Dragon's Dogma is easily one of my favorite games of all time. I've had Dragons Dogma on both PS3 and Xbox 360 and respectivly played a crap ton of it. When this came out for PC I was so ecstatic I could barely contain myself. What suprised me even more was on how well a port this is. I've never used the PC controls but from what I've gathered from people that do use them they are quite good, I personally perfer a controller and doing everything with a controller was how the game was meant to be played. The controls are fluid and responsive and combat never gets old. Every hit is satisfying, with hard hitting attacks the game breifly pauses for emphasis on how big of an attack you are doing. The magic system is bold and powerful and is very satisfying to use/see. The story is about average and I never really cared a whole lot for it. I understand most of it and I appreciate it for what it is but I couldn't really care less. That's not to say that its bad, just not the main reason why I love this game. The progression in this game is spot on where there's always somewhere for you to go next for a challenge♥♥♥♥♥whoppin'. The class system allows for a flexible play style, whether you want to be a giant sword wielding badass or a quick agile dagger wielding assassin wrecking havoc on everything in site. The loot is rewarding to find and getting that one peice of armor or that weapon you've been going after for an hour is satisfying and actually means something. After you complete the "end" of the game a whole nother area opens up that is ripe with loot and challenge. The world gets signifigantly harder and the best loot in the game can be aquired. The Ur-Dragon (A post "end" game boss) is fun to fight and can certainly give you a run for your money, while the loot you get from him is the best in the game excluding the Dark Arisen equipment. Speaking of Dark Arisen, I just finally finished it after having this game for a multitude of years and I have to say, Bitterblack Isle is hard. The enemies will kick your teeth in if you are not prepared and the whole place is dark and eerie. The DLC will take a while to get to because the minimum level I would reccomend you be before even attempting it would be 60, which is post "end" game content. The final fight for the DLC is hard and rewarding and the loot you get from it is amoung the best in the game. I've dumped over 55+ hours on one save, beaten the game twice, and just completed the DLC and I'm no where near done playing. The amount of side quests are rediculous and completly opptional, but highly rewarding. I'm only level 83 while the level cap is 200. I have so much more to do and yet I keep coming back to this game. If you are looking for a game with great RPG elements, a fantastic party system, tons of gear, tons of replayability, and loads of content then look no further than Dragon's Dogma.

Late to the party, but since the DLC for DS3 is about to drop, I’ll give my two cents for anybody wanting to check out the original, before playing the others: DO IT.
10/10, Game of the Decade. By a
margin.
You need to not be in a hurry, and you need to enjoy exploring an open world.
You need to not mind turning back because You Are Not Prepared™… yet. There are other ways to go.
You need to observe enemy attack patterns, be open to using the environment, and consider
your combat options, before engaging. You can build against any playstyle, and you can change playstyles and gear, as the situation calls for.
You need to not mind getting ganked occasionally, either in PvP, or, more disturbingly, in PvE (looking your way, Ornstein and Smough).
You also need to not mind a healthy dose of angst, though tempered somewhat by a fair amount of humor.
The world is built around a couple of central hubs.  This makes it easy to get from one area to another, particularly later in the game.  Shortcuts unlock, so that the majority of the fighting can be avoided, once an area is explored.
Progress is saved as you go, so any decisions you make regarding, e.g., killing NPCs, or the order you progress through areas, can have permanent consequences, at least for that playthrough. But honestly, this is what makes the game engaging, and replayable.
Multiplayer (PvP/co-op) fits in seamlessly with PvE. You let yourself be summoned so you can help kill a boss. Does that qualify as a boss fight, PvE, or co-op? Now the host gets invaded. Is this still a boss fight? co-op? PvP? ALL THREE? What about being Gravelorded (dumps extra PvE content into your world)? Is that PvP? Or PvE? Or PvE until you invade the player who is Gravelording you, then PvP? Does this make you the aggressor? HE’S THE ONE WHO STARTED IT! /sigh. Then there are all the different phantoms (colors), related to PvP/Co-op type....
More seriously, the point is that one kind of play can instantly (either intended or otherwise) morph into something else. Multiplayer, in all its forms, is where the replayability – and the rush – lies, in spades.
One last thing. Maybe because Dark Souls requires some level of patience, there seems to be a lot less PvP trolls, gogogoers, whiners, etc. Yes, they exist (e.g., in Darkroot, and Dark Anor Londo) and are the ones you hear about, but by and large, PvP in Dark Souls is…
, in a way that PvP usually
. Or maybe it’s because the game’s been out so long out that players are just happy to have somebody there. Same goes for co-op, there are still a lot of people out there who want help.
So yeah, 10/10.
N.B., I
ding FromSoft on the sh*t mouse support and 30 FPS, but both can be fixed. Thanks to the brilliant Dark Souls community the DSFIX and DSMFIX mods are available and 100% necessary. For better multiplayer connectivity (and to see who the hell is Gravelording you), also get DSCM. Without these mods I never would have played.

Ok... I love the Dynasty Warriors series and have been hooked since DW2 on the PS2. Then when they added the Empires versions, I went all in. I currently own DW6 Empires on 360 and that is my favorite to date. When I heard that they were releasing DW on PC, I couldn't wait and had to try it out.  If you have played DW in the past, then this game will look very familiar and play just like you would expext.
If you have never played DW before, it is an interpretation of "Romance of the Three Kingdoms" which tells the story of feudal lords trying to restore the Han Dynasty or seize power for themselves. What this means is that it takes place in China approx 280 ad, you choose a warrior you want to play as and then get to fight in a battle. Each battle will have different objectives and they are also timed, the battle is filled with thousands of enemy solders that you get to fight with timed button mashes (there is a little more finesse to it but that is how the combat works in a nutshell). It isn't too serious and the voice acting is... well it is there. It really is just a fun game to go through and cause as much havoc and destruction as possible.
And now for a quick review, graphics are the best in the series to date, however they are still sub-par for pc games in general. The controls are clumsy at times, but stay true to previous DW titles, unfortunately so does the camera. It appears they tried to incorporate the Empires idea into it, which allows you to choose your character and plot a semi-linear destiny for them while trying to win favor of the emperor. There has been a ton of stuff added to the weapons and combat part, allowing you to carry 2 weapons into combat and switch between them semi-seamlessly is pretty neat, but overall it is just like every other DW title.
I do recommend this game and especially for previous fans of the DW series. However, I think the $50 price is pretty steep for anybody other than fans of the series.
I will answer the burning question many of you have: Yes, this is Dynasty Warriors. It works just as well as the console versions, and perfectly with a controller.
If you enjoy Dynasty Warrior games, or have in the past, but took a break then this is absolutely the perfect time to gcome back in. This game is my favorite by far.

Does the game have flaws? Of course! What game doesn't? Have you played Fallout 4? So any excuse of, "Oh, this game is too old" or "Oh, this game has bad graphics" or even "Oh, there are already 3 sequels to this game (almost)" is...well inexcusable. So please, if you consider yourself a gamer of any level, or any genre, this game is one that you must add to your library of experiences. Trust me, it'll be worth it. Shepard out.

I don't really understand why this was cut into acts. Anyone who was interested has been waiting YEARS for it to come out (to the point where they probably didn't think it would ever actually come out at all), so why not just take a little more time to complete everything and release it once? What have they been doing for the last 6 years? 2 hours of gameplay is not reflective of a 2.5 million dollar kickstarter and 6 years of work. For a game split into acts I wasn't assuming it would be very long, but I really didn't think it would be this short and shallow.
For anyone who was a kickstarter backer I'd reccomend waiting until the entire game is out before starting so you don't feel let down.
For anyone who is interested in buying it, wait until all four parts make it into a cheap bundle and buy it then. The cost per part will not be worth it at full price, especially if each act is only 2 hours long.

Oh, man. Hiveswap. The game long awaited by the Homestuck fandom. Long awaited by me. I was really excited to play it, but once I opened it up many of my worst fears came true and most of my hopes were crushed. I like the plot and the storyline and all that jazz, I'll give you that, but the gameplay. The gameplay is sort of decent at best. Now, I'm not sure if this is because my computer is just a tad bit out of date, but a lot of the cutscenes are very laggy and some of the frames blur together into a glitchy amalgamation. Half of the time when I'm in a battle, attempting to do something will make the game freeze, and the only way to keep playing is to force quit it and load it up again. About 20 minutes of my gameplay is me crashing it by making a wrong choice in battle, and going back to try and correct my mistakes. It's the game we've all been waiting for, but in my opinion, there are too many bugs and glitches for the game to be ready for the market. What Pumpkin Games just HAD to put out a release date when the game was in this stage. I am a Homestuck fanatic, but I gotta admit, the game needs a LOT of bug fixes. Although it may have its major downsides, I still reccomend the game.
TL;DR:
It's a decent (at the least) game if you are a hardcore Homestuck fan like me and have been awaiting it's release for a VERY long time. 3.8/5 stars.
It's a very bad, extremely buggy (at the least) game if you have never heard of Hoemstuck and want to get into it by playing this. 2.5/5 stars.
EDIT: 9/20/17
Oh my god. The new update is perfect. It fixed EVERYTHING I just listed up there that made the game horrible. Once again, this fandom and series has managed to capture me with it's perfect imperfection. 5/5 stars!

Splinter Cell has always been one of my favorite stealth games (right up there with Deus Ex) and Blacklist is cerainly no exception. I genuinely feel as if this is one of the few franchises out there that has consistently gotten better with each new entry. That being said, a good bit of Blacklist is taken from Conviction and revamped or overhauled while the rest is all new; this is speaking purely in terms of gameplay and mechanics mind you.
Everything can be customized this time around. Your weapons. Your gadgets. Even your suit - which is segmented so as to offer customization on a piece-by-piece basis. Said upgrades arepurchased with cash, which you earn by completing mission objectives and the like. You're given up to three loadouts to tinker around with for easy access, too. Your mobile command center - a flying fortress that puts Airforce One to shame - can also be upgraded in a variety of ways to help missions go more smoothly. Pretty straightforward stuff that still adds a lot of depth to an already amazing game.
There's a bit of an open-world free-roam aspect to the game. Don't get too excited though as it's not what it sounds like - and let's be honest, legit open-world free-roam would pretty much kill a game like this. Still. What they've done this time around is tie the multiplayer and co-op missions into the game in such a way that you can transition between them and the single-player missions seamlessly from the mission map aboard your mobile command center. You can even have the game find a partner for you if you're lacking chums who play the game or they're just offline and of course there is a matchmaking system in place for the multiplayer. All missions (single-player or otherwise) can be replayed at any time, just in case you missed something or you just happened to really enjoy yourself the first time through.
The story is great too, of course! Sam Fisher has aged quite well over the years and is still a proper badass, having finally been given command of his own team and operation. Unfortunately, the circumstances are rather grim - a group of extremists calling themselves the Engineers have threatened to attack a major US city once every week until every last US troop is brought home from overseas. An ultimate deadline of one year was given and it's anybody's guess what happens when the year is up!
If you would love to experience a stealth game. Then this is the sweet spot.

Pillars of Eternity (PoE) is an absolutely terrific game. It's not just one of the best 3rd person isometric RPG's of recent years. It's one of the very best period.
PoE's main selling point, in my humble opinion, is how it immerses players rapidly and completly. The story is great with many smaller plotlines all across the map, sometimes quite literally. Your primary character is built at start but you gather the rest of your party as you go along. There's stuff to do everywhere and I've come back to several locations just to find out I missed stuff. What really helps is how the areas ooze flavour with the right look and feel and plenty of flavour text everywhere.
In party creation Obsidian really shows this game was created through Kickstarter and community support: don't like the characters the game throws at you? No problem, just hire an adventurer and built one to suit you. It allows you to tailor the experience the way you like it. Now, the game party members add their own story to the mix and the tend to be fun and capable anyway so you can go both directions. But as an example: unless you build a Fighter or Paladin yourself you find yourself short of a tank for the first few hours of game play. So hire an adventurer and set off. Absolutely fantastic and 100% geared towards offering an experience you can tune as a player. You can go through all of this in any way you like. Want to be a beneficent hero? No problem. Want to be sadistical piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥ No problem. And the world responds to that in all sorts of little things. Again: you get to tune your own experience which is a great selling point for this game.
Graphics wise the game isn't anything special. But it runs extremely well and the graphics work well and fit the game. You're not going to get blown away with minute details or spectacular effects but it hasn't bothered me. This game is all about content and immersion and it scores off the charts on both off these aspects. The music is much of the same. Not spectaular but it fits the game and most importantly; it doesn't grate the nerves.
Pillars of Eternity is one of the very best 3rd person isometric RPG's I have ever played. I consider it right up there with Planescape: Torment for those you know and remember that legendary game. Yes, I really think this game is that good. For anyone who enjoys RPG's this game is a no-brainer: get it. For everyon else: get it. it's that good.

Absolutely fantastic game. Perfectly captures the feeling of classic Infinity Engine games but also holds it's own with an amazing story, outstanding voice acting and really well fleshed out companions (big highlight for me)!
The dialogue system is very robust and greatly add to the actual role-play element of the game (Obsidian are great at this). I played as a female elven ranger, who was passionate, honest and benevolent and the game reflected my actions and the reputation I gained. Also, the quality of the writing is superb! This is a huge plus because half of the time spent in the game is reading text, and it's so worth it.
The combat is a solid variation of the classic RTWP formula and the nontraditional classes fit really well in the game. I like that it caps at Lv12, as I prefer to be the underdog rather than overpowered, since this is more akin to tabletop RPGs (low level is when it's risky and exciting!). There are plenty of side quests, tasks and bounties to dig your teeth into if you like a good challenge. If you don't, a lot of the encounters have nonviolent ways to resolve them too, which is also very useful at times.
The stats and whatnot are somewhat unique, taking ideas from the old AD&D 2nd Edition up to more modern concepts. I won't go into depth about it, but some things I liked about their system was how each major stat has some value to every class, with dual benefits (eg. Might gives you more Damage and Heal) or how item's stat buffs don't stack (you can't have 2 items that buff the same stat).
The backgrounds and other artwork are absolutely beautiful. I'd go as far as saying it's one the best looking games I've ever played! It's like playing a painting. The music feels like Baldur's Gate or Lord of the Rings and is epic when necessary, charming when wandering around town and immersive enough to never feel tiresome.
Oh and the UI is much better than the old IE games. Lot's of info gets logged in your journal and it works really well (it also writes your biography as you play!). With the party stash loot isn't a hassle at all (unless you play with one of the restrictive game modes).
As a fan of the classic IE games this hit my sweet spot in a major way and I spent pretty much a whole week glued to the game until I finished. Now I look forward to doing a play-through as an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
They are still patching up some bugs (never encountered any serious ones) and still balancing a few things I believe, so feel free to wait as they iron out the kinks, but honestly I can't recommend this game enough. It's my favourite RPG since the Baldur's Gate series and I can't wait for any upcoming expansions/sequels.

Really liked the tactical combat in this game. Primarily emphasizes preparation, using narrow doorways to your advantage, and generally positioning your folks properly. This leads to delightfully varied and challenging encounters. Do note, however, that micromanagement is also an important part of combat (they even tell you that when you're choosing a difficulty level), so if you don't like that sorta stuff, this game might not be your cup of tea.
When it comes to story and such, I almost don't know where to begin. The world in this game is really creative and unique (just the fact that it's more of a fantasy version of the Age of Discovery rather than medieval Europe is refreshing), your companions are all interesting characters (really felt like I was friends with most of them, rather than being their leader), and since it's an Obsidian game, there are some really delicious philosophical ponderings here and there.
Special mention goes to all the different dialogue choices you can make, though. Instead of just being different solutions to quests and such, there are also plenty of options that exist solely for the sake of roleplaying, to further flesh out your character's motivations and so on. That's really neat.
If there's one major gripe I have with this game, though, it's that pathfinding can be really rubbish sometimes. Seeing folks politely waiting behind their allies because they don't realise they could go around that guy in order to bludgeon someone is something that happens too often.
Oh yeah, and you can get at least three cats and a piglet in this game (but you can't give them little hats or armors, which I hope will be remedied in a future expansion).
Even better than Baldur's Gate - if such a thing is possible.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding Chocolate-Caramel Cream Pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
All-purpose flour, for surface
Chocolate pie crust
1/2 cup sugar
1/4 cup cornstarch
3/4 teaspoon salt
2 1/2 cups whole milk
4 ounces bittersweet chocolate (preferably 61 to 70 percent cacao), finely chopped
4 large egg yolks
1 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
2 cups Whipped cream
2 tablespoons caramel
1 thick block bittersweet chocolate, room temperature, for garnish
Directions
1.
On a lightly floured work surface, roll pate sucree to 1/8-inch thickness. Fit into a 9-inch pie dish. Trim edges, leaving a 1-inch overhang. Tuck overhang under dough so edges are flush with rim, and crimp edges. Lightly prick bottom of dough with a fork. Refrigerate for 30 minutes.
2.
Preheat oven to 350 degrees. Line dough with parchment, and fill with pie weights or dried beans. Bake until edges begin to look dry, 20 to 22 minutes. Carefully remove weights and parchment. Bake until crust is darker around edges and bottom looks dry, 10 to 12 minutes. Let cool completely on a wire rack. (Chocolate crust can be stored overnight.)
3.
Whisk together sugar, cornstarch, and salt in a small bowl. Heat milk and chocolate in a medium saucepan over medium-high heat, stirring occasionally, until chocolate melts.
4.
Whisk 1 cup hot milk mixture into sugar mixture until smooth. Whisk milk-sugar mixture into the remaining milk mixture in the saucepan. Cook over medium heat, stirring constantly, until bubbling and thick, 4 to 5 minutes total (about 2 minutes after it comes to a boil).
5.
Whisk yolks in a medium bowl until combined. Pour in milk mixture in a slow, steady stream, whisking until completely incorporated. Return mixture to saucepan. Cook over medium heat, stirring constantly, until it just begins to bubble, 1 to 2 minutes.
6.
Remove from heat, and stir in vanilla. Let custard cool in saucepan on a wire rack, whisking occasionally, for about 10 minutes.
7.
Pour custard into chocolate crust. Press plastic wrap directly on surface of custard. Refrigerate until custard filling is chilled and firm, at least 4 hours (or overnight).
8.
Gently fold caramel into whipped cream, then spread the caramel whipped cream over pie. Using a vegetable peeler, scrape chocolate block at a 45-degree angle to make a small mound of shavings, and sprinkle over whipped cream. Serve immediately, or refrigerate and serve within 2 hours.
Tip
The caramel mixture must be very cold before the whipped cream is folded in. Otherwise, the whipped cream will collapse.

If you ever wanted to play something that feels like a cross between the best parts of EverQuest, Gothic 1 and Skyrim, but programmed by Japanese, this is it.
The fact that this is an eastern studio trying to make a western RPG makes this extra quirky. Some elements are almost too by the book (the architecture, setting, the weird archaic English), but then others are fairly exotic: Healing by creating zones of restoration with a spell? Refilling stamina for casting by eating mushrooms? The pawn system where you get other players' party members to join yours? It feels odd but not unpleasant in this atmosphere.
I'm playing it with a caster character right now and the pawn system works well, I can get enough tanking or ranged DPS from the AI. Your pawns behave more or less sensibly, but you can customize their behavior using potions and commands if you want to change some basic trait.
One of the best things is travelling at night. You don't really see far even with a lamp (that's why I mention EverQuest) so a simple walk through a forest makes your neck skin crawl as you listen for enemies. There could be chimeras, dragons, an ambush of sorcerers or simple little goblins.
This great sense of atmosphere continues inside dungeons. The graphics may not be the best, but shadows dance and light feels natural. This combines with great echo effects and positional audio. You are able to pinpoint the location of an NPC that is speaking even when his speech has to go through two rooms and two hallways in a dungeon.
They also nailed character progression. You feel seriously weak in the beginning, and can't go everywhere because some places are guarded by things that rip your eyes out. But levels really mean tangible improvement and so if you retry getting to an area ten levels later, you discover that you can suddenly explore another third of the map.
There are small niggles, like boring inventory management, but being able to store items and use most things from storage when appropriate can help here. Also, the difficulty curve is steep in the beginning and then flattens. I'm still enjoying it.

This is a surprising game in both good ways and bad. But the upside is so good that the bad can be forgiven (at least for me anyway).  So what's surprising?
1.  Early in the  game, it's recommended that you rest, but when you go to your house can you sleep in your own bed?  Of course not.  But you can go to the inn just  around the corner and rest for 50G.
2.  Early on, you can go to the beach and shoot birds with magic or arrows and get XP and credits for doing it!
3.  The combat is just crazy fun. I wasn't expecting that.
4.  You can pick up enemies and throw them, kinda like in professional wrestling.

7.  You can pick up kindling but you can't start a fire.

9.  There is no real story early in the game and I don't care.
10. Did I mention that the combat is awesome!

Couldn't delay the mission because the escortee showed up and followed me everywhere.  Ended up groping around in the dark (dark is seriously dark by the way) beside a cliffside for a long way and ran into a couple of big beasts (trying not to spoil anything) which were OP and killed my crew off pretty quickly.  I tried to find a way around them and discovered  a ranged weapon that made it ridiculously fun and easy to destroy the beasts from afar.

Seriously, did I mention that the combat is great. And fun and quirky!  The lack of quick travel and the lack of places to rest means you will want to remember to save your game. A lot!  If you try this game be armed with a sense of humor and you will have fun!

A wonderfully unique take on ARPGs that even with all of it's faults IMO deserve more recognition for it's achievments.
Pros:
1.The first and most innovative mechanic, namely the Pawn system might by itself be enough to sell it for many searching for new mechanics in this genre. The ability to completely creat and personalize a primary NPC companion that then gets hired by other players is something that from my knowledge has not been done before or not this way at least.
2.As the store page would indicate the big boss/monster battles are it's other most well known mechanic. Dragon's Dogma manages to make the mechanics of the game feel like you are actually fighting something that could theoretically exist.
As in they feel, move, act and react surprisingly natural. Fighting a griffon that won't sit on the ground, no problem just set it's wings on fire and it's grounded. A Cyclops not feeling your blows, if arrow at the ready aim for the eye. Chimera overwhelming you with it's diverse range of attacks, just start going for the one body part that is giving you the most trouble.
3.A slightly different take on the usual fantasy story, with a believable enough world and a very interesting lore-mythos for that world.
Cons:
1.Even though I like the story it's takes quite a while before you start understanding what exactly you are and are meant to do in the overall scheme of things.
2.Few characters feel like they actually are important or are interesting enough to remember. Even the ones that do have personality are in end not that relevant in the story.
3.This one might not be 100% true but from what I saw and read on forums talking about this game, a lot of content was cut. And I mean a lot ( if those rumors are true).
What that means is that while what we have is IMO really good and satisfying, as you play the you start feeling like it's not really as big as impressions first gave. And the number of monsters and bosses start feeling repetitive sooner than many would hope.
(4). I am not sure if this is really the game itself or steam messing up but it seems that achievements are incredibly frustrating to unlock. By now I should have had about half or more but they just won't register.
10/10 would make an orc army again.

I guess I like this game? It has an immense amount of problems which are really irritating, but overall the game is decent. There's as much or more wrong with the game than right, but melee combat in the game is enjoyable enough to counterbalance the problems.
Pros -
Fun combat mechanics, battle is decided more by skill than by quality of gear.
Co-op available for most areas until the boss is defeated.
Good storyline.
Wide variety of weapon types and strategies are viable to play through the game with.
Cons -
Horribly optimized. (This comment is obligatory, and I assume everyone already knows this. I'm just covering my bases.)
Co-op can't be played unless you opt into being invaded and PK'd by players using vastly overleveled pyromancy to kill you. There is no way to play co-op without pvp. Non-optional pvp with players who go out of their way to make the pvp unfair is the single worst feature of this game.
Co-op is glitchy, there aren't a lot of servers for co-op online anymore, finding a specific player's sigil without mods is extremely difficult, and even with a mod, still sometimes impossible.
A vast majority of the game difficulty is just working around bad mechanics, and has nothing to do with the game actually being hard.
If you are looking for a difficult game, you're going to have to deliberately make the game difficult (don't level up, don't upgrade weapons, ect), by default the game is beatable by any player with a vague amount of patience.
Lock-on system is pretty bad, and will sometimes kill you if you attempt using it (locks on to creatures you can't see and tries to get you to fall off the environment).
Using projectiles for long range attacks is tedious, clunky, and rather inaccurate. Assume all projectiles have an effective range no further than you can lock on.
The camera in general is pretty bad, particularly if you haven't turned off "Camera Auto-Recovery" in the settings, which is on by default.
The community detest new players. Don't expect any assistance or advice other than "git gud" and anticipate being invaded every time you reverse hollow. TIP: Entering the white mist to a boss banishes invaders - I'd imagine alt-f4 works as well.
I'd rate the game around 8/git gud - and probably worth the $19.99, but if you're buying it outside of steam, certaintly wouldn't pay any higher than that.

Update:
*Still no Narrator between missions.
*Still extremely limited number of units allowed on screen, negatively impacting gameplay.
*Over $100 worth of DLC for the so called "Complete Edition"
*Online Multiplayer? What's that?
*Non-Playable character models still crappy, makes some cutscenes unwatchably bad.
*Textures still largely low quality, giving game a very dated look.
Koei is likely to see negative reviews like this and think:
"PC gamers just don't want Dynasty Warriors"
To which I say:
"Dear Koei; I wouldn't have bought it in the first place if I didn't want Dynasty Warriors on PC, you made top seller on your first day, but this is a terrible port and you people have a history of crappy ports and generally suck at supporting your games."
So that said, like many of Koei's other ports this game just falls short of all of the potential of the PC. It has no online multiplayer, inconsistent and often low texture quality on environments and especially on non-playable characters even during cutscenes, a unit limit far lower than what most PC's can handle, and no narration between missions (seriously how hard would that have been?). Some have also reported game crashing bugs, but I haven't encountered any.
On the positive character textures and models for playable characters tend to be pretty good, and there are a ton of characters to play and a wide variety of weapons to choose from, as well as several modes of play. Voice acting remains hilarious which I believe is intentional.
However the lack of narration between missions really hurts immersion in the story and feels uncanny and painfully silent after the fully voice acted cutscenes and battle speeches. Poor textures and extremely limited number of units allowed on screen also both serve to make the game feel unpolished on the PC.
The lack of online multiplayer also really hurts the experience. Dynasty Warriors has tremendous potential here, and it's potential that is being entirely wasted.
Koei has traditionally assumed that PC gamers just hate Dynasty Warriors, failing to understand that what PC gamers actually hate are broken glitchy terrible ports. Past PC ports such as Dynasty Warriors 6 Xtreme Legends were so broken that stores pulled them off the shelves, and received pretty much no support whatsoever.
Hopefully this game making top seller on Steam will show Koei that the market is there for games like Dynasty Warriors and their previous assumptions were fundamentally irrational non sequiturs. Here's hoping for better ports in the future...

Ugh, where to begin on this? I've only played about 2 missions in this game before I had to stop, so I don't quite have a lot of details about the game itself. If you've played any other Dynasty Warriors game before you already know what to expect from the gameplay. If not, it is a ridiculous, over the top hack n' slash game loosely based on the book series "Romance of the Three Kingdoms". The gameplay itself is fun, and its mostly about spectacle fighting, but there is a bit of difficulty and a high chance of suddenly being killed from only a few hits on the harder difficulties.
So what's actually new in this version? More characters, more weapons, more stages, Lu Bu gets his own personal story mode in the same category as Wu, Wei, Shu, and Jin (honestly this just sounds like a DLC pack more than anything). The game is addictively fun especially if you like spectacle fighters or fast paced hack n' slashes.
So what are the downsides? Well its a below average quality PC port. My first and most pertinent issue is texture flickering. The textures on a lot of ground flicker like crazy around any hills, and sometimes disappear completely. This is the reason I could only play 2 missions before I had to stop. I've attempted messing with the graphics options but there seems to be no way to fix it in game (if anyone can find a fix for this, PLEASE let me know).
Second problem: The graphics options menu. For a PC game it has very few choices for graphics settings. The major issue here though is the resolution setting. Instead of a drop down selector you have to scroll through each possible resolution, and the game reloads in the new resolution and asks you if you want to keep the new setting. This is just frustrating and pointless.
Third problem: Control displays. The game features fully rebindable controls for every action in the game, and thats wonderful, it really is. The issue is that no matter what you set the controls to, or if you're using a gamepad, the game will always display keyboard controls on the menus, and in game they just show a random key with a picture that vaguely describes the action you would do if you hit that key. The question is, what key/button is it? It's a guessing game that requires you to continuosly refer back to your controls to figure out what does what.
Final problem: This is more of a personal issue, but the overall graphics quality. I understand that the DW series has never won an award for amazing graphics, but playing this even on the highest graphics settings I feel like I'm playing a PS Vita or old XBox 360 game on my PC. The graphics feel like an overall downgrade from the original DW 8 on XBox 360. I get that not everyone has a monster tower of a computer that can run anything a person can dream up, but I'd at least like to play something that doesn't look like it belongs on a portable system.
The second, third, and final problem I can live with and still whole-heartedly recommend this game, because at the end of the day, its all about the gameplay with this title, but the first problem physically harms my eyes on most stages. I will still recommend this game, its still fun as all hell, but I don't recommend playing it too much until the texture flicker is either fixed with a patch or someone finds a work-around to make it stop. Til then I suggest refraining from excessive play times.

Speaking as a longtime Homestuck fan, I'm sadly disappointed by Hiveswap.
I'll first outline the positives and negatives.
Positives
- An incredible, immersive soundtrack. I regret not purchasing this with the soundtrack included as the soundtrack is my favourite part of this game.
- Jam-packed with pop culture references and callbacks to the original webcomic.
- Many great nostalgic 90's references.
- Very witty writing.
- Gorgeous environmental art.
Negatives
- The art and animation is inconsistent, there is a dip in quality as the game reaches it's conclusion.
- For the $10AUD I paid for this, I really did expect there to be more content. I was able to finish this game at my own pace, whilst interacting with everything I could find in the world, in just under 2.5 hours. The pricetag is fairly hefty for what little playtime you're getting. Whilst I understand that this is only the first act in presumably many to come, value for money needs to be taken into consideration here.
- For a point and click game, it's incredibly vague. I had to consult a walkthrough several times just because the game often doesn't make it clear enough what steps you need to take.
- The battle system is quite confusing, and is in desperate need of a tutorial. Whilst it's not set up for you to fail (at this point) it can be quite frustrating.
- The GUI doesn't make it clear enough as to what items you're utilising.
Some improvements that could be made.
-Cutscenes need to be better optimised.
-GUI and strife/captchalogue system could use some tweaks to help make it clearer what you're actually doing with it. Visual feedback is important and unfortunately somewhat lacking in this game.
-Some form of tutorial.
-General polishing of the story and reasoning behind the items you're required to pick up.
-Some new sound effects - that one constant bleep sound began to do my head in very quickly.
-More content for what you're paying for - just because it's only one act doesn't mean it can't be more indepth.
Do I believe this was worth the several year wait since the Kickstarter project? No, I would have expected several more acts to be released in this time frame with a much higher level of polish. This game pays homage to years of dedicated Homestuck fans, with clever callbacks and references, however it's just not
for what you're paying for.
I was so excited and enthralled as soon as the game started, but my enthusiasm very quickly dulled as I found myself getting confused and frustrated quickly, and before I knew it the game was over.
Here's to hoping Act 2 is an improvement of Act 1.
Wish it was longer.

Played through the full Act in two and a half hours, with only one puzzle that truly stumped me (and then was actually easy for me to solve) - absolutely worth the $8 for the game if you want the first chapter of a fascinating story with gorgeous art, engaging characters and a true sense of humor. People who worked on this game worked on the likes of Undertale, Unbeatable Squirrel Girl (the comic), the original webcomic Homestuck whose multiverse the game is set in, webcomic Neo-kosmos and many other highly regarded narratives and works of art.
Play this if you like stories, if you like fun, if you like 90s references or if you just like good characters, regardless of whether you're a homestuck fan or not. It's worth the $8.
If you're reading this after playing, and you like the game, the writing style, and the world(s) the game is set in, consider checking out the webcomic that started it all, Homestuck. It's a long read, but the depth, characterization, humor, animations and plot make it more than worthwhile.
Looking forward to Act 2 and onwards!

Guess I should review some of the games I spend countless hours on.. So here it goes!
-First off this game is REALLY FUN. Especially if you (like me), love large scale RTS/PVP games. Remember Starcraft 1 Online!?! Man those were the days.
-Art of War: Red Tides captures alot of this, with a new spin. The MOBA feel and PVP relient system keep things interesting and even more so with the tactics. That's my favorite part, on the fly tactical strategy. Whether its pulling of a rush early game when they have no way to defend, to a game changing Missle Strike; its an old enchanting feeling in a fresh package. And its free so... worth a shot.
-Graphics are good, and I run it pretty well on a 5 year old PC. Despite crashing and bugs, it runs fairly smoothly.
-The Devs seem to be keeping up with patches, balances, and bug fixes from the last week I have been playing.
- The only downside I have seen thus far is it's a little grindy to unlock everything but its also kind of nice as it gives you time to craft your ideal army. You can pay of course to unlock units, but screw that. Everything can be unlocked by just playing.. NO P2W. Also the crashes get annoying but I am sure that will be addressed promptly.
-The matchmaking is a little wonky but usually its not too long. But if someone quits you have to wait all over again (usually). It's way better to just minimize and browse Reddit while you wait.
--All in all I'd give Art of War: Red Tides a solid 7/10 as of right now. It has so much potential and I cant wait to see where this goes. Give it a try, im sure you wont regret it. (again it's free)

Who is this Game For?
==================
When Dragon’s Dogma first released back in 2012 on last generation consoles, not many knew what to expect from the brooding title boasting a true challenge. Demon’s Souls and Dark Souls at the time both proved to be incredibly popular with their highly demanding takes on action RPGs, yet they relied on closed, overbearing atmospheres to deliver their key sense of dread. Capcom’s Dragon’s Dogma was wide open, and free in a way that neither of those two games could be.
Is it good?
=================
The combat system allows for one notably unique feature; your hero is able to grab enemies, sometimes heroically grappling the neck of a chimera, and other times desperately clinging to a cyclops’s legs hoping somehow this will help. For larger creatures, you’ll find yourself climbing across the expanse of their bodies, which is a lot less sensual than it sounds. There’s plenty of excitement to be found as you find yourself scaling one of the many necks of a Hydra, aiming to chop of one of those viscous heads.
First and foremost is upgrades to visual fidelity and performance. Dragon’s Dogma: Dark Arisen was always a pretty game, but the shift from last gen to PC has definitely delivered a welcomed facelift. A full range of options are available to your particular rig, including 4K support and up to 150 frames per second (talk about silky smooth). Along with these options comes support for the 360, Xbox One, Steam and DualShock 4 controllers as well as Steam amenities like Trading Cards, Big Picture, Cloud save, and Achievements.
Does it have any problems?
========================
Unfortunately, for as engrossing as Gransys is, the lack of a straightforward fast travel system means that it's nearly impossible to not get sick of it. While the tweaks in the Dark Arisen expansion made getting around slightly more bearable, teleporting can only be done via expendable items, and only to an extremely limited number of warp points, most of which players need to place themselves. Even being able to run without quickly depleting all of one's stamina would have helped to alleviate this issue, but as it stands, players will inevitably spend a lot of unnecessary time retracting their steps.
It got especially tiresome for me late in the campaign, when the game developed a nasty habit of asking me to trek all the way back to places immediately upon returning from them. I was just at the Greatwall, game. Why did you tell me to return to the hub if you were gonna make me walk all the way back in the very next mission?
Final Thoughts!
====================
What you essentially have here is a definitive edition of one seriously amazing action RPG. Dragon’s Dogma: Dark Arisen manages to live in the same vein as the Souls, sporting the darkness and challenges so many players have come to desire, yet forges an identity all its own. Dragon’s Dogma: Dark Arisen doesn’t adhere to a formula, it creates a sweeping experience, one whose strengths you won’t find elsewhere. The title’s move to PC, even three years in age, has made that fact shine once again.

What can I say about this game? It's great! Well its great and.. has a few interesting design decisions that are downright confusing. The combat in this game is fantastic and feels thought out, with the various classes and how your character changes based on them. The items look great and there is a very large amount of character customization. However this is where one of the "weird" design decisions comes into play - the stat leveling. Stat leveling is handled per level up based on what class your current character is using. So, for example, if I am using the Fighter class it levels up a certain number of stats comparable to the other classes. This is where the design decision gets odd - it doesn't tell you natively what these stats are! While this doesn't matter to a large extent as the game is, without a doubt, pretty darn easy. What it does do however is make you unsure of which class benefits you the most and often times can lead to frustration as you spend a large chunk of time playing a class only to learn it leveled up some stats more then another class would of.
The other design decisions are things like having only two built in waypoints, and while you can find more waypoints that are "portable" and "Placeable" it adds to the travel time hugely. The story itself is just a side thing and can, and in my opinon, should be ignored. The game actually shines more in randomly encounters and end game then anywhere else.
To sum it up.. this is a great RPG with amazing fights and great enemies. Weird design decisions aside its a joy to play from start to finish!

Other people have spoken on Dark Souls more effectively than I can, so I'm just going to say a few words on this specific version of it. The Dark Souls PC port is not very good. It's playable, but it seems to have framerate inconsistencies on rigs that should be able to handle it just fine and without a fan-patch, its internal rendering is locked to a 1024x720 resolution, meaning it's gonna look subpar on anything significantly better than a 1360x768 monitor. The fan-patch in question, "DSfix," does go some distance toward mitigating the porting issues, but it's not a flawless patch by any stretch. The game also does not have any sort of "borderless windowed" fullscreen mode, so it's not a game you can play while retaining access to your desktop (the game even vanishes entirely if you so much as click on anything displayed on a second monitor), which is especially irksome since Dark Souls does not allow the player to pause. There is no means of multitasking between this game and another application, even for simple chatting purposes.
The only perk to playing this on PC is mods, the configuration options for this game are bare-minumum, and this game really was designed with a gamepad in mind. If you have a PlayStation 3 or an Xbox 360, it might be more convenient to get Dark Souls for one of those, instead. Quick research says the PS3 version is JUST SLIGHTLY the better of the two console versions, if you have the choice between the two, but apparently framerate issues still plague console versions to some extent in this case, too, so it might just be a preference issue for most players whether they go PC or console with this one.
I can confirm that Dark Souls works with an Xbox One controller on PC without issue.

Let me start off with saying that I actually enjoyed this game quite a lot.
To be honest, I loved this game.
It had potential to be the best game I have ever played so far.
Why the negative review then? Oh let me tell you.
I was afraid to buy this game because I thought it's going to be too hard for a casual player like me and I did not want to waste money on yet another title that would just sit in my library unfinished forever...
But oh, was I wrong. I fell in love with this game, it got me hooked up from the very beginning and it even kept me awake at night just so that I could finally beat this boss (
)!
But despite being one of the greatest games I have ever played in my entire life, this game is broken.
The PC port is a joke.
In order to make the game playable I had to spend 3 hours looking for a solution online, because it would be unplayable otherwise. I had to download mods and set them up properly for the best experience possible.
After spending this much time I finally got to play the game and I enjoyed the hell out of it. I loved the challenge and I loved the amazing feeling of accomplishment whenever I beat a tough enemy.
I felt like I was lacking something, because most of the time I wasn't able to connect to any other players or see their summon signs or anything, but I didn't mind. I enjoyed the lonely single player experience anyway.
And after spending a little bit over 20 hours with this game it suddenly stopped working.
One day after work when I wanted to continue my quest to discover the fate of the undead the game just wouldn't launch anymore. I would get an error every single time I tried to launch it.
I tried many things to fix it, like reinstalling the mods that allowed me to play in the first place, tinkering with the configs, running it as admin, running it in compability mode and I just kept getting this damned crash at startup.
So I gave up.
I am writing this honest review to warn you about this game.
It's definitely a great game. But is it really worth buying it if you may end up just not being able to play it at all?
I will try a fresh reinstall and a couple of different things and if I manage to get it to work I might as well change this review into a positive one, but right now it just doesn't deserve it.

I don't even know where to begin because I have NEVER had this problem before. What problem am I referring to you may ask? The problem where a game doesn't work. Well technically it works, but if I were to categorize it I would have to put Miscreated in the "WTF" category.
I cpmpletely understand that this game is "pre-alpha" and that everything about a game in this stage is basically an "experiment" for the devs to figure out what works and what doesn't work. I understand that I'm not to expect a perfectly complete and polished gem, but more of a freshly mined, rough around the edges rock with the potential to becoame a sparkling beauty. I get that... I understand... Which is why I usually don't mind frequent crashes, weird physics defying objects, bad graphics, screen tears and glitches and everything else that comes with a "pre-alpha" game. So far durring my gaming career I have bought numerous "pre-alpha" stage games and I have been happy with all of them... Until now.
I personally do not even feel right to give a review for Miscreated because I honestly haven't had the chance to even experience it for what it is or what it's supposed to be. The only things that I have actually been able to do in Miscreated is walk, run, punch the air, swim, starve and drown! Thats it, nothing else, game over. The very first time I decided to give Miscreated a try I had to go into the settings and make some changes. The resolution was way low and the game was in "window" mode. This is where I encountered my first problem. My rig is a high powered 4K gaming beast and Miscreated started the game off in an extremely weird and very low resolution. I can't remember what the exact number was but I do remember that I was below 720 (I'm thinking that it was either 705 or 715) and the opening start screen looked horrible. I immediately set the res to 3840 x 2160 and bumped everything in the graphics department to max and hit apply. When the game reset itself to my settings it looked great and a giant sense of relief came over me (the original opening menu screen looked so bad that I was scared I wasn't going to be able to play the game at all). Now that the game was ready to be played I tried to possition my mouse over the player set up category. I say try because my curssor would only move about three quarters or less down the screen... Not enough to reach the player set up option. I stayed calm. This has happened to me before and all I had to do was "tab" and "arrow key" my way through the options. So I did. I made it to the player set-up category and prepared to make my character or at least I thought I was going to create a character. All I did was decide on my players name... Bummer. I was hopping to create my character with a plethra of cool options and tweaks, but all I got was a lonely black screen asking me to type in my characters name. Again, no big deal... The game is in "pre-alpha". After I typed in my name I again "tabbed" and "arrow keyed" my way back to the menu screen and decided to go ahead and join a server.
WOW! There were hundreds of servers and most of them were largely populated! This a good thing! This means that despite the few problems I encountered really were no big deal and that I was gonna be able to finally kick back and enjoy the game! I couldn't have been more wrong! I tried to join several servers and all of them would go through the motions nad suddenly reset my screen. By reset I mean the screen would flash and the list of servers would reappear asking me to pick a server as if nothing happened. After about 13 attempts I decided to go back and give the controls a quick once over. In doing so I discovered that some of the key-bindings were really weird, but for the most part the controls were set out just as they are for almost every other PC game... Space/jump, ctrl/crouch and so on. After learning how to control my avatar I went back to again try and join a server and AGAIN I was confronted with the same outcome. I decide I was going to try 10 times and if I couldn't successfully join a server I was gonna call it quits. Wouldn't you know it that on the 10th try I finally made it!
So there I was in the middle of nowhere. Nothing but the wind blowing and the grass swaying. I did my little "see if everything works" dance and took off walking. When I got tired of walking I decided to run. I did this for about 10 minutes and the game suddenly crashed. In the blink of an eye I went from running in the wind to staring at the "server select" screen! BAHH HUMBUG! I had homework to do and decided to take a break, do some homework and come back to Miscreated later. That was yesterday.
Today I decided to give Miscreated another go. I expected that I was going to have to change the resolution and graphics settings again, but I didn't which was great! I was starting to get that "I'm gonna get to play a new awesome game" feeling all over again... I was excited. I even got through on the first try! I couldn't believe it. The very FIRST server I tried was a success... WRONG!!! For some weird and unknown reason I spawned underwater in the middle of the ocean (or at least I think it was the ocean). I took me a good while to figure out what in the hell was going on. When I spawned in, all I could see was blue and all I could hear was a very strange "wooshing" sound. At first I thought I spawned off the map somewhere. Then I saw a bubble, followed by multiple other bubbles! I then pushed the "w" key and I saw my hands! After that I knew I was freakin underwater. Way off in the distance (and I mean waaayyy off) I could see the very faint outline of some mountain tops and a little to the left of that I could see what appeared to be modern winmills or a "wind" farm. It didn't take me long to decide on what to do so I began swimming toward the wind farm. I didn't make it. I starved before I reached the shoreline.
Just because I spawned underwater in the middle of the ocean doesn't mean I was gonna give up. That was just bad luck. Wrong time, wrong place sort of thing... I highly recommend this game. This game takes the previous Splinter Cell games, takes the good parts and distills them until you get a Splinter Cell that we had been waiting for.
The single-player and coop can now be played three different ways, each with its own rewards: you can easily choose to go all-out Assault, shooting and blowing up everyone as loudly and messily as you can; or Panther, killing everyone as quietly and unnoticeably as possible. And finally, we have Ghost, the hardest of the playstyles, but the most rewarding if you have been following the series from the first game. There's nothing quite like sneaking into and out of a building filled with hostiles undetected. The in-game cash reward when ghosting is pretty nifty too.
You are now not limited to only one path towards your objectives, you can find all sorts of other ways to move forward in a mission. You may even find different paths on different playstyles.
AI can be a crapshoot sometimes, either being as deaf as possible on one moment, to suddenly being hyper-aware and shooting you in a moment's notice.
For true ghosting fans, Perfectionist difficulty brings you back to pre-Conviction gameplay, taking out Execute (but not marks) and takedowns from the front. AI is quicker to respond, and you take more damage on this difficulty.
Single-player missions can be quite short, but can be replayed with different playstyles to enjoy them. Same can be said with the coop missions.
And the multiplayer is nothing but icing on the cake: bringing back Spies vs Mercs was probably the best thing Ubisoft did for the series. Play either as a Merc, shooting and blowing up Spies to complete your objectives. or as a Spy, moving in the shadows using your gadgets, waiting and then moving in for the kill to complete your own objectives. Gameplay is not like your usual FPS slugfest, you have to be coordinated and know your equipment in order to win. Maps are well-thought of, giving Spies enough room and multiple ways to move across the map, but at the same time giving Mercs a enough line-of-sight if paying good attention to his surroundings.
SvM Classic is the same as Pandora Tomorrow's SvM, 2 players on each side, no customization and the maps are considerably darker than on the other modes. The other modes bring you customization for either side, giving you certain abilities depending on your faction.
Some notes:
1. Cloaking for Spies and Drones for Mercs aren't the best suit gadgets, Overcharge and Disruptor for each respective side is sometimes more invaluable for winning a game.
2. Mercs: look behind, look above. Often times, doing this will save you and your team a lot of problems.
3. Spies: don't even think about going head-to-head in a shooting match with Mercs, they will shoot you down to the ground, and then some. Only shoot when you can net a guaranteed kill, or if you want to distract.
4. For either teams: communication is the key! Use the in-game voice chat to coordinate with each other, this will net you more wins over the long haul.
All in all, as I said from the start, I highly recommend this game, and it's best enjoyed with friends, either on coop or on SvM. We finally get the Splinter Cell that we have been waiting for, especially after the joy that was Chaos Theory and disappointment that was Conviction.

On the game itself - I've played almost every Splinter Cell game (SC1, Pandora, Chaos Theory, Double Agent, Conviction) obsessively since the franchise began.
I was one that hated (ok, disliked) Metal Gear and loved SC's methodical and open approach to stealth, and would play the games over and over, and did Ghosts runs/No disturbing enemies and no alerts.
I rented and finished Conviction in 1 day and actually enjoyed it as brainless fun even though it was the least favourite of the series.
I had hoped that Blacklist would be the return to SC's former glory.
-------------------------------
Unfortunately, while Blacklists incorporates stealth elements back into the game... it feels very restricted. The levels are on rails and the enemies perform the same routines over and over.
There doesn't seem to be variation in AI pathing and behaviour, everything is scripted in a very linear manner.
If you follow specific timings you can automatically get through stealth sections as a routine. It almost feels like a bot could be programmed to run through the levels because of how little randomness there is.
The KB + Mouse controls are very awkward and more than once Sam climbed over a car instead of shifting to an adjacent side. This is one of those games where you need a controller, and that's understandable given SC's console origin.
All in all - I recommend RENTING this game if you're playing SP. I haven't tried the MP yet so I can't comment on it. If you have a console, go down and rent this from the shop, it's not worth buying IMO.

Being one of the first success stories of Kickstarter, Obsidian Entertainment received massive funding for Pillars of Eternity. As you play through the game you can see that money was well spent creating and polishing up an astounding amount of lore. It is at times overwhelming how much content and text was written for this game.
The story is set in the world of Eora where you as a foreigner arrive in Dyrwood in search of a place to settle. Through unforeseen circumstances you are attacked and forced to escape to the nearby ruins, where you witness a grand supernatural event which awakens newly found powers in you. So you begin your quest to find out what has happened to both the world and you yourself.
Mechanically it is much like you would expect a classic RPG to be. You create a character -
- and start your adventure. Throughout the game you meet new people to group up with and can hire and create new characters if you feel like you wish to have more control over your party of 6. Fighting through realtime combat which can be paused to issue commands, earning reputation, questing, exploring and even developing a stronghold of your own, the game has a variety of different things to keep you busy.
My only real complaint is that the story took a little bit too long to really get going. The last third of the game was definitely my favorite simply because you finally understood more of the underlying story and what your overarching goal is. Before it seemed at times a little trivial to be questing and earning reputation with only glimpses of the underlying story, which made me lose a bit of interest. Still, wanting to find out what the story is all about made me push through the boring bits and finish the game.
If you enjoy more of the action side of the RPG genre, be aware of the amount of reading involved. Pillars of Eternity is a great classic RPG and for fans of old Black Isle games like Baldur's Gate, this game is definitely a must buy.

This is an amazing game.
I have a copy on Steam that I have modded, but I also have a DRM-free version that I played through the vanilla game with. And as far as a review is concerned, that really needs to be about the game itself in its native state. The mod community is vibrant, however, so that's a plus. I won't say more than that so I can move on to the game itself.
Starbound is, clearly, inspired by Terraria. For me, it offered far more entertainment and replay value than its predecessor, however. The cultures found within the game, many of which you can choose to play as, have rich histories and backstories. The dialogue is clever and fun, never taking itself too seriously while staying true to the game's lore. Colonies can be built for a single species, or as a multi-special complex. You can build from scratch or take over abandoned homes and bases. You can even clear out the prior inhabitants violently, if you're that sort of player.
You can garden... and there are many options for farming and cooking... but you don't have to. After spending many hours in Stardew Valley, I wasn't in the mood for more farming. So I bought canned food and played all the way through without planting a single seed. Which game elements you focus on are completely up to you.
I had fun with the story, even if the storyline itself is a bit recycled, as the characters still shone, the lore was intriguing, and the battles reminded me of my Mega Man days... with better music. And again, the story is optional. There are some great perqs for moving through the progressive stages of the story, but they aren't necessary if you just want to explore the galaxy and build an apartment complex on an asteroid.
The art is colorful and well-rendered, the music is fitting and upbeat most of the time, and the gameplay is largely intuitive and clear.
Is anything imperfect? Sure. I was not a fan of the red cursor... I am guessing it was designed to be inobtrusive, but I found that my eye had trouble tracking it from time to time, which was an occasional problem in battle. But it was not a major issue, and some may have no trouble at all with it.
Inventory management could be improved. You can auto-arrange your personal inventory, but for some reason you don't have that option in exterior storage windows. That would be helpful.
The game modes make sense, from worry-free Casual to eat-to-live Survival or even permadeath on Hardcore... but asteroids are a special kind of terrible. You can lose everything if you fall all the way through a field on Survival. (Not on Casual, and on Hardcore it doesn't really matter, because your game is over at that point.) There is no retrieval option, and no way to know it will happen. Even in boss fights, you will not lose items in your inventory, and planetside you'll lose them, but you can go back and get them if it's the same play session. But asteroids? Yeah, I don't quite understand the logic.
Anyway, overall, my gripes are minor. There's exploration, discovery, crafting, and often some destruction of the local flora and fauna as you set about saving the galaxy -- or not -- at your own pace.
It's a truly great game, and one I have really enjoyed playing. Games like this are the reason I game, and the reason I buy up all sorts of games I hardly spend any time with. I do it because I know that periodically, a gem like Starbound will come along, and I don't want to miss it. I'm glad I didn't miss this one!

This game is the closest that walking dead fans have, to live out their zombie apocalypse. It's GTA4 + Rebuild + Sims + Stalker rolled into one. You have complete open world and almost all fully-accessible building interiors. There's dynamic day/night cycle, lighting and noise triggers to allow stealth tactics or zombie luring. There's finite resource management and car availability to encourage strategic survival planning. There's RPG leveling of abilities and character investment paired with perma-death, to emphasize the importance of survival and careful play. There's base management allowing for custom facilities and perks. And lastly, there's infinite drama. Your growing band of survivors will need to get along to ensure group survival and prevent rash decisions and their untimely end. All your actions have weight even when logged off... the game world persists and you would be wise to log off with your group morale in good standing. There's a real sense of accomplishment with each playthrough. Rick Grimes, logging off.

Wow. What an incredible journey. My hours count right now is from me completing the main game, all optional areas and bosses, and the DLC. There's nothing quite like finishing a Souls game (this is my 3rd, after Demon's Souls and Bloodborne).
This game is just as hard as you've heard, at least in the beginning. Sort of how college classes make the first semester really hard to weed out those who aren't dedicated, Dark Souls does much of the same thing. This game is hard, but it's not impossible. Once you learn the many systems in the game, you'll be cruising. With that being said, there are a LOT of different systems, ways to play, and afflictions/buffs/abilites to learn. My biggest advice for this is: Ask questions. I strongly recommend reading a guide; not to know how to beat everything, but just the beginning of the guide to learn how the systems in the game work. Also, I personally used a guide as a form of checklist, just to see which areas were intended to be next. I don't recommend reading one to learn where every item is and how to beat every boss. Figuring that out yourself is much of the fun in this game.
The Dark Souls community is also very much alive and well, and extremely helpful. Yes, there's always the person that tells you to "git gud," but many members are still active and available to answer questions or even help out in your game. I personally had to request help with the final boss, and had someone agree to help, and help me beat him, within 14 minutes of me posting my request for help on the Dark Souls discussions page (Thanks MobiusPizza!).
This game is also masterfully crafted. The developers created a game that is dark, foreboding, but also has some of the most intricate strategies and gameplay systems I've ever seen, and they all work flawlessly. From combat, to there being extrordinarily few bugs, to the atmosphere and graphics in general. This was very much a labor of love, and From Software should be commended for this enormous, and extremely riveting experience.
Be warned though, once you start playing, and start winning, it's very difficult to stop. The adrenaline rush following every encounter can be intoxicating, and most of my playtime listed has been in the last 3 weeks. It's addictive, in a masocistic sort of way, but enthralling upon completion of a particularly difficult area.
All this being said, I STRONGLY RECOMMEND YOU DON'T PLAY THIS IF YOU ARE NOT A GAMER, A CASUAL GAMER, OR, IN SOME CASES, A SEMI-CASUAL GAMER. This game requires so much dedication, patience, tolerance for failure, and optimism in almost hopeless situations. If you don't consider yourself a gamer, are a new gamer, or otherwise don't play games often, don't get this game. I can almost guarentee you right now that you won't get past the first or second boss.
But, if you do game often, or have a number of games in your Steam library, you've probably already heard of this game. You might know people who play it. You've undoubtedly heard of the immense difficulty. Do yourself a favor. Forget everything you think you know, and click purchase. Enjoy.
This is one of the greatest gaming triumphs you can have (upon completion) in your gaming career. And it should speak to the immesurable appeal to this game that most people who have beaten this game, have beaten it more than once or twice. I've heard of several people beating this game 5 or more times. This game also has NG+ (New Game Plus), where upon completion, all your equipment, levels, and upgrades carry on to the next playthrough. Enemies also become much harder, and the game becomes more difficult. Each playthrough is like beating it for the first time (albeit you know the systems, bosses, locations, and more the next time around).
Overall, not the greatest game I've played, but definitely one of the best.

Really fun game, and obviously challenging. You're not given advantages in this game. Your advantage is that you are player controlled, and the enemies are AI that can be predicted.
The story is all told through lore, for the most part.
You can kill pretty much any NPC you see.
The maps are very well connected, making the world a bit more fun to traverse.
One thing that some people may find frustrating, while others find immersive is the fact that you are given little to no guidance. There is no mentor in this game, there is no real end goal for quite a while. One of the most immersive parts of this game is that you really arent anyone super special. Your importance comes from your actions, not the other way around.
Unfortunately, the multiplayer doesnt usually work, which takes out a large portion of the game. It's basically a straight port from console too, so it really isn't optimized for pc. But, thats what mods are for. I recommend the Dark Souls Connectivity Mod (DSCM) and DSFix.
I would also not recommend playing this with a mouse and keyboard, as this really isnt made for that.
All in all, if you are thinking about buying this and it sounds like the kind of game you would like to play, odds are it probably is. It's not as impossibly hard as people make it out to be, but it is challenging. It's definitely not for everybody and it's meant to cater to a more seasoned gamer, but it does it well.
You will get frustrated. You will get angry sometimes. But you will also do things you didnt think you could, and beat monsters you never thought you would. It's an expeierence, and I would recommend it to anyone who likes RPGs and knows thier way around a controller.
Definitely worth the $5 this game goes on sale for so often.

Dark Souls is an acquired taste.
Initially, you'll be really off-put by it's difficulty. And to be fair, is is a very very challenging game. Though I make the argument that most of this challenge comes from assholish enemy placement or just bad game design in general, most of the game is a legitimately fun experience and all of the challenges are completely fair. I've put in over 150 hours since my last review of this, and I grow to like the game more and more. I'm currently on my 8th playthrough, not counting NG+.
The character creator isn't as indepth as the future titles, but that's not too much of a bad thing. It's still very simple. And you can get into the action without fiddling with a menu for half an hour.
The game is VERY VERY VERY open-ended. Not as much as Dark Souls 2, but there are enough weapons to suit any playstyle, or make any character you want. You could sink countless hours into this game just starting new runs with weapons you've never tried before.
Another thing this series is famous for. PvP. This is kind of a mixed bag for me. On one hand, you have twinkers who beat the game at a low level just to go back to the start to grief with endgame equipment. Then you have exploiters who use♥♥♥♥♥♥like backstab escapes or lagstabs or just general tricks they use to get an easy win.
On the other hand, You have some actual people who don't play the game exclusively for PvP. I have a lot of fun fighting people with average builds, not just ones specifically designed for PvP. But you know what else I love?
All of the AMAZING and MAGICAL moments I've gathered from the online mode. My favorite moments of PvP include:
-Tricking a NG+ guy off a ledge with poison mist, getting me 50k souls.
-There was a point where someone just stood by a ledge, trying to bait me over. I shot him once with my bow. It did about 1300 damage for some reason.
-I once invaded a giantdad while giantdadding
-The time I repeatedly tossed myself at a naked gravelord servant while "Dual-Shwielding". She ended up giving me 10 twin humanities and a thief mask+10. This was at a very low level.
And There's just so much more that I know I can experience.
Now, I did mention bad game design. I do love this game, but there are some things about it that I never liked, and they're only slightly better in later playthrough since you know to avoid them. Half of the boss fights are AMAZING, but then you have things like the Stray Demon/Demon Firesage, Centipede Demon, Bed of Chaos, Capra Demon... And several others, they all just have a really flawed design to them. Also worth mentioning is Seath. The first fight with him is forced failure, and you're still punished for dying, but he's pathetic when you meet him again. There's also some bad enemy placement, like the Archers of Anor Londo. There's the issues with bonfire warping, And what seems to kill me the most: Bad level geometry.
But even with all of that, I still love this game. I feel like writing some guides for it to help other people with the parts I had the most trouble with. It has it's faults, but if you can adapt, learn, and perservere, it's not as hard as it seems.
But watch out for this version of the game. You'll need DSFix, DSCM, and possibly PvP Watchdog. It's a buggy mess of a port. And Namco has the worst cheater prevention imaginable.
Love this game and everything about it.

The enemies are more of an annoyance than anything else, and it's very difficult to dodge their projectiles as your character is rather large. And even if you do get hit a lot, you can easily craft a cheap healthkit that heals most of your bar. Speaking of the crafting system, you can also make grenades. But i rarely found myself using them, aside from when they were required to bypass obstacles, they can also be used to perform an air dash move, but this needs to be charged up and so is only useful in specific situations.
All in all, I think this game isn't really that good. If you like platformers such as megaman, then i'd recommend buying it during a sale. But other people probably won't enjoy this.
