Over the years the RPG on computers has evolved into something that is a hybrid of FPS/Third Person with an RPG element. Even FPS and Third Person games have begun this transformation taking on RPG elements.
Pillars of Eternity is a step back to the pure essence of the early forays of the RPG world into the computer. It takes some of the tech advancementsa we have seen and combines it with the classic style and game play of the early days of computer RPGs.
Gone is the twitch gamer mentality that has so invaded the RPG world and in it's place is the slow, methodical game play that drew you into a story. This is a game that will not impress you with eye candy and glitz, it is more than skin deep.
If you love RPGs and loved the classic RPGs beofre they tried to become FPS, then you will love this game.

After just finishing this game I am giving it a solid 7/10 - which means it's a good title, there's just some areas where it falls a bit flat.
Strong points:
- Great atmosphere, immersive world.
- Overall good quests
- Most companions have an interesting background and personality
Weak points:
- UI is not on par with 2015. While this is a revive of the genre, it doesn't have to bring back the frustration of the 1990-s UI! Also it loves to bug a lot (for example you equip an item that grants you a spell, but you don't see it in your bar until you reload)
- Stealth options are minimal and bland. Yes, you find the odd hidden object or door, but too rare. Most of the time you use stealth mode only to detect traps, which in itself doesn't make much sense - traps should be detected by a high PER char regardless.
- Due to the isometric view, the combat can get difficult when you can't see your guys because of a tree/rock/ruin in front of them.
- While the story is interesting in act 1 and 2, it really falls flat in act 3 - I personally was disappointed and kindof rushed the end just to get over with it.
- The stronghold ends up being just a Copper Sink, with no other real influence over the world or quests or anything meaningful.
- Lackluster Skill System - out of the already few options (5!), only 3 make any real difference.
- Cosmetic dialogue choices - even though there are many skill checks, few of them alter the outcome in any way. What's even more disturbing is that only your main character's stats matter towards these skill checks, which doesn't make much sense in a party based game...

In April of 2009, Andrew Hussie posted the first live updates of his comic Homestuck, although calling it a comic does not give full justice to the inventive ways that work played with the medium. It would take seven years to complete, but it was largely created by a single man, and it was massively long. It's impressive it did not take even longer.
Andrew Hussie is a gifted writer. His comic is inventive, funny, and he did a remarkably good job of writing the complicated story as he went without tripping over himself. The characters were multi-faceted and interesting, the world was well developed, and the exposition was never dull to read. His artwork was also excellent - low detailed and made for speed, but expressive and visually appealing, and although he was a crude, novice animator, he had a real talent for making engaging flash videos. He was especially good at timing the action to a piece of music, which was even more impressive given that the songs were composed first, before the videos were even conceived. There was a constant sense of learning and escalation in the delivery - it began with simple GIFs and short flash projects and expanded to include inventive 10-minute short films. That progression made a nice motif for a story with themes of adventure, discovery, and coming-of-age.
The music was always done by volunteers. Homestuck's website carries two contributor pages - one for music and one for art. Beginning from a little over a year into Homestuck's run, Hussie would take some art submissions for use in his comic. At first this was only for the larger animation projects. But it grew increasingly more frequent, and when the comic ended, one could be forgiven for thinking that Hussie was no longer contributing to Homestuck at all: the final panels and the last animation were done entirely by others.
This of course brings us to Hiveswap, a kind of side-story video game set in Homestuck's multiverse, the creation of which, unbeknownst to the people who backed it on Kickstarter over five years ago, hardly appears to have involved Andrew Hussie at all. He is credited by the game as a writer and producer, and information from Hiveswap's dedicated tumblr indicates that he acted as a kind of creative consultant to the real brains behind the project: Cohen Edenfield.
Who is Cohen Edenfield? According to an autobiographical update on the Hiveswap tumblr he is an English Lit graduate who shared an internet forum with Hussie over a decade ago. The body of his previous work consists of a twitter feed and Hiveswap's promotional material. Before release this did not encourage positive speculation: his former work is written in an insufferable self-aggrandizing voice that tries too hard to be funny.
But to his credit, his scripting for Hiveswap is not that bad. It's hard to say how much Hussie's advice helped, because What Pumpkin have been tight-lipped about the process of their development. About the only thing we do know is that they repeatedly failed to deliver on the release dates they promised, and that the project changed hands at least twice. But for the most part the dialog in Hiveswap is tolerable, and occasionally even funny. Edenfield does sometimes lay it on thick though. In Homestuck, the main character had a book titled "Colonel Sassacre's Daunting Text of Magical Frivolity and Practical Japery." It's a minor joke how overly long and whimsical that title is, and it works for Homestuck's outwardly quirky tone. In Hiveswap, a book is similarly titled "Pistols to Pelts: How to Turn Sweet, Intelligent Animals Into Weird Rugs and Stuff." The first example works because it's actually a plausible title, but the second really overdoes the joke and bungles it.
In Homestuck, the child characters have complicated, ever-changing views of their parents and their relationships. They were confused about who they wanted to be and what their roles in life were. All of this is to say that it did a good job portraying adolescence. Hiveswap doesn't really have that. Joey is fully decided on how she feels about her parents. She shows next to no self-doubt, and her dad is cartoonishly negligent to make that work. It's the same with the story's themes of revolution: the alien regime is entirely, ridiculously wrong and the characters are plainly meant to rebel against it. What exactly is that meant to portray? That monarchy and genocide are wrong? In conversation, the characters spout their life-stories unprovoked, especially Joey in the final scene of the game.
To be fair, this is only the first episode of many, and the later acts might resolve some of these story issues. I wouldn't be too surprised if it at least turned out to be a nice, classically structured adventure story with some decent character arcs. That much potential is there. The backgrounds are nice to look at and the animation is generally good, although there is a problem of the game being so visually cluttered that it sometimes hides the things you need to interact with, and there seems to be no way to tell what's a usable item and what's just background besides mousing over it all. The music is fine and works for the atmosphere but it's not memorable, so that I wouldn't recommend buying the soundtrack. Toby Fox has done much better musical work than this.
And I understand that it isn't fair to compare such a short game to something like Homestuck. That's the point though. Adjust your expectations accordingly: Edenfield is no substitute for Andrew Hussie, and Hiveswap is not and will probably never be Homestuck. In one news update on the Homestuck website, Hussie promised that this game will play with the medium as much as Homestuck itself did. Nothing like that has been displayed so far. This is a decent, standard-fare modern adventure game, completely toothless in terms of both puzzles and story. I'm willing to give it a thumbs-up in Steam's system, and I would score it about a six and a half out of ten. But the recommendation is conditional: if you don't like adventure games this won't change your mind. And if you haven't read Homestuck, your time is much better spent with that.

***THE LAST PART OF THIS REVIEW CONTAINS MINOR SPOILERS***
EDEN* is a visual novel about a romance that slowly blossoms in the face of an ending world.
EDEN*: The Positives and Negatives
+ Very good writing, feels very authentic a lot of times.
+ Beautiful imagery.
+ Amazing soundtrack, that, despite looping a little, never gets old.
+ Great middle part, this part is almost perfect in my opinion.
+ Interesting main protagonists.
- The first 1-2 hours of the story aren't the most interesting and, honestly, got boring at times.
- Half of the cast are forgettable, and not present for long.
- I know it's a visual novel, but this game would be so much better with a "choose what path you wanna take" style gameplay involved. The ending in particular seems to be able to move in many directions that all seem awesome, so interactivity would have been very much welcome.
Overall, if you like visual novels, this one is very solid.
***MINOR SPOILERS WILL APPEAR FROM THIS POINT***
Personal Opinions:
I liked EDEN* a lot. I spent about a day playing through it, and I do not regret doing so. It's a great experience, but it's not without flaws. I'll praise the game first though. The writing is solid. It's suprisingly authentic, and you really believe a lot of the conversations the characters have. The music is f*cking amazing, and I could listen to the OST for hours. This also goes for the beautiful scenery and overall visual presentation of the game. The most important thing in the game is the love story between out two protagnonists and, honestly, it's really heartwarming. It never really delves into creepyness or goes to another extreme, the love story is right where it should be.
Now let's talk about some of the negatives. The first 1-2 hours spent inside of the facility are boring. Plain and simple. Sure, we get the necessary information about the characters... but that's it. Nothing else. The story only gets amazing when the perspective shift solely to our two protagonists, but it just only happens after a mediocre at best opening. Also, the ending. Now I know, this ending made people cry, and the love story was indeed, pretty tragic. So why didn't I cry? Simple. I kept thinking about other possible endings that made more sense in my head, espicially after they threw in the detail that one of the characters "had a wish to see the protagonist one last time". Instead, the ending we get it the one where the protagonists stay together, removing any logic from that scene where it clearly shows that the side characters are concerned. If you want us to care about the side characters, don't base the ending SOLELY around just the protagonists. If you want us to care about the protagonists, don't throw in statements about the side-characters, focus on the main two!
So, after all that ranting about the ending, do I hate it? No. I just got really confused by the writing near the end, but I think I'm probably the only one to do so. I had the same reaction to the ending of Life is Strange, which people seemed to love, but I didn't. Most people will fall in love with the ending, if they don't tend to overanalyze things like I do. The ending is still heartwarming and indeed sad, and you'll probably shed a tear or too.
Not to mention that the 3-4 hours between the beginning and ending are the best parts of the game. They are so perfectly written, deciding to focus on the main characters, rather that dragging in several other characters, like the beginning and ending did. This part is what I love most out of the whole game.
In conclusion: While the beginning fails to completely impress me, and the ending is quite confusing in terms of the direction it really feels comfortable going in, I still had a lot of fun with EDEN*. In the end, it is the writing that makes a visual novel, and the writing is fantastic. The "visual" part of visual novel, the scenery and the music, are also breathtaking on their own. I wrote alot about the ending of the game, and how I wish it had more choices, but in the end, it's still a good ending. I'm probably also the only one who think it isn't perfect, so don't mind my opinion too much on that point.
EDEN* is a game I recommend to any visual novel-lovers, fans of love stories or simply bookworms. It's a great tale, that is worth playing through. If you aren't completely sure, wait for a sale, and it will DEFINENTLY become worth the amount of money you pay for it.

That sinking feeling of impending doom never stops. It's like day 3 of majora's mask, except extended for like 8 hours.
The main theme would be "(no)Regrets" and "Accepting the inevitable", but taken to extreme levels.
If you have trouble coping with any of these, I wouldn't recommend going into this unprepared.
Regardless of previous experience with sad novels, eden* had me crying internally halfway through even before the sad events happened because I wasn't expecting plot curveballs and indeed, they never came. The reader is given the burden of shouldering all of the characters' emotions, building up to an obvious tearjerking ending that unfortunately, couldn't be happier.

I guess I like this game? It has an immense amount of problems which are really irritating, but overall the game is decent. There's as much or more wrong with the game than right, but melee combat in the game is enjoyable enough to counterbalance the problems.
Pros -
Fun combat mechanics, battle is decided more by skill than by quality of gear.
Co-op available for most areas until the boss is defeated.
Good storyline.
Wide variety of weapon types and strategies are viable to play through the game with.
Cons -
Horribly optimized. (This comment is obligatory, and I assume everyone already knows this. I'm just covering my bases.)
Co-op can't be played unless you opt into being invaded and PK'd by players using vastly overleveled pyromancy to kill you. There is no way to play co-op without pvp. Non-optional pvp with players who go out of their way to make the pvp unfair is the single worst feature of this game.
Co-op is glitchy, there aren't a lot of servers for co-op online anymore, finding a specific player's sigil without mods is extremely difficult, and even with a mod, still sometimes impossible.
A vast majority of the game difficulty is just working around bad mechanics, and has nothing to do with the game actually being hard.
If you are looking for a difficult game, you're going to have to deliberately make the game difficult (don't level up, don't upgrade weapons, ect), by default the game is beatable by any player with a vague amount of patience.
Lock-on system is pretty bad, and will sometimes kill you if you attempt using it (locks on to creatures you can't see and tries to get you to fall off the environment).
Using projectiles for long range attacks is tedious, clunky, and rather inaccurate. Assume all projectiles have an effective range no further than you can lock on.
The camera in general is pretty bad, particularly if you haven't turned off "Camera Auto-Recovery" in the settings, which is on by default.
The community detest new players. Don't expect any assistance or advice other than "git gud" and anticipate being invaded every time you reverse hollow. TIP: Entering the white mist to a boss banishes invaders - I'd imagine alt-f4 works as well.
I'd rate the game around 8/git gud - and probably worth the $19.99, but if you're buying it outside of steam, certaintly wouldn't pay any higher than that.

What's up guys.  I just got Savage Lands included with the recent Humble Bundle.  To be honest, I'd only known of the game in passing through random store items.  Originally I bought the bundle for Rust but after playing both games, it seems to me that even at this stage of the game, SL is a much better game.  In Rust I ended up just running randomly around an island full of little bases with security doors looking for naked guys to bludgeon.  There was nothing to pick up and nothing to do.  SL on the other hand seems to have a much more immersive and interactive world.  Here are a few pros and cons based on my short time with the game thusfar...
Pros:
-Graphics look great and the lighting effects are done well.  Night can be nerve-wracking as you have to make sure you're in a safe place to wait it out.
-The crafting system is intuitive and points you in the right direction in making and obtaining items.  Some things aren't well explained though (finding a crafting table, smelter?, and where to get components from).
-The setting really draws you into the game world and there is just enough story content to build a believable setting for your character to exist in and build their own narrative.
-SL has a local game option.  The fact that Rust is a multi player game is the biggest drawback.  It's hard to get immersed in a survival game where you start out with a rock and the rest of an island's population is mowing you down with flame throwers and automatic weapons.  This doesn't fit the scenario at all and SL has much more technology appropriate things to create.
Cons:
-The world really needs to be much larger.  Even though I'm still on the first island of 3 I've heard, it seems that the game world is limited.
-More items to craft and structures to build would be excellent.
-I've come across some weird bugs that I hope will be fixed.  The first is killing an animal close to a set of rocks or structure.  I once killed a deer and its body clipped inside rocks and I couldn't loot the meat or hide.  A boar killed once fell against a stone tower structure and I couldn't access it either.
-AI in some cases needs help.  The large boar attacks with a jumping snout push motion and just jumps forward clipping all over the place.  It doesn't turn its body or vary attacks.  You can easily just jump to the side bullfighter style and easily kill it.
I know this is an early access game and many of the bugs hopefully should be fixed by general release, but overall very good and the best game in the Humble Bundle assortment by far.  A real steal!

Game : Splinter Cell Blacklist
Score : 7/10
Summary :
Overal Splintercell Blacklist brings back the old feeling Chaos Theory used to have, It's a game where the developers acctualy did their best to bring back that good old feeling of trying to stealth past enemies without being deteced, something that Double Agent lacked in my oppinion. The singleplayer is a nice storyline with a nice extra added feature to upgrade your plane, upgrading this said plane will give you advantages on the battlefield, from better radar to better goggles.
Considering i have played every Splinter cell series ever released on PC i think i know what i'm talking about by saying this is probably the best Splinter Cell they have released since Chaos Theory.
When it comes to Multiplayer they worked hard to try and get that old feeling back that Chaos Theory used to have, unfortunately i still feels a bit chunky sometimes however i have over 100+ hours in on Multiplayer, i have to say tho, i played it without a proper team, if you have friends that want to play it aswell i can easily imagine you hit the 200+ hours.
The Coop is pretty good aswell, although i suggest playing that with a friend aswell on LAN or Teamspeak, it makes the experience so much better!
All in all this game surpasses Double Agent and Conviction by far, they really got the old Splinter Cell feeling back and i for one can not wait until they start working/releasing the next one!
Good things about Splinter cell Blacklist
- A nice new feature to upgrade your plane to make things a bit easyer in Campaign Mode
- They smoothened out the upgrading/buying of new gear
- Good gameplay, after 5/10 minutes of playing i got the feeling back and it felt like i never left
- Versus/Multiplayer is a HUGE step forward and getting close to what Chaos Theory used to be
- No significant gamebreaking bugs
Bad
- The launch was a bit bad with Multiplayer not really working although all issues are resolved for me
- At the start of Versus you feel overwhelmed by not knowing all the controls
- I understand some things change, but i don't like the new voice of Sam Fisher :'( nor that he looks younger!
- I hope they release some patches with new maps somethimes ( NOT DLC the game on itself is expensive enough )
All in all Tom Clancy's Splinter Cell Blacklist is a nice addition to the Splinter Cell franshise, if you liked Chaos Theory i suggest you buy this one as well.
-Please note this review is written on the base of my oppinion.

WARNING: SPOILERS AHEAD!
So, I finally got around to playing this game that so many of my friends told me was such an amazing game (also, none of whom warned me that this was Elevators, the RPG). Now, before I get into my full review here, let me give you my overall opinion of the game. It was a lot of fun, and the main story line was awesome and had me hooked from the beginning. I'd say that overall, I'd give it a 4 out of 5, I liked it a lot, and would recommend it to anyone that is a fan of RPG's and good sci-fi.
Now, that said, there were some things that I really disliked about this game. The biggest one, and the reason it's 4 and not 5 stars, is the side quests. They felt repetitive, needless and uninteresting. They all involved driving around in the Mako, the worst part of this whole game in terms of game play, IMHO. The few that did have interesting stories (the rouge VI on the moon, the Cerberus story) all seemed to just end, with no real resolution or even feeling of a cliffhanger. They just... ended. I killed the last gut, quest over, return to the Normandy to turn in the quest. After that happened twice, doing more side quests just felt... pointless. I probably missed out on a good chunk of the game because I skipped a LOT of the side quests due to a serious lack of interest. And I find that particularly dissapointing because the side quests in Dragon Age: Origins were so much better. I realize that DAO came out a year later, but still... disappointing nonetheless.
All that said, the Citadel Side Quests were almost the exact opposite. I participated in news stories that later showed up in the elevators, I helped people out and those stories felt resolved, I discovered clues that related to the main quest, even if they didn't directly effect it, and I never once felt bored running around the Citadel talking to NPC's (or shooting up clubs). These quests felt fun and unique and complete; everything I want from a side quest.
Another gripe was the way the party was handled. Now, this is a smaller gripe, because I realize this game is older, and Bethesda seems to have learned their lesson in later games, but still... a lack of a loyalty/"do they like me" meter was kind of awkward. I would have conversations or do loyalty quests and have no idea of the choices I made had any effect on the character.
That said, the party members themselves were really well done. All of them were interesting, well voice acted and unique. I honestly had trouble picking who to take on missions a lot of the time, because I liked all the characters so much.
Finally, my last gripe is this: I felt like the choices I made during the main quest had no real effect on the overall story. Again, I'm making comparisons to DAO, which may be unfair, but as I played DAO first, I can't help but compare them. In DAO, while my choices didn't effect the fact that I had to battle the dragon at the end, they did drastically effect the ending of the overall story, and I felt like they had weight, and consequences beyond just setting up the next game. In ME, however, it kept feeling like no matter what I chose, nothing really major changed. Save the Council? Humanity gets a seat for their sacrifice and major role in stopping the bad guys. Don't save the Council? A shiny new one shows up, and the same outcome happens. I mean, short of having one, maybe two, party members not show up at the final battle, nothing at all was effected by my decisions during the game. I mean, I realize they will in in the next one, but as far as the outcome in the end of this one? Nope, nothing, and that kinda sucked.
All that said, though, as I stated at the top, the game was, over all, really fun. While the side quests were boring, the main quest was not. The story was fascinating, fun, well-paced and well written. If I viewed this as an interactive Sci-Fi movie, it is awesome! The villians were all well done, and well voice acted. I loved most of the aliens (I was a little disappointed with the Assari, AKA the Fan Service aliens, but only a little), their background and the sheer amount of detail that went into this game.
I also liked the game mechanics. Taking cover became important, and the way poping up form behind cover was just a load of fun. Some fights were simple run and gun battles, while others required me to actually strategize how to beat the enemies (again and again a few times). As noted above, I wasn't fond of the handling of the Mako, but otherwise, the controls were just fine.
TL/DR: The game was overall very fun, and the main story line was gripping and kept me playing all the way through. Side quests were obring and repidtive, and it felt like my choices didnt have an over all effect on the ending of the game, but neither of those stop this game from just being really good and a lot of fun.

Combat.
you get an initial choice of 3 basic classes:
fighter (sword and shield)
strider (daggers and bow)
mage (uh magic)
the combat consists of light attacks and strong attacks, as well as up to 6 abilities that consume stamina when used.  many abilities have much higher potential for damage than either of your basic attacks, but many of them are also more defense/utility focused.
abilities are important.  initially i had issues with the combat, as i was trying to get by just blocking and attacking as a fighter.  this works on basic monsters, but anything tougher will break your guard and take little damage if you use this strategy.  you need offensive abilities to deal significant damage and break guard, and you need defensive abilities to effectively block or tank or dodge anything substantial.
Pawns.
you create a NPC character (pawn) in addition to your own character, and you customize his/her class/abilities/gear as well.  you can also take on up to 2 other pawns for your party.  these additional pawns are taken from a database that stores every player's main pawn.  you're probably gonna want at least one pawn to heal you (tho you could just wharf down curitives like a madman instead).
Fast travel?
mentioning this here because it took me a bit too long to realize this myself.  there is fast travel, but you need to place the travel points (portcrystals) yourself.  it also apparently required a consumable items (ferrystones) in order to fast travel to these locations, but this updated version of the game grants you an "eternal ferrystone" (that can be reused indefinitely) very early on.
So.
this wasn't really much of a review, just an overview of what you're getting yourself into.  the game's pretty good.  I hope they make a second (and that it's on pc).  seems like a perfect game for co-op, but it doesnt have any.  oh well.

Icing on the cake would have been a ledge climbing mechanic such as metroid fusion-onwards and this game would have stood its ground with the greats, probably knocked out a few.
as it stands now however it's still an amazing game. i you HAVE the money, i suggest you buy it even if just for the sweet sweet nostalgia value

Simply an amazing game, the game takes everything from games like Baulders Gate and Icewing Dale and combines them with modern mechanics.
Endurance/Health system:
The endurance/health system is a system in which, instead of having one pool of life you get two, endurance and health. Endurance is the amount of 'health' you have durring combat, if it is brought down to zero you get kocked out for the fight. Health is the total pool that endurance draws from, once Health is reduced to zero you are put into a killable state, where if hit while in this state you can and will die. Mechanics such as these help take old ideas and put new and modern spins on them.
Stronghold system:
Along with that there is a keep system in which you get to own a stronghold! With the keep you upgrade it, and gaurd it. Your stronghold serves as a main base of opperation in which you can rest, leave companions and do numerous other things i will touch upon later. Upgrading your stronghold allows you to get numerous different benefits, (most of which benefit the keep or you when your at it). Upgrading the keep allows you to gain presteige and saftey. The keep also serves as a front to a large well crafted dungeon which you can delve into. Along with your keep being attacked and a couple other cool minor additions.
Story/Lore:
I havn't gotten that far into the story but from what I have done it has been a very well put together and solid universe with a stream of neverending lore and stories. They have a cool background idea that is well developed and looks like it will lead to an amazing story.
Quests/Side Quests:
The first game I have wanted to be a completionist without feeling like it is a hassle to complete... Thats all I have to say.

This game is essentially the love child of Terraria and No Man's Sky (or rather, what No Man's Sky
have been); it is a 2D sandbox/adventure/crafting/survival game, and you can freely explore the in-game universe and everything that it has to offer (dangers included). It also has Workshop availability, if you want to mod the game to your tastes.
If you fall under any/all of these categories...
• You like Terraria
• You enjoy space-based games
• You enjoy sandbox/adventure games
• You like playing multiplayer with friends in those above-listed game genres
• You like having the option to stray away from the main story of the game without being punished for it
• You are sorely disappointed with what No Man's Sky wound up being and need something to fill the void in your heart
...Starbound is your game, without a doubt. I bought this game during a sale, but now that I have been playing it for a while and I can see just how fun it is, I would have gladly paid full price for it.

I've been with this game since it's humble beginnings, and watched it grow. There were some "rocky" periods during it's Early Access stage but I had patience to spare, so it didn't bother me as much as it bothered most.
That said, I've played the game throughout it's many different phases. I've seen it through times both good AND bad. In the end, some things have been left out entirely, some things have been watered down to the point of blandness, but there are still many things in the game to love and some new stuff that's wildly amazing.
Returning Players will have many gripes. But they've already bought the game. As a new buyer, you want to know specifically what YOU'LL be upset about.
Honestly? The only things I can think of that are directly negative are the Techs, Weapon Crafting, and Difficulty Settings.
1. Right now, Difficulty is broken down into three modes: Casual, Survival, and Hardcore.
Casual disables dropping items on death, allows you to teleport back to your ship from underground and removes the hunger bar. Survival has all those things.
Many, MANY players prefer a mix of the two (basically Survival sans the item drops). Fortunately, there's a mod for that ("Disable item drops for Survival").
2. List of craftable weapons is bland, even from a newcomer standpoint. Chucklefish seems to be going all-in with their randomgen weapons. I mean, they're NICE, yes... but... look up the Weapon Fusion mod, anyway.
3. And finally, Techs. They're rather bland and unhelpful. I suggest the "Energy Dash Restoration" mod and the "Phase Shift Module" mod.
That said, this game has a lot to do. Make your own farm so you have a steady supply of food and buffs, host a colony so you can get paid by your tenants, and of course save the universe from a nigh unstoppable tentacle beast.
And if you want more? This game has full mod support through the steam workshop, making fine-tuning your game as easy as looking up a mod you like and hitting the 'subscribe' button to add it instantly to your game.
The vanilla game won't disappoint you, but a few mods don't hurt neither.

Lets be real here, As far as "problems" go with this game, its mostly how long this game took to come out. End of the day though, if they hadn't been over zealous about release dates, i don't think this would be a problem, the game came out in reasonable amount of time (a little over 4.5 years from the blank slate to the finish) which isn't unusual for games, especially one with so many complications, and this being a first time company.
With 10 hours and 100% completion of act 1 on record, i think its time to put in my review. First off, the art goes without saying in that is extremely attractive and well done. Although the characters themselves and much of the art did mimic the simplicity of the Homestuck style, the backgrounds were rich in detail and the animations smooth in movement, excluding from the nasty loading screens however, which hopefully will be fixed in a patch. Despite the clutter of some of the characters homes; such was well placed and built on each's personality very carefully, as well as many enjoyable references to the time period this game was set in. The plot was quite enjoyable for just being the beginning to the story, as the main character Joey interacts well with both other characters, and background characters, even ones we had presently been aware of were we fans of Homestuck itself, were handled well in explanation. It's especially important to notice that this game has very little relation to Homestuck at all, except for the apparent fact it is the same universe. A few people have been overlooking plot points as "probably references to Homestuck" but in fact I personally found very little references to the webcomic myself, and the ones that did exist explained themselves rather thoroughly, In fact, putting Homestuck aside entirely, people can still easily understand and enjoy this game.
There are of course, a few things on the downside to it. Theres a bird that dies, rather sad, some slightly strange interactions, and bugs in loading between cutscenes, as well as there being a deal of typos (specifically a name recall fail with several of your item uses) when interacting with your Deercat in the final cutscene. I was also a bit puzzled by the fact that e consistently mention the troll main character bleeding under the rocks (presumably to death?) up until the point where we move him out, and he is inexplicably scarcely injured. they did draw the Deercat bleeding, although i have some suspect drawing the troll not bleeding was to keep a rating, since his blood is red?
The game was a little short, I completed my first run in about 4-5 hours, including the annoying cutscene lag, but completed a speed run in under an hour, with similar lag issues. I hope that the second act will be greatly longer, with that release being without the cutscene lag, but regardless, I'll probably end up playing and enjoying it as well. I'm a simple person.

This game has done what so many games try to do, but so few succeed.  It has introduced new ideas in storytelling, artistic elements, and gameplay all at the same time without resulting in a convoluted mess.
The adaptive narrator in Bastion (Logan Cunningham as "Rucks") contributes so much to the immersion and enjoyment of the story that the player finds himself doing things just to see what Rucks will say about it.  His deep tones and modern vernacular differ from the stiff prose of traditional narrators, connecting the player with him.
Seriously, the narrator is such a huge contributor to this game's successful implementation that one couple had him narrate their wedding in real life and the deluxe versions of this game had ringtones and notification tones with his voice narrating your every day life.  (My favorite was "Sorry to interrupt", raising eyebrows in many situations at my exceedingly polite phone).
The post-apocalyptic world with the techno-pseudo-western soundtrack brings a familiarity of cult classic sci-fi such as Firefly.  The player gets a sense of bleakness, but also one of hope (that feeling of pioneering and a new world with new rules).
The mechanics blend role-playing with a mostly action-based hack n' slash.  There is crafting.  There is town building.  There is skill tree branching.  There are challenge zones to allow for additional power-leveling and skill access (sort of like Bayonetta).
The main character, "The Kid", is loosely defined and a little mysterious for reasons explained in the game.  This allows the player to feel curious about finding out more while also allowing some flexibility for player choice.
Other characters are similarly guarded and mysterious.  Throughout most of the game, other characters are no more clear in their roles or intentions than the protagonist.  However, this is not a lack of direction as much as an open door to possibilities.  The player's mind may wander while considering the motives or actions of those he meets.  Multiple playthroughs will have different results, but certain characters may become clearer across multiple meetings.  There is depth here, but it feels as if it holds the player at arms length until a certain amount of involvement is met.
The iso-3/4 view with a floating land mass look for all of the generated maps has a painted look, somewhat similar to Squaresoft's gorgeous Legend of Mana-- and evokes a similar sense of whimsy and fantasy.  So much of this game is innovative that it is easy to undersell the tremendously beautiful graphics.
If you have not played this game, you have missed out on a game that supports the notion of video games as interactive art.  I invite you to rectify this wrong and let Rucks narrate your life for a little while.

My god. I don't even know where to start with this game.
This game is a gem. All my complaints surrounding the game are nitpicks at best, and my compliments are utmost and sincere. If you're alright with dedicating yourself to this game from start to finish, learning it inside out, then it will be the thing that gets you up in the morning. It will change your outlook on life, it will make you yell and cry and cheer till your throat is sore.
I can't tell potential new players anything past the gameplay without spoiling it for you. Its story is a tearjerker with no happy endings. The NPCs are memorable, the side quests reveal a lot about those characters' relations and why they're where they are, and despite the ambiguity, there is a thriving community based solely on the lore. This is an old ♥♥♥♥ing testament of a story, people.
Gameplay-wise, it fits its themes brilliantly, and as VaatiVidya once said, the biggest thing about this game is that it has the player experiencing everything the Chosen Undead does. Death becomes an obstacle to surpass, both in lore and the game. Many players "go hollow" and give up on the game, leaving out of frustration, anguish, or confusion, but those who press onward are greatly rewarded. Humanity is a rare but sweet find, for many reasons: not only do you gain access to the help of players who are online (and trust me, this game will never NOT have people online, not while r/DarkSouls continues to thrive with thousands of people logging in daily), regain health in the short term, kindle bonfires, and best of all, get a higher chance of receiving sweet loot.
The combat is genius, with few weapons in the game being bad. Some people can cheese bosses with the Gravelord Sword, or harass others early-game with the Drake Sword, but you will never see a weapon beside the broken swords in the very early game that have no good use. In fact, it's highly recommended you learn to use your starting weapons without elemental upgrades, as they become most trustworthy as time goes on. Every weapon has two phases, a wind-up and the execution, which give most if not all weapons in the game a chance to be parried, with the exception of gigantic boss attacks. Despite bad netcode, PvP is satisfying due to the balancing of armor and weapons, and so long as you're okay with being bested by Soul Level 1 gankers every once in a while, it's an enriching experience.
I give some tips to anyone reading this, that will make your first playthrough much, MUCH better.
-Don't use any of the gifts in early game except either the witch's ring or the Pendant. The Master Key is great if you know the ins and outs of the game, but only once you know the game is it recommended you use it. Believe me, you can't beat Blighttown going through New Londo Ruins in your first run without preparation.
-Don't use any guide except ones based solely on combat or PvP. Learn the maps firsthand instead of relying on instructions to get the "best loot."
-Stay Human as often as you can. You may be invaded, and it may suck when you lose your humanity, but it keeps you connected and invested in your character. My first successful run (only a few days ago!!), my character was held to a standard of humanity. I would not let him go Hollow. And you shouldn't let yours, not for long.
-Don't get mad. If you get mad, take a little bit off, jack it, eat, nap, shower, smoke some dank whade, but don't play while you're full tilt. It will only make you madder. I almost went hollow out of anger, and it's not a good feeling.
-Don't be afraid to die. It's a learning experience. Just try to make it further each time. It's the whole reason behind getting back to your bloodstain: get past the last obstacle that killed you, take a few extra steps, and eventually you will succeed at little or no cost except a few Humanities.
-Parrying is the answer to a lot of things. Learn it, and learn your enemies so you can parry them. Parrying stuns the enemy, gives you ample room to decimate them, and takes very little of your precious stamina. Even if the enemy cannot be blocked or parried, you can benefit through reducing the recoil of blocking with a parry-block/partial parry. The only exception I can think of right now is the final boss, given every time I parry his first swing, I take a♥♥♥♥♥♥load of damage. But that's one boss out of, like...20+.
I want to give an example of death as a learning experience. It's an early boss, and I know you'll benefit from hearing it. When you first meet the Capra Demon, his fight is purposely unfair. The arena is tiny, and immediately upon walking through the fog he's ready to slam you. The dogs in the area are also an unfair trick, to make your character flinch. However, the entire point of this is not to take it personally or get mad at the game. Instead, learn more each time. The first dog is on the right side, and Capra quickly takes you on with a slam, so the best thing to do here is not to attempt to kill any of the dogs, but raise your shield and sprint/roll toward the stairs. If you time it right, there's a second dog at the stairs, ready to hit you. You don't need to be afraid, simply attack it back, or evade it in favor of getting up to the end. After that, all you gotta do is kill the dogs and beat the boss in your own time. It's easy, other than the unfair setup of the fight.
Good luck, and please, if you get this game, don't go hollow. It's a waste of money, not to mention a sign you've been bested by a video game. Cling to your honor, win through force of will, and learn to love the game as so many before you have. Reignite the Age of Fire, or usher in the Age of Man. Either way, you win.

For God's sake, save your money. This was maybe the worst story I've ever experienced, in any medium.
It should be, but isn't, broken up into two distinct episodes. The first half is a fairly decent, if cliche-riddled, suspense plot, and the second half feels like a too-long epilogue that eventually festers into 3-4 hours of syrupy, sentimental loli fetish scenes. In both halves, the story goes out of its way to deflate elements of narrative tension that it bothers to introduce, with antagonists literally just stepping out of the protagonists' way.
The writing itself is verbose to the point of smothering the emotional impact that a scene might have. Characters will repeat a simple statement three or four times in the same scene, contributing to the problem of scenes that go on for 2-3x longer than they need to. There are many scenes that are repetitive or pointless (and still go on for 2-3x too long). Props, symbols, and images are repeated constantly, leaving them shopworn. Added for good measure is some cheap moralizing about taking care of the planet, the "appetites of those in power," and a few other super-deep subjects. Ryou even says "Sometimes, even pointless conversations can teach you a thing or two," without apparent irony.
Speaking of characters, they're more stock than Getty Images. For brevity, I'll talk mainly about the Gary Stu protagonist: He kills without a flicker of emotion, flies a helicopter, cooks breakfast (which he does over and over), and generally does anything the plot needs him to do with no previous setup. He can also completely abandon his professed love for violence and following orders, opting to dedicate his whole life to taking care of his loli. If this sounds like it could maybe be a character arc -- trust me, it isn't. His change is quick, complete, and virtually conflict-free. His old life doesn't come back to haunt him or lure him back to his past ways. I think there's one line, as he's serving his bedridden daughter figure dinner or something, where he mentions not liking how domestic he's become, but he doesn't actually experience any tension or conflict because of it -- he keeps it up, getting even more pathetic as he goes along. He also treats the female lead like an idiot, points his gun at everybody, and does some highly rapey stuff to a throwaway character who's introduced toward the back end of the story. Great guy.
So, what actually works in this game? The sounds effects, music, and voice acting are all fine to my ear. The art is nice, and really deserves a better story. I wouldn't mind this style becoming the norm for VNs. There's a warm glow to the scenery and lighting, and camera focus is used really well. The character designs are okay to good, and the blinking and moving mouths add to the immersion in a big way. But for whatever reason, characters tend to "dance" through three or four poses in a single conversation -- it can get a little distracting, like watching the exaggerated gestures and expressions of an actor in a silent film. Still, it's doesn't detract from the visuals too much, and some of the poses are cute.
There are many, many problems with this game -- more than I've mentioned here. I can't recall being more disappointed.

It's a touching visual novel with linear story. Great artwork, music and voice acting. The VN is quite long, but this in itself isn't a bad thing. The story makes ample use of flashbacks / flash forwards to show how past interactions of the various characters affect their future situations, and to gradually show how various factors add complexity to what first appeared to be simple events (e.g. the main character getting assigned to guard a "relaxed" research facility, despite his special forces background). Having said that, the pace does feel sluggish at times. The characters are interesting enough, and their eventual fates felt reasonably realistic given the circumstances. It's not really a "game" (due to its linear nature), but if you seek a long kinetic novel with good production values, IMHO this is a good buy.

WARNING: SPOILERS AHEAD!
So, I finally got around to playing this game that so many of my friends told me was such an amazing game (also, none of whom warned me that this was Elevators, the RPG). Now, before I get into my full review here, let me give you my overall opinion of the game. It was a lot of fun, and the main story line was awesome and had me hooked from the beginning. I'd say that overall, I'd give it a 4 out of 5, I liked it a lot, and would recommend it to anyone that is a fan of RPG's and good sci-fi.
Now, that said, there were some things that I really disliked about this game. The biggest one, and the reason it's 4 and not 5 stars, is the side quests. They felt repetitive, needless and uninteresting. They all involved driving around in the Mako, the worst part of this whole game in terms of game play, IMHO. The few that did have interesting stories (the rouge VI on the moon, the Cerberus story) all seemed to just end, with no real resolution or even feeling of a cliffhanger. They just... ended. I killed the last gut, quest over, return to the Normandy to turn in the quest. After that happened twice, doing more side quests just felt... pointless. I probably missed out on a good chunk of the game because I skipped a LOT of the side quests due to a serious lack of interest. And I find that particularly dissapointing because the side quests in Dragon Age: Origins were so much better. I realize that DAO came out a year later, but still... disappointing nonetheless.
All that said, the Citadel Side Quests were almost the exact opposite. I participated in news stories that later showed up in the elevators, I helped people out and those stories felt resolved, I discovered clues that related to the main quest, even if they didn't directly effect it, and I never once felt bored running around the Citadel talking to NPC's (or shooting up clubs). These quests felt fun and unique and complete; everything I want from a side quest.
Another gripe was the way the party was handled. Now, this is a smaller gripe, because I realize this game is older, and Bethesda seems to have learned their lesson in later games, but still... a lack of a loyalty/"do they like me" meter was kind of awkward. I would have conversations or do loyalty quests and have no idea of the choices I made had any effect on the character.
That said, the party members themselves were really well done. All of them were interesting, well voice acted and unique. I honestly had trouble picking who to take on missions a lot of the time, because I liked all the characters so much.
Finally, my last gripe is this: I felt like the choices I made during the main quest had no real effect on the overall story. Again, I'm making comparisons to DAO, which may be unfair, but as I played DAO first, I can't help but compare them. In DAO, while my choices didn't effect the fact that I had to battle the dragon at the end, they did drastically effect the ending of the overall story, and I felt like they had weight, and consequences beyond just setting up the next game. In ME, however, it kept feeling like no matter what I chose, nothing really major changed. Save the Council? Humanity gets a seat for their sacrifice and major role in stopping the bad guys. Don't save the Council? A shiny new one shows up, and the same outcome happens. I mean, short of having one, maybe two, party members not show up at the final battle, nothing at all was effected by my decisions during the game. I mean, I realize they will in in the next one, but as far as the outcome in the end of this one? Nope, nothing, and that kinda sucked.
All that said, though, as I stated at the top, the game was, over all, really fun. While the side quests were boring, the main quest was not. The story was fascinating, fun, well-paced and well written. If I viewed this as an interactive Sci-Fi movie, it is awesome! The villians were all well done, and well voice acted. I loved most of the aliens (I was a little disappointed with the Assari, AKA the Fan Service aliens, but only a little), their background and the sheer amount of detail that went into this game.
I also liked the game mechanics. Taking cover became important, and the way poping up form behind cover was just a load of fun. Some fights were simple run and gun battles, while others required me to actually strategize how to beat the enemies (again and again a few times). As noted above, I wasn't fond of the handling of the Mako, but otherwise, the controls were just fine.
TL/DR: The game was overall very fun, and the main story line was gripping and kept me playing all the way through. Side quests were obring and repidtive, and it felt like my choices didnt have an over all effect on the ending of the game, but neither of those stop this game from just being really good and a lot of fun.

They replaced the voice of Sam Fisher, so prepare yourself for that downside if you're a fan of the series.  It's weird to not hear the voice you've grown up hearing for the character, but I got over it fairly fast.
The coop elements are great in this game, with some missions that are entirely coop oriented.   It captures the feel of the older games where you and a buddy could just sneak through entire areas stealthily, with some areas being high action and fast paced.
If you hated the last of the series, this one probably won't turn you around.  The game play is mostly the same, just with a few different gadgets.
You have to solve some missions without alerting enemies or being detected, forcing stealth game play at times.  Others you're given more freedom to beat them however you please.
I had a ton of fun playing it, with a few hair pulling moments in coop where we'd have to replay an area several times due to one or the other half messing up something.

I was surprised by Blacklist, it's a lot of fun for a Tom Clancy game made post golden era. The story is alright in single player, nothing to write home about. Love all the weapons/gadgets you can unlock by playing, with the need to earn virtual money to buy each one, I spent a lot of time re-doing missions/co-op to earn more money for all the items. Re-doing missions with different loadouts or going different playstyles is a lot of fun.
The co-op missions are even better online, and a lot of fun. Just wish they had built in VOIP as it's sometimes hard to tell your teammate not to do something stupid.
The PVP multiplayer is kind of meh. Yes they brought back spy vs mercs but it just feels very unbalanced and unfair at times. It really comes down to being a spy, hiding in a shadow, run up to merc, press x, boom merc is dead, rinse repeat. Gets old.
OTHER than that, the CO-OP is fun, the single player is fun, and it's a lot of fun unlocking everything and re-doing missions. Well worth it for less than $30. (check Ebay, you can usually buy a key from there for around $20)
Better than conviction, but not all stealth like the old games.  Worth a try at a discount.

The sequel to Splinter Cell: Conviction is as good as it gets. Deeper weapon and gadget customization, new moves, and a fair story make this game a good buy for stealth action fanatics and gold for Splinter Cell fans.

Like a love-child between Conviction and older Splinter Cell-games (DA, CT etc). Can be played fast paced or all sneaky-like. Several ways to neutralize hostiles (lethal or non-lethal). The multiplayer's balanced and fun

To conclude, Splinter Cell Blacklist offers a full package that dances with several styles to create an encompassing game that covers all bases with ease. The story is interesting, the characters well realized, and the gameplay of a high caliber as expected from game number six in the series. With single player, co-op and multiplayer, there's enough to sink ones teeth into for quite some time, and so the question remains, is Blacklist worth a purchase, and more importantly, better than Conviction? The answer is obviously yes on both counts, making Blacklist not a massive leap forwards in terms of new features, but perhaps the most slick and accomplished game of the series to date.

I don't usually write reviews for games, but I felt compelled to this time. I didn't find out about Pillars of Eternity in time to back it on KS, but I began supporting it as soon as I learned of its existence :)
As a kid I played the old Infinity Engine games. I think my first was Fallout 2, then Fallout, then Planescape: Torment, then everything else. Basically, I cut my teeth in gaming on some of the best (arguably the very best) Western-style CRPGs ever made. It gave me a sincere appreciation for storytelling in games that has served me really well since, though I think any fan of RPGs remembers the dry spell in the 2000s where it looked like CRPGs might irrevocably change to something much lamer, or just not get made anymore. If I had to pick a game that ended that negative outlook, probably The Witcher, by my reckoning, and it has been a great deal better since. I guess it's a real resurgance of craft and storytelling in CRPGs :)
This game is the best one out of any that I've played since Planescape: Torment, though. Bar none. It has an engrossing story, a brilliantly realized and organic (but mystical!) setting, places that feel truly alien through sincere and earnest effort on the part of the developers. Interactions with NPCs carry the dramatic flair that a VERY good dungeonmaster can bring to a P&P tabletop game, and that feeling is only further enhanced by the clever system of scripted events in the game that have multiple stat or skill checks and require some thought to navigate without peril. They don't happen often enough for you to start predicting every time you'll have one, but they do happen often enough that they are a serious gameplay element and not a gimmicky afterthought. The user interface is a brilliant combination of accessibility and feature-richness, evoking the Infinity Engine interfaces in general but without their frustratingly restrictive control schemes.
I haven't played enough to assess how the game will be in retrospect, after the story has ended. But I am absolutely enthralled by my role in the story so far, and I am not looking forward to the end of it so much as having gone on this awesome gaming journey. You don't get stuff like this often. Buy it, if you're even a little interested you ARE the type of gamer it's for. This will rekindle any person's love for old CRPGs, and I bet it'll make a lot of new fans too!

A.R.E.S. is a shooter/platformer game starring a robot in his quest to protect humanity. Any similarities with other famous titles end there, as the flagship high attention to level design that is so present in most installments of Megaman games is completely ignored with this game.
I completed my first playthrough of A.R.E.S. on the "Hard" difficulty so I cant speak for the normal one. As said in my intro the biggest point of disappointment in the game was the level design. There is a total of 5 levels in the game, all but the last one very straightfoward in the sense that you just have to move to the right while killing enemies... But that's it. The enemies are seemingly placed at random in the levels (Which also have almost no variation. We could describe all the scenarios as "orange factory", "red factory", etc) neither enemy placement or overall level details and progression had any though put into it.
Another point that juts out when playing the game is it's controls. You move with the left control stick and shoot 360º with the other stick, using the "A" button on the xbox 360 gamepad to jump/double jump. You start right off the bat with the ability to double jump and because of that all platforming segments of the game have to be based around it. This is really bad because the jump itself is very awkward, and when most of the game depends on it that can be a very frustrating experience. You will more often than not simply do the "double jump" animation instead of doing the first one, which will make you fall to your death a lot.
Although failing a mission is simply considered a "slap on the wrist", because the game instantly lets you continue from the last checkpoint with no "Continues" system implemented.
Another detail that shows how uninspired the levels are is the fact that all of them have an obligatory "Enemy gauntlet" room, where you have to stay in a single screen fighting some waves of enemies until the game is satisfied.
The bosses, aside from the last one, are actually ok when compared to the rest of the game. Although they dont have many attack patterns and are mostly just giant damage sponges they are far from the worst problem the game had.
The game tries to give you various shallow mechanics, like having 2 types of granades that clear different obstacles and having you craft your items (Like grenades, health pickups and upgrades) from fallen enemy parts and even giving you the ability to call from air support to deal damage to all enemies in the screen, but due to the short lenght of the game (About 1,5h from start to finish) they are as previously mentioned shallow and are only there as failed experiments. The game also gives you multiple weapons but I was never complied to use them, prefering to stick to my default blaster that was already upgraded to the final level (3).
Overall A.R.E.S. was a very unpleasant experience, showing that it takes more than a couple of capable people to make a satisfying game. The game is short, uninspired and terribly bland and that's what makes it get an overall 3/10 from me.

Best game of its type since Baldur's Gate 2.  Which.... well I guess that's not saying much since there haven't been many but...
Great writing on par with Planescape Torment (though lacking the same depth, somewhat), good interface, interesting, intuitive yet simple combat system.
Little threadbare in some places.  Item diversity could have used some work, as could the crafting system.  And there were some great opportunities for player-specific interaction when backgrounds/homelands/races etc intertwined that were left unexplored.  Also no romance options, which was a bummer, since those were some of the best story sections of games like Baldur's Gate 2.  You could tell they wanted to do everything but ran out of time or money at some point.  Looking forward to expansions/sequels/new games of the same type now that Obsidian has decent proof that games like this can make a profit.
Just... if you liked BG2, buy this game.  Buy it to relive the nostalgia of playing a story-heavy well written game of this type.  Buy it to encourage game devs to keep making these.

With 10 hours and 100% completion of act 1 on record, i think its time to put in my review. First off, the art goes without saying in that is extremely attractive and well done. Although the characters themselves and much of the art did mimic the simplicity of the Homestuck style, the backgrounds were rich in detail and the animations smooth in movement, excluding from the nasty loading screens however, which hopefully will be fixed in a patch. Despite the clutter of some of the characters homes; such was well placed and built on each's personality very carefully, as well as many enjoyable references to the time period this game was set in. The plot was quite enjoyable for just being the beginning to the story, as the main character Joey interacts well with both other characters, and background characters, even ones we had presently been aware of were we fans of Homestuck itself, were handled well in explanation. It's especially important to notice that this game has very little relation to Homestuck at all, except for the apparent fact it is the same universe. A few people have been overlooking plot points as "probably references to Homestuck" but in fact I personally found very little references to the webcomic myself, and the ones that did exist explained themselves rather thoroughly, In fact, putting Homestuck aside entirely, people can still easily understand and enjoy this game.
There are of course, a few things on the downside to it. Theres a bird that dies, rather sad, some slightly strange interactions, and bugs in loading between cutscenes, as well as there being a deal of typos (specifically a name recall fail with several of your item uses) when interacting with your Deercat in the final cutscene. I was also a bit puzzled by the fact that e consistently mention the troll main character bleeding under the rocks (presumably to death?) up until the point where we move him out, and he is inexplicably scarcely injured. they did draw the Deercat bleeding, although i have some suspect drawing the troll not bleeding was to keep a rating, since his blood is red?
The game was a little short, I completed my first run in about 4-5 hours, including the annoying cutscene lag, but completed a speed run in under an hour, with similar lag issues. I hope that the second act will be greatly longer, with that release being without the cutscene lag, but regardless, I'll probably end up playing and enjoying it as well. I'm a simple person.

ARES is a Megaman clone where you try to save the world against some catastrophe with assistance from your special suit and an ally to give you guidance. I played with a gamepad, so movement is with 1 stick, and shooting is with the other. The story was not the most gripping, standard save the world type stuff. Your suit makes you immune to some chemical that is being released, which is why you are mostly going alone.
I found the enemy types to be pretty repetitive at the beginning. It seems in the first level I fought about 100 copies of the same 3 enemies. The boss design was a little lacking. The best strategy seemed to be to hide out in a corner or tank the fight. The controls were somewhat sloppy. It was difficult to get the tight movement necessary to dodge some attacks.
The graphics are bright and colorful, but I found the animation to be choppy. The environments didn't really do enough to draw me in to the game. Seemed like I was just fighting in giant labs of warehouses. The soundtrack does a little to pump you up, however. It may have been the high point.
I feel that there are enough entries in the Megaman/Metroidvania platformer genre that are more worthy of your time than ARES. Try it if you are a huge fan of these games and are running out of quality options, but I cannot recommend it to everyone.

Let's start with the obvious: Will you enjoy this game if you have never read Homestuck?
That's hard to tell. Being a Homestuck fan, I spotted lots of references that added to my enjoyment of the game. That being said, the game is focussed on new characters and their stories. Important characters to Homestuck only have a role in how they have affected Joey's and Jude's lives. Additionally, concepts that would be new to someone are viewed from the perspective of a character who has never encountered them. So when the description says you don't need to have read Homestuck to enjoy this game, it's technically true.
But will you?
In my opinion, there are plenty of players who will still enjoy this game.
Are you a fan of the old adventure games from the 80s and 90s?
Are you a fan of 80s and 90s nostalgia?
Do you like excellent game music?
Do you like enjoyable characters and good stories?
Do you like witty and interesting writing?
Do you like beautifully stylized art?
Then you will almost certainly enjoy Hiveswap.
However, there are still two more things to consider for this purchase.
First: difficulty. The game seems to intentionally avoid the frustrating pixel perfect, guide dammit moments of oldshcool adventure games. But perhaps it tries a bit too hard. There was only one puzzle I really felt I had to think about. The rest were just a matter of course in exploring the game. It definitely creates the feeling that this is more of an interactive narrative then a true adventure game.
Second: length. It took me around four hours to beat this chapter. That's a nice bite of game, but it definitely left me wanting more. This also brings the value proposition into play. Personally, I believe I got more than my money's worth. But some people may be hesitant unless they can catch it on a sale.
In the end, I believe Hiveswap is a wonderful story based game with excellent characters, writing, art and music. I think any number of players may enjoy this game, whether you've read or enjoyed Homestuck or not. Hardcore gamers may not find the meat they desire here, but anyone with a spare $8 would be well served to at least give the game a try.

Absolutely wonderful game. You have big boss/creatures battles, which you can tackle in multiple ways, you can climb them holding on for dear life and hacking away at them, you can stay at a distance throwing spells or shooting arrows, or you can just send in your pawns to do the work. The pawns are your 3 AI companions, one pawn is your own and you can customize it any way you choose, and it learns from how you play or tell it to play and tries to follow that. The other 2 pawns are ones other people have created as their main pawns, and you can summon them to your world. You can not customize them, but you can switch them out easily.
There are 9 different classes in the game and it is very easy to switch between them, even with the most basic skills they are good enough if you let your pawns pick up the slack. You're not locked in into your choice as with most other RPGs and in fact it is beneficial to explore the classes as you can pick up some skills which are class specific but carry over across all classes (augments). That's why you will be able to find just the play style that most suits you. Your main pawn can also switch classes in the same way, there is only a slightly smaller class selection for them.
The story is interesting enough, but it isn't really explored much. Mostly you're just picking up quests in the hub areas and going out into the open world to complete them. Which is fine, until you're returning to the same exact spot for the 8th time and you have to run all the way there every time. There is the possibility of fast travel, but it's limited to where you can fast travel, you can find Portcrystals and set them down somewhere in the world, then you can fast travel to there any time you choose. However you would need to know the game to know where the best spots for placing them are. Thankfully the monsters you encounter on the way have a varied style of fighting, it's just a shame that the monster variety doesn't improve until after you've "beaten" the game.
This is a great game, hampered by the feeling that it wants you to do the same thing over and over again, and that's really where you have to know if you can endure the grind or not. Although just going through the main game will not be too repetitive, anything past that and it's Grind City all the way.
8 / 10

Arbitrary crafting system and stiff inventory system is a quality combination. UI outside the average of combat, is stiffer than statue depicting rigor mortis. Different menus with little or no function, combined with horrible shopping, equipment and rubbish inventories no mater the age of the game these were and are crap.
In every "rpg" you usually get to haul rubbish around to use or sell. There's plethora of♥♥♥♥♥♥that drops from monsters, could but many MMO's in shame and all can be either combined to make usable♥♥♥♥♥♥ more♥♥♥♥♥♥or "upgrade" your♥♥♥♥♥♥  There's a combine option to smash two random pieces of crap together to make something... except there are so many items and only so few combinations that are most of all logical. I really wanted to love this game. In a way I still very like it, but in 2016, where there are games far better I simply cannot recommend it.
Who is this game for? Probably for people who enjoy monster slashing, especially bosses fights. Yes! That is what shines here, but it also does not at the same time. Every single time when you travell, you meet the same bunch of monsters in the same places. At first it is not annoying, but after a while, when you have to go the same route for yet another and another and another and another and another time... You simply know every single time you will be attacked, you will have to fight and already know how to do it. There is no surprise here. Monsters simply respawn after you leave the area! Your killings are insignificant.
On the other hand, when you fight them, especially during night time, when you cannot actually see them all, and they call reinforcements, it's just fun! You fight, kill, more come, more die and there seems to be no stopping to it and yet, after a while, when you return to area, they are there again. Waiting to be slaughtered by your might.
Ohhh yes for You are mighty after a while! They are not even a challenge, just sheeps ready fo slaughter. Boss fights on the other hand can be too challenging at the beggining but after a while you just grab, press the same buttons for a while and slaughter them like they had no meaning at all.
I love the design of areas, darkness in dungeons, they are trully perfect. When you dwell in ruins, catacoombs etc. you can trully enjoy your time. It is in a way similar to Dark Souls, sometimes you can't know where your feet take you. On the other hand journey to these places can waste you so much time, you simply don't want to explore it anymore...
But if above does NOT bother you, you may find a lot of fun in this game UNLESS! Yes, unfortunately there are two other major things which infuriate me. First is the terrible User Interface. Oh dear... DO you perhaps remember Gothic 1? Many people accused it of having the worst UI ever. Imagine that this game is even worse then this... It's purely work of evil! You have to navigate through countless pages eg. to exit the game you have to exit to menu, then click to enter the menu, wait few seconds for it to load, click exit the game, approve of exiting and finally! And its just when you want to quit it. Please don't make me describe how it works during gameplay...
Where UI was not a strong point of Gothic, story is where it shined. Story of Dragons Dogma shines... NOT! It's terrible, generic and soooo much disappointing. If you don't care for story, for making the same stupid quests in the same places for the same rewards, want to smash enemies and kill boss or two, then it's the game made specificly for you. But when you expect an RPG to be a ROLE playing game with deep story, many choices in open world, stay away from it, as story sounds fancy, but execution is sooo lack luster. Yeez!
Buy it on sale maybe, buy if you don't have anything else to play, but be prepared for a game, which could easily beat a lot of games, but was soo terribly executed.

I don't understand the positive reviews.
To me, the worst part of this game is what the developers did to your companions, the "Pawns". They have litterally no personality. It's right there in the game, it tells you this. So why bother with them at all? Why make them human-looking when they could have been awesome golems or robots and still carry the same weight story- and lorewise?
And you can't control them, at all. No scripts like in Dragon Age, no pause -> issue commands -> watch them happen or top down tactical menu for increased battlefield overview and control. Nope, nothing but three different generic commands that don't work.
Shame.
Other than that, I agree to what other people are saying about the "open world". Yes, you can explore places... but you will die. There is no visible level indicators on the enemies so, when I wandered off into the wilderness and encountered my first bandits or lizardmen I thought "Aha, my army of magic Pawn-people and I, the chosen one, can handle this!". I could not. I was one- or two-shot to death. Again, and again, and again. With no "quicksave-key" it gets tedious to save all the time you explore in case you suddenly encounter an enemey that is too strong but has nothing to give this away to the player.
There are so many more things in this game that are just poor design choices but I won't go in to them. Instead, if you want to see what people who play it a lot and got invested enough to actually care did, check the mod scene. If you disregard all the nude-mods, most mods involve "no carry limit", "no stamina drain when running" and changing the way leveling shapes your character.
Don't buy it. Instead try Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning, much better in every way, or The Last Remnant. The Last Remnant has a similar "not directly controlling your companions in battle" thing, but is better.

So let's get this out of the way first: This game is not a very good port. However,it's not the worst, either. The game is very much playable in my experience, though some Windows 8 users have reported issues. If you run that OS, I suggest you look into that in more detail before buying this game.
Now, on to the actual gameplay. If you've never heard of Dynasty Warriors before, allow me to give you a rundown: You are a General in ancient China. One of around 80 choices. You are given a sword, axe, spear, one-handed miningun with a bayonet attached, or some other totally-historically accurate weapon for ancient China. Your mission, should you choose to accept it, is to take to a historic battlefield of the Three Kingdoms Era and hack and slash your way to the enemy commander using a simple system of light and strong attacks.
Sound repetivive? That's what most people think. However, like I said, this game has over 80 characters to choose from, with their own unique moveset, as well as special attacks known as Rage attacks, Musou attacks and EX attacks. On top of that, there is 5 different storylines, each with two branches, to go through, as well as an ambition mode, a mode where you lead your own path to conquering China, as well as a Challenge mode and a "Free Mode", which allows you to replay Story mode levels with any character, (normally in story mode, you have to choose between a set number of characters who actually participated in the Historic battle) and has several side objects for every single one.
Since the game is simplistic at it's core, it's a relaxing journey through one of the most interesting Historical periods I know of.  It's got content to last for months, even years. There's a pretty good reason why Dynasty Warriors has gone up to 8 games in the main series. I highly reccomend any who have not yet tried this game to give it a shot and see for themselves.
