In the genre of Zombies/Zombie survival, there are a lot of duds. Games that don't really live up to the genre's hype. Infestation: Survivor Stories, Dead Island, several others. This indie title does what no game has really done, made a great game out of the genre. Made an amazing game out of the genre, in my opinion.
In this game, you start out as some random guy in the beginnings of a zombie apocolypse. You find a group of people, then it turns into more of a survival management game. You have to deal with problems in your group, such as anger issues and fear, you have to befriend and keep the morale of your fellow comrades up. And, of course fight zombies. Now while the combat in this game isn't amazing, its actually really fun. Its simplistic, it doesn't try to over complicate things. You wanna smash a zombies head in, right? Of course you do, and you can do that easily. With a gun or with a blunt weapon. I enjoy the combat, but it is still in my opinion the weak point of the game.
Managing your community, building new training facilities, sleeping areas and medical stations, and recruiting other survivors are a large part of the fun in this game. Its so satisfying to run through a zombie hoard and save a group of people, then have them befriend you so you can switch to them.
I really enjoy that you can't just use the same character forever. They will get injured, sick, and tired. Eventually you'll need to switch to other characters. That's why it is important to do things like anger management missions and afraid missions, to befriend people in your group so you may switch to them.
The visuals are fairly impressive, but nothing amazing. It runs perfectly fine on my GTX 660 with everything turned up. it definitely looks better than the xbox version, but it will not visually wow you in any way. Although the zombie design is quite impressive.
My one bugbear with this game is the ammount of stuff it throws at you at once, then puts it on a time limit. I can understand why you need to do things quickly, but when i still need to gather food and medicine for my group, and then I recieve 5 other messages about missions I need to complete quickly, it can get frustraiting. Really frustrating, especially when it makes me lose influence with my tribe. I think they should either cut back on the ammount of missions you get at once, or eliminate the timer. The former sounds better in my opinion.
Reguardless, this game is amazing. And even when it isn't discounted, its only 20 bucks. So incredibly cheep for a game this fun. This game has raised the bar in the Zombie genre.
Despite of the downsides as you can read in the majority of reviews, it a must for a zombie fan. Worth every penny for its price. Dont you want to play "walking dead" as it should be?

8/10 - A highly entertaining killing frenzy amongst funny looking creatures with silly names.
This game takes some of the highest-grossing elements of action-rpgs that came up in the past years and combines it with the successfull franchise of LotR. A good idea, that was realised almost perfectly.
ME:SoM has much to offer for ARPG and Tolkien-Fans. Also, if you liked climbing on things and stealth-killing enemies in Assassins Creed or beating the living hell out of thugs in the Batman Series, this Game is likely perfect for you. Besides the familiar and well balanced gameplay, this game has to offer a pretty good storyline with a nice character development. The only downsites here are the endless upcome of sidemissions, that distracted me too much from the story, the lack of different races and characters of the LotR universe and a pretty lame bossfight at the end. The atmosphere is quite nice, but the two large sections the game offers are fastly explored and get boring after a while. Nevertheless the nice soundscape and the enemies and creatures roaming the lands of ME:SoM result in an immersive atmosphere. The graphics are very good: a low amount of loadingscreens but a stable framerate at high settings on a average system. The mainstory is quite short, but there is plenty to do in the world of ME:SoM. The DLCs offer some more information about characters of the story, some more gameplay features (sadly even more quicktimevents) and a more challenging alternative gamemode.

I have played at least a couple thousand videogames over the years, and this is one that has stuck itself in my head as one of my favorites. Climbing enemies, remembering their weaknesses, levelling all the vocations to gain access to their passives for all the others. Not just that, but as far as ports go, this is a fantastic one. I've had no issues with the keyboard adaptation, with performance, or even with managing pawns again.
This is the sort of game that makes you remember your finest moments, like holding onto a griffon as it climbs into the air, attacking it until it loses control, and holding on for dear life as it spirals into the ground. Or grappling a deer and then throwing it at your pawn, who learns from your playstyle and then proceeds to toss the deer back to you, creating a game of catch that'll last until you're giggling too hard to catch the deer before it gets to its hooves and runs off. Changed class to a Paladin and I couldn't swing my weapon overhead.... Broken class. Game got boring real quick.

Combat 8/10
Its definitely fun, and although there are not a wealth of skills that can be used (most classes can use 6) the skills themselves change gameplay to the point where you can create a different playstyle for each vocation (profession, there are 9 total). The hack n slash will keep you going, but ultimately most of the lower level monsters are too dumb to be a challenge. The late game monsters get easier the more you learn their weaknesses, and fighting them is extremely fun. Not all vocations can block or dodge (the fighter can block, strider can dodge, mage cant do either). Its worth to note that some vocations have skills with invulnerability frames built into them, allowing you to dodge huge monster attacks.
Visuals 7/10
The graphics themselves as well as the ambiance/environment are pretty good. There is a day and night cycle which is pretty well done. Not sure how long each lasts (an hour?) but night can get really dark. Hope you bring enough oil for your lantern, or else you're kinda screwed!
Equipment/inventory/crafting 7/10
The equipment is well done. I enjoy starting off with nothing but rags and slowly making my character more badass, and there are some badass weapons in this game. The one thing that makes no sense to me is the clothing system which adds to your armor total. For inventory, there is a bit of realism. Instead of being able to carry thousands of pounds, your speed is effected by weight. It adds a bit of micro management. Crafting is basic, you gotta go out and kill stuff to collect their remains, and voila. You can upgrade items up to three times normally, plus 3 additional dragonforged levels.
Map/quests/voiceovers/pawn system 9/10
I have explored the entire map, in terms of size it doesnt compare to Skyrim but hey few games do. Quests are alright. There are kill count, collect, find rare item, escort, plus some other type quests. The voiceovers are awesome, they can get a bit annoying, but I'm constantly surprised at how helpful some of the pawns can be. I swear, some of the female voices sound eerily familiar (main chick from farscape and kusanagi from ghost in the shell). Oh yeah, pawns! They are your party members. You can create one of your own and hire up to two created by other human players! Its pretty sweet, just visit a rift crystal and start searching. They will do everything from offer advice, collect stuff (sometimes they take their sweet time), and of course jump on huge monsters and start stabbing them! Dont worry, if you get too far away from them they'll port to you, and its impossible to steal from other players pawns. The pawn system is something that could have gone horribly wrong but instead went terribly right.
Anywho, this game is well worth the time and money put into it. There are some glaring "wtf is this" mechanics and moments, but mostly its smooth sailing. As with most games, I wish it lasted for longer, but hey the developers did a great job so credit to them. I look forward to their next rpg. I would definitely buy it.

Game is extremely meh. It's repetitive, grindy, and feels incomplete/unfinished especially with its joke of an ending. Base building is super shallow and relationships between survivors are nonexistent. AI is atrocious for survivors and zombies. If you're in a siege mission, then all your AI companions do is stand still and board up windows while the only thing that zombies do is attack the boarded windows. Big ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s don't enter the house, they just ram into it which damages the boards. You literally have to exit the house and kill the zombies outside to progress things.
Your survivors constantly go missing/get stuck/need to be rescued, hordes constantly spawn, infestations constantly spawn, special zombies constantly spawn, etc. The game simulates itself when you're not playing it so if you don't want to come back to a game where all your neighbors are dead, all your supplies are drained, and your group is missing, then enjoy babysitting constantly to quit the game on a good note. You can also just keep the game indefinitely paused to prevent this.
There are few home sites, and only 2 of them are any good.
Scavenging is pointless if you play for long periods of time. Despite having a day/night cycle, days only pass during simulation. Supplies only drain when you're not playing the game and you can easily overstock on everything in about 30-45 minutes.
The game is also incredibly easy. After clocking in about 30 hours, I only died once and that's because I was trying to make my experience as hard as possible.
Mechanics are easily abusable. Stuck alone with no health and a feral chasing you? Switch to a character in your home base and then switch back to your character. He/she will teleport immediately back to base.
Game is very short too. You can easily beat it in 8-10 hours.
I guess the best thing I can say is the port is very faithful to the 360 original. They even ported over all the bugs and glitches!

I'm shocked to see all the negative, and "whinning" reviews here. I give a lot of credit where its due for animation and wonderful art. Not sure where people come off saying the animation wasn't great, to me it felt just like reading the comic but at a faster pace, amazing music to go with it. This was a beautiful game, with great characters, thrilling plot and I honestly can't wait for more. There was a lot of excitement to be dealt with since the beggining.. The writing was funny, relateable, and kept me wanting to know more of how everything was going to play out.
Now I saw one revew saying there wasnt much character backgrounds or deveopment, and mabye that might have been because it was only the first freaking act (so we cant say for sure there wont be more character deveopment) but I beg to differ. You dont necessarily need to click every gosh darn thing in the game, but doing so gives you a lot of insight how each character thinks and their backgrounds and past. Which is exactly how the webcomic was, so I really like that it gave us the freedom to do that on our own whether we wanted to know more or not.
If I had to critize this game, it would be the battle scenes. Honestly it took me a while to figure out what to do before actually solving the puzzle. I guess they wanted to keep the homestuck feel to it, which it clearly did with the looped annimations and funny comments with each of your actions but it could've helped to explain how to properly initialize each action.
Anyway, this is only act one and I already love the first characters introduced to the story and I sure as hell enjoyed the funny chatroom conversations. I think that was an improvement instead of going throuh a whole list of text. I like you can click for the next text and even add a few of your own choices to see thier reactions to eachother. This was great, I could give it a 8/10 rating overall, only lacking two points because the battle gamplay and the overall short game time.

This review is more of an emotional sight on the game, than rather pointing out the aspects of the game and it's mechanics etc.
I think the first thing I want to mention about Eden* is that this is a once in a life time experience.
I have spent a lot of my time reading stories/books or whatever came under my eyes, but Eden* stood out from everything I have ever experienced.
I have to say that I'm still new to the Visual Novel genre and after I played two Sakura Games, I kinda thought that all the Visual Novels point out in a more "feminine sexy direction".
Even though that can be entertaining to a certain point, I was really glad to find out that this is not what all Visual Novels are about.
Since Eden* could be called a sci-fi genre I was kinda sceptical at first, since I enjoy the medival age over any futuristic genre, but I'm really glad I gave it a go, because I would have missed a masterpiece of art, graphics, voice acting, story, music and an emotional expirience.
I'm still lacking words to actually point out how good it is, since it's way to spectacular to really put everything in a review or even on a thought itself.
I do wanna point out the music for itself as well. I still cannot really tell if the music is incredible sad or unbelievable beautiful. But it comforts the story and the dialogue so well that it's always on point.
Even if you take out the music itself I could listen to Eden's* tunes everyday without playing the game just because it's so amazing, heart touching and it feels like opening up a gate into your very own imagination.
Even though I finished the story it feels like it never ended. I have played the second half of this game in one go because there was no way for me to stop in the middle of this beautiful story but afterwards I was kinda sad.
Sad that I've read it in one go. Sad that it actually ended. But on the other hand this is a story so perfect that even if the story is over, even if the world would end, it still continues.
And still I have the feeling that I want to experience this even further, even after the game has ended.
This story would not change if you read it a second time, but it wouldnt lose its power either. It is rare for me, that a story brings me down to tears, but that term would be way to less to describe the state this game left me in. I have never cried over a story for more than 3 hours STRAIGHT. Just because it was so beautiful and heart breaking in the same time. And I do know for myself that I will play this game over and over again, countless times and the fact that I cry would not change. I think it would be a shame not to cry at this brilliant story. It deserves to shed some tears.
If you have the time, the patience/concentration and the interest to experience a story beyond any expectations please give Eden* a chance.
I do wanna point out in the end that all the small details that may be just everyday things become a part of the big beautiful scenery, so it is worth to give everything a second look and thought.
With this I feel like I should come to an end even if I still got countless words that I want to say about this story, but after all, this story speaks louder than any voice/text or review could.
Thank you for taking the time to read my opinion about Eden* !
And for everyone out there, if you look for a story so perfect end emotional that it will for sure stay in your mind over a very long time get Eden* and have yourself that incredible experience.

Splinter Cell Blacklist is my favorite stealth game of the year, perhaps even contender for GOTY. I loved Splinter Cell every second I played it! A solid entry in the SC, but still not it's best. As someone who enjoyed the improved tactical options and fluidity of movement in 'Conviction', I can say this takes that even further. Options to complete missions completely undetected, or by taking out enemies quick and quietly are a blast. I understand why the 'assault' option of guns blazing is there, but it's really not that much fun for me. It doesn't feel like how an operative like Sam Fisher is meant to operate. My biggest complaint is that while this is the best splinter cell gamer mechanically, and is plenty of fun, it doesn't feel much like a 'sam fisher splinter cell game'. The character is not there. It's not too shallow to say, but  a new actor created dissonace I could never fully ignore. A new character, under the tutelage of Sam Fisher would have been more interesting, and understandable, especially considering how much younger Eric Johnson--Sam's actor--is. Lastly, the dissonace is a matter of the game's general tone, as well.  You can be stealthy, but it's to a backdrop that's still  too actiony, too Jack Bauer, and too bright.

I'll say after finishing Eden* that it was quite a ride.
Very much a novel, just with some voice acting and very nice visuals going along with it. No real choices to make during the game, so won't get that kind of gameplay out of it.
But I can say it was very much worth getting. For a summary that talks about the planet's final love story, it certainly delivers on that front. You know how it is going to end, but it takes nothing away from the power of the story. It's one of those times when you know how things will turn out and it's all the more impactful because of it. Finding out how things ended up like this and the journey the main characters went through.
In terms of story and characters Eden* just delievers. I also appreciated the strong art and visuals. It is just japanese voices and english subtitles, but the voice acting is top notch. A nice touch as well that you do get to see lips moving as the characters talk so it really does feel like you are watching this story from up close. I don't think the story would have been as good if the MC wasn't as complete a character as the rest of the cast and you had dialogue options popping up. Everything just worked for the sake of the story.
Took me about 12 hours to get through it. Might take others a bit less time, but if you are letting all the characters speak their voiced lines then it will take a good while. Definitely worth what I paid for such a strong story. And got to me enough that I wanted to write up something about it.
It is a story that will leave a bittersweet feeling behind, but if that doesn't bother people then I wholly recommend it.

This game is a polished one. It has been written with the finest ink, composed with passion and made with perfection. It has awesome story, captivating moments, originality and of course, terrific voice acting. Some say it's annoying, but I see the grief, sorrow and misery beneath each line. Everyone is desperate, yet cheerful, in a black sense of humour. There are eleven classes, in which you can find anything that suits you. A classical Barbarian of good health? A Cipher who can read your minds? The classical Fighter? The noble or not so noble Paladin? The far-reaching Ranger with his/her pet? The intelligent, acute-minded Wizard? The Chanter who sings in battles? The Druid who is one with nature itself? The sure-handed Monk? The sinister or benevolent Priest? The cunning and agile Rogue? All of them are found here. I have not played so much, I admit, but I have tried many of the classes, and the game is well-balanced. And I'm hungarian, so it is worth mentioning the Budapest Art Orchestra, who composed the mesmerising tunes for this game. Rest assured that it will take hours of your lifetime wandering. There are some bugs, I know, but these guys are working hard to stomp on all of them. You will get an absolutely amazing game for your money, it is worth every single cent that you will spend on.

So now that I've just beaten this game and every single boss in it including the DLC bosses, think its about time i wrote a review on this game.
Though I did have experience with other Fromsoft games (Bloodborne and DS3) this game was still actually fairly challenging, but overall it didn't feel like it would've been as hard if it were my first Soulsborne game as everyone claimed it was. I remember around when this game was new that plenty of people claimed this game was way too hard to actually beat and I never found myself in a position of giving up. If you're jumping into this game without any previous Souls games experience its gonna take some getting the hang of things to actually survive.
Now with that out of the way and going on to an actual review, there weren't actually that many issues i had with this game and I dont have a lot of negative things to say about it. In fact I personally think statistics-wise, this game does it all the best. Switching armor and gear for resistances, poise, and using different weapons to beat different bosses was actually a really cool kind of strategy for me. I feel like different shields in this game actually had some kind of use to them compared to the other Souls games, at least compared to DS3 which I didnt really find a good use for a shield. And again, switching shields to resist different attacks gave me some more thinking and strategy as well. The world design for this game is extremely pretty especially for how old the game is. I'm always completely immersed in games like this and I enjoyed the exploration of almost every zone... except the Demon Ruins cause there wasn't really much to see. I liked how the dodging in this game is more realistic I guess, you actually have to dodge away instead of being able to dodge and gaining invincibility frames. The way everything works in this game feels so much better to me, slower but still much more i guess polished because the statistics felt like they actually mattered. I'm not 100% sure if I prefer this one compared to everything else but it's very close to the best if anything.
The only negative things I can think of about this game are how easy it is to get trapped into a corner by a ton of regular monsters and die because you either can't hit them all fast enough before getting staggered, or not being able to roll through them. I also don't really like how humanity works in this game because I would always find myself out of humanity if i died and then something stupid happens like getting trapped in a corner and dying once again before I'm able to recollect all my souls and humanity. Honestly that's more of just me being bad but I like the idea of being able to dodge out of corners you were being trapped in which I think they used in DS3. The game is also a little glitchy in certain places cause I kept falling through the floor. Wasn't entirely game breaking though
Overall I think this game is spectacular. I liked the majority of the boss fights and adventuring throughout every zone in the game. I found very little problems with the game at least in my opinion and is completely worth the buy next time you see it on a sale. Especially if you want a game that you could easily put a lot of time in. 9/10

The game has large amounts of strategy involved, and at the moment there are so few guides written on it that it is basically anyone's game. If you absolutely require a Starcraft, CnC or Supreme-Commander style RTS then go pay money for those. This is unique, brilliant, endless, and very fun to get into.
This game has one of the best real-cash economy systems i've ever seen. Completing battle and daily missions will reward you with gold, which can be used to by units early if you absolutely must have some. There is the option to unlock those units for no cost other than your time, and there is also the option to pay IRL cash to get them. Regardless of your choice, the units balance out to an extreme degree and i never find myself without a response (unless i forgot to read the unit's tips page and have no clue how to counter it. In that case GG, but if you made it this far into the review you probably dont mind reading two sentences).
In conclusion, this evolving game is among the best out there right now and I would call it a must-play for anyone into unique or genre-changing mechanics.

Before I start I would like to say that I bought Starbound Early Access on Day 1. The game was quite bland so I prompted to wait for 1.0. Now that it's out I can say that it almost never changed. Of course there's more content, but nothing was truly interesting in Starbound. I forced myself to enjoy it just so that 15 bucks I spent years ago would not go to waste.
I will not touch about the story and progression of the game, because many other reviewers have talked about that.
Starbound is a shallow unoptimized game. Don't ever buy the game if you don't have a powerful PC because once you get a big ship with decorations, full crew and containers it will destroy your frame rate. This also applies for when you build a fairly big base with at least 10 colonists. The frame rate is not the only problem but also the existence of a "lag" akin to delays one can see in a multiplayer mode.
I would also like to say that the minimum requirements listed on the Steam page is absolutely not accurate. The recommended CPU is at least an i3 and for GPUs, a "Discrete GPU capable of directx 9.0c ". I have tested the game on two computers with both i5 3GHz and GPUs of AMD Radeon HD 7k and NVIDIA GeForce 920m. Early in the game the framerate and the "multiplayer lag" is not very noticeable but once I started upgrading the ship and building a nice base with a bunch of colonists that's where I saw the huge performance issue. Once it starts this issue continues on to even areas with not much things to render, as if the game was trying to process other stuff that was not on the area my character was currently on.
Moving on from performance issues, many features in Starbound are not very interesting. The Starbound universe is big, and so is its repetitiveness. So many planets, but most of them look or feel the same. There are so many NPCs in the universe, but they always just give random dialogue depending on the "personality" given to them. The quests are almost always the same, fetch something, kill people, give me stuff, deliver this to someone, rescue a friend. Sounds good? No it doesn't, the quests don't encourage exploration especially since a lot of the quests can be done on the surface of a planet. There is absolutely no incentive for exploring underground other than finding ore, and it is possible to find the rare ores even in the shallow parts of a planet.
The game advertises itself as open world but it does not feel that way at all. The universe does not move when the player does not move, as if there wasn't any life to it.
Nothing actually struck me about Starbound other than the amount of content the game has.
So is the game worth spending 15 USD on? Perhaps people with really nice rigs might be able to appreciate this game better, but for me I regret supporting Chucklefish.
If you have any reactions to my review, please do so in a civil way. I will delete comments at my discretion.

I like this game a lot, mainly due to the fact that modding is encouraged.
The combat is better than it's biggest competitor (Terraria), and the weapons feel a lot more interesting and fun to use.
The armor is nice, everything can be dyed as well or un-dyed.
The ships are your substitute for a home, you can pretty much do everything on them, and you would be unwise not to put all of your crafting tables and supplies on your ship.
This can sort of make building your own home on a planet a pointless endevor for those who are not simply completionists looking to get all of quests completed which require a settlement.
For those who do love building their own bases and houses it can feel slightly pointless in this game, as there are many randomly generated castles, bunkers, temples, cities, settlements, science facilities, ect ect.
Which is one of my favorite aspects, exploring these places.
But if seeing predone buildings already sculpted doesn't deter you from making your own, then you will find that this game has a near endless supply of objects, bricks, and themes.
The story is a bit played out, nothing you've never heard before 100 times in a fantasy game.
And sadly the missions, while fun and interesting the first time, are very short and there are not many of them.
You can probably complete this game in a few hours if you just sit down and do it.
It suffers from that problem most people say no man's sky has.
It's a vast ocean, but it's only 2 feet deep.
That is how this game can feel after playing it for more than a few hours.
At some point the planets will all start to look alike, the enemies will all start to seem the same, and the quests literally are all the same.
I still recommend this game however, because it can give you quite a few hours of play time.
But if you're looking for a game where you actually have a good reason for exploring the trillions of planets in it, this isn't it.
you'll explore maybe 10 planets as you work to getting the best armor and equipment you can.
Then you will find yourself just skimming the surface of high threat planets in a minute or two looking for something in a chest you might like.
But everything will pass you by pretty quickly.
But the game is still worth the price tag.
For the combat, the items, the races, the missions(though short lived) the modding, and the hope that they will add more content.

The story is based off the Romance of the Three Kingdoms historical novel, but since it is a video game they have fantasy elements and change some things to make it more exciting.
The Story Mode has a bunch of cinematics before and after battles that help tell the story and they are alright for this type of game.
The graphics seem to be based on the PS3 version of the game, but they still look better than the PS3 version due to higher framerate, resolution, and I think they added a few things in the graphic options that make them look a bit better.
Overall the graphics are average for a console port of a game, but the gameplay is the best part of the Dynasty Warriors series.
Those who know the Dynasty Warriors series will be familar with the hack and slash gameplay. You can control a hero from a roster of 82 characters, each with their own individual design.
The game is mostly about using weapon attack combos to defeat hundreds of enemies and other officers through battles in the game. There is a lot of flashy effects for the weapon attacks and special musou attacks which make the game more exciting.
You can obtain new weapons to equip your warriors with and each warrior can use two weapons and switch between them in battle. You also can level up each warrior to level 150.
There are story missions for the three major kingdoms (Wei, Wu, Shu), and the Jin and Lubu forces. As well as a Free Mode to replay story and other battles, a Challenge mode that has arcade type battles, and Ambition mode where you can upgrade a camp and conquer territories.
I purchased the game because I am a fan of the Dynasty Warriors series and I don't own a PS3 or PS4, so I can't get Xtreme Legends unless I pay $50 for this on Steam or go out and buy a PS3 or PS4 and pay $60 for the PS4 version or $70+ for the PS3 bundle.
The graphics seem fine to me, they aren't amazing, but they aren't bad either. I played the Xbox 360 version of DW8 and they seem to be a bit better, but the graphics aren't as important as gameplay with the series.
Online multiplayer would've been a good bonus feature, but I don't think its a mandatory feature for the series. I have never played online in the past titles, I usually play solo or split screen. If you need to have online multiplayer then pick up the PS4 version instead.
The game has been running great and I haven't had any technical issues yet.
Only complaints:
- DLC is now avaiable, but the price is a bit high (though the DLC is optional and not needed to enjoy the game)
- Would be nice to see controller buttons instead of keyboard buttons when using a controller.
- Depending on controller may need to remap your controls.
Overall it is a good game if you are Dynasty Warriors fan or someone who likes hack and slash games. It is cheaper to buy the PC version (North America - USD) than the console version as well which is a plus. Should be glad they brought Dynasty Warriors 8 game to Steam!
There seems to be some people having issues with the game crashing, freezing, not starting up, etc. I haven't encountered any of these issues yet, game has been running perfect on my machine. The explosion of survival games in recent years has been fascinating to watch, because everyone has a different idea about what makes them appealing. There are some like Subnautica that go light on the survival elements to emphasize exploration and building in a vibrant world. Then there are others like The Long Dark that push you to learn and master the mechanics to survive in brutal conditions. Savage Lands appears to go in a third way, opposite the ones I just mentioned, and I'm not really sure that's the best direction to strike out in.
Savage Lands casts you as an outcast, sent to the frozen reaches of not-Skyrim presumably to die. You can customize your waxy, lumpy character with mohawks and tribal tattoos before embarking upon your exile, but harbor no illusions of making Goku or Kanye West with the handful of options present. Once you arrive in the arctic wasteland you're given a laundry list of survival tasks that act as a tutorial, directing you to chop wood, gather stones, and hunt animals. It doesn't actually tell you HOW to do these things or WHERE to find them, but I was able to puzzle them all out in fifteen minutes or so.
From there you're on your own. The landscape is helpfully dotted with ruins of shacks, cabins, and villages which you can repair with the right resources. This makes a good first goal once you find your footing, working your way up the extensive structure tree from workbenches to smelters in order to patch up your new home. In the meantime you'll have to attend to your survival, represented by two bisected gauges. The top one is health/temperature, restored with bandages and fire, and the bottom is stamina/hunger, restored by eating and not running around all willy-nilly. It's arranged in this way so that hunger and temperature can eat into your other resources if left unchecked, which becomes a major consideration in blizzards or on long treks.
As you scavenge across the land you'll find notes scattered about that give bits of lore or hints at how features like armor work. You'll also find quite a few points of interest like ruined forts and towers that usually contain some loose tools to appropriate. The other thing you'll find are monsters, and in no short supply. Your starting area is mostly populated with rabbits, deer, and the occasional brittle skeleton that needs to be smashed. Travel more than a hundred meters in any direction, though, and you'll have wolves tearing your throat out. Preparation is a must for longer journeys, as just one tough foe getting the drop on you can spell disaster. They won't give up once they spot you, either, a fact I was distressed to learn after leading a wolf back to my camp.
There's plenty more to be distressed about, too. Creatures in the world have some of the worst collision and hit detection I've ever seen, vibrating through rocks and walls and hitting you from a yard away. If you're not beating on monsters you'll probably be beating on mineral deposits, because mining is key to progression and takes a ridiculously long time to dig out anything more valuable than coal. Other resources like clay are bound to be a complete mystery unless you try literally everything or consult a wiki. And in a perfect example of how little quality-of-life there is here, a basic container to place in the world takes fairly advanced materials to make, meaning all your junk is going to be sitting in a pile in the snow for a few hours until you can finally craft a ♥♥♥♥ing wooden chest.
I would be more willing to stick out the rough gameplay if the game had some other appeal, but it really, really does not. You may have noticed that the screenshots on the store page have a lot of similar daytime scenes. That's because this is probably the grayest game I've ever played, and that's counting stuff like LIMBO. The world is almost completely devoid of color; the snowfields are gray, the foliage is brownish-gray, the stonework is blueish-gray, even the monsters are all grays and browns. There's not much detail to the models either, and the animations tend to be slower and stiffer than you'd expect.
There's certainly potential in Savage Lands, but it won't be realized without some major overhauls that probably aren't within the scope of the project. The visuals are a dreary mess and the progression is needlessly tedious and complicated. And even if you come to grips with that, you're likely to be eaten by a wolf or a dragon and spat out to the main menu. I get the appeal of open-world survival Skyrim but this is missing so many simple balance and accessibility elements that I don't know how you get there from here. If this game ever shapes up I'll revisit the frozen hells therein, but until then I have little interest in sticking it out.

Browsed through the crafting menu, gathered supplies for Bow and Arrows, shot some boar and deer...cooked the meat this time and survived Night 2. Figured out how to mine flint and metals, finally. Built a workbench to craft bags to expand inventory, I now have 6.
Random attacks by skeletons and one brave boar, but I stay within short range of my now repaired buildings. The dragon has not bothered the small area that I have stayed in. Starvation is the most diffiult part of starting out, imo. I have almost 3 hours put into it and two deaths.
This game does have a learning curve and is a bit clunky (which is to be expected in Beta), but isn't too hard if you are patient which is required in a survival game where you're not the top of the food chain. The graphics are not the best, but that will more than likely improve in the future.
Use common sense, or you die.

Salutations gamers; renowned reviewer T Swag here coming at ya with a brand new review for my new favorite game, Overwatch, So without further ado lets jump right into it. Let it be known I have been a long time loyal fan of the previous Elder Scrolls games so needless to say I was very excited to play the latest installment. I began by starting up a grand campaign eager to jump right into the action and cycled through the fourteen base factions in the game. After thorough review the Saxons were the disgusting Germanic tribe of choice for me. Once ingame I realized immediately that the game had improved its map design and I was impressed with the family features having been overhauled to have more meaning. I immediately went and attacked the Franks and much to my chagrin I was paddled by them due to a poor military decision. Combat is good, even better with mods. Units are more responsive to your commands and the AI seems to actually have a will to win rather then unfasten their tunics and bend over like previous Battlefield installments. After my great defeat I began to notice the vast amount of factions on the map and most of which were unavailable to me in the faction selection, my serotonin began to dip.  I once again navigated to the store page to feast my eyes not on the one, two, but EIGHT DLCs available for purchase which all add up to a whopping $81.22(CAD)! More than the base game! The Blood and Burning DLC especially caught my eye, pay for blood and gore effects?! I began falling ill and felt pains in various areas of my body. I decided to head to my local hospital for evaluation and I was greeted with some devastating news... I now have cancer. My doctor asked me about my lifestyle choices. "Have you ever smoked?" "No never" "How has your diet been" "I always eat my raw venison and take my 42 suppliments!" "Have you ever been witness to abhorrent marketing practices?" I then realized it was in fact, the developer/publishers DLC structure that gave me cancer.   In conclusion, Watch Dogs 2 improves upon its strengths, and corrects quite a few weaknesses, however it seems there is a breach in the hull, that breach being the deplorable DLC structure. Whether it was Creative Assembly's idea or SEGA's who knows but it ain't right my friends.
Regards,
T Swag

I adore this game! The writing is hilarious - full of clever wordplay and pigeon antics and witty dialogue, but it also delves into some affecting subject matter (absent parents, classism, toxic friendships) with sincerity and sensitivity. The characters are really lovable, especially the main playable character Joey and a certain sport-loving butler boy. The soundtrack is terrific, with loads of catchy beats and haunting melodies - if you loved Undertale's music you'll be well at home here since Toby Fox co-composed! The backgrounds are absolutely gorgeously drawn, and they complement the writing by giving you a strong sense of the characters’ lives and interests. The character designs and animations are just as wonderful – Joey’s nervous fidgeting, peppy tapdancing, and acrobatic pirouetting are endlessly cute ‘n charming. The animations have a snappy, bold, keyframe-heavy style – maybe some extra in-between drawings could have been added here and there, but given how enormously time-consuming hand-drawn animation is I understand why they used their frames economically. It already looks gorgeous and communicates the characters’ personalities perfectly anyway!
Don’t feel discouraged if you’ve never read Homestuck - you don’t need any knowledge of the comic to enjoy Hiveswap since the story is so far self-contained and set years before Homestuck’s events. Long-time fans will find tons of subtle Homestuck references hidden throughout the game, some just for fun, others filling in characters’ pasts and adding an extra layer of intrigue.
My only complaint is that there’re a few minor bugs and typos at the time of writing, but these will all likely be patched by WhatPumpkin soon. The most bothersome one is a resolution/camera-panning hiccup that can appear the first time you launch the game, but it’s easy to fix since the bug seems to disappear for good if you relaunch the game after changing your resolution settings.
Overall I give Hiveswap five out of five transuniversal tapdance teens… I can’t wait for Act 2!

This game manages to be simultaneously fantastically nostalgic for anyone who's read Homestuck, and completely approachable and fun for anyone who hasn't. 100% worth giving $50 of my 8th grade Christmas money to kickstart this back in 2012.

Loved it! Very immersive game!
Length:
Took me about 30 hours to finish the main story
(while doing many side missions), without rushing it.
Gameplay:
The combat feels great, it's fluid, responsive,
and it rewards a lot you for NOT button smashing.
As the game progresses, new abilities are unlocked, and that works against repetitiveness.
I must say... OMG, the animators did an EXCELLENT job!
During regular combat, I never thought "oh, it's this killing animation again".
And it was 30 hours!
A few fights with beasts had repeating animations though.
And some stealth kills sometimes repositioned the target noticeably to begin the animation.
The parkouring elements gave a feeling of freedom. The world is large and carefully designed.
Graphics:
Beautiful, detailed, realistic. The only negative thing was some flickering shadows during cinematics.
Almost solid 60 FPS using custom medium-high settings on a GTX960.
Story:
The main story started quite captivating and promising, but that faded slowly.
I was neither satisfied nor disappointed at the ending.
The main missions were usually multiple parallel stories.
It felt good that you had multiple options for a "main" mission.
Mixed with Uruk politics and their related missions and side challenges, it didn't feel dull.
Audio:
Nice music that fitted the atmosphere at any given moment.
Satisfying slashing sounds!
Well done voice acting! I frankly thought to myself "these are actually real people speaking!".
Final notes:
It seemed to me that the developers wanted to avoid any annoying elements.
It was the minor details. They WANTED ME to enjoy this as much as possible! Thanks!

An open world that enables hack and slash, time-slowing archery, stealth and dagger assassination, riding mounts, and controlling orcs and beasts. You are free to go about killing and doing the story missions to your own liking, whether through stealth approach, head on, or strategic planning through mind controlling the enemy.
The story was ok, but the ending was a bit disappointing. I recommend this game if you enjoyed what's stated above. In terms of achievements, you can 100% the story in approx. 26 hours. Achievements, on the other hand, are harder as there are two DLC achievements that require you to complete a list of challenges in under a constricting time limit. Beware that some achievements can be obtained through the story or as you progress, but can be skipped over because of a small error. Due to the error, you may have to restart certain parts again.

All of this is based on my opinion.
GRAPHICS: 9.5/10 :
This game is beautiful and the draw distance even on my computer setup is pretty impressive, there are a few in game *using game engine* cutscenes for the main story and a few pre rendered cutscenes. I rarely came across clipping or clipping issues, particles looks great. Not perfect but damn good.
SOUND: 10/10 :
The soundtrack , the sound effects, the echoing, the voice acting, and many other effects are used with great care in this game and give it a pretty awesome feel and pace to the game. Very much what you would expect from a LOTR games.
GAMEPLAY: 9/10 :
Fantastic climbing, responsive controls, just enough enemy variety to keep it interesting, with the opportunity to really just go into a group of Orcs and just start destroying them one by one. You get melee sword action, stealth gameplay, and ranged combat. This all makes for a fantastic experience that only near the end got a little stale for me. I am not the biggest fan of quick time events but this game used them in a decent way.
Pros: Graphic, bloody, gruesome, fast gameplay, propped up with a great story that helped me understand the lore of the one ring how it was made, what happened to the ring maker, seeing another story unfold in a great way. This game will give you hours and hours of fun either creating a army or orcs or destroying every last one of them. Or you could just do both and still have amazing fun.
Cons: at the end of the game the gameplay got a little stale as many of the things you have to do at the end are things you have had to be doing for the last 15 hours or so of gameplay. This for me meant that at the end of the main story I was really looking forward to playing another game.
The middle ground: I bought this for 10$ and to me it was worth easily 2-3 times that amount in gameplay ,story, and fun factor and that is not something that happens too often. If you can get this game for less then 30$ or cheaper i suggest you do so as you will not be dissapointed. I find it really hard to find any real flaws this game has, considering i got almost 40 hours of playtime out of it and had lots of fun 95% of the time, and i still have some things to 100% still as at the end of the game i only had 80% of the game complete and that was without the DLC i have yet to play.
Final say: If its cheap and you have been thinking about it just get this game, it will be a good investment in my eyes.

,as now I'm reliving the game, I will say some of my feelings.
Eden* is my favorite one in the VNs I have played/experienced, although I didn't go over as many as some VN fans. And Sion is the person I love best, in my own heart. My portrait is Sion's back shadow.
Talking about Eden* in Minori's history, it is another pinnacle production after having a great success in
, at that time they have really much money to produce a same-level production.
Whatever the resolution of the game, artwork of background&character,movable emotion CGs,almost every element in the game, has reached a height that few opponent can compete with.
The artwork of the game is mainly presented by ちこたむ&KIMちー, not ななお なる in former productions of Minori, but the artwork is still exquisite.
Comparing with others, Eden* is not a long story, won't cost you too much time finishing all of the story.But all main character have their enough full characteristic in this story.
The illustration is also different from other VNs, with lots of static illustrations of the event, while many others use set painting plus background. Showing more storytelling attribute in the whole story.
The opening is not the production of Makoto Shinkai, but can say it from his disciple, with lots of style of Makoto Shinkai.
You may not find such a shocking PV among many VNs, when you see the glass shatter and the ruin collapse into pieces, background turn into grass at the moment Ryou and Sion hold their hand, and the surrondings suddenly change into wide angle view of  blue sea and sky with the running of Sion.
The script, or the story by IURO, has a big framework,but much simple and obvious
story-line. But you can see it pays a lot of work in completing the characteristic in every main character in the game, like Ryou, Sion ,Elica and so on.
Some might say the end of word is not an important part of the whole setting of the story,but I think that it is not the whole and most important part of the story, but the element of it. The crucial part should be the story between the characters in the story.
Or, simply saying, a love story in a dying planet.
, of course the setting of the end of the word is the foil of the atmosphere and melody of this beautiful and ,well, tearjerker story.
Although the story doesn't have many choices for you to decide, but it is coherent. In other words, it is not an adventure game,seems more like a long story that let you to read.
The OP and bgm is from Tenmon,or Shiragawa Atusi,which also produce the bgm of ef, although many bgm can be seemed as the modified tone of the theme song Little explorer, but when you play the game, you can find the whole story is more colorful and lively with these soundtracks. Though the character voice and the artwork of the game is better than many opponents,but the soundtrack is the assistance of letting the game more than touching your heart.
In the opening of the game I see Sion running on the grass with Ryou at her side, and standing on the small hill, with
, it gives me a strong feeling of getting rid of constraint of the institution, walking freely on the new world with Ryou.
I see the ending of the story,but I still feel so sad when it comes to the farewell in the setting sun.
In the epilogue of the story, looking at the happy and warm, sweet story finally comes to the end, making me awfully sad, even if I have known that the end is unavoidable, I can't stop the sad feeling spread out of the screen, into my heart.
Though I have forgotten how to cry for many years, but looking at the end of the story,and
like the final detainment, describing the reluctant of the world and love with Ryou from Sion,I feel so sad that I can't say any word.
Though Eden* was released in 2009, debarked steam in 2015,but it is still can be one of the best Japanese VNs ever.
So, if you haven't experience the charm of Japanese galgame ,and/or don't like too many choices in the game, Eden* would be your good choice.
Thank you for reading.

So now that I've just beaten this game and every single boss in it including the DLC bosses, think its about time i wrote a review on this game.
Though I did have experience with other Fromsoft games (Bloodborne and DS3) this game was still actually fairly challenging, but overall it didn't feel like it would've been as hard if it were my first Soulsborne game as everyone claimed it was. I remember around when this game was new that plenty of people claimed this game was way too hard to actually beat and I never found myself in a position of giving up. If you're jumping into this game without any previous Souls games experience its gonna take some getting the hang of things to actually survive.
Now with that out of the way and going on to an actual review, there weren't actually that many issues i had with this game and I dont have a lot of negative things to say about it. In fact I personally think statistics-wise, this game does it all the best. Switching armor and gear for resistances, poise, and using different weapons to beat different bosses was actually a really cool kind of strategy for me. I feel like different shields in this game actually had some kind of use to them compared to the other Souls games, at least compared to DS3 which I didnt really find a good use for a shield. And again, switching shields to resist different attacks gave me some more thinking and strategy as well. The world design for this game is extremely pretty especially for how old the game is. I'm always completely immersed in games like this and I enjoyed the exploration of almost every zone... except the Demon Ruins cause there wasn't really much to see. I liked how the dodging in this game is more realistic I guess, you actually have to dodge away instead of being able to dodge and gaining invincibility frames. The way everything works in this game feels so much better to me, slower but still much more i guess polished because the statistics felt like they actually mattered. I'm not 100% sure if I prefer this one compared to everything else but it's very close to the best if anything.
The only negative things I can think of about this game are how easy it is to get trapped into a corner by a ton of regular monsters and die because you either can't hit them all fast enough before getting staggered, or not being able to roll through them. I also don't really like how humanity works in this game because I would always find myself out of humanity if i died and then something stupid happens like getting trapped in a corner and dying once again before I'm able to recollect all my souls and humanity. Honestly that's more of just me being bad but I like the idea of being able to dodge out of corners you were being trapped in which I think they used in DS3. The game is also a little glitchy in certain places cause I kept falling through the floor. Wasn't entirely game breaking though
Overall I think this game is spectacular. I liked the majority of the boss fights and adventuring throughout every zone in the game. I found very little problems with the game at least in my opinion and is completely worth the buy next time you see it on a sale. Especially if you want a game that you could easily put a lot of time in. 9/10

Ok, I'm going to be honest here. Eden* is one of the best stories I've ever experienced in any medium. It is an absolute masterpiece, and that's not hyperbole. If you're looking for a brilliantly-crafted story that has tragedy, intelligent characters, meaningful dialogs, romance done right, and bittersweetness all around, look no further. It also has one of the most interesting fictional characters I've seen (Sion), and her interactions with the main protagonist (Ryou) are fascinating.
One more thing to note. Much like the movie "Full Metal Jacket", Eden* is split into two distinct halves, and in my opinion, the second half is where the VN actually starts. The first half is moderately interesting, but fairly dry, and for me mostly exists as necessary backstory and character introduction. The second half is where Sion really shines and the VN properly begins.
That being said, $20 is a steal for a story you'll never forget.

Lok’tar humans!  Azbolg the Gaming Orc to review the quasi-renaissance fantasy Pillars of Eternity by Obsidian Entertainment.
A grass roots crowd funding campaign, with over 77,000 backers, raising over 4 million dollars, as it recreated, and maybe surpasses the magic of the classic 3d isometric games of the 90s, the Baldur’s Gate series.  If you are a fan of that series, this game is a definite full price buy, with over 70 hours of content, and if you’re not familiar with the classics of ye old times, and are a fan of real-time strategy, D&D party mechanics, epic storytelling with a vast an immersive world, this game is also for you.
The game begins in a detailed character creation with some new races that I haven’t seen before since my time in Azergoth.  I picked a Wind Godlike Cypher, since I’ve played almost every combo in these kind of games, and this race class combo was refreshing to see something new and creative.  After seeing what kind of companions you can get, I would have re-rolled to an evil halfing monk with the evil voice, since there isn’t any monks companions in the game.  This isn’t a big deal though, because you can hire a custom adventurers of your exact choosing similar to the character creation process at any inn in the game.  It scales off your level too so don’t get too hung up about it.
The game takes place in an immersive world of Eora, inside a nation known as Dyrwood.  Your character witnesses a ritual and awakens, where you are known commonly as a “Watcher.”  You are now like the boy in the six sense, but hopefully less oblivious, you can speak with dead people, and touch objects to get visions of their past.  Your journey is more or less open-ended, guided by a quest journal.
The music is incredible.  A mix between Lord of the Rings, and also brings back memories of Conan the Barbarian running the fields with his Asian nomad companion, but after listening to it on its own, outside of the game, it reminded me of a mystic mystery, which is what this game is.
The unpredictability, and freedom this game gives you, is what keeps you addictively playing like a gamer craving midnight mountain dew.  For example, a boy will tell you a secret if you get him a knife made out of special metal.  You can intimidate him and throw him to the curb like the little snot that he is, or go talk to the merchant who sold the knife to some adventures who you can buy it from or attack them and take it by force, and still decide to kick the puny human kid anyways.  Or it could be as simple as breaking up a drug dealer’s den only to find out things aren’t what they seemed.  There are so many outcomes and options, and it’s up to you as the player to be bewildered by how open all of them are too fit your character’s play style.
A feature Pillars of Eternity has superior to the Baldur’s Gate series is that it allows you to have a stronghold which you can improve upon with time and gold.  It’s too bad you can only build one feature at a time though, but the options are so dynamic and fun, you can even repair the dungeon to imprison people in across your journeys.
Another epic feature of the game is the endless paths below your stronghold.  A standalone game within its own right.  The map is remarkably creative, none like I’ve seen before.  The winding twisting paths are mysterious as you venture forth through the depths to discover who built it.  It is so massive and epic, and addicting!
A few negative criticisms about the game is that you pretty much have to read the whole story’s dialogue.  So you if you are lazy and don’t like to read detailed and captivating storytelling, then this game is not for you.  So accidently you might read and miss some over some key plot points, partly because the dialogue is so rich.  Also sometimes the NPCs will voiced randomly at times, and other times will not be voiced at all, which tells me either that the dialogue was changed or the voice actor couldn’t act it all out, which is disappointing since the voice acting is great, but overall this breaks the immersion.  I wish this game was completely voice acted, even with all the coughs, yacks, and other things, which I hope a sequel or expansion will bring.
A few tips that I can suggest to you if you are going to play it are to turn up the graphics, since they are set a the middle by default, and also you can key bind abilities by moussing over them and hitting the key you want them to be bound too.  If you find the game is too easy, you can raise the difficulty, but I haven’t even at normal difficulty as some casual fights require pause-by-pause tactics.
Pillars of eternity is a vast D&D party adventure with epically rich storytelling, and those fans of these type of strategy RPG games will find that this game not only stand among the classics, but in many ways surpasses them with its unique take on a forgotten game style.  Azbolg gives this game 9 Orc axes out of 10.

Space exploration has never been more fun or customizable in such a small game. The game puts you up as the lone survivor of Earth after being destroyed. Only you can unite the six main races and destroy what is threatening the entire universe.
The crafting is pretty straight forward and the combat is fun. The bosses can be a challenge, but they are pretty straight forward. Each world is randomly generated and that adds to the fun of being a space explorer. Planets filled with villages and monsters that can add loads of quests! This is unfortunatly where the game falls apart.
The quests are all the same. Talk to this person. Get this item for this person. Destroy this person to help this person. It gets pretty pointless in doing said quests when they say, "Deliver this note for me," and the person you are delivering it to is right next to them.
The main goal I had was not completing the story though. It was upgrading my ship! Upgrading was so much fun and the fact I can customize it anyway I want adds to the joy of games like this. After that though what else do you do? You can beat the main story, but what fun is that when the final boss...... I won't even discuss it. All I'll say is everything led up to that moment. And it was severely underwhelming.
Overall I give the game a 6/10. Crafting and procedurally generated planets can only get the game so far. Exploration is fun, but tiresome after so long. The final boss was also extremely disappointing especially after all that build up.

I cannot see this game ever coming out of early access in a state much better than it is now unless they totally overhaul the game. The developers seem to have ignored getting the basic mechanics right before creating a fully fleshed out world. This is a major red flag that they aren't in it for the long run and simply rushed something playable to make a quick crash grab.
The sound effects are really jarring and don't fit the theme of the game at all. A Michael Bay noise happens every time you complete part of the initial tutorial. Your foot steps sound random and swap between sounding like you're a bug skittering and wading in a swamp. Gathering cotton sounds like someone hitting a kick-drum.
The animations and combat are very basic. For example, a pig simply slides forward in a static motion and moves its head slightly to hit you. If you hit a mob,  a cheesy looking red glow appears.
The concepts of the game seem great, and the screenshots make the game seem immersive and unique. But once you see it all moving it is unfortunately very difficult to appreciate with next-to-no animation and a world that looks like a low textured version of Skyrim. Even Skyrim wasn't popular for its graphics back in 2011, but they are still better than this game.
I would love to be proven wrong about this game but all the signs of what's there make it look like it was a rush of asset and sound creation to create something that would seem unique and look good, simply to sell well on Steam.
If you like hardcore, medieval games then there are plenty of others that are more promising, such as Life is Feudal, Glora Victis and Mortal Online.

Savage Lands isn't a phenomenal game, but it is a competent survival game. It isn't like other sandbox survivals in that it has much more lore, sort of unique enemies and a general goal. It is an overall enjoyable experience even if it lacks some polish. Here's a pro-con list, because they're easy.
Pros
+just-right map. The map feels neither too large nor too small. Dangerous enough to make you think twice about certain trips, but not enough to feel unfair.
+Difficulty. A lot of people used to complain about this but there is no permadeath or character progression. Death only makes you lose items which can be recovered. So while it may be difficult, it isn't too punishing.
+multiplayer. I haven't played multiplayer yet but it is a great and common addition to survival games. With the small map and more goal-oriented gameplay I can imagine it would be fun with a group of cooperative friends.
+Interactive and active developers. This is an early access game, and many early access games have developers that avoid the community or give up on the game or let development come to a standstill. This game has none of those problems.
+Base building. Though the base building is in it's early stages and has an admittedly small amount of structures, it is a fun part of the game.
neutral
~Crafting. Crafting is a mixed bag. It suffers from the same issue that games like Unturned (in the 2.0 era) suffered, and that is a complicated multi-level crafting system. For example, if you want to make bronze armor you need to first craft hardened leather armor, which requires leather armor and a few other items. You also need bronze, which requires tin and copper ingots which requires tin and copper ore. You also need various small things like bronze rivets and nails which require more bronze. So the crafting can take a while and some effort to make your way through the levels, getting more complicated as the items get better and also requiring higher tier crafting, smelting and forge structures, and while some of the complexity is annoying, it isn't a terrible system. I would say just remove some of the clutter items like rivets and it would be a good system.
~Combat. This game is more combat oriented than other survival games might be, with enemies spawning almost everywhere, which is a bit of a shame because the combat is mediocre. The game has various weapon types bu they all have long clunky animations and they leave you guessing as to their range, maybe you can hit that enemy 6 feet away, maybe not the animations are too poor to give any indicator. The enemies have the same style of fighting as well, but that's a good thing, they telegraph their swings giving good time to react, dodge and counter. This gives the game an unpolished, indie, pseudo-Dark Souls feel to it's combat.
Cons
-bugs. Currently the game has a few bugs, nothing game breaking except maybe the one that causes no enemies to spawn on the second island. Hopefully the developers can sort that one out, but overall I find the game to be relatively bug-free.
-Performance. The game doesn't run all that great. Nothing new for indie early access survival titles but it would be nice to see some better optimization.
-variety. There isn't all that much variety in the game. It feels as though there's three stages (corresponding with the three islands, which might be a design choice), beginner where you're just running around in the beginning trying not to die and scraping up various crap you find, intermediate where you have a small base and you collect nice ores and craft a suite of tools and armor, and the final stage where you're fighting giants and dragons and working with the highest tier armor. But it feels like the high-tier armor and weapons are only marginally better than the mid-tier stuff, and you really only end up crafting 2 sets of armor through pretty much the whole game. It would be nice if the higher tiers of armor had a less marginal increase of stats and perhaps a minecraft-esque system of "to mine gold you need iron, to get iron you need stone" to facilitate working your way up the levels.
A fun, if flawed, game that could use some improvement, but is ultimately enjoyable. And if you get it for cheap on Humblebundle, it is absolutely worth it.

I do recommend to purchase this game but only when it is on big sale and I will explain why in details.
First of all, I have to be honest - I am SC fan and I was playing the series right from the first title. And yes, I do not care about graphics - more about overall atmosphere. Though I do care about how devs supporting their product.
The game has very good single player and if you play it right it feels like that old SC's that I loved so much - you can do the things silently or even without touching anyone (there are some counter-examples though). I have to mention "train break-in" and believe me you won't be happy with this situation if you are fully stealth player. Overall, single player is a good way to entertain yourself for another day or two but that's all. If you are the "loud guy" you can also re-play everything as panther or assault. The only question remains is why those awesome night infiltrations have gone? You encounter only several in this installment.
CO-OP. Well, it took the best features of SC Conviction co-op and executed them just perfectly - it is another great game to play with a good friend of yours for some time. The only thing I don't love is that it is way too short (I am also extremely dissapointed with that Briggs'  missions never-ending bug, but let's keep it aside as it might get fixed). It's an outstanding co-op if you play it right - you have all the tools you need but if you fail to deliver you are the only one to blame.
However, the thing I was so excited about is SvM (Spies vs Mercs). This was initially introduced in Pandora Tomorrow and in next installment, Chaos Theory, it keep many gamers entertained for years. Double Agent also presented us with SvM but it was not so popular. With no SvM in Conviction I though that the series is getting worse (like many others on the market, sadly) but SvM got its place back in Blacklist. It is so much fun that you can play it for hours and hours, again and again. It is almost perfectly balanced, and, aside for some bugs, you can equally good play as a merc and spy and there is no loosy side really. You might think that one side is better than the other one at first, but as soon as you start to use your equipment properly and your skill increases - you will see that SvM is balanced nicely. I was in worldwide top 15 at the moment of writing so I do know what I am talking about. What about modes - I was so hooked by SvM Blacklist that I abolished that SvM Classic mode, which many claim not to be classic (and I agree with them). They re-introduced Deathmatch as well, which still looks weird for me, even though my beloved Chaos Theory also had one. For newcomers I recommend to try out SvM Blacklist and SvM Extraction.
Points are - if you are looking for Chaos Theory Redefined - Blacklist is a good choice as it is Chaos Theory ideas blended with some Conviction mechanics. If you are looking for exact copy of Chaos Theory or Pandora Tomorrow - you better look for an unsold copy of CT or PT at your local store - Blacklist has different focus - it is more action-driven than Chaos Theory (single-player and co-op) and  more diverse in terms of SvM. Yet it has many bugs in each of the modes of game so you have to live with it. However, as I have been playing CT for years I glad I now have something else to play.

Full discosure, I used to be a huge fan of Homestuck and backed this game on Kickstarter, so my impression is not so much "I paid $8 for this; was it worth it?" and more "Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥this game actually came out; is it any good?". For instance: the game's got a ton of dialog, and it goes on longer than I'd like, but I enjoy slowly getting to know the characters' via their banter and the jokes sometimes make me cackle with glee. However, I almost didn't realize that because it's exactly the same way I felt about Homestuck five years ago, and I took it for granted here. So yeah, take my praise with a grain of salt.
This game is a bunch of fun. The strife puzzle-solving sections are especially good, because they're inventive combat that leverages the game's true strength: Having jokes written for pretty much every ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t combination of inventory item and puzzle object in the game. The puzzles aren't insane - you're not going to be spending an hour wandering around before you think to use "Fork" on "Pile of Spaghetti" to turn it into a fake hairdo - but they're odd enough that you'll try a couple wrong options, and there will always be something written for it. Hell, one time when I was stuck I tried to use a pile of pogs on a staircase crammed with guns and there was a response for *that*. I got into a fight I didn't know how to win and resorted to throwing everything in my inventory at the monster, and the monster replied with a pun for every single one. I might replay this game and just spend all my time mashing my inventory on the environment.
Speaking of replaying, the game's pretty short! About three hours, I think. I super wanted more - but I know there were some (for high values of "some") production problems, and I'm really glad they spent the money and time they had left on making a short game that's crammed with jokes and crazy visuals rather than a longer, blander game.
Speaking of crazy visuals, holy♥♥♥♥♥♥this game looks crazy good! Every scene is crammed with excellent ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t going on, weird things scampering outside the windows, every shelf jammed with trash literature and nonsensical occult bric-a-brac and leg lamps and conspiracy theory diagrams. It's awesome.
So yeah! I recommend this game, and I'm definitely gonna buy Act 2.

Homestuck fan or non-Homestuck fan, I think Hiveswap is enjoyable by anyone who plays it and enjoys games involving a good story. I have to warn anyone who wants to buy this game: do not buy this for the puzzles. The puzzles and combat (which itself is still a puzzle, really) are fairly easy. Hiveswap is enjoyable mostly for its story and flavor text when trying to solve puzzles. If you're still here knowing that the puzzles aren't too amazing, then go for it. At eight dollars, this game is certainly worth it. There are many complaints about how short it is, and it is short, but it's not like it feels incomplete considering the price on it. It left off at a good point, and while I'm going to hate to wait for act 2, the game gives you enough content. If we had to wait another 5 years, then yeah this would be ridiculous, but What Pumpkin said that it shouldn't take nearly as long for act 2 to be released.
The game breaks down into about three different categories. I'll briefly talk about each one.
Exploration/puzzle solving: Like I said previously, the puzzles aren't anything special at all, but they're still fun for the most part, and the exploration to figure out the puzzles is entertaining due to the flavor text. However, I wouldn't buy Hiveswap if you're in it for the puzzles.
Combat: The combats are actually small puzzles. You have to use the resources you have along with the terrain around you to defeat enemies. There were a few times that I got frustrated with the combat because the game didn't do a good job of visually displaying the problem with why <insert some item/ability> didn't work how it should've, but it was only like two times, and it did make sense afterward. Might've just been me brainfarting, but I do think there could've been better telegraphing for some of the combats. I really enjoyed this kind of combat/puzzle, however. It felt pretty rewarding to escape or defeat whatever it is you're facing, and the little quips used when you attempt to do something were a nice touch. Overall a small part of the game, but pretty enjoyable when it was there.
Story: I think the best parts of the story are the interactions between characters. The interactions feel natural and stay interesting throughout the entire game. This was definitely my favorite aspect of the game, especially after interacting with the thing in the attic (no spoilers). The interactions were completely solid. As for the other aspects of the story, such as reading your diary or looking at pictures of family on the wall, etc., I enjoyed the sort of "already know but thinking about" perspective. It feels natural and gives you an idea about how the characters feel about each little story blob.
Yes, there are references to Homestuck in it. While they were very enjoyable, they're a small part of the game that aren't required to pick up on at all for a full enjoyment of the game itself. This game makes you care about the characters within itself, not characters from another story.
I would certainly recommend this game! There are people who definitely wouldn't care for Hiveswap, don't get me wrong, but I think Hiveswap has a lot to offer to people who like more story-based games. I hope this review was helpful in your decision!

You choose a class and level your characters just like any other RPG game, but the combat is a real-time 3rd person shooter. Leveling up is just as important as your ability to dodge enemy fire, use cover, and score headshots for critical damage. The game also has different difficulties settings to choose from in case you need to lower it.
Aside from combat; you can literally spend hours at a time just going around exploring, talking to people, and reading codexes you come across (bits of information about certain guns or whatever). Some people love this stuff, others hate it, so its purely preference if you'll like it or not. The main highlight of this game though is the option to choose your own path/dialogue. You can pretty much apologize to someone, agree to disagree, or sometimes just straight up punch them in their face. Then the next time you meet this person down the road, IF you meet them again, they'll remember how the previous conversation went and it affects the feel of the game. It might even open or close off certain things. The overall core storyline of the game is the same though, you can't change that. It's also a trilogy. Certain decisions you make can span from game 1 game into the next if you transfer save files.
-
Cons: A few times playing this game I had to load an older save file due to some weird glitches happening. Maybe 3 times in 50+ hours of playing. (only lost a total of 10 minutes of playtime or so). Other than that the game ran fine for me.
