text:
This is both a great Total War game and by far one of the most frustrating to play late game.
Because surviving is the goal, empire-building comes with some severe barriers to entry, most notably the gigantic cost to convert city centers or colonize ruined settlements.  Late game, assuming you're like me and build an empire anyway, you have a ton of territory to defend from the Huns and you'll likely be at war with enough or powerful enough factions to limit how many forces you can bring to bear on the Huns.  This works out ok for Germans and Vikings, it makes the game challenging but not punishingly so.  If you settle or start further northeast though you are ****ed.
This is immensely frustrating because the Slavs are among the most interesting factions to play, their units are unique, they are immune to winter attrition (a helpful boon), their minor temples can add fertility to a region (a godsend as each "chapter" opens with a global cooling effect that drops the fertility of a ton of regions by 1 each "chapter"), and they can colonize ruined settlements without cost.  The problem is that Huns not only spawn with most if not all armies stacked full of top tier units by the time Attila emerges, they ****ing respawn the turn after you kill them.  This is fine for Germans, Vikings, Celts and literally anyone who doesn't have a steppe empire, but it ****s you so hard if you play Slavs or make a steppe empire as fresh hordes instantly spawn on your ****ing doorstep repeatedly until you kill Attila, which you have to do three or four times before Huns can no longer spawn new hordes.
Even assuming you don't have wars with anyone else, and you will, fighting the Huns can overwhelm you easily as you can't afford to keep too many troops sitting around defending territory and if a Hun horde is present, they rarely come in less than two, then none of your units in the region can regenerate. Because the Huns aren't really paying for their unlimited hordes you can spend tens of thousands of gold desperately fighting them off and still end up in dire straits.  None of this is helped by the fact that Huns have inexplicably fantastic infantry and artillery on top of their monster cavalry, this is a major problem for me because I could probably hold the Huns at bay if not for the fact their armies are so well rounded that they excel in pitched and siege battles even when they're outnumbered by a sizable margin. Not to mention the Huns will burn any city they encounter to the ground, which weakens your already strained economy and undoes potentially hundreds of turns of progress.  I like that this game is challenging and has a bunch of mechanics to make late game difficult but it's frustrating as **** to watch the empire you spent over 100 turns building burn down around you as you desperately try to kill Attila and stop the respawning hordes.
In conclusion, this game is a ton of fun to play for 100 turns.  I love razing settlements and watching fire engulf the map, the buildings are much improved from Rome Total War 2, the graphics are better, and you can make early game easy on yourself by playing as various barbarians or you can make the game a frantic struggle from the get go if you like a challenge by playing as Rome. Plagues no longer totally wreck armies or towns, although they now last for varying periods of time and can easily spread from one settlement to another even if you have good sanitation.  It has the best of what Rome Total War 2 had to offer and so much more.  But the **** the Huns.  They need severe rebalancing, don't give them great infantry and artillery (which they really shouldn't have), and when a new horde spawns it should take four or five turns just like it would to recruit a normal army so that you have a little breathing room.  I don't mind having three of the eight (there's always eight hordes at a time by late game) hordes rampaging through my territory at a time, but if they keep respwaning endlessly near or in my territory a turn after I beat them I will get zerg-rushed to death regardless of how good I play and how many armies I set aside just to fight the Huns.  Or better yet just give the Huns eight awesome hordes by late game and do away with the respwaning entirely, save for maybe Attila's horde.  I know the obvious answer is don't colonize the steppe, but it's so much more limiting if I can't, it basically forces me to fight just Germans and West Empire or just Eastern factions and East Empire with a dash of Huns on the side for each scenario.  There's no other spot in the game where you're stuck between the Sassanids' allies, the East Empire, eastern Germans and incoming Hun hordes and the idea of forging a kindgom in such a tough spot is immensely appealing.  The Huns would still be hard to beat even if you rebalanced them as I outlined and it would still make for a fun challenge.  But as it is now it's impossible, for me anyway, and worse its really ****ing frustrating, enough so to make me outright quit campaigns I was otherwise very much into.

I like Total War. Got back into it recently. I wasn't really impressed with the game. Then I saw the full retail price for the DLC. Yeah. That really turned me off of the game. The grand campaign period and factions are really interesting, around the time of barbarian invasions and the historical fall of the Roman Empire. The Last Roman campaign is set in Justinians reign trying to reclaim the Western Roman Empire in the A.D 500's. The Charlemagne campaign is set during the time of Charlemagne, who founded the Holy Roman Empire in A.D 800. Atilla Total War thus bridges the Dark Ages between the classical and medieval world, which is a fascinating and underrated period.
Many of the features in Atilla are refined or expanded from previous games, and simply make sense. The AI is more intelligient in battle and in diplomacy. The political/family system is refined and intricate. RTW 2 was a trailblazer with the internal politics, Atilla really made it work. Religion, sanitation, agriculture, conquering settlements, rebuilding razed settlements etc. all work well.
I have had a lot of fun playing my first campaign: fighting for my Garamantian empire and building a dynasty (I've already played more than I did in RTW2, in a couple of weeks). Its a great game, so I'll playing many more hours of it.
I would consider that Atilla Total War is the greatest Total War of all time and the true and worthy successor to RTW 1 (and Barbarian Invasion for that matter).
The only issue is that with so many features and happenings there is a lot of keep track of (RTW 1 had a better notifications system).
Also, check out the medieval 1212 A.D mod - amazing.

The Binding of Isaac is guilty of making me lose my sanity. Not that I was sane to begin with, I just feel more insane as a result of playing this game.
The Binding of Isaac's story is weird. It has an opening which tells us a sort of real, sort of not real, story. You'd need to play through the whole game to actually learn the story, so I'll give the simple version. And by short version, copy and paste the intro because I can't be asked to explain the story.
Isaac and his mother lived alone in a small house on a hill. Isaac kept to himself, drawing pictures and playing with his toys as his mom watched Christian broadcasts on the television.
Life was simple, and they were both happy.
That was, until the day Isaac's mom heard a voice from above: "Your son has become corrupted by sin! He needs to be saved!"
"I will do my best to save him, my Lord," Isaac's mother replied, rushing into Isaac's room, removing all that was evil from his life.
Again, the voice called to her:
"Isaac's soul is still corrupt! He needs to be cut off from all that is evil in this world and confess his sins."
"I will follow your instructions, Lord. I have faith in thee," Isaac's mother replied, as she locked Isaac away in his room, away from the evils of the world.
One last time, Isaac's mom heard the voice of God calling to her:
"You have done as I asked, but I still question your devotion to me. To prove your faith, I will ask one more thing of you."
"Yes, Lord. Anything," Isaac's mother begged.
"To prove your love and devotion, I require a sacrifice. Your son Isaac will be this sacrifice. Go into his room and end his life as an offering to me, to prove that you love me above all else!"
"Yes, Lord," she replied, grabbing a butcher's knife from the kitchen.
Isaac, watching through a crack in the door, trembled in fear. Scrambling around his room to find a hiding place, he noticed a trapdoor to the basement, hidden under his rug. Without hesitation, he flung open the hatch just as his mother burst through his door and threw himself down into the unknown depths below.
Now for the part I can be bothered to write. The gameplay. Ever wanted to shoot bullets in The Legend of Zelda? Too bad you shoot tears. Tears which, may I add, can completely vaporise flesh. Tears which can be altered to RNGJesus's will. Your tears can be altered by stats our general effects which can be given to your tears. Tears which explode, tears which freeze enemies occasionally, replace your tears for a laser, replace your laser with a beam of blood and, my favourite, make your tears into the shape of bananas.
I mentioned stats. Lets talk about that(s). There are 9 stats. The first being health, this increases your survivability. There are three types of hearts: Red are replenishable and are generally the main source of health you will have, Soul hearts are similar to red hearts but are not replenishable and, finally, black hearts. Soul hearts but they damage enemies when depleted. Next stat is speed. Walk faster. Then there's range. Shoot further. Next is tear rate (called tears in game). This determines how fast you shoot. Shot speed. Self explanitory. Damage. How much damage you do. Luck. Determines certain things like room drops and certain tear effects. Devil Deal chance. A Devil Deal is where you bargain with the devil to give them your red hearts (or soul hearts) for cool♥♥♥♥♥♥(items). The chance for a Devil Deal is determined by your actions in game. Taking damage means you have a lower chance unless the damage is done to a soul heart or black heart. And Finally, the Devil Deal's enemy: the Angel Deal. Angel Deals give you free stuff which is better than the Devil Deal (sometimes). To get them: don't take Devil Deals. This segways into our next topic, rooms. There are normal rooms where you kill enemies, item rooms where you get an item at the cost of a key, Shops where you spend money to get items, health, keys, etc and finally, boss rooms, fight bosses to move to the next floor and get a free item.  There are also hard challenges where you can win cool items, these are difficult though.
There are also characters which I will quickly go over.
Isaac: default stats
Magdeline: sacrifice speed for health
Cain: sacrifice health for luck, speed and damage
Judas: sacrifice health for all out damage
???: Isaac with more speed and soul hearts instead of red hearts
Eve: Sacrifice damage and health for a demon form at 1 heart + extra speed
Samson: Sacrifice fire rate for increased damage every time you're hit
Azazel: BLOOD. BEAM. FLIGHT. BLACK. HEARTS.
Lazarus: Free revive for less luck.
Eden: RNGJesus
The Lost: One hit you're dead in exchange for unlocking the best items in the game.
You can unlock these characters through simple (yet challenging) challenges
Thought I was done? I literally only covered Rebirth.
Afterbirth adds two new endings, more challenges, new items, fixed mechanics, more enemies, new floors, new bosses, more regular rooms a new gamemode and new characters. This expansion adds more and it really expanded what we knew as Isaac. There's not much to explain without spoiling the game, but the point is. New. Better. Cooler. Stuff.
The two new characters are
Lilith: have a little helper which shoots tears for you instead of yourself. You can double this buddy temporarily.
The Keeper: Remember The Lost? Have coins for health (which you can't increase). Also, have a slow triple shot and -2 luck stat
Imagine all of the above except
.
. In all seriousness AB+ is very hard. And it did literally add what Afterbirth added. One new character:
Apollyon: Start with a void which sucks stuff up at your will for stat upgrades
The achievements are made stupidly hard. And the challenges added are the same. I do not enjoy myself when getting to the harder achievements.
Also. MODS. Want to BS your way through the game using a console? SURE YOU CAN. Play people's creative mods for fun if you don't want to take the game seriously. The game is also being constantly updated

An unusually long kinetic novel (no choices/only one ending) featuring full Japanese voice-over.
I was hesitating to play it because the character art is uninspiring. There are chlichés like oversized breasts, a cute army girl and a cute housemaiden. Part of me was afraid a cute magical cat-girl would appear next but thankfully I was spared this. Luckily the protagonist is not some silly perverted fool tripping into his own personal harem he has secretly dreamed for but a rather cold-hearted war veteran, and there are a couple other characters of that sort that you wouldn't necessarily expect in your more ordinary anime.
Despite some initial bumps and doubts the game is rather profound and thoughtful and has a better world and story to tell than most other KNs/VNs I have played. Their unoriginal exterior and cliché-like introductions aside the characters were likeable and quite well written and had more depth than meets the eye. The game features a pretty interesting pre-apocalyptic sci-fi scenario that has you experience the final phases of mankind fleeing earth due to a bright red star that appeared in the sky and is said to destroy it. It's featuring some genuine sci-fi elements but isn't dwelling on the technical terms of it as much, it's more about the people and how they handle it all. This and the extensively designed background art (particularily skies and clouds) remind me fondly of the Makoto Shinkai animes that I had seen many years back.
The music deserves some mentioning too; there is plenty of it, it fits the situations nicely and is memorable. I intentionally stopped progressing at times just so I could listen to it more. It features contemplating, sad and upbeat tunes and I wasn't surprised to see that other players were wondering if it was available separately (it isn't in the West afaik, but there is a playlist in the main menu and I guess one can try YouTube or sorts).
I don't think I would've touched it anytime soon if not for the "overwhelmingly oositive" Steam reviews. Thanks to them I put my initial doubts aside and it didn't took me long before I liked it, wanted to see how the story works out, had it touch parts of my heart in several ways and realized that this game is one of the better, higher-value kinetic novels to be found. It raised my bar of expectations towards any other KNs/VNs I will be playing in the future.

Ah minori.  A galge publisher which I will forever remember by IP blocking all non-Japanese visitors and blame all of us gaijin as responsible for their own country tightening laws regarding erotic games.  How does a game from a publisher like that get an official English translation and got put on Steam is beyond my imagination.
Of course, you all know this is Steam, thus there is absolutely no conventional erotic content in this visual novel.  Forgive me being too lazy to search the internet on whether the actual sex scene got cut for the English release, or was it nonexistent in the original version.  It is irrelevant, because a sex scene in eden*’s story and the mood would be an intrusion, rather than enhancement, and I’m glad that there is none for me to see.
Although far from being a bad vn compare to rest of the genre on Steam, I don’t feel eden* is worth of the $20 asking price.  Gorgeous background CGs coupled with dubious character sprites/portraits of inconsistent style; nicely tuned soundtrack but eclipsed by mediocre voice acting… I can’t pin down what exactly went wrong in the production phase… but something definitely was amiss for such swing of quality in different departments.
Story of eden* is largely a fairytale-ish romance.  (And by “romance” I don’t just mean a love story, but rather a tale of emotion and human nature.)  Background setting: The world’s scientists somehow are convinced that the world will end in about 100 years.  World war then broke out; half of human population died, and the rest formed a unified government and started to build spaceships.  The plan is successful; nearly everybody on Earth got evacuated in the end, and the story really begins on one couple who chose to remain on Earth to live together and eventually faces the inevitable.
Of course, there would be a few more to the story than that which I would not spoil.  The plot does introduce a few more elements to aspire intrigue and perhaps the readers’ tear… but when the time comes, the ending is largely predictable.  I know it’s beside the point and focus, but the vn never tried to explain what exactly is the nature of this “Armageddon” event, and the story doesn’t elaborate on it, deliberately I shall say, which is irritating even more.
So in the end, I feel the story couldn’t leave a positive impact.  It is partly due to the premise of the story is built too much on a hypothetical and fantasy world setting that is far too removed from current reality.  Or maybe I’m just not into love stories about people who know their life would soon end.  It is fine, though, like not all people enjoy horror game/movies and not all like the science fiction genre.
In conclusion, if you dig for a story like this, then you can safely ignore everything I wrote above.  Otherwise I would advise caution, because in the end the experience which this vn brings might very likely not worth the money—and more importantly, the time—you spend reading.

This prettymuch hits the exact point I expected it to between the previous action-centric and pacey Conviction, and the older considered and more ponderous outing of the series.
Let's get the major criticism out of the way first.  These characters and this tone really doesn't gel in that quiet way that the original Splinter Cell did.  The happy trio of Grim, Sam and Lambert doesn't exist here - and while that fits the story evolution of the series, they've ended up with a bizzare mix of personal and international stakes.  This game has a public face to the enemy - an actual named villian - and a buddy-movie style revenge plot.  These all lack the simple yet effective subtley of a man trying to quietly protect his daughter's future while never being acknowledge outside of the team.
On to the positive.  This merges prettymuch all of the best bits of the stealth-centric AI from the series - the defensive door-camping and quick-storming from Conviction, with the slow escalation of awareness from Chaos Theory.  This is a stealth game that really lets you mess with the AI - without them seeming completely stupid.  Mess with them too much, have one too many of their buddies go missing and they become far more aware - a neat feature that really sells the idea that you're trying to outsmart people and not purely mechanical systems.
The range of difficulty settings and what they change is really nice - pushing you more and more towards a stealthy/ghosty playstyle the harder it gets.  This goes hand in hand with some nice score scaling - with avoidance being scored above confrontation, and containment being scored over escape.  It really pushes the correct ethos of a stealthy game without ever penalising you should you make a mistake, or simply not want to play that way (barring mission specific objectives cos PLOT happens).
It's nice to see the range and use of gadgets return to use and the loadout system is a neat idea - though I can't help but feel like so much of it is more or less completely pointless.  Some of these seem to exisit purely to make the game harder and for those that need to collect unlocks and achievement hunt.  I think the general idea is good, and it is nice to be able to actually pick your own gadget and weapon loadout rather than be forced to use things you don't like - however it feels like missed potential for some variation in tactical choices - rather than it essentially coming down to a handful of weapons/gadgets that are just going to be better most of the time.
I like the way they've handled the shorter replayable mission chunks for coop/solo play too - clear differences in the objectives and playstyle of each so you can pick a mission that suits the type of play you want at that moment.  This is something I really hope they expand and this might well be the first game I've ever bought where I really want them to release mission DLC.
The best praise I can give BL is that it's greatest failing is not capturing CT's tone - in many, many other ways it's a better and more evolved stealth game than CT ever was.

That, along with the fact that the fantastic structures are inhabited by painfully obvious RNG scripts (I won't dignify them with the term AI).
I feel that, if Starbound - with it's myriad of races and architecture - were a proper RPG, I might enjoy it much more. As it is, the main quest is 5 dungeons, and the settler quests are just RNG fetch/kill quests without any real narrative or reason to them.
Not to mention there's only 7 armors in the game, of which 3 are stat side-grades, and all the rest race-specific are re-skins; and all found/dropped armor is always stat-less cosmetic stuff as well... I don't know, the game just seems like it's made for social-minded people to screw around in. I'll give it a token play-through when it's launched, but I'm not holding my breath or anything.

You might have been expecting an actual review, but whether you’re grilling, baking, boiling or broiling, here are some helpful tips for making perfect spaghetti every time.
FOLLOW THESE STEPS
Boil water in a large pot
To make sure pasta doesn’t stick together, use at least 4 quarts of water for every pound of noodles.
Salt the water with at least a tablespoon—more is fine
The salty water adds flavor to the pasta.
Add pasta
Pour pasta into boiling water. Don’t break the pasta; it will soften up within 30 seconds and fit into the pot.
Stir the pasta
As the pasta starts to cook, stir it well with the tongs so the noodles don’t stick to each other (or the pot).
Test the pasta by tasting it
Follow the cooking time on the package, but always taste pasta before draining to make sure the texture is right. Pasta cooked properly should be al dente—a little chewy.
Drain the pasta
Drain cooked pasta well in a colander. If serving hot, add sauce right away; if you’re making a pasta salad, run noodles under cold water to stop the cooking.

Just have a look at the following cons:

I'm not usually one to write reviews for games, as I don't really consider myself a great critic, but this one deserves it.
I've been a fan of the Baldur's Gate series and played every game like it that I could get my hands on.  This game is loosely based on those, at least in it's style.  It's very D&Desque and I love it.
The class system is pretty simple, and the stats aren't overly complex like some games can make it.  The customization depth for your characters is fantastic, especially considering that even fully zoomed in you can't see nearly as much detail as the editor shows you on your character.  The campaign party members are fun, memorable, and endearing, and the voice acting is great.  But I think the part I've enjoyed the most is the vocabulary.  I'm not the most educated person, but I've read a lot of books, so it's not often I come across words that I've never seen before, and this game has thrown quite a few of those my way.  It's weird, but I actually enjoyed that part quite a bit.
But on to the actual game.  The gameplay is pretty simple, as I said it's very D&Desque.  If you've played any of the Black Isle PC games, you'll pick up on this one right away.  The classes are pretty well balanced, and like most games of it's type, the combat in the early game is quite challenging but once you get a good party rolling, it becomes much easier.  Balancing a team has been fun and easy, you have classes that very clearly fit in certian roles (tank: paladin or fighter) and while there are healing abilities, potions and spells, this game takes a twist on the typical HP/healing mechanic.  Which is confusing at first, but has added that extra something that makes this game stand out from the obvious sources of inspiration.
The equipment is great, too!  There are a few weapon types, and you can dual-wield, single-weapon, sword and shield, two-handed, range and all that, and no matter what ranged weapon you use, there's no need for ammo!  But even within each of those styles, there are different weapons, and those have their pros and cons (estoc is a two-handed sword, lower base damage than a great sword, but has damage reduction, which punches through some of the opponents armor).
The concept behind armor is also awesome.  Heavier armors give you more protection but reduce the frequency of your attacks, so while everyone can wear the highest defense armor without any training or skills required, the drawback is your team attacks much slower than if you put them in weaker armor.
And every piece of equipment can be customized through a very well thought out enchantment system.  You require ingredients which be found or bought, and you can make each piece of gear tailored you how you want it (assuming you have the right ingredients for the enchantments).
The combat is fun, and while most encounters aren't going to take a lot of strategizing, there are quite a few that make you pause and issue every single order as the battle unfolds, leaving only your most powerful and lucky characters standing afterwards.  You have the option to make custom characters for your party, so you can tailor the party to be EXACTLY what you want.  That being said, the game gives you characters in the storyline that fill every role in a party, so no matter what character you make, the party fills and balances nicely with whomever you choose.  There are definitely some good team make-ups, but since healing isn't exactly healing in this game, there's no "required" class (like how D&D requires a druid or cleric since there's no way you can get thru any series of fights without healing or you otherwise have to rest every fight).  You do need the classic roles of tank and DPS, but I've been running without a conventional healer and been doing just fine.
I don't even think I'm halfway through this game, and I'm loving every moment of it.  The only problems I've had with games of this type is how some fights are so ridiculously hard that they actually♥♥♥♥♥♥me off out of sheer frustration. This game flirts with that line.  There have been some downright insanely tough fights, but never overwhelmingly difficult where it makes me want to not play for a while, but rather restrategize and try again and again... and again.
Overall, this game is incredible, and I highly recommend it if you like RPGs.  If you're a fan of the old Black Isle games (Baldur's Gate, Icewind Dale) you HAVE to get this game!  Gripping story, fun characters, great mechanics, excellent customization options (and I don't just mean looks, but almost every aspect of the game let's you tailor to what you want) and this game is a definitely a must have.

First off, this game can start off really slow, almost at a crawl however after you reach the main city of Gran Soren the game really takes off, the character customisation - albeit a tad dated - still stands up especially in Dark Arisen where you have all the DLC.
The classes available are vaired and fun, you start off with the basic holy trinity (Warrior, Rogue and wizard) but as you progress 6 additional classes are added, three of which are unique to your main character alone - Magic Warrior being my personal favourite - on that note you also get a partner in crime in the form of your personal pawn who can be fully customised in terms of appearance and class you can also summon additional two pawns created by other playesrs (sometimes this can be a tad unfair if you summon high levelled pawns in low level areas)
The story is fairly basic, sing along if you haven't heard this already, "You are X person who - through no fault of his own - becomes a chosen hero who must fight against the forces of evil and goes on a valiant quest with a band of heroes."
The combat is fast paced and fun, which is to be expected when you have the creator of Devil May Cry on your team (Hideaki Itsuno) I have to mention one thing that really sat well with me however, in most fantasy games when you have a large two handed sword you swing it around as if it weighed nothing ans it doesn't feel like you're using it properly, but in Dragon's Dogma two handed swords looks, and feels like you have some real power in your swing, attacks have a slow built up and you have a good constitution so you can ward off light attacks, suffice to say you real feel like a tank. I also have to mention that you are able to climb onto large enemies Shadow of the Colossus style and can really lay into them.
All in all I can't express enough how much I like this game, highly recommend.

Eden, this is one of the best romance visual novels I've seen and enjoyed so far, it wasn't much of a fan service (which, was perfectly my taste, except for maya's part) but it mainly relies on it's story plot, normally visual novels would go with a steady story about love in different ways, not complete romance but with comedy and ecchi. Eden was different, in a lot of ways, it has emotions, it shows us how horrible humanity is, it shows us how would the world rot and it shows us how hope still exists in the darkest ways.
I've never gotten so addicted to reading a visual novel for 6 straight hours, slide by slide, munching on each and every word... Eden has reminded us of a lot of things, Ryou Haruna, the main character of Eden was a boy who had been given birth in a village on a certain mountain that gathered people that did not want to evacuate to space, eventually they began to fight back to the army since they were capturing them and evacuating to space, ofcourse a lot of them had gone "missing". After a certain while, one day a felix that had escaped from the No.703 Facility escaped to the mountain, her name was Natsume, who eventually became like a sister for Ryou, people started disappearing more and often, at the end even Ryou's' parents, the whole mountain was left with Nastume and Ryou, they had enjoyed the time, but it wasn't long. The No.703 facility staffs had traced her down and had forcibly taken her from Ryou, giving him ultimate despair and made him join the army, to see his sister again. A world where you can make an innocent child who just wants his sister that was going to die within a year, kill people, and by that I meant a lot of people, Ryou had stepped his way up the military and did everything he could, basically killing everything he can to reach Natsume, even his emotions, even his memories for Natsume, at the end all she did was left a shadow in Ryou's heart to keep fighting, but for no reason since she's already dead after a year she was captured back (felix's end of life span). In reality people keep hurting each and other every day, they take, they gain, but they lose as well, no one has ever thought of stopping, they hadn't, they couldn't, and that's how monsters were created, monsters to the society, but horribly sad.
Sion was another case, her very existence were a disgrace for humanity, the sadness she gave me was a kind that couldn't be expressed by tears, but rather, a smile that couldn't explain human emotions, it was sad, but also breaking my mind. Sion reminded us of the balance in the world, you take, someone gains, you enjoy, someone suffers, you live, someone dies, but the world isn't completely balanced as well, humans have broken it, they took away freedom to continue living, but they didn't give happiness, there were those who had happily evacuated to space, but there were also those who wanted to stay on earth no matter what comes next. I'll get straight to the point now, Sion was created for humanity's survival, she had led the evacuation project for 100 years, right when she finishes it, she wanted freedom, she wanted to try things on earth, try things for life, but the united government had taken that away, they wanted to keep her alive and show her off as hope, she had worked on for 100 years straight, no complaints, yet she couldn't enjoy freedom in her last few months of life. At the end, Sion did escape with Ryou, the government had to announce they found Sion dead in an accident for test, but Sion's death did not bring sorrow only, it also brought hope, it empowered people they have to keep moving on, to carry on the death wish of their savior...
Things have been completely ridiculous, the war that started before humanity was destroyed almost destroyed themselves, they never realise technology made life comforting but could also destroy humanity on another hand... I once thought about it but never made a fuss, now that I read Eden, it made me understood how selfish governments are, they wanted stable economics, society, but not people's happiness. Eden's definitely the game where you want to be sad, but as you feel sorrow, you might feel that you couldn't cry for it. (seems like at the end, Ryou had also broken down due to Sion's death)

Do not think of this as a game. Think of it as a novel. There are no choices to make. It's simply a linear story.
That said, it's a very interesting story and it's very well-told. The characters are nicely complex and nuanced, as is the overall plot. What I find most interesting is the way it puts a spin on the traditional concept of "moe" (which I usually abhor).
This is a love story, but it's not at all smutty. I can count the number of moments that come anywhere close to the usual fanservice that plagues anime and the like on the fingers of one hand.
The story got me to cry, but only because I let it. I went into this looking for an emotional binge of sorts, and that's exactly what I got. I also got a few more profound things to think about--not life-changing, but very interesting.
For what it is, I give it an A-. :)

I'll start off by saying that, spoiler alert,
However, with that out of the way, Middle-earth: Shadow of Mordor is some of the most fun I've had in a video game ever.
I've been a fan of this type of combat forever, the so-called Arkham combat/freeflow system type of thing, and the game utilizes this type of combat really, really well so I was immediately drawn to it. It's incredible how fun it is to murder orcs left and right in this game, absolutely astoundingly fun to play.
The story is engaging, the voice acting is great, the game is even hilarious if you listen in on orc conversations whilst hiding on a roof or in a bush or something.
The atmosphere is phenomenal, as is to be expected from anything Lord of the Rings-y in my opinion. The world is great, there's a bunch of things to learn and have fun with if you take your time to read item descriptions and stuff and if you're not into that, they even have voice acting for a bunch of item descriptions and lore that really helps immerse you in the game.
The game really comes into its own with the use of the Nemesis system. Essentially, the game's own built-in rank system of orcs that is affected by YOUR actions in the game, like who you murder, who you run away from, etc. It keeps the game sorta fresh and it separates it from a lot of other games in the same genre.
In short, Shadow of Mordor took the best parts from the Batman Arkham series and dropped it into a Lord of the Rings meets The Hobbit sandbox open world game and it's truly astounding how good the end result is. Highly recommended.

Lowering difficulty is not a problem, but the game was not adjusted to be both easier AND fun. It's just an unchallenging game that will probably bore you after a while, even if it is very short.
That is because the game misses the point that games like Mega Man had few levels because the difficulty was so high that it would take you a while to beat. This is short, easy and with few variations. But the soundtrack is not too bad. The problem is that if you're in the target audience for this game, you probably know of better games and expect something you won't get out of this.
And that is the biggest argument against this game. It's not that it's not that great, but it's that even at a price tag of only $9.99 compared to bigger budget titles, there are much better options everywhere at a lower or very similar price, like buying Mega Man X on Virtual Console or other retro-styled games like Super Meat Boy or VVVVVV or you could always just save that money for a higher costing but way better alternative.

Where do I start? The story in Blacklist is decent.. It's pretty much cliched from a lot of action movies.. IN terms it's pretty much 'Guy wants to end the reign of powe the USA has. You're our only hope for stopping him.'.. It's a decent plot but nothing you'll remember. However, the gameplay is what really shines in Blacklist.... Long time fans of Splinter Cell like me will feel right at home with this installment in terms of how it will take stealth gameplay... A variety of non lethal gadgets, google upgrades, level design centered around exploration and stealth, with so much more.. The game also takes your performance on three levels. Ghost, Panther, Assualt. Ghost is centered on all stealth. Avoiding enemy guards, non leathal takedowns, etc. Stealth in this game is the primary focus as playing in a manner for Ghost, will get you the most cash at the end for upgrades. Panther is still being sneaky but you take care of threats with lethal force. This includes but not limited to mines set up on patrol paths, using weapons, slitting a guard's throat, etc.. Assualt was created to appease the ones  who wanted to treat it as a 3rd person shooter... Anything from unsilenced AK-47s to grenades that set people on fire... However, Panther is the way to go in this game if you want to kill everything in your path..... The AI in Splinter Cell is not the greatest in the world but for a stealth game, it's probably my favorite. Killing a guard and leaving the body in the open, will have all surronding guards go on high alert. They will change all patrol patterns and begin to hunt you down. If you're spotted, you have a few seconds to take care of the guard before he can shout out that he found you and open fire... Conviction players will notice a few key gameplay elements taken from the game and put into Blacklist. Last known position, is a highlight of Fisher on his last location if the guards are firing on you. This also plays a key factor in Blacklist as well. Once guards find where you are at, all guns are on you and they will supress you. Depending on your location, they might try to go around and flank you or just throw a grenade in your direction. Mark n Excute is there as well, but I barely used it since most of the time, I was killing guards with my sexy knife. In all, Splinter Cell Blacklist will not be a great jumping off point if you're new to the series. However, fans of games like Chaos Theory will be in love with how much Ubisoft had pushed for the game to have stealth.

Y'know... After watching review video after review video on Youtube I originally thought this game wasn't worth even $5.00. However, after giving into the ever-so-attractive Steam sale, I decided to give it a go. I am impressed. The amount of freedom is great. I can choose where to stay, what supplies to collect, what defenses/assets to build, and who to play. Another great thing is that the freedom isn't too overwhelming either. I never felt lost, or confused as to what to do next. Everything was easily understood.
The graphics are decent. It's certainly not Dying Light quality graphics, but the visuals aren't ugly either. They're Xbox 360 quality graphics (since this is of course a PC port). Not saying that's bad, but it's not using the PC hardware's full potential. The combat is intense. You can easily get surrounded by a horde (or three is you're unlucky like me) and find yourself being pulled apart by a unique zed. However, the combat isn't too frustrating either. Sure, I've lost a couple good "Heroes"... Mainly because I decided to go it alone.
Now, one thing I thought was necessary but wasn't included was: Why can't I load supplies into vehicles? I wasted so much time driving back and forth from the home to a supply cache just picking up one bag at a time. If I could load said supplies into the bed/trunk of a truck/car that would be a great addition. Another rather frustrating piece to this game is the mouse sensitivity. One little jerk of the mouse sent the camera spinning at 3,000 miles per hour. The driving camera also, at times, was impossible to control.
Overall, I rate this a 7/10. The fun factor, free-style play, freedom of where to live and build, and multiple playable characters are great. The camera controls are very quirky at times, and driving back and forth over and over to clear a supply cache can become time consuming. However, these issues certainly don't hinder the fun-factor in this game. I recommend this to anyone who enjoys a good zombie survival game.

What gets to me is the way the story/main quest is structured.
Scan some decorations, do a dungeon. Repeat 4 times. Open the gate and [not available in nightly]. I'm sure that when it releases and all the lore books (now PGIs) are available, it would make it a bit more interesting. But as it is, relying on a bunch of text to make it more interesting is not the best approach. I'd much rather experience some things, it IS a game after all - albeit a sandbox.
My problem with the game's flow is that it's kinda bland. And unless whatever's behind the gate acts like a Wall of Flesh, ushering in all new monstrosities and gear, it's kinda meh.
That, along with the fact that the fantastic structures are inhabited by painfully obvious RNG scripts (I won't dignify them with the term AI).
I feel that, if Starbound - with it's myriad of races and architecture - were a proper RPG, I might enjoy it much more. As it is, the main quest is 5 dungeons, and the settler quests are just RNG fetch/kill quests without any real narrative or reason to them.
Not to mention there's only 7 armors in the game, of which 3 are stat side-grades, and all the rest race-specific are re-skins; and all found/dropped armor is always stat-less cosmetic stuff as well... I don't know, the game just seems like it's made for social-minded people to screw around in. I'll give it a token play-through when it's launched, but I'm not holding my breath or anything.

I would tentatively recommend this game, but anyone familiar with other Infinity Engine games (such as Baldur's Gate) should be aware that combat is a bit chaotic and silly/unpolished.
For example, 1vs2 fighters where you face two enemies (in the first town), one of them can engage you while you and the other enemy run in circles around the stationary guy. Forever. Similar pathfinding oddities are found throughout the game.
It doesn't help that targeting spells is unncessarily difficult due to the lengthy but random delay - for example, the same priest might be able to cast a heal spell immediately but incur a 5s delay at other times (compared to, say, Baldur's Gate where a fireball always takes 2.4s to cast).
You might also encounter large enemies who literally block your view of the entire party, making targeting spells impossible.
I also don't think that combat avoidance is done consistently enough to be a selling point - some enemies you can avoid, but you'll also be forced into unavoidable enouncters. The game loves to take your controls from you for this, leaving your party badly positioned in an ambush.
Save often, and be prepared to reload after cheap/ "bovine excrement" deaths because fights tend to fall into two categories:
1) Fights that can easily be beaten with reasonable strategy (use tanks to block chopepoints while you wittle down the enemy with 2nd line pikemen, archers and casters).
2) Fights that start with an enemy mind controlling your entire party, or with paralyzing your entire party, or stunning your entire party  - either way, everyone will be dead by the time you regain control of your cleric.

TL;DR: Game is great, but has some problems to be expected in EA. Overall: 8/10 (for early access)
Since many of the reviews that I've seen for this game are mostly people trying to be funny, or just people leaving reviews that are short, I decided to share my thoughts about this game as in depth as possible. That being said, this game is currently early access so of course it isn't complete. Normally I'm against buying games in EA or pre-order, but I couldn't resist this one. Also, this review was written with about 3 hours of gameplay under my belt. It may not seem like much time to get an idea of what a game is like, but with the limited content, I did almost everything you could. Anyway, let's begin:
Pros:
- Survival/Open world/exploration
- graphics are great, but still could be a little bit better
- very atmospheric and immersive even as it is
- day/night cycle
- random weather (really forces you to adapt in some situations)
- player is actually pretty hardy, doesn't die too easily (I haven't died yet with 3 hours of gameplay)
- supplies are scarce, just like they would be in a real situation like this
- sharks seem to be attracted to blood
- sharks add a great sense of fear when exploring the ocean
- really makes you feel like you have to survive by picking and choosing everything
- even the temporary UI looks great IMO
- night time isn't so dark you can't see, moon lights up the island a bit
- doesn't hold your hand, throws you right into it
Cons:
- VERY small islands
- no caves (devs, I would really love to see bigger islands with caves in this game)
- not much to craft
- not much to do (island hop and dive, forage for food - that's about it. It's survival, sure, but it feels like it's missing something still
- tiger sharks are SO aggressive. They'll constantly knock you off of your raft and force you to fight them to leave an island
- no other animals except for aquatics (fish, sharks, turtles, and stingrays - that's about it)
- some weapons are weaker than they should be (machete is almost useless for chopping down palm trees, use it for sharks only)
- very limited in what you can do/what there is to do
Now that is just a list of things that are good and bad about this game, as for my experience with the game, I must say that I'm impressed. The game itself is visually compelling - the underwater scenes are glorious and the textures are pretty great everywhere else. Also, it's VERY atmospheric. I really felt like I was lost on an island trying to survive while playing this game. That's a huge plus for me. I just wish that there was more to experience within the game. I would love to see bigger islands with cave systems that are inhabited by animals like rodents, monkeys, deer, etc. It would be really cool to be able to hunt and trap them. The items that you can craft are pretty functional, but other than the few items that you can craft, there's not much more you can do in that category which is a bit of a disappointment.
There were also a few bugs that I've come across like getting stuck inside your life raft, but after jumping, I was able to fix that. Also, sharks seem to defy the laws of physics, glitching right through the boundaries of shipwrecks occasionally. This can be a little scary when you're first starting out or in dire need of first aid.
Overall, this game is simply amazing, but I'm hoping that the devs expand on it quite a bit. I'm hoping to see a lot more content and a lot of interesting sites to explore.
A note to the devs:
Here are my suggestions for content, hopefully this is seen.
- CAVES - I really want to see this implemented
- bigger islands - the small islands are kind of boring, bigger would be better because then there's more to explore
- multi-storied shelters - ability to customize shelters in general really. Also, ladders and stairs.
- fishing - It would be great to be able to craft a fishing rod and fish with it
- hunting - bigger islands, throw in some animals and let us craft bows and traps. It would be epic.
- binoculars that actually work - Seriously though, currently they're useless.
- more items to eat/forage for - maybe add some banana trees and the likes
- SCUBA/snokel gear - I think some of this is already in the game, but if not, DO IT.
Thanks for the development of this game. I really enjoy playing it and it's a lot of fun!

- Not bad combat system, but still needs a lot of work
- Really creative items can be created (I love the respawn item and that if you kill somebody you can just put his/her head on a spike right infront of your house)
Cons:
- I think some of the mobs are way too powerful.
- Also they are glitchy (sometimes they just disappear)
- The spawn system is a joke currently. One island is full of animals and mobs and the other is just plain empty.
- There are a lot of materials that are not implemented yet (I never managed to find iron, gold, lion flower etc., but maybe I wasn't really lucky with them)
- The mining is just tedious
- It doesn't matter if you have a betterm hammer you won't be able to mine more or faster
- Terrible inventory system
- Not easy to play with your friend (can't create groups)
Overall:
Only buy this game if you are brave enough to bet on the developers for future updates. Currently I don't think it's worth 14,99 euros but definitely worth to buy it via Humble Bundle (as I did ;)).
I will update this review maybe a year later. I hope the devs will work on this game! :)

Review for alpha version 0.02.H1:
First of all, if you liked the movie "Cast Away" with Tom Hanks, you will love this game very much.
This game is just so beautiful, it has just extraordinary good graphics, very detailed and also the light- and shadow-effects look so good, you will fall in love with the sunrise/sundown and maybe with the bright shining moon, too. The whole carribean island setting is just amazing. Also the underwater-world is super detailed and beautiful. I haven't seen a game looking this good very often, especially when it's an early access alpha game.
You play a lone survivor stranded after a plane crash on the ocean. After landing on the first island with your life-raft, you have to do, what every survivor has to do in this situation: find water, find food, build a shelter, make a fire. You will find lots of resources to achieve your goals. Also you can search in the water for useful stuff, dive down and maybe you'll find a shipwreck and discover a real treasure (no gold). And of course you can also paddle to other islands around you, there are dozens of them, BUT watch out for the hungry SHARKS! They will overturn your raft (if you're lucky enough) and then you have real problems! Better get back on the raft ASAP!
In my current game (6,5 h) I survived for 9 days so far, found lots of food (crabbes, fish, potatoes, coconuts), crafted some tools, started to build a house and a bed and checked out a few islands.  I even got my raft flipped over by a shark (almost♥♥♥♥♥♥my pants), but was fast enough back on there.
And I still have to learn things to survive longer, there is just so much do discover already. Because in this game you have to find out everything yourself, there are no plans of how to craft this or that, you have to try it out, what I find pretty cool, just put every craftable item on a stack and see, what you can do.
Same with the exploring, just keep your eyes open for everything useful on land and in the water. I think, I still haven't seen all of this game yet, but I am very impressed so far!
I actually can't understand people, who rate this game negative, just because it's an alpha version and because there is so much work to do. People, it's an early access alpha build, just v 0.02, that means, the game is not finished and the developers want YOU to try the game and help them with the developing process by telling them what you like and what you would like to see in this game, report bugs and stuff! If you like the game so far, but think, it needs some work, than SAY IT, you can rate it positive AND say, what you don't like!
My conclusion: This game ist just amazing, very nice concept, great graphics and lots of things to do and to discover so far, even in this early stage. I bet, when it continues getting updated regularly, than this one will probably become the best survival game in gaming history, even if it takes a lot of time! I will wait for it!
And the 15 bucks for this game are well invested, because you will get everything that's still to come for free, a finished game of this kind will cost you at least 30 bucks! Actually, just the beauty of this game is worth the purchase!

I normally never write reviews, but with the amount of negitve reviews that I've seen for this game I have to weigh in on it.
First: this is an early access game, it does show, and there are definately areas for improvement, figureing out crafting is dificult, and sometimes you can easily forget that not everything you can craft show up in the main crafting interface. Played for awhile, but the gameplay is repetitive and unbalanced.
They added two new maps, one you fight over a dragon that can push like crazy (and later the standard soul essence dragon bonus), another has crates in the air crates so you need anti-air and later you can defeat & recruit the giant mechanoid thing.
My biggest qualm with the game is the balance. Balance is terrible, one of the worst I have seen. You have the units which are never seen or used because everybody knows they suck compared to the rets, then you have the "OMG this unit is so OP" because you have to essentially buy it with real money.
One of the units people will say is pay2win a lot if HEF flamer (the high ingame money/real money ver of flamethower guy), but is he? Yeah, pretty much he is. Before you upgrade your mines you gain 25 resources per second, basic units cost 100-200, flamer guy is around 400 and expect him to kill 800-900 worth of units before he kills over. Counters? Air units, flamer guy has no anti air, he can't pewpew (what's the sound effect for fire?).. fwoosh you while you're in the air! That's why you pair HEF flamer dude with cheap♥♥♥♥♥anti air units like sniper, this duo of sniper guy and HEF flamer dude will just zerg rush the map.
You now dominate the early to mid game, sure the enemy might try use another pay2win unit like sawblade slave against you but the great bromance of HEF flamer dude and sniper guy can not be torn apart by puny mortals.
If you have not won already then your ancestors are probably ashamed of you, but do not despair, now is not the time for seppuku. The enemy is mounting some type of counter force at there base, click missile strike (click bombing run if they are cheating/used telepathy) and blow up their counter forces.
Now all you need to do is mass produce marauders/butchers as your front line and siege tanks/ancille as your ever encroaching wall of ranged death. At this point the enemy will probably just stop building new units because your 20 siege tank/ancille wall is spawn camping anything that pops out. You can now walk off and pee/watch makeup tutorials by Michelle Phan, or try rearranging your desk feng shui until you get the victory pop up proclaiming you MVP.
Should your opponent be Terran and following the same path as you.., well then you just need to click faster than him, produce units quicker and row row fight the powa-cheating jerk who stole your build. You have a pop cap of 60 so flood the map with tanks.
Oh right, there are 3 races in this game, not just Terran. Atlac are the ninja themed race who produce flying whales and various colourful (mainly blue) cosplayers. They have an invis ninja melee unit, but he is crap compared to Terran infiltrator because he is ranged and deals pure damage (kills their late game units). They have the lowest population cap at 50 because their gimmick is they have energy shields. Atlac players will typcially field legions of ninja who will die instantly to HEF flamer and give a Terran player gold. They will be holding out for mid game where they produce their tanky unit Varja, and mix in some supporting range. Later on they may try to produce the aforementioned flying whales - these are really good, Atlac have likely have already already lost the match and not gained the 7200 resources needed to unlock their first whale or they unlocked them and they shot got shot down by the 7 Ancille the Terran player mass produced.
Atlac commander skills range from shooting orbital lasers at you, making their forces invisible, teleporting their next wave and being huge jerks and swapping your forces into their strongest tower.  Use false rally to make their waves walk into your towers.
The third race is Yaoguai, they have the biggest pop cap at 70, this is because most players just spam kamikaze sheep or beetles at you for awhile and then sell them to buy tanky bear vanguard or bone dragon/devourer.
Yaoguai have commander skills such as making a fish swim through the ground and bite you in a large aoe, Sacrifice that sucks in ALL biological units (including their own team) and then explodes - does not matter because you will have switched to mechanical tanks by the time they get the gold to use it, and mind control which only has half the duration on mechanical tanks. They have shuriken panda which are good vs mechanical and can shred through tanks up close, and Markcat that uses AoE to bomb areas with arrows - potentially killing off a lot of your infantry.
So I played all 3 races, in all seriousness I found Yaoguai the most fun and versatile to play, followed by Atlac, but playing Terran was the most boring and OP. Game balance is pretty screwed up, I like the game concept and kind of want to change it to recommended, but I just got so bored.
If you play the 3v3 ranked mode (take turns producing units) then be prepared to get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off, first you have to spend time waiting for a match, then the ban commander skill, ban unit phase, then *each* person has like a whole 60 seconds to choose their 3 commander skills and which race they will play, so if you are like player 5 then you may end up waiting 4-5 minutes..., and then.. player six does not click ready and you have to go queue all over again, turns out that same guy is in this lobby too and..he forgot to click ready again and you have to queue again. Does not happen all the time, but happens a fair bit, so if you play then choose 1v1.
On the positive side, I heart the little unit forces, and some of the designs are pretty cool. I read all the Sun Tzu quotes on the start splash screen so I am not a master of warfare.
So yeah, the game is free and it is early access, if they can fix the balance issues on some of the paid units and balancing out the races & commander skills (+ the lobby problems) then I'd recommend it. It is pretty dull to spam the same units to win matches and you a loss.
One thing the developers could consider is putting a cap on certain units so they can't be spammed and it'd force players to make more mixed armies to support them.

This game has gone in the wrong direction since the beta.
I wont cover microtransactions of power because thats pointless to argue at this point (aka should be astetic only not power ie. buying all the best units first and stomp all new players and no one ever fixes it)
Lets be clear first, alot of what was in beta was overpowered I think many of us can agree.
But the attempts to balance things while headed in the right direction, is moving down rather then up.
The difference of power is too skewed now between the factions.
Many units feel either too weak now or too strong, and any effort to counter them with units that take advantage of their particular weekness also falls short too often in my experience.
Unique units within the factions seem to have done a 180 since the beta as well, those units that no one built since then are now the only units people build.
Over spamming of a particular unit is a problem more so now then back in beta, for a game that advertises STRATAGY, there is very little of it here.  You can win by either spamming a very strong early game unit or wait till late game and spam one end game unit till the cows come home and just simply steam roll an opponent.
There needs to be a proper balance set of damage/support/tank/utility units to provide you with the gameplay you wish to use.  This is underminded when you can spam sky yoshies and eat litterally the entire wave before they get to attack.
One method to balance this was reducing population count and wave stacking limits, however this too seems to have failed.  The population cap is not EQUAL for each faction, so one faction will get a population advantage or disadvantage naturally.  The wave spawn limit is only restricted to population PER WAVE, the game does not recognize when the stacking as reached such a porportional advantage to the winning player, that not only is continuous spawning redundent, but the ability for the loosing player to have any hope of pushing back is almost impossible if not so.  Now if its clear that the loosing player is going to loose reguardless thats because they were unable to outplay their opponent, but when the battles become so one sided within the first 10 waves, I see a huge problem.
The defence turrets need to be stronger I feel.  As mentioned before for the game to be over so fast, the only means of padding for players to figure out what needs to be built is to fragile to be conciderd an "assist." Sieging should be a result of a player being able to produce a powerful wave that is able to crush the counterplay options of the defending player.
This ultimately results in COMPOSITION, it sould not be based on the fact that I spammed the crap out of an advanced unit or strong basic unit that can attack both land and air to the point that it is my ONLY army unit.
I would rate this game 6/10 because the core of the game is good and I'm obsessed with the Atlac faction's art design...but the game just has to many fundamental and superficial weaknesses for me to reccomend it in its current state.

Bastion is a beautiful game. Each of the stages are hand painted and if you stop and look at them the detail is clearly there. That being said, very few of the stages stuck out or were memorable for me. Some were notably different (Jawson's Bog, Roathus Lagoon, Colford Cauldron) but everything in between kind of blurs together, as most of them have a “grassy ruins” motif. Thematically this is excusable because the Calamity did send Caelondia into ruin. I imagine a lot of it is probably just shambled buildings in easily inhabited places like grasslands or forests. This didn’t necessarily make for a boring time, as I did like the overall aesthetic. A majority of the enemies encountered are not exclusive to one area and a lot of ground patterns are similar, so I would have liked some more distinct features that really make each area it’s own.
Whether you love it or hate it, the narrator is what truly made Bastion a unique game. I had never played a game where instead of reading most of my exposition, a real time narrator told me what was going on. Every tonic, every idol, every weapon, there was a specific voice line that tied in a tidbit of flavor. It helped flush out the world in my mind. Logan Cunningham truly did a great job as the voice of Rucks.
The plot is relatively simple, which I can understand being boring for some people. I like the concept of scavenging and exploring, especially in a post-apocalyptic setting, so I wasn’t disinterested in the game by any lack of depth in narrative. Most of the characters have little development but I still felt that I was able to sympathize with them. Oddly enough, the characters being flat actually worked for me. Everyone is somber and only let small personality quirks seep out. These are defeated people. Having their world in shambles is enough for me to justify them having meager personalities. Whether that’s subtle design or laziness is up to you.
This is one of the best parts of the game. It helps set the tone so well, all I can say is if the demo isn’t enough to influence your decision on picking this up, search the OST on Youtube. Even in a lot of the “Would not Reccomend” reviews, many say they enjoyed it regardless of their overall opinion of the game.
Combat felt tense (as it should be most of the time) and sometimes frustrating. To an extent it reminded me of Dark Souls. It is rather unforgiving which encourages you to not just mindlessly dodge roll around the platforms. You have a limited number of healing potions and if you die, you have to restart the entire level. Button configuration can be cumbersome if you’re not used to it. It definitely took me a bit of practice to get it down before I felt like I had a good muscle memory (I was using a keyboard and mouse). I’m sure this will be a big turn off for people who want more simple gameplay.
Once and awhile certain ranged weapons had a hard time hitting enemies despite my cursor being exactly on top of them. The actual hitbox would be immediately around the enemy and would change color appropriately (teal to red). Occasionally I would be able to walk over small holes in the ground, making for some inconsistency in what parts of platforms you can and can’t fall through. These things happened infrequently for me, but felt like they were worth mentioning.
The variety of weapons in the game is nice, although there were a couple that I felt were not as good as the rest. There were a couple configurations that I liked switching between, but not a single combination that I felt was the “best.” Levels do force you to use newly found weapons for a period of time, but as long as you’re attentive you can find an Arsenal that will let you switch back if you don’t like it. It’s also important to note that once you’ve bought an upgrade for a weapon in the Forge, you can change it to the second choice in that tier for free. Many games punish you for making the wrong choice by charging for a skill reset, so I appreciated that flexibility.
The Idols were the one thing I found myself having to look up. There is a general description of what they do, but no specifics on how the mechanics work. Unless you want a challenge I would suggest not using them. You find plenty of fragments normally throughout the game so the minor bonus they provide was not worth the powerful drawbacks. I think the only one I had on the entire game was Pyth.
I don’t think Bastion is an amazing game, but it is rather good.

I've played through this game a couple times now, it gets more and more interesting as you learn and pick things up you didn't in previous playthroughs.
It's one of those games you need to play at least twice.
The Stranger narrates your way through the story, you'll que some voice lines that you may not otherwise by doing things like smashing objects picking certain weapon combinations. He'll tell you stories and hum and give you funny little quips from time to time.
The soundtrack is amazing, it's got everything from banjo to violin to piano back to electric guitar. All of it is origional music by a man named Darren Korb, and I reccomend checking it out even if you don't play the game (it's free on YouTube!) My favorite is "Brusher Patrol," personally.
And the artwork looks like it's painted, I've stopped to stare at the background just because it's so pretty - plants that swirl, rocks that float, skeletons of monsters I'd dare not meet in a dark alleyway. My only issue with this is that because the background is so nice The Kid (your character) looks a little out of place, like they ran out of time to make his character model more polished. That being said, however, all of the other characters look nice and fluid.
This game doesn't have any "hard mode" or "nightmare night" levels, it's as hard as you make it through a system I very much like - The Pantheon. If you feel like you've mastered the game, just pray to the gods and boy howdy will they ruin that thought for you. Enemies that regenerate, become untouchable, reflect attacks, and - oh yes - explode.
I reccomend this game to anyone looking for a game that's not Tripple A, big title, shoot-em-up. A game that's story heavy and beautiful, one that brings you back time and again. That being said, this is only an 8-10 hour game (depending on how long you stop and smell the stinkweed) so it's a shorter game. There's no hidden levels or puzzle solving or "complete this mode and unlock this other mode!"
There are Proving Grounds to complete and journeys to Who Knows Where that will get you more materials and story, fleshing out the characters and places.
You know - just play it already, Check out other Supergiant games if you like this one, they're a small company and could use all the support they can get.

Bastion is a combat focused RPG set in a post-apocalyptic world. You play as someone only referred to as "The Kid", and start the game on a floating rock in the sky with no explanation as to why or how you are there. A lot of the game's charm comes from its narrator, who reveals all the mysteries of the Calamity throughout your play through.
The game is great, but I would only recommend it if you enjoy playing a game for the story. Otherwise the games minor flaws will point themselves out to you and ruin your experience. Highly recommend if you love story driven RPG's, this is a must play for you.

Got the game on sale for something like 10 or 20 USD. What I found was amazing, almost making me regret not paying full price.
Following the (very arguable) failure of Total War: Rome II, CA (creative assembly) released Total War: ATILLA.
They set forth looking to fix the failure of Rome II, but what they did was instead so much better than a mere fix. What I found instead was something astounding, I never thought to see ALL of these features jam packed into the VANILLA game. You can migrate to a new territory when you lose everything or even start out as an actual rebellion via one of the tribes, or fight as the great huns or even the roman empire(s, west and east) themselves, all via vanilla standard purchase.  All of the graphical bugs as far as I have seen from Rome II are fixed, and even vastly improved. Throws my GPU out of the water after taking a sledgehammer to it. And my generation is only a few years old- as in, it's the 4th or mabye 5th best on the market as of writing this. This isn't because the game is not optimized, but because the graphics are that good.
Music is vastly imrpoved in my opinion too, unlike the second rome game where I had to use the first romes music to feel truly immersed, this has its own music set that does it just fine. The attention to detail is amazing, you can actually see the townspeople flee in terror when you are sieging, and they made it so towers and gates are not borderline invincable (Rome 2 >.>)
You can literally burn entire regions to ashes and destroy entire settlements, never to be inhabited again.
Overall, I'd rate it a 10/10.

"On this quiet, ending world... I'm experiencing my first and final love."
In general, the opinion of people regarding visual novels is that of disgust due to it's association with it's 18+ counterparts and games like nekopara. (Not that they are necessarily bad games).
eden* however, is a completely different kind of novel from the differently garbed anime girls throwing themselves at the protagonist's feet in a different interpretation of love.
The basic premise of eden* is a love story between two very different individuals.
Right off the bat, from the preview alone, the art, the music, the smooth animation already grabbed my attention.  Believing it to be a truly exceptional work, I wanted a copy of eden* the minute I saw it.
It lived up to my expectations.
Yes, it isn't perfect, the upsize/fullscreen isn't as good, the characters eyes are a little too large for my liking.
But still, in spite of all that, eden* delivers, and what a story it has delivered. The art, the characters, the voice acting, the music, the CGs, the finale and more. Each and every bit of eden* delivers and brings the story to life. To me, the story is not particularly long, at 7-8 hours, yet in game, that time is both fleeting and eternal. At times it feels so excruciatingly long, and at times it passes by so quickly.
And the ending, my sweet merciful (whatever religious figure you believe in or don't for that matter), the ending. Though the read through left me with a sense of melancholy and sorrow at times, at the ending i do not believe it's possible not to shed a few tears.
Words alone cannot convey what a wonderful piece of work eden* is.
Words alone cannot convey what a touching tale eden* is.
I highly recommend it.

The quality of this game depends on when you joined the TOTAL WAR series. I joined with Medieval Total War II. There will always be bias towards or against a game based on previous editions of the series. For those of you coming into this without playing the rest of TOTAL WAR you will be pleasantly surprised with a decent, challenging game. There is a lot to focus on all at once and you will stay busy on the battlefield or with politcal events.
For those of you who have been playing the rest of the series, I recommend this game with a bit of caution. The political system is revamped and makes it seem like more of an empire building game than a war game. If your preference is more war oriented, it will be hard to focus on just that. Faction politics does require attention. The game does have nifty new details to keep track of a legions health, integrity, etc. Also, the skill tree for characters and legions is much better designed. Instead of seeing options a few at a time when leveling up, you can see the whole skill tree so you can plan ahead of time.

I've played and loved all Splinter Cell games since it's debut in 2002. This one is at least as good as Chaos Theory. Awesome story, flawless gameplay, many upgrades for weapons and gadgets. A tense atmosphere and super exciting locations (breaking in and out of Guantanamo Bay, holy ****).
The Multiplayer is intense, the coop levels differ a little in quality. The best once are the 'coop-only' missions. I haven't enjoyed playing coop in a game that much since ... well... ever.
There a few downs though:
The graphics are a little outdated, especially the facial animations are really bad (Sam is an exception). That doesn't bother much but the game runs comparably slow (which was already a problem in Conviction).
The two DLC contain about 20 items. 3 suits and one weapon are usable, the rest of them is absolutely useless because you unlock much better stuff after a few hours of playing.
The biggest problem for me personally is Micheal Ironside not being the voice of Sam. That alone cost a lot of atmosphere and somehow deminishes the 'Splinter Cell feeling'.

Respect of previous releases, this Splinter Cell sets appart. Not so linear as the previous ones and, more based in small missions, that together form an story but, with way less depth than in previous ones.
But, action has been clearly enhanced and, the game has now some kind of RPG mix, allowing you to evolute your suit and weapons, as well as the headquarter technology to help you in future missions.
Each mission gives you points, depending on several characteristics, and those points are used to improve your gear and gadgets, what is an interesting approach.
Movements of Sam are perfect, very fluid and realistic.
New interesting Multiplayer games, with some surprise challenges in the ShadowNet (some kind of aleatory or special missions).

State of Decay is thrilling. You're dropped into a zombie infestation and forced to manage your resources and survivors. There are various missions that pop up alongside to main story and if you ignore them your survivors can get injured or die. The zombies are easy enough to deal with, but if you're out on your own and you make too much noise you can find yourself being swarmed by all sides. A few lucky grapples by the zombies can leave you in an undead dogpile, slowly being torn to shreds. Once a character is dead it is gone forever.
There have been times where I find myself surrounded and being beat down, and after barely knocking them off I stumble towards a car out o breath, zombies running after me and trying to grab me. One bite away from death I get into the car and drive off with several zombies hanging on banging at the doors. I can't remember the last time a game has made my heart race so much. There is so much character development and macro management in this game that you really feel like you're "surviving" rather than adventuring.
Now for the flaws. The game is riddled with bugs. It's annoying to be heading into a dangerous area only to have your partner teleport back to base for an "Angry resident" mission. The zombies often clip through walls and into the floor. Sounds don't always play and cars can get damaged on invisible bumps. But none of the bugs are really gamebreaking and they're easy to shrug off. The resource management part of the game is too simple. There's supposed to be some sort of resource usage where some of your food/ammo/medicine are used up each day, but it seems like I'm always at max resources and the only thing I ever NEED to gather is building supplies for more upgrades at base. Because of this there's always more than enough time to do every side mission and there's no sense of urgency in the game.
A few minor tweaks could make the game so much more difficult and so much more exciting. Side missions should force you to choose between saving a survivor or gathering necessary resources (think XCOM). Outposts should require a person there to be useful (instead of giving resources and killing zombies as an autonomous house), making you trade labor for safety. Resources should decay faster so you actually have to spend time scavenging inbetween or during missions. There are a limited amount of resources on the map but I haven't even come close to depleting them all. Before I moved my base to a new town I still had unsearched houses a two minute walk away.
Overall the mechanics of the game are solid. THe game is enjoyable and exciting. With a few tweaks to make it harder could make it a game of the year. If you're thinking about buying it, buy it. If you'e not, buy it anyway.
