Amazing Open-World Survival type of Zombie game.
It's not really about if you can survive with a single character. You are able to control different characters, equip them with weapons and such. Your characters get tired from running, killing and scavenging. So you have to be careful not to get exhausted while you are too far from home.
It also comes down to having enough supplies for your community to survive as well. Make sure your 'Home' is safe and that everything has enough food, ammo and medical supplies.
You can send out members of your community to scavenge places, but be prepared to come to their rescue if they get in trouble.
Different take on the Zombie Apocalypse, not about killing as many zombies as you can or surviving for as long as you can with a individual character. But make sure your whole group survives and do as good as possible.
I strongly recommend this game to anyone a fan of Zombie Survival type of games, and don't mind having to manage supplies and your playable characters, making sure they are not too exhausted.

You take over towers & try to cover the map (sort of like being the prom king or voted most successful kid at your high school). You play as Celebrimbor & are against a character who I believe is your uncle? Anyways, that is pretty fun stuff. It is all very, very political & there is loads of intrigue and suspense as to how things are going to go. There are couples, coalitions are formed & disbanded, there's rivalries, long-running dramas, it's pretty interesting, this world.
Sorry but the Nemesis system is stupid & discourages people from trying because the punishment for failure is too severe. Makes people too cautious. I can say that now because the new game from that developer, Mad Max, is fairly similar in a lot of ways but doesn't have the nemesis system. You complete missions for money for car parts, gas & food, & you have a pad you live in with people you are affiliated with, & the gameplay is fun even if things get stale after a few hours
Storyline: I found the set up plot where I see the character's wife get captured & get a sense for why he is doing all the things he is doing to be the best part of the game, & that exposition took place right away & then I was able to do my own thing with that in mind. That was of great interest to me. The story is an open-world simulation of Middle-Earth where you complete goals for cash, XP points which you use to make changes to your character, & new gear.
In any case, I've thought about these topics quite a bit & came to the conclusion that the negatives outweighed the positives & I turned my attention to different games that were more well-thought out, specifically Max Payne 3 & Depth

You might have been expecting an actual review, but whether you’re grilling, baking, boiling or broiling, here are some helpful tips for making perfect spaghetti every time.
FOLLOW THESE STEPS
Boil water in a large pot
To make sure pasta doesn’t stick together, use at least 4 quarts of water for every pound of noodles.
Salt the water with at least a tablespoon—more is fine
The salty water adds flavor to the pasta.
Add pasta
Pour pasta into boiling water. Don’t break the pasta; it will soften up within 30 seconds and fit into the pot.
Stir the pasta
As the pasta starts to cook, stir it well with the tongs so the noodles don’t stick to each other (or the pot).
Test the pasta by tasting it
Follow the cooking time on the package, but always taste pasta before draining to make sure the texture is right. Pasta cooked properly should be al dente—a little chewy.
Drain the pasta
Drain cooked pasta well in a colander. If serving hot, add sauce right away; if you’re making a pasta salad, run noodles under cold water to stop the cooking.

So... at this point I've put in about 45 minutes of time into the game. Let me tell you of my first 45 minutes. I spawned on the beach somewhere. I proceeded to run around for a bit and eventually figured out the preset controls for this game are pretty darn funky. I fixed them to the best of my ability and carried on. I found some remote houses and found some alright loot, nothing too note worthy. Kept looking around, looted a log yard and a cell tower. Eventually my eyes layed apon the greatest sight I was yet to see in the game. A town. I rushed to the town, each step filled with uncontrollable amounts of exictement. There was loot in the town. And I was here to take it. First a gas station, then some houses, a parking lot, and a crashed helicopter. I eventually found myself in a clothes store, ready to get myself a new look. But little did I know that the greatest thing I'd ever seen in the game was in that store. A sheriff's hat. As soon as I saw it I knew what my responsibilites were. I must become the sheriff of this town. Who was going to defend it if I didn't?
With a new found purpose in my step, I continued scavenging the town for useful supplies. For whatever reason, after I put that hat on, I began to find the clothes that any respectable sheriff would wear. Boots, gloves, even some sunglasses. Then, in the third story of an apartment building, my first firearm. A bolt action rifle of some kind. I knew it was a sign. It was destiny that I was here. I was meant to be the champion of this town. Out the front door and down the street I went. House after house I sifted through looking for the means to defend this town and myself. It was when I was on the fire escape of another apartment when I saw a car drive by. Want to take a guess at the type of car? None other then a cop car.
I knew that I couldn't let the driver leave without somehow interacting with him. My fingers raced over the keyboard as I told them that I was here and who I was. "Sheriff of this town" is who I said I was. When I saw them turning the car around to come back down the street, I turned and raced down the apartment stairs out to the street. Slowly the car approached me... I was ready.. Justice was going to be served one way or another. My game then immediately prompted to crash and turn my screen black.
10/10 would sheriff again.

I'm not much of a review writer (I think I've written maybe two before this one), but...this game's deserving of a good review, and as I finished my first playthrough earlier today it seemed the ideal time. Unfortunately, I'm not a wordy person, so I'll point out some quick bits and leave the description of the plot out apart from some very simple comparison to its grandparents:
Story - 6/5. Seriously, it's so multi-faceted, between the main questline and all of the side quests, it's the type of story we haven't seen since the good old days of cRPGs (aka Pillars' grandparents!). Other, more recent RPGs are definitely steered towards the action side of things, and while the Bethesda games do have a fairly expansive story/lore (well, fond memories are especially coming to mind about Morrowind when I'm thinking of that), there's just something great about a game's story relying a lot on making the player read.
Combat - 5/5. I've never been the best at party-based RPGs (though they're very probably my favorite style, go figure), but playing through this game has been a real learning experience. While it's not super dense, it's not too simplistic either, and it allows you to play it however you will. Eventually I got to the point where I could tell which battles required strategy to win decisively and which I could just essentially auto-smash. The variety of combat styles available through the different character classes is great, and the two unique classes added to the eschelon were fun and interesting to learn and play. There was only one battle which I ended up taking an alternative method to solving...needless to say, I tried to persevere and win it out through blood and steel, but all that was happening was my party's blood was being spilled at alarming rates and their steel was being dropped by their limp, lifeless corpses.
Non-combat gameplay/exploration - 4.5/5. One of the first things which really impressed me about the game is how a character's stats and skills regularly affect gameplay outside of combat. Whether it be in conversations or scripted events or what have you, I regularly saw options I couldn't go with (a few of which unfortunately made my character act contrary to the sort of personality I'd developed for him throughout the game) and many which I could. My only complaint about this system, and it's a small one since in reality it just gives me more reason to go back and play again as different styles of characters, is that none of your companions' stats or skills can be used in any of these situations. I understand that your PC is, of course, front and center and does most of the talking, but I found myself wishing on occasion that I could have had my companions weigh in a bit more.
Pets - unrated/5. I didn't, in all honesty, see the point of having the pets around. They didn't detract from the experience at all, but they didn't add to it much for me either. They just sort of followed us around, all behaving as placidly as the others while all sorts of crazy situations unfolded around them.
Stronghold - 4.5/5. Only complaint about the stronghold is
. I enjoyed piecing the place together, and it added a fun little side-mechanic to distract me on occasion.
Music - 5/5. When it needed to be atmospheric, it was atmospheric. When it needed to be a bit tense and...battle...ish....it was that. The music was well composed, varied and interesting.
Graphics - 5/5. I love this style!
Replayability - 5/5. The amount of variation possible between playthroughs is obscene depending on race/background/class/personality/decisions/penchance for violence/completist attitude/etc etc etc.
There are still a few bugs/glitches/typos in the game, but I know the guys at Obsidian are working on getting it all ironed out.
Final thoughts - I can't wait to get around to playing through this again, though I'm going to take some time off between playthroughs so I don't tire myself out of it (and so I can give some much needed attention to other games I've bought lately). I saw an interview with one of the creators stating that they're already working on putting together a story for a substantial expansion (YES!), akin to those expansions from all the older classics of the genre. This game, man. It's worth your time and money if you're into this sort of thing, and it's got me eagerly awaiting any future developments. A game destined to remain in the glorious halls of classics.
TL;DR: 5/5!

Pillars of Eternity is one of the best RPGs I've played. It's far from perfect - there are certainly things I were disappointed by or felt could have been done better. The stronghold is poorly implemented and mostly busywork. Items can sometimes be a little boring. The AoE radius of spells seem to be distributed haphazardly, almost randomly, balance-wise. And for my laptop at least, loading-screens take a bit long at 5 - 10 seconds - especially annoying at the aforementioned stronghold where heading to the inn for resting and then out to adventure again will take at least 6 of said loading screens. And I have some disagreements with decisions made by the dev-team stemming mostly from my own subjective likes and dislikes. Any of these could get fixed or improved through patches and expansions, but they might also not be.
Don't let any of these nit-picking complaints prevent you from playing though! In most respect, it's a lovingly crafted game, with fun combat (although I suppose a caveat that I, unlike apparently many, like the RTwP system a LOT should be added here) vastly improved from its Infinity Engine origins, an immersive setting clearly crafted with love from its admittedly somewhat generic base concept and now brimming with its own characterization, interesting story and lkeable characters makes it a very solid game indeed. I've certainly not regretted buying it at any point, and while I hope any future expansions or sequels will improve on the game and work out the kinks that always come with new games in new engines, I can nevertheless heartily recomment Pillars of Eternity for any RPG fan!

Ah the binding of isaac, this game has come a long way from newgrounds and I can't express enough how much I love this game. Here is a basic short overview of what this game gives you if you buy.
Story: TL;DR your mom has to kill you you are scared by that and you try to escape only to find a trap door instead, In this trap door is where the game starts, simple and easy to understand.
Gameplay: This game resembles the legend of zelda by a mile so if you like the dungeons of zelda then this game will feel like home. Each time you play you get a different seed (level layouts) so this makes the game feel new all the time.
Fun Factor: This game at least for me reaches really high levels of fun since I enjoy the legend of zelda alot so once again if you dont like zelda or anything like it you might want to pass on this game, but that being said getting crazy item combos is always a blast.
Not So Fun Factor: Some runs take a really long time to finish once you unlock more chapters, also in the challenges if you pick up an item you have not seen it wont count toward certain achievements. I understand for alot of the challenges but the challenge purist should be able to count, these are just nitpicks but I can't say theres nothing wrong :p
Difficulty: This game starts off normal but gets harder as you go on unlocking more areas to go to each run. The real hard ships come from the characters more so since there are easy and hard characters to choose, like isaac is an easy character and blue baby is a harder character etc. Also theres a normal mode and a hard mode which makes it so anybody can play as they choose, I always play hard mode since it only chooses more difficult rooms and make less heart drops. But for tips and tricks I cant really say much since its a pretty clean game so just keep playing and you will get the hang of it. try to not get hit no matter what but once you start to get better try different harder characters to master isaac.
End Game Content: Well as of writing this review afterbirth+ has 2 days to come out so thats 1 thing but before that dlc there was afterbirth whitch came out a year ago. There are lots of achievements to get lots of items to unlock and once afterbirth+ comes out, there will be a infinite amount of content to make and download form others since that comes with a room editor and other mod tools. I highly recommend getting 2 dlcs and the soundtrack too its really good and the dlcs are amazing you will get plenty of hours from this game even without the dlcs but more with them!
Wrap up: So all in all this game is a wonderful rouge like zelda game whitch inspired lots of other games to give this genre a try, so I fully recommend this game to anyone who enjoys that sort of thing I know I do!

*Basic knowledge shown from the beginning of the game is revealed in this review*
8/10: Soundtrack
The soundtrack is nice, but never stands out. It matches with the mood quite well and is never irritating.
11/10 Visuals: A kinetic novel always needs less work, however, the opening and the animated visuals with multi CGs are still fantastic. The amount of CGs make me forget that they're even considered CGs because it feels like it blends in with the story so well along with its frequency. Their mouths move and they blink in every single scene. That is absolutely amazing effort. The opening looks like an anime. The art is so beautiful and impressive.
10/10 Atmosphere: The writing style, audio and visuals were put together to create such an amazing atmosphere. It may be just a kinetic novel, but the way this visual novel was made creates such an amazing atmosphere. When they were in the mountains, I felt ultimately relaxed, but when they were in the facility, I felt more tense. This adds to the feeling of the reader to emphasize with those who stayed in the mansion for so long.
9/10 Plot: Almost a masterpiece! The plot is quite sensical, however only a few small things were never explained. The small things unexplained were not the main point of the plot, so know not to worry. A majority of the plot was explained. The plot is quite sensible and consistent. When I expected the plot to end, it wasn't even close to the end, in fact they covered a majority of plot holes. The plot went about excitingly or gently, never rushed.
9/10 Characters: The character development was magnificent and each character has more to them than just their looks. Every character shows their stupidity and smarts in different subjects. Their intelligence is also consistent, as well as their personality. Every small thing said shows each character's personality. Each character has a voice actor. They all have clear and voices that match the tone of the scene. Their emotions are easily felt with each character's feelings. By the end, every single character has their endings explained.
9.5/10 Overall: Needless to say, amazing work.

Total War: Attila has contained some of the most most unique and fun strategy gameplay I've ever experienced. In most strategy games, strategy is all that matters. Army comp, numbers, etc. But with the Total War series, a good General can exploit real world advantages, such as terrain, weathering, and deployment of units. Instead of Starcraft-esque battle ball, Total War employs high risk chess moves, feinting a flank or hiding units in forest, deceiving the enemy until the proper time to lay the crushing blow. If you are at all interested in this game, I suggest giving it a try. The learning curve has been a bit steep in the first 24 hours or so of gameplay, but I currently am spreading time between 3 separate campaigns and am excited to play each for very different reasons.
Not a perfect game, but overall is good. Recommended.

State of Decay is an open world zombie game where you get to swap around from survivor to survivor, trying to build up your home base and keep as many people alive as possible. There's some story in here too, but it's not why you came here. You came to kick zombies in the head!

Other zombie games out there are either:
1. Completely broken (The WarZ, DayZ) and unplayable
2. Way too hardcore and punishing, not for having fun, and only multiplayer (Project Zomboid, Rust, DayZ, Left 4 Dead series, etc...)
3. Lacking all kinds of features that make it a fully fledged open world survival game (all of the aforementioned)
This game not only is immersive (singleplayer only) is playable and doesn't have many bugs, and gives you the "fun" factor that is missing in all of the other zombie games, you get to actually experience killing zombies without dying in 2 hits or being killed by another player for the lulz. Permadeath is a thing in this game, but you will barely experience it.
Some people will not like it to not be very challenging, thus the DLC came with, enhanced difficulty and other options.
All in all, a very fun open world survival game that deserves your time.

If you like zombie slaying and saving survivors, but always wanted the experience to be a bit more personal, this game is for you.

Time becomes a big issue in this game, you won't have enough of it be everywhere and do everything, some things simply have to be prioritized. You may WANT to help those farmers out, but you have a team member in trouble and your base is nearly out of food and ammo...
All up, SoD is a pretty well rounded sandboxey survivor sim. Few bugs to speak of, and I've never felt this invested in a zombie game before.  Definite thumbs up.

While I've only sunk maybe 15-20 hours into this game so far, what I can say is this:
If you like crafting, collecting, building, rich lore and space exploration, this is a game you'd be into. After a long, long love afair with Stardew Valley and some difficulty getting my head wrapped around this games somewhat sticky controls, I can see myself sinking further and further both in time and immersion with this fantastic game. Filling in the gaps between Stardew Valley, Minecraft, Terraria, and No Man's Sky, Starbound is both an amalgamation of these engines and games while existing as its own bright star among dozens of similar crafting-sandbox-type releases. For me, it's one of those games that I'm thinking about and planning for while I'm not playing. Where to go next? What to build next? What resources to mine or grow?
The storyline, while I haven't completed it, and the quest structures are admittedly a little boring and repetitive, but I don't believe that significantly affects the gameplay or the player's freedom to sink time into what they're into, be it collection, building, or collecting fuel (a terrifiying, anxiety-inducing venture, just you see) and crusing through the universe.

What gets to me is the way the story/main quest is structured.
Scan some decorations, do a dungeon. Repeat 4 times. Open the gate and [not available in nightly]. I'm sure that when it releases and all the lore books (now PGIs) are available, it would make it a bit more interesting. But as it is, relying on a bunch of text to make it more interesting is not the best approach. I'd much rather experience some things, it IS a game after all - albeit a sandbox.
My problem with the game's flow is that it's kinda bland. And unless whatever's behind the gate acts like a Wall of Flesh, ushering in all new monstrosities and gear, it's kinda meh.
That, along with the fact that the fantastic structures are inhabited by painfully obvious RNG scripts (I won't dignify them with the term AI).
I feel that, if Starbound - with it's myriad of races and architecture - were a proper RPG, I might enjoy it much more. As it is, the main quest is 5 dungeons, and the settler quests are just RNG fetch/kill quests without any real narrative or reason to them.
Not to mention there's only 7 armors in the game, of which 3 are stat side-grades, and all the rest race-specific are re-skins; and all found/dropped armor is always stat-less cosmetic stuff as well... I don't know, the game just seems like it's made for social-minded people to screw around in. I'll give it a token play-through when it's launched, but I'm not holding my breath or anything.

You might have been expecting an actual review, but whether you’re grilling, baking, boiling or broiling, here are some helpful tips for making perfect spaghetti every time.
FOLLOW THESE STEPS
Boil water in a large pot
To make sure pasta doesn’t stick together, use at least 4 quarts of water for every pound of noodles.
Salt the water with at least a tablespoon—more is fine
The salty water adds flavor to the pasta.
Add pasta
Pour pasta into boiling water. Don’t break the pasta; it will soften up within 30 seconds and fit into the pot.
Stir the pasta
As the pasta starts to cook, stir it well with the tongs so the noodles don’t stick to each other (or the pot).
Test the pasta by tasting it
Follow the cooking time on the package, but always taste pasta before draining to make sure the texture is right. Pasta cooked properly should be al dente—a little chewy.
Drain the pasta
Drain cooked pasta well in a colander. If serving hot, add sauce right away; if you’re making a pasta salad, run noodles under cold water to stop the cooking.

Well, it's finally here. This game has been through STUFF, alright. Alleged theft of kickstarter money. Overestimated budgets. Development of this game was restarted twice. It took, what, four years or something for this thing to release? Point is: I've been wanting to play this game for a long time. One question remains, though: Does it hold up to half an eternity of being hyped up as "The Homestuck Game"?
Let's look at the facts. Or the opinions, I guess.
PRESENTATION: 4.5/5
The game is beautiful, both visually and acoustically. Though much of the soundtrack isn't usually the kind of music I personally enjoy, the game was definitely pleasing to look at and listen to throughout. Not much else to say on the matter. I'm not really a stickler when it comes to presentation, but I can see that HIveswap's Music and Art team did their best, which is definitely enough in my book.
STORY, WRITING, CHARACTERS: 5/5
If there's one thing people should read Homestuck for, it's probably the music I mean come on the music's great go listen to it right now. But if there's TWO things, the second one is definitely the characters. Hiveswap, in my opinion, lives up to its legacy here. Which is fascinating, because there's really only a handful of characters in Act 1!
As for the writing, there are lots of great jokes in Hiveswap. If you're going to play it for that, though, remember to combine all of the things, as this is where most of the humor is stashed away.
GAMEPLAY: 1/5
Look, I'll be honest: Hiveswap is easily one of the worst Point and Clicks I've ever played, gameplay-wise. This is mainly due to one thing: Lack of Difficulty.
The game is super easy. Some What Pumpkin employees must've thought they were making a modern FPS, because this game has so much handholding it's not even funny. Here's a little taste of what awaits you in Act 1: Throughout the entire game, you are required to combine items in your inventory ONCE. There's dozens of situations where just LOOKING at a problem tells you how to solve it.
If a What Pumpkin employee reads this (which is highly unlikely, but still), PLEASE, for the love of gog, MAKE ACT 2 MORE DIFFICULT. This is embarassing.
Also, make it longer. You can beat the game within two hours, even if you don't know what you're doing.
These issues go hand-in-hand, and they both seriously need fixing.
OVERALL: 3.5/5 Hats, to keep it real
Despite all my nagging about the lack of difficulty, I still thoroughly enjoyed Act 1 of Hiveswap. In spite of all its gameplay-focused shortcomings, I don't think gameplay is what most people want from this game. But as for me, I just... I really, REALLY want Act 2 to be enjoyable by a wider audience.
If you're a fan of Homestuck, it's a must-have. If you want an extremely short and easy, but cleverly written game, the game is also recommendable.
But if you're looking for a Point and Click Adventure where this cleverness extends to the gameplay as well? Hiveswap Act 1 is just not for you. Go read Problem Sleuth instead.

I funded this game (Senator Lemonsnout is sitting on the shelf right behind me) 5 years ago, and given the horrors Andrew Hussie has gone through trying to get it made (being outright conned and robbed from by one studio, and dumping another before making his own from scratch), I had long written off it ever being completed. Glad to be wrong!
I am SO glad that he went with 2D instead of 3D. The artwork is super-saturated and gorgeous, there's a huge number of text slapbacks to "squawk like an imbecile and♥♥♥♥♥♥on your desk" attempted shenanigans, and practically every pixel is flooded with homestuck lore, there for fans (like figuring out that Joey's babysitter is Rose's mom as a teenager) but not needing explanation to enjoy the game.
There are some visual glitches that need fixing (sometimes cutscenes misfire), and I think it should be slightly more obvious where exits are (and some more care should have been taken to maintain room orientations, at least as you enter and exit). The biggest problem is that it's TOO SHORT. I am going to play it again to overdose on interactions, but even doing a bunch already, it took less than 4 hours to finish, and I didn't feel like I was rushing (I was enjoying myself too much).
Hopefully the game does well and he makes more chapters. At least he's got the framework for the game done this time, so it's mostly going to be content development.

That said, the models it does already have are great, the face tracking is very good even if it gives me a lazy eye sometimes(maybe I just have a lazy eye lol), it's fun to play with, and it's great if you want to stream but don't feel confident enough to show your face. I still think it's worth buying if you want to play around with it for streams, so I'll give it a thumbs up, but there's definitely a lot of obvious improvements that can be made and hopefully will be soon in the future.
Looking forward to what Facerig brings in the new year!

If every single day in the world could be your last, how would you choose to spend it?
eden*: They were only two, on the planet. is a fully-voiced kinetic visual novel (meaning there are no branching paths) developed by minori and published by MangaGamer. eden* explores the story of Ryou Haruna, a young killing machine that ranks as one of the best soldiers on the force, on his new assignment in a quiet island. Wondering why this settlement would need so much protection, he soon discovers that it is the home and workplace of a girl named Sion, who is hard at work developing ways for the people around the world to leave Earth before an unknown calamity.
Right off the bat, I’ll have to praise the game for its incredible pacing, writing and voice acting. Not once did I ever feel bored while reading through eden*. Each scene only lasts a few short minutes so you’re never forced to go through a large chunk of it at a time, but at the same time the writing is so good that you’re always wondering what happens next.
The kinetic style of eden* doesn’t hamper the story it tells. It perfectly complements the story by providing you with great illustrations and emotional music that really makes you feel every scene. The world is well-built, the graphics are beautiful, the characters are engaging and the voice acting is top-notch.
It’s very difficult to review a kinetic visual novel without spoiling anything important. I will tell you, however, that I was hooked basically from the very first scene, and more than a few tears will be shed by the end.
I highly recommend this game for fans of great stories. I also recommend you to not look at how much the game takes to complete to really feel that every day could be your last.

I have pre-ordered this game a long time ago and actually haven't touched it for a while, having forgotten about it after a while.. One day, my internet was ♥♥♥♥ed, so I was desperately searching for some kind of source for entertainment and spotted this game on my desktop, which made me think - "Oh, this game, I completely forgot about it!". The first couple of hours into the game, I was constantly wondering how this story was going to expand from here, because for me, the ending was spoiled, due to the nature of the description given to this game. This, I thought, might make the whole VN underwhelming, but I was completely wrong. The overall shell of this VN is easy to figure out, in the early stages of this VN I couldn't help but be sceptical overall about this. The whole trailer type video shown in this page is also a big spoiler for me, as it shows the two main characters already in the mellow state. I couldn't stop wondering about how these two main characters, both seemingly cold-blooded with no humane emotions to be seen, were going to develop. This VN starts off in an oddly relaxing manner, it feels like this game's just going around in circles with its story at times, but after having finished this game, I can't help but appreciate the amount of time I was given to get attached to the characters (deeply, deeply attached). The pacing is incredible, looking back at how the whole entire story has unfolded, in a slow, majestic manner. This game knows to take its time with the story. This game seems to have all the time in the world, contrary to the inhabitants of this small world, the measly human race, desperately struggling to survive the end of the world. Things seem uneventful, duty for the main male protagonist also lacking any kind of action. The seemingly static storyline put me off at first, but as I've mentioned before, this is crucial for this story to have any kind of impact on your feelings, so bear with me on this and this game will show you its worth in full display. Something which has caught my attention very early on into this game is - the incredible dialogue between characters, it's seemingly flawless and the usage/timings of specific words are impeccable, they were incredibly poetic and have made me quite envious of the writer! The way this story develops is simply amazing, I couldn't expect when or how this story would expand, due to the nature of this VN, only sloooowly..and slooooowly.. revealing each and every part of the story, completely trapping me in the game, unable to stop pressing the space bar! I was so absorbed into this game, I had forgotten that it has become midnight, I had forgotten to breathe regularly and ended up having to do it manually! (I guess that's what you call "breathtaking"?) Once the story had started to gain momentum in the storytelling aspect, it has gotten too interesting for me to let go of and time was seemingly flying! (though my clock says otherwise) The main female (Sion) protagonist's character development is astonishing, I knew something had to happen in her for this to be the "Earth's last love story", same goes for the male protagonist. And I was correct, something DID happen (what a surprise). The game had become a feels trip, I cried so many times and so much that I've lost count. "I have become too attached for my own good.." is what I was mumbling, while wiping my tears. *sniff* Yes, if you're wondering about the art and all the other things in this masterpiece, you won't be disappointed, though I expect you've already seen this game's trailers and what not, the art just gets better and better, same with the soundtracks, so you won't need to worry about these aspects being a potential sacrifice in order for them to have created the incredibly immersive and simply touching story. Sion's VA is incredible, she has simply pummelled my heart constantly, with her flawlessly delivered, impactful lines. So I have looked her up on the internet, only to find that she doesn't seem to be well-known at all and by that I mean - she hasn't been a part of many games/anime/vns so on so forth and it's very saddening for me, as I was ready to watch/read what other great things she might have had in store. This is the first game to make me feel my heart wrench, I have actually felt the pain in my chest and the inability to calm myself down from the sadness during and after. The ending of this game has left me in a dazzled state. As the credits were rolling, I was simply staring up ,while lying on my chair, thinking about nothing, absolutely nothing, as this game has left me speechless, accompanied by the feeling of emptiness.
I give this game 10/10 with no doubt, this deserves more than just a glimpse. Delve into it, experience true melancholy and a feeling of amazement, followed by the feeling of accomplishment after having finished this game, which is truly worth your time.

If you like to play as Rome, this game is not so great (almost nothing like Rome 2's Rome, basically a different Rome). Not only is it extremely hard, almost impossible to win (because everyone is trying to kill you, pretty much), but it gets buggy (probably for all factions), so it is not as smooth as Rome 2, for me. Sometimes I have seige artillery that is defending a city or on a fleet and it will not obey orders. It either does not fire or fires at the wrong target.... They took out a lot of the things that I loved about Rome 2. Garrisoning cities is harder to do and manage. Most ships cannot ram, only board and light on fire, certain ones can, but that often turns into a melee fight anyway. Garrisoning cities is hard to do in this game. It's harder than ever to maintain public order and now you have to worry about sanitation or your cities become sick and your armies die. Regiments are small, only groups of 56 men. Then you have hordes of tribes running through your lands and declaring war. These tribes steal your food when they are in your lands, so you have to kill them or you starve. The hordes don't take your cities, they burn them to the ground or damage them to the point where you have to abandon it because you cannot afford repairs... Everytime an army, no matter how small, seiges your city, it costs about $1000 gold in repairs.
If you're a hardcore total war fan that loves challenges, this is it. Prepare to spend days and days just trying to maintain public order and an income while defending your cities with small garrisons vs huge armies (so you cannot afford to ever auto-resolve)... Prepare for your allies to randomly attack you. Prepare for the Picts and other factions from the other side of the map to land on your shores and raid your cities. Prepare to not really play the game, but witness the fall of Rome as despite your best efforts your death will be:
1. Be conquered by the shear amount of units
2. Rebels take over, because public order is hard to manage
3. Run out of money, cannot replinish units, get conquered
4. Run out of food, starve to death
5. Abandon all of your settlements to only the ones you can defend, run out of money or food, die.
6. A combination of all of these.
If you love killing Romans and taking their lands this game is good other than the buggyness. I don't see a lot of differences between each army, just lots of levy spearmen...
I really like how they make fire a formidable weapon. Fire can burn and spread and kill in battles. I like the greater deversity in cities and how you can upgrade their defenses by building better walls.
I'd likely not mind the challenge if I did not have irritating bugs happen now and then.... I mean, the real Eastern Roman Empire survived, so can we. If you're the Western Romans, there is really no hope for you.

It is clear that Treasure's Mega Drive releases in the form of Alien Soldier and Gunstar Heroes play a huge part to A.R.E.S. design with huge epic bosses, eight directional firing and an emphasis on weapon power-ups more specifically. While it would seem from the offset that the folks from Extend Studio know what they're doing, sadly A.R.E.S.  never quite manages to capture the precise beats of the controls and core mechanics that made both of the mentioned games as exciting as they were in the early nineties. My biggest gripe with A.R.E.S. is that the controls never do what you want them to, even with an Xbox pad. It really hurts the rest of the experience when the game pegs a wealth of secrets accessible only through exploration and careful platforming. This wouldn't be a problem if all the actions in the game didn't feel a chore to commence as the lumbering animations making double jumps especially hard to predict and all-round not fun to do. Despite this fatal shortcoming,  I will give A.R.E.S. credit for it's soundtrack which, like the Mega Drive games I mentioned, feature memorable tracks for each level. Still, Would I concluding recommend this game because of that alone? No, not really.

Dragon's Dogma is hands down one of the greatest RPG titles I've played. The introduction throws you into a fantasy universe that begs to be explored. Fighting dragons is common in these games, but never have I felt such fear from one that steals your soul and becons you to find and slay him. A journey worth remembering, and even exploring over and over again with 9 different playstyles and several followers that don't actually act like complete idiots. The story is vague, and very open to interpretation, but after completing it I sat back and thought "did I just play this game, or did it play me?".
That may be a controversial pro for this game, but quite honestly, that's what video games have always been to me as a gamer. Something to really test my overall understanding, and if you can sit back and just enjoy an experience, then that's what Dragon's Dogma will do for you.
10/10, currently playing again.

Let me start this straight : This game has its troubles.
It has not the most breath taking graphics
It's AI has some issues from time to time
A good chunk of its quests don't make sense and story is kind of a mess
But the core gameplay is just genuine fun. Fun as in new games should have at least these systems : Ability to climb on large monsters/grapple smaller ones and the Main Pawn sharing system ( You basically share the latest save of your Main Pawn with it's Inclinations - which is how the AI will work with you- Equipments, Stats, Augments and abilities.)
The fighting is oh lord so responsive and dynamic, one minute you are attacking from afar with let's say a bow and the next second you are rolling about trying to get a good momentum to jump on some dragon do get to its heart.
In the end of the day, having this game in your library is a good thing.
Things to fix for a sequel (and please Capcom, stop with this MMO formula ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t and make a second singeplayer entry ! ) :
-Splitscreen/multiplayer : I didn't understand why this wasn't a thing taking that you had a obligatory Main Pawn following you about and being a main plot line in the game even. I can understand that the game is then more difficult to players that somehow lose the Main Pawn ( It can die and then disapear until you visit a Riftstone). Splitscreen is really simple to add with a drop-in/drop-out system, with 2nd player taking control of the Main Pawn.
-Lipsync. Enough said, just please add some deatils for the dialogs suchs as : Moving lips. And when there's moving lips, make them sync with what's being said.
-More player-friendly stats-growth.
- Change the rating system of the rented pawns so you can rate them even when they die rather than having the owner getting a unfamous 3 stars - no comments - no gift reward for sharing is work.
- Better story. Well, this is tricky. The main plot line is fairly simple - and it's fine like that- and makes sense through the game and even further once you work for all the ending achievments. But the secondary quests that link to it. Please. These are a mess.
-Having less reskins and more unique items. - with the enchants being visible, that'd be nice
Anyway, the game is still incredible and show some really interesting points. I wouldn't give any numerical rating because it makes no sense but I'd say Go for it, buy it and play it. Really immersive.

For historical use, my old review:
Yes, yes, YES!!!!! I've been waiting for a survival game like this for a long time. It's not perfect by any means, but it's the closest game I've played that fit my zombie survival needs.
PROS:
-Base building is cool
-Going on runs for supplies is fun
-The zombies can be a ♥♥♥♥♥, but they can also be easy
-Each character has a pretty good back story, and most of them get told(unless you kill them)
-If you die, you're dead. Your character is gone and you gain a new one at base, and you lose any story lines that they could produce
-special zombies
-House moving
CONS:
-Wish it had personal needs(food and water) that I had to keep up with
-So far the games been a tad easy, but I've not done much of the "main" missions, and the DLC will fix that too
-I'd like better control over a party member if I have one(tellling them to pick up reasores or dropped packs)
-And more squad based controls would be fun
-You can't send your friends out on the slower/easier missions(like scouting out or getting building marterials) in the same way it works with Assassins creed, that would add more risk/reward to the game
All in all though the game is still fun and it's so far the best survival game I've found that lets you do all the stuff you can.

Mass Effect is an action role playing third person shooter game, developed by BioWare. Releasing on Xbox 360, PS3 and PC. The game was released in November 2007 as a timed Xbox exclusive, but eventually got ported to PC in May 2008.
The game starts out with you being able to fully customize the appearance of the main character, male or female, abilities, and background story.  The game play is based a lot around a squad of three characters including you. There are six difference “classes” that come in the form of important characters that you encounter throughout the game. Each of these classes will level up, and have their own special abilities and talent tree to select from.  The talent tree is very detailed, allowing you to spec each class into specialized roles which you will take on different missions depending on what enemies you will be facing.
The game’ combat system is primarily in real time, but you can pause at any time to give orders to your squad. I however found this to be a very negligible feature as I had no use for it all, I don’t think I used even once. The combat is very easy to get to grasps with. A really good cover based system is included, with some really tight controls to boot. Whilst you do have unlimited ammo for your weapons, you do run the risk of overheating your guns if you just continuously fire, meaning you have to take breaks in your onslaught for a few seconds at a time or you can simply switch to one of your many other weapons. I liked the idea behind not having to scavenge around for ammunition, its 2183…it’s all lasers for gods sakes! :)  Another key game play element comes in the form of the dialogue and morality system. A really good portion of the game takes place in dialogue scenes with NPCs, your answers really do matter and can sometimes change the course of events which carry out for the rest of the game. I am not normally a fan of games which have too much dialogue, but I was completely intrigued to explore each dialogue option to delve deeper and immerse myself completely in the story. Different actions and different results will affect your morality, completing the main missions don’t really add much to the system, but a lot of the game’s side missions make you choose a “good” or “bad” resolution to them, which really makes you think sometimes.
Mass Effect is almost ten years old now, and whilst it is showing its age, it is certainly still an OK looking game by today’s standards.  All of the animations are really crisp. The textures aren’t all high resolution, but you have to remember the age of the game when playing. The facial modelling of all of the characters is done very well too, and even betters some of the recent titles!
I played Mass Effect on the medium difficulty level, and I found the game to be challenging enough so that I wasn’t breezing through the game, but not so hard that I felt I wasn’t able to progress without having the need to grind a few levels before taking on a certain boss or mission. The only times I did find myself getting stuck, is purely a UI issue, rather than the gameplay. The game doesn’t do a fantastic job at telling you where to go next; you have a lot of maps to be able to look through, but no help at all comes for many of the side missions for where you need to go, meaning I had to look up a few of the missions online to be able to work out where to go.
The majority of the game’s levels are really well designed. There is really only one main hub of activity in the game which has an open world feel to it, and that is the Citadel. You will find a good portion of the game’s side quests in this location with plenty of NPCs to interact with as well. Each of the game’s main missions takes place on a different planet, and that planet will also have a handful of side missions for you to complete along with the main story. I would urge people to check them out as they are well worth your time, and I didn’t at any point feel like I was completing the same type of mission over and over again. All of the side missions add a great deal of story which also keeps the lore crew happy as well.
I have recently just finished my second play through of Mass Effect, the first being a few years ago now. The most recent play through of the game took just under 20 hours to complete, this is with me being in OCD mode and completing all of the side missions, exploring all of the levels and interacting with any of the NPCs I came across. There is a deal of replay ability with Mass Effect, you can of course ramp up the difficulty, but you can also play the game in different styles using the morality system, and changing the gender of your character to also effect relationships with your crew members.  I would even say I could squeeze another two play throughs out of Mass Effect before I would find it hard to find something new to come across.
Technically, right now I have to say Mass Effect does have a couple of issues running on newer operating systems. Whilst I didn’t have any crashes or major bugs, I did have a few performance problems with the odd stutter every now and again. I am pretty sure it is not hardware related as my PC is more than capable of running current titles on 4k with high settings. Another pet peeve is that I wasn’t even able to run the game on 1080p; you have to put up with the lower Xbox360 resolutions. I didn’t play with a controller, as I am more interested in being more precise with my aim than anything else to be honest.
My conclusion on Mass Effect is, that whilst many of you will have probably already played and finished the game, I would still class this as a must play title for our recent memory. It is the start of a truly fantastic series, and one of the standout titles of the last generation of games. It is showing its age slightly, but Sci-fi fans will want to start here before stepping foot into the Mass Effect world.  If you can look past the aging graphics you have an absolutely stellar story and hella fun gameplay with some heavy RPG elements.

A powerful story about love, life and what it means to live. The story involves the final days of the planet Earth which may seem like a cheap way to inject drama but, honestly, that part of the story may as well be an aside. The fact is that the main story is between our two main characters and it could have just as well been told in another setting while still remaining as powerful. It's very well written with one caveat...
The pacing for the first half is incredibly slow. If you're not a patient person, you may have trouble dragging yourself through it. Speed reading or skimming along until the main characters get together wouldn't be a terrible idea if you feel yourself getting disinterested because there is a great ending to this story, despite the slow start. This is a long story and they get together at about the midway point so you won't be robbing yourself of much by skimming a bit. Lastly, just an FYI, this is a kinetic novel meaning there are no choices, branching paths or interactions.
As far as the artwork goes, it's mostly top-notch. The characters are often incorporated into the backgrounds instead of the standard VN format of having a background layer with static "pop-up" characters in front of it. There are a few frames of Major Inaba that are comically bad and I question how they ended up in the game when the rest is so well drawn but aside from that, it's all very beautiful.
In summary, it's a great story if you have the time (and a little patience) to put into it. A bit slow to start but it has a fairly powerful finish. I recommend it.

Hooray! It's yet another Early Access, Unity-based craft-to-survive game!
It should be a crime for a game that's as hilariously glitchy as Savage Lands to take itself so seriously. Stuff that isn't missing is just plain broken. Rocks and chunks of ice float in the air, and world collision seems more of a suggestion than a rule, with deer swimming through cobblestones and wolves leaping inside solid rock. Enemies respawn by popping into existence anywhere they please, and hitbox detection is so janky you'll spend most of your time wildly swinging tools around air trying to find that one magic spot.
The feature request and bug lists alone are a riot, and the fact that the devs are so standoffishly indignant about it just adds to the comedy. A pause button? That's not part of our design principle! Console commands? We don't think you need cheats! Crouching? Sneaking? Nah, just try to stay behind some trees, it'll be fine.
I can totally understand why this game has found its niche as a $1 tier Humble Bundle title; For $15 it's an insult -- for a buck it's a punchline.

When I think of A.R.E.S., I can't help but think of S.T.A.L.K.E.R.. They're totally different games; ARES is a 2D action-platformer and STALKER is an open-world FPS, but they share one critical thing: nobody expects their acronym to actually stand for anything. It's the name of the main character; any further explanation is left to the imagination. However, with only four letters, it's not terribly difficult to guess what they might be.
Always Riddling Enemies with Shots
ARES: Extinction Agenda plays something like the Megaman series if it was invented twenty years later. Controls boil down to variations on jumping and shooting, the former feeling fantastic and the latter feeling less so. The combat is fast and frantic; if you manage to get a bead on them, enemies die in seconds. You aim & fire either via mouse cursor or analog stick, making attacking & dodging independent. This is for the best, as ARES moves a tad too ridigly for its own good especially when it comes to the air.  The designers seem to have been at least somewhat aware of this, and tend to stray away from insta-kill death pits, which can swing the difficulty from challenging to frustrating. Overall, the gameplay remains solid and plays to its best points, though there are speed bumps along the way.
The game also includes a ranking system for each level, influenced by a number of simple factors. Did you find the secret area? Did you get hit? Did you go through quickly? It also takes into consideration a combo system, which counts the number of consecutive shots you've landed without taking damage. It's a simple system that rewards skill and practice well. The issue, however, is that it trivializes slower weapons when you can get six hits on enemies that would normally only take one or two. It's a small problem, but a definite oversight.
Animations Rarely Exceed Substandard
ARES' aesthetic appeal is a mixed bag. In screenshots and stills, the game look marvelous, and rightfully so; the environments are carefully detailed, maintaining a consistent art style that's a pleasure to look at. Sadly, this means little when half of the animations look like something off of an old Flash game. Most of the time, you're too preoccupied by the fast-paced gameplay to notice a laughably strange wiggle-to-death animation, but it becomes hard to forgive when some of the main bosses disassemble in the same spectacularly shoddy fashion. Overall, the graphics are well done but inconsistent.
A Really Excellent Soundtrack
One of the best aspects of the game is its soundtrack (which is free to listen to here:
) Electric guitar combines with industrial synth to amplify the already intense environment. It's a really standout part of the game, definitely worth picking up separately.
Actually Rather Enjoyable; Short
At its best, ARES is explosive. Satisfying shooting, detailed graphics, and a supercharged soundtrack all combine to make ARES' high points memorable. However, the game fizzles out far too soon, lasting only a couple hours. Enjoy it while it lasts; its replay value is limited.

This game is a must-play for RPG enthusiasts.  Casual gamers might tire of its systems.  Play it if you have the time and drive to experience a masterpiece story with moderately-challenging strategy.  Extremely long-winded review forthcoming.
I just completed my first playthrough - totaling 85-92 hours.  Range given as I was AFK once or twice leaving the game running, so Steam "Hours Played" is not entirely accurate.
What can I say?  All the positive things that reviewers say about this game are true, and the negatives are trivial enough for me to nearly ignore.  I will mention them both below:
The best pros are that the narrative is excellent and carefully woven.  The game is immersive, with a classy high-fantasy soundtrack and beautiful atmosphere.  Voice acting is excellent, where it is to be had.  Love the idea of a stronghold, it was nice to feel ownership over something that grows and evolves as you sink coin into it.  Combat was as challenging as it was meant to be.  I played on Normal during first playthrough, which felt like Core Rules in Baldur's Gate I and II.  Character customization is vast, which is daunting at first but adds to replayability.  I now want to play a second time as another class, with a different party configuration.  The morality system is also great, and intricately woven into the game's story.  Instead of the D&D alignment system, dialogue choices lend themselves to behaviour, which grow stronger the more you use them.  For example, I chose mostly honest/benevolent choices on a good playthrough.  Where no clear "Good" or "Evil" choices exist, there are choices such as rational, which I would associate with "Neutral" alignment.
The worst cons are that the party AI is mildly broken - I had to disable auto-attack early on because party members would engage their own monsters, which was far less efficient than clearing one by one and often resulted in death.  It would be great if scripts were available a la Baldur's Gate series.  The voice-acting is not present in every dialogue with voiced NPCs, which a lot of people found annoying; it didn't bother me, though.  There were also a few bugs which patching seems to resolve.  I would have preferred subtitles on every interaction such as selecting a character, similarly to Baldur's Gate series, but that's a minor complaint.
I should take a moment to point out the Kickstarter supporter content in-game.  In terms of Pro/Con, this is "Neutral" to me, as without backers this game wouldn't have been made, or made in the same way.  It makes sense that the devs honor those who have contributed and offer rewards accordingly.  That said, I can take or leave the added content, and it doesn't really bother me.  As for the "Soul Stories" or gold-plated NPCs, I found myself lazing beyond clicking to learn about them past the first few major areas.  The stories behind each are great, and are like books of additional content in other games, but they are not necessary to experience the core story.  Some people find the in-game 'memorials' to take away from immersion, but they didn't for me: After I learned what they were, I just stopped clicking on them.  I would advise that you do the same if such things bother you.  Ultimately, what the memorials reminded me of were tombstone etchings from old D&D games (ie "He's dead, Jim" from Warriors of the Eternal Sun).
On backer content - The recent news about Obsidian changing supporter content that was deemed inappropriate is also trivial, as it does not affect core story/gameplay.  To focus on such things when an epic of this gravitas comes along is akin to poking out one's own eyes.  This is Pillars of Eternity, not Pillars of Absurdity.  Whatever side you're on or arguments you believe are more important...  Just shut up and enjoy the game, or get lost.
All in all, it's a solid game that is worth any RPG enthusiast's time.  Having played a 'good' character making benevolent/honest choices, I look forward to exhibiting reactions to an "evil" playstyle, making aggressive/cruel choices.  I may play a third time to see how a rational/deceptive character may fare, dishonest but not good or evil.  On my next playthrough, I will up the difficulty from normal to hard.  I have not tried trial of iron mode that forces you to use one save, though perhaps I'll try it on a third playthrough.  Same goes for expert mode.  Some of the Steam achievements (such as Soloing) are nuts to me, but I applaud those who choose to challenge themselves thus.
If I had to rate this game of 10, I'd say 9.0/10 honest review, 9.5/10 with the "Inifity Engine Nostalgia Factor".
Cheers and have a happy Eternity experience.  Fingers crossed that we will see a sequel before long!

Good points

Classes are balanced
Deep good story
Main storyline and lots of side/sandbox elements don't feel like I am being rushed or forced into anything
Cool stronghold with lots to do/develop
Bad points
Little slow (though it is what I was expecting)
Classes are balanced (for instance mage spells have really low range making positioning a lot harder)
Defense system makes it hard to make dedicated defensive characters (Deflection (AC) Reflex Will Fortitude defenses so its hard not to have a weak point and armor damage reduction is similarly spread out so its almost impossible to have a set of armor thats just good (I keep about three sets for my tanks to switch between depending on what we are fighting).
Conversation options can be really stat/class dependant (restarted about halfway through playing a cipher with high resolve just to have the options I wanted in come converstations/quests/storylines).
Overall my complaints are very minor and the game takes me back tp the best era of PC RPG gaming and continues where it left off.

Prepare for your allies to randomly attack you. Prepare for the Picts and other factions from the other side of the map to land on your shores and raid your cities. This game is fantastic and deserves far more attention than it gets or has ever got. As somebody who was recently trusted into this game blindly I feel like I can say that without bias. Anyway, the main gist of it is this game is a blend of exploration, survival, and action mechanics that work very well together.  You are given a main story, and after the tutorial mission is over you are thrust into the universe with a ai guiding you.  It is all randomly generated except for the main story missions and allows players to get a lot more action than you would expect in this type of game. Comparisons are drawn between this and Terraria, which are partially accurate partially not. It has the core game play style from Terraria, the very open and huge universe to explore of FTL or No man's sky, and the story structure of open world games such as skyrim. What is does to separate itself from those games is have a quirky sense of humor, a need for Every resource you can find, and a surprisingly well integrated multi-player (except for people being able to steal you're things). Even with all of these things in mind, it's not a tough game to learn, I learned everything I needed to know within the first hour with no guides. It is a game that does not hold you're hand but gives you enough to work with. Basically, if you have made it to this point in my review, buy this game. It is 15$ and it is better than most triple a games. It also wouldn't hurt to bring a friend along, because if you get someone else who will work well with you, this will be one of the best experiences you could have.

Shadow of Mordor is a game that defines the 7/10 rating. It is intensely average in almost every way.
The story varies, sometimes its good, sometimes its straight up mediocre fan-fiction. Especially with its self-references like quoting Lord of the Rings, and even a LOTR title-drop that is one of the worst lines I have ever heard. "There can be only one...Lord of the Rings." is a real line that exists in this game. Its so forced and corny, and has no place being in a game trying to take itself seriously, and the inclusion of a character for no other reason than to have one character from the films/books in the game, its never justified. The ending sequences crosses into straight bad fanfiction.
Gameplay is good, but thats because its batman, down to the button combos and most of Talion's abilities. You like Batman? You like this. The main issue with the gameplay is after a certain point it becomes a joke, Talion becomes absurdly overpowered and you can clear out 50 orcs in no time at all, without struggling for health once. (Just stack runes that heal you on the use of any drain/brand on your dagger, and combat drain to restore all HP, which you can do twice, per 5-hit combo...) This also heavily hurts the real focus of the game, the "Nemesis" system.
The nemesis system is a fun, but flawed system. Its fun to play with, it really adds to a sandbox game, but it doesnt really work like they clearly intended. The intent is clear that you have actual nemesis, who come for you, and its a constant back and forth, and you are trying to manipulate tyhe captains so you can work your way to the higher ranks and take out the big fish. The reality is more of a cluster♥♥♥♥. The difference between a rank 1 captain and a warchief is barely noticable, save the warchief has a lot more defenses around him and you have to do a quest to make them even appear, otherwise you can pretty much kill anyone, at any time, at your discretion.
Thats also what makes the game fun, it is a true sandbox, and the results are sometimes pretty damn amusing. Having a captain you killed come back for revenge, only to finish his speech while you have your combo charged, and kill him in one finishing move? Hilarious. And it never fails to make me laugh when a area just turns into a clown car of captains, you move in to kill one, just to discover another one was right there, then have a nemesis come to kill you, then have a new captain who was hunting you show up, and its great.
I would love to see this system in more games, especially a more comedic tongue-in-cheek game.
The game is fairly short, you get 20 main missions (most fairly short), 24 rescue missions (they are all the same type of mission in different areas, recycled over and over, far too many of them in the game imo) 30 "Weapon" missions (10 for each of talions weapons), 20 open world challenges, a mercifully small handful of collectables. And a handful of recycled random missions that come up for the nemesis system, where most of the padding lies. Depending on how much you goof off exploiting the nemesis system for your amusement, the game is between 12-24 hours long.
Its a fun game, and a good one to kill time while waiting for another game to come out, but dont expect anything to blow you away.

Yeah, okay, sure you're a Homestuck fan. So am I. But I actually know what I'm talking about and enjoyed both Homestuck and Hiveswap: Act 1.
After developement hell, this game finally gets released. My review will be more based on the game itself and less about what people hoped it would be.
Hiveswap: Act 1 is the first of 4 episodic Point and Click adventures and is supposed to set the tone for the rest of the series. Besides a few visual glitches and some spelling errors, it's done it's job at introducing characters and setting up the story for the other 3 acts. Visually, the backgrounds look amazing, the animation flips from fluid to choppy, and mechanically, there isn't a puzzle too hard to figure out with all of the visual cues you're given. A new feature packed along with the game is the dialog response for each combonation of "inventory item X item/environment". No longer will you get the same old "You can't do that." over and over. Each interaction has something different to say, and can encourage the player to try to combine everything out of curiosity. The soundtrack is composed from James Roach and Toby Fox, both of which are very talented musicians. If you get the chance, you should buy the sound tracks for each act. You're bound to fall in love with at least one song. (Also, I don't believe "The Grubbles" have had a chance to play yet, and the two songs released are pretty damn good as well. So hang on to your underwear when they finally make their debut.)
Now onto the Homestuck Perspective Review.
LOTS of references to Homestuck. Being based in the same universe, it's really unavoidable. For anybody who's kept up with the story, you're going to be combing through this game with a super secret cypher thats not easily obtainable. Plenty of stuff will already be common sense to big fans of the series, while everyone else will be just as clueless as Joey Claire. And for those that are wondering what is up with the combat system, it's modeled after some of the early Homestuck flash fights. If it doesn't make sense, it's not supposed to. It's purely cosmetic.
With the tone set, Act 2 is going to deliver just as well, if not better. Let's just hope it delivers on time!

Hiveswap: Act 1 was an absolutely fantastic starting point for the new series.
If you enjoyed Homestuck immensely, wished to play a Homestuck style game based upon the format the webcomic was in, or just wanted more out of Andrew Hussie, Homestuck, and MSPA Adventures, this is absolutely the game for you.
The game is moderately short, I beat it in 2 hours and 13 minutes, and its generally a Point-and-Click game with a set storyline.  The style however very clearly shouts Homestuck, with the visuals and all references to pop culture still prevalent, and a few puzzles, minigames, and even Strife sequences to play in.
Overall, I was definitely happy with Hiveswap, and I'm looking forward to Act 2 and the rest!

Plus a sequel?? Or maybe they'll just split up the Acts between 2 games..
Either way, it's gorgeous, funny, has awesome music and tons of Homestuck easter eggs (of course); really worth the wait considering all the trouble Hussie and the WhatPumpkin? development team had to go through to get this game made. Absolutely fantastic.
**And like other reviewers have been saying, you don't even need to know that much about Homestuck to get into it. You like old style point and click adventure games with aliens, charming sibling banter, possible world threatening scenarios and weirdly absent parental figures? Totally a game you should check out.

A truly fantastic and great game. Though I'm incredibly late to the party, I'm glad I finally decided to play through and beat this game. For the most part, it's a 3rd person shooter, but it's not typical. At the same time, the gameplay isn't exactly groundbreaking. There's elements of customization, minimal squad control that makes this game stand out from other 3rd person shooters, and space navigation that isn't too hands on.
What really grabbed my attention about this game was its immersiveness and the setting that is gradually revealed to you. For the most part, the story isn't also particularly original *SPOILER WARNING* it involves you chasing after a rogue alien who's attempting to bring the downfall of all known civilizations in this game's galaxy. Though that isn't quite original, the way the story is revealed to you is quite interesting. Through journal entries, conversations, and general observations, you as a player begin to learn about the setting of this game. Though it's not essential to the game, you can exhaust character conversations in order to be better informed of what's going on outside of the game's storyline.
Overall, I rate this game a 4/5 and I highly recommend it if you're into action RPGs and enjoy science fiction as much as I do.

Original review: Ok, Im sure the team behind this game worked hard on it, because it shows. Impressive graphics and a great opening sequence prove this. I hate to give a negative review on any game, as it takes a lot of time, dedication and hard work to create one. But I also want to  warn anyone out there to be wary of purchasing this game, and invite you read my review please. I also will answer any questions you have.
"Early Access" is no excuse for this.  I read a lot of  reviews for this game before buying it, All of which were positive, encouraging anyone who likes survival or open world exploration to get the game. Since I like both genres, i decided to give it a try. The beginning of the game starts strong but soon falls flat. I begin the game in a plane, mixing a cocktail beverage only to soon find the plane diving to the ocean. I plunge into the water and then swim out of the wreckage and into a conveniently placed life raft. I see a nearby island and slowly row towards it while the wreckage burns and explodes behind me. As if things couldnt get any more dramatic, a shark circles my raft. I scramble to reach the land, jumping out of the raft and running through the shallows as the shark gives up his chase. I was very excited to get started on my survival quest. The game doesnt hold hands, (Which I like). With no directions or hint on what to do, I soon find an axe and make a fire and shelter and I kill some crabs to eat. I decide to brave the shark infested waters and scavenge the nearby sailboat and plane ruins underwater. I come back up to the surface(With my non-upgradable inventory of 8 slots full) and decide to tinker on my island a bit more before nightfall. But then I find that I have depleted all of the resources on my small island. By small i mean around 50x70 meters. When morning comes, I embark on a journey with my raft full of my collected trinkets and find that my raft moves very slow loaded down so i throw most everything overboard (assuming I will find a large island containing more trinkets) and head to a nearby visible island.
This game sounds pretty good as of now, Doesnt it? If my review stopped here, Im sure you would buy it. But this is where I insist you wait until after the game is finished to buy it.
As I reach the next island, I am confused as to why it is a cookie-cut replica of the previous island. A few new sticks to grab, new rocks to sharpen but its the same size and nothing of interest is found other than some binoculors in a nearby box. I try to look through them only to find that my character peers over the top of them instead and the view is only magnified by about  2x. I  somehow happen to spot another island, however, so I head to it. When I arrive, I notice, to my surpise, another replicated, small island with a few more rocks and sticks. No new ruins, No enemies, no caves or landmarks. I play on, surviving, eating, sitting around fires at night, and "exploring" during the day only to find more replicated 50x70 meter islands. Nothing new, no land-based enemies or new tools. A quick search of a guide shows that there are around 15 craftable items, A shark as the only real enemy and nothing I didnt find in 25 minutes of gameplay. You can however, build a boat motor and raft and use it to "explore" More hollow, small, replicated islands and "survive".

If you are a normal human and want to play an early access survival game, try "The Long Dark". It is a survival game done right, And has many more places to explore and things to do. If however, you are a well behaved (and well used) aching prisoner, or a slave locked away in a dungeon, yet have access to Steam, You could play "Stranded Deep" to kill time in between your torture sessions and reamings. Not much to do or see here quite yet, unfortunately.
