People often look at Supergiant Games as one of the best indie developers, and after playing This masterpiece, I believe them. Bastion was their first game, and what an amazing game it is! I’m here to tell you exactly why you should buy Bastion.
You play as a boy, who’s name is unknown, so we just call him The Kid. The World has been destroyed after “the calamity”. Most people have turned into dust, and the world has broken into a bunch of floating islands. In case of events similar to this, the people of Caelondia was told to meet up at the bastion, a place built for situations like this one. Once The Kid arrives at the bastion, he finds only one person, an old man. He is the narrator. Later in the game, you'll find other survivors. The story starts of a bit slow and is a bit hard to follow, but after a while, I understood most of what was happening. The ending of this game is really good! It was surprisingly emotional, and will stick with me for a long time! (At least throughout the week.)
The game has a top down view, which I didn’t have any problems with. The ground will appear as you explore, and the color palette is very nice to look at. I didn’t like the design of the kid too much, but the animations are alright. To be honest, I thought the visuals were only okay. They look alright, but it isn’t what I’m gonna remember this game for.
What I am gonna remember this game for however, is the awesome narrator! Throughout the game there is this man who will narrate everything you do. While it might sound annoying, it is the polar opposite! Almost all the story of the game is being told by him, and he also responds to what you do in the game. One time, I was in a place with a lot of boxes. Being the completionist that I am, I started breaking everything, just in case there was something hidden in them. But while doing this, the narrator would comment on it. I don’t remember what he said, but it was something like this. “The Kid continued to break all the boxes because he thought he would get something from it.” He also comments on how good you are. There is a part where you’re riding a ship called Nelly. Once that part was over, the narrator said something like: “Do you know how many times that kid fell down from nelly? Not even once.” He will also comment on your playstyle, like which weapon you choose. In short, the narrator is awesome, and is a big part of why this game is so great!
The music in this game is really good! It might be one of my favorite game soundtracks of all time! You can buy it for 70 nok, which is around 8,5 dollars. While I won’t spend that much money on it, I will most likely pick it up on sale!
While the combat isn’t the best, the game's weapons makes up for it! You’ll get a lot of weapons, and they all feel unique in their own way. The game gives you a lot of freedom on how you play it. You can use the weapon you start with through the entire game if you want, because the weapon upgrade system makes every weapon useful! You can have around five upgrades on each weapon I think, but for every upgrade there are two options to choose from. The upgrade system makes each weapon highly customizable. The way your bow works might be quite different than mine! But if you don’t like what you chose, you can always change it at the bastion for free! You can have two weapons with you at a time. No weapons are better than others, so you can choose the ones that suits your playstyle the most! I always had a bow with me, and in the other slot i mixed it up a bit. By the end of the game, I always went with my trusty bow for long range attacks, and the musket for when the enemies got too close for comfort. To upgrade your weapons you need special items. These can be found around the world, or won at these “proving ground” levels. These levels will test your skills with a certain weapon. There’s three prizes: The first is for completing the challenge, The second for doing it very good and the third for doing it almost perfectly. These challenges are pretty fun, and some of them are actually pretty hard! The best prize is always a special attack. Just like the weapons, there are tons of special attacks in this game. You can choose one at a time, and they are activated with the right trigger. These range from a really powerful arrow, to my favorite: trapping all the enemies on screen! You’ll need black tonics to use these attacks. Black tonics are found all over the world and can drop from enemies.
The gameplay section ended up being half a page worth of talking about weapons, so I ended up splitting the gameplay into three sections.
Just so you know, I played this game with a controller. I didn’t test the keyboard controls, but the controller worked just fine. When you take damage, you can restore it by using health potions. These work exactly like the black tonics. You use a healing potion by pressing Y. The goal of the game is to collect these shards. There’s usually one in each level. You use the shards to build buildings in the bastion. You can choose which one to build first, but by the end of the game you’ll have every building anyways, so it doesn't really matter which one you choose. When playing the game, I found the levels to be really creative and fun, but thinking back, I can only remember a couple. The level design doesn’t feel very special. The game is very linear, but that isn’t necessarily a bad thing. What is a bad thing however, is that when you pick up a new weapon for the first time, it will replace the one you’re using. You get the weapons in the middle of a level, and you can only change back at the bastion! It makes you test out every weapon, and not just sticking with the ones you know. What is annoying, is that the weapons you pick up aren’t upgraded, and the ones you used are! You’ll experience a massive dps downgrade whenever you get a new weapon, and it’s really annoying!  I get why they made it that way, but it's still annoying!
This game is an action rpg, and has some rpg elements. First of all, there’s a leveling system. you’ll need xp to level up, and you get it from killing enemies. when you level up, your max hp will increase, and you’ll unlock a new perk point. There’s a lot of perks in this game. They can do stuff like increasing your health potion capacity, and more interesting stuff, like getting hp for killing enemies, at the cost of lowering the hp you get from health potions. You can change your perks at the bastion. There’s also special challenges you can do that’ll give you money. You’ll finish most of them by the end of the game, all I had left were some weapon challenges. You can also activate disadvantages that will make the game harder, but you get more xp and money. These can be activated or deactivated at the bastion, and when you die you’ll get the option to deactivate them. You also have a shop where you can buy upgrade materials, special attacks and perks.
I love this game! The story is good, the music is amazing, the narration is clever, and the gameplay is fun! The game also has a lot of replay value, and I want to jump back in it and play the New Game Plus right away! I know what you're thinking... 'But Chris, I already have all the card drops from this game by just sitting idle in the main menu..!', well shame on you! There's actually a decent attempt at a classic genre on offer here.
It's a 2.5d side scrolling game, which reminds me of Metriod, Mega Man and all the other games from the NES/SNES generation I grew up playing. The level designs are simple, but have scope for secret areas and discovery, while the music again is a fantastic tribute to the genre and era it's attempt to reflect.
Boss battles reflect on the genre well too, with each boss having set pattern attacks you can learn and counter. Weapon upgrades and suit upgrades are there too. All in all this is a fun little game, and fans of the genre should check it out.
Gameplay wise I'd recommend investing in a 360 pad, or something with Dual Analog sticks, as the game supports 100% (even the force feedback), and plays a lot smoother for having one too.
Overall advice would be - give this a game a chance. If you see it in the sale pick it up, if only for the brief chance it'll remind you of the fun you had as a kid.

I am not really sure what to make of the final version of Starbound. I bought this in it's early stages of development, and I have to say first off that I think it was a real mistake to release the game so early. It was literally years away from completion when it was first released. Way, way too early. Anyway, on to the final version, and I think I prefer the earlier version!!! The earlier version was more of a sandbox idea, you could just wander about and build things. The final version, though, I really find the alien creatures very annoying. They always attack you and seem able to kill you with just a few hits. When you are trying to learn the game, and more to the point when you are more interested in exploration and building rather than fighting, their constant presence of atacking creatures is very tiring. And I also have some objection to the fact that most alien cratures would be unfriendly. It would have completely changed the feeling of the game had they mostly been friendly instead. There really should be an option to disable or at least reduce the numbers of them. They are literally every ten feet in the game.  So I guess whether you like Starbound very much depends on what you expect from the game.  Recommended? Well, like I said, depends what you expect from the game. I will say yes, but like me you may find it a bit annoying.

I'd like to start this by saying I don't write many reviews. It's not that I don't think I can, and it's not because I don't think other games deserve them. There are a lot of games that deserves much praise and admiration. However, when this game strikes a special cord for me.
It's a relatively short game. Don't go into this expecting ten hours of entertainment. This is just one part of a larger whole.
It's on tracks, this is not a choose your own adventure game. It's a story-telling narrative.
As stated before, this is just part one. Part one took a very long time to come out. I can't say when the next part will be out, and you might want to save playing this until all the pieces are released.
It does it's job fantastically. It tells a story, gets you interested in the quirks of the characters. It flows smoothly from one point to the next in that style Hussie became famous for.
Though the game itself is linear, the things you can discover are so vast that in this short game you can and will spend more time reading about wall posters than advancing the plot.
Almost true to the description, there are very few generic 'combinations' in the game. Almost everything you can use on something else gets its own unique flavor, even if it doesn't work or do anything special. The few times that something lacks interaction or has a generic default are far between, and hardly immersion breaking. I was never quite left with the feeling of "I have an axe, but I need a hammer to get past this wood because it has nails." that you might get in older point and clicks.
Last but certainly not least it's beautiful. The work put into the assets and the way everything is composed is both beautiful and true to the original Homestuck style.
I'm happy with the end result, even if it took a very long time to get here. Now I'm just waiting eagerly for part 2.
This is a beautiful, charming game, a tad on the short side but overall an amazing experience. Kudos to the What Pumpkin team for their exceptional work, and looking forward to the following acts!
Short and sweet. Definitely worth the wait.

FOR A NOT HOMESTUCK:
Pros:
+Incredibly adorable, if you're one of those people who can live off a game by how cute the characters are, then you can go ahead and stop reading here.
+Art is perty
+Humor is fairly on point, it won't really miss any beats
+Music is lovely

Cons:
+Some poorly telegraphed puzzles
+They don't even really try to give you an illusion of choice, mistakes you make are forgiven instantly to make room for a sloppy combat system and a linear narrative that they give you dialogue options for - for what I can only see as no reason- nothing you say or do can change anything and yet they still give you choices to do things for cheap 'interaction'
+AN ENTIRE SERIES OF PUZZLE PIECES THAT YOU GO THE WHOLE GAME WITHOUT USING. People are going to say "oh but this is chapter one, they'll probably use them later."- and I retort with, I don't care. If they are going to release this product as is then I am going to judge it as is.

+The game leans almost a bit too much on the text logs, and more to the point this entire first act is basically doing the housework to move you up to speed with the lingo, but since it has to do that your overall experience will suffer for it unless you're super into these characters
+You might find 1/3 of the characters annoying. Oh wait there's only 3 characters.
+Short play time. 3 hours. Act one. At the time of writing there is absolutely no scheduled release date for act two on a game five years in development and 3 years past initial scheduled release with vague development timelines leading up to this.
+A character switching mechanic that never gets used
+Spelling errors
FOR HOMESTUCKS:
Pros:
+All Pros mentioned above

+Jude is Cute
+Xanax or whatever his name was is adorable
+References I guess...
Cons:
+All Cons stated above

+Literally nothing new to anything you already knew besides 3 new characters
+I cannot overstate how dissapointing the combat system is
All I can really hope is that the next three sections they take the few criticisms they get to heart (because love is blind, and so is fandom) and make chapter two at least worthwhile for the 2 and a half hours it'll take to beat that. Also ADD TRICKSTER MODE.

Shadow of Mordor is a game that defines the 7/10 rating. It is intensely average in almost every way.
The story varies, sometimes its good, sometimes its straight up mediocre fan-fiction. Especially with its self-references like quoting Lord of the Rings, and even a LOTR title-drop that is one of the worst lines I have ever heard. "There can be only one...Lord of the Rings." is a real line that exists in this game. Its so forced and corny, and has no place being in a game trying to take itself seriously, and the inclusion of a character for no other reason than to have one character from the films/books in the game, its never justified. The ending sequences crosses into straight bad fanfiction.
Gameplay is good, but thats because its batman, down to the button combos and most of Talion's abilities. You like Batman? You like this. The main issue with the gameplay is after a certain point it becomes a joke, Talion becomes absurdly overpowered and you can clear out 50 orcs in no time at all, without struggling for health once. (Just stack runes that heal you on the use of any drain/brand on your dagger, and combat drain to restore all HP, which you can do twice, per 5-hit combo...) This also heavily hurts the real focus of the game, the "Nemesis" system.
The nemesis system is a fun, but flawed system. Its fun to play with, it really adds to a sandbox game, but it doesnt really work like they clearly intended. The intent is clear that you have actual nemesis, who come for you, and its a constant back and forth, and you are trying to manipulate tyhe captains so you can work your way to the higher ranks and take out the big fish. The reality is more of a cluster♥♥♥♥. The difference between a rank 1 captain and a warchief is barely noticable, save the warchief has a lot more defenses around him and you have to do a quest to make them even appear, otherwise you can pretty much kill anyone, at any time, at your discretion.
Thats also what makes the game fun, it is a true sandbox, and the results are sometimes pretty damn amusing. Having a captain you killed come back for revenge, only to finish his speech while you have your combo charged, and kill him in one finishing move? Hilarious. And it never fails to make me laugh when a area just turns into a clown car of captains, you move in to kill one, just to discover another one was right there, then have a nemesis come to kill you, then have a new captain who was hunting you show up, and its great.
I would love to see this system in more games, especially a more comedic tongue-in-cheek game.
The game is fairly short, you get 20 main missions (most fairly short), 24 rescue missions (they are all the same type of mission in different areas, recycled over and over, far too many of them in the game imo) 30 "Weapon" missions (10 for each of talions weapons), 20 open world challenges, a mercifully small handful of collectables. And a handful of recycled random missions that come up for the nemesis system, where most of the padding lies. Depending on how much you goof off exploiting the nemesis system for your amusement, the game is between 12-24 hours long.
Its a fun game, and a good one to kill time while waiting for another game to come out, but dont expect anything to blow you away.

Splinter Cell: Blacklist is one of the best games of 2013. Many were disappointed in 2010s Splinter Cell Conviction, which was more like an action game with stealth elements, adding new features like the mark & execute system, but also limiting the players experience by tight, limited corridor levels packed with little armies full of enemy minions.
With Blacklist, Ubisoft promised us a kind of back-to-the-roots approach to the franchise, a game in the style of classics like the timeless Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory. Did they keep their word? No, not exactly, the game offers strong stealth elements while also allowing gameplay in the style of a third person shooter. Its kind of a marriage beetween the old school stealth games and a solid shooter. Its kind of the opposite of the direction that Conviction took back in the day. While Conviction limited you in your possibilities of gameplay, it featured an intriguing good story, really fleshing out Sams character for the first time in the series in my opinion. Now Ubisoft decided to make a game with one of the best overall gameplay mechanics of 2013, but letting you fight stereotype terrorists with one of the weakest antagonists of this year. Sam Fisher in this game is more like a renegade Commander Shepard stripped of his intelligence and humour, completely different from the caring father figure he was in Conviction. (Also bring Michael Ironside back as Sam Fisher)
The Developers spiced up the stealth action gameplay by adding different types of enemies. Now you have to deal with heavies, dogs, drone technicians that disrupt your goggle and elite troopers that can spot you through cover and smoke. In the later levels of the game it is often impossible to take the enemies out by tons of silenced headshots, because you'll encounter guys with helmets and armor that can take a ton of damage before they go down. This makes stealth really worth doing, which is something that I praise this game for. But you also have the option to gun down your enemies, which is possible but frankly alot harder, nearly impossible in the mentioned later levels. So you either go for the hunter stealth approach, picking your enemies off one by one with lethal or non lethal takedowns or completely evade any enemy and fights.
And this is where the heart of the game lies down. Trying to get through the level without attacking anyone, only using your gun as a last resort, while playing on a high difficulty level is really intense, which isn't common in modern games anymore. Being spotted in games like for instance the Batman Arkham series always lets you escape by your grappling hook or fight your enemies off in open combat. If your spotted in perfectionist mode while having your stealth gear on (the game offers a great amount of weapon/armor customization for your playstyle, which is awesome), you're pretty much dead instantly.
From the technical aspect, the game is pretty solid. It's by no means a beautiful game, based on the Unreal Engine 2,5, but it gets the things needed for a stealth game right, like lightning and shadows. I haven't encountered any gamebreaking bugs or glitches, and the game is fortunatily relatively free of scripts that limit your progress in the level. The only thing that's really annoying it that everytime I get disconnected from the internet and reconnect, the game changes to window mode, but I don't know if this is a common issue.
If you're looking for a good stealth game with well done action elements, this game is for you.

I don't know I can say anything new about ME that hasn't already been said. It's a popular game series, the first one is over ten years old, and there are going to be more than enough reviews on here already that discuss its pros and cons. People will be bringing up how the first game has too much inventory management, or how levels progression is a little uneven (starting with too low of skills then gaining ground too quickly), or how solid characterization and story feels in ME 1 compared to others in the Shepard trilogy.
That being said, I still can't help but speak up and say: yes, these games are incredible. Yes, these games are worth being played. Yes, these games are worth talking about.
You can go to other reviews if you want to know how well the controls handle and other such game mechanisms. For me, it is sufficient to say the game is incredibly fun, and while aspects like inventory management might not be perfect, it never detracted me from my overarching, overwhelmingly positive gameplay experience. So I'm not going to talk about controls and graphics and the like. I'm going to talk about what means the most to me about the ME series: the story.
What makes the ME trilogy my favorite video games ever played is story. Don't get me wrong - I have a whole lot of fun shooting things. But there are lots of shooter games. That's not what makes ME special. What makes the game special is its characters, its plot, its world, its emotions. I consider ME an incredibly powerful story, perhaps even ranking amongst some of the most impacting stories ever told.
The first time I played ME 1, I remember having some slight challenges integrating into the universe. A lot of information about the universe is dumped upon you in a short amount of time. I would not say it is overwhelming, but it is something that, at least for me, was initially hard to keep everything straight. On my first mission, I already had to juggle information about geth and spectres and the Alliance and turians and human colonies like Eden Prime - and what was this about some Prothean ruin and what did it have to do with galactic matters? That said, I don't know how they could have handled information distribution any better, and one does find oneself emerging into the game, its world, and its lore seamlessly over the course of gameplay. You do successfully integrate into the world, and once you do, you become lost in it.
One of the things I appreciate most about the ME trilogy is that nothing is truly superfluous. Sure, there are side missions galore that seem to have nothing to do with the main plot. But I am impressed as a storyteller. Seemingly unrelated side missions tie into the overarching plot of the trilogy. By the time one enters ME 3, you realize that nothing introduced has been random additional information. Even simple events in the side missions get some growth, development, storytelling, and resolution. It's very satisfying to experience. You don't just meet some random guy Conrad Verner. You see where he ends up. You don't just help Rita's sister Jenna in the first ME game. You see her again. You see where she ends up. You don't just stop some random rogue VI on Luna. You see where even THAT ends up, too. Everything all ties together for the final efforts of the third game - and the way these get wrapped up gives a satisfying sense of closure, of completeness, of storytelling done right with a lot of careful precision and attention to detail.
That's only the side stories.
ME's main story is one that resonates with the heart. I feel that, of all the games in the Shepard trilogy, the first Mass Effect game has the best-structured story. The plot arc and its execution is impressively well-formed from a storytelling perspective, resulting in a narrative that is cohesive, memorable, and satisfying to experience. It is a well-formed adventure, making every step of the journey, start to end, engaging, enjoyable. Many stories have hiccups along the way, some portion of the story that does not carry through as well as the rest... but I feel as though ME 1 is solid from the second it starts to the second the story concludes.
As far as world-building and characterization are concerned, the first game is the least developed. Part of that's just the nature of being the first game, though - its purpose is to establish the story and characters; the other two games can then grow from it. I like to say ME 1 is best for plot structure, ME 2 best for characters, and ME 3 best for emotion. The player falls deeply in love with all the characters during the ME 2 missions, but might not be QUITE as gripped by the team in the first game. You are only just meeting the team, only just getting to know them, only just forming bonds with them. I still don't think the treatment of character is BAD in the first game - I did find myself latching onto Kaidan, Wrex, and Garrus readily enough in the ME 1 missions - and I did find myself quite emotional about certain impacting moments with characters - but character interactions only improve as the story continues. You don't *quite* get the howling-with-laughter moments in ME 1... but the first game is important for establishing these characters, helping you see how they tick, and helping you charge through Citadel space in an unforgettable adventure. You still have good times talking to the characters! You still can feel the essence of their personalities. You care about them by the time you get to Virmire! You still walk away from the first Mass Effect game feeling as though your experiences were memorable with the characters you met.
And by the time of ME 3? These characters resonate deeply within you; they are extremely three-dimensional, to the point they feel real.
An unforgettable story is part of the legacy of the ME franchise. It feels AMAZING stepping through ME 1 and ME 2 as a galactic hero. And then there are the characters - another astounding legacy of the ME franchise. The last thing that makes these games a sample of the finest storytelling is that the decisions you make critically matter.
As you're all going to know, RPGs allow gameplayers to make decisions that affect the outcome of your adventures. The ME trilogy is a series where your choices make *critical* differences... these are high-impact decisions, and what you choose profoundly alters your experiences in the game. Squadmates live or die depending on what you do. Civilizations could fall if you make the wrong move. These are not light choices to make... you CAN lose your teammates... nobody is safe. That level of high-stakes decision making is what makes the games so powerful to play. You are fully immersed into the world and what you do profoundly MATTERS.
The more I learn all the options you can select, and all the ways in which the story alters itself based upon your decisions... the more I'm in awe. I don't know that it's anywhere close to possible to experience all the ways the trilogy can go. The writers think of everything - if you romance X character in ME 1, then Q character in ME 2, then return to X in ME 3, and take them on Z mission, there will be unique dialogue. If you lose V character in ME 1, don't make W action in ME 2, lose R character in ME 3, and gain # amount of reputation points... then someone else might live. Who lives, who dies, who comes back into your life, how they come back into your life, what they say, how they say it, what they do, why they choose to do it... everything from the tiny-little-details (whether or not they sang a song to you during freetime) to the big impacts (like whether or not they even lived) is all accounted for and integrated into gameplay.
Maybe I can't say anything profoundly *new* about ME, but it's still worth saying. Of all the games I have played, of stories I have experienced, few have come remotely close to the immersive, engaging, and emotional world of ME. I could not recommend this story enough.

If you knew the world would come to its end, how would you spend your remaining time on Earth? If you are Haruna Ryou, you take this opportunity so that you can live the last happy life on this dying planet.
NOTE: This is a slow paced visual novel. There are only a few jokes here and there to lighten the mood sometimes. Otherwise, this VN can take 10+ hours to read, so if you don't have the patience and you just want to finish a story quickly, this VN probably isn't for you.
This is a kinetic VN, meaning that you read it as if it were a story book. There are no choices to make so just sit back and enjoy the story (and keep tapping the space bar to move to the next line of text if you don't have Auto forward turned on).
To put it short: The world is coming to an end. People are preparing to evacuate from Earth. Creatures know as Felixes have helped humanity with the evacuation, including one particular Felix, Sion.
Warrant Officer Ryou is a deadly soldier who struggles to find the reason why he wants to fight and what his goals in life are. He is assigned with a comrade named Lavie by his lieutenant to protect Sion.
The story is told in flashbacks. The story begins with the present, with Ryou and Sion living together. Afterwards, we go back in time and see how things came to be.
There is a reason why Minori's name is on this VN. The scenes are very well done. They are simply, yet beautiful. Character designs are nice. While the building interiors may look generic, there is usually that light streak that helps add some "life" to the scenes. Characters will also blink (it's not much, but its at least better than looking at a still , unmoving picture).
Maybe I love the Opening them for eden too much. The soundtrack consists of soft piano music in the background that helps accompany certain scenes. When dramatic scenes start to roll in, you will feel it.
The voice acting for this VN is superb. None of the dialogue feels rushed and it feels as if the characters are having a real conversation as they usually would. When things get serious, you will definitely hear it coming.
Like I said before, it's best to enjoy eden if you have the patience for this story. This story can be considered a love story".

I had high expectations when I saw that this VN had high ratings in Steam but was rather disappointed.  My first impression was something like "Kazami Yuuji meets Reverie Planetarian" but the end result was a rather weak plot.   Planetarian made me cry like a child and Grisaia made me gasp, but Eden didn't make me shed a single tear.
Comparison with other VNs aside, the story in general was pretty bland. Whatever excitement I got from the "research facility" arc disappeared completely in the arcs that followed. It's like they tried to follow the mirror image of the plot mountain, starting with the climax and ending with exposition. The story became some bland slice-of-life between Gary Stu and Mary Sue. It did a good job tying plot elements together but it all felt unnecessary towards the end, messily resolving any conflict.
It's a well-spent 10+ hour story, a calming ride, a relaxing experience... but it doesn't feel like it's worthy of its high ratings. I'm glad I bought this at a discount - I might've had buyer's remorse if I had bought this at full price.

[Disclaimer] This review contains very minor spoilers. And for those who do not wish to read the entire length of my review, a TL;DR is located at the end of the review summarizing my thoughts.
[Synopsis] Over a hundred years ago, humanity learned of a humungous comet, one massive enough to obliterate Earth itself. Now, as the day of destruction closes in, most of the human race has already evacuated into space in search of a new beginning. This escape is largely due to the accomplishments of a woman named Sion - a genius scientist born as a part of a new race of intellectually-enhanced humans created for the sole purpose to find a method to counteract humanity's extinction. It was at this time that she met Ryo, a soldier seemingly void of life and purpose, who was ordered to become her bodyguard. Now, let the curtains rise on the last love story on earth…
[Review] Eden* is undoubtedly one of the best and most touching VNs currently available on Steam, and is a must buy for anyone looking for a beautifully written and somber story accompanied by fantastic visuals and music. Though there are certainly flaws within the VN itself, I believe the pros far outweight the cons of this VN.
Pros:
• Characters - Each and every one of the characters is written with care. Though each falls into a certain trope in their early stages of development, depth is carefully layered upon each character that far surpasses their original trope.
• Music - Eden* has some of the most pleasantly somber tracks I've heard in any VN. Many classical instruments are used including the violin and the piano.
• Voice Acting -
• CG/Visuals -
• Pacing -
• Translation -
Cons:
• Price - For a 10 to 15 hour VN (varies on whether you choose to use the autoplay feature and/or skip voice acting), $19.99 is a pretty high price. Though I'd love to say it's completely worth it, I'd recommended waiting for it to go on sale. Fortunately for me, I was able to pick Eden* up months after release in a very cheap Humble Bundle deal for less than a dollar.
• Certain Facial Proportions - Eden* has some of the biggest eyes I've seen since CLANNAD, so for some it might be a turn off. Additionally, Ryou has the most awkward looking facial features in many of the CGs he's included in.
• Minor Distracting Fanservice - Though fanservicey shots are used extremely rarely (taking up less than 5 minutes in total screentime), I find it still worth mentioning that there are a few CGs which included some unnecessary fanservicey elements to them.
• User Interface - Compared to other VNs of similar quality, Eden* has a very basic UI.
• Animations -
• Plus MOSAIC (18+ additional content) - Entirely unnecessary. Unless for some reason you desire the eroge content the game offers separately (only available on MangaGamer), I wouldn't touch this.
TL;DR: A little slow to start, but the tears will rain soon enough.

At best, A.R.E.S. is competent. It doesn't know whether it wants to be Mega Man or Metroid, and suffers for it. The level design includes both large multi-scrolling rooms and more platforming-oriented sections, and it's never entirely clear which drops are bottomless pits and which lead to other parts of the stage. I'm also not happy with the upgrade mechanic, which encourages literal grinding as you kill enemies for the three types of items that are needed to upgrade your weapons. The controls also feel a little slow, with the dash move in particular always feeling like it's just a little too long to execute and traverses just a little too short a distance to avoid enemy attacks.
At least the boss fights are pretty fun, and it's entertaining when you get into the groove of blasting enemies and jumping from platform to platform. But all of its other problems make it hard to recommend. You could do worse, but you could also do a whole lot better. Try Cave Story+, Noitu Love 2, or They Bleed Pixels if you want to play a really good action-platformer.

I've played this game since before version 1.0 and in its various stable, unstable, and nightly states. Early on, I would have told you the game was alright, but the devs didn't uphold their initial promise of quick updates delivered at least weekly. Eventually, they got updates to a good state, even through a company headquarters move, that also involved moving the development team. For a time, the game was fun, but aimless.
Things have changed for the better, in my opinion. Where before, the pacing of the game was entirely based around when you felt like moving to the next tier via "crafting" the next boss, there's now a semi-decent plot to go with the experience. The gameplay has gone from from a largely procedurally generated effort with teired sectors of difficulty, to a more controlled, somewhat precreated effort with a nice bit of RNGesus goodness to keep things fresh. The result is that while planets still can feel same-y, there are actually secrets on and under the surface to keep things interesting, like dungeons, "mini-dungeons" (which are never bigger than a screen or two), and challenge rooms. Sadly, the storyline happens mostly outside of the RNG-generated worlds and instead takes place inside contained missions that have you teleporting to places you can't actually reach via flying around space, which feels like a missed opportunity, but this allows missions to structured properly outside of the rest of the game's sandbox, but unfortunately locks out out of tile manipulation, so your actual skills at combat and platforming will be tested.
There's still lots of questionable design choices in Starbound, like that AI is often dumb and reacts oddly to actions such as crouching (I had one gun toting enemy just stand in front of me and let me take pot-shots at him until he died without reacting while I crouched behind a two-block high cover, for instance). A lot of the progression is locked to an "item scanning" system that may have you flying around to several planets hunnting the villages of a particular race that may or may not have all of the items you need to scan in it. The inventory has expanded into a tabbed system that forces items into their own individual categories, which keeps your equipment and the various terrain blocks you'll inevitably pick up separate, but it can make finding a particular item hard in a pinch (are my torches that I use all the time with my equipment and various upgrade items? No, they're with the furniture). The game also likes to "blank" out your hotkeys when you don't have any more of an item, whereas other games would leave a greyed-out "zero" indicator until you have more of a given item. There is also no dedicated "exit all dialogs" button, as far as I can tell. A friend of mine had more of an issue with this than I did, expecting "jump" to close all open dialogs, like inventory, container, or shop dialogs. But these are mostly nitpicks.
As for new features, one thing I've particularly enjoyed that didn't exist in the earlier versions of the game that I played (there was a large gap where I'd stopped playing the pre-1.0 game) is the colony system. Previously there were tons of fancy towns, villages, or even just houses in the game that held native residents that... didn't do anything. These have been overhauled considerably to where they can now tell when you've destroyed property and may turn hostile to you. Also previously, you could attack the citizens of these towns accidentally, whereas now you can't attack them without first making them hostile. Where the colony system comes into play is that now you can build your own colonies from scratch, and by using race, job, or just special themed furniture, you can choose what types of people live there. There are guards, chefs, merchants, plain old villagers, and more. I'm currently trying to get a themed set for an All-Seeing Knight that involves building furniture with disembodied eyes. From the improvements to villages and the ability to make  your own, there's also procedurally generated quests you can get from any of the NPCs involved that can give you items or even a new member for your ship's crew, which is part of the ship progression path to add new rooms and functionality to your ship.
Again, the game is a much stronger game than it was pre-1.0, and I liked it then. I've made multiple characters and had a great time while I've played it. The performance problems of pre-1.0 have been worked out, there's a strong progression backbone, and most of the gameplay and pacing issues I had problems with have been ironed out. Definitely a good game, especially if you're coming from something like Minecraft or Terraria and want something a bit more rooted in a linear plot, but with enough of that procedurally generated goodness to keep things fresh.

I've had my eye on this game for quite sometime since it's early access release in 2015. But recently it went on Humble Bundle so I figured I give it a shot. Now, I did not go into the game expecting an MMO version of Skyrim, Unreal Engine quality graphics, or anything of that nature... needless to say this game is quite fun. Not sure why people are complaining about difficulty because it's not a hard game...
Positives:
* Easy to pick up
- I didn't have any issues picking up the basics of the game, it was simple and straight to the point (gather, hunt, craft).
* Story/Lore
- despite it being an open world survival sim. There are books, pages, and other things that         really add depth to the world of Savage Lands, including an origin story of the lands.
* Enemy modeling
- very nice models and the creatures in the world are also pretty interesting, though, nothing original, still pretty awesome designs.
* Multiplayer
- For you and a bunch of friends.
Negatives:
There are a few things I would like to point out that are a bit out of place.
* First off, there is no female gender (at least not yet).
- so fellow female gamers have to create a male character (which isn't game breaking but diversity would be nice).
* World details and textures could use more polish.
- The enemies and character armors look nice but next to the textures of the world they stand out a bit. (again, nothing major. Just minor adjustments to make it a bit more enjoyable.)
* A small tweak in spawns.
- I spent about 2hrs in my first playthrough exploring and aside from the dragon on the tower the only things that tend to appear every now and then are grunt skeletons, a few rabbits, and only a few deer. I did however run into an armored skeleton which was pretty tough.
Overall I am really enjoying this game. I see the devs update on a regular basis so I hope there are more additions to keep this game alive and growing. I also recommend this game if you like surival or open world games.

I had a really good time with Shadow of Mordor, even though it is not without it's flaws.
The plot is pretty ordinary, and paced pretty badly. The character development is such that it is hard to really care about the outcome, and at by the game's end it becomes clear the plot was litle more than window-dressing for the gameplay itself.
This is where SoM shines: borrowing from and refining Arkham-style combat mechanics, the game includes stealth and open combat sections as it tasks you with killing orcs, gaining intel on their captains, killing them, and moving up the chain in perpetuity. The game's early challenge makes certain captains memorable and thus your nemesis - killing them is it's own reward if they were the one to burn you last time round. Those organic sections of gameplay are extremely rewarding, and it's a little bit of a shame when the convoluted plot gets in their way. One small criticism is the game's early challenge dissipates when you begin unlocking some of the more overpowered abilities - it's still fun, but less rewarding in terms of difficulty.
It looks pretty, and ran very nicely for me despite being extremely close to the minimum requirements. The game-world is engaging especially for Lord of the Rings fans, placing you in familiar areas and with familiar characters and enemy-types. The voiceacting particularly deserves praise.
Overall, Shadow of Mordor is well worth the price of admission thanks to compelling and rewarding gameplay. If you're prepared to look past a weak storyline, and the difficulty plateau in the latter half, you'll have a grand time.

The earth is about to be smashed to bits by a red star. Having known this for 100 years a certain someone was instrumental in creating a space program so man could escape. People were not given a choice on if they could stay and die so many were outraged. Some also refused to believe the end would ever come. Thus the world has been in a constant state of martial law style war. The main male character is former special forces and a ruthless killer in his own eyes totally full of sin. Will he and the countless other people he meets find an internal sense of redemption or a way to atone for the immense guilt they feel?
Well obviously art and sound are top notch for a VN. I mean just watch the preview video. The story has a nice way of coming full circle and telling stories within stories. The whole story itself is by no means short like most VN titles bosting over 10 hours of story.
It ends up very difficult for a rational person to find any point in some of the decisions made since there is really no reason things had to turn out so heart wrenching if you think about it after your done with the game. This is a kinetic novel so choices do not exist. It's actually kind of a shame that choices don't exist because the option to make this into a Clannad type visual novel would have made more sense even if the story suffered slightly. In the end this game reminded me a lot of Clannad the anime series because it felt like it was purposely set up for feels even when it didn't make a whole lot of sense.
If you don't mind emotional stories with well developed characters this is a must. So far it is the best VN I've experience on steam easily beating the rest. Unlike many other steam VN's that have hentai on other sites this one has it available on other sites, but it actually is separate and makes little sense with the game if you go that route. Thus the steam version is actually better in my opinion because it won't make you wonder about that other content that makes little sense with the story. Even if I do think the story purposely makes the reader sad by having the characters purposely choose the more painful route even though there were way better options available I still respect it none the less.
I would say about $15. To be honest I usually don't value VN games at a high value so this is actually rather up there for me. Especially since I normally say $1 per hour of gameplay. Except this time the story, sound, and slight animations make it worth the extra $0.50 an hour.

This kinetic novel follows the point of view of a young man who has seen more combat than he should have. He enters a mysterious facility and meets a girl who has more to her than meets the eye. No, I promise you I have not confused eden* with Planetarian. That said, if you enjoyed Planetarian, then I think you are very likely to enjoy eden*.
The visuals in eden* are good. In addition to having a variety of poses and facial expressions for each character, the characters are shown to blink and their lips sync with the voice acting. There are many CGs and each one is beautiful to see. Several locations even have multiple CGs and this gives the impression of a changing camera angle. I like it.
As eden* is a visual novel, the topic of H-scenes should be raised. I did some research and discovered that the H-scenes are apparently bonus content to unlock in the main menu after completing the kinetic novel once. This means that the H-scenes are not at all relevant to developing the canon storyline. So don’t worry about characters suddenly referring to something that happened during a deleted H-scene. That said, I also read that the H-scenes add more depth to each character despite being non-canon. Anyway, it should be well known now that if you want to see H-scenes then you should buy directly from MangaGamer.
The sound is good. The background music sets the mood well. However, it does not loop well because the end of the music fades to silence before starting again. The voice acting is good. I did not find any characters irritating to listen to. I think the emotions contained in the voice acting were appropriate for each character and the situation.
The story is told using flashbacks, and it makes some of the plot developments easy to see coming. The setting is easy to follow. The plot is decent and enjoyable, but it is not great. The translation is good. There are a few instances when I think a native English speaker would find the text unnatural but the text is still grammatically correct so it can still be understood.
Overall, I enjoyed eden* and recommend it to people who enjoy visual/kinetic novels. It is not a great kinetic novel, but it is good enough to deserve a place in the visual/kinetic novel library.

A.R.E.S: Extinction Agenda is a side scrolling action platform game.
You play as a robot called ARES through linear levels with mid-bosses and bosses at the end of those levels. As you defeat enemies and blow up crates, you can find three types of resources which can be used to upgrade your abilities and weapons. You acquire more weapons as you progress through the game.
The storyline is nothing amazing, but engaging enough. The game itself looks beautiful and plays like the old Megaman X games on the SNES. The levels have varied enemy types and can be challenging. There are also several difficulty modes and a ranking system based on how well you perform in each level.
My only complaint is that it is far too short...with only 5-6 levels, you can finish the storyline very quickly with full upgrades. The DLC for the game simply includes alternate skins for ARES and music, nothing that really adds to the gameplay.
The game itself is great, but you don't get very much for what you pay. I also doubt any further DLCs with expanded levels or extras will be added. I hope if they ever release a sequel, it will be much longer.

These are things ANYBODY would say about A.R.E.S.: Extinction Agenda after roughly ten minutes of play.

This isn't Baldurs Gate or Icewind Dale. It's not even close. It's way better.
Obsidian reactivity is everywhere, with multiple endings to quests, different ways to influence your companions and a storyline that is similar in theme to Mask of the Betrayer and Planescape Torment.
The backdrops are influenced by the Infinity Engine games, but with more interactivity with the environment. Much of this takes place the form of text cutscenes - storyboards that allow some player agency, usually through item or skill checks. These can help you skip past a section of enemies or find hidden treasure.
As a backer of the Kickstarter, I'm pleased to see Obsidian do well with a game they've always wanted to make. It looks successful too - here's hoping they can do more games like this. I wouldn't mind seeing another game in this engine, with their kind of reactive storytelling.
The next one up is Torment: Tides of Numenera from inXile. That has Black Isle and Obsidian alumni (Kevin Saunders, George Ziets, Colin McComb, Adam Heine) working on it, so my hopes are high.
Pillars of Eternity certainly sets the bar.

TL;DR: Really captures the BG vibe. Highly recommended for fans of the IE games. Writing is solid throughout, even if some companions are a bit flat. The new mechanics are a mixed bag of hits and misses. Wish there was a higher level cap. Glad I backed it, and can’t wait for the expansion and future continuations of the series.
If you miss the good old days of BG, do yourself a favor and just buy this now. For those of you who have managed to miss one of the best CRPGs ever made keep reading for the rundown.
PoE uses a RTwP system with plenty of options for auto-pausing, as well as a slow mode to briefly slow the action down and get your tactics set. While your uncontrolled party members lack an AI like BG (used spells on their own based on AI chosen) they do auto attack without input.
A lot of the more complex rules are gone and things are much simpler for new comers (no need to know what THAC0 is). Many abilities have a limited number of uses per combat and other have a limited number per rest always providing choices in combat. At higher difficulties the number of enemies grows, you get higher enemies types (Black Ooze > Lesser Black Ooze), and the number of camping supplies you can carry is extremely limited (Hard and up). Depending on how much problems you have with combat this could be an issue. Crafting has also been added, though it’s far from a great implementation in my opinion.
The diversity of races and classes doesn't disappoint. Each race has a choice between two subraces which gives them a racial bonus. Many of the races, and classes, will be familiar in general make up to normal fantasy tropes, but there's also some unique things like God touched (the lack of a helm is a drawback) and Ciphers. Character creation overall is pretty good and adding in custom portraits is quite easy.
Some of the newly designed systems do fall a bit flat though. The new stat system really lowers the importance of min/maxing. On the one hand this means casual players won’t be stopped by bad builds, but people who enjoy character building may feel let down by the diminished emphasis on stats. XP is no longer given on a by kill basis, instead being rewarded for bestiary additions. For example, a little bit of experience the first few times you fight a monster till you know everything about it, then none at all. Depending on play style this can lead to a fair amount of unrewarding combat.
A minor complaint includes most NPCs not feeling as interesting as BG. The low level cap (12) is disappointing, though understandable. You will most likely hit the cap long before the game is over if you pursue most side quests. After that point the lack of character progression feels a bit unrewarding sadly. Considering they designed a ruleset from scratch and had a limited budget it’s understandable, but still a bit of a let down. I expect this ground up design is also the reason for the limited number of abilities and spells compared to AD&D.
Unfortunately at the time of this review there are bugs. Obsidian is still patching, but their official communication regarding it has been pretty poor. However, they are an established midrange studio so we know it's coming, eventually.

I had a chance to play Dark Souls years ago, and I've wanted the game ever since. So I already KNOW I like it, I love the feeling of being able to control my character in a fight rather than facing vaguely in a foe's direction and hitting buttons to apply some damage, or scooting around a bit and hitting buttons to apply some damage. It reminds me of Die By The Sword in that respect -- there's a retro moment for you -- although the two games took very different approaches, with DBTS focused on weapon movement control and Dark Souls foremost on combat maneuvering control and learning when to use each skill. The feeling of having achieved something through skill rather than just large numbers and maybe good timing, upon beating a foe that was hell to get past, is like no other game I've played. And in spite of all you're about to read, I do recommend it, but with one caveat which many others have mentioned before me... Especially if you play KB&M-style rather than using a controller.
If, like me, you are a diehard keyboard-&-mouse gamer by preference, necessity or both, yes you can still play this game on PC. But know going in that the recommendation to use a controller isn't a suggestion, it's a warning.
The job done porting this game from console to PC is a well-known unfunny joke where keyboard and mouse support is concerned. It's so bad that, both now and back when I could try the game before, I wondered aloud how much someone made in kickbacks from Xbox controller sales because of this! It's a visibly half-egged effort; they didn't even bother to show keyboard equivalents in onscreen tips or main menu instructions, those all still show the Xbox controller buttons regardless of what control method you're using.
-- You can download the player-made DSfix and DSMFix mods from a trusted source to at least sort of fix the game's keyboard and mouse support, as well as open up some display options and a better resolution selection, another area in which this port falls embarrassingly short of the mark. Spend some time setting them up properly. The instructions I had didn't make it as clear where certain files need to go as it looked like, so I followed the instructions to the letter and some mod functions didn't work until I figured it out. Oops.
This is in order to avoid things like the camera spinning wildly (on faster mouse settings) or swaying drunkenly (on slower settings) at the tiniest shift of the mouse, which was my "welcome to Dark Souls, baby" moment. Unless you feel like playing Dark Souls "Drunken Master Style", you probably won't enjoy that any more than I did. Many thanks to the modders who put in the time and effort to fix things like this, by the way. But even with the fixes, the camera behavior in this game may well drive you crazy: movement keys operate independently of the camera, which is great for some situations -- you can see a boss while maneuvering around it -- and ghastly for others --  such as suddenly reversing direction without falling to your death because the camera's still facing the other way. It can be reset behind your character (there is no 1st person cam) with a separate keystroke or a drag of the mouse, both of with have their downsides (such as, the camera's positional reset key also serves as Target Lock-On Mode's toggle. This can be a problem). But there's no way to set it to continue doing so automatically for situations in which this would be useful.
-- Web search is your friend. If you're having trouble translating from Controllerese to interpret the onscreen tips, the solution is likely to be already mentioned online.
Here's some examples of translated-to-Keyboardese commands mentioned only in Controllerese in the ingame tips:
Options Menu (Where your character status, gear, equip & unequip items, and game control panes are found. The key for this is End, rather than ESC as in many games. Can be remapped to ESC.),
Looting corpses or accessing messages and bloodstains (Action/Gesture key. Put this somewhere you can reach it in combat for easier retrieval of your green demise bloodstain, in case of a second death),
Using spells at the very beginning of the game (you can't do this until you obtain an item you need for spellcasting. So when you can't cast your spell in the first few rooms, that's normal. You should have it before the end of the tutorial/first game stage),
Kicking (Tap Run Forward + Normal Attack keys AT THE SAME TIME. Hold+tap or asynchronous keystrokes won't work),
Jump Attacking (Tap Run Forward + Heavy Attack keys at the same time. Same notes as Kicking),
Jumping (1. Hold Run Forward key, 2. continue holding RFand also hold Spacebar [or whatever you ressigned it to] until you see your character enter Sprint animation, 3. release Spacebar while still holding RF key and quickly tap Spacebar again.
If a combat skill doesn't work, make sure the game's Options menu is closed (default to return to previous menu or exit  menus: Backspace key), as you can't perform some actions if it's open, even though you can still move your character around.
Dark Souls also has bizarrely limited keyboard rebind support. It refuses to acknowledge that the F-key row even exists (or tilde, or punctuation keys, or number keys...), and the numpad is only slightly better off, being usable to reassign the main arrow key functions, and not actually usable for issuing commands in play. If not for the game's reputation for poor K&M support, I'd have wondered if I'd finally facedesked on my keyboard one time too many.
Some people will tell you to just buy a controller and 'git gud' if you want to play Dark Souls, possibly with a "lol" in there somewhere. But for me, even though in this instance they have a valid point about controller being what the game was made for.... When I saw what a truly pathetic job was done of keyboard and mouse support... well, later edit here: I resent using a controller for one game because someone didn't do their job right (or actively decided not to do it) on this deservedly much-requested port. This is also a part of why I waited so long to get the game, I resented spending much on it unless this issue got a functional official fix. HOWEVER. I've made peace with a controller, reluctantly, now that I've found one I can use comfortably. Using it resolved some technical problems (game would blackscreen-lock while playing). I'm still disgusted with whoever handled that part of the port to PC job.
I already know it gets better with practice. I spent my first play session bumming around the starting two rooms and hall mastering moving around, and the second using tutorial-level mobs as practice dummies, before I even approached the boss fight at the end of the level. It took quite a lot longer than usual, but there was a distinct moment after several reconfiguring tweaks to which keys do what to suit how I address the keyboard, when I started to "click" with the controls and things (mostly) happened the way I intended them to. For now, I almost don't use the mouse at all in DS, even though I'm normally a kb&m-combo player, while I've read that others do the reverse and bind everything to the gaming mouse buttons. Find what works for you.
So, yes. I will slowly 'git gud' just like with any other game I feel is worth the effort, or I'll die (and die and die and die and die) trying.  Because it's Dark Souls, and it's worth it.
And if you're game for this in spite of the hassle of setting it up and mastering the controls, if I haven't scared you off yet, then get the game, get mauled a lot, get good and kick some butt. :)

I'm torn on this one.
I really really REALLY want to love the game, but in the current way I can't recommend it to anyone.
Would I really care about it if I would not be familiar with homestuck fandom? I doubt it.
It lacks the substance, lacks the proper character development and generally lacks the charm that homestuck had.
I'm not saying it is bad, it is just not what I expected. Worst, it reminds me of exactly the same problems that Armikrog had.
PROS:
Yes, it is really, really well drawn.
CONS:
1. First of all, it feels dated and unfinished. The game was in production for 5 years and you can feel it. Manual save system for 2h game looks archaic. Menu elements looks half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ The game is buggy. It's rough around the edges. Art quality is inconsistent.
Map layout is bizzare. A lot of game elements can be accessed from a very specific angle even if they visible on other screens. For example, in the 2nd act security terminal is visible but you can't access it *UNLESS* you realize that you have to change the view.
There is an option to swap characters, but there is no gameplay mechanic to utilize it. Why is it there?
Combat/ability system looks unfinished. Once again, it feels like a forced addition that can be entirely cut from the game or be replaced by the scripted scene. I can't exactly say what feels wrong about it, but it feels wrong. Also, those abilities can be probably used, like, two times in the entire game? Why coudn't they just add another option to the popup menu and call it a day?
Those are minor complaints, but they are important, because they form the overall game impression, and generally break immersion for me.
2. It has a soul but it has *WRONG* soul.
The broad appeal and the art direction they took is understandable, but in my opinion it is detrimental to the game.
In Homestuck art always feels second to the content, and the whole aim of the narrative was to create this bizzare "meta" atmosphere.
I don't see it in the game. They tried to make classic golden age adventure with a team and creative lead who does not have experience in this field. As a result we have a game that has all of the weaknesses of the genre and none of the strengths of the Hussie. It is an attempt to play on the foreign field and I don't see the reason behind it.
Why creating another beautiful but mediocre adventure game? There are plenty of them, and it is very difficult to compete with them having such a small team. The game does not try bring anything new or try to achive anything notable rather than being very ambitious but very minor omage to the niche webcomic.

While the game is clearly not finished and I wasn't expecting to like it when I started playing, I do recommend it for those who enjoy multiplayer crafting/survival. This review is current as of v0.8.3 build 306 (11th August 2016). Update: I've been out wandering all over now, even almost climbed a dragon tower before I found out you can't. At this point in time I feel there need to be more to do and would really like some buildable stairs and platforms.
I have not encountered death from the dragon once (even walking right up to it's tower) as some others seem to (I think it got patched) and most of the wildlife is easy enough to kill, at least on the starting island. I've started several new games and every time the dragon has stayed away. Once you venture across the long bridge the enemies (skeletons) seem to get better equipped and can kill you quite quickly, and there are other things lurking in the woods.
One thing the game doesn't have which I would like to see is skills you can buy with experience from things you accomplish, such as being able to sprint longer, freeze/starve more slowly, harvest more ore from mining sites before they are depleted and increase weapon damage or armour protection. This isn't a huge thing missing from the game but I feel the experience would benefit from having at least some small ways to improve your character.
The biggest issues I've had so far are;
- the interface isn't explained (it's not incredibly complex but a short tutorial to tell you what's what and how it works would be helpful). For those wondering, you can split a stack of items by holding shift and clicking with LMB, and items can be quickly picked up in the inventory by double-clicking with LMB.
- on some games the wildlife decides to just randomly stop spawning in certain areas for a while (in my first game my friend and I began starving after day 2 because there was nothing around to kill).
- most physical structures have to be built from your journal in the house tab, which is confusing and nothing tells you to look for them in there. Campfires, walls, buildings, traps and various crafting stations are all in your jounal and not the crafting menu. Once you select something to build you put down a blueprint where you want it (mousewheel rotates) and the blueprint then shows the materials needed to build it, which you can add all at once or bit-by-bit. A problem with this is that if you have items on the ground near a blueprint you can accidentally add materials while trying to pick up your stuff.
- a few of the items you build in the crafting stations are world-placeable (like chests) but when you make them there's no placement interface, so you end up placing them down only vaguely where you want and with no control over the direction the objects are facing. Furthermore these objects can be knocked over and off surfaces by enemies but you walk right through them and cannot pick them up or adjust them to keep your base tidy.
- The only way to unbuild structures it to tear them down and weapons (even stone swords) deal more structure damage than your basic clubs and hatchets, so as soon as you hit tin you'll end up using weapons for everything since they can harvest resources as well. I find this odd.
- There are some issues with server hosting. Server privacy is almost nonexistent unless you set a password. Even when I set the game I was hosting to "friends only" I still had random strangers joining every now and then (not a lot of them, but even one is too many). On top of this there are very few things you can do as the host and none of the options are presented to you when starting to host your game, you have to find them in the options menu while playing.
- Both the food you eat and the food you keep don't last long enough. Especially considering you're in a very cold area, meat should last longer than it does before spoiling (and there's nothing in the item details to tell you how long it lasts). On top of that everything you DO eat doesn't keep you going for long. If killing a boar the same size as myself only gives me one piece of meat then by golly that piece of meat should keep me going for at least a few days! Because of these issues you'll spend a lot of time hunting and foraging, unless you got lucky like me and had one wild boar after another wander straight into the abandoned village (seriously I killed more than ten of the things while just standing around working on building stuff).
- Some things are intuitive, like the fact that you have to mine metals, but others aren't. When I wanted to get clay I had to google it, facepalming at the fact that I have to smash it out of rocks. Thankfully this only seems to be the case for a few items.
- Creatures often go straight through rocks and other barriers that you have to go over/around. This is a real issue when you think you have that deer cornered and ripe for stabbing and he just vanishes into the rock face. This only seems ot happen with part of the rocks and I think they get stuck in there sometimes because they don't always come out the other side.
- A minor gripe; I once found a compass and was annoyed that I had to hold it in my hand to tell direction. Normally it wouldn't be a bother but with so little inventory space the item wasn't worth the bother to take with me, so I dumped it. Extra equipment slots for things like this would be useful, and having them add a compass bar to the interface instead of holding up the object too. Furthermore as far as I can tell nobody from the abandoned settlements thought having a map would be a good idea despite apparently having enough paper to just leave lots of notes laying around. Even if there isn't a "you are here" marker on them, having some maps of each area to add to your journal and a compass bar would be really nice.
- Another minor gripe; In character creation you can only create males, colours are limited to the realistic natural spectrum and half of the tattoos make the characters look like they are wearing t-shirts. Small things really, but I want to have a pink mohawk! D:<
All in all I find it fun so far, just watch out for those skeletons, they're surprisingly quiet when they come up behind you!

There’s a serious lack of drive behind the story and it’s entirely masked behind shallow side quests that offer very little relief from the repetitive hack and slash nature of the game. As the main story progressed towards the end, I found a slight build up towards this Black Hand character that slaughtered my beloved wife and son. That was a disappointment. The final scene was a sorely brief experience with very little satisfaction (your girlfriend probably says the same thing). If you like a historically masked hack and slash then sure, go buy the game. However, and although I got all the DLCs with this edition, I won’t pursue the additional content purely on the basis that it’s a boring game.

This is a really good game in a rare sense.
Most games make themselves fun by giving you some stuff early on that becomes inferior quickly, thereby forcing you to have to buy their currency or items in a similar fashion (Items that are helpful in your current area, but quickly become inferior.) And if they don't do that, then they just tend to get boring fast, require low or no skill whatsoever, or require TOO MUCH skill for you to handle. TBoI (As i call it) manages to require a ton of practice and skill while maintaining its fun factor, by making it a gamble at the same time. But the items it gives you can be helpful later on and in your current state. (Brimstone - My Opinion), or completely screw your play over (Bob's Brain - Literally every player's opinion ever) Some items just help you out, (Pentagram - Damage Up) And some combine extremely well, (Pyro + Pyromaniac - 99 Bombs + Immunity to bombs [Respectively])
But Overall, it is an extremely fun game that you can easily get lost in, and punch several (Hundred/Thousand) hours in without getting bored. And community mods just extend your gameplay further (Anti-Birth), but some mods aren't all so well. (Couldn't find an example).
Thank you for reading this review, so have a good day. (And avoid Bob's Brain!)

Very solid single player zombie game-- I've always looked for an open world zombie simulator like this one, and I'm fairly hooked now that I've found it! There's a pretty decent story, lots of stuff to do, and many cool things to factor in like being in charge of bases that you can upgrade, or the ability to barracade yourself inside a building to practice your shooting on passing zombies, and many more.
I especially love the mechanic of having to gather resources and survivors for bases-- you often have to bring sacks of food/building material/ammo/fuel back to base in order to keep morale up, survive, and build stuff. In fact, base management is probably one of the most in depth systems this game has to offer, letting you move base location to a wide variety of spots, establish outposts based on how big your home base is, and creating a self-sufficient base that can grow food and has everything you need.
That said, there are a few things that might turn some people off. For one, while this is an open world game so to speak, there's only 3 towns, and they're rather tiny. There is a decent bit of wide open area as well and you won't be short of things to do inside the towns, but if you're looking for a large expanse to explore and scavenge, you won't find it here.
2nd: The game is pretty damn easy. It's really hard to die, even if you lose all your health you just spam spacebar for a revive. If you die again after that in a fight, you lose that character and maybe the ones who were fighting with you, but it's very rare that you die unless you afk in the middle of the road(That's how I lost Marcus, the main character :( )
Zombies are easy to kill and you don't have to avoid getting bitten. In fact, hordes of zombies(10-15 zombies roaming together) can be killed in a few seconds by just running them over with a car, which you can do several times before the car takes significant damage.
Overall, it's a great game still, and I would definitely recommend buying it if you enjoy doing objectives and following a storyline while still having the freedom to pretty much do whatever you want/go wherever you want in the map provided. I currently am still having a blast several hours in, which is more than I can say about a lot of the zombie games recently released! If only there was a way to have a multiplayer system in this game though....

***This is a spoiler-free review!***
I wish there was an option between "yes" and "no" for recommending a game on here. Because my response varies based on what you're wanting this game for.
Do you like Homestuck and want to get a little more into what kind of place Alternia was, and have a good chuckle every now and again? Then yes, I recommend it.
But as a point and click game, regardless of what franchise it's tied to, I can't in good conscience recommend it as-is.
My favorite part of P&C games is the puzzles. Even when I don't get them myself, I like seeing how clever they are in the end. But a lot of the puzzles in Hiveswap that stumped me wound up having really bizarre and illogical solutions. A lot of parts felt really over-written, and that in the process of trying to cram as many jokes in as they could, they also put in far too many red herrings that then became more frustrating than funny. On the flip side, some of the puzzles seemed like they could have had a little more player involvement, but were largely just handed to you.
There's also a particular minigame that I wasn't a fan of that was required for you to proceed, that required you to look in multiple places on the screen at once. It wasn't that difficult conceptually, but the execution wasn't great.
The UI could have used a little work, it wasn't entirely intuitive and there was no real guide to how to use some of the buttons. There are also a lot of typos in the dialog, as well as a lot of very blatant bugs. More than once, a button would come up, giving me a dialog option, but it would be completely cut off.
These issues would be a lot more forgiveable if this was an early access game, and if it hadn't taken as many years as it did to be released. I understand that there is some unofficial banter about monetary issues, but given that I've heard competing rumors, I can't really take that into account. Still, money issues aside, I don't think it would have been particularly hard to at least run a spell check on your dialog.
That said, the characters are cute, and while the story is a little slow to get going, once it does it's pretty fun. I imagine it will feel a little more fleshed out when there's more actual game to play. The art is, of course, lovely and the colors are vibrant, while the world is well-populated and lived in.
So if you want to learn more about trolls, this is the game for you. But if you only want to play a good point and click game, I'd wait until they release a patch or two.

I am not really sure what to make of the final version of Starbound. I bought this in it's early stages of development, and I have to say first off that I think it was a real mistake to release the game so early. It was literally years away from completion when it was first released. Way, way too early. Anyway, on to the final version, and I think I prefer the earlier version!!! The earlier version was more of a sandbox idea, you could just wander about and build things. The final version, though, I really find the alien creatures very annoying. They always attack you and seem able to kill you with just a few hits. When you are trying to learn the game, and more to the point when you are more interested in exploration and building rather than fighting, their constant presence of atacking creatures is very tiring. And I also have some objection to the fact that most alien cratures would be unfriendly. It would have completely changed the feeling of the game had they mostly been friendly instead. There really should be an option to disable or at least reduce the numbers of them. They are literally every ten feet in the game.  So I guess whether you like Starbound very much depends on what you expect from the game.  Recommended? Well, like I said, depends what you expect from the game. I will say yes, but like me you may find it a bit annoying.
