Stranded deep is without a doubt the greatest survival game i have ever played, even in its current unfinished state, its still an excellent minimalistic survival game. if you're a fan of the movie "castaway" starring tom hanks not only will this serve as an experience faithful to the movie but also fans will eperience a few treats and secrets catered just to them.
First of all, the game looks beautiful, not only is it good graphically but it runs incredibly well on my system and so far i have experienced almost no slowdown. visually the game is pleasing. when your thinking of your stereotypical castaway scenario, stranded deep is a perfect match. aside from the few lighting bugs i might have experienced, almost nothing in the game stands as a reminder that what i am playing is simply nothing more than a simulation.
Immersion is clearly a massive focus in this game, the crafting system is almost entirely without a menu, and the only instance you ever need to look at one is when your opening up your inventory, pretty much everything you can craft right in front of you, the only real hassle you might experience with the crafting system is having to travel to get to other islands to get more supplies. which is especially important if you want to build a larger house, the first time you play it sharks will definitely be your biggest challenge, the game focuses on realism and the only enemies you need to face are your own mortal  follies, and of course, sharks and poisoness fish.
Exploration is what truly makes this game an impressive survival experience, often you're going to have to get out of your comfort zone to be able to get the most out of the game and in order to get higher tier equipment the game encourages exploration. the game has a weather system and the devs are currently planning on adding a temperature system. often times ive found myself getting lost at sea during storms so players are encouraged to focus on using landmarks such as buoys, and other islands, and compasses players can find in sunken ship where they can get items that cannot be crafted. however exploration in this build of the game is almost essential, if you want to be able to build a decent house without having to sit around for hours on end for your trees to regrow you need to be willing to explore other islands, without getting distracted and wasting your rather limited inventory space on items you find on the way.
so far even in this stage of development there aren't many bugs, from the occasional lighting bug, and the ability to literally surf from island to island with nothing but a palm tree. the biggest bugs so far has been sharks, and despite the development teams best efforts to fix them, they are still just as much of an issue, if not more than the games initial release.
so far this game has been wonderful. if you enjoy the forest but want a more realistic and/or less buggy experience this game is a definite must buy. this game was definitely worth every 15 dollars. considering this game is going to go through many potential changes and improvements this game definitely has room to double in value.

I haven't been playing visual novels for years now. Around the time that I got involved with adult responsibilities a couple year back, I involuntarily stopped sparing time for the genre. Thanks to a friend's insistent screenshot sharing of many beautiful VNs, I noticed that I've been missing pretty artwork and superficial stories in a very girly manner. I gave up and decided to give the genre a go after a long time. My first pick though, being anything but superficial, left me thoughtful and shaken.
is a tale of compassion, free will and tomorrow. It is the tale of a world coming to its end. It all started with the appearance of an ominous red star on the sky. After through research, scientists agreed that it is the first warning sign of the end. It took a hundred years for mankind to prepare themselves for a major immigration project to evacuate the planet and search for its destiny elsewhere. During these final moments of the worn planet earth, there are yet things to wonder and chains to break. Between a stoic soldier, a secluded genius, a kind maid, a broken warrior, a regretful commander and a loud journalist;
is the tale of breaking chains.
The game is designed to be a kinetic novel - which means a visual novel without any choice options. You only keep reading and watching the story as it unfolds. In this manner, it cannot wholly be defined as a game. The quality of CGs and the labor put into artwork are far beyond your casual visual novel though. Characters present a full selection of animations, including moving eyes and lip synch with Japanese voice acting. Voice acting is also beyond the par, as if taken out of an A+ anime series. Translation from Japanese to English is great - which is a rare case in any media - and manages to deepen the mood furthermore. The game is quite long so to say; if you'll be waiting for voice acting you can expect an average game time of 13-15 hours.
I'd love to share some character details, but any relevant information about identities or backgrounds would be downright spoilers. Have you ever watched
? With After Story part of course. If your answer is no, it is a huge recommendation. If yes, you already know what kind of soul wrecking experience that you are getting yourself into. You'll remember Sion and Ryou's story for a long while.

I never believed myself to be the visual novel type person.  Games where you just read text always seemed boring to me.  I usually play more RPG/Adventure type games where you actually DO things with your characters, not where there is a set, linear outcome.
But this game truly altered my views on visual novels.
I like to think of my myself as a rather "tough" individual when it comes to watching movies and playing games and not getting genuinely sad or "immersed" with the characters in the story.  Not so with this game.  I can count no less than 3 times when I had tears in my eyes playing this and many many other times when I felt concerned beyond what I can describe for the characters within this game's incredibly well-presented story.
The story combines science-fiction with romance to create a very interesting situations.  And the use of suspense, oh my God.  The feeling of: "NOOOOOOOO, not now!" or: "That's not good..." will grip you and tear you apart all throughout the story.  It's fantastic.  Truly fantastic and engaging.
The game's soundtrack is beautiful.  Although at points I have wondered: "Oh boy, that song again?" it does not detract from the game in any way.  Although a few times when it kicked in it scared me, I remedied the issue by turning BGM down just a tad in options.  Then no problems.
I thought the art style was sort of weird at first, but now it is very appealing to me.  I guess it may be my sister's very awkward views on what is anatomically correct, but I promise this game's art is quite incredible and that my sister is full of crap.
In terms of characters, their development, and how they change over the course of the story, I've never experienced anything quite like this.  Some of the most powerful scenes I've ever seen have come from this game.  I cannot applaud Minori, the creator of this work of art, enough for the beautiful creation I have just witnessed.  This is off the grading scale.
I'd have to invent an entirely new grading scale to accurately rate how good this game is to me.  But I'll spare those details.
I came, expecting it to be a "crappy harem" with a "strange" art-style and only one, "dry" ending.  Plus ew, all that text you have to read and potentially "bad" voice actors/actresses.
I left feeling completely different.  Changed.  Soothed, if you will.  Also, I must say my prior judgements are unfathomly incorrect.  If you have any/all of those like I did, play the game.  You will see what I mean after completing the game.  You will be most surprised.
The game has an overwhelmingly positive rating, and I am proud to contribute to that.  As my first ever review for a game, I am most satisfied it is with this glorious visual novel.  I played.  I cried.  I left feeling at peace and satisfied with my purchase.  Money well spent.
TLDR:
Recommended.  :-)  Very highly recommended.  :-) :-) :-)
PS- And don't rush through it, whatever you do (I didn't, although towards the end I was quite anxious to see the ending, although I never skipped anything).  Enjoy it.  And remember, do not suppress your tears.  Or I probably would've cried a ton more, and especially audibly at no less than 3 parts in the game.  Part of enjoying games like these are to truly take in their beauty and let your emotion express itself, as it should be allowed to.

Haven't played much yet, so not sure if this review is reputable but I'll go on what I like about this game.
Pros:
-Simple but fun platformer gameplay, interesting weapons and low learning curve which allows casual gamers to pick up and have fun
-Amazing narration which is on par with "The Darkest Dungeon" for me personally, Everything is narrated by "The Stranger" from progressing levels, to upgrading "The Bastion" and equipments which all give you context and witty comments
-Low system requirements make this a good casual game to play on low end PCs or laptops
-Detailed and vibrant graphics which still look good in 2017 considering that the game has aged quite a bit
Cons
-Non at the time of the review
Overall, Bastion is a unique game with solid witty narration, assortment of fun weapons, and simple mechanicals that remain challenging enough to keep you on your feet and kill off boredom, I highly recommend picking up Bastion for yourself and having a go.

Pros
- Combat is balanced. The game encourages diversity unlike society.
- Narrator. His deep voice soothes me while mindlessly hacking away at the game's monsters. His sarcastic responses when I f***** up are pretty damn hilarious.
- Artwork. The game's world is unique and vibrant with colors. Enemy design are also unlike any monsters from other games.
- Music. I particularly liked how the music is muffled while in the pause menu. Also, music choice for ending is the best.
- Story. The story hooked me as I progressed. It started pretty fast, but half-way through the game you'll be up to speed.
- The ending. The choice between restoration and evacuation are pretty damn good.
- Length. After rushing through the game during my second playthrough, I was pretty surprised to see that almost all the level can be completed within 2 minutes while on my first, levels can be completed in no less than 10 minutes. Thie levels provides enough content for first-time players to explore everything while simultaneously providing the second-time players the ability to breeze through them, making the journey towards the second ending not that much of a hassle.
Cons
- Some platforms look solid, thus when stepped over I fell. It happened to me once or twice during my 8 hour run.
- Some issues using keyboard + mouse combo. Firing then trying to dodge will let you dodge towards where you were firing, not towards the movement key you were pressing.
Things to Note:
Who Knows Where with 10 shrines are sooooo hard. I gave up and collected all the other achievements. This is as far as I could go.
Recommendation: Buy it if you like a story-rich game with a balanced combat that doesn't feel repetitive.
Price: Buy it full-priced if you can. The game is worth every dollar.
Peripheral: Controller when playing through the story, keyboard on some proving grounds. I had completed my first run with a controller and my second run with a keyboard + mouse and I must say that the game responds fluidly towards the controller. There are some parts that require the no aim-assist of the keyboard like the bow and the mortar proving ground, but the controller is much better responding than the keyboard.
Great game, great sound track. A must buy imo. If you have a few spare bucks, buy this game. You wont regret it

This is probably the best zombie game I've played. The gameplay is survival based and pretty much anything can happen. You must find a place to hang yer hat, build up defenses, and gather supplies. Lead a group of survivors and see them sort of flourish or drop the ball and see them all get killed...and then start up as somebody else somewhere else. Pretty cool.

What with the recent surge in popularity concerning survival drama, zombies and psychological haunting in the media, it's hard to separate the wheat from the chaff, particularly in video games, as more often than not a purchase is required to get the best idea of whether or not you'll find it to your liking. Not all zombie games are created equally, and many of them aren't even created intelligently.
State of Decay is one of the few that was made with incredible forethought. The controls feel real to the situation, and the emphasis on discretion and forward thinking when engaging of evading zombies makes this perhaps the best zombie game to have been released in the last 3 years. It's markedly different from the fast-paced zombie shooter action of Left 4 Dead, and much more similar to the ghouls one might expect from World War Z (the book, -not- the moronic Brad Pitt movie), the Romero zombie series, or Walking Dead. If this is not your flavor of zombie, I would not discard the idea of this game just yet anyway.
The strategy involved in the game, which consists setting up homes, using space efficiently, raiding abandoned areas for supplies and making outposts for make areas safe to travel through; really gives one the sense that there is an undeniable system of cause and effect throughout the game. Overworking the main character by making him run around all day finding supplies will encourage the players to switch between characters, each with different attributes, in order to shoulder some of the work load, allowing you to develop the characters abilities as you see fit- even taking some of them as partners when you need an extra hand on risky endeavors. Morale plays a big part, as unhappiness will breed dissent, prompting some people to leave, and at its worst, may prompt some to commit suicide.
The weapons and combat are realistic, and generally not out of place. They range from weak-yet-pragmatic 2x4s to rare-yet-powerful grenade launchers. They may even consist of useless weapon replicas or improvized gear. Everyday items have their place, too- medicine will restore health (some of them at the risk of addiction), items like firecrackers and timers will provide loud, obnoxious distractions to draw in the undead, and molotovs serve their decidedly effective purpose of incinerating groups of ghouls.
What I like most are the effectiveness yet riskiness of gun-use, which without the aid of supressors (which work -exactly- as they do in real life, not actually reduce sound to a sharp whistle) will draw in more undead than you may have ammo for- even the use of vehicles to get around has its risk, causing substantial noise in populated areas, and while most undead can be easily run over, they will undoubtably damage your car over time, causing it to explode- and once the heavier and deadlier Juggernauts start appearing, completely nip the idea of using them as weapons in the bud for smarter players.
The plot is fairly generic, predictable in many ways- you become part of a group of survivors during a zombie outbreak, where the military is containing the undead threat (poorly). You deal with various survivors ranging from well-meaning farmers, insidious gun-runners, a totalitarian governor and rebels within the military. It's not groundbreaking in any way, but there are a few story elements that are well-executed, and the game does a good job conveying those tired and perhaps overused tropes in a way that makes it seems moderately new. The experience of being a survivor is more the games focus, and it's in this respect that the game succeeds.
I would not hesitate to recommend this game to anybody. It's worth the price even when it's not on sale.

Dark Souls: Prepare To Die Edition is a beautiful, rich experience. You are The Chosen Undead, the one prophesied to escape the Northern Undead Asylum and find out the truth behind the Curse, as told in a story handed down in the land of Astora.
It's a game that I have a hard time deciding the best way to describe to my friends and family, it's an action adventure hack-n-slashy game set in a grim world where the light is fading and men are cursed to reincarnate endlessly upon death, eventually becoming hollow, a mindless husk.
At it's core is a philosophy of not shoving story down your throat beyond what's nessecery to understand going on. For deeper insight into the world around your, as your journey alone through a cold and dark world, the player is required to piece together, whether from dialogue or from the description of some items. Along side that philosophy is a rule: The game is tough, and you WILL bleed and you WILL die, but it is always fair in it's heavy handedness. When you die, it is generally your fault (Outside of co-op pulling the entire planet on you and PvPers with tryhard builds, of course. There is also an encounter with two OP archers in Anor Londo, but they can be gamed with poison arrows without much fuss) which is sadly a thing that was lost in translation with Dark Souls 2 and 3, were they gleefully padded difficulty for the fanbase to eat up.
Gameplay wise, you're never told what you can and cannot do with your character based on your starting class (which is more a template, than anything else) If you want to be your typical spellsword who combines equal part martial prowess and magical skill, all you need is the stats and spells. If you want to be a madman who runs around naked wielding nothing but his fists, you could do that. I wouldn't recommend it unless you're either very good or incredibly masochistic, but you could.
Unfortunately with Dark Souls 2, and more recently 3 being out, I fear that the multiplayer isn't as lively as I imagine it was at launch, but you can still have quite a lot of fun.
Mechanically, it's behind Dark Souls 2 and 3 in terms of polish, considering they wanted to release this ASAP due to fan demand. Graphically, it might not be the prettiest thing, but it has a certain style and charm to it that 2 and 3 simply lack.
All in all, this game is a masterpiece, that was unfortunately somewhat let down by 2 and utterly disappointed by 3, where it became more about mindnumbing difficulty than the experience. Still, get it, it's an amazing game.

This game is beautiful. This game is beautiful and it will run on my mid-range laptop in 1080p at 40-60FPS. It is slightly buggy, yet it exceeds all competitors. It's smooth, it's not often laggy, it's better than DayZ, Rust, Ark, any of those games, and the optimization is clearly insane. Good on the devs. If this review was on eye candy alone, it would get a 10/10.
That being said, for me, it suffers from the same problem many other games in the genre suffer. Too much time and walking required to get to the point where the game is fun (having a weapon, a few bandages, water and food) and then as a result, so much to lose when you die (which unfortunately, can occur from lag).
To be honest, the main reason I stopped enjoying DayZ back when it was a mod was the removal of the starter pistol. Why? Well, although I love survival and crafting, I also love blowing zombie heads off. In DayZ the problem is that without that starter pistol, you were instantly killed on site by basically everyone for a can of beans. The community of this game is far better and that is less likely to happen, but honestly, I liked when DayZ started you with a leg up, I wish this game did also.
I just don't have hours a day to dedicate walking from potential weapon spawn to potential weapon spawn, car part spawn to car part spawn, food spawn to food spawn, just to enjoy the cool features the game has to offer.
I'm requesting a refund and going to support the f2p survival/crafting game Unturned and buy premium access. That game doesn't take itself too seriously, and the penalty of death is not hours of hard work being destroyed. Some people love this style of game, but I really hoped this was going to offer a slightly more arcad-ey feel than DayZ in regard to combat and progression while also prioritizing careful management of food, water, and medical supplies.
I have no ill-will against the devs. What they have managed to achieve with this game is amazing, and I love the extreme level of optimization even for an early access game. Despite this, I can't recommend it as a game because, well, it isn't really very fun. Have fun walking.

What with the recent surge in popularity concerning survival drama, zombies and psychological haunting in the media, it's hard to separate the wheat from the chaff, particularly in video games, as more often than not a purchase is required to get the best idea of whether or not you'll find it to your liking. Not all zombie games are created equally, and many of them aren't even created intelligently.
State of Decay is one of the few that was made with incredible forethought. The controls feel real to the situation, and the emphasis on discretion and forward thinking when engaging of evading zombies makes this perhaps the best zombie game to have been released in the last 3 years. It's markedly different from the fast-paced zombie shooter action of Left 4 Dead, and much more similar to the ghouls one might expect from World War Z (the book, -not- the moronic Brad Pitt movie), the Romero zombie series, or Walking Dead. If this is not your flavor of zombie, I would not discard the idea of this game just yet anyway.
The strategy involved in the game, which consists setting up homes, using space efficiently, raiding abandoned areas for supplies and making outposts for make areas safe to travel through; really gives one the sense that there is an undeniable system of cause and effect throughout the game. Overworking the main character by making him run around all day finding supplies will encourage the players to switch between characters, each with different attributes, in order to shoulder some of the work load, allowing you to develop the characters abilities as you see fit- even taking some of them as partners when you need an extra hand on risky endeavors. Morale plays a big part, as unhappiness will breed dissent, prompting some people to leave, and at its worst, may prompt some to commit suicide.
The weapons and combat are realistic, and generally not out of place. They range from weak-yet-pragmatic 2x4s to rare-yet-powerful grenade launchers. They may even consist of useless weapon replicas or improvized gear. Everyday items have their place, too- medicine will restore health (some of them at the risk of addiction), items like firecrackers and timers will provide loud, obnoxious distractions to draw in the undead, and molotovs serve their decidedly effective purpose of incinerating groups of ghouls.
What I like most are the effectiveness yet riskiness of gun-use, which without the aid of supressors (which work -exactly- as they do in real life, not actually reduce sound to a sharp whistle) will draw in more undead than you may have ammo for- even the use of vehicles to get around has its risk, causing substantial noise in populated areas, and while most undead can be easily run over, they will undoubtably damage your car over time, causing it to explode- and once the heavier and deadlier Juggernauts start appearing, completely nip the idea of using them as weapons in the bud for smarter players.
The plot is fairly generic, predictable in many ways- you become part of a group of survivors during a zombie outbreak, where the military is containing the undead threat (poorly). You deal with various survivors ranging from well-meaning farmers, insidious gun-runners, a totalitarian governor and rebels within the military. It's not groundbreaking in any way, but there are a few story elements that are well-executed, and the game does a good job conveying those tired and perhaps overused tropes in a way that makes it seems moderately new. The experience of being a survivor is more the games focus, and it's in this respect that the game succeeds.
I would not hesitate to recommend this game to anybody. It's worth the price even when it's not on sale.

Despite some initial bugs, this is a real gem of a game that brings back memories of great games like Neverwinter Nights 2.  I vastly prefer this to Divinity: Original Sin. Why?  In this game the party size can be up to six members (plus pets) and the character class system is more diverse and complex.
Six characters are needed for this game because they implemented a system whereby party formation and positioning (and micromanagement) are absolutely necessary.  Well armored characters form a front-line that locks up enemy melee from getting to your squishy casters and ranged fighters.
Even so, casters and others are not necessarily forced to be squishy.  Nothing stops you from throwing heavy armor on your mage and having them cast cone or beam attacks from the fore.  They will suffer mainly from a penalty to speed, low hp and a lack of defensive specializations, but it is quite doable.
In addition, the stat system breaks the long-standing D+D paradigm and makes every stat useful for every character type instead of cookie cutter builds that focus on 2-3 useful stats.  For instance, Might affects healing and damage, both physical and magical.
Highly recommended as the best fix for old-school RPG nostalgia.  I sincerely hope that Obsidian uses this engine to make many more games.

I've spent quite a bit of time in this game, and feel like I've barely scratched the surface. I haven't even messed with the enchantment system yet. There is a learning curve to some of the mechanics in this game (eg: magic system), but once you get used to how they work, they're easily managable. I'm going to cover all the basics here, but it won't take long.
Gameplay: If you're familiar with Baldur's Gate or Dragon Age Origins, you'll find yourself right at home here. Pause and play is featured heavily here, and everything is responsive. The spells in particular feel great.
Graphics: It's not going to push your hardware, but what's here is gorgeous. The attention to detail is what will amaze you the most.
Sound: Great soundtrack. I could put this in rotation on my phone. Seriously. Voiceovers seem sparse at times, but when you realize how much is here, you realize it would take forever to record all this.
Story: Where this game shines. There is so much going on here, and it is a fresh take on spirits, souls and their correlation to Gods/Religion. And, the Lore. Good, God the Lore. So much to soak in. All of it is interesting.
Overall: Just an amazing game. Through and through. Very well executed, and so engrossing. I do not want to put this game down, and I imagine I'll jump right back in as soon as I finish it.

Make no mistake the A.R.E.S. is a short game. A playthrough on normal difficulty lasted me under two hours. However, if you're an achievement hunter, some of the hoops you'll have to jump through will undoubtedly prolong your game time.
Despite its brief presence, I can't deny that I had plenty of nostalgic fun with A.R.E.S. As an avid fan of the old Megaman games, I was pleased to see this specific genre of platformer resurface amidst the flood of first person shooters. The game is fast paced, action packed, and on the hardest difficulty, near unforgiving.
With this diamond in the rough lasting just as long as a movie, there is absolutely no reason for you to not give A.R.E.S. a shot.
Grade: B-

50 hours into this game feels like the right time to start a review. The fact that I'm 50 hours in and yet have barely scratched the surface of this excellent game, should tell you something about the size and density of this nostalgic throw back to the Infinity games of yore.
The first thing likely to strike you will take place in the character generation screens. It's easy to get so involved in this process that an hour will easily flick by. I can think of few games since the Baldurs Gates series or Icewind Dales that have had that effect, perhaps Skrim or Morrowind, but again this just proves the richness of the characters and backgrounds on offer here.
Once into the game proper I felt instantly transported to the Baldurs Gate and Torment era. A little further scratching showed that whle POE has stayed true to those great games it does not feel like a game of that generation. Indeed Obsidian have managed to create a modern and innovative RPG that feels just as right in 2015 as would have in 2000 at the height if the Infiity engine age.
To name just a few of the things on offer here, player choice, great NPC interaction, a rich and diverse world and an even richer and diverse story.
So far I can't find a lot to fault. If I had to come up with one negative it could be that I will struggle to go back and play the likes of Baldur's Gate and Icewind Dale again, as finally they will feel aged and matched, if not bettered, by a modern RPG.

This is, in my opinion, one of the best Total War games.
Rome 2 was an utter disappointment. It was perhaps the most expected, most hyped game in the series, yet failed to deliver. It was riddled with bugs, major features were removed or streamlined, and while it had its strengths, the weaknesses far outnumbered them. Attila then essentially took the formula of Rome 2 and hugely improved it. The result is, to me, one of the most well balanced, most entertaining games they have made so far. The graphics are amazing, the ambience, well, they really managed to represent the chaotic, semi-apocalyptic feel that, to the population at the time, is what they must have felt like seeing an empire such as Rome fall, and all the changes that came with it.
The gameplay is really good as well. As mentioned, everything is well balanced, the campaign map, the empire building and its management, the battles and recruiting systems, it all falls into place and is really intuitive once you understand the basics. It's in essence Rome 2's simplified, streamlined gameplay, but with some actual depth and immersion to it, which actually makes it entertaining.
My only real complains about Attila are the number of DLC's which can be quite costly if you intend to buy them all in order to fully experience the game, and the "fake" difficulty that is seen on their most recent products. For instance, the fact that the roman roster is too weak when compared to their adversaries. How come a legionnaire with full body chainmail, helmet, big sword and shield + all the training and discipline they are known for, can barely hold against a bunch of famished barbarian tribesmen with nothing but regular old clothes and a simple spear and shield? I get that it's to make the "last stand" feel even more intense but... oh well, fortunately, these and many other similar complaints can be easily solved with a visit to the workshop and a couple clicks.
Speaking of which, another great thing about this game is how moddeable it is. Still no campaign map modding though, which absolutely sucks.
All in all, this is a very good game. Few other games have been so rewarding as how you feel after facing dozens of enemy factions, famine, disorder, disease, civil war, invasions and skirmishes against a dozen more enemies... and surviving the Hunnic doom stacks.. and then you not only save the Western Roman Empire from total collapse, but actually lead it to greater prosperity and power. Or taking one of the barbarian factions that start with just one region and a ragtag bunch of misfits as an army, and lead them to actually dismantling the Roman Empire and estabilishing your own semi-medieval kingdom.
The replayability is immense, even when playing the same factions.

This is one of my favorite visual novels by far, I have of course read it entirely despite the hours played. Thats just becuse i'm a bit of a pervert and decided i'd rather read the 18+ version, which btw changes the story in no way. It just adds some extra bonus 'alternate' scenes if you know what I mean. ;)
First things first this is a kinetic novel, in other words there are NO choices, and therefore only one ending. The closest parallel I can draw from the steam library is Planetatian, which btw is another great kinetic novel, if a bit shorter.

The story in this one is for the most part pretty predictable, in so much as you know what the ending is going to be basically from the get go. This is not actually a problem though as for this visual novel, it is the journey, not the destination that you will enjoy. The plot is vaguely similar to the anime plastic memories if you have seen it, and if you have then you will know to prepare for some hardcore emotions throughout, so make sure to pack some tissues.
I liked all of the characters and enjoyed their interactions with each other, although the main character was perhaps a bit unlikable at the start but by the end he had really grown on me.
The animation and CG design was really top notch, the artwork is one of the best i've seen visual novel wise. The soundtrack was good as well, really fitting the mood for the most part.
To sum up, this is an amazing visual novel and is well worth your time to read it. Having said that, this is my first real review so It may be a bit shoddily written but I hope I have articulated how good this is.
Personally I would suggest getting it on mangagamer though, I believe you get a free steam copy anyway, as that version contains bonus scenes that require just as many tissues as the main story, though for a bit of a different reason.  ( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°)

First minutes in the game:
Wow, the game seems to have changed a lot since last time I played it, It even have a tutorial! Wow!
I believe there will be lots of things to do, oh, just popped up a quest of finding a gate, I'll try to open it...
Sometime after opening the gate:
collect 20 iron bars to make full armor set, complete a mission, collect 20 tungsten bars to make a set, scan floran objects, complete a mission,collect 20 durasteel bars to make a set, scan hylotl objects, complete a mission,  collect some kind of bar to make a set, scan avian objects...
That is most likelly the main quest in the game, without counting that everytime you start a new character, you are forced to see the same story from Esther.
Exploring the worlds in the game are still quite vague, because most likelly, unless you are looking for ingredients dropped from certain monsters or ores to make a set, or crafting, you will see yourself running from left to right, or from right to left of each world you visit, looking for dungeons or towns, for at least a few percentage of chance of getting a better equipment than the one you are using. After exploring for some time, you'll feel the necessity of buying a hoverbike, because you will grow tired of the same enemies over and over, and the same unrewarding exploration.
The good point, is that now guards no longer nags you to sheathe your weapon, but you still have to beware not to attack a citizen or guard by accident, since that Guard does not know how to arrest you, neither how to "forgive and forget".
Also counting that if the guard is chasing you, other guards in the way of that guard chasing you may also have the death wish the other guard had, which means that you surelly are in problems, and the only way of resolving the situation would be killing the guards.
Also talking about towns, towns now offer you unique items for sale, being that finding an Avian shopping village will be very nice, if you like to buy things, since their variated inventory will most likelly have all items of a set you may get interested into completting, the bad, is that the merchants are complete morons, they usually leave their shops, so you need to find the owner of the store so he can move to his stall, the problem is that once the shop owner reaches his shop, they may decide to idle away just after they reached it, meaning you have to catch them again, and then click them asap once they reach the shop.
Also, It is very unusual for a shopkeeper to leave his store hanging around while waiting for costumers, which makes things not be very much... Realistic.
Other point that were added in the game, also includding towns, is that npcs can occasionally give you quests, which you can complete to gain loot bags, which can come weapons, armors, useable items and upgrade items, beside the quests sometimes can be quite a chore, they sure are quite rewarding, aswell as you can end up having the npc as a recruit for your ship's crew, and you get quests where new merchants appears on the map with their unique items, aswell as rescued npcs moving to the town, making it bigger in population, which is also awesome, the problems with it actually, is that it is very easy for you to accidentally abandon a quest, the other problem is, I'm not sure if anyone else have this issue, but when it comes to a quest of defeating a named bandit, the bandit, beside having an absurd defense, it can also 2 or 3 hit kill your character, making the quest demi impossible for you to complete with the planet's tier equipment, unless you make a box around them with some tile, and fill the box with lava to kill them and complete the quest, but the bad of using that method is that a recruitable bandit may not be able to be recruited to the ship due to that.
Another thing that were implemented into Starbound, is the possibility of creating your own village, yay!!!
You can create your own town with your own houses, furnish them, and then a tenant will spawn based on the
kind of furnitures in your town, sounds awesome, isn't? But it is! The tenants of your town can even give you quests,
Even mod races that have it's own kind of furnitures setup in their house, can be spawned.
But again, the problems are, if you want to spawn a certain kind of citizen, you will have to look up in the starbound
wiki for what kind of furnitures are of x type, because the game itself will not tell you, and if you get a quest to spawn
a certain tenant by using that x type furniture, you will also look in the web, unless you use the Colony deed of the quest
giver, then send a huge **** to the quest giver and cancel the quest.
And now, the Crew, your very own ship crew, they can be recruited by spending some time doing quests at the towns, or in your own colony, each crew member have it's own class, which will prove certain benefit in combat or in the ship, unless it's a janitor. They seems to be more durable than your character, plus can be proved to be of good aid to you during your quest in the galaxy, that if they weren't dumb.
I'm not saying that they will be a complete burden to you, but they will not try to avoid traps, and neither leave a lava or poison spot they have fallen into, being that you have either to run away from near the crew member to make him leave that spot either by moving or teleporting, another problem, is that once they are defeated, you must go to your spaceship, and then call them back to the team, since they seems to not know the way back to you, which is annoying, even more when you are deep underground, and it were annoying to reach where you are at.
And to finish, the missions, the missions can offer you challenge, aswell as unique loots, plus they can be farmed by repeatedly entering the mission and going through it and beating it's boss. Now to the downsides, some missions you can easily run through the enemies, or just avoid them by jumping, or grappling the hook, making your dungeon run be more like a rogue like game, and for some reason, 1.0 update made Missions be very expensive on game requirements, being that the old Floran Party mission, which is currently the Floran Tournament, I guess, the floran mission at the quest line, it used to run very well on my pc before the update, now, I need to restart the game, and then bet that the mission will start without throwing me back to my ship, and if I am able to start the mission, I have to hope the game will not crash while moving through it, I'm not sure why that happens, but I believe it's because of the new way maps are handled in the game.
I guess that's all for my review.

For those that are pondering buying the current "3 for a dollar survival game tier" via a bundle site:  It's been a couple of months since I installed and retried this game, but as someone who tried it at different stages after paying a retail price for it and also gifting it to others I feel obligated to post the blunt truth.
It is one among many  indie games that had some good ideas and intent, and apparently some very earnest hard work leading to producing a somewhat functional early access game with a bit of atmosphere and promise.  The controls and feel were awkward in my early trials, and only got worse when I tried it in later patches.  Yes, there was more effort invested and more content, but in terms of true gaming enjoyment I deem it a failed investment.
If this had been a school project produced by my nephew I'd have patted him on the back for his accomplishment and proudly played it for a few weeks before dumping it.  Instead, it has existed as a commercially priced game by yet another dev that bit off more than they could chew.  I recommend that you instead invest your 33 cents into some emojis you like rather than wait for this project to ever achieve its promise.

I had a chance to play Dark Souls years ago, and I've wanted the game ever since. So I already KNOW I like it, I love the feeling of being able to control my character in a fight rather than facing vaguely in a foe's direction and hitting buttons to apply some damage, or scooting around a bit and hitting buttons to apply some damage. It reminds me of Die By The Sword in that respect -- there's a retro moment for you -- although the two games took very different approaches, with DBTS focused on weapon movement control and Dark Souls foremost on combat maneuvering control and learning when to use each skill. The feeling of having achieved something through skill rather than just large numbers and maybe good timing, upon beating a foe that was hell to get past, is like no other game I've played. And in spite of all you're about to read, I do recommend it, but with one caveat which many others have mentioned before me... Especially if you play KB&M-style rather than using a controller.
If, like me, you are a diehard keyboard-&-mouse gamer by preference, necessity or both, yes you can still play this game on PC. But know going in that the recommendation to use a controller isn't a suggestion, it's a warning.
The job done porting this game from console to PC is a well-known unfunny joke where keyboard and mouse support is concerned. It's so bad that, both now and back when I could try the game before, I wondered aloud how much someone made in kickbacks from Xbox controller sales because of this! It's a visibly half-egged effort; they didn't even bother to show keyboard equivalents in onscreen tips or main menu instructions, those all still show the Xbox controller buttons regardless of what control method you're using.
-- You can download the player-made DSfix and DSMFix mods from a trusted source to at least sort of fix the game's keyboard and mouse support, as well as open up some display options and a better resolution selection, another area in which this port falls embarrassingly short of the mark. Spend some time setting them up properly. The instructions I had didn't make it as clear where certain files need to go as it looked like, so I followed the instructions to the letter and some mod functions didn't work until I figured it out. Oops.
This is in order to avoid things like the camera spinning wildly (on faster mouse settings) or swaying drunkenly (on slower settings) at the tiniest shift of the mouse, which was my "welcome to Dark Souls, baby" moment. Unless you feel like playing Dark Souls "Drunken Master Style", you probably won't enjoy that any more than I did. Many thanks to the modders who put in the time and effort to fix things like this, by the way. But even with the fixes, the camera behavior in this game may well drive you crazy: movement keys operate independently of the camera, which is great for some situations -- you can see a boss while maneuvering around it -- and ghastly for others --  such as suddenly reversing direction without falling to your death because the camera's still facing the other way. It can be reset behind your character (there is no 1st person cam) with a separate keystroke or a drag of the mouse, both of with have their downsides (such as, the camera's positional reset key also serves as Target Lock-On Mode's toggle. This can be a problem). But there's no way to set it to continue doing so automatically for situations in which this would be useful.
-- Web search is your friend. If you're having trouble translating from Controllerese to interpret the onscreen tips, the solution is likely to be already mentioned online.
Here's some examples of translated-to-Keyboardese commands mentioned only in Controllerese in the ingame tips:
Options Menu (Where your character status, gear, equip & unequip items, and game control panes are found. The key for this is End, rather than ESC as in many games. Can be remapped to ESC.),
Looting corpses or accessing messages and bloodstains (Action/Gesture key. Put this somewhere you can reach it in combat for easier retrieval of your green demise bloodstain, in case of a second death),
Using spells at the very beginning of the game (you can't do this until you obtain an item you need for spellcasting. So when you can't cast your spell in the first few rooms, that's normal. You should have it before the end of the tutorial/first game stage),
Kicking (Tap Run Forward + Normal Attack keys AT THE SAME TIME. Hold+tap or asynchronous keystrokes won't work),
Jump Attacking (Tap Run Forward + Heavy Attack keys at the same time. Same notes as Kicking),
Jumping (1. Hold Run Forward key, 2. continue holding RFand also hold Spacebar [or whatever you ressigned it to] until you see your character enter Sprint animation, 3. release Spacebar while still holding RF key and quickly tap Spacebar again.
If a combat skill doesn't work, make sure the game's Options menu is closed (default to return to previous menu or exit  menus: Backspace key), as you can't perform some actions if it's open, even though you can still move your character around.
Dark Souls also has bizarrely limited keyboard rebind support. It refuses to acknowledge that the F-key row even exists (or tilde, or punctuation keys, or number keys...), and the numpad is only slightly better off, being usable to reassign the main arrow key functions, and not actually usable for issuing commands in play. If not for the game's reputation for poor K&M support, I'd have wondered if I'd finally facedesked on my keyboard one time too many.
Some people will tell you to just buy a controller and 'git gud' if you want to play Dark Souls, possibly with a "lol" in there somewhere. But for me, even though in this instance they have a valid point about controller being what the game was made for.... When I saw what a truly pathetic job was done of keyboard and mouse support... well, later edit here: I resent using a controller for one game because someone didn't do their job right (or actively decided not to do it) on this deservedly much-requested port. This is also a part of why I waited so long to get the game, I resented spending much on it unless this issue got a functional official fix. HOWEVER. I've made peace with a controller, reluctantly, now that I've found one I can use comfortably. Using it resolved some technical problems (game would blackscreen-lock while playing). I'm still disgusted with whoever handled that part of the port to PC job.
I already know it gets better with practice. I spent my first play session bumming around the starting two rooms and hall mastering moving around, and the second using tutorial-level mobs as practice dummies, before I even approached the boss fight at the end of the level. It took quite a lot longer than usual, but there was a distinct moment after several reconfiguring tweaks to which keys do what to suit how I address the keyboard, when I started to "click" with the controls and things (mostly) happened the way I intended them to. For now, I almost don't use the mouse at all in DS, even though I'm normally a kb&m-combo player, while I've read that others do the reverse and bind everything to the gaming mouse buttons. Find what works for you.
So, yes. I will slowly 'git gud' just like with any other game I feel is worth the effort, or I'll die (and die and die and die and die) trying.  Because it's Dark Souls, and it's worth it.
And if you're game for this in spite of the hassle of setting it up and mastering the controls, if I haven't scared you off yet, then get the game, get mauled a lot, get good and kick some butt. :)
[Edit: formatting fixed. Also, ahem, missed a spot, so that's back in now.
I'm still loving the hell out of the game, although I've shifted to playing in offline mode as I don't have any interest in the PVP aspect of the game. I've also learned that while I enjoy this game, that does NOT extend to Dark Souls 2. As for Dark Souls 3, I don't have it... Yet.]

PC Gamer likens this game to Mega Man, and that's not a bad comparison.  You take the role of a powerful robot trying to free hostages from a space station overrun with an army of robts run amok.  The stages scroll both vertically and horizontally, and you earn new weapons each time you defeat one of the boss characters.  You also acquire spare parts that can be "recycled" into repair kits, bombs, and upgrades to your existing weapons.  Using a controller, you have full directional control of your weapon, and you'll eventually earn a Mega Man-style slide to get into small places and attack your enemies.  The game is pretty short but has 2 difficulty levels and Steam achievements to add replay value.  If you're a fan of old-school action-platformers, give this one a try, especially if you find it on sale.  Be careful of scrolling into a new area with a chasm nearby, though; you can accidentally walk off before you're fully aware of what happened.

I eagerly got behind this Kickstarter project a few years ago and am incredibly impressed; the hope that the 'spirit' of Baldur's Gate would be reinvigorated in contemporary gaming was also accompanied by an anxiety that I was merely desperate to revive my childhood as a late 20-something year old.
Few games since Baldur's Gate and Planescape Torment have gripped me and kept me yearning for more, and now, after impatiently waiting for its release, I have sacrificed sleep, temporarily suspended social and career ambitions and reconfigured my life towards solely experiencing as much of this game as possible.
PROS: Countless improvements that certainly elevate the game to a more seamless experience; most notably an array of features that serve to peel away the redundant and potentially boring aspects of the game, like travelling (fast speed mode) and a whole host of pleasant adjustments that could repel newcomers to the genre, or those easily tired of the grind.
The graphics are/will always be a contentious point of discussion; old school gamers will feel accustomed to them with the gorgeous 2D painting and artistry - as a kid who grow up in this genre, I feel right at home. However, newcomers who have been brought up on 'gaming' revolving around stunning photogenic realism, the sight of 2D top-down gameplay may initially repulse.
The strategy: Fun and the game throws quite a challenge early on; as I learned the new Engine I was able to adapt and start finding success with the strategy and effective micromanagement to sustain myself at Normal and Hard difficulties.
I find myself compelled to clear the last room before switching off and in true AD&D fashion, it's an insatiable hunger that grows with dungeon clearing and quest-hunting.
CONS: Little to complain about, though a few aspects of the game have begun to mildly irk me, particularly the soundboard utilized throughout the game; repetitive sounds and music in bars and taverns has started to reveal certain 'notes' that I continuously pick up on (key voices in the bar) and whilst seemingly petty, it does provide a repetitive feel and a lacking sense of 'new' as I progress to new areas.
Additionally, I would have liked more potential NPCs to utilize in my party.
The story is good and I feel like I have barely touched on it, as my time has been spent clearing dungeons and gearing up my crew.
The new classes are certainly a plus - I do like the idea of the Chanter and Cypher.
However, I do remember more variation in the skill choices from Neverwinter Nights and such, particularly with the class expansions - I am not keen on seeing expansions being constantly required to extend what gameplay should be available from Day 1, though as an ambitious kickstarter project I can overlook these wild dreams.
At 36 hours in, I give the game a 9.5 - the game is true to the fans of the genre, innovates quite a number of features, though by this point of the game elements such as the music/sound effects have become repetitive and that *can* produce a more 'grinding' experience when I inevitably drown out the atmosphere and forward march.
A fantastic achievement for a resurgence of AD&D (at least for my kind) and I look forward to subsequent titles.

So where to begin. I will say that I purchased this game based on my experience playing BG 1 and was looking forward to a return to that genre. Having come from Obsidian I expected alot. After beginning my experience I will say I had a love/hate relationship with this game for about the first 8 hours the game finally began to click and I couldn't stop playing. Is this game the spiritual successor to BG 1? Answer: No. Its a good attempt however BG 1 set the bar very high it is an unrealistic expectation. Is PoE great in its own right? Answer: Yes. While lacking many of the little nuances that made BG1 great it does it well in other areas. The mechanics are well done once you figure them out. Combat is smooth and graphics with the updated engine are nice. The story I enjoyed however I don't think I enjoyed the companion's stories as much as I enjoyed BG 1. To me they were pretty anti-climatic. I had no bug experiences like many people (knock on wood). My only real disappointment is crafting was rather bleh, very limited, not enough choices. If you are looking for a return to this genre then this is a good game, if you are expecting it to be BG 1 or its successor you will more than likely be disappointed. All in all I would give this game and 8 out of 10.

I'll keep this short for you: If you know what TSR, Black Isle, or Interplay are, you'll either nod knowingly or have things to flame me about, by the end of this. If not, you might have some poorly informed opinion-hate for me by the end, anyway. For safety's sake, if you still defend -- say, the D&D alignment system, assume you will hate this review, and me. Oh well.
BUCKLE UP AND BRANDISH YOUR D20'S!
This will come as a strange response, from a player of older cRPGs, such as the Baldur's Gate series, Icewind Dale, Neverwinter Nights, and Planescape Torment, but, after playing Pillars of Eternity through to its resolution, I suddenly come to realize that the Infinity engine has not aged well.
The entire game is plagued by cliches of Tabletop gaming, and does little, either to adapt them for PC gaming beyond what Baldur's Gate and its successors already did, or to turn the conventions harshly on their head, the way Planescape: Torment's story was able. Even most of the enemies are ripped remorselessly from your Saturday night campaign, and given mildly gaelic redubs; Ghouls are Guls, Vampires are Fampyrs, Banshees are Cean Gwla, but it's blatantly transparent. The variety of enemies is even drastically down, from say, Baldur's Gate II. (You've got your typical 'horrible' living dead, bad-mouthed bandits and fanatical ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ zealots, some slimes, some beasties, trolls, dryads, and dragons. Yay. I probably missed something and will be narked at about it. Bring me back killing my own mortality.)
Worse yet, I never felt the story came to any decent level of 'resolution', for my character--one needling plague of open-ended gameplay that eternally haunts.
For perspective for current gamers who are some five paragraphs in, and have never heard of Gary Gygax--if you felt like, say--the ending to Fallout 3 was stupid (having an anticlimactic final battle, being guilted to martyr yourself needlessly to someone else's morality, or suffering a lousy ending because you weren't a completionist when it came to sidequests), you'll feel cheated by the end of PoE, even when you think you're heading toward the ending you want--simply by the system of flags and scripts that determines what disappointing exposition scene you get. (No, Fawkes. You're not denying me my destiny, now get in the '♥♥♥♥ing' GECK chamber. I have a dog to walk away with while the narrator smugly talks about War. No, I am not buying the expansion DLC!)
While the end boss to PoE is wholeheartedly on the opposite end of the difficulty spectrum to Fallout 3's ending, you can bet that the outcome doesn't justify the effort.
Again for perspective, Torment's boss can be killed in dialogue, but provides a massively more satisfying resolution, that resonates with the overall 'message' of the game. The big bad of this game, by contrast, utterly refutes every line you throw, regardless of stats or what you've accomplished, to the point that you may as well fast-forward to immediate combat (--and past that, just turn on cheats, mouse over him and hit the key to shut him up.) Afterward, the game gives you the ending it has mathed out that you maybe could want, if Obsidian didn't have to spread itself thin covering all the bases (and you'd best bet they had to, the title was nearly their swan song.)
Even these things weren't dealbreakers, alone. What truly threw me out of the experience was simply reaching the end stretch of the game, and realizing just how little has changed from older cRPGs in the engine--in fact, in terms of gameplay, things have taken a backslide, in the sense that the descriptions for the function of many of PoE's items are vague at best, and the merits of many of the different stat tweaks and perks pale in comparison to just exploiting the shoddy AI of the Infinity engine. Many encounters I won simply by targetting a single difficult enemy and having a character run around in circles to distract it, or spamming summons and pinning the enemies in corners, while my expendable characters took their time shooting. And if I feel like I'm coming up with tricks to outsmart bits and bytes, and doing complex math before battles, rather than winning out of a sense of skill... welp... Screw math, I'll save that for making stock investments. Back to games that make me care, rather than teabagging my corpse over algebra.
MY BURNING QUESTION: IS +10 WILL more valuable than HITTING THINGS FOR 1.2x more DAMAGE?! I HAVE NO IDEA.
What made sense as a general guideline for pen-and-paper get togethers over chips and Mountain Dew has never worked particularly well as filler for functional gameplay, on Infinity's part. Hearing the same statistical song and dance try to dress up as something new and improved over twenty years later just makes me groan.
Point in Case: Borderlands 2 has a jumbled mess of statistics handed to me to sort out, for its guns--but I can tell what 'fire rate' or 'pellet count' or 'reload speed' are, without a glossary. If I get an amazing weapon, I can tell it's amazing at a glance, and it feels like an event. I know what elements on weapons are effective against what kinds of threats, at a glance, without a monster encylopedia. More to the point, the struggles of Roland and the Crimson Raiders, and the humour of characters like Hammerlock and Claptrap, keep me going in spite of needless number crunches that the devs may as well have handled. Pillars of Eternity gets as far as 'telling' me to care, and then 'literally' sets all my efforts on fire to advance its shallow tale, within the second act.
One particularly egregious example: I kill a raving mad local lord who is driving his village into extinction, and appoint his idealistic cousin as successor. By the end of my overly arduous final boss-fight, hidden numbers assigned with dealing out the game's ending montage have determined that my old foe gets up from being dead, goes even crazier, and wipes out everyone in said village before the end credits can even roll. And I have no say in it--how was I supposed to forecast that? ♥♥♥♥♥♥move, game. Imagine if Handsome Jack got away with nuking Sanctuary despite your best efforts defeating the Warrior, in Borderlands 2. How lame would that be?
But since I'm not twinking out six me's with optimum gear and stats, maybe I'm not doing something right. I'll never know--I'll be playing other things. Tip for you geniuses of metagaming preparing to flame me: none of the enemies provide combat exp, and the level of encounters scales with your level. Fighting trash mobs produces equivalent results to running to the far end of the room. Have fun with your grind.
In summary: Pillars of Eternity neither renews the Infinity engine's myriad wrinkles, nor does it tell a particularly fresh or engaging tale. It's not particularly horrible either--just woefully over-promising, mediocrity on all counts. It was a lukewarm reminder that old things can get a second chance to show how well they've festered, and that's all a good little twink can ask for: spoilt milk and stale cookies with a great big fat +10 to some stat I'll have to look up the applications for, on the end.
There's always Torment: Tides of Numenara, coming Q4, right?

I read mixed reviews of this game before I bought it.  It was a friend of mine who eventually said I should play it and I am glad he did!
Like all RPGs you start off in a smal area with very few skills and have to skulk around avoiding enemies that are much stronger than you are.  You do some small things and gain experience and build and build and build until you can take on 3 war chiefs and all his minions at the same time.  That feeling of power you get at the end of the game is hard won, but it is won, unlike some games where the bad guys seem to upgrage to keep pace with you (e.g. the other from-a-film title, Mad-Max).  Also unlike Mad-Max, where they trap you in a room until you die or prevail, you always have the option to run, regroup and come back stronger.  Even if you die the worst that happens is the boss guy gets promoted and you have to find someone else to fight until you are strong enought to face them again,
For those of you who have reservations like I did I am here to tell you that this game is a great RPG and better than most on the market today.
Really good story, and the combat mechanics area really fun, you will enjoy slashing heads off of the enemies.

State of Decay does a lot of things really well. Due to the randomness of the missions/npc interactions however it can feel a little stale at time times. Occasionally, when things go really poorly you can end up feeling ripped off by the random events as well. An example of this that occured for me was when, while I the player was away slaughtering zombies, one of the less important npcs caught the plague back at base; no biggy, I thought. Who cares about that guy? Then upon returning for a rest after some excellent zombie related road rage, I find that the unimportant npc also randomly killed the two main characters of the game. The characters that you start the game with, the only ones I cared about. Much sadness and anger ensued. It wasn't about the fact that they died. It's the apocalypse, sure most people will die. But it just hurt me that they died alone, with no cutscene, no heroic sacrifice. Not even a corpse to t-bag. They were just gone, and a random entry about them taking some plague to the face was in the journal. Admittedly this really hurt any further motivation I had to continue playing. I am now very tempted to restart the game. We will see if i press on or not. But either way, besides the tragic nonchalance of how this game kills important characters while you arent even around it is pretty badass when it comes to the general zombie killing mechanics and has a thick atmosphere of freedom, which is exactly what you want in an open world game.

So, here's a review from someone who technically skimmed through most giant texts in homestuck and enjoyed the first Act better than the others starting with when we started following the trolls, noticed i say I like it better, dosen't mean I dislike it, very different things, anyways, starting with the quick version :
+ Pretty good visual, music, despite me reading that some peeps had problem runnin' it, i haven't had any issue at all.
+ Quirkly well written, ignore the confusing names, they're just a joke most of the times.
+ Not old king's quest level of ''ey kiddo, forgot something back there? start again you dumb f###''
+- For me it isn't that big of a deal, but it's rather short, a lot of quality, but i clocked 3 hours, prolly 4 after the achievement hunting, which are fun in this, unlike in some games where it is ''finish the game on extra hard where if you step on the floor too hard you blow up in pieces I'M LOOKING AT YOU EVIL WITHIN YOU MOTHERFU---''
- Pigeon Betrayal and Violence.
- Not enough of the Heiress, but enough to base fanart on, i like fish ladies, any problem with it? hu? you talkin' to me sod?
- For reals tho', there's way less things to examine than expected, for the amount of clutter, also, maybe a Encyclopedia function? where you can read what every new world or item you find is? i mean, yeah most people won't read it, but yo Hussie if you think your fans ain't gonna spend 10 hours reading everything about whatever weird troll things they find, well, you really don't know them.
- Gotta wait for the next Act, feels...familiar, the feeling of emptyness and wanting more, nostalgic even, in a bad way.
This is very much a story in the same world, yes, and, for most of the part, it's quite stand alone, there's many nods, and many things aren't explained but the core is just new kids and new trolls, so it's...easier-ish for someone who never touched that crazy comic to just play it.
That said, there is so many things unexplained but i guess, and i guess if you read the comic you'd be like ''oh yeah, SCUMARCHFLOOPYWWEIRDWORLD totally know that'' , tho' most of those are just quirky silly names, but yeah, we're again in control of kids that serve as our views, and most of the nescessary things are explained well enough and fast enough to not annoy old fans, or alienate newer ones.
The art is amazing, visually and musically it's outstanding and hey, it's made on Unity, which despite it's bad press due to its moronic ''Free stuff you gotta have our logo, and that logo goes on ♥♥♥♥♥♥ games cause of course clueless dummies won't buy it, so basically in good games that uses your engine, no one would find that they are using said engine cause they bought it, should be the opposite, do you get what i'm saying? why you reading this? go play the game DA''.
Lenghtwise i've clocked about 3 hours shoving everything into everything cause thats what you do in point n' click games, it's short yeah, but hey, it's one Act, maybe this will have 10 Acts, who knows, even so, it dosen't overstay it's welcome but i see why the riders of the hype would be disapointed, it does leave you wanting more however.
This is kinda of a more focused Homestuck, the texts are more to the point, i mean, Homestuck got carried away so much that i'd just be tired afterwards, and the art style seems to be the perfect evolution of the original comic.
Back to Homestuck Act 1, this reminds me a lot of it, and i enjoyed it, the feeling of discovery and silly puzzles and shenanigans, it's something it was lost after a while, and it's here again, obviously since this is LITERALLY a point n' click game, an obvious one yeah but i have enough nightmares of the old king's quest games, so thanks for not following that hell.
I really look foward to Act 1, and, should you play it? Hrm, maybe? I mean, if you never read the comic you'll be a bit alienated, but not as much as you expect, there's enough explanation to get you to speed, on things that matters that is, so yeah, can't say, it's on you, do what your heart tells you kiddo, my best of luck to ya!

While not perfect, this game has been greatly enjoyable.
The save system and possibility of sudden death leads to some frustration.  I'm on my first playthrough and I lost my main character around hour 10 of 20ish.    Would have really liked a save to reload at that point.    I've since picked up a 3rd party mod/save tool to avoid catastrophic failures.
Plus the aiming reticule is on the small side and zoom is underpowered.
With all that said, its been a blast.   I'm not normally a zombie fan, but the combination of strategy, missions, first person shooter/beat em up is great.    I've been playing it as often as I can get away... just one more mission, just one more supply run - or I'm running away and want to get safe before shutting the game down.
In general its not overly difficult, but occasionally it will throw a curveball at you and its suddenly down to boots (always good to have a 2nd melee) and hoping to get lucky since running may not be an option.
Graphics/controls are ok.    Animations/gameplay is great (beyond a few control quirks).
Itemization is good, base building is somewhat simplified but still a good aspect.
Randomization is good, variety is great as well.
Best part is that out of probably 20+ characters I've had in my group, you start getting attached to a few of them and trying to build them up.    Then it gets even more tense in one of those boot heel fights.

Hello random person! Bringie the Knight of Void is here to help you decide whenever or not to give this game a chance.
First important thing: quite obviously, this is a Homestuck inspired game, so there are many great references for Homestuck fans (would feel unfair if there werent since we waited so goddamn long for it.) BUT if you´re not a Homestuck fan, its okay! the game itself does a great job of being indipendent, so there is no required Homestuck knowledge to enjoy it. But if you enjoy the game experience, the mechanics and the storytelling, i´d wholly recommend Homestuck for you: Act 1 is a bit slow, but once you get past it, you´ll discover a rich world full of complex characters and excellent story and humour.
Now, without futher ado, lets review the heck out of this game.
Lets start with the esthetics and animation. The colors are beautiful, the visuals vibrant, and, should i say, alive. Each character has a set of tiny animation while standing, walking etc. There are animated leaves, moving chains, closing doors, each detail carefully taken into consideration. Fighting sequences are fluid and fun.
Music created by crazily talented duo of James Roach and Toby Fox (the latter being composer for quite a few Homestuck songs before moving to create his own game, Undertale. Undertale itself is also an excelent game worth checking out once you´re done with Hiveswap). The tracks are lovely and i myself am a happy owner of Hiveswap OST, definitely worth investing in if you´re electric/chiptune/orchesta enthusiastic.
The characters are unique, with their own quirks and interests. You mainly get to play with two out of four characters in this act, so i believe others get their turn in Hauntswitch (Act 2). But even with two characters, you get plenty of fun and experience a lot through them.

Game mechanics are simple and easy to use. The essencial of Hiveswap is to click everything, combine everything, and use objects on everything. if not for plot advancement then definitely for hillarious text that always pops up.
Probably the strongest aspect of the game, as mentioned above, is writing. Andrew Hussie has plenty of experience, and knows how to make funny, sad or silly commentary whenever needed. The storytelling is masterful, and i must admit i was close to tears about twice.
As for negatives (every game has its bugs afterall), my personal problem was with short animated sequences, because they were choppy. But seeing as i have outdated computer with not very strong graphic card or CPU, i say its due to technology i am using, rather than the game itself.
Another problem with the game is that at perhaps three points, i didnt know what to do. Again, understandable, since this is point-and-click game. You just gotta use your brain (or mouse and desperately click on everything again, like i did :D )
Lastly, the game isnt very long. it took me 5 hours to finish it and get most of achievments (still planning to play it second time to get remaining 5), but you need to remember there is a whole lot more coming. The story had only just begun.
In conlusion, Hiveswap is a tribute to Homestuck fans who will happily get nostalgic over their fandom years, as well as a well-made visual adventure novel for people that want to get into world of mysteries. Go try it on your own, and i believe you wont be disappointed.

I understand discovering how a new weapon upgrade or shot works is part of the fun factor for it, but a slight guide or some tips would be appreciated for the less experienced players or just general tips. I didn't know what I was buying into, only that it was an RPG of some sort.
2 weeks later I emerge from Mom's basement, the sunlight scorching my retinas and scattering light across stacks of printed gameFAQ guides. Empty dorito bags tumble out the door, as the stale air within escapes like a vacuum; strong with the scent of gamer gunk™ and dead memes. Father stumbles down the stairs, mouth agape at the wasted figure before him.
"My son!", he exclaims, casting his eyes over the atrophied human in front of him. "Have you returned to us at long last?"
He trails off as I open my mouth, my breath short and ragged as I struggle to breathe the O₂-laden air. My voice wavers and cracks, as weeks of decarbonised Mountain Dew Gamer Fuel™ has coated my larynx in viscous phlegm. I manage to draw air, grasping at my throat in futility with my gnarled and carpal tunnel hands.
"What is it, son?", Father wails, "What ill-fate has happened upon you, betwixt this dozen-and-half suns? Is the ordeal at an end?"
I am able to utter but a singular decree, with what little air I can muster into my rapidly deflating lungs.
"Bitterblack Isle level 12 to 120. I haven't touched the story yet..."
