An excellent, well written RPG epic that brings back a sense of exploration and wide eyed wonder back to the CRPG genre.
Definitely a must for fans of the infinity engine classics, it feels just like the first time I played Baldur's Gate many years ago andis refreshing that it doesn't lead you on a clear path, letting you explore and find your own way through the multitude of amazing locales of the game's world.

It's the Infinity Engine as you remember it, now how it actually was. The game brings the original sense of adventure and exploration and adds 15 years of UI and gameplay refinement on top of it. The worldbuilding is excellent, the quest options are immense, and the combat manages not to get old over the course of 50+ hours.

The story is well-done, but unfortunately Infinity Engine-style games should have been left in the past.
The bad combination is:
1. a large party
2. a complex combat system
3. real-time (with pause)
4. unsophisticated party-member AI
Even on 'easy' difficulty, to perform as well as expected in combat one needs to be pausing *constantly*, making it painfully obvious that at least one of the above design constraints is incorrect. Turn-based would be so much more satisfying. Better party-member AI would also help. A smaller party *might* work all right, but even so there are probably too many options to juggle between even three or four active characters, let alone six.
A modern Infinity Engine game with no glaring flaws at all. If you like BG / IWD you'll like this.

First, I'll tell you what you won't be doing while playing Pillars of Eternity:
You won't be spending hours moving through vast empty areas fighting worthless mobs and picking up every weed that grows. You won't be mashing "A" for awesome, or "B" to win. You won't be wasting time with pointless, souless fetch quests without any sort of character or story development. And you won't be watching most of the story through interminable cutscene after cutscene, wishing you had just a little bit of influence in how it all unfolded.
Pillars of Eternity DOES feature:
The pinnacle of real time with pause combat. It's tactical, it's challenging, it's easy to pick up but difficult and rewarding to master.  A great narrative adventure that doesn't ignore player agency, like so many other RPG's do. A world that is rich with lore and isn't afraid to show it's dark, ugly side, a lot. Also characters that will keep you engaged in every single detail and word that is spoken.
If you're a fan of the BG games, well you're probably already playing, as this is a modern BG 3 in all but name.
However, if you are any sort of RPG fan AT ALL, this is a game you NEED to try.
You'll wonder how on earth you could have ever though spending hours picking up iron ore and healing herbs, had any business being in an RPG.
Easily one of the best RPG games I have played in the last 10 years.  The gameplay and story are both phenomenal!

An incredible example of what can be achieved through Kickstarter support, Pillars is an impressive paean to old cprgs of yore (Baldur's Gate, Planescape Torment, Arcanum, the original Fallout games) while still learning from its contemporaries (Skyrim, Dragon Age, Fallout 3 & NV). Pushing thirty hours into the game, I still feel as if I've barely scratched the surface. I will come back and review the rest of the game upon completion, but for now I'm having a great time.
The basics of the game mechanics & systems are easy to learn, but they're much harder to master. I've ran into a few fights that trounced me soundly, only to return victorious after reading the in-game journal a bit closer and adjusting my strategies. I'm playing on normal, and I expect my understanding of the rules to be challenged even further on subsequent playthroughs using higher difficulties and optional restrictions while achievement hunting.
Perhaps excepting easy difficulty (I don't know as I'm not playing on it), this isn't a game you can brute-force your way through without learning at least the basics of the underlying rules system. If you're familiar with tabletop RPGs or the details of the old Infinity Engine games, you will adjust quickly. The rest of you should take your time to learn a bit each time you run into a fight that pushes your abilities. You will do better in subsequent fights, and you will come to appreciate the level of work Obsidian put into the behind-the-scences systems.
Additional playthroughs will also be required to see more aspects of the story. Certain choices you make build (or destroy) reputation with various people and factions, opening up new pathways while closing off others.
Obsidian has shown committment to the game's continued quality by quickly issuing a patch that addressed a serious item bug. Addons, DLC, expansions (whatever you want to call them) are already in the pipe.
The game's quality is, thus far, exactly what you should expect from Josh Sawyer, Tim Cain, Chris Avellone, and the rest of a crack team of rpg greats under the leadership of Feargus Urquhart (If those names don't mean anything to you, then you have a lot of very good RPGs to discover. I envy your fresh perspective).
This is Obsidian's finest game yet.
gameplay 10/10
story/characters 9/10
music/sound 9/10
visuals 8/10 (Absolutely nothing wrong with them, but if you're expecting Skyrim, it may take a bit for you to adjust and appreciate what's here)
overall 9/10

Baldur's Gate, Icewind Dale, Planescape Torment.... games from the past that have a special allure and held many fond memories. Though Bioware took some steps in bringing the AD&D style forward in games such as Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic and Dragon Age and such, all of their games are fun and impressive in their own rights. But something was lost in translation over the years. Pillars of Eternity very successfully revives the genre.
PoE brings back the isometric top-down PoV over rich and beutifully constructed environments, as well as some very familiar user interface designs that really help the nastalgic sensation.
It is however its own game in its own universe, not part of D&D nor the Forgotten Realms for that matter. This allows the game to have a little more creative freedom and not bound by a pre-existing world. The world of PoE can be explored through countless books found throughout the game and by following the quests and questlines.
The only negative critique I can offer is the character portraits and their design seem a bit rushed. There are numerous portraits available but some of the designs are the same image just re-rendered different hues. And there seems to be a lack of variation. I love the nastalgic effect the crew at Obsidian were going for but with these 3-D modelled characters it would almost make sense to use a icon of the rendered model for the portrait. But after you pick a portrait and get deeper into the game the portraits become less and less important.
If you enjoyed the classics, you'll enjoy Pillars of Eternity.

Edit: Okay.. I can't recommend this game. :\ The saving is just too awful. I've lost 30+ minutes over and over again.. not because I'm not saving; I'm saving as often as I can.. but any enemy still being "in combat" will stop you from saving.. problem is that, in the wild, you very often have endless strings of weak enemies or small groups of somewhat tough enemies, and then suddenly a gigantic chimera jumps out of nowhere and is destroying your party. No big deal, right, just run away? HAH. You can't. Your idiot pawns will ignore your frantic efforts to tell them to follow you, turn around and just get one-shotted again and die, over and over. You can't run, you can't save often enough, I'm just about to quit even trying to play.. There's nothing "challenging" about being unable to save reasonably often and wasting my time repeatedly because of a poorly developed save feature. It's basic stuff, we've had saving for quite a while now, it shouldn't be this hard.
Extra edit: Just spent a ton of points on forward roll.. And it doesn't work? I have daggers equipped, it shows on my UI, but holding alt and hitting space with a direction pressed doesn't dodge at all. The keyboard bindings also like to change every time I launch the game slightly, which is extra annoying. It's a bit silly to have issues this basic right from the get go. I get that people seem to be pretty fond of this game, but you can't just blindly ignore bugs like this on release.. it's pretty weak.
Overall it's pretty decent - I still wish steam had 5 options for recommending, from basically 3 being neutral, 4 being pretty okay and 5 being awesome. This one is like a 3.9 for me.
Why? It's clunky. I know it's a console port and, honestly it's WAY better than most..  but it's still clunky. The controls are sometimes unresponsive and I've had to use work arounds to get some of the controls to work with mouse side-buttons and things like that. The autosaving is downright worthless, it's easy to lose 30+ minutes when wandering in the wields. Your NPC pawns are pretty stupid, I've had them get stuck down a small ledge or behind a rock while I'm being beaten to death, and none of the beckoning or commanding them to do anything helps at all.
And the best of all - fighting a monster you MUST flee from, it just regenerates limbs over and over.. Your NPCs constantly yell "run run" while standing in place and dying repeatedly.. no amount of spamming the "come here" button does anything, they just run back in to fight and die. Again. If you're going to have NPC-heavy stuff like this the players NEED to have the ability to RELIABLY manipulate them. This was by far the most obnoxiously frustrating part of the game for me.
Navigating menus is clunky as can be, as you'd expect from any console port - it always seemed kinda lazy, to me, to not go in and really re-work it to be far more intuitive so we don't have to sift through sub-menu after sub-menu since, y'know, PCs have mice and all, but hey.
That said, for $30 and the gameplay offered, it's still kinda borderline. The bugginess and awkardness for $30 pushes me into not recommend, even if just barely.. But there's not much in this category available on PC and I'd like to see more, albeit more polished and smooth, but hey. It's better than nothing, I guess..
It runs pretty damn smooth so far with settings cranked up on a GTX970 so no real complaints there. Combat is about 80% fun and 20% annoying - the annoying is mostly from the ridiculous amount of time your character will lie on the ground defenseless, be unable to dodge, etc., which results in you dying in just a hit or two.. at which point you better have manually saved relatively recently.
That said, thre's a decent handful of "classes" - ranging basically from warrior to rogue to wizard, but with a sorta double-up system. Warrior warrior is a big beefy all fighty guy, warrior wizard has a magic shield, etc. There's pure and hybrid, and they seem to have a decent range of skills and abilities which are unique, and I like that.
The dialogue is, overall, pretty decent. It'd be better done if the devs were more tempered in their implementation though - being told the fiftieth time, without leaving an area, that a map is useful for finding out where you are makes you really roll your eyes and wonder who thought that was clever dialogue to have spewed repetitiously. It's like those really mediocre fortune cookies that aren't fortunes but just lame obscure advice. Aside from some dumb thing like that, the chatter and such hasn't really been a distraction to me and has a bit of variety, even if it's sometimes very uninspired (finish a quest? Great! A companion wants to talk! What their insight on this development? "We finished that quest." Yeah thanks for that sherlock.)
The graphics are pretty solid when cranked up, and the sound effects are good. Decent-ish spell effects, nothing stellar yet. Soundtrack? I honestly can't recall any of the music being remotely remarkable at all, so I'm startled they have a soundtrack up for sale for so much, but maybe I've just not heard the good ones yet or something.
Overall, it's totally playable and seems pretty decent-to-good, depending on your preference and control scheme and all that. It's no AAA open-world as PC folks are used to, but it's nice to get our hands on a DECENTLY well done port of somethin' from console with some genuine value to it, quirks aside.
The stupid, stupid NPC AI plus the horrendous saving are the two biggest complaints.. I've last 20-30 minutes of playtime over and over because there's just no chance to save.. tons of stupid weak enemies keep assailing you for an endless amount of time, NPC pawns are being stupid, you never get to save, then die for some inane reason or another. That's not fun at all.

Alright, so life relented long enough to spend a little more time in-game and check out the last few weeks of updates.  Here's the report:
First off, the dragon.  Because who liked "flaming death from above every 3min" as a tutorial?  I'm happy to report that he is no longer a spawn-camping ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.  I'm actually not sure how to get his attention now since he ignored me on the first and second island both.  Tsunderagon?  Thankfully, this means players have to chance to get established and figure out what they're doing.
They've added some new books laying around that discuss weapon and armor factors, though the books are somewhat widely scattered and don't address some of the missing information about weapons (range and speed, most notably).  There are also a number of new loot items laying around near the starting area.  An extra axe, some basic armor, and more flint help get things rolling; a compass and fur armor (which both require metals from the second island to make); and a tin battle axe rounds out the lot.  Some of them are in odd locations, so I probably missed others.  All together, this helps ease new players in (honestly, the Fur armor might be a bit much, but I can't complain), though it is still a good idea to start a character in a completely new world to pick things up before joining a friend's world for coop since the loot takes quite a while to respawn.
There's still a lot of other issues to note, though.  Gathering anything mineral-related is still quite tedious.  Maybe some people like it, but it strikes me as time padding.  12 hits with a tin hammer (the best you can get early) to get a 1 piece of copper ore (of which you need a dozen or so along with more tin and coal to make something useful).  It adds up very quickly into lots of time standing around hitting rocks.  Put another way, some people have found it worthwhile to devise farming runs for the nodes to reduce time spent gathering minerals.  It just doesn't feel right here.
The crafting menu is still very annoying to use, especially when you aren't completely sure what something in the miscellaneous section is named (great example is when you go looking for nails because you see they are needed to repair a building, but they are actually named "Bag of Nails" in the rather long, alphabetized list).  Not being able to scroll a list when the mouse is over an item is frustrating, likewise the same issue when you have an item picked up in the poor inventory system.  Speaking of the inventory, I hate it.  I get what the intent is, but the implementation is very clumsy and makes finding anything an unnecessary chore.  Buildings/crafting stations are still all together in a 4-per-page list that would really be better served by a section in the crafting menu, though perhaps there is an issue with the coding (since they go to outline-placement mode instead of producing an item) preventing this.
Some bugs/design issues:  It looks like they're in the middle of some terrain changes on the islands.  Especially on the second island, there are a lot of rocks and other objects floating a few feet off the ground in many places.
With regards to the warmth mechanics, it still feels odd to me that it not only reduces your max health but also your actual health.  I get that it's supposed to be another layer of the survival gameplay, but it's really annoying to need to bandage myself just because I went outside for a few minutes before coming back to warm up.
Combat is... dull, I suppose is the correct work.  Yeah, your life is on the line with vicious monsters, but you just trudge around swinging mechanically.  There's no real intensity to it.  "Strafe around it in a circle while swinging" seems to be almost a one-size-fits-all tactic, and survival is more about whether you've farmed materials long enough to make the best available equipment than learning the enemies and playing well.
Overall, it seems like there is a desire to avoid out-of-character tutorial information, but I'm not sure whether that is appropriate to a game demanding you make survival choices.  If the character has the know-how to make a leanto, it seems reasonable to inform players of how to do so within the system.  Likewise with the fact that some mineral resources are found in discrete nodes while others are randomly generated by bashing any rock.  If they want to keep it completely in-world, a few more books in the starter area mentioning the basics would be great for new players.
There needs to be a decision on which direction to focus on for the moment:  Either improve the crafting side of things with better interface and more options (particularly with regards to structures) or emphasize the exploration and combat side with improved enemies (at the moment they seem mechanical, have 1 or 2 attacks that frequently have janky hit ranges, and depend mostly on huge health pools and damage compared to the player).  Right now it feels like the game is trying to do too many things at once, but I think some focused attention in each area one at a time will really help.  My personal preference would be the combat system since the game doesn't really fit the builder/crafter mold.
I still think this will eventually be a great game.  While I'm about to have even less time available, I'll try to check in every month or two and see what's changed as long as the devs keep pushing steady updates.

---Spoilers ahead!---
The game is set in the regions of Gondor/Mordor around the Black Gate during the times between The Hobbit and The Lord of The Rings. You play as Tallion, a Captain guarding the Black Gate. The region has long been unsave because of marauding orks who slowly take over. A part of the families stationed at the Black Gate don’t think it’s safe anymore and wanted to leave. They are called outcasts because they are seen as traitors. Later in the story they play an important role.
During the opening sequence the player gets to know some of the game’s mechanics. Fighting with the sword, blocking, running as well as stealth. At first those are somewhat unfamiliar as they replaced the typical L-Shift to sprint with Space. It ends up working splendid though as Tallion jumps over small obstacles on his own, so a jump isn’t really required anymore. Pressing Space to sprint is a lot more comfortable and I appreciated the inclusion quickly.
Back to the story: during the opening sequence we also witness how The Black Hand kills Tallion and his whole family and that everything he experienced was a memory of him as a sort of Spirit. His spirit and the spirit of an yet unknown wraith are somehow connected after the execution. Later we learn that this is the spirit of Celebrimbor, the legendary Elven smith who forged the rings of power.
The player is then somehow given corporal form. The goal is to draw out The Black Hand who are responsible for binding Tallion between the world of the living and the world of the dead.
In order to draw them out however the player has to go through the ranks of the Uruk army. The player can use wraith powers to interrogate lowly Uruks and find out the identity, strengths and weaknesses of the captains. They can then be sought after in different missions that pop up on the big, open world, map. Speaking of which, fast travel is possible to several towers of light that can be unlocked. One can also go after them without the information of strengths and weaknesses, however it is a lot more difficult and dangerous as they can be resistant to some of the players powers.
It is not exactly clear to me how it works, but I think that the first Captain who manages to kill the player becomes the Nemesis. He instantly gets a strong boost in power and is immune to a lot of your own powers. Even if killed the nemesis returns several times which can be frustrating. It is claimed that he wasn’t killed off completely, or maybe resurrected? It is unclear.
Frustrating as it may be, it’s still cool to have this arch enemy whom one wants to kill over and over! Parallel to this the player also meets Gollum. He hopes that Celebrimbor has the One Ring with him. Hence he tries to help him uncover his lost memory by showing him the way to relics of the past. Touching them results in a cutscene playing. It unveils a part of Celebrimbor's story. These get increasingly more difficult to uncover.
Throughout the game the player can also uncover artifacts and runes which uncover bits and pieces of the lore that revolves around the game.
Last but not least I want to mention the Branding mechanic. It allows the player to take command over the orks, as well as over the captains and warchiefs (after those have been weakened).
However in the first part of the game the player does not have this power and has to kill all 4 (remaining) warchiefs.
Killing all of them opens a new path in the questline: Helping the Outcasts. They have hidden away in a cave. After earning their trust by helping the leader rescue his wife, he sees the power the player possesses. This gives him the idea to destroy the monument the orks have been building in Saurons honor.
After this has been done the first, and unfortunately, most challenging of the three members of the Black Hand arrive to investigate.
After he is taken care of the player meets a woman (Lithariel) who somehow knows Tallions name and invites him to come with her to her mother who apparently wants to speak to Celebrimbor (yes she knows that too, through her mother). She leads the player to a completely new world.
Arriving there the player completes some tasks and is rewarded with the brand ability. The new task is to brand all the warchiefs to build up an army and storm the black gate. During the time here the player also encounters a dwarf with whom the player goes hunting and learns the mechanics of riding and controlling certain creatures in the world.
This is a way to introduce this mechanic to the player, and it’s a very compelling one as the story behind the dwarf is very interesting.
Back to the main storyline. After branding all the warchiefs Lithariel, who has been raiding the uruks forts, is captured. The player has to rescue her. This has probably been put in place to show that Tallion is still human. Surprisingly it works and it doesn’t feel annoying at all. Lithariel is portrayed as a total badass and rescuing her feels satisfying and rewarding.
The only really disappointing part of the game is the ending.
It’s a lazily done quick time event fight against Sauron. I couldn’t believe it. After I had played such an amazing game this is how it had ended. Story wise it was okay, setting up a sequel and being interesting. But gameplaywise I was simply shattered. It was way too easy and I don’t understand why this has been done.
After the main story line has been completed the player can explore the game further and finish all the different challenges that upgrade the weapons and collect all the story bits.

Not my cup of tea. It's not really a bad game, but just not enough to hold my interest. It's essentially an isometric combat-based RPG, kind of like Diablo without randomized levels, loot, skills, etc... The combat is ok, and there's a good variety of weapons, but you choose only two for any given level. And the levels are fixed, so if you want to play through again then you will be playing the exact same levels over and over. It's a fairly short game (less than 8 hours to complete), which is actually a good thing in my opinion. There are a good number of additional difficulty options you can assign as desired, and a lot of achievements to unlock, but for hard-core gamers, I just don't think it will be worth the effort.
The one thing it has going for it is story, and a narrator that constantly narrates every move you make. But it's just not that interesting.
This would probably appeal more to a younger crowd, like 10 year olds.

* The story so far is interesting, taking place somewhere before the begining of the events in Homestuck (haha who am i kidding, pinpointing a beginning on the homestuck timeline is like trying to find the mean between zero and infinity), and the humor is cyoot.
* The gameplay is standard point and click fun, EVERYTHING is interactable with EVERYTHING, so if you're the type of peep who likes his games slow and rich, this can work very well for you. Puzzles are interesting but nothing you cant solve, so it's not gonna be one of those games you need to open the wiki for to search how to progress.
* This game doesn't require any fancy computer parts to run, and it ran smoothly on my potato i3 intel hd graphics 4600 on the highest definition, so if you are low end, you can purchase without fear.
with all that, here are some noticable cons:
* The most noticeble one: it's SHORT. Like, I'm a nerd who likes to use all the interactability and slow down to read in some parts, so I got 6 hours out of this game. But a man who likes his game fast and to the point, and people who just want to get on with the story, will finish it in 3. But you know a game is good when the most noticeable bad thing with it is it being too short. Hopefully the 2nd act comes withing less than a year, but you know how it is with homestuck titles. One can only hope.
* With the intentions of this game to be a complete standalone title and people not needing to read homestuck to enjoy it, you will miss a LOT if you didn't read it. I'm not saying you CAN'T enjoy it without Homestuck; but the first act fails to explain itself many times, if you're new you would miss half the jist. Maybe it's a way for the game to stay mysterious for the second act, but I know it's going to annoy some people.
* The game is simplistic, and can be predictable at some points. If you are searching for hardcore puzzles and mindblowingly complex gameplay, im afraid you wont find it here. The point of the game is to enjoy the feel, story and characters (which are all adorable btw), not to win.
* It had some visual glitches at some points, but that was because I was messing with the screen resolution while tabbing out. Also it had some lag loading certain clips, but nothing to worry about.
* Not even a con, just my petty nitpick: it has nothing to do with Sburb, at least not now. I know it's supposed to be focused on the troll-human relations, switching planets yadda-yadda... But what I personally liked best about Homestuck was Sburb, the concept of a game being connected personaly to you, with kids learning and becoming gods and most importantly: adults. Again, this is just a nitpick and I know it wasn't planned to be connected to Sburb in the first place but... A man can dream right?
I give a score of 7/10, great for me, maybe not much for other people. It's only 8 bucks anyway, you're not risking much by buying it, and I can say with confidence that 3 hours of this 8 buck game is more fun and rich than 1.5 hours for 15+ bucks going to a movie.

It's a game that requires determination, and trial and error. With every death you suffer, you learn more of the enviroment and the enemies you lost to. The first time you meet a particular enemy and they murder you horribly, it's easy to feel like it's just plain unfair or annoying. However, the more you fight them, and the more you play the game, the more you learn about combat and their weaknesses. Those hollow spear soldiers that always have their shield up and take their sweet time attacking you? Punish their constant guard by kicking them, then follow up with attacks. That terrifying black knight at the beginning? He's easily parried, and by the end of the game you'll be killing them with ease.
The lore and atmosphere is fantastic too, you're making your way through this crumbled kingdom full of undead and demons, piecing together the history of the world and it's inhabitants.
It's got it's problems though, the PC port is not great so you'll need to get used to the jittery camera movement and XBOX button prompts, and you'll need to memorise the controls too. The lock-on switching is ridiculously sensitive, you need to keep your mouse perfectly still or your character will be twirling around switching between enemies.
I'd recommend these mods which make it a lot more bearable:
PVP Watchdog - Since they moved from GFWL to Steam, hackers are a bit of a danger. Luckily with this mod you can detect hackers (their name will show up in red when they connect with the reason why they're flagged) and you can press F1 to kick them out. It also shows the current time and how many nodes you're currently connected to, which are both nice features.
DSCM - This connectivity mod fixes the multiplayer as it's possible to not be connected to any nodes even though you have a perfectly fine connection. Make sure your steam name doesn't have any unicode characters in it though, or you won't be able to connect to any nodes. You can also force connections with this mod, meaning you can guarantee you can find your friends' summoning signs.
DSFix + HD tecture packs - With these you can make it look beautiful. This game's internal resolution was set to 1280x700 to help consoles run it without much issue (although I hear they still have some problems in Blight Town) but this mod changes it to 1080p. It has it's own anti-aliasing though, so you'll need to turn it off in the game's setting or you might have some problems.
It's like Stockholm Syndrome, the more I played it despite it's difficulty and technical issues the more I loved it.

An incredible example of what can be achieved through Kickstarter support, Pillars is an impressive paean to old cprgs of yore (Baldur's Gate, Planescape Torment, Arcanum, the original Fallout games) while still learning from its contemporaries (Skyrim, Dragon Age, Fallout 3 & NV). Pushing thirty hours into the game, I still feel as if I've barely scratched the surface. I will come back and review the rest of the game upon completion, but for now I'm having a great time.
The basics of the game mechanics & systems are easy to learn, but they're much harder to master. I've ran into a few fights that trounced me soundly, only to return victorious after reading the in-game journal a bit closer and adjusting my strategies. I'm playing on normal, and I expect my understanding of the rules to be challenged even further on subsequent playthroughs using higher difficulties and optional restrictions while achievement hunting.
Perhaps excepting easy difficulty (I don't know as I'm not playing on it), this isn't a game you can brute-force your way through without learning at least the basics of the underlying rules system. If you're familiar with tabletop RPGs or the details of the old Infinity Engine games, you will adjust quickly. The rest of you should take your time to learn a bit each time you run into a fight that pushes your abilities. You will do better in subsequent fights, and you will come to appreciate the level of work Obsidian put into the behind-the-scences systems.
Additional playthroughs will also be required to see more aspects of the story. Certain choices you make build (or destroy) reputation with various people and factions, opening up new pathways while closing off others.
Obsidian has shown committment to the game's continued quality by quickly issuing a patch that addressed a serious item bug. Addons, DLC, expansions (whatever you want to call them) are already in the pipe.
The game's quality is, thus far, exactly what you should expect from Josh Sawyer, Tim Cain, Chris Avellone, and the rest of a crack team of rpg greats under the leadership of Feargus Urquhart (If those names don't mean anything to you, then you have a lot of very good RPGs to discover. I envy your fresh perspective).
This is Obsidian's finest game yet.
gameplay 10/10
story/characters 9/10

visuals 8/10 (Absolutely nothing wrong with them, but if you're expecting Skyrim, it may take a bit for you to adjust and appreciate what's here)
overall 9/10

Baldur's Gate, Icewind Dale, Planescape Torment.... games from the past that have a special allure and held many fond memories. Though Bioware took some steps in bringing the AD&D style forward in games such as Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic and Dragon Age and such, all of their games are fun and impressive in their own rights. But something was lost in translation over the years. Pillars of Eternity very successfully revives the genre.
PoE brings back the isometric top-down PoV over rich and beutifully constructed environments, as well as some very familiar user interface designs that really help the nastalgic sensation.
It is however its own game in its own universe, not part of D&D nor the Forgotten Realms for that matter. This allows the game to have a little more creative freedom and not bound by a pre-existing world. The world of PoE can be explored through countless books found throughout the game and by following the quests and questlines.
The only negative critique I can offer is the character portraits and their design seem a bit rushed. There are numerous portraits available but some of the designs are the same image just re-rendered different hues. And there seems to be a lack of variation. I love the nastalgic effect the crew at Obsidian were going for but with these 3-D modelled characters it would almost make sense to use a icon of the rendered model for the portrait. But after you pick a portrait and get deeper into the game the portraits become less and less important.
If you enjoyed the classics, you'll enjoy Pillars of Eternity.

For those of you chasing that old school RPG dragon like I do, this is the game for you. It takes every thing that made the Dungeon Seige and Neverwinter special and VASTLY improves on it. I am 24 hours in and this game just keeps getting better.
Old School feel with the perfect amount of new age touch? Check!
Perfect amount of difficulty? Check!
Multiple options to customize how combat works from real time to turn based? Check!
Dragons? Check!
Amazing story with great voice acting and dialogue? Check!
The ability to replace the characters you dont like with ones that you hand created simply by talking to an in keeper and hiring an adventurer? Check!
Fully upgradable castle complete with the ability to hire guards, lock up prisoners, that just so happens to be built upon an extremely difficult dungeon that you can explore to your hearts content? GOD DAMN CHECK!
Really, the only thing I was going to complain about was the exp system, but even that has grown on me. You dont get exp from killing monsters. You sort of have a hunting log, where you get exp until you kill so many of a certain monster then the exp stops. Basically, you can only learn so much from killing the same thing over and over again, until you have to move on to stronger or more unique monsters.
It has a few bugs here and there, but nothing game breaking and the ones that are there, the developers have been knocking out in droves.
Video game companies that take care of their fans and value their input are a dying breed. This game is a product of a company that wants it to be all it can be and not just what it has to be to make money. It really is everything you would expect from Obsidian and so much more.

Now the game itself is one of those "the whole is greater than the sum of it parts" as nothing sticks out as average/nor brilliant (except the AI of your companions in fights which is average, but you should micro manage them any way). *Really minor spoilers* The story is above average, but do not expect anything groundbreaking, it is still the same old "you are special" fantasy stuff with the schizo sidekick, a nerdy scientist/history scholar companion etc. *Really minor spoilers* I am especially enjoying the hard mega dungeon, when I backed the game it was something that looked especially cool and it really is. If you want to dip your feet in a fantasy RPG, this is a great game to do it, if you are someone who loved the old Infinity engine games you MUST buy this game, seriously what are you waiting for?

Short Review: I recommend it, but only if you know what you're getting into.
Long Review: Dragon's Dogma is an interesting game.  It's a bit like if you were to take elements from Skyrim, Dragon's Age, and Dark Souls and smash them together into an RPG made by Capcom.  Sounds like a perfect idea, right?  Well... I didn't say they took the BEST things from each game, just, "things."  The story is really just... bland and forgetful, but the combat, though tricky at first, is SOLID.  Oh my goodness.  Playing as a long bow man, it's amazing.  Pulling out and shooting 10 arrows at once is fantastic.  That being said, the damage is a little weird at times because of creature levels.  Like, I'm sorry, if I shoot a fully loaded set of 10 arrows right in the face of a bandit, he should die, not just get knocked back a little bit, but I digress.
As far as a PC port its... mediocre.  It's not optimized all that well for the resolution and textures you get, but by no means does it run super bad or look terrible, it's just obvious that this is an older game.  As far as mouse support in the menus it's non existant.  I REALLY would've liked to have the option to scroll instead of having to click EVERY slider and move it to preview things or sell items.
All in all, it's definitely worth the price of admission if you get it on sale. (11.99ish)  There's a lot of running in this game, so make sure you pick up your infinite ferry stone in your inventory at the main Inn before you do much, or else you'll literally spend like 30 minutes running in one direction because of the lack of fast travel.

Replay value comes from the fact that you are scored at the end of each of five chapters. On the normal difficulty setting, you can only reach A rank, however on Hard, you can strive for SS. You may think that since I have only played for about 3 hours I have no right to write a review, but I’m starting to fear that I’ll burst if I hold this in. I may update my review if I ever manage to finish this game or my opinion changes.
I still remember the first visual novel I ever played. It had pretty bad graphics with broken anatomy for the character portraits, very few CG’s, 12 different soundtracks of horribly repetitive music, several flaws in its coding which made things confusing at times and not the best English. But the fact stood that a single person with English as a second language had worked and produced an amazing visual story with deep characters that touched the heart.
Eden* is the exact opposite. The graphics are beautiful, characters have animated eyes and mouths, there are a huge amount of CG’s, fully animated opening, beautiful soundtracks and sound effects, full voice-acting, perfectly coded and excellent English text. But Eden* with its mind-numbingly dull story and flat characters have succeeded in completely killing my interest for visual novels. Eden* is for some reason passed off as a visual novel but is really a kinetic novel.
From the moment I started up Eden* I was bored, but told myself that I was being unfair and should play more before passing judgement. But no matter how much further I went things never turned out interesting and the story only became duller and duller. At certain parts of the story there were moments that could have been interesting but was completely cut out and skipped over because god forbid we have something remotely interesting.
The protagonist is Ryou Haruna who is the most perfect boy in the world, the best soldier of them all, dark and totally edgy, has a dark past and charms all the girls simply by existing. He is a terrible person but the story progresses as if he’s a good person with characters magically being in love with him and completely trusting him for no reason.
Other characters include Sion who is the most perfect loli in the world, the most intelligent being on the planet despite not being able to wash her own hair and everyone calls her “the messiah”. Elica who is a ditzy maid that takes care of Sion. Lavinia who gets her panties wet over bladed weapons and Inaba who drinks on the clock.
I couldn’t for my life care for any of the characters or their backstories and only found them infuriating. Every character’s personality is horribly typical and cookie-cutter. All I needed was an introduction and then I had immediately grasped their entire character and could predict their actions from there on. The conversations between the characters are so flat and unrealistic it feels like everyone is talking to a wall.
When I read the description, saw all the good reviews and saw that it was developed by the popular Minori I honestly expected a good story with deep characters. For the first time I wish that Steam issued refunds. The only consolation I have is that I bought it on sale so I didn’t suffer the full blow of the 20 euro that this game is selling for.
I would not recommend this for anyone with regular standards. If you however have a strong liking for dull storytelling, underdeveloped characters, anime characters whom look like they’re 12 years old and old-fashioned cheesy drama this would satisfy your needs.

Eden is a visual novel set in the near future with Earth on the brink of destruction. We see the story through the eyes of an elite soldier called Ryou Haruna who is a personal guard to Sion, the Earth's lead scientist. We are just a passive observer and have no control over anything except when to start the next line of dialogue. There are no decisions to be made or any dialogue choices here. It does make your character more interesting and it makes for some pretty tense situations in where you hope he does the “right” thing. But that also means you will be doing nothing but right clicking from start to finish which can be a turn off considering it is a lengthy game that took me about 12 hours to complete.
Options menu doesn't have much to it but a very neat feature is that you can turn off individual characters voice actors if you don't like there acting. Can't speak of the quality of acting as it is all in Japanese with subtitles being in English. Starting off you are in a field with Sion and it's all calm and happy. After a short while you are teleported back to the events that got you there which was kind of daunting and that intro served no purpose other then taking the impact out of scenes, as you already know both Sion and Ryou will be fine. Anyways, after the intro you will be on your way to a secluded island masion which is housing the renowned genius Sion who is working on her lasts steps to get mankind off of the dying planet.
Even though the world is about to end and Sion is nearly done with her work there are infiltrators that want to kill her. The game does not handle intrigue and mystery well. For example someone says “She is a...” and the game fades to white and teleports you to another point in the future leaving you clueless as to where you are or what you are doing now. If you don't want us to know about it yet just don't bring it up. Another scene has you killing an infiltrator but you never see it happen, instead you are teleported a bit forward in time after the murder happens, leaving you wondering “Wait. He is dead now? Well, okay then.”  It does this every time something mildly interesting happens which makes the game an utter chore to play until you escape the island.
Characters don't help at all either. Most are very unlikable which would be perfectly fine if they didn't try to play them off as good guys later on. Especially your character. He is supposed to be some elite solider that doesn't question orders but comes off as an extremely paranoid antisocial psychopath. That would make sense though the game never builds him up as a character or shows what he has been through to make him so psychopathic. Seeing his transformation from a sad kid to a hardened soldier would have been a much more interesting tale than anything on offer here. It is an interesting setting, humanity went bunkers after the red star in the sky was confirmed to destroy Earth and started a World War. Afterwards they focused on escaping the dying planet but some people refused to leave and started a guerrilla style war against the government.
But no, there we are stuck in a mansion with a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ protagonist and nothing much of interest going on. It really picks  after you escape the mansion though. As to be expected from this game it doesn't tell or show about your journey or how you avoided the military after escaping, you just teleport to a safe house. In that environment is where the game really shines. Sion being sick to the point of dying any moment really tugs on the heart strings. She is a super genius but she has been so sheltered that she does not know how to do the most basic of things like cooking or brushing her hair. You take on a father like role until things get romantic which is uncomfortable considering she has the body of a child. That is very late into the game though, do not be expecting a romance game, it is more of about taking care of a dying “child”.
Late in the game they also introduce the only other decent character besides Sion. It is entertaining watching our psychopath Ryou bully her, though Ryou will never become a likable character. Eden does a far better job mixing day to day comedy and sadness in events leading into the end of the world than trying to tell an actual narrative. There is nearly no “fan service” except for one scene showing a girl in a bikini which was a nice change a pace from most Visual Novels.  Our character does like to stare at breasts though and probably spends more time looking there than at their faces. You can also buy a different version over at
that features H scenes if you are interested but the story is perfectly fine without it.
One thing that really helps set the mood is the amazing soundtrack featured in this game. All the songs are top notch and really amplify the powerful moments. Artstyle is great though the environments are nothing special. This is a strange title. It does nothing right story-wise other than get you to care about Sion. If it didn't reveal right off the bat that you will escape safely there might have been some tense or interesting moments in the mansion which is a shame as the intro served absolutely no purpose. Eden did something right though since even if we all know how it will end you can't help but see it through to the end. It's not awful but it is a very slow burner and has neither the characters, the overall objective or the story to hold your interest until you reach the good parts. Something like finding out secrets about the facility, having the infiltrators be an actual threat or having meaningless dialogue options would have done wonders to alleviate the boredom. When all is said and done the last few hours are pretty memorable and emotional which does save the game in my opinion. Recommended to Visual Novel fans with a lot of patience.

I do really like this game, and I have gotten my fair share out of it, but now i'm coming back to write a review.
As you can probably see, i've spent a good deal of time in this game. It is a really well made game, for the most part, but to be honest, it's just not
When I played it at first, for the first long time I thought it was great, and the game definitely is worth the money, but as time went on I realized this game really isn't that fun. It is a perfect example of a mile wide and an inch deep. There is so much stuff you can do, but not much of it is varied. There is so much for you to see, but after awhile that gets old too, and it takes a long time to do it as well. There are tons of cool little dungeons and buildings on planets, but it takes ages to find good ones and when you do find one they do... Next to nothing. With recent updates you can get crew for your ship and villages have quests, but they're all cardboard cutout carachters and quests. Not very interesting.
My main problem is the combat system. It's awful. It feels super damn clunky and nowhere near satisfying. Long cooldowns, unsmooth movements, and the monsters you fight are borderline childish levels of cartoon. The boss fights feel the same way.
This game is, still, in my opinion, amazing. ---Spoilers ahead!---
The game is set in the regions of Gondor/Mordor around the Black Gate during the times between The Hobbit and The Lord of The Rings. You play as Tallion, a Captain guarding the Black Gate. The region has long been unsave because of marauding orks who slowly take over. A part of the families stationed at the Black Gate don’t think it’s safe anymore and wanted to leave. They are called outcasts because they are seen as traitors. Later in the story they play an important role.
During the opening sequence the player gets to know some of the game’s mechanics. Fighting with the sword, blocking, running as well as stealth. At first those are somewhat unfamiliar as they replaced the typical L-Shift to sprint with Space. It ends up working splendid though as Tallion jumps over small obstacles on his own, so a jump isn’t really required anymore. Pressing Space to sprint is a lot more comfortable and I appreciated the inclusion quickly.
Back to the story: during the opening sequence we also witness how The Black Hand kills Tallion and his whole family and that everything he experienced was a memory of him as a sort of Spirit. His spirit and the spirit of an yet unknown wraith are somehow connected after the execution. Later we learn that this is the spirit of Celebrimbor, the legendary Elven smith who forged the rings of power.
The player is then somehow given corporal form. The goal is to draw out The Black Hand who are responsible for binding Tallion between the world of the living and the world of the dead.
In order to draw them out however the player has to go through the ranks of the Uruk army. The player can use wraith powers to interrogate lowly Uruks and find out the identity, strengths and weaknesses of the captains. They can then be sought after in different missions that pop up on the big, open world, map. Speaking of which, fast travel is possible to several towers of light that can be unlocked. One can also go after them without the information of strengths and weaknesses, however it is a lot more difficult and dangerous as they can be resistant to some of the players powers.
It is not exactly clear to me how it works, but I think that the first Captain who manages to kill the player becomes the Nemesis. He instantly gets a strong boost in power and is immune to a lot of your own powers. Even if killed the nemesis returns several times which can be frustrating. It is claimed that he wasn’t killed off completely, or maybe resurrected? It is unclear.
Frustrating as it may be, it’s still cool to have this arch enemy whom one wants to kill over and over! Parallel to this the player also meets Gollum. He hopes that Celebrimbor has the One Ring with him. Hence he tries to help him uncover his lost memory by showing him the way to relics of the past. Touching them results in a cutscene playing. It unveils a part of Celebrimbor's story. These get increasingly more difficult to uncover.
Throughout the game the player can also uncover artifacts and runes which uncover bits and pieces of the lore that revolves around the game.
Last but not least I want to mention the Branding mechanic. It allows the player to take command over the orks, as well as over the captains and warchiefs (after those have been weakened).
However in the first part of the game the player does not have this power and has to kill all 4 (remaining) warchiefs.
Killing all of them opens a new path in the questline: Helping the Outcasts. They have hidden away in a cave. After earning their trust by helping the leader rescue his wife, he sees the power the player possesses. This gives him the idea to destroy the monument the orks have been building in Saurons honor.
After this has been done the first, and unfortunately, most challenging of the three members of the Black Hand arrive to investigate.
After he is taken care of the player meets a woman (Lithariel) who somehow knows Tallions name and invites him to come with her to her mother who apparently wants to speak to Celebrimbor (yes she knows that too, through her mother). She leads the player to a completely new world.
Arriving there the player completes some tasks and is rewarded with the brand ability. The new task is to brand all the warchiefs to build up an army and storm the black gate. During the time here the player also encounters a dwarf with whom the player goes hunting and learns the mechanics of riding and controlling certain creatures in the world.
This is a way to introduce this mechanic to the player, and it’s a very compelling one as the story behind the dwarf is very interesting.
Back to the main storyline. After branding all the warchiefs Lithariel, who has been raiding the uruks forts, is captured. The player has to rescue her. This has probably been put in place to show that Tallion is still human. Surprisingly it works and it doesn’t feel annoying at all. Lithariel is portrayed as a total badass and rescuing her feels satisfying and rewarding.
The only really disappointing part of the game is the ending.
It’s a lazily done quick time event fight against Sauron. I couldn’t believe it. After I had played such an amazing game this is how it had ended. Story wise it was okay, setting up a sequel and being interesting. But gameplaywise I was simply shattered. It was way too easy and I don’t understand why this has been done.
After the main story line has been completed the player can explore the game further and finish all the different challenges that upgrade the weapons and collect all the story bits.
I completed the main story line including some diddling around, just running around in the world killing orks in about 16hrs.
I really enjoyed this game. It can get a bit repetitive but it's worth picking up on a sale. The nemesis system is unique and interesting, and the combat feels great. Definitely worth playing.

First of all I just want to say that this is a GREAT game and I absolutely love this game and would recommend it, but that does dot mean that this game is without faults.
I'll get all the bad things out of the way first
1. DLC spam. I hate that I love Total War so much that I'll waste whatever money to get whatever DLC pack that comes out and tbh they're not always worth it, plus the ammount of DLC they push out absolutely bleeds us dry considering that a lot of these factions are indeed copy paste.
2. Too well balanced. The balance of the factions is almost too good at least compared to Rome 2. multiplayer is static and I have found that I have to try very unorthodox armies to spice multiplayer battles (which usually results in my defeat)
3. Wasted potential. Attila was already an improvement over Rome 2, however my biggest complaint about Attila is that the DLC and updates felt rushed and some DLC packs almost felt rushed like the Slavic Nations Culture Pack imo.
but in seriousness, everything that came after launch felt rushed so they could start advertising Total War: Warhammer earlier and now CA treats it like the middle child.
Now time for the positives (Thanks to anyone whose made it this far)
1. Awesome Mechanics. The added mechanics to this game over Rome 2 like the Horde, Raze, colonisation etc... is fantastic. This is truly what Rome 2 should have been, this is what we were expecting in 2013 and CA really did make up for that with Attila
2. Game Aesthetic. this is my personal opinion really, but the transition from the ancient era to the middle ages have always been one of my favorite time periods. The dark, gloomy vibes the game gives off the feeling that the world as you know it is coming to an end with the Huns descending on your doorstep. From the map appeal to the Unit Variety and choice of Factions is great and I never get tired of seeing my legions of Romans being crashed upon by waves of Sassanids and Barbarians.
3. Battles. What can I say besides that I love it. Cavalry finally operates like it should, Elaphants are not too strong, but remain an impactful tool on the battlefield. Infantry has good mass and the fatigue rate is a lot better in this game since it always bothered me that units in Rome 2 could always run from one side of the battlefield to the other while only being active or a little tired.
All in all I'd give Attila an 8/10, it's a solid game with good replayability and enough things to do that you'll never truly be too bored. truly worth every single penny I spent on this game.

I didn't like this game, for a multitude of reasons. But, before I say them, I'd like to say that CA did some things right. Most notably, the bug-ironing-out on launch. By and large, this game's was one of the smoothest launches bug-wise in Total War history. However, it really does little long term merit.
First of all, optimization. Or, rather, the lack thereof. I've seen far better optimization in Rome II, which is saying something. You'd need an inordinately costly PC to get  60 FPS consistently, and even then, best of luck to you.
Next, copy-paste factions.... they did way too much of that, especially with the Germanic factions, in that most of their rosters are exactly the same with a different color scheme. I wish I was joking, but alas, I am not.
Finally, the unit balancing in more competitive multiplayer. I haven't played MP in this game for performance reasons, but the unit balancing really put me off the idea of starting. Say, for example, ages ago, the Athar's chosen from the Empires of Sand DLC. Cheapest and deadliest infantry/berserker unit around. It make meals out of far more expensive units. I think the OP unit of the day now are poison archers, but I'm not sure if things have changed all that much since the Slavic DLC.
And finally, this is an abbreviated version of why I dislike this game.

Attila's got a different "feel" from most Total War games. You can play as one of the smaller, emerging nations, nipping at the heels of the larger empires to claim what you can, or play as one of the Roman Empires and try to stave off the encroachments of your rivals. The worsening weather will tighten your food supply, and entire cities can be wiped off the map. And then there are the Huns, threatening everyone with their scorched-earth policies.
The whole game feels like a long struggle against the darkness. That makes it difficult, but also more rewarding if you can bring order to the chaos. Or, just sit back and watch the chaos engulf the Western Roman Empire. That's fun, too. (If you play, do take at least one turn as the WRE, just to see how crazy it gets.) The politics system takes a little getting used to, but it's easier to figure out than in other games. Plus, arranging marriages and assassinating people is cool!
Overall, I think Attila might be my favorite Total War so far. Every faction I've played feels really different, and the "deterioration" of the world gives it a unique flavor. Just don't be too upset if the Huns burn your cities.

While the game does have it's issues (Mainly the engrish and some bugs here and there), the devs keep in touch with the community and so far have focused on what is most wanted/needed. As for the P2W complaints; Everything can be unlocked with the in-game currency aside from skins and boosts, which provide no advantage whatsoever. There are no units, runes or gameplay content of any kind locked behind a pay wall. However, it IS possible to unlock certain units with cash, which may feel unfair at first glance. But these units as well as their counters can just as easily be unlocked for free. The game is very generous with it's gold (Daily quests, daily gifts, achievements, etc), so it isn't like a moba that takes a month just for one character.

Short Review: I recommend it, but only if you know what you're getting into.
Long Review: Dragon's Dogma is an interesting game.  It's a bit like if you were to take elements from Skyrim, Dragon's Age, and Dark Souls and smash them together into an RPG made by Capcom.  Sounds like a perfect idea, right?  Well... I didn't say they took the BEST things from each game, just, "things."  The story is really just... bland and forgetful, but the combat, though tricky at first, is SOLID.  Oh my goodness.  Playing as a long bow man, it's amazing.  Pulling out and shooting 10 arrows at once is fantastic.  That being said, the damage is a little weird at times because of creature levels.  Like, I'm sorry, if I shoot a fully loaded set of 10 arrows right in the face of a bandit, he should die, not just get knocked back a little bit, but I digress.
As far as a PC port its... mediocre.  It's not optimized all that well for the resolution and textures you get, but by no means does it run super bad or look terrible, it's just obvious that this is an older game.  As far as mouse support in the menus it's non existant.  I REALLY would've liked to have the option to scroll instead of having to click EVERY slider and move it to preview things or sell items.
All in all, it's definitely worth the price of admission if you get it on sale. (11.99ish)  There's a lot of running in this game, so make sure you pick up your infinite ferry stone in your inventory at the main Inn before you do much, or else you'll literally spend like 30 minutes running in one direction because of the lack of fast travel.

I really liked this game for the first nine months that I owned it-- I was able to operate it on my netbook, an Acer Aspire, which is impossible with most graphics intensive survival games; important life/food bars and menus were easy to see and use; overall, the game was very intuitive and easy to figure out; multiplayer was a dream come true in ease; and even though some game graphics were less than realistic or laggy, they were real enough that when you went wolf hunting in the woods with a pack of your buddies, you felt like you were really there, in the moment.  I tried the beta, but it wouldn't really run well on my netbook, so I stuck with the original game; not a problem, since either option was supported by the game.
Then, after a couple of busy months of not having the time to play, I came back to the game only to find that none of my hard built characters or original game were playable any more.  I had to start everything from scratch.  My new character woke up in what had been the bad-running beta world, naked, freezing, and horribly video-lagged.  The all-important life bars were no longer well-designed for easy tracking, and my menus were unresponsive.
As of now, this game, which I had highly enjoyed, has been killed for me through the development process.  At any given time that may change, but personally I'm not going to keep checking back just to see if maybe I can play again.  If you're the kind of player who doesn't mind spending a hundred hours building up characters and equipment just to have it all rendered unplayable when developers decide to head off in a new direction, this is the game for you.  If you're the kind of player who buys a game because you like playing the game and also like knowing that the game requirements are not going to change unexpectedly and render your purchase unplayable at any given moment, this is not.

So my first experience with Savage Lands was great. I wandered around the island, got a friend to play with me, built a house, took over a small village, got killed a bunch of times, eventually learned how to hunt wolves... we got pretty far. There was a LOT of cross-country running because we died and had to go back to our bodies across the island. But it was fun.
Left it behind for a while. Picked it up a while later..... here's what happened.
- friend and I both made new characters
- Loaded into the game
- friend loaded into the game
- found ourselves dying repeatedly on an island
- we just screwed around next to a tower with a door that wouldn't open
- random person joined our game, immediately made the best gear and gave it to us
- random person proceeded to lead us through the entire game in what might be a speedrun, from one island to the next to the next
- random person helped my friend and I reach the dragon himself (who, by the amount of limbs, is actually a wyvern not a dragon but that's neither here nor there)
- three more random people joined the game
- cue twenty-minute battle with the dragon in which we died a lot and there was a bunch of random naked people running around in the ruin trying to pick stuff up off their own dead bodies
- dragon was killed
- my friend and I decided to stop playing the game for the night
.....so that's what happened. The game was super laggy for both of us, which wasn't the lovely old Savage Lands I had remembered, but I think that in the future that issue will be fixed. I wouldn't necessarily buy this game right now, but I'd definitely keep it on my wishlist or keep following it for updates if I were you and I hadn't bought it yet.
I should probably also point out that I didn't buy this game, I won it in a giveaway. So this review isn't altered by anger or pleasure at spending money on something.

I received Miscreated as a gift from a friend, looking to branch out in my survival games. I was growing tired of DayZ and thought this game might be better. However, this game is in dire need of optimization.
Pros:
-Alt-Look: I love being able to run forwards and look around me. It's incredibly satisfying.
-Spacebar=Jump: You don't miss it until it's gone.
-Visuals: By golly it sure looks pretty.
Cons:
-No Friend Tab In Servers: I really wish I could be able to find my friends' server.
-No Way To See What Server You're In
-Superlag
-Inventory System Could Use Some Work
-Music is total garbage
-Character Models Look Like Low-Quality Cartoons
-Broken Melee System: Go ahead, try to hit a zed or another person. I dare you.
-Loot Spawns Are Non-Existent: I shouldn't have to search for 15 minutes to find a can of food or, rather, anything at all. I've played for nearly 2 hours and found 1 melee weapon. I asked a guy in chat if he had anything useful and he said that 45 minutes got him some clothes and a couple cans of food.
-Food And Water Start At 80%: You mean to tell me I spawn with absolutely nothing and I'm already down food and water? Bull.
-Food And Water Decay: Way too fast. You're constantly in worry about starving to death or dying of dehydration.
-Servers Are Very, Very Unreliable
This game should be free-to-play until they optimize it a little bit more. Keep it on your wishlist and come back in a few months, maybe then it'll be worth the money. I'm sorry my friend spent money on this for me.

Usually I write reviews when I am done with a game. This game is going to be the exception to that rule or at least the first exception to that rule. The reason why I'm writing this review now is because I have basically seen all the game has to offer and I am just finishing up on collecting the last few unlockables.
Let me start by saying that this game is a really good game. It can go from making you love it in one moment to making you scream in frustration in the next. If you don't know what the game is about you basically play as a little kid that has to make his way through randomly generated floors and you kill enemies with your tears. It is unforgiving as hell, since your character is really weak to start, and is almost entirely down to your skill at dodging things and luck. I'm not one to enjoy luck-based things, however, due to the randomness of this game, it is endlessly replayable. The floors aren't the only part of the game that is randomly generated. Every floor has an item that changes the way your character works and with hundreds of different combinations of items, every run will be unique. Now, when I say run, I mean, the game is a roguelike and features permadeath. Don't let this put you off as it will be quite easy to get good enough at the game that you can complete a run and then it comes down to just completing each milestone for all the characters.
The characters in the game do feel very different. Although they don't have too many differences, they all have very different playstyles. Most of the characters are enjoyable with the exception of the purposefully difficult characters which are there just to test you.
The game has an incredible soundtrack and the artstyle, while being simplistic, is cool and is surprisingly detailed. I would definitely recommend this game as it is a very fun, highly replayable and challenging game.
The only time the game really makes you feel like it is badly designed is when you get unlucky and get some terrible rng but that is the way the game is designed. It doesn't care about your feelings.

As a Homestuck fan, I was going to get this regardless but this is honestly just a very well done and fun little game. It's a Point & Click adventure that's beautifully done and well written. Is you don't know the webcomic that won't be an issue as the game generally explains everything with the in-player interactions.
Pros:
-Text for almost every interaction with the scenery and invertory items
You can honestly use like every item on one object in the background and get interesting text and jokes/puns with very few exceptions. Heck you can even use items on each other which yield some funny results.
-Well written
From the characters to the descriptions everything feels just well done and authentic. Though it is written in a 2nd-person style which might seem weird at first, you'll get used to it and this style works for the benifit of the game as you get the character's thoughts on whatever you've clicked on.
-This ain't a fairytale
The trailers and images make it seem like a fun little adventure and it is, but there's themes in this game that are not all sugar and spice. It never gets bloody and nothing really dark happens but these themes add to the characters and makes them and the situations they're in seem real. It also makes you sympathize with them too (if you're worried about the potential themes because of triggers I'll leave a list of them at the end of my review).
-Puzzles
The puzzles are mostly simple until you get to the battles. Battles in this game aren't really battles but act more like puzzles themselve in order to win which is pretty cool.
-Music
This music is very, very good and fits with whatever is going on scene. I'm not really surprized by this because the webcomic always had good music and it's obvious they brought people who contribute to it here on the game like Toby Fox (the man who created Undertale which makes me wonder when this game is going to get it's own version of Megalovania because I want it)
-Cheap
Honestly I was surprized this game was so cheap but it makes sense since it's a short game, speaking of that...
Cons:
-Short, like, VERY short if speed running
The game is very short if you just do the puzzles, you could probably beat it in 30 minutes top but that's not what these game are for. You're ment to explore and interact with stuff and that easily adds a few hours onto it. Another issue with the game being so short is that there's only so much plot and in hind sight there's really not a lot as it leaves you wanting more. It honesly only feels like the introduction to the game and then some.
-Character animation (more of a pet peeve)
This may just be me but when I saw the introduction cutscene and then the animation of the character in the acutally gameplay section I was put off because it wasn't as smooth as I was expecting it to be. It took a minute to get used to but after that it didn't bother me in the slightest, it was just a bit jarring at bit.
The Conclusion:
Overall, it's a very fun click & point game that is short but is also cheap. If you got the money to spare and you like these type of games even a little bit I'd say get it. There's more to come in the future and if it's anything like the webcomic we'll get up to 6 Acts where Act 6 feels like 5 acts on it's own merit to the point we got acts in Act 6 itself (e.g. Act 6 Act 4, it was very silly with how long Act 6 was getting). Oh and let's not forget the intermissions, there were several of them in the webcomic that would later tie into the main story...

Excelent RPG in the vein of IWD and BG series.  Just finished the game on normal and it took me about 46 hours doing approximately 4/5ths of the side content.  My party was level 11 when I finished.  Excelent story, great writing, interesting companions and the combat was fun once you get the hang of it.  Also, a lot of variety in terms of character creation (which is a big deal to me atleast) - races, sub-races, and backgrounds all have an effect on stats and interactions.  Their is a lot of replay value here as well - all the classes play differently and there are many choices as you progress that effect the story.  If you enjoy old-school RPGs with real-time combat then you should definitely pick this one up.  I'll highlight below some of my pros/cons, overall I would give the game a 8/10.
The good:
- Great story, emotional, good pacing, interesting twists and the ending was great IMO.
- RTwP combat is a big pro for me.  I hated the combat in D:OS and was very relieved that the real-time combat worked will in Eternity.
- Huge variety of spells and abilites (over 300) plus talents and class specfic perks add a lot of variety to combat.  My PC was a wizard and there is a lot of spell variety.  Plus you can learn new spells not just at level up but by buying/looting spell books from other wizards and copying them into your book.
- Lots of options for character creation, classes all play differently, character choices effect stats and abilities.
- Lots of side quests, some of the main side-chains allow a lot of choice in how you want to handle things and what faction/s you want to support.
- Well writen companions that have important interactions with the story and have their own motivations that can impact the game.
- Stable, I experienced no bugs either major or minor in 45+ hours.  The ranting about bugs seems to be very very overblown.
The not so good:
- Somewhat limited in how to respond to certain situations that have a major impact on the story.  Would have liked to see more options.  Usually you only have 5-6 responses.
- Some stats are not conveyed particularly well in how they effect combat so there is a learning curve.
- Druids and cyphers seem overpowered in AoE and single-target damage respectively.  Druids are noticibly more potent than mages at present and have higher defenses.
- Music is hit and miss, but mostly good.  Some of the songs get repeated to nausea inducing levels, however.
- No spell interations, this may be a design choice or lack of time related, I'm not sure which.  But spell/ability ineration is a newer RPG idea that would really add depth to the game (one of the few area where D:OS is superior).
- Not a lot of portrait variety at character creation.  You can however add your own custom portaits very easily.  Community will likely start pumping out extra portrait packs like they did with NWN/BG
The bad:
- Visuals aren't very impressive and there are few graphics options.  No in-engine FSAA so the characters often look very blocky, even when zoomed in.  Maps and spell effects look much better, but could still use some improvements.
- Voice-acting is very hit and miss in terms of quality.
- Enemy AI is sketchy.  Example - certain enemies seem designed to speficially prevent any type of control since they can teleport directly to your squishies.  Enemy agro priority is also unpredictable in some cases.
- Enchanting interface is very obtuse.  Numerous times I had enchanting points on an item still available and could not upgrade the quality.  Also it would frequently tell me I didn't have the required reagents and when I bought them it would then say that the item couldn't be further upgraded.  This is very annoying.
- Not a lot of variety in terms of locations - forest, medieval town, cave, ancient ruins with some varietion.  Would like to see more variety in the future.
Overall the positives very much outweigh the negatives in my opinion.  I have been waiting for a return to the old-school RPGs and this game did not disappoint. Personally I would put this game way ahead of D:OS - the combat is much better, the narrative, companions, and story are much better and the various secondary systems and crafting are more intuitive.  There are certainly things that need to be fixed/improved either through patching or in the expansions (two planned at present), but if you like old-school RPGs then you should definitely pick this one up.

Simply put, this game is amazing.
After the nightmare that wa Rome II, Attila seems to stand on a much more stable ground than what Rome II gave us back in 2013. The new fire effects, coupled with the Blood and Gore involved when engaging in melee and long-ranged missile combat all make Attila look and feel fresh. It was a surprisingly good first few hours that I wasted whilst trying to properly learn the game when I decided to forgo with the prologue; and in my opinion, this is the best way to learn how to play the game. It never felt draggy, nor were its battles boring (unlike the long, extremely drawn out battles in Rome II). Whereas in Rome II, you'd see men standing around doing nothing while their friends engaged in combat, there is a lot less of that in Attila. A lot less, not completely absent mind you.
The battles wasn't the only thing to get a revamp however, as the Campaign Map certainly feels more intuitive and less 'boring' than what we got in Rome II. First off, it must be said that Attila plays more like a Survival-Strategy game than a 'conquer everything' type of work, as roaming hordes threaten every single city you have, regardless if it was in the outer borders of your Empire or nestled deep inside its core.
What's more is that the game doesn't require you to have all cities in a province/region before you could start issuing edicts.
All in all, a very good game that I recommend for everyone to at least try.
