This game has potential but th current state is rather unsatisfying. It takes about an hour to find out almost everything this game has to offer yet. There is no storyline besides surviving alone on a cluster of micro islands surrounded by sharks. You start by collecting sticks and stones, build some crude tools, cut down a few palm trees, build a fire pit and a crude hut, while eating coconuts and roasted fish. Then you run out of stones or tools or wood and hop into your life raft, trying to reach another isle alive.After endless minutes of boring rowing a shark appears, topples over your life raft and bites you into pieces. Yes you can fight back, but underwater sharks dominate you and your weapons seem to do not much damage at all, neither spear nor knife or axe. If you get wounded, you bleed. Next time you step into the water to catch some fish, Mister Shark comes for you faster due to that. You haven't found a piece of cloth or ducttape to make crude bandages? You are doomed. You will not die fast, but it takes many days to get your health back to try another journey to an island, in the meantime your island will hold no more trees or stones to make a fire.
Basically survival in such an environment should be harsh and painful. But in games, deadends just are joykillers. Yes, you will have to start over after losing your paddle out on the ocean while being attacked by a Tiger Shark. You can build a raft but you can't use it without the paddle. Tools break after using them several times, always make sure you have enough material at hand to build a new one, otherwise you can just go drown yourself.
The graphics are ok but not the best that can be seen at the moment. Especially objects in the distance are rendered so crude and looking alike, you have not even a tiny chance to judge which island is which. Placing of islands is weird, they all seem to sit in a symmetrical pattern map, rowing towards one doesn't brng it closer to you gradually but in huge steps. Suddenly you are in front of its shore...
Objects and environment like the ground don't iteract well at times. Especially when you drop stuff on other stuff, the physical engine looks weird. Sometimes items float above the ground for no reason.
Environmental events like rain or hot days don't seem to have much impact on you (getting sick? growing thirstier than on humid cooler days?). I wonder if the weather model was meant to be realistic. During July there should be heavy rains and rainstorms, even Tsunamis. It should rain heavily every day for a few hours. I wonder if the devs found this to be too annyoing.
The material balance is off, 1 wood stick makes a small fire that burns for hours, but 8 such sticks make a full raft. It's ptetty abstract. A palm tree gives you 4-12 sticks, before you get them down to sticks you cut the tree into logs, I expected the logs to be the building material for raft and such, but currently they are just for the purpose to further wear down your tools.
I don't know what took 1.5 years of development time here. There is not much landscape to be developed, wildlife is limited to a handful of crabs, small fish, sharks and stingray (I read whale somewhere). Natural phenomena like storm/wind seem to be rare, at land they don't have any impact (I expect some heavy rainstorm to damage my hut or sweep my coconuts into the ocean or the life raft from the beach...nothing like that happened. Ok, I didn't get beyond day 6, but other people played 22 days or longer and already said that nothing changes at all.
So basically, the idea is good, the setting is interesting, graphics ok, controls also work (minor bugs everywhere), but after a few hours of playing you just don't know why you should try to continue. Just to see how long you can make yourself repeat everything over and over again? Islands could be much more diverse, this would make you want explore more. So, I guess, this game needs another years or so of content development and fine tuning. At least there are no zombies. 15€ is still to much fo what you get at the moment.

This game is a true masterpiece. The thing that held the game back was the fact that it started as a XBL game. Which means that they had a 2GB size limit, limited hardware to work with, and a control system more tailored to consoles than PC. The PC version has been given a bit more love by adding higher resolution, better graphics, a full M+KB control scheme, and smaller touches to take advantage of stronger PC hardware.
That doesn't diminish what this game HAS managed to accomplish though. It's incredibly ambitious for a downloadable game, and is executed very well. The survival aspect can get hard at first, and lacks a good tutorial to explain all the systems in play, but once you get past the learning curve the game is incredibly fun. The combat and exploration all makes sense in a zombie apocalypse world. In many instances, it felt like a single player version of Day Z, and it's definitely what War Z WANTS to be but failed.
The game is already not very expensive at full price for what it offers. Definitely pick it up when you can. A sale is just a cherry on top of this very good ice cream. If you're a fan of zombie games, you won't want to miss this.

After all the trials and tribulations and sweat and tears, after waiting patiently and not-so-patienty for five (count them: FIVE) whole years for this game, Hiveswap is finally here! And it's actually pretty damn good!
...ahem. Look, it's hard for me to stay calm and collected about this, okay? But putting aside my fangirl bias for the moment, there's no denying that Hiveswap is a success story. It's a fun and enjoyable adventure game that will delight both long-term fans of the Homestuck webcomic and complete newcomers alike.
My god, they're beautiful. Filled with personality, vibrant colours and a million little fun details, every single backdrop is a joy to behold. I often found myself pausing and simply appreciating the art, trying to take it all in and find any hidden jokes. The character animations were also nice and smooth, with different body language given to each character, and the animated cutscenes looked amazing. All in all a very eye-pleasing experience on all counts.
the music is good. Let me ask you something, have you ever listened to Homestuck music that wasn't awesome? If you don't actually know the answer to this question, it's "No I haven't, all Homestuck music ever created is genius, implying Homestuck music can be bad is a paradox unto itself and a punishable offense." I mean okay, maybe the first couple of tracks are not
memorable, but once you get to the strife battle music it's absolute headbangers all around. (I'm seriously kicking myself for not buying the soundtrack edition, if you're reading this DON'T MAKE MY MISTAKE just go for it.)
Hussie, you magnificent ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, you've done it again. You've struck gold. The game is joke after joke after joke, followed by slightly depressing introspection, then followed again by even more jokes, usually of the black humour variety. And it's all done in Homestuck's inimitable signature style, with the meta narration that's speaking directly to you the player, or maybe it's the character's inner narration, or maybe it's the character acknowledging the narrator? Also, puns. If you've read the comic you know EXACTLY what I'm talking about, and you will feel immediately comforted by the familiarity of it all. If you
read the comic I'm still willing to bet you'll be amused, or at the very least appreciate the unique sense of humour. (and hey if you like the game you can always give homestuck a try
actually you know what nevermind)
Speaking of, I
to mention all those sweet sweet Homestuck references! I was honestly a bit worried about this part, afraid they'd be clumsily shoehorned in just for the sake of fanservice, but nope! They're all subtle and seemingly innocuous, more like a sly wink than an obnoxious honk. The end result is that fans will feel the exciting jolt of recognition that comes from having extra context, while newcomers won't feel alienated and probably won't even notice the reference flying over their heads. (At least until you get to Alternia. Then those who've read the comic will be completely at ease in the familiar environment, and those who haven't will uh.... will be thrust headfirst into a super weird, vaguely disturbing alien world where everyday objects are bug themed and have bizzaro names instead? Have fun with the culture shock!)
As for the storyline, since this is only Act 1 the game understandably spends most of its time introducing the world and setting up the pieces, with the mystery behind the plot creating more questions than answers. However where the game truly shines is in the characters. One of Hussie's greatest strengths as a writer is his ability to create memorable lovable characters, and he's worked his magic once again. All the new kids are cute and endearing (Joey is
and I will love her forever) with their own distinct personalities, and all their interactions with each another are incredibly fun to read. They're definitely worthy additions to the Homestuck pantheon of characters.
When it comes to point-and-click games, Hiveswap is admittedly on the easy side. You will never be stuck with incomprehensible puzzles or need to consult a guide to proceed, and you'll naturally obtain all useful items during normal exploration. You also can't die/fail, so even if you're having trouble with a sequence you can just experiment with your inventory till you get it. And trust me, you really
want to experiment, because all items can interact in all possible combinations and give funny lines. Let me repeat that:
And I'm not talking about lame variations of "I can't do that", I'm talking genuinely funny and long lines, in the writing I praised so much before. I'd honestly argue that reading all these descriptions is the meat of the game, so if you prefer exploration to puzzle-solving in your adventure games this will be right up your alley.
To be fair, the game is also on the short side, though I don't think that's a particular downside. After taking my time and going slowly I finished in about 4 hours, which may not sound like a lot but it actually felt good enough for me. There's a ton of content (unless you rush, and why would you?) to go through, and the overall quality plus the cheapness of the price make it hard to complain.
If you're homestuck trash like me then you already slammed that purchase button the second it appeared. Enough said.
If you're a Homestuck fan who is apprehensive after being burned one too many times, fear not: It's a good game. I mean it's not the second coming of christ or anything so don't get your expectations TOO high, but it's also not some soulless money grab. It's obvious a lot of love and care went into this, and playing it will remind you why you fell in love with the comic in the first place.
And if you've never heard of Homestuck and never plan on ever changing that, you absolutely have a place here as well. This is a charming and funny adventure game that will keep you entertained for an evening or two, and you're bound to enjoy it if you're a fan of the genre.
To sum up, Hiveswap is a fun game that left me very satisfied, and I'm eagerly awaiting its continuation with Act 2.

An excellent story that will leave you thinking and embracing someone you love.
Although some parts of the story seem like they go on a bit longer then needed, these 9+ hours took me on a journey of Earth's final days with a man that was searching for something he didn't know he needed and a girl that saved mankind, locked in a golden cage. I played hours at a time, wanting to see what was next and was not disappointed. With some Visual Novels (VN), it should be pointed out there is no game here, there are no choices and this is purely a voiced graphical story similar to an amine or movie.  The voice actors were decent but were not able to live to full potential due to characteristics of some of the characters, but did as good as that would allow.
The art was well done, but with most VNs there were a lot of re used images at times but nothing detracted from the story. This version is rated for Everyone, but the original is Mature, however I do not feel anything was lost with a few scenes being implied instead of shown.
Overall I am glad I picked this up, if you are new to this style of "game" I would recommend trying the demo (if still available) and maybe waiting for a sale on steam. If you do pick it up, just be sure to maybe have some tissues near by.

It is hard to rate this game, as I did find the game's first 20 - 30 hours amazing - which is more game time than most standard AAA released today.  However, after playing that long you will start realizing some serious flaws in the game...
* All the classes will start to feel the same
* You'll start realizing the limitation of the skills system
* Main quest starts strong, however, gets weaker later on
* Visiting dungeons starts to feel like a hack and slash (every room/hallway filled with red to kill)
-  Hardly any unique loot to find
- This promotes their simplified enchanting/upgrading system (know all recipes, upgrades level capped)
* No experience from killing enemies after logged in bestiary
* The companions have banter and seem fleshed out, but seem to be missing the flair/annoyances to be remembered
* Stronghold could have been better implemented.
-  Also hate that some events could start while traveling and go away before you reach your destination to enable    event
There is more, but I guess I am being a bit nit picky.  Perhaps future installments of PoE will expand/improve, but as a stand alone game for isometric party based RPG, it is far from reaching the BG series/DAO.  Would definitely wait for the game to be 50% off, especially if you're expecting BG series/DAO.

So. I noticed that people are griping about features that were removed in the older versiojns. I never saw that, and while yes, it does kinda seem like techs suck now, but flying sounds a little on the OP side. Mechs sound fun but aren't too practical for exploration.
Now, I've already completed the story and am now playing through with a second character with some items passed down from the first. Exploring is still fun even though Ive seen every planet. I've barely even tried fishing yet. And sometimes the planets can generate very strangely and give an interesting little surprise with biomes, such as bioluminescense biomes generating in volcanic planets (and ember rain always seems to hit right as I find those, heh) and other biome generation that hilariously breaks logic six ways to Sunday.
For a 2D game, some of the landscapes are downright gorgeous. You almost don't want to destroy them, but sometimes you just gotta get the unique tree type there, especially if the foliage generated in your favorite color. You could spend ages collecting them all just for the hell of it. Also geode biomes. What would be amazingly awesome is if they could generate in other colors.
Weapon progression is alright. Challenge rooms are an excellent source of good weapons, and once you start getting legendary goodies you're generally pretty well off. Personally, I've found 3 Ex Machinas on one character... My luck in video games tends to be very stupid. It's either really good or absolutely horrible. As for armor progression, you actually need to do a bit of work to get the best armor. And unless you want the Perfect Set, you need to actualkly make a decision as to how you want to play and get T5 and T6 armor to match.
If you're the creative type, GET THIS GAME. You'd be amazed at what you can do with a 2D space. Whether you're making pixel art or a home for yourself, the possibilities are endless with all the themes out there.
One of my favcorite features is how mod-friendly this game is. Me, I love mods. There's mods for mechs for those who want that back. There's mods that make the game easier or harder. There's ones that add old features and new techs. There's the Phase Shift tech mod for those who want to fly again (and go through walls and be immune to damage as a result of basically becoming a ghost). Mods that change worldgen. New races. More furniture and cosmetic items. Vehicles. Damn near EVERYTHING. Unless you're the type to prefer vanilla, go check out the Workshop for this game.
To end this off, sure, the story and armor progression can be easily rushed by mining planets of a certain tier, crafting the EPP and armor you can now make with those materials and rush the whole story, the game is far from over when the story's done. You can do whatever the hell you want. Look for planets that break logic and see just how broken it can get.  Build the base of your dreams. Pimp out your ship. Catch fish and make an aquarium. Grab critters and make a critter pen. Maybe even try to collect them all and display them. Collect pets. Collect other things. Build massive colonies with furniture looted from dungeons. Get a vehicle and go nuts with it. There's MUCH more to do than gather resources and go through the story.
And hey, it's still better than No Man's Sky!

Summary: Best RPG I've played since Divinity Original Sin, which in turn was the best I've played since the original Dungeon Siege.
Pros:
1) The depth of content offered by this game is fantastic. A rich world providing lots of distractions and things to keep you occupied, and a healthy main quest if you want to simply run through from start to finish.
2) Near perfect character customisation. From your main character to your custom followers the level detail you are able to go into really satisfies my autism. The only change I would make is not having character alignments being bound to the class, so I could choose for example to be an evil or benevolent Gold Pact Paladin. Others may disagree.
3) Great visuals. While people shouldn't really be playing these games for the visuals, having good looking scenery, lighting and spell effects really adds to the overall immersion provided by the game.
4) Companions. A good selection of companions to choose from - minus the ones you can create yourself - each with a back story and companion quests add to the overall, rpg-ness of the game. All of them do however come across rather likable in their own way which is bit of a downside, I would like an unlikable companion that just pisses everyone off to make the party a bit more spicey.
Good but could be improved:
1) Combat. The real time combat in this game is generally very good and with the difficulty turned up can be really challenging, but at times it can also be rather repetitive. When crawling through the ruins of Cad Nua for instance, there are A LOT of encounters and as a result they become rather formulaic, performing the same rotations and when one encounter doesn't go as planned, reload and repeat. This will probably not be an issue for a lot of people but it is something to be mindful of.
2) Interactions. Character and NPC interations are very good and provide a good choice of options. Most of the time. I would like further interactions based on character and party alignment / reputation. People are scared if your evil, children are scared if your a priest, etc.
Cons:
Music. The music in a game like this could really enhance the mood, however I found it rather lacking and repetitive, and at times there was nothing playing at all where it really could have made a difference. A minor criticism but one that really impacts the mood and feel of the game. Imagine watching LoTR without the music.

Disclaimer: This piece was not intended as a review. Therefore it is written with a lot of personal opinions from me as a gamer perspective. This has little to no analysis as me the game designer.
The short version is that I greatly enjoy Pillars of Eternity. It brings some old school game design and emotions back to the industry. There are moments where a critical eye towards modernizing aspects would've been welcome. I would personally enjoy it if games like these would maintain their old format with modern elements. That way this genre can be revitalized and enjoyed for generations to come.
–-------------------------------------------------
I can understand how some might find the pace slow. Thankfully I play a wide range of games going from the past paced Wrack to turn based games and everything in between. Each genre has its own pace to work with and switching between them can be tough as a gamer. It took me a while to get used to the pace of Serious Sam and Wrack, because everything is so damn slow these days to begin with. Even the "fast" shooters are really slow compared to games in the past. I didn't even notice this until re-playing some of them. Not so weird seeing how most "fast paced" games are made with console controllers in mind. Those are just slower to begin with and have invaded PC gaming as well. In that regard I can somewhat understand how some people might have trouble getting used to the slow pace of Pillars of Eternity. Simply because its on the other extreme end of the pacing scale.
So far I've restarted Pillars a total of 3 times. But I always end up going back to the same party build up. You need 2-3 tanks to get by. Especially against larger groups of opponents. In that regard I find that it doesn't really matter what kind of a character you make yourself. You'll have to make one to fit one of the group roles.
The battles won't drastically change all that much. Only the interactions with the world and dialogue options will alter. Even that seems to be limited. I clearly see old DnD dungeonmaster techniques in which you create the illusion of freedom and diversity. Your character might not have 18might to scale that wall. But hey just have Eder do it for you and then drop a rope so you'll still end up on top of the wall. You'll never really have a win-lose situation due to that. Only in places like Raedric's hold you actually have 3 choices on how to enter his hold and deal with the situation. Downside is that if your main char lacks the stat to climb vines you won't be locked out of that route and have to use one of the remaining entry points. You will get the option to have one of your party members to take your place. One hand that is only logical and real since you work as a team. Other hand you won't get any real win/loss situations.
Different dialogue options is more fun. At times you do get some results that are different then another playthrough. Especially since it is also combined with your reputation. As well as the reputation how how you usually respond such as diplomatic, cruel, benevolent etc. Also nice that, just like D&D, there are different DC's (difficulty checks). There are chat options at 13,15,17,20 etc which unlock different responses and interactions. Catacombs under Defiance Bay is the first place where you'll actually notice this aspect most clearly. How you developed your character and gained reputations will matter. Choices you made up to that point will have their impact. Something you don't really see in many games.
Combat is clunky as hell. Even if you enjoy turn based like I do it still is annoying at times. I can understand how many of us, me included, like games that capture that old school feeling. That doesn't mean games like this need to be full with outdated game design philosophy. Some elements would benefit from being modernized while maintaining a critical eye on the how. With all the spells and skills available it is only normal to use pause a lot and have a relatively slow pace. There simply is a lot of depth and choices that need to be made almost constantly. Sure the tanks do nothing but use knockdown combined with a load of passives to engage large groups of opponents and staying alive. But the rest of the group is a lot more work. Especially with cone shaped AoE spells that require some to get into proper positioning in order to work. Strategically this type of combat is fun and challenging. But at times it simply isn't intuitive and smooth...with moments that are downright unresponsive. With large fights the screen gets cluttered with all those little boxes above the character's heads and spell effects and the rings on the ground indicating what's going on. I would've loved if games like this would incorporate a camera that you can rotate just like Grim Dawn has.
Which brings me to the Graphical Aesthetics. As always I love it. Everything blends well together. The first time you temporarily lose camera control for a small "in-game cut scene" conveyed the emotion of nostalgia and familiarity. This looks and feels like those old school cRPG's which most of us love. You see the love for D&D world building and tales of a fantastic story. The art style and how certain elements get portrayed early on in the game immediately set the right tone. It felt as if I had missed it more then ever realized. Almost had to pink away a tear in the corner of my eye. On the other hand it also has a downside in modern times. All art is pre-rendered and has to be fully loaded when entering a new area. Which means A LOT of annoyingly long loading times. Something that would occur less with 3d models that would be rendered by the graphics card when getting near the location. And using 3d models would also let people rotate the camera for a better and clearer overview of crowded battles. Question remains how going to 3d models would effect the aesthetics of the entire game. Would it effect it in such a way that those conveyed emotions would no longer be generated?
Regarding modernizing games like this... Well I don't want them to become fully fleshed 3d open world games. Let them be isometric, top down or whatever. But that doesn't mean some Quality of Life changes can't be made. For example the TAB button is getting worn out drastically. I move a lot in stealth and after every move action I press the TAB to see if there is something hidden. If you have a high enough perception you'll notice things without using this method. When it comes to D&D, especially since 4th Edition, I found passive Perception and active Perception a very pointless mechanics. The same is being used in Pillars of Eternity it seems. It is something that needs to be looked at. Then find a proper solution for this mechanic.
The group stealth issue still annoys me. After your characters reach lvl 3 or 4 they are becoming truly powerful. No more issues of survival, lack of damage or whatever. They feel solid like adventures should. The rogue, combined with the right passives, will cut through opponents like a knife through hot butter. That is awesome and what we'd expect. However the other aspects of a rogue don't work well at all. Placing traps seems rather pointless. Out of the many that I've placed in front of a door that opponents have to run over...only 1 actually activated. Using Stealth to sneak into a room and ambush opponents with a first strike isn't going to happen...EVER! I've been investing in stealth for all members in the group. It has happened how the entire group could stand beside a troll without it noticing us. But using the backstab of the rogue...still not happening. Something is seriously flawed here. The rogue needs to be able and use stealth on its own for the combat aspect. Outside of combat you simply select the rogue and move it on its own away from the group. Such as scouting ahead and removing traps for example.

Okay, I love this game. I've, across the entire series, hundreds of hours. I even enjoy the pvp even when I lose most of my battles; they are always exciting. What I love about dark souls is a marriage of two things: combat and atmosphere. The combat in this game is quite similar to the previous entries. Mind you, I value PVE over PVP for this series.
If I want to fight players I'm the sort who goes to mobas or FPS (though For Honor looks promising as Dark Souls moba). You will probably have read that the unique feature in this is adding weapon arts to the mix which makes fights very dynamic, fluid, and grants many combat styles despite there being a prevailing R1/parry meta (but if you play pvp, meta will always determine how well you will do, whether you choose to join the currently favored style or not). The biggest problem with pvp is that the invader is too gimped to compete. Invasions are plainly a♥♥♥♥♥♥move, but should the invader have to contend with 3 total opponents? Perhaps they should have gone the older route in disabling certain healing options.
Apart from pvp, the bosses are generally thrilling. Some are easier than others and to the point that they are somewhat disappointingly simple  like rolling invincibly by Vordt or cleaving the hell out of the Deacons, but may the lore make up for these flaws. There are cinematic fights that are also challenging such as the Abyss Watchers and truly tough and frustrating fights like the Nameless King (not to brag, I beat him at the third try, but a brand new character, I somehow died repeatedly... repeatedly 10+ until I decided to summon). Overall, I think Dark Souls 1 has the best bosses, but this one has a bit more challenge than DS2 sans DLC.
I will end this short review with the lore. I fell in love with the lore with this game. It took long enough, huh? I played every game, except for Bloodborne, and somehow it was DS3 that broke me in. I love the lore and how we can learn a story by the items and aesthetic. I did learn a few things here and there in the series’ previous installments, just the gist. This one had stronger references to the first game, so I began to form ideas of my own and wondered about ideas of others due Miyazaki’s way of telling a story according to scenery, item descriptions, and placement of NPCs and their appearance. It’s just so rich. It’s a game series like this that makes for an engaging, interpretative storytelling. I actually was very disappointed that Miyazaki stated that he was finished with the Souls series because his mind provided me with such an immersible experience.
By the way, the graphics are so damn good. I love that there are individually unique stones arranged here and there. I read some reddit post that explained it perfect. DS1 has the best bosses, DS2 has the best DLC, and DS3 has the best graphics… or something like that.

I like this game. I love the concepts, I love the environment, it does not love me though. Good, I like a challenge.
For an early access I admire the dev team dedication to this, I support it wholeheartedly, if they can pull this together then it's a wonderfully engaging game.
When you first get in then the early access aspects of it are obvious, the creatures do wierd things when trying to kill you, the wild boar will do a growl and then fire off three rapid jumps down the road. Wolves will growl at you and pounce on where you are standing, if you move anytime between the wolf getting ready to attack and the 30 second warm up routine before it does then you are treated to watching it jump into empty space, at which point you smack it (if you haven't figured that out then you were eaten by your first wolf).
You will freeze to death the first time you are in there
You will freeze to death again
You will starve and freeze to death
You will begin to know what you are doing
You will know why you froze to death, you are learning, freezing, and learning.
You will figure out the crafting system and make some stone tools
You will freeze to death again.
So after much of this, you eventually build a place and start getting armour together.
You will go adventuring
You will find Kruul and you will take him on with the stone axe you made.
You will die
You will try and retrieve your stuff, Lord Kruul will kill you
At this point you begin to understand that you need to think about what you are doing and why. You need to plan your moves, or you will die.
You will build stuff and become stronger. You will venture forth with confidence, you will die again. I love it.
The game has its bugs, but I'm confident that the dev team are comitted to this. I do recommend it, certainly if you like to see something being made and anticipating how the next version is going to take it, it's an adventure in its own self.

Visuals:
======
I like the visuals. The world and items look nice, everything has a matching style. Even without anti-aliasing it looks really good.
Gameplay:
========
The controls are nice, everything works as intended. Controller support is very good, didn't play it with mouse and keyboard though.
Characters:
========
I think my main problem with the game is, that I can't identify with the character. In most games you have a moment of desperation, something that sparks even a little fire of emotions in me, the death of an NPC, who was valued by the playable character, something that makes me either love the playable character or hate the NPCs.
In this game there is nothing like it. There is no background on the playable character before you wander off into the unknown, there is no information on the enemies. They are just something that attack you for no apparent reason. Other than "oh, they are probably the enemies, I should fight them because they want to kill me for no reason", there is nothing that makes me want to fight them.
Difficulty:
=======
I don't like the difficulty. I tried the "normal" mode, wich was kind of hard. The general difficulty of this game is hard, I'd say. Then you have the "no-sweat mode", a mode that still lets you die, but not for good. You press a button and rejoin the current fight without losing anything. In that mode the game is more of a story, than a game, since you just have to mash the attack buttons and can revive yourself after a death again and again.
Problem is: I want a game, not a story. Paired with the unlikeable characters a too high or too low difficulty makes me not want to play the game anymore.
Which is why I stopped.
Conclusion:
========
Not for me. I need to emotionally connect to the playable character, either because of cuteness, coolness, sadness, happyness, you name it. I can't connect to "the Kid" at all.

The gameplay is one of a classical 2D isometric hack and slash, with different weapons and skills to use. What makes the game stands out is its gritty, enthralling narrative and the vibrant music.
The soundtrack and sound effects react to the player's moves and actions, and as the player progresses the narrator tells more of the story. The downside is that one can miss some explanations while the player is focused on battling monsters and surviving an ambush but this is a minor detail.
Thanks to the narrator, the game has a "film noir" feel to it, although the story is not told from the main character point of view, and the atmosphere is peculiar as the game takes place after an end of the world event called "the Calamity", lending it a sense of loss and melancholy blended with a wild west tone, served by a superb musical score and two beautiful songs.
The story may not be without plot holes, the gameplay may be pretty simple (there is even a no-sweat mode for people who want to take it easy) but you can pick this game up just for the narration and its soundtrack.

People say this game is basically a mash-up of the Batman Arkham and Assassin’s Creed series, and from what I can tell (having never played Assassin’s Creed) this is an accurate description. So if you like either of those games, you will most likely enjoy this.

The intriguing Nemesis System turns the orc armies into an evolving hierarchy, with battle-hardened enemies you may have defeated several times before becoming an entertaining challenge to take down.

Even now, long after release, this is a solid game to go back to for some entertainment.

Now, when I first caught eye of this game I couldn't help but sighing and thinking to myself: "Not another zombie-game". Don't get me wrong, I love zombies and the zombie apocalypse concept. There has just been so many zombie games as of late that the idea of yet another had dried up for me. But this game really got me hooked. The survivors you play and manage become a sort of investment as you level them up, as they can easily get killed even if they're far down the skilltree you've been working on for the specific survivor.
A downside is that the random missions are essentially repetitive, aside from the main story missions, they can and due to the survival aspects of the game, will grow tiresome.
Which brings me to the main story line. It's nothing new in the story being told, which I don't really have a problem with. Seeing as the only option imaginable, during a zombie apocalypse, would be to adapt, overcome and survive. The only problem with it, is that some of the missions has a time window, and if you miss that, the mission are gone forever unless you restart. So make sure you keep track of your time, in case you await sunrise, or want to complete some other missions first. Although the game really peaks my interest by being so open, the main protagonist can actually die, or you can complete the game without playing with him at all. There's a vast open world for you to explore, and seeing how you constantly have to work for finding food and other resources, it keeps you pushing forward into it.

So uhm, State of Decay. Bit of a funny story regarding this. From what I understand, it started out as an Xbox Live Arcade game , and a very well done one at that.
I bought this during the Early Access phase, but I can safely say I'm satisfied with the purchase. It has a rather appopriate pricetag of €19, and it fits the content. You won't find yourself spending a hundred hours with it, but you may return to it a few times.
State of Decay is a zombie open world sandbox game. There's really no other way to describe it. There's no protagonist, no overarching plot of "stopping the big bad". It's all just surviving. If the character you play dies, you take control of another one. Over time, your group of survivors and the compound/safehouse can grow or shrink, depending on how reckless you are.
The world itself is fairly big and allows for a good deal of free roaming. There are cities, open fields, rocky mountains, and pretty much all houses and buildings can be entered. I suppose you could call it the open world game to accompany the Walking Dead.

There's no food, there's very little money around, hordes can pop up all over the place, and there is climate change that forces you to move south to be able to feed anyone at all.
Where in Rome 2, other factions sort of waited around for you to attack, in Atilla, you're constantly worried about what's on parts of the map you can't see: because horrifying things are happeing out there for sure.
I've been impressed with the AI in this as well, though this has the Arcade-style combat that they've had since Shogun 2.

Oh, Mass Effect. 9 years or so after the XBox 360 release, and I'm still playing this. My entire family knows the theme music, the order in which I visit planets, and the companions that I prefer.
I only just downloaded the PC version, and my experience with ME is even better. No longer do I have texture pop-in that lasts for 5 seconds or more. No longer do I have ridiculous load times when entering and exiting the Normandy. No longer do I feel like I'm controlling a drunk rhino when I'm planetside in the Mako (although this is a minor improvement, at best.)
To give a quick synopsis of the plot: a surprise attack on a small colony reveals a galaxy-wide threat, which ONLY YOU and your motley crew of diverse personalities and skin tones can counter.
A quick overview of features:
STORY - Incredible. Still one of the best, if not THE BEST, stories that I have encountered in a video game. Interactions between your hero, your companions and crew, and the large cast of supporting characters are interesting and feel like they matter. There are all the elements of a good story: beginning, rising action, climax, falling action, satisfying conclusion, twists and turns, and emotionally gripping moments that will have you biting your lip and agonizing over the choice you have to make.
Oh yes. THERE IS CHOICE. The choices range from minor decisions that only impact your immediate mission, to game-changing choices that affect you to the very end (as well as in later games.) If this was a linear story, it would be good. Add in a moral system, and it becomes epic.
CHARACTERS - I love these people. Not only has Bioware created some really diverse and believable alien races, but their motivations and interactions feel real. Granted, there's a fair bit of stereotyping: the militant aliens, the sneaky aliens, the wise and peaceful aliens... but, there are also some aliens that manage to break the mold. The humans are also recognizable as the kind of people that you would meet in your life: as a military vet, I laughed out loud at some of Ashley's lines, and Kaidan uses appropriate military jargon several times.
VOICE ACTING - Pretty good. I find male Shepherd's performance to be one of the weaker ones, but he's still great. Tali can grate on you after a while, and waiting on the Elcor voice actors to finish their lines is a bit tiresome. HOWEVER, these are all really minor complaints when you consider the overall quality of the voice work.
GAMEPLAY - It was really fantastic when it released, even though it has visibly aged with the release of the rest of the trilogy. Controls on your ground vehicle are the stuff of nightmares, and thresher maws will have you fleeing in terror. Your companion AI can go from really awesome to facepalmingly bad in a single battle. If you're not in it for the story, the gameplay can be a little off-putting - it's not the best 3rd person shooter on the market. However, it's good enough to keep you moving forward as you wait for the next story moment.
The difficulty is adjustable, and there's a pretty smooth learning curve. Probably the area that I find most frustrating is the inventory. Holy crap, you pick up so many useless items, the armor upgrades are sporadic at best, and you'll be at your money cap about 3/4 through the game if you sell everything that's unneeded. The modification system is messy, and I find myself randomly equipping mods on my companions more often than not.
The "main missions" are really, really fantastic and varied. The side missions are less exciting, and the uncharted planets are straight-up boring. But, they're all strictly optional, as there's no level limitations on your main missions.
TL;DR - Buy this game immediately. Not only does this game stand up well on its own, it is an entry point into an amazing series. Even though you can do the Genesis thing to make the choices for 2 and 3, it pays to play this game first to experience the story in its fullness.

After all the trials and tribulations and sweat and tears, after waiting patiently and not-so-patienty for five (count them: FIVE) whole years for this game, Hiveswap is finally here! And it's actually pretty damn good!
...ahem. Look, it's hard for me to stay calm and collected about this, okay? But putting aside my fangirl bias for the moment, there's no denying that Hiveswap is a success story. It's a fun and enjoyable adventure game that will delight both long-term fans of the Homestuck webcomic and complete newcomers alike.
My god, they're beautiful. Filled with personality, vibrant colours and a million little fun details, every single backdrop is a joy to behold. I often found myself pausing and simply appreciating the art, trying to take it all in and find any hidden jokes. The character animations were also nice and smooth, with different body language given to each character, and the animated cutscenes looked amazing. All in all a very eye-pleasing experience on all counts.
the music is good. Let me ask you something, have you ever listened to Homestuck music that wasn't awesome? If you don't actually know the answer to this question, it's "No I haven't, all Homestuck music ever created is genius, implying Homestuck music can be bad is a paradox unto itself and a punishable offense." I mean okay, maybe the first couple of tracks are not
memorable, but once you get to the strife battle music it's absolute headbangers all around. (I'm seriously kicking myself for not buying the soundtrack edition, if you're reading this DON'T MAKE MY MISTAKE just go for it.)
Hussie, you magnificent ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, you've done it again. You've struck gold. The game is joke after joke after joke, followed by slightly depressing introspection, then followed again by even more jokes, usually of the black humour variety. And it's all done in Homestuck's inimitable signature style, with the meta narration that's speaking directly to you the player, or maybe it's the character's inner narration, or maybe it's the character acknowledging the narrator? Also, puns. If you've read the comic you know EXACTLY what I'm talking about, and you will feel immediately comforted by the familiarity of it all. If you
read the comic I'm still willing to bet you'll be amused, or at the very least appreciate the unique sense of humour. (and hey if you like the game you can always give homestuck a try
actually you know what nevermind)
Speaking of, I
to mention all those sweet sweet Homestuck references! I was honestly a bit worried about this part, afraid they'd be clumsily shoehorned in just for the sake of fanservice, but nope! They're all subtle and seemingly innocuous, more like a sly wink than an obnoxious honk. The end result is that fans will feel the exciting jolt of recognition that comes from having extra context, while newcomers won't feel alienated and probably won't even notice the reference flying over their heads. (At least until you get to Alternia. Then those who've read the comic will be completely at ease in the familiar environment, and those who haven't will uh.... will be thrust headfirst into a super weird, vaguely disturbing alien world where everyday objects are bug themed and have bizzaro names instead? Have fun with the culture shock!)
As for the storyline, since this is only Act 1 the game understandably spends most of its time introducing the world and setting up the pieces, with the mystery behind the plot creating more questions than answers. However where the game truly shines is in the characters. One of Hussie's greatest strengths as a writer is his ability to create memorable lovable characters, and he's worked his magic once again. All the new kids are cute and endearing (Joey is
and I will love her forever) with their own distinct personalities, and all their interactions with each another are incredibly fun to read. They're definitely worthy additions to the Homestuck pantheon of characters.
When it comes to point-and-click games, Hiveswap is admittedly on the easy side. You will never be stuck with incomprehensible puzzles or need to consult a guide to proceed, and you'll naturally obtain all useful items during normal exploration. You also can't die/fail, so even if you're having trouble with a sequence you can just experiment with your inventory till you get it. And trust me, you really
want to experiment, because all items can interact in all possible combinations and give funny lines. Let me repeat that:
And I'm not talking about lame variations of "I can't do that", I'm talking genuinely funny and long lines, in the writing I praised so much before. I'd honestly argue that reading all these descriptions is the meat of the game, so if you prefer exploration to puzzle-solving in your adventure games this will be right up your alley.
To be fair, the game is also on the short side, though I don't think that's a particular downside. After taking my time and going slowly I finished in about 4 hours, which may not sound like a lot but it actually felt good enough for me. There's a ton of content (unless you rush, and why would you?) to go through, and the overall quality plus the cheapness of the price make it hard to complain.
If you're homestuck trash like me then you already slammed that purchase button the second it appeared. Enough said.
If you're a Homestuck fan who is apprehensive after being burned one too many times, fear not: It's a good game. I mean it's not the second coming of christ or anything so don't get your expectations TOO high, but it's also not some soulless money grab. It's obvious a lot of love and care went into this, and playing it will remind you why you fell in love with the comic in the first place.
And if you've never heard of Homestuck and never plan on ever changing that, you absolutely have a place here as well. This is a charming and funny adventure game that will keep you entertained for an evening or two, and you're bound to enjoy it if you're a fan of the genre.
To sum up, Hiveswap is a fun game that left me very satisfied, and I'm eagerly awaiting its continuation with Act 2.

I bought Dragon's Dogma: Dark Arisen on PS3 even though I don't own a PS3 because I had heard it had fights similar to Shadow of the Colossus which is one of my all time favourite games.  I had to borrow a PS3 from a friend of mine and he didn't get it back until this was released for steam.
I really like this game and I recommend it to anybody that likes serious fantasy RPGs.  The atmosphere of this game took me back to my days of playing the Ultima series on my Atari computer and to playing Dragon Warrior (now Dragon Quest) on my NES which I don't feel many games do anymore.  My favourite thing being that monsters don't scale to your level so you will walk over the early creatures when you come back as a seasoned warrior, but if you go somewhere you shouldn't be, you will die.  I absolutely hate scaling in games because it feels like I'm not progressing anywhere since every fight is the same and every fight feels drawn out.  As far as fighting being like Shadow of the Colossus, I don't really agree since those fights required climbing and you didn't really have stats.  You can climb in Dragon's Dogma but it is nowhere near as good nor required.
The pawn system is fine, they're just like party members in any other game except you don't control them and they don't do what you want.  They are fun to make though and it is fun to rent other people pawns just to see what they like in a companion.
This game definitely has a lot of play value.  The main quest is a good 50 hours the first time if you're not rushing and the Dark Arisen content is another good 20 hours.  You can also do new game plus and play through the game again with your experienced characters and all items brought over.  Chances are you missed some quests on the first playthrough so it's nice to be able to experience them without having to start over from scratch.
Oh, I should also mention that the port works perfectly on my PC and I actually enjoy it a lot more than playing on the PS3 thanks to the higher resolution and smooth frame rate.

Summary: Best RPG I've played since Divinity Original Sin, which in turn was the best I've played since the original Dungeon Siege.
Pros:
1) The depth of content offered by this game is fantastic. A rich world providing lots of distractions and things to keep you occupied, and a healthy main quest if you want to simply run through from start to finish.
2) Near perfect character customisation. From your main character to your custom followers the level detail you are able to go into really satisfies my autism. The only change I would make is not having character alignments being bound to the class, so I could choose for example to be an evil or benevolent Gold Pact Paladin. Others may disagree.
3) Great visuals. While people shouldn't really be playing these games for the visuals, having good looking scenery, lighting and spell effects really adds to the overall immersion provided by the game.
4) Companions. A good selection of companions to choose from - minus the ones you can create yourself - each with a back story and companion quests add to the overall, rpg-ness of the game. All of them do however come across rather likable in their own way which is bit of a downside, I would like an unlikable companion that just pisses everyone off to make the party a bit more spicey.
Good but could be improved:
1) Combat. The real time combat in this game is generally very good and with the difficulty turned up can be really challenging, but at times it can also be rather repetitive. When crawling through the ruins of Cad Nua for instance, there are A LOT of encounters and as a result they become rather formulaic, performing the same rotations and when one encounter doesn't go as planned, reload and repeat. This will probably not be an issue for a lot of people but it is something to be mindful of.
2) Interactions. Character and NPC interations are very good and provide a good choice of options. Most of the time. I would like further interactions based on character and party alignment / reputation. People are scared if your evil, children are scared if your a priest, etc.
Cons:
Music. The music in a game like this could really enhance the mood, however I found it rather lacking and repetitive, and at times there was nothing playing at all where it really could have made a difference. A minor criticism but one that really impacts the mood and feel of the game. Imagine watching LoTR without the music.

Disclaimer: This piece was not intended as a review. Therefore it is written with a lot of personal opinions from me as a gamer perspective. This has little to no analysis as me the game designer.
The short version is that I greatly enjoy Pillars of Eternity. It brings some old school game design and emotions back to the industry. There are moments where a critical eye towards modernizing aspects would've been welcome. I would personally enjoy it if games like these would maintain their old format with modern elements. That way this genre can be revitalized and enjoyed for generations to come.
–-------------------------------------------------
I can understand how some might find the pace slow. Thankfully I play a wide range of games going from the past paced Wrack to turn based games and everything in between. Each genre has its own pace to work with and switching between them can be tough as a gamer. It took me a while to get used to the pace of Serious Sam and Wrack, because everything is so damn slow these days to begin with. Even the "fast" shooters are really slow compared to games in the past. I didn't even notice this until re-playing some of them. Not so weird seeing how most "fast paced" games are made with console controllers in mind. Those are just slower to begin with and have invaded PC gaming as well. In that regard I can somewhat understand how some people might have trouble getting used to the slow pace of Pillars of Eternity. Simply because its on the other extreme end of the pacing scale.
So far I've restarted Pillars a total of 3 times. But I always end up going back to the same party build up. You need 2-3 tanks to get by. Especially against larger groups of opponents. In that regard I find that it doesn't really matter what kind of a character you make yourself. You'll have to make one to fit one of the group roles.
The battles won't drastically change all that much. Only the interactions with the world and dialogue options will alter. Even that seems to be limited. I clearly see old DnD dungeonmaster techniques in which you create the illusion of freedom and diversity. Your character might not have 18might to scale that wall. But hey just have Eder do it for you and then drop a rope so you'll still end up on top of the wall. You'll never really have a win-lose situation due to that. Only in places like Raedric's hold you actually have 3 choices on how to enter his hold and deal with the situation. Downside is that if your main char lacks the stat to climb vines you won't be locked out of that route and have to use one of the remaining entry points. You will get the option to have one of your party members to take your place. One hand that is only logical and real since you work as a team. Other hand you won't get any real win/loss situations.
Different dialogue options is more fun. At times you do get some results that are different then another playthrough. Especially since it is also combined with your reputation. As well as the reputation how how you usually respond such as diplomatic, cruel, benevolent etc. Also nice that, just like D&D, there are different DC's (difficulty checks). There are chat options at 13,15,17,20 etc which unlock different responses and interactions. Catacombs under Defiance Bay is the first place where you'll actually notice this aspect most clearly. How you developed your character and gained reputations will matter. Choices you made up to that point will have their impact. Something you don't really see in many games.
Combat is clunky as hell. Even if you enjoy turn based like I do it still is annoying at times. I can understand how many of us, me included, like games that capture that old school feeling. That doesn't mean games like this need to be full with outdated game design philosophy. Some elements would benefit from being modernized while maintaining a critical eye on the how. With all the spells and skills available it is only normal to use pause a lot and have a relatively slow pace. There simply is a lot of depth and choices that need to be made almost constantly. Sure the tanks do nothing but use knockdown combined with a load of passives to engage large groups of opponents and staying alive. But the rest of the group is a lot more work. Especially with cone shaped AoE spells that require some to get into proper positioning in order to work. Strategically this type of combat is fun and challenging. But at times it simply isn't intuitive and smooth...with moments that are downright unresponsive. With large fights the screen gets cluttered with all those little boxes above the character's heads and spell effects and the rings on the ground indicating what's going on. I would've loved if games like this would incorporate a camera that you can rotate just like Grim Dawn has.
Which brings me to the Graphical Aesthetics. As always I love it. Everything blends well together. The first time you temporarily lose camera control for a small "in-game cut scene" conveyed the emotion of nostalgia and familiarity. This looks and feels like those old school cRPG's which most of us love. You see the love for D&D world building and tales of a fantastic story. The art style and how certain elements get portrayed early on in the game immediately set the right tone. It felt as if I had missed it more then ever realized. Almost had to pink away a tear in the corner of my eye. On the other hand it also has a downside in modern times. All art is pre-rendered and has to be fully loaded when entering a new area. Which means A LOT of annoyingly long loading times. Something that would occur less with 3d models that would be rendered by the graphics card when getting near the location. And using 3d models would also let people rotate the camera for a better and clearer overview of crowded battles. Question remains how going to 3d models would effect the aesthetics of the entire game. Would it effect it in such a way that those conveyed emotions would no longer be generated?
Regarding modernizing games like this... Well I don't want them to become fully fleshed 3d open world games. Let them be isometric, top down or whatever. But that doesn't mean some Quality of Life changes can't be made. For example the TAB button is getting worn out drastically. I move a lot in stealth and after every move action I press the TAB to see if there is something hidden. If you have a high enough perception you'll notice things without using this method. When it comes to D&D, especially since 4th Edition, I found passive Perception and active Perception a very pointless mechanics. The same is being used in Pillars of Eternity it seems. It is something that needs to be looked at. Then find a proper solution for this mechanic.
The group stealth issue still annoys me. After your characters reach lvl 3 or 4 they are becoming truly powerful. No more issues of survival, lack of damage or whatever. They feel solid like adventures should. The rogue, combined with the right passives, will cut through opponents like a knife through hot butter. That is awesome and what we'd expect. However the other aspects of a rogue don't work well at all. Placing traps seems rather pointless. Out of the many that I've placed in front of a door that opponents have to run over...only 1 actually activated. Using Stealth to sneak into a room and ambush opponents with a first strike isn't going to happen...EVER! I've been investing in stealth for all members in the group. It has happened how the entire group could stand beside a troll without it noticing us. But using the backstab of the rogue...still not happening. Something is seriously flawed here. The rogue needs to be able and use stealth on its own for the combat aspect. Outside of combat you simply select the rogue and move it on its own away from the group. Such as scouting ahead and removing traps for example.

Pillars of Eternity is a well-written and strongly executed spiritual successor to Baldur's Gate II. No RPG in the last decade can hold a candle to its immersive role-playing experience or engrossing, highly believable world. This modernized take on the classic CRPG is a must-buy for any fan of the genre.
Below I will list a few points from the perspective of a veteran gamer who values immersion in his RPGs above all else, and will attempt to measure it against one of the greatest RPGs of all time.
Pillars is much easier to play than the
trilogy, doing away with several annoyances Infinity Engine veterans won’t miss:
++ Flawless path-finding
++ Sexy as ♥♥♥♥
++ Excellent UI design
++ Level design plus “fast mode” saves a ton of time
++ Tutorial, though heavy, is very informative
+ Tooltips!
+ New stash system for painless inventory management
+ Flags for stat-qualifying conversation options
+ Quest notifiers
+ …and much more!
++ Options to turn off most of the above if you feel it interferes with your role-playing
++ Does all of this while retaining the feel of classic CRPGs (major nostalgia bonus)
At the systems level, Pillars biggest departure from classic CRPGs lies in its new attribute and skills system. To me this has been a mixed bag:
+++ Every attribute and skill has a place in conversations and scripted sequences
++ A ton of options for each class, much more customization than classic CRPGs
++ Updated reputation system is excellent and works as intended
++ Very challenging early game– hallmark of the classic RPG
++ Every attribute influences combat, no dead-weight attributes
+ Skill system allows more freedom for customization
+ Mastering new attributes is a fresh challenge for RPG vets
+ Can build custom NPC adventurers whenever you want
- - - Classes are not nearly as unique as in classic CRPGs
- - No multi-class / dual-class, classes all have same XP chart for leveling
- - Leveling up doesn’t have the occasional power spike that was so satisfying in BG
- - No alignments! This affects companions most, more on that below
So to sum up there is a big tradeoff here: much deeper customization at the cost of much weaker character identity / personality on each character sheet. Is this modernization worth it? Depends on the player.
In general, combat in Pillars is much more enjoyable, though
still does some things better:
+++ More combat, challenging combat –closer to
than
+++ Limited resting plus “per rest” and “per encounter”  system rounds out encounters!
++ Melee engagement completes the positional party-based combat feature-set
++ New damage-type and defense-type systems are excellently executed
+ New friend/foe AoE mechanics add a bit more depth
+ Modernized combat UI with AoE overlays decrease yolo-ness of spell-casting
+ Item enchanting adds customization to combat style
+/- In general, more abilities and options, less impact of each individual ability
- - - Spells and abilities feel nerfed compared to classic CRPGs
- - Not as many crazy encounters as in BG.
- - Challenge is more in mastering the system than in new encounters.
- AoEs everywhere, not enough single-target spells
First off: good effort by the new narrator, but not even close to the narrator of Baldur’s Gate!
Obsidian’s writing may be its greatest strength as a studio, and I would say that several of their sequel projects exceeded the writing quality of the original (
,
,
).
In my opinion:
+++ Better high-level concept, deals with religion, philosophy and identity better
++ Original world, characters, etc. are extremely fleshed out
+ Main player arc is basically same story as BG, but written better
- - - BG still tells the small stories better, with more detail and broader range of outcome
- - Writing feels rushed sometimes
The companions, though, are where Pillars loses clearly to
:
- - - - - - - - - - Nothing close to a Minsc :(
- - - Less personality range of companions. Companions are not differentiated strongly
- - - Weaker classes and no alignments means companion identity and opinions are not as convincing
- - Companions rarely interact directly with other NPCs and events. When they do, feels forced.
- Less companions
Aside from my
(shared by many), Pillars has significant weaknesses in its systems-level representation of characters, and therefore clearly falls short of
in storytelling.
The obvious complaint here is that
is bigger, takes the player to more places, and exposes the player to a wider variety of characters and factions. No comparison can be made until Obsidian is done with the Pillars franchise– which hopefully will not be anytime soon.
However, in many cases, Pillars is
and
, leading to some significant drawbacks:
- - - In BG, you can walk into a random house and start a huge quest, not the case here
- - - Very few chances to permanently gain (or lose) stats
- - - Related to above: less consequences for decisions and therefore less interesting choices
- - - Conversation and NPC interaction in general is not as varied as in Baldur’s Gate
- - Only one stronghold type, less replayability with different classes / characters
- - In general, items feel less unique– especially when compared to Baldur’s Gate
- Curve of item acquisition is more linear, so no dramatic item-based power spikes
- Effect suppression system is healthy for game systems but disappointing for player
Pillars is not
, and was not designed to be, but its choices above make it modern at the expense of the “anything can happen” feel of
. As a role-playing game, the balance feels more like a smooth and guided experience– cleverly giving you the trappings of choice and freedom, while remaining very accessible.
The result is a game with strengths that most players will experience, but lacking in the varied details and unbalance that made
so special. I would submit that those small details: silly side-quests, ridiculously unfair interactions, huge amounts of content almost completely hidden, etc. They are the quintessence of the open-world RPG experience.
There have been many advances to systems design since BG2, and Pillars exploits them to its full advantage. However, in many cases it does so at the expense of immersion. In the end, Obsidian has made conscious choices to make an experience that carries the torch of classic CRPGs in a new, accessible package. As they have said, Pillars does not replace the Infinity Engine games.
Pillars of Eternity is a great RPG, and the best RPG of the last decade. With updates, expansions and sequels it may become the greatest of all time.
But for now, and in my humble opinion,
retains its seat as the king of CRPGs.

Phew, where to begin with this game. A lot about it is so amazing that I hardly know where to start.
So, let's start with first impressions. The trailers are very good at giving you a feel for the atmosphere of the entire game. The positively manly narrating voice is present throughout the game and tells you the entire story as you uncover locations and enemies. Don't confuse it for exposition because it's really interesting as a story mechanic.
Ininitally I needed to get the hang of the controls and gameplay. This topdown beat-em-up style game is something I rarely play but this game definitely nailed it. I went from "Never did this before" to "Mastered every individual weapon's challenge" before the end of it. The challenges are also a really cool way to learn the weapons and earn upgrades for those weapons. The ability to also challenge yourself by activating "Idols" is also amazing. They give you the option to earn more currency but make enemies harder, or give more exp but makes certain enemies tougher to beat. Amazing if you like a challenge and want some added replay value.
I won't spoil any of the storyline but if you get invested in it, it can definitely jerk a tear by the end. Something that's even more the case because of the amazing soundtrack that plays beautifully into this.
All things considered this is one of the few games that I would still buy even if it was priced higher.

State of Decay is a single player zombie survival game where you must scavenge supplies, set up outposts, help people out, but most of all: Survive.
While the zombie scene has been beaten like a dead horse, (undead horse maybe? Ba-dum-tss,) this game is actually not half bad.
Let's start with the graphics, here. While the graphics aren't anything to write home about, there definitely are uglier games out there. However, I've never been one to care much for graphics. Graphics are not the core of a game, nor do they, or should, rather, effect the enjoyment received from playing. That role is in the gameplay department.
Gameplay is pretty good. This game doesn't try to be a horror game, yet I have freaked out more times than I care to admit when I'm scavenging around for medicine, ammo, or weapons and a zombie horde hears the glass I just accidentally broke and starts sprinting towards me, and I have nowhere to run. Now I must rely on my half-broken bat and a revolver with only 11 bullets to spare.
For any zombie fan, this is a hidden gem. I highly recommend this game for anyone who likes zombies and fresh ideas.

TL;DR - Brilliant storyline, immersive galaxy and worlds to visit. The characters and chemistry between you and character you meet are one of the things that makes Mass Effect so great. A truly brilliant RPG for those who love Science Fiction and action games.
As you can tell by the amount of time I've spent playing this game, I've done quite a few playthroughs (I've lost count of how many times I've played Mass Effect, but it's an abnormally large number). Bioware really has a knack of combining a great storyline and character development together with gameplay and customisation. Of course, this was before EA really got them by the balls and milked their franchise dry.
- The story (as mentioned many times above) could not be any better;
The different plot points blend together perfectly; the introduction of Saren Arterius, the Geth, the Citadel and your Spectre ranking, it all just comes and goes so well. The interaction with characters and potential romance options really puts the player in the game and the experiences really stick with you.
- The lore/canon behind the different points of the game and the background to the game is brilliant; I've spent many hours external of the game reading up on the Mass Effect Wikia page about different planets, key events (like the discovery of the Mass Relay near Pluto) and the technology seen within the game. Players can learn everything and more about the Mass Effect universe without even leaving the game, the codex contains lots and lots of sub-sections pointing to various information about the universe, with the player being able to add more and more accessible canon stories to the codex by interacting with certain items or buildings in game.
- Character customisation is really in-depth and customisable; right off the bat, you are given the choice to edit your character's name, appearance, classification and background story. The appearance customisation options are alright, it's pretty default across a lot of RPG games. The class system is great also, with different classes offering the player different weapon choices, in-game powers and abilities. By selecting a character's background story, it really allows you to set up your characters morals for whatever way you wish to play;
, you have those choices in Mass Effect.
- In-game levelling up and point assignment to you and your squadmates works very well; you have lots of options to add points to specific abilites that will become more accurate, powerful or varied with you and your team in combat and in dialogue. You can also access all your squad's character profiles on the Normandy and customise each one individually, as well as assign different squadmates to you with different missions.
- The variety of weapons and mods available is huge to say the least; you can modify any weapon to have different effects on enemies, have a fast fire rate or more accuracy to name a few, as well as purchase or loot newer, more powerful weapons and equip them to you and your squadmates. The same is said for armor and omni-tools, which too can be upgraded by newer items.
- Off the bat I'm going to appeal to any of you graphic predators; this game is not high-end, cutting edge in the graphics department, it's pretty meh for a game that came out in 2007, compare to the likes of Assassin's Creed or Crysis that came out the same year. But available mods can greatly improve in-game textures and such if it really bothers you.
- In-game, the mechanics of combat and everything combat-related is not really that great; the whole cover system, FOV and freeze screen selection is alright, but the newer Mass Effect 2 and 3 definitely improve on this game's mechanics.
- The exploration options in the game are pretty linear, but definitely better than Mass Effect 2 and 3. Every world just kind of looks the same but in different colours or with a few different bases re-arranged. The mako is also a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to command around when exploring, getting stuck on mountain sides or in ditches and causing a lot of awkward situations.
this game and it's counter-parts are my pride and joy of video games. The game overall is so well made and the elements of it just work together fantastically, and for
(or wait until the Steam sales, where I've seen it sell for £1.99 many times).
I highly recommend you invest in this game if you like RPGs, Science Fiction or want to play a game you'll get lost in over and over again, for hours on end.
