Just finished the game at 51% completion after 34 hours. It should be possible to finish the main story alone under 30 hours, but I enjoyed taking some time off to add progress towards the side-quests. I still ended my run with a shoddy percentage of completion though, the reason being that this game is on my backlog, and I was out to reduce that list as quickly as I can. Here's what I can say about this game:
Pacing for the early game feels slower than the rest of the game. I'd say the pace picks up rapidly around the part when you start going deep into the skill trees and acquiring combat finishers - these skills tremendously reduce the amount of time you spend in combat sections, so if you're aiming to finish the game as soon as possible, you should look at finishing a lot of power struggles early so you can unlock the later tiers ASAP. There were also more story sections in Mordor versus Nurn, so the early game might feel a little more extended than the mid-game. It's definitely not a bad thing, though - the story itself is riveting enough even for non-LotR fans like me (yet).
Combat is very deep, to say the least. This game will pit you against the world and require you to deal with numbers and single out enemies in equal measure- lore-wise, you might be out to hunt Uruk Captains and Warchiefs one-on-one (that's what it means to have a nemesis, right?), but this is also a spectacle fighter at its core, so that also meant that you're gonna have to learn how to dance against a dozen blades at the same time. Mastering the rhythm of using your Combat Finishers and keeping your hit counter alive is the name of the game here, and oh boy, it is very satisfying to use these finishers. Also, every Warchief and Captain has certain Strengths and Weaknesses that distinguish them from the rest of the enemies - this degree of uniqueness makes the Nemesis system work because you can't approach Uruk leaders in the same way. You have to investigate the Uruk leaders using Intel (which you can either telepathically extort from enemies literally marked as Intel, or you can gather them from corpses or texts spread across the world) in order to know their vulnerabilities, since they can turn the tide of battle. Imagine charging into an Uruk stronghold before knowing that the Captain is a Berserker who is immune to Combat Finishers - you're gonna have a bad time if you suck at parrying, that's for sure. But, if you do your homework well enough to discover that this same Captain is vulnerable to Stealth finishers, well, now the siege is a piece of cake, since you can one-shot the enemy with a backstab or a drop kill. Runes, which you use to enchant your weapons and get certain combat bonuses, can only be obtained through Uruk leaders - the reason why this is mentioned in the same vein as Intel is because exploiting weaknesses to kill a leader guarantees the drop of a rune related to that weakness; i.e., if you stealth-kill a Captain/Warchief vulnerable to stealth, they're guaranteed to drop a dagger rune.
The Nemesis System makes all these components work and keeps the game from going stale to a certain degree - you're not the only one out to kill Uruks, since these ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s also hate each other and they'll do background off-screening against each other on the side to rise up the ranks. It also adds weight to every victory and loss, since losing meant that your enemies will grow stronger, and winning harder fights ups the rewards for  Power Struggles, events that affect the power ranking of the involved Uruk leaders and the Exp. and Power rewards gained for finishing them. My story involved a particularly dastardly permutation of a Captain named Barfa the Brawler, who eventually became my Nemesis. It was beautiful, in a way, because that dude was the very first Captain I met on the Black Road. Dude was a beast with the Combat Master strength and Invulnerability to Stealth (and a poisoned weapon), and this beast beat me in the early game at least 7 times in a row, not only because I was a limp waffle with parrying in the early game, but also because fate decided to ♥♥♥♥ me over several times by guiding no less than two captains to the vicinity every time I fought him. It took me the Fire Arrow skill to put this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ down (along with 2 random captains who "happened" to be in the area). It was pretty fun chasing the guy out of anger, not so much the feeling of seeing his power ranking rise from like 8 to 16 by the mid-game because I couldn't settle the score.
However, I mentioned "to a certain degree" because it WILL get repetitive in the late-game, and unavoidably so, the reason being the game's implementation of its character progression system. First and foremost, the skill tree doesn't behave like a skill tree from Borderlands or Etrian Odyssey, for example - it does not restrict you to a certain set of abilities and force you to pick a branch, simply because  you can get every skill in the tree if you have even the slightest patience to grind for XP. I thought that skill progression was weird in the sense that you're simply gated by the number of levels you have - the skills you have are pretty generalist and there's no tendency towards any particular playstyle because the skills themselves don't restrict you that way. You don't feel like growing as a swordmaster or an archer or a rogue (which, I think, are classes that fit the weapons you have which are the sword, bow, and dagger), which, coming from games which have specialist skill trees like Skyrim and Borderlands, is unusual. You progress through the skill tree both by gaining ability points from levels (from EXP) and unlocking skill tiers from Power (gained from Power Struggles) - simply put, even if you get a lot of EXP from side-quests and amass a lot of ability points, you are gated from accessing later abilities if your Power level isn't high enough. This facilitates a much more grind-heavy environment because you have to grind TWO parameters instead of just one (which is usually just EXP in most games). The Nemesis system is novel in the way it adds another dimension to the narrative and the gameplay, but the novelty is also quickly worn down by the levelling system because it forces you to exhaust the combination of nemeses you can face for Power Struggles.
Graphics is really good, I guess? I had to downscale to 1366x768 and reduce a lot of settings to low just to hit 50+ FPS on my laptop, but even so, the game looked great and sharp. Voice acting is great (I have my reservations with regards to Celebrimbor, who always seemed to sound like a villain even in scenes where he shouldn't).
Level design is very good. It plays and feels like an Assassin's Creed game with the way you can wall-climb and parkour against the environment, and there are lots of things to do in the overworld for the completionists, like the Legend of Azkar/Acharn/Urfael side-quests and Outcast quests, without feeling as overwhelming as AC's. I think that's good praise, seeing that Shadow of Mordor occasionally plays like a stealth game. However, the stealth aspect of Mordor is faulty only because of the dumb AI - they're smart enough to gang up on you in combat, but they're freaking dumb when it comes to noticing you and tracking you once they do spot you. They will forget you if you climb high enough, and even when you're sneaking in plain sight, they're blind as bats even in broad daylight.
I highly recommend this game for the combat system and the story.

2. The upgrades are overall, well thought out and fun to use. It encourages exploration without making it neccessary and achieves a good balance of challenge. The best part about the upgrades is that you never feel overpowered since the enemies could always overwhelm you with numbers, making the game challenging even after you beat it. Aside from the aforementioned upgrades that should not be unlockables but given to you standard, it's a good and meaningfull system.
3. The story is  both the best and the worst part of the game. The actual story of the game makes me feel like it wasn't just written but rather vomited through a pencil. It goes from a tolerably generic revenge story to a complety bonkers side story about someone who beside sauron also happens to be the lord of the rings. It reads like the worst kind of fanfiction, the one who is happy to step all over the story, and miss every single point the character made through the story so long as cool stuff happens. I tried to research more about the universe to see if it made sense then, but that made it even worse. Aside from a few references to Morgoth or the Asumarils or the original corruption of the elves that became orcs, it also kicks the cannon in the stomach, completely missing the point of everything that happened in the Hobbit, The Lord of The Rings, and the parts of the extended universe I read about, made even worse by the fact that the cutscenes have very high production values and the story is well voice acted, as if someone actually thought this was a good idea.
Now you might be thinking how the story can be the best part of the game after my rant. Easy, the real story is not whats in the cutscenes, it's what you make up through the random encouters with randomly generated captains. Imagine in your head that you are not in mordor but in some random (insert name here) fantasy world and the game becomes leagues better, as you shape the story the way you want it while it intwines excelently with gameplay.
Overall This is a great game and I would recomend it to anyone, after I tell them to ignore the main story.

I bought Dragon's Dogma: Dark Arisen on PS3 even though I don't own a PS3 because I had heard it had fights similar to Shadow of the Colossus which is one of my all time favourite games.  I had to borrow a PS3 from a friend of mine and he didn't get it back until this was released for steam.
I really like this game and I recommend it to anybody that likes serious fantasy RPGs.  The atmosphere of this game took me back to my days of playing the Ultima series on my Atari computer and to playing Dragon Warrior (now Dragon Quest) on my NES which I don't feel many games do anymore.  My favourite thing being that monsters don't scale to your level so you will walk over the early creatures when you come back as a seasoned warrior, but if you go somewhere you shouldn't be, you will die.  I absolutely hate scaling in games because it feels like I'm not progressing anywhere since every fight is the same and every fight feels drawn out.  As far as fighting being like Shadow of the Colossus, I don't really agree since those fights required climbing and you didn't really have stats.  You can climb in Dragon's Dogma but it is nowhere near as good nor required.
The pawn system is fine, they're just like party members in any other game except you don't control them and they don't do what you want.  They are fun to make though and it is fun to rent other people pawns just to see what they like in a companion.
This game definitely has a lot of play value.  The main quest is a good 50 hours the first time if you're not rushing and the Dark Arisen content is another good 20 hours.  You can also do new game plus and play through the game again with your experienced characters and all items brought over.  Chances are you missed some quests on the first playthrough so it's nice to be able to experience them without having to start over from scratch.
Oh, I should also mention that the port works perfectly on my PC and I actually enjoy it a lot more than playing on the PS3 thanks to the higher resolution and smooth frame rate.

There's very little bad things to say about this game. Specially since this version fixed most of the problems with the old one.
Lets see... the "Most important person to you" (or romance, if you want) is a little convoluted, and you have to go through lots of trouble just to get the person you want, and not someone else by mere accident.
Graphics are slighty outdated but you can easily get by, the game is beautiful, with tons of vistas and places worth of screenshots. Enemies are very detailed as well, and very lifelike (especially in the case of the large monsters).
I loved the story. Its a little convoluted at first, but the Dark Arisen expansion shades a lot of light in the original's plot, provided you look for the pieces of text in Bitterblack Isle and aren't too busy trying not to die.
Which brings me to gameplay. Its is superb. An ARPG done extremely right. Fights with small monsters are agile and require quick thinking, with block or counters or dodges, or accurate spell casting required (dependant on class). Big monsters are methodical and require specific strategies, like climbing them to attack weakpoints, for example.
Multiple class system with growths and abilities of each, some of which can be mix matched, mainly passives.
Its a must buy. And if you get it on discount, its an absolute steal. Get it!

Hello, finally finished this game on the hardest difficulty settings and wanted to post my thoughts, I'll try to cover up spoilers as best I can.
I've put a lot of hours into this game, on various different playthroughs each with a different method of playing, those being Companion playthrough / solo playthrough / minimalist playthrough.
**DISCLAIMER** To start of ill point out that my experience with this genre is limited to this game alone and it may be that you are reading this knowing more about how these games work than I.
To kick off right from pressing play this game immediately grabs grabbed my interest by dropping me into an event that was covered in mystery, straight it made me want to dive into it no boring introductions to plot smack bang right in the middle of something.
Following this little introduction I was given the hero creation screen, to a depth I didn't expect.
The game offers you 6 races, each with a number of secondary "habitat" options (these add to bonus stats for min/maxers)
following that there are 11 classes all that can be built in their own way, then lastly the creation is finished with some personalisation/previous job roles that adds a few extra stats and gives you a starting armor / weapon set.
At no point in the lower difficulties have I felt a need to build my character or her companions strictly in a single linier direction, though in the higher difficulties you may find that the opposite be true.
**COMBAT**
following this and the opening story portion I very quickly found that this games combat was going to slow my progress down a bit, immediately following the easy monsters in the "training" portion of the game. I died. Needed to restart everything all over again (hardest difficulty) You CANNOT rush this game's combat.
that being said the combat in this game never got boring, each pack of monsters offered a different challange and seperate strategy with the number of different resistance types making it so that there wasn't an all rounded effective method of nuking monsters as I also quickly found out. I died again, wondering why my cool fire spell wasn't killing anything.

and take note, on the higher difficulties the game produces more mobs and higher tier creatures in packs at a higher density as on the lower difficulties.
**THE PRESENTATION & STORY**
throughout my 80 hours of playtime, this games art never once felt to much. The colours were very well blended, with great still painted background artwork and the 3D npc / character models fitted superbly on them. movement was very smooth, soundtrack and foley was great, spell effects were pretty and not to over the top they even included incantations which I personally thought was rather neat. so all that gets a big thumbs up from me!
The story and it's delivery was interesting and well paced all the way through, mainquest was entirely voice acted, side quests had great mini stories and some were branched of the main quest. there's public tasks you can do, super crazy hard bounties for the try hards that want a rediculously hard challange and a few more progression aspects in your stronghold.
so theres plenty of stuff too keep you busy in the world of Eora!
In addition to all the above mentioned the game also offers a lot of very small packets of information and secrets, adding to the story telling that you gain through the abilities you gain throughout the game being that each of the attributes have both combat and social implications.
Each playthrough is a different adventure, tailored exactly how you want it to be with the world reacting around you in accordance to your actions the fate of Eora is in your hands!
This game gets a 9/10 from me!

Usually I write reviews when I am done with a game. This game is going to be the exception to that rule or at least the first exception to that rule. The reason why I'm writing this review now is because I have basically seen all the game has to offer and I am just finishing up on collecting the last few unlockables.
Let me start by saying that this game is a really good game. It can go from making you love it in one moment to making you scream in frustration in the next. If you don't know what the game is about you basically play as a little kid that has to make his way through randomly generated floors and you kill enemies with your tears. It is unforgiving as hell, since your character is really weak to start, and is almost entirely down to your skill at dodging things and luck. I'm not one to enjoy luck-based things, however, due to the randomness of this game, it is endlessly replayable. The floors aren't the only part of the game that is randomly generated. Every floor has an item that changes the way your character works and with hundreds of different combinations of items, every run will be unique. Now, when I say run, I mean, the game is a roguelike and features permadeath. Don't let this put you off as it will be quite easy to get good enough at the game that you can complete a run and then it comes down to just completing each milestone for all the characters.
The characters in the game do feel very different. Although they don't have too many differences, they all have very different playstyles. Most of the characters are enjoyable with the exception of the purposefully difficult characters which are there just to test you.
The game has an incredible soundtrack and the artstyle, while being simplistic, is cool and is surprisingly detailed. I would definitely recommend this game as it is a very fun, highly replayable and challenging game.
The only time the game really makes you feel like it is badly designed is when you get unlucky and get some terrible rng but that is the way the game is designed. It doesn't care about your feelings.

Phew, where to begin with this game. A lot about it is so amazing that I hardly know where to start.
So, let's start with first impressions. The trailers are very good at giving you a feel for the atmosphere of the entire game. The positively manly narrating voice is present throughout the game and tells you the entire story as you uncover locations and enemies. Don't confuse it for exposition because it's really interesting as a story mechanic.
Ininitally I needed to get the hang of the controls and gameplay. This topdown beat-em-up style game is something I rarely play but this game definitely nailed it. I went from "Never did this before" to "Mastered every individual weapon's challenge" before the end of it. The challenges are also a really cool way to learn the weapons and earn upgrades for those weapons. The ability to also challenge yourself by activating "Idols" is also amazing. They give you the option to earn more currency but make enemies harder, or give more exp but makes certain enemies tougher to beat. Amazing if you like a challenge and want some added replay value.
I won't spoil any of the storyline but if you get invested in it, it can definitely jerk a tear by the end. Something that's even more the case because of the amazing soundtrack that plays beautifully into this.
All things considered this is one of the few games that I would still buy even if it was priced higher.

I've got 13 hours playing, 90% of it spent looking for food and water, and at this point I doubt I'll ever pick it up again. It feels like a poorly made DayZ with better graphics. Having known everything I do about it now before I made a purchase I would not have purchased the game. Trying to play without people is not fun at all, you'll spend more time looking for food than anything else in this game which is not what I wanted. I expect survival games to be more realistic, not I need to eat and drink fifteen times daily. Miscreated falls short in every aspect. Here's why:
1) Food/water consumption is out of control. The amount they have you eating and drinking would actually be fatal to the average human.
2) There's a body temperature meter yet no functionality. I can be ~40 decrees C with no impact, even though that's a medium grade fever.
3) Zombies/Mutants eat damage. I understand an ax taking a few swings if you are hitting the body; however, three shots to the head with an ax isn't fatal? Yet on the other side they hit the player, with bare hands mind you, for ~20% of your life.
4) There is base building, but zero environment interaction. Which is pretty crazy considering in this situation most people would just board up an already standing structure rather than build something from scratch.
5) Like stated earlier, you'll spend 90-95% of your total time looking for food and water. I think I only got to actually talk to four or so people that I didn't already know.
6) The map is WAY to small. You can cross it in the matter of minutes thus ruining the whole point of the game.
Unless there are some HUGE changes to this I would not recommend it to anyone. Hopefully the devs care enough to fix these huge issues, then maybe the game could be fun. They've lost me though. If you're just now thinking of getting this game only do so if you want to spend all your time searching for food and water to get three hit killed by a mutant. Otherwise, look else were.

Pros:
- Great variety of guns/melee weapons/explosives/medical items to find and manufacture.
- Not a large map but reasonably sized for the duration from start to endgame
- Permanant death due to lack of manual saves makes for more careful usage of your characters. This might be a negative depending upon how this is personally viewed upon but this can be easily bypassed by making a manual backup of the savegame.
- Additional upgradable facilities can be built for your base ala X-Com depending on your needs with other members boosting the efficiency if a related skill is present. For example, a survivor with medical skills will boost the healing chance of the medic bay.
-Resource management and scavenging makes the world seem more realistic as resources are finite in a world of zombies and you will have to be careful in how you use them.
- RPG and skill elements makes for an interesting choice in decisions to include or exclude other survivors from your enclave. There is also interplay in relationships between the members of your enclave.
Do you keep the survivor with chef and blunt weapon skills but with really abusive attitude which lowers the morale of the whole camp or decide to select him to go on a "suicide" mission? The choice is yours.
-The atmosphere and art direction of this game is excellent and evokes a real sense of isolation and terror of an small american rural town over run by undead.
Cons:
- Graphics are servicable but "level loading" prone to lag especially when a new area comes into range. Shadows are not really well done and the lighting at night is really too dark so you'll have to adjust the gamma manually to suit your tastes.
- The randomly generated daily missions do get stale after the 30th time you are called out to rescue a missing party member or lift a siege of zombies on a house of NPCs. There needs to be more variety in the random missions.
- There isn't much interaction with other survivors other than to constantly assist them with various tasks like finding someone missing or helping them with a zombie attack until they trust you enough to want to join your enclave.
They could be more dynamic, eg. patrolling the area around their home, helping you out when you are attacked in the area or even robbing you or attacking your base if they are hostile.
- Outposts are over-powered in the sense that once you get a group of them surrounding your home base and activate the flame mines, no zombie horde could get thru which somehow diminishes the sense of fear and urgency in a world over run by zombies.
Summary: 8/10
Overall this is a great open world zombie game especially when considering the price. I have gotten more enjoyment from this game then some other full price AAA titles. Of course the game is not perfect but i'm hoping a sequel or a full on expansion DLC (not the DLC breakdown which only made the game run without a storyline and limits and with a few new weapons and characters) would improve upon those shortcomings.

Okay, I love this game. I've, across the entire series, hundreds of hours. I even enjoy the pvp even when I lose most of my battles; they are always exciting. What I love about dark souls is a marriage of two things: combat and atmosphere. The combat in this game is quite similar to the previous entries. Mind you, I value PVE over PVP for this series.
If I want to fight players I'm the sort who goes to mobas or FPS (though For Honor looks promising as Dark Souls moba). You will probably have read that the unique feature in this is adding weapon arts to the mix which makes fights very dynamic, fluid, and grants many combat styles despite there being a prevailing R1/parry meta (but if you play pvp, meta will always determine how well you will do, whether you choose to join the currently favored style or not). The biggest problem with pvp is that the invader is too gimped to compete. Invasions are plainly a♥♥♥♥♥♥move, but should the invader have to contend with 3 total opponents? Perhaps they should have gone the older route in disabling certain healing options.
Apart from pvp, the bosses are generally thrilling. Some are easier than others and to the point that they are somewhat disappointingly simple  like rolling invincibly by Vordt or cleaving the hell out of the Deacons, but may the lore make up for these flaws. There are cinematic fights that are also challenging such as the Abyss Watchers and truly tough and frustrating fights like the Nameless King (not to brag, I beat him at the third try, but a brand new character, I somehow died repeatedly... repeatedly 10+ until I decided to summon). Overall, I think Dark Souls 1 has the best bosses, but this one has a bit more challenge than DS2 sans DLC.
I will end this short review with the lore. I fell in love with the lore with this game. It took long enough, huh? I played every game, except for Bloodborne, and somehow it was DS3 that broke me in. I love the lore and how we can learn a story by the items and aesthetic. I did learn a few things here and there in the series’ previous installments, just the gist. This one had stronger references to the first game, so I began to form ideas of my own and wondered about ideas of others due Miyazaki’s way of telling a story according to scenery, item descriptions, and placement of NPCs and their appearance. It’s just so rich. It’s a game series like this that makes for an engaging, interpretative storytelling. I actually was very disappointed that Miyazaki stated that he was finished with the Souls series because his mind provided me with such an immersible experience.
By the way, the graphics are so damn good. I love that there are individually unique stones arranged here and there. I read some reddit post that explained it perfect. DS1 has the best bosses, DS2 has the best DLC, and DS3 has the best graphics… or something like that.

If it matters, I've read Homestuck all the way through and I did back this game on Kickstarter.  It's just the first act right now so obviously I can't rate the full game experience, but here's what I can say.
I'm giving Hiveswap a thumbs-up because I enjoyed it, and because I think it (for the most part) succeeds at being what most people expected it to be, but I only "recommend" the game under very specific conditions.  I meet these conditions, but I don't think most people do.
This is a good expansion to the Homestuck universe, sure.  So if you already know you love Homestuck, you probably want to get it.  But, if you already know you love Homestuck, then you already bought this game before reading this review.
The thing is, that's ALL it is.  It's an extension to Homestuck.  If you ignore that part and review it as just a game, it's a pretty bog-standard adventure game in the style of "rub all inventory items on the scenery until something happens".  That part, alone, is not worth the asking price in my opinion.  What IS worth the asking price is if you wanted to see more of the chaotically dense worldbuilding and goofy IM conversations that Homestuck had.
It's not BETTER than Homestuck, though, and while Homestuck is humongous and free, Hiveswap is tiny and costs some amount of money.  Well, Hiveswap is comparatively tiny, anyway--it's a short playthrough from beginning to end of act 1 (2-3 hours), but it's also dense with descriptions of all the stuff in the world you can click on, not to mention unique reactions for attempting to use different items on those same things.  But Homestuck is still massive in comparison to all that.
I'll say that Hiveswap is better than Homestuck in two major ways: The art is way better, and it gets to the meat of the universe-spanning stuff way faster than Homestuck does.  So although Hiveswap is shorter than Homestuck, that also means that it isn't the same slow burn that Homestuck is, and I'm sure that would make it a better experience for some people.  (It also means a whole bunch of stuff is dumped on you at once with very little introduction, but then again, being confused and overwhelmed by the complexity of the story is part of the Homestuck experience.)
But would I recommend the game to anyone who hadn't already tried Homestuck to see if they like it or not?  I don't think I would.  I'd be more likely to gift this game to someone in an attempt to get them interested in the idea of reading Homestuck.  Except I wouldn't do that either, since I'm not THAT big a fan of Homestuck.
I dunno.  Hiveswap is okay, but the only consumer advice I feel comfortable giving is "read Homestuck first to decide whether you would enjoy this or not".  You should probably give it a pass, otherwise.  If later acts turn the game into something truly unique, I may change my mind on that.

Really just not a good game altogether. The problem is really with the inbalance in playable nations. The East and West Roman Empires along with the Sassanids are massive, and it's practically impossible to keep most of the territory you start off with, much less gain any. The "Great Migrators" are incredibly hard to play as, because your two fledgling armies are usually wiped out before you can establish yourself. The huns are just as bad, as it's difficult to expand your numbers very much while conquering territories, and in the end the Romans have 10x the amount of troops you do. In the other, smaller nations, you may have short campaigns, conquering a couple territories, but you will then have nowhere left to expand besides the behemoth Roman or Sassanid Empires. There are also a lot of other things I dislike about the game, like the useless pikemen, the DLC after paying $60, and how incredibly over-powered some units are, but the main thing is the time period and the available scenarios. This game is simply not worth your money, although you still want to buy Empire, Napoleon, or Shogun if you haven't already.

Video version of this review:
To start this off, this game has the worst tutorial ever. They tell you what to do, but they don’t say the controls. I couldn’t figure out how to reload until I went to the options, and found out you have to press the middle mouse button. WHY?! That's literally the LAST button you’d expect to use to reload a gun with. Well, at least they allow you to change the controls.
Chaser wakes up with no idea who he is, or what he’s doing in this space station. These polygonal military ships enter the station and the soldiers start murdering a bunch of unarmed workers. Seriously, some of them even try to surrender, but these soldiers just won’t take any prisoners.
All the soldiers are after you, and it is unclear why, which is what Chaser is trying to find out. At least after losing his memory, he still knows how to use a gun. So you fight your way through the station, and leave in an escape pod, heading to Earth as the station explodes. Every so often we get some flashbacks of Chaser’s previous life. Apparently he was a part of his own little group of rebels before being attacked by soldiers. Geez, what did this guy do for everyone to want to kill him?
Chaser looks like he's not even alive. The facial expressions are non-existent. And your character tends to stare into nothingness like a doll. I know this was made in 2003, a time when character models did indeed look lifeless, but it seems a lot more creepy to me in this game.
I wish he was a silent protagonist, because this guy’s voice acting is just awful. The rest of the voice actors aren’t anything that special either, but none of them even come close to the level of awful as Chaser.
Anyway, you meet someone named Mike Gomez, and he strongly advises that you get out of the city as fast as you can. But you are taken in by this group called the Family, run by this guy named Vallero, who inserts a device into your head called a spider. If you get too far from the city or do anything that Vallero doesn’t like you doing, he can make it explode, and then you’re history. Luckily, Mike knows someone who can help you get rid of the Spider. But you have to play along with Vallero for a while. You eventually meet up with the lady who helps remove the spider. But then you are attacked by Vallero’s men, and are branded a traitor for being in cahoots with their enemies.
This game can be a little ridiculous when it comes to saving. The only autosaves you will come across in this game are at the very start of each mission. So if you don’t save anywhere between the start and end of a mission, you have to start all the way from the beginning of it. So you’ll want to save as often as you can.
I hate the level design in this game. I had to go through a lot of trial and error during the first stealth mission, because sometimes, I'd get confused about where I'm supposed to go. The only way I would know that I'm going the wrong way is from Mike telling me I'm at the wrong door. There are so many doors, man. Sometimes what you say isn't 100% clear. In some other levels, you aren't exactly told what area is what, so you have to walk around and try every door until something happens. I hate this, because there are too many doors, and I can't always tell which ones I've tried or not.
This game has too many dead ends, in my opinion. There are very few that I feel actually belong there, but when a series of doors leads to absolutely nothing, I have to wonder, WHAT'S THE POINT? Some paths even loop back to a previous area, which is also pointless, since I have no reason to go back in the first place.
It doesn’t seem to matter what difficulty you choose, it’s a lot easier to die from enemy fire than I’d like it to be. At one point, I had full health and armor, but I managed to die from only two shots from a shotgun. It’s absolutely ridiculous. Even Half-Life is more forgiving than that.
Not sure why they decided that having enemies pop up out of nowhere in an area I already cleared was a good idea. Seriously what’s the point? Is that just supposed to add to the difficulty? Because to me, all it adds is annoyance.
The sniping mission is by far the easiest and most boring mission in the game. And the underwater mission is the absolute worst. My character keeps moving in directions which I can guarantee I am not moving him in. It’s really hard to navigate in this place, because looking around is really disorienting. You are supposed to touch these yellow lights, which turn blue after you touch them. They sort of make a trail for you. But there’s this giant room, where I cannot find the next light to save my life. I’ve been swimming in this area for literally 10 minutes, and haven’t found the way out. So I had to look up a video. Honestly, why was it necessary to go through a ship anyway? Don’t you think it would have been easier to simply go around the ship instead?
Eventually, you head to Mars in search of more information about what’s going on. I’ve been here for not even a minute, and everyone is trying to kill me. You end up getting arrested, and have to escape from jail, with an old friend of yours, apparently. You free all the prisoners and continue your search for the exit. But what I don't get is why are the prisoners shooting at me? I freed them from this place. I did absolutely nothing to warrant this.

Date Completed: 1/1/17
# of Hours: 221 Hours (pretty sure I left it running on my computer a couple nights overnight)
Replayability: Yes
Game Type: Open World Roleplaying
Score: 8 Decapitated Uruks out of 10
Spoilers below: Yes
Overall Thoughts:
The game starts off with a bang, throwing you immediately into shoes of a ranger faced with death all around him. As he kneels beside a corpse you think, "oh his friends died", and with a series of flashbacks it fills you in with a compelling backstory that makes you immediately feel for Talion as he mourns the death of his son and wife, taken in front of him in a gruesome way.
And then, just like that, it immediately throws you into the game. Confused, I wasn't sure how much time had passed between the events just replayed, and Talion's resurrection at the hands of an elf ghost. I spent a good while assuming years had passed only to be (what I can only now assume) an immediate transition. The flashback story telling was nice, giving you glimpses into the Lord of the Rings mythos. While I didn't come to care for Celebrimbor, I loved to see and learn through his eyes how and why the rings where created. The side quest missions were short and sweet that I didn't feel a dread in trying to finish them because I knew they'd tell me a fun story in a short amount of time, introducing new characters that incrementally moved the plot forward.
Overall, the Orc battle system seems to be the most entertaining part of the game, and I spent hours trying to wipe out the entire board (p.s. you can't). Each orc leader has it's own set of weaknesses, and playing against them was fun, branding your enemies, and setting up traps even more so.
However, the boss fights themselves lacked the epicness you hope from all the build up. The Hammer fight played out much like any other orc Warchief, the Tower attempted a new strategy of sneaking up on the boss and draining him that finally played out overly simplified with a button press hold to finish him, and the last boss battle of the game was over in 30 seconds in an interactive cutscene.
The combat was interactive with a nice play between stealth stabby, ranged slo-mo headshots, and up in your face orc countering and combat finishers that it kept entertaining. Unlike other games (Elder Scrolls), I found myself actually using all three weapons on a constant basis because each was very balanced, and the game expected them to be used in tandem. The talent tree and new abilities that came with it didn't add anything overly new or exciting, instead opting for incremental improvement, but I found that to be fine in this case.
Shadow of Mordor benefits greatly from the Lord of the Rings mythology, and relies on your knowing it pretty heavily. I found myself googling character names, and reading backstory to understand what was happening. For the die hard LOTR this will be a pleasant addition to the mythos. For those interested in the books and movies, it's a nice tease to get you to learn more. For those who want a roleplaying game with a self contained story, look elsewhere.
Gameplay Mechanics:
This is a game that challenges you not in the combat or play style, but in the sheer number of orcs that it will press on you at any given time. Stealth is your ally, although fighting twenty orcs at a time is rewarding in itself. With no true leveling up, all advancement is done either through ability points in the talent tree, or rune upgrades on the weapons.
Weapons
Shadows offers you three weapons you have at the beginning of the game that cannot be traded, bought or sold. A bow, a dagger, and sword. Each allows you to unlock rune upgrades (a total of five) with Mordor points obtained from completing quests such as helping free slaves. Runes are obtained any time you kill an orc leader. These runes allow you special upgrades such as the chance to set someone on fire, regain focus, etc. All weapons are very balanced, and each used in its own situation. Whenever the bow is used, time is slowed and can be used during combat. The dagger can only be used when you are in stealth, instantly killing enemies or brutalizing them to scare other orcs. The sword is used when in open combat to counter and finish orcs.
Weapon Special Abilities
Each weapon also has it's own special abilities. The Bow allows you to Shadow Strike and Shadow Kill enemies, instantly moving to their location and attacking them when targeted by the bow. The sword allows you to stun enemies, entering into a quickly timed hit succession ending with a brutal finisher. The dagger allows you to stealth kill, and brutalize enemies, stabbing them repeatedly to scare other orcs around you.
Talent Tree
The talent tree unlocks about six tiers as you gain more power (obtained from killing Orc leaders, gaining power equal to their power rating). Once unlocked, you spend abilities points gained from getting experiences (also obtained from completing quests). The talent tree gives you certain abilities such as throwing daggers, mounting beasts, or pinning orcs by shooting their legs. Everything here seemed incremental, not game changing, but they were fun none the less.
Health and Focus
The game gives you a health bar, which can be upgraded with Mordor points throughout the game, and works very similar to any health bar, regaining health slowly over time. Health can also be completely regained by eating herbs found plentifully throughout the maps. Focus only comes into play when using the bow, and slows time as you shoot orcs in their face, depleting quickly the longer you keep using the bow. It to also regains focus over time as you stop using it.
Nemesis System
The game gives you a grid of 4 rows of Orc Leaders, which remain shadows until you interrogate orcs, or steal intel, revealing who and where they are, as well as their weakenesses and strengths. You can then mark them, allowing you track them down and slaughter them, using their weaknessess to kill them quickly (or sometimes instantly).
The fourth level of Orc leaders are the warchiefs, and it's these that you have to take down throughout the game. They have bodyguards that will accompany them into battle (unless otherwise turned or killed prior to engaging them), and can only be made to come out once you've fulfilled a certain requirement such as stealth killing a certain number of their followers.
Maps:
There are really only two maps to the game, revealed through from the fog of war but reforging ghost towers (think assassins creed). Each has about 6 sections with orc camps, and various side quests in each section.
Stealth
Stealth is a big part of the story as you sneak through bushes, or crouch along rooftops over orc heads. When stepping into an orcs line of sight (depending on distance) you will immediately be noticed, forcing you into open combat, or there will be a slow yellow filling timer above their heads that allows you time to move out of sight and maintain your stealth. Once broken, other's will be altered to you presence, and in strongholds, an orc may even raise an alarm, attracting a horde of new enemies to your location.

I love CRPGs, and this one is well done. You can tell it's designed by people who listened to their fans, and also people who have played CRPGs. This game is truely a spiritual successor to the Baulder's Gate series. It's been a joy to play the game. I haven't finished yet, but I'm probably 65% of the way through the game.
If you like CRPGs you'll love this game. If you haven't played a CRPG before, Pillars is a good one to get your feet wet on. Just make sure you spend some time reading the way combat works or else you may find yourself somewhat frustrated.
Pros
+AMAZING voice acting. On par if not better than Dragon Age.
+Good storyline, good setting background. Your introduction to it can be kind of head spinning, but there's enough reminders to keep you on track.
+Lots to do and see. There are tons of quests to keep you busy, and the locations are diverse.
+UI is clean, effective, and intuitive.
+Combat is very complex, which means there are a lot of approaches you can take to building your party the way you want.
+Generally bug free. I only ran into a few minor issues, and most of those have been immediately addressed by the developer's recent patch. Game is also very stable. I alt-tab out constantly and have never had it crash on me.
+NPCs you can play with have very distinct backgrounds, and are all very interesting. I love NPCs that I can relate to. They add a lot to the game.
Cons
-Item bonuses and enchanting generally is pretty boring. Flat bonuses that just make you better. The items you FIND are interesting, but the stuff that you can add is very bland.
-The endurance/heatlh system just seems wierd to me. Generally your characters just get knocked out, but sometimes they die. How much damage blows through from endurance to health is not intuitive at all.
-Money becomes kind of worthless towards the middle of the game. The game lacks any "super high priced, super high quality" vendors that would allow you to save up and spend your cash.
-Could use a few more NPCs. Not every class is represented as an NPC, which means you need to make custom characters if you want access to certain classes in your party.

People spend a lot of time reminiscing about their gaming past. Few sub-groups do this as vocally and with as much affection as fans of traditional RPGs like the near-legendary Infinity Engine games: Baldur's Gate, Neverwinter, etc. This might be because so many of those gamers found these games in tandem with traditional pen-and-paper RPGs, which is understandable when you see how much similarity there is between the two.
Publishers and developers of course play on this nostalgia and claim that their title will be the game that ushers in a resurrection of the classic RPG - a grand return to the days of high adventure. And of course they are consistently wrong because pitching a 50+ hour game with thousands of pages of text to read through is a hard sell.
Fear not these false prophets, though, for Obsidian has delivered unto you a second coming of traditional swordplay, wizardy, and esoteric lore. Lead us not unto Dragon Age. Deliver us from The Witcher. For Pillars of Eternity is the power and the glory. It's every D&D session in a moldy basement, every late Saturday night in the cold glow of a CRT displaying Icewind Dale, distilled into one game and freshened up just enough to make it more functional to a current audience. And that's it. It's a very *pure* experience. I can't give it better praise than that.
This shows you what a team can do when the budget isn't being poured into marketing, graphics, and bloated staffs. Exemplary work.

Let's get the bad things out of the way first.
Cons:
- Terrible default controls
That's about everything I hated in this game, but after much strategizing and rebinding, which involved:
- Moving the map scroll keys from the directional pad to WASD
- inventory to C,
- map to TAB
- next char/prev char to Q and E respectively,
- reveal interactable objects to V
And a whole bunch of other QoL improvements. The general idea is to completely remove my reliance from the other half of the keyboard, particularly the right side since I am right-handed and that's reserved to my mouse. Infinity Engine games needed this option like real bad. My settings are not intuitive for the casual gamer, but Diablo 3 taught me there were better ways to access my inventory besides going all the way to I. And Diablo 3 is pretty casual.
But once all these are set, and I got used to my own controls, I am able to immerse myself in the game completely. No more glancing on the keyboard, no more groping for the right key - my eyes are on the game 100%, enjoying the sheer narrative bliss, the engaging tactical combat, and the captivating story that keeps me at the edge of my seat.
This is a true successor to the infinity engine games. I would love to see Baldur's Gate on this engine, with its stunning visuals, pleasant to the eye yet evokes the imagination. This is the enigma that Bioware left behind instead of improving upon. While Dragon Age: Inquisition is a glorious adventure in its own right, my heart belongs to Eternity!
Long live Obsidian!

Game is in early access, so it is rather buggy still. And by rather buggy I mean invisible players, dying from exiting a car driving at 2mph, or exiting in a location with a tight fit. Sometimes players are invincible, either by another bug or they are using cheats.
Fuel and oil often bugs out of cars, as well as other items getting stuck in inventory slots.
Cars flip way too easy as well as explode when you touch an invisible wall, and there are plenty of invisible walls. All in very stupid locations, like right off the side of the road.
Weapons misfire when clicking items in inventory.
Bullets sometimes dont register damage. Cars lag when driving, arent synched with other players view of them. Not to mention the constant microstutter when driving cars, regardless of specs or internet speed.
NPC enemies sometimes despawn and even spawn out of nowhere.
Player bodies despawn before you can loot them quite often. People alt+f4 to escape death as well, and the time you need to alt+f4 (when the game freezes every 30 minutes) it wont let you.
Dropping items on top of any static object will often cause them to fall through that object down onto the terrain. So dropping an item on the second floor of a building will cause your item to fall through the floor and the next floor, down to the ground. Even when dropping directly on terrain the game will sometimes glitch the item out and cause your item to fly across the map.
There are countless other bugs that plague this game regularly. But despite them all, I have been alive for over 20 hours straight without dying on a KOS server. Killed at leat 50 people, driven and traded a dozen cars. Stockpiled weapons and ammo for friends and gunfights.
But all in all, I would pass on this game for now. Wait for it to enter retail release because the alpha is way to buggy.
This game will likely die off after Escape From Tarkov comes out anyway, and this game will likely still be in beta.

Let me start by saying the game isn't bad, it just isn't worth the asking price.
Miscreated suffers from persistant game breaking bugs and a community as toxic as any other survival game out there. There are some redeeming points however.
Pros:
Nice graphics
Large map
Vehicles
Cons:
Performance Issues
Low Player count.
lack of loot variation
Survival is a joke
Griefing
PvP issues
Server issues
AI
Base Building
I'll just touch on the most important issues here, so this isn't too long of a review.
Performance: Many players suffer game breaking performance issues. The optimization is extremely lacking. Sometimes the game is running at 60+ fps, then seconds later I drop to a slide show 5 fps for apparantly no reason what so ever. I have had a consistant error where my game instantly crashes if anyone lights a torch within my view. I've asked about it on several threads and every last one has received no response whatsoever. Several performance hiccups have persisted since launch, with no end in sight apparantly.
Low Pop and Loot: This is one of the worst parts of the game. Servers can't even support 40 players for a humungous map. Many many times I've traversed the entire map without meeting a single living individual. From brightmoor to the new city, not a single other player. On the off chance you do meet someone, there is a 90% chance they are simply going to shoot you, so you'd better just shoot them to be safe. The complete lack of frequent player interaction is a huge disappointment for Miscreated.
The Loot is even worse. Food and water are literally so abundant that the ENTIRE survival aspect of the game is ignored. You can't go through one house without finding enough food and water to fill you up. There is absolubtely ZERO struggle to survive nature. As far as the other loot goes, once you've played for an hour or two and learned where each type of loot spawns, you will be fully geared within 30 minutes of spawning. Food, clothes, guns, ammo, a tool or two, all within 30 minutes if you know how to look. Aside from that, majority of the items are entirely generic and similiar. All the gloves are exactly the same, just different colors. Same for hats, jackets, everything.
Server Issues: Many players who bought the game cannot even connect to it, under any circumstance. This has been present since launch and still is not resolved. Some servers will completely wipe with no warning or explanation. Some servers (such as Aus1) will continue running, yet every player structure on the map vanishes, and the server has to be rolled back. just type AUS1 in the discussion threads to see numerous posts about problems show up. Some servers drop off the list for no reason, with no explanation given, only to reappear later.
TLDR:
The game has a few good ideas and high points, but it is severely tied down by performance issues, server issues, and horrid balancing. Alpha or not, there is no excuse for the same bugs to be present for over a year.

Here we go;
Bastion is one of those games that definitely gives you an indie feeling the whole way through. Let me highlight the phrase "the whole way through". This game keeps you gripping your controller and never lets you put it down. The story is so engaging I found myself reacting to it in ways I thought only books could invoke. The narrator really makes you feel like a lone wanderer, ready and eager to take on the powers that corrupt his path of freedom. The art is a never-ending dreamscape with such a rich, surreal concept of animation and detail that I forgot tilesets were even involved. The music was so well chosen that I didn't even notice it (It mirrored my mood and empathy for the story perfectly). Now to the gameplay. While I would have been happy with a single attack one weapon combat system since this story carries itself; The game gives some surprising effort into the combat system. While it is nothing extravagant, and they glamourize simple stat perks a little bit, It all fits into the character of the game. They go further and include multiple weapons with different special attacks. I guess what I'm getting to is, if you got bored of the combat, it's most likely your fault for not taking advantage of the ability to switch things up at virtually any point in the game.
TL;DR
Pros:
Story, narration, art, music, all 10/10
Combat system is simple BUT EFFECTIVE 8/10
cons:
No sequel.

6-9 hours that I enjoyed every second of.
Very reminiscent of Legend of Mana, or Secret of Mana (though to a lesser degree).
This title hearkens back to the SNES/PS1 days of extremely advanced, colorful animation that is executed to the highest degree in this game. It's gorgeous.
The combat is also very responsive and diverse with plenty of customization to suit your playstyle; it's classic Secret of Mana style (think ARPG, but with blocking and more movement, positioning).
It's completely 2D for the most part until you complete it and you unlock jumping.
I recommend this game, but give a caveat to older players like myself: This game is outstanding by todays standards, but if you can remember Legend of Mana, or Secret of Mana, its content pales in comparison and you should not expect to get that amount of game delivered for the purchase price.
The musical score and narration (the narrator is outstanding) also add a distinct flavor to it, which is, in my opinion, the contribution of this game to the genre.
In short: Rejoice, this is a great game; very fun content, but in a small  6-10 hour dose, but let us not forget the titans of this genre. Thanks developers, but if you could do something like a Legend of Mana, please do. Please remember the 90's and 80's.

I have to say that I was skeptical about this game. I bought it included in a Humble Bundle a few years ago (I bought the whole bundle to get my hands on something else in the pack). A few days ago I opted to install it and see what it was. I didn't bother looking at reviews or play throughs.
From the moment I dropped into the world, I was wowed by an interesting concept for dungeon development, a beautifully rendered game world, and a great soundtrack. When I realised that the narrator was actually responding to what I was doing in the game I was pleasantly surprised.
As I get deeper into the game, the mechanics are deceptively simple. The difficulty ramps up quickly and mobs are increasingly difficult and one needs to master all the elements of game play (and each weapon). It reminds me of the old NES games in that the first few levels seem easy and each subsequent level gets just a bit harder until you're swearing at your monitor.
The big downfall for me on this game is the repetitive missions. Every mission is, well, just like every other one. Thus far, in my experience, there hasn't been a puzzle of any sort to be solved or a variation on, "we need these things, go find one of them here:"
I will say, if you haven't tried it and can find it under $10 (US), it is worth the investment. Each level can easily fit in between meetings or on your lunch hour. It's a nice palate cleanser for the long sessions you may put in with other games.
All-in-all, for me it's about a 7.5/10

There are some negative aspects that make the game less enjoyable and if they were improved on, it would make this game perfect. I recommend buying the game on sale and also buying the Empires of Sand and Age of Charlemagne DLC's. Finally, to make the game truly enjoyable and get rid of some negative aspects, add many mods to it. I really enjoyed this game
Pros-
-The story is well crafted and you can tell alot of effort was put into it. It has lots of twists, turns, and reveals that are pretty good. Not mind blowing, but still, its one of the highlights of the game. Theres alot there if you want to dig giving players a choice in how far they want to go into the lore of the worle.
-Interactions with your squad members are memorable and personal. Each has distinct personalities and underlying motives that are there if you spend the time to get to know them all
-The branching diolauge paths are great. Give some depth and a player's touch into the game. Not super deep and many diolauges still lead to the exact same result but thats ok.
-The settings were pretty good. It was really neat to go explore all these planets and choose in what order you were to do it in. The aliens and universe created here are also interesting and thought out.
-Runs well on my crap PC and also has a widespread texture mod for those who seek higher fidelity.
Cons
-Elevators. There are alot of them. Most I assume are disgusing loading screens and it really gets old fast especially when in some situations you go through one elevator, get out, walk a bit, then go up another.
-Combat. While it is good I wouldnt call it great. I played on the hardest difficulty with AI actions turned off for my squad mates and one of two things would happen in combat situations: my main character could just wipe out all the enemies without the help of my squadmates so I have no reason to even have them do anything, or when I do need them they are HORRIBLE at staying alive. Even when you direct them towards cover they very often come out for no reason and die. Somtimes you plan a combo of abilities on a enemy all at once but one squad member decides that its just not happening today. It got annoying. Also I didnt like that you had to pick your squadmates from the begining of the mission when you have no idea whats in store. They all have different abilities but only a few combos cover everything so it locks you out of doing certain combos of characters you may like. Overall it is an ok combat system, that with some tweaks could be really really good.
-Driving sections - controls are kind of slippery and every driving section all game has the same 3 or 4 enemies making them really easy and really boring
-Enemies. There are only about 10 enemys in the whole game if you dont count reskins. Kind of a a let down.
-Final Boss- Ended up just being the main bad guy with the abilities of one of the enemy types you have fought all game with a stupid amount of health and rocket launchers added on. The universe is on par with stories like Star Trek and even Star Wars with clear inspiration from those universes. This is easily one of the best, if not THE best scifi RPG out there. Its a great series, if you exclude ME3.
I'll sum up what makes this masterpiece great in a simple list forn
PROS:
-Great voice acting
-Great characters and villains
-Although the Reapers are somwhat generic "ancient evils" they're still very interesting
-The fully voiced protagonist with two genders shows how much work they put into the dialogue and making it as emersive as possible.
-leads into a great trilogy (excluding the second half of ME3)
-all races are interesting with lore behind them
-different planets and have their own culture and feel. Lower-Citadel is a robust cyberpunk-like underworld where anything goes while Noveria feels like the Hoth we never got to explore (until SWTOR came along)
-the atmosphere throughout the game is strong. You really do feel like the captain of a spaceship, exploring the universe and learning new things
CONS:
-meh gameplay. Significantly improved in ME2
-graphical glitches present in this version and vary between person to person (judging by community posts)
-Kaiden is almost as bad as Alistair
-A lot of your choices don't really matter. The game gives you the illusion of choice. It make impact ME2 somewhat, but the choices you make in ME1 and 2 make no difference whatsoever in 3
-Male Shepherd in this game has a very wooden voice actor. Femshep does a much better job. Mark Meer improves his acting in ME2
-Shepherd overall isn't a very interesting character after the 10 minute intro. You can choose his/her origin story which is great but it's only loosely referenced in the game and it doesn't make as much an impact as your origin does in Dragon Age: Origins (another great RPG by BioWare)
-most of the time, you're only fighting Geth which is a shame since the galaxy is booming with much more life. It gets stale seeing the same model fall over and over when you could be fighting a limitless amount of different species. Some planets let you fight rachni and krogan but these moments are few and far between. It feels like wasted potential. Again, ME2 improves on this.
To sum it all up, it's a flawed masterpiece. The atmosphere, story, and characters are fantastic but the ho-hum gameplay and wooden protagonist leave a lot to be desired. ME2 is an overall better game but this game remains my favorite in the series because it gives you a sense of curiosity and wonder that only few games manage to give me.

While I can see why people like this game, I'd like to warn against the hype.  Not because of the things everyone is saying are bad about this game, (the MAKO, crappy RPG/shooter hybrid combat) but because of what people like - the story.  This is a game that promises great story and characters, but delivers on neither.  The developers do a superb job building anticipation, giving a sense of a wider world, but do absolutely nothing with it - just a by the numbers "save the galaxy from evil invaders" plot that could have been copy-pasted from a Michael Bay movie.  Make no mistake, this is not Planescape: Torment or Fallout 2, but a game whose story, although carefully polished, says absolutely nothing.  The characters in your party are sometimes interesting (the tech-alien girl is decent) but are mostly flat, having nothing much in the way of a character arc and only a single motivation.  This is exacerbated by the clumsy dialogue system; not being able to see what you're going to say is crippling on its own, but restricting to four options removes all subtlety from interactions.
If you compare it to the likes of Skyrim, sure, the story looks pretty good.  But that game has vast, open landscapes to explore, a reasonably deep customisation system, and more importantly a mod community that can make the game whatever you want it to.  Mass Effect (and its sequels) really have nothing but their story (and some pretty graphics) and there's just not enough there to justify the time you'll spend on this, let alone the money.  If you want to play a modern story-based RPG, the Witcher series is superior in story, character depth, story interaction, *and* has decent combat.  Alternatively Alpha Protocol has a similar style to Mass Effect, but characters you will take more than thirty seconds to figure out.

Truly, this game is one of the greatest experiences crafted by Obsidian Entertainment.  The story telling in this gem is one of a kind, and each character you come across on your journey leaves a lasting impression.
If you are a fan of the traditional style Role Playing Games of old, Pillars of Eternity is simply a must try.
One bit of note I will make for those who have not yet bought the game, it is a mature story.  There are many subjects covered that sensitive people may find offensive, yet that is also what makes this game so unique and enjoyable.  The developers at Obsidian were clearly allowed to put their hearts into Pillars of Eternity without fear of holding back their creativity.
The gameplay requires proper strategy and liberal use of the space bar to pause the game during fights.  Some fights will also be nearly impossible if your character is not strong enough to rise to the challenge, so don't feel discouraged if you are defeated early on.
Having taken at least fifty to sixty hours to finish the story, I can say that the game will keep you entertained for quite some time.  The side quests, normally nothing of importance, all feel meaningful and let you see the outcome of your choices while still playing.  Clearing out monsters from an abandoned building will help a distraught traveler set up shop and open a new inn for example, and many more memorable quests await.
Of further note is the fact that each person you add to your party develops and reveals their past over time.  Eventually, the quests they give you can change their perspective on life in Eora, for better or worse.
Will you be the champion the Dyrwood needs, or will you take advantage of the chaos?  Make the choice, in Pillars of Eternity.
Combines the tactical nature of Icewind Dale 2 and Baldur's Gates Storyiine very well.

I loved this game when I payed full AAA price for the console and now it's even better on the PC port. Capcom, a AAA title, returned to work on this game and delayed for 3 years in order to make a good port for PC: 60 FPS, added content in BitterBlack Isles, and the ability to mute the Pawns. There is still only 1 save file, so that may be a bummer to some people, but the class system is flexible enough that it dowsn't really matter. I do feel spoiled with the improved Fast Travel system. My console opinion of the old fast travel system that cost money every time fast travel happened was that it was tedious, yet appropriate.
This is a game frequently compared to Skyrim and Dark Souls, but in my opinion falls comfortably in the middle, especially in difficulty, combat techniques and class systems. It also has some elements of Shadow of Colossus in that you can climb larger monsters to fight them.
The classes themselves, I'd rate an A-. I have played 8/9 max characters (not assassin). They definitely all have pros/cons, and inherent difficulties with enemies. For those who haven't played the game, there are 3 basic classes, 3 advanced classes, and 3 hybrid classes (the fun ones). Out of the 9, I most enjoyed and played a lot of the Warrior (advanced Melee) and the Magick Archer (hybrid Magic/Rogue). The Warrior played like an aggro, hack and slash character. They excel at strong arming multiple enemies, and drawing attention away from high damage output mages. They are also horrific at fighting magic based enemies and have few tools to deal with overbearing enemies. Magick Archers have incredible utility, but lack the ability to aggro or apply burst damage in certain scenarios. Despite these debilitations, it is still possibile to overcome these weaknesses by building a team of pawns that compensates for these weaknesses. They can at times seem too OP, even in hard mode.
The story is mediocre at best, and the whole pawn system seems like a last minute effort to replace a would-be multiplayer system. The pawn system is fine, but not great. The pawn system is where you make a permanent AI companion in your party and you can rent 2 other players companions and form a 4 person party.
Hard mode is also somewhat dissatisfying (I'd give it a B). Enemies have slighly improved AI, and are sometimes higher leveled, but you get compensated by receiving more gold. After about level 20, the extra gold allow you to equip yourself with gear that overcompensates for hard mode.
But at the end of the day, I would rate this game in my top 3. Why? The combat. The climbing on top of a cyclops as he tries to shake you off, reaches for you like a fat man trying to wash his back without a loufa, jumping off just before that he pile drives you into the ground. Fights are exhilirating and the combat system is intuitive and provides depth. Each combat school is also very distinct. Magic is full of vulnerability and preparation and the reward of insane burst damage, warriors aggro and control a fight, rogues whittle away at armor points and weaken enemies.
Conclusion: buy it win it's on sale. buy it when it's full price. Buy it when it doubles in price. It's one of the few games I would pay full AAA price for

This had the potential to be a truly enjoyable "so-bad-it's-good" type of game for me, but the damn thing just drags on and on.
The story is just ridiculous enough to be enjoyable--it takes itself seriously, but between the terrible voice acting and the incoherent nature of it, it's just all laughable to me.
The gameplay by itself is a bit frustrating, as enemies will often times appear out of thin air, especially if you manage to find a way to circumvent the normal path you're supposed to take. In one instance, there's a door on one of the levels (after the lighthouse sniper mission) that was supposed to be opened from the opposite side I opened it on, and 3 guys just appeared and started shooting at me. Also, it seems fairly arbitrary how often the AI will actually hit you--sometimes I'd be standing 5 feet away from a guy and his shots would go wide, but I'd be standing a mile away and he'd drain my health from full to dead in moments...maybe that's just me, though.
Another REALLY frustrating thing is the fact that there's absolutely no report for people shooting rockets or explosives at you. The screen doesn't really differentiate between a bullet hit and a rocket hit when you're in the middle of a firefight, and enemy rockets are whisper-quiet when fired, meaning you don't always realize you're being blown up.
Lastly, the game just drags. There are just too many levels, with you mostly just doing the same monotonous thing over and over again.
Overall, the game obviously has some development talent behind it, but it feels rushed and unpolished. The laughable moments get fewer and far between, and I had to keep my nose to the grindstone to finally beat it. I honestly wouldn't recommend it, on the grounds that it just starts getting boring after a while.

The first thing that caught my attention, for better or worse, was the $20 price tag. I was skeptical at first, since I had heard nothing of this visual novel, and it didn't seem to be very prominent on forums or other gaming sites. Thankfully, the summer sale reduced the price to about $8, and I bought it. After reading all the way through, I completely understand the price point. eden* has absolutely gorgeous artwork, a sweet, melancholic soundtrack, an intriguing and engaging story, and complex, relatable characters. It was developed by minori, a small studio known for their most famous visual novel series, Ef: A Fairy Tale of The Two. eden* took me about 12 hours to read through with auto mode on. It is a kinetic novel, which means there are no player choices, just straight up reading.
eden* was originally released as an all-ages VN, with an eroge side story named Mosaic releasing later. There is no sexual content in the Steam release, and you will not be missing out on any story or character details if you buy it here. If you're looking for something to fap to, you're in the wrong place. eden* was published by MangaGamer, who also brought Higurashi and Go Go Nippon to Steam.
eden* takes place in the near future, where mankind has predicted the death of the world. Scientists concluded that Earth will die in approximately 100 years, and began to frantically find a way to transport humanity to space to live on. Because of the pressing time limit and the magnitude of the situation, two major events transpire: all of the governments of the world join together to form the "Unified Government", and a certain doctor had the bright idea to genetically enhance a handful of humans. These creations are dubbed "Felixes" and their main perks are that they are intellectually superior, and their bodies stop aging after a certain point. These Felixes greatly accelerated the research for space travel, and a new project was initiated: The Earth Evacuation Project. The head of the project, a girl named Sion, is the alpha felix, the cream of the crop, if you will. The story revolves around her.
Unlike most VNs, the protagonist has a name, a face, and a personality. His name is Haruna Ryou, a Warrant Officer in the Unified Military, who is assigned to a research facility in the middle of nowhere with the vague objective to "protect it". He has quite an impressive track record in the military, only volunteering for the most dangerous missions and showing no mercy or remorse. Most of his comrades fear him and respect him from afar. Another Warrant Officer by the name of Lavinia F. Asai (Lavie) is assigned to be his partner. I feel as though revealing more would ruin the experience, so moving on.
eden* is a kinetic novel. There are no choices at all. Just relax and read through the story. Depending on how fast you read and if you listen to the voice acting (every character is fully voiced, Japanese only), it can take 10-12 hours to complete. It has a rather small native resolution of 1024x640, and there are various graphical options available.
What sets eden* apart from other VNs is the characters being given life through subtle animations. They blink and their lips move when speaking, as opposed to the standard static image. One can turn off these animations through the options if desired. Functions such as saving and loading are not part of the text box, but reside in a small bubble that appears when moving the cursor to the bottom right corner of the window, Windows 8 style. That deterred me at first, but I quickly got used to it.
Some of the highlights of eden* are its spectacular artwork and music. The use of lighting is fantastic, giving a bloom effect when outside and limiting it indoors to create an oppressive, somber tone. The characters themselves are simple, but attractive. Sion's large red eyes are incredibly alluring. The backgrounds are detailed and polished. Many of eden*'s still images are wallpaper-worthy. For most of the VN, melancholic piano music fills the silence. In moments of tension and suspense, it switches to a more chaotic, impactful rhythm. The music also plays a role in the storyline, which I find refreshing. eden*'s opening theme, "little explorer", is sung by Harada Hitomi.
If you have $20 to spare and are looking for a good VN, look no further. eden* is a fantastic and heartwarming experience that gives perspective on morality and humanity. The art is gorgeous, the characters are diverse, the plot is engaging and impactful, and it will most likely make you cry by the end. Make the purchase. Spend the 12 hours. It's worth it.

I finished this in 9 hours, so the story is fairly short for a visual novel. The plot is fairly straightforward, and the characters aren't developed enough for me to feel empathy for them. The premise is interesting, but isn't fleshed out much in detail. Since this was done by Minori, I expected more. If you have never played a visual novel, and just want a taste of what it is like (style, pacing, etc), this is okay as an introductory title; however, it falls flat if you are looking for rich characters or plot which is what one comes to expect from quality visual novels.
