If you tracked your gameplay, you'd find maybe ... 70 - 80% of your time in the game is spent watching your hammer hit rocks for mining ore, or your axe hitting trees. The rest of the time is spent scrabbling for food, hiding from things, and running from things. And trying not to freeze. Not freezing is a theme in this game.
After hours of that, you've hit enough rocks to get enough things to make a better hammer, so you can hit fewer rocks. This takes the pressure off a bit, and not long later you'll have a leather vest, a tin hat, a tin axe, a backpack full of food and bandages, and you'll be ready to cross the ice to the next island. Where you will be one-hit. Tin hats aren't very good.
This should be really boring. It sounds really boring. But after lots of rock-hitting and pig stabbing, you build a shack and step inside. You feel funny. It's quiet. There's no wind. You're not scanning the area for things that one-hit you, or edible meat creatures. You're not eyeing your freezeometer. You feel safe. That's when you see you've been tense since you fired up the game. Something's always coming to kill you, if only hunger and cold, and if you're not paying attention, they'll get you. You've been a hunted animal. But now you have shelter, and some stuff, and you can think about turning the tables. Carefully.
In short, it's got the things I look for in a good survival game.
It's not perfect. It feels like it hasn't really gelled into a coherent game yet, but what it does so far ( survival ) it does well.
p.s. When you are just starting out, you'll usually encounter a giant boar and maybe a wolf or two. You will die if you wail on them with your stick. Don't panic. You have more time than you think. That giant boar will run towards you and stop. Then it will do some yoga, which apparently is what pigs do when they want to kill you. Then it will leap at where you were standing when they started their attack yoga dance. Just step to one side ... and wale on them with your stick. And repeat. Then you eat them.
The game is fun to use! Although, the face tracker won't or can't track my face. Is there a problem?

Very cool to play with and lots of fun.

What I love about dark souls is a marriage of two things: combat and atmosphere. The combat in this game is quite similar to the previous entries. Mind you, I value PVE over PVP for this series.
If I want to fight players I'm the sort who goes to mobas or FPS (though For Honor looks promising as Dark Souls moba). You will probably have read that the unique feature in this is adding weapon arts to the mix which makes fights very dynamic, fluid, and grants many combat styles despite there being a prevailing R1/parry meta (but if you play pvp, meta will always determine how well you will do, whether you choose to join the currently favored style or not). The biggest problem with pvp is that the invader is too gimped to compete. Invasions are plainly a♥♥♥♥♥♥move, but should the invader have to contend with 3 total opponents? Perhaps they should have gone the older route in disabling certain healing options.
Apart from pvp, the bosses are generally thrilling. Some are easier than others and to the point that they are somewhat disappointingly simple  like rolling invincibly by Vordt or cleaving the hell out of the Deacons, but may the lore make up for these flaws. There are cinematic fights that are also challenging such as the Abyss Watchers and truly tough and frustrating fights like the Nameless King (not to brag, I beat him at the third try, but a brand new character, I somehow died repeatedly... repeatedly 10+ until I decided to summon). Overall, I think Dark Souls 1 has the best bosses, but this one has a bit more challenge than DS2 sans DLC.
I will end this short review with the lore. I fell in love with the lore with this game. It took long enough, huh? I played every game, except for Bloodborne, and somehow it was DS3 that broke me in. I love the lore and how we can learn a story by the items and aesthetic. I did learn a few things here and there in the series’ previous installments, just the gist. This one had stronger references to the first game, so I began to form ideas of my own and wondered about ideas of others due Miyazaki’s way of telling a story according to scenery, item descriptions, and placement of NPCs and their appearance. It’s just so rich. It’s a game series like this that makes for an engaging, interpretative storytelling. I actually was very disappointed that Miyazaki stated that he was finished with the Souls series because his mind provided me with such an immersible experience.
By the way, the graphics are so damn good. I love that there are individually unique stones arranged here and there. I read some reddit post that explained it perfect. DS1 has the best bosses, DS2 has the best DLC, and DS3 has the best graphics… or something like that.

So. I noticed that people are griping about features that were removed in the older versiojns. I never saw that, and while yes, it does kinda seem like techs suck now, but flying sounds a little on the OP side. Mechs sound fun but aren't too practical for exploration.
Now, I've already completed the story and am now playing through with a second character with some items passed down from the first. Exploring is still fun even though Ive seen every planet. I've barely even tried fishing yet. And sometimes the planets can generate very strangely and give an interesting little surprise with biomes, such as bioluminescense biomes generating in volcanic planets (and ember rain always seems to hit right as I find those, heh) and other biome generation that hilariously breaks logic six ways to Sunday.
For a 2D game, some of the landscapes are downright gorgeous. You almost don't want to destroy them, but sometimes you just gotta get the unique tree type there, especially if the foliage generated in your favorite color. You could spend ages collecting them all just for the hell of it. Also geode biomes. What would be amazingly awesome is if they could generate in other colors.
Weapon progression is alright. Challenge rooms are an excellent source of good weapons, and once you start getting legendary goodies you're generally pretty well off. Personally, I've found 3 Ex Machinas on one character... My luck in video games tends to be very stupid. It's either really good or absolutely horrible. As for armor progression, you actually need to do a bit of work to get the best armor. And unless you want the Perfect Set, you need to actualkly make a decision as to how you want to play and get T5 and T6 armor to match.
If you're the creative type, GET THIS GAME. You'd be amazed at what you can do with a 2D space. Whether you're making pixel art or a home for yourself, the possibilities are endless with all the themes out there.
One of my favcorite features is how mod-friendly this game is. Me, I love mods. There's mods for mechs for those who want that back. There's mods that make the game easier or harder. There's ones that add old features and new techs. There's the Phase Shift tech mod for those who want to fly again (and go through walls and be immune to damage as a result of basically becoming a ghost). Mods that change worldgen. New races. More furniture and cosmetic items. Vehicles. Damn near EVERYTHING. Unless you're the type to prefer vanilla, go check out the Workshop for this game.
To end this off, sure, the story and armor progression can be easily rushed by mining planets of a certain tier, crafting the EPP and armor you can now make with those materials and rush the whole story, the game is far from over when the story's done. You can do whatever the hell you want. Look for planets that break logic and see just how broken it can get.  Build the base of your dreams. Pimp out your ship. Catch fish and make an aquarium. Grab critters and make a critter pen. Maybe even try to collect them all and display them. Collect pets. Collect other things. Build massive colonies with furniture looted from dungeons. Get a vehicle and go nuts with it. There's MUCH more to do than gather resources and go through the story.
And hey, it's still better than No Man's Sky!

There's very little to interact with.
Some units have an active ability, which is a singular button that does a singular thing on all your units of the said type(all that are in effective range of something for the ability - which makes it even more casual friendly). Inherently very boring to me, and requires minimal skill as it's virtually always best used immediately.
The whole game you simply playing clicking units to create in your next wave, with a sporadic ability. It all feels very much like a simple mobile game with fancier graphics.

It's easy to get lost in this pretty picturesc post-apocalyptic theme park. The graphics are gorgeous (relative), models look pretty good, nice textures. The lighting though, the LIGHTING IS NICE! I love the long cast shadows and the way the light penetrates tarps and curtains casting their color on nearby objects. There's so many post processing effects that just look so nice and sell the environment. Even with all the graphics on low, the game looks nice. The engine was a good choice.
The weather also helps to set the feel of the game. There's several grades of rain/storms, tornadoes, a really fantastic fog, and more! Terrain is pretty good, but not perfectly realistic. They should study some terrain maps and come to an understanding as to how erosion cuts into hills and mountains, that would inform their design choices better, but it's pretty good. LOD textures are pretty horrendous and they need to figure out a way to populate distant hills with the illusion of trees rather than making them♥♥♥♥♥bald when you're far enough away. Godspeed on that. The stars don't match up to a real sky so you can't navigate by them, the time cycle is too fast, so it's difficult to judge East from West by the position of the sun. You end up just getting to know the terrain anyway. Overall, the Map is small but growing.
There's no armor, but there is also no equipment damage. Food, guns, car parts, clothes, and such just grow in houses and all, like in real life, and you go and harvest them. It's a game!

I had really a lot of fun in this game - and the fact that its still somewhat active after all this years ( in a time where game servers die after a couple of years) already says a lot.
And the best news is - a new team of devs started to work again on this game ( September 2016 ).
So if you look again through your hundreds of games in your libary and dont know what to play - just give ZPS a try.

You have no idea what I've been through regarding this game.  I was one of the Kickstarter backers who put money towards this five years ago.  After five years, I expected more.  I really did.
I could go on for hours, almost as long as I've played the game itself, on all the things I hate about it.  It's really pretty, I'll give you that.  All the art, the references, the artifacts laying about, and the attention to detail in a purely visual sense is very strong.  It's meticulously crafted for the time period.  But in a point-and-click adventure game, it's kind of hard to know what's interactable and what's not when the background is so busy.  And in a 2D format, everything is warped to try and appear 3D, so your depth perception is thrown off.  Is that a hallway, an alcove, or a shelf?  Can I click on it?  WHY NOT??  I got lost in the ♥♥♥♥ing ATTIC.
Plus there's the clunky menu that (spoilers) ironically often gets in the way of the puzzle's solution.  You gotta close it to see everything in the whole screen.  ***And there's no WASD controls.***  You have to not only click on everything to use or interact with it, in an already disorienting setup, you also have to click on arbitrary points of what might be floor somewhere at some unknown distance.  If you click on something that is not floor, it will give the same message as when you inspected it the first ten times, all of which will be preachy and smarmy.  This will happen over and over, by accident.
In a game that is 90% walking and using items from your menu on things in the environment, it sure makes it hard to do those things well or differentiate from them.  That is the first big gripe, one that will break the game singlehandedly in most people's eyes.
Meanwhile, the same looping midi track is playing over and over in the background.  You'd think composers with such experience in the indie game scene (the legendary Toby ♥♥♥♥ing Fox being one of them) would have thought of making the soundtrack a little more tranquil, or just less in-your-face all the time, especially in the troll segements.  Nothing makes an obtuse, buggy, utterly garbage puzzle more infuriating than also having obnoxious band music playing on loop.  Here's a hint: loud, obnoxious music only appeals to us if it's FUNNY.  That's why Horsecatska was so popular, Mr. Roach.
And speaking of hints, hoo BOY HOWDY do we have a segue there.  The hint button is the most infuriating piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥you'll ever find in a game.  Navi from Zelda has nothing on the hint button.  At least Navi would tell you something useful some of the time, and her only flaw is that she would tell you too much too often.  But the HINT BUTTON.  It is not a hint button.  It is the greatest crime ever conceived by a developer: a feature which has no use.
The hint button does nothing.  Ever.  It's not a glitch, it's not a bug.  It just makes fun of you for clicking on the hint button.  You expected help?  In a game where nothing makes sense and the controls are garbage?  It's not like this is Zork here, we aren't typing commands into a prompt.  But apparently when you're stuck and can't find any sort of solution (and here's the kicker: (spoilers again) you are ALWAYS trapped in a room.  It is almost comical how stupid the hindrances become to your progress through this quadriplegic art mural.), it decides to say nothing of your situation and MOCK YOU FOR IT.  It's a "make fun of me" button.  For how sensitive and bleeding-heart the writers were about big game animals and ♥♥♥♥ing security cameras, they sure love to trigger people.
After a certain point, the hint button just stops saying anything.  It would make sense if it started taking things seriously as the game progresses, and only make fun of you in the opening area when things are easy and (supposedly) self-explanatory.  But nope.  Its only purpose is to antagonize you, and then cease being funny.  It's the lack the lack of being funny that gets me.  It's like every piece of progress punishes you for you for daring to proceed, in the only way possible, by design.
You noticed the redundant words up there just now?  Get used to it.  There are grammatical errors and copy flubs throughout.  In a text-heavy game, just within the first few sessions of me playing, I've found six textual and punctual errors in the narrative prompt itself.  Missing periods, repeating repeating text, and just and just failed grammar in general
This has absolutely nothing to do with the characters' spoken words or typing quirks either, both of which are essential spice to the dialogue both here and in this game's source material.  This is just the writers being careless and not as diligent as I, which is a shame since they are supposedly older, more professional, and should just ♥♥♥♥ing know better.  This game was written in 2012 goddammit.  You should have found these by now in your last half a ♥♥♥♥ing year of bug testing.  I certainly noticed and I've only had the game for two days.
The very last question of this game, since it was set in the Homestuck universe(s), is "Is it funny?"  Well, it wasn't written with the sharp, cynical, nihilistic wit of Hussie, so no.  It was written by some vegetarian Tumblrite or something when Hussie couldn't give enough of a♥♥♥♥♥♥about his own game to bother after the first developer he chose to make this game embezzled him and then his father died.  I guess your ghost writer being a total pansy is the lesser of two evils.  They still burned through the better part of two million dollars pushing this platinum turd out on their own.
Oh, and did we mention that after the five years of development hell, the game was delayed another eight months for bug testing?  AND IT'S STILL BUGGY.  Eight months is enough to create a whole damn game, and they couldn't even get the screen to center properly in that time.  I CAN SEE ANOTHER PANEL FROM DAMMEK'S LIVING ROOM IF I WALK AROUND TOO MUCH.
You wanna see what kind of game the Homestuck fandom makes?  This is it.  All doodle, no substance, and definitely zero fun.  Just like the SJWs who were fallen back upon to create it.
I mean, in conclusion, I should have expected as much.  This game was in development hell for several years, been through three developing houses essentially, and the only thing that's stayed true since the start was the gorgeous concept art which is the strongest point of the whole game.  Hell, I don't think they'll even need a "making-of art book" for their backers since the whole game is basically an interactive, annoying, hard-to-navigate art book that shouts preachy vegetarian slogans at you whenever you click on one of the taxidermied trophies.  Of which there are many.
Please, for the love of God do not buy this game.  Not until several patches have been made, preferrably ones with the words "we're sorry" in it.

Hiveswap is a really fun game that blends the humor of Homestuck, the puzzles of adventure games and a surprisingly moving story into a stellar first act.
I'm someone who picked up Homestuck late so I didn't spend the years waiting for it to finally come out. I read it and then saw a trailer for it a few months later. That said I was very excited but also knew how the game was probably going to be utter garbage. It only makes sense. So I'm really happy that this game actually really nails what made me fall in love with Homestuck while not leaning so heavily on it to collapse.
Joey Claire is a fantastic main character, isntatlly likable as she looks through her room, remembering good times and bad as she looks through her house. Her relation with her brother is sometimes contentious, but ultimately loving. Seeing her naviagate her feelings for her father, her mother and the relationships she might have in the future was honestly one of the most interesting parts of the game. I put so many items together to see if it revealed another tidbit.
That's not to say their isn't a great sci-fi plot going on. If you can swallow that their are suddenly monsters out of nowhere you'll have a lot of fun. Newcomers will love learning their first tidbits of the world while longtime fans will enjoy all the little nods to things from the comic. I don't want to spoil much but there's a lot of exciting stuff going on.
The puzzles are good, never feeling like the worst of adventure games, solutions always makes sense. Having combat be it's own puzzle is great and removing the risk of dying there is a smart decision allowing you to play around to find a solution or just to find the perfect bad pun attack name. The second half gets a bit more obtuse but not to a point of being that difficult.
The art is incredible. Beautiful 2D animation and backgrounds make the homes of the characters feel lived in and very unique. You'll want to look at everything and you basically can. Little touches such as the way the kids draw or the toys they leave behind make their world feel so much more real and really bring this to the next level.
Basically this is a great game that worls great for old and new fans.

Story's a bit garbage, but the Arkham-esque gameplay is really fun.  The open world stealth and combat has been so good it's actually pulled me away from Far Cry for a while.  And getting to play Orc Political Simulator on top of that is simply fantastic.
You can carefully build a particular orc up all the way to warchief just to tear him down for the epic rune.  You can farm on a larger scale, leaving captains untouched until they hit the level cap and then WHAM.  You can safeguard your favorites, branded or unbranded (though the latter takes a little more care), moving them into whatever position of power you deem appropriate.  You can prune like a gardener, weeding out captains with skills you don't like.  You can pick one particular orc to terrorize over and over just because you can (and if it's a warchief whose bodyguards all share the same fear, all the better).  Or you can decide to clear the slate and go on a massive murder spree, just to get a new batch to mess with all over again.
You can even decide to just sit and watch who does well on their own and who gets smacked down.  You'll get crazy stuff like an orc with a flaming weapon deciding to duel another captain with a fear - or hate - of burns.  An orc without monster slayer who decides to go hunt a graug with only a pack of basic warriors at his back.  Or, the most baffling and somehow most common oddity, an archer who decides he really wants to fight with that other captain that has invulnerability to ranged.  Unless he's also got flaming weapon or explosive arrow, you can guess how that works out.

I would not recommed this game in its current state.
Pros:
-Attractive game
-Many different weapons to unlock and upgrade
-Cheap
-6 different game modes and varying options for hosting servers
-Has a few single-player missions.
Cons:
-This game currently has a terrible player base. It is littered with under 13 year olds that spam the chat, randomly leave mid-game, and last but not least, they 'roast' you because you're getting 'beef' with their 'bros'.
-In this game you earn xp to unlock new weapons and level up. However once you get to level 25 or so, it becomes difficult to earn these levels, simply because of this: In the game you have an xp multiplier. The xp multiplier increases for certain things. If you have wind on high, it increases. If you have maps on random, it increases. If you have a certain gamemode (rebound) it increases. And last but not least, if you have the one weapon mod on, which basically doesn't let you choose weapons but instead gives you one random weapon, then the xp multiplier increases.
This system means you can't play the game in the way that you will enjoy, because the xp multiplier will be at 0.58x if you have certain server settings on. meaning, if you earn 20xp, you will be given 10xp instead.
-A few of the weapons are very silly, and by silly, I mean random. Now random isn't always a bad thing... However in this games case, it is. For example, a certain weapon called molehill: Molehill is a weapon that you shoot underground, it will then rise up in a totally random direction and geometry, meaning, if you shoot the weapon towards your enemy (aiming under ground), it is very possible that it could come back at you and hit you instead.
There are a wide variety of these random-path weapons, making the game displeasing in certain situations.
Well, there you have it folks, I suggest NOT to buy this game in its current state. Maybe a year later the developers may see this and make this game glorious, but today I am afraid, is not that day.

Takes a fairly simple set of mechanics which allows you to spotaneously clone and swap to a new version of yourself, and uses it to create a whole slew of often very clever puzzles. (As well as a very rapid if somewhat disconcerting method of getting around.)
If that was all it was then this game would be good, but there is a lot more here, it looks fantastic, the sound is suitably ambient and responds well to the events of the game, and the universe its set in is surprisingly fleshed out considering you are stumbling thorugh a dead space ship with only a few terminals to inform you. It makes me curious about what else is going on in that world, on the other stations, on Earth etc.
On top of all that, the story delves in to open scientific questions and philosophy regarding the mind, aliens, mortality, etc. It reminds me a lot of the book Solaris by Stannislaw Lem, and has a bunch of the same themes.
It takes about 4 hours to get through, much longer if you want the extremely tricky achievements that flesh out more of the world, but Ive already played through once more and will probably do so more times when Ive forgotten enough of the solutions and situations it throws at you again.
Its a fantastic game, atmospheric, compelling, even on its surface its a very satisfying puzzler, but if you want to look in to it more its about as deep as any game ever has been.

I just bought the game recently, after reading all the reviews posted on Steam, which were not very good. English is not my mother tongue, so my apologies in advance about it.
I'm not very demanding about the graphic quality (in fact, I play in medium configuration level, just imagine) and find them acceptable for the price of the game. I agree that they are not the last generation, but by the type of game and the price, I see them appropriate.
I am not a reviewer, but since SP2 was added, in which they have solved most of the problems users complained about months ago and because nobody has dared to make a positive assessment, I have decided to publish this comment.
The game has some high hardware requirements, but to medium configurations it runs well and I have not found any bugs. The game is user friendly and the learning curve is simple. I have played a lot of ATC games and although this is not the most professional I have tried, it is nice to be able to play without having to write endless cryptic commands. In addition, compared to most, obviously (and despite the low quality some complain), the graphical interface is very nice. It is not a professional game, but casual instead, and funny.
Here, some suggestions about my experience in this kind of games. Most should be easy to implement in a future SP:
- I will love to have a blinking PAUSE signal when I have the game paused.
- A skipping time button when you found your airport with no planes till the next strip together with (not instead) the accelerated time.
- Keyboard shortcuts for the commands. I mean, after you click in a plane or plane strip and get the callsign, would be lovely that the commands were numbered and you can press 1 for “Taxi to”, 2 for “Cleared for”, etc… and later 1, 2 or 3 again for the second row of orders (Runways if you had choose “Taxi to”, for example). The use of the ENTER key as "Send" would also be advisable.

This game is an intensely satisfying rogue-like adventure with a minimalistic story littered with vague symbolism that must be seen by winning several times in different ways. If you've never played it and have avoided spoilers you will likely "finish" the campaign several times before you unlock the real final levels, and then the game get's far more challenging. You have to be smart and use the game's mechanics to your advantage if you want to have a chance, and since wins constantly unlock new items and greater levels of challenge the game grows with your experience until it becomes a total mess of varied items, effects, and enemies. You must use the keys, bombs, and coins you collect carefully in order to succeed.
Combat boils down to two basic elements: realtime bullet-Hell dodging and twin-stick shooting. Hit enemies with your tears and don't let them hit you with themselves nor tears of their own. Simple, right? But then there's the other aspect of play: stuff. Passive items, charge-holding items, trinkets, and consumable pills and cards can change how your tears travel, replace them with a room-traversing beam or bombs, and effect your health, speed, damage, and firing rate. No two things in this game have the same effect and all of it is interesting, though some combinations are strictly horrible and screw you over big time. Make sure you learn what everything does while the game is still easy or you'll be jumping to the wiki constantly.
Furthermore, different characters in the game have different ways of recovering health, shoot tears differently, start with unique things, and must be used to complete the game for more achievements and unlocks independent of what you've done with the other characters.
The normal and hard modes are the traditional meat of the game, and require you to traverse through rooms blindly as you search for the treasure room that contains one extremely helpful item, the shop room where you can buy more items with coins, and the boss room you need to pass to progress of each floor, potentially discovering arcades for gambling, dice rooms for randomly changing all kinds of things, bedrooms for recovering health, crawl spaces below rocks with extra rewards, and sacrifice rooms for those who aren't particulary attached to their lives. Moving through a particular run fast enough will reveal secret bonus challenges in their own rooms, and devil or angel rooms can spawn if you perform certain actions before beating a boss. Here's a hint: try not to take too many hits. Not taking damage on a floor is extremely helpful here.
Then there's greed mode, which is just a massive store attached to an arena room with a couple of treasure rooms, a cursed room, and a lot of enemies. There are ten main waves per floor and one bonus wave, the first ten rewarding you with coins and the bonus wave unlocking a devil or angel room. Be warned that the final boss for greed mode is insanely tanky. You have to be damn good at this game before you can actually beat this mode.
Finally there are easter eggs in the menu you can find that will completely change the gameplay even more. I won't spoil what they are or how to find them, but I will tell you that some of them lock achievements so be mindful of that.
And that's just the vanilla game.
There is an annoying fog effect in the base game that I refuse to bother with, but that's totally fine because there's a website dedicated to mods for this game, and playing with mods does NOT turn off achievements nor unlocks. I recommend you get the Afterbirth expansion, and I'm certainly getting Afterbirth+ when it comes out, because mod support is only going to get better with that release and the UNDERTALE mod is already fantastic. There are mods for player characters, models, statistical information, tooltips for special rooms, new special rooms, and all manner of cosmetic changes so the game can basically be whatever you want it to be.
My biggest gripe is that the local coop feature is a bit limited, but as a singleplayer experience this game rules.

I played the game back when it was in Early Access and the main thing I enjoyed about it was how open it was. The only thing standing between you and the rest of the universe were some upgrades you needed to make to your ship. It was a more casual experience, though you would have to face bosses to progress.
Now, the experience has changed for both better and worse, in my opinion. The initual quest line to repair your ship is non-negotiable without mods or other cheats. You're stuck orbiting a single planet until you go through the 3-5 quests necessary to get your ship repaired. At the end of that quest line is a dungeon (called "missions" in Starbound) that you have to beat without dying, otherwise you'll have to start over. There is a save point near the end of it, at least, but you still have to make it to that save point before you can skip past all the stuff you slogged through before.
I have a huge issue with this because of where the game was in Early Access. It felt very restrictive when they first introduced quests, and it still feels that way far too early in the game.
Fortunately, after you complete the initial quests and mission, you at least get the ability to browse the planets closest to your current location. The real meat of Starbound is its collection of planets with randomly generated creatures and places to explore. You can even customize one of these planets to make your own homestead and village. They've done a much better job of supplying you with the tools to do that, thanks to the work they did in Early Access.
You also have  ship to customize. It starts out small but gradually you will make it larger and  can make the interior look as weird as you want. I fell in love with the game because of this feature. Having your custom base go with you as you travel the cosmos is a huge plus.
There is an option to skip random quests that come up, so you're not forced to take every quest you come across. I appreciate that, because right now all I want to do is explore. I'll feel the weight and responsibility of the main storyline later. Right now, I just want to club cute animals and take their loot.
I can't make a solid comparison between this and No Man's Sky, because I haven't played the latter. But I can say that with the way that No Man's Sky was described, they were more than likely aiming for a 3D version of Starbound. If you feel like NMS is missing several key space exploration elements, I recommend giving Starbound a try. It has a plot and quests for people who need that in their exploration games, but it also has nearly unlimited possibilities for exploration and colonization.

I stocked up so many hours due to playing this game alot during the Early Access phase, eagerly waiting for better changes. Some updates during Early Access required you to start a new save altogether, so that played a huge part in me wasting my time on this thing.
The story mode for this game was obviously hacked together in a couple of months before the final release since the developers realised that they had to push out the game from Early Access one way or the other.
The campaign/story revolved around retrieving gemstones that would represent each race.
*There are no missions revolving around Humans (im not counting the intro because that barely had any gameplay) or Novakids, which means that only 5 of the 7 races in-game have the proper representation in terms of quests and missions.
Novakids have no presence in the story altogether.
Progression involves you tediously scanning pieces of furniture from the settlements of each* faction to unlock their missions and upgrading your EPP (some weird lookin life support device on your back that you have to cover up with cosmetic vanity items.) so you can hop to planets that have "harsher" conditions.
The monsters you encounter on the overworlds barely pose a threat, since the game conditions you to fight in a way that leaves the enemy no chance to even hit you.
Surviving enemy attacks relies on you walking backwards and trying to bonk them back with a sword constantly with anything you have. Enemies that can actually put you in danger are just outnumbered by the amounts of mediocre enemies this game throws on you. The monsters that are the most entertaining to fight against aren't randomly generated.
The above problem is exempt from boss battles.
Some of the boss fights you encounter in the missions of the story mode are probably the only fun thing that you are going to get to fight, but there are too little of those in the game, and that statement only goes for SOME of the boss battles in the game.
I feel like the game could've used more missions and bosses.
The only interesting part about this game for me was just collecting equipment by strolling around the surface of every planet I came across.
Collecting the equipment was fun compared to actually using it, take this statement as you will.
Fishing and fossils are pointless fluff.
If you are one of those types of people that get joy and fun out of dressing up your character, get this game.
If you are looking for gameplay that can rival Terraria, you aren't going to find it from this game.

The pros heavily outweigh the cons, but there's still something to say about them:
It's a good idea, with some deep lore hidden here and there... But the concept of running around and scanning things just to fill up some progress bar doesn't really appeal to me.
Although each race is unique, with their own cultures and traditions that you continually unravel, scanning a few sprites to progress makes it feel all a bit shallow.
Now I may not have an incredible, high-tier computer but it should be capable to handle these graphics.
The main problem for this comes from the weather and other effects. As soon as that rain falls or that snowstorm brews, your frame rate drops.
A small issue none the less, but still something to look into.
(in co-op, at least)
A friend and I jumped into this game from the very beginning until the end, and, I don't know about him, but I really did admire this game; with the space setting, beautiful graphics and smooth combat... However, with two people, it was just too easy... I admit there was one boss where we struggled, but once we figured out what armour was, the rest of the game was a cake walk. Everything took a single try and it would be over before we really got to enjoy the fight... It felt somewhat incomplete when we finished the game.
I suggest adding a new, harder difficulty where the enemies you face are more and more powerful (with more HP or damage...), the more players there are.
In conclusion, although I may just be a little picky for what already is an incredible game, there are still some things that can be worked on and improved.
These comments aside, I would still recommend this incredible game to anyone who even shows the slightest interest in this genre; and I will continue playing it, hoping, maybe one day, there may be an update to fix all these small problems.
Or I might just have to suck it up...

Bastion is a fun little gem of a game from a tiny team of passionate developers. It is an isometric action adventure RPG that tells the story of the Kid in the aftermath of a disaster called the Calamity.
There are three things that instantly stand out as you start a new game:
As mentioned above, Bastion is an RPG. The gameplay is pretty run and gun. You kill and roll your way from Point A to Point B, get what you need and fly back to your home base. You are introduced to several weapons throughout the game, which are upgradeable. You can acquire various passive buffs and you can buff up the enemies for extra XP. The game gets increasingly fun as you unlock more things. Levelling up can take a while though.
Bastion has a decent story with extremely well written dialogue. The story is short (3-4 hours) and tight and does not overstay its welcome. It feels like it ends exactly when it needs to. There's also New Game+ and Score Attack mode. Pretty self-explanatory.
Overall, Bastion comes off as a charming little game that oozes art, love and passion from each of its frames. Defeinitely pick it up either on sale or at full price as soon as you can.

Savage Lands is a fantasy, survival, crafting/building game. Reminiscent of games like RUST, and ARK, or even at times, similar to games like Minecraft. Savage Lands features some realy wonderful aspects, and a challenge that is sure to be rewarding when you succeed. You're stranded on an island (procedurally generated) and it's COLD! As you try to survive, you must gather wood, stone, ores, and leathers to build fires (for keeping warm), structures (again, helps you stay warm, and lets you build a base of operations), tools, weapons, armor, and lots of other items. The crafting is robust, and fulfilling. The gathering is beautiful and less monotenous than games like Minecraft. As you start to get better tools, weapons, armor, and a base, you are able to take on bigger challenges, and eventually, you move on to different areas and really lets you feel progression.
Pro's:
Strong Survival Elements (You are constantly getting cold and will die if you don't warm up. Clothes, and fires, and houses help keep you warm)
Strong RPG Elements (build weapons, and armors, and fight enemies and get stronger to take on stronger enemies!)
Great Multiplayer (Whether playing with friends, or strangers, the multiplayer is VERY rewarding and fun. Surviving is always better with a partner.)
Fun Server System (You can create your own server and make it public, you can turn PvP on or off for extra challenges and even a fun role playing (pretending you're the actual character, not a player in the game, but the person surviving) experience!
Con's:
VERY High system requirements ***
Game is not very optimized (Even on low graphics settings, you still may experience some lag or hang ups)  ***
Secondary Notes: (not pro's or cons)
Frequent updates and patches (with a timer on the main menu showing when the next update will be) show that the devs are active and trying to offer the best game they can. Sadly, they aren't working on some very important things, like optimizing the performance. Also, because of the poor perfomance on most machines, some people are unable to play (I can play just fine, but I was not able to play with my brother) and this makes some people upset that they can't play with friends, or even they can't play themselves. The game is absolutely terrific, but it requires an omnipotent machine to play.
***EDITS
The system requirements have been fixed, and this game is far less taxing on your system. They've also worked wonders with optimization as well. This game is better now than it was when I purchased it!

I would not recommed this game in its current state.
Pros:
-Attractive game
-Many different weapons to unlock and upgrade
-Cheap
-6 different game modes and varying options for hosting servers
-Has a few single-player missions.
Cons:
-This game currently has a terrible player base. It is littered with under 13 year olds that spam the chat, randomly leave mid-game, and last but not least, they 'roast' you because you're getting 'beef' with their 'bros'.
-In this game you earn xp to unlock new weapons and level up. However once you get to level 25 or so, it becomes difficult to earn these levels, simply because of this: In the game you have an xp multiplier. The xp multiplier increases for certain things. If you have wind on high, it increases. If you have maps on random, it increases. If you have a certain gamemode (rebound) it increases. And last but not least, if you have the one weapon mod on, which basically doesn't let you choose weapons but instead gives you one random weapon, then the xp multiplier increases.
This system means you can't play the game in the way that you will enjoy, because the xp multiplier will be at 0.58x if you have certain server settings on. meaning, if you earn 20xp, you will be given 10xp instead.
-A few of the weapons are very silly, and by silly, I mean random. Now random isn't always a bad thing... However in this games case, it is. For example, a certain weapon called molehill: Molehill is a weapon that you shoot underground, it will then rise up in a totally random direction and geometry, meaning, if you shoot the weapon towards your enemy (aiming under ground), it is very possible that it could come back at you and hit you instead.
There are a wide variety of these random-path weapons, making the game displeasing in certain situations.
Well, there you have it folks, I suggest NOT to buy this game in its current state. Maybe a year later the developers may see this and make this game glorious, but today I am afraid, is not that day.

If you were given the power to instantly create a clone out of nowhere and be able swap bodies with it at will...
Don't you think it's wrong to just swap bodies without the clone's consent? But does it even HAVE the capacity to get offended? Does it even HAVE a "self" to begin with? Since it's technically just a copy of you in space? Does it even matter?
The game mechanics of The Swapper ties in well with it's style of narrative by showing the consequences of owning the power I mentioned. By tackling philosophical themes like "the self" and conciousness, The Swapper offers a sad yet innocent story that may or may not get you thinking about your actions. The visuals also add up to this theme with it's dark atmospheric motif with lots of eerily realistic textures decorating the environments... Beautifully put together and no heavy hardware required in order to run it smoothly.
The level designs are excellent~
The Swapper's spacial reasoning puzzles feel very similar to Portal, There are times when you think that the level just seems impossible to solve, but you know damn well in the back of your head that you just need to git gud.
So in my opinion, if you love the Portal franchise, you'll love The Swapper~
Happy Swapping~

Story's a bit garbage, but the Arkham-esque gameplay is really fun.  The open world stealth and combat has been so good it's actually pulled me away from Far Cry for a while.  And getting to play Orc Political Simulator on top of that is simply fantastic.
You can carefully build a particular orc up all the way to warchief just to tear him down for the epic rune.  You can farm on a larger scale, leaving captains untouched until they hit the level cap and then WHAM.  You can safeguard your favorites, branded or unbranded (though the latter takes a little more care), moving them into whatever position of power you deem appropriate.  You can prune like a gardener, weeding out captains with skills you don't like.  You can pick one particular orc to terrorize over and over just because you can (and if it's a warchief whose bodyguards all share the same fear, all the better).  Or you can decide to clear the slate and go on a massive murder spree, just to get a new batch to mess with all over again.
You can even decide to just sit and watch who does well on their own and who gets smacked down.  You'll get crazy stuff like an orc with a flaming weapon deciding to duel another captain with a fear - or hate - of burns.  An orc without monster slayer who decides to go hunt a graug with only a pack of basic warriors at his back.  Or, the most baffling and somehow most common oddity, an archer who decides he really wants to fight with that other captain that has invulnerability to ranged.  Unless he's also got flaming weapon or explosive arrow, you can guess how that works out.

This game I would say is unique and interesting.... but I wouldn't reccomend buying it quite yet.
All in all, stranded deep is a pretty fun game. You get to survive, like in Castaway! You can even find an in-game equivalent of Wilson! Sure, it has a lot of bugs, but they will all eventually get ironed out. The game is in early access right now.
The main reason I reccomend waiting on Stranded Deep is, when it comes down to it, there isn't really a large amount to do in-game yet. Your actual crafting is severely limited, letting you only build crude tools and basic homes. The only way to get anything really useful is to scavenge from wrecks in the ocean, and that is extremely time consuming. You have to paddle a long ways to another island, then swim around it, dodging the sharks and searching for more wrecks. Then, once you've cleaned it out and crammed what you can into your extremely small inventory, you'll go dump it back on your home island and repeat the process. It quickly loses its appeal after searching five ships and only finding some compasses and gas tanks. You can travel the ocean faster by building a speedboat, but this first requires discovering around 6 engine parts from- you guessed it- wrecks.
Stranded Deep currently lacks very much to make it interesting, as all you do is beat coconuts on rocks and scavenge from ships, and occasionally try to fight a shark before realising you're an idiot for trying to fight a shark with a pocketknife. The game has a TON of potential, and seeing as how it's only on version 0.2, the developers are very likely to add in more engaging activities to keep it interesting. So, I would reccomend getting Stranded Deep- but only once the game has recieved some more content.
Also, killing sharks with a pocketknife is awesome.

I kind of thought I was done with zombies.  They're everywhere these days.  TV, movies, and of course, video games.  State of Decay uses them a bit differently, though.  Most zombie games (L4D, Resident Evil, etc) use zombies as cannon fodder, and arm you to the teeth so you can mow down hordes of the undead and feel like a real badass.  In SoD, you feel all too human, for the most part.  A single zombie? Pssh, please.  Two zombies? Okay, still not a big deal, but I better make sure one doesn't get behind me.  Three zombies?  Might be better to leave.  Five zombies?  Screw this, I'm out,
The game is about surviving, and combat is a last resort.  As an indie game, the combat is actually a little clunky, and things tend to get janky at times: zombies (and you) will occasionally clip through walls or fall through the world, or you may dart forward two or three feet, but most of the time it's pretty solid.
If you want to actually feel like an average Joe in the zombie apocalypse, pick this one up.

The pros heavily outweigh the cons, but there's still something to say about them:
It's a good idea, with some deep lore hidden here and there... But the concept of running around and scanning things just to fill up some progress bar doesn't really appeal to me.
Although each race is unique, with their own cultures and traditions that you continually unravel, scanning a few sprites to progress makes it feel all a bit shallow.
Now I may not have an incredible, high-tier computer but it should be capable to handle these graphics.
The main problem for this comes from the weather and other effects. As soon as that rain falls or that snowstorm brews, your frame rate drops.
A small issue none the less, but still something to look into.
(in co-op, at least)
A friend and I jumped into this game from the very beginning until the end, and, I don't know about him, but I really did admire this game; with the space setting, beautiful graphics and smooth combat... However, with two people, it was just too easy... I admit there was one boss where we struggled, but once we figured out what armour was, the rest of the game was a cake walk. Everything took a single try and it would be over before we really got to enjoy the fight... It felt somewhat incomplete when we finished the game.
I suggest adding a new, harder difficulty where the enemies you face are more and more powerful (with more HP or damage...), the more players there are.
In conclusion, although I may just be a little picky for what already is an incredible game, there are still some things that can be worked on and improved.
These comments aside, I would still recommend this incredible game to anyone who even shows the slightest interest in this genre; and I will continue playing it, hoping, maybe one day, there may be an update to fix all these small problems.
Or I might just have to suck it up...

(Keep in mind that I have over 100 hours on Origin and another 100 hours on Xbox, with a total of 9 full playthroughs across all three games with plenty more playthroughs on the other games.)
I have tons of games in my library and love most of them, I've been holding off reviewing a game until I really felt I understood every aspect of the game and done all there is to do. Mass Effect is my absolute favorite series and will be until my death, it is an amazing game and has a beautifully crafted storyline. In this review I will go into detail on most aspects of the game and will explain both the good parts of the game as well as the shortcomings of it. I will keep this review as spoiler free as possible as well.
Right from the beginning of the game, even in the character creation, you feel like you are really in this universe. It really immerses you into the world and lore of the game. As you play through the game the storyline may seem to slow a bit as you’re doing your side quests and exploration but it will always feel like you’re doing something to help advance personal storylines of people that will play some role in Shepard’s mission. As you play through the other games in this series these storylines arc out more and more and intertwine in ways that you wouldn’t imagine. It is truly the single best part of the game and completely makes the game.
The gameplay can be sort of clunky at times, especially during fights. The cover mechanic is a nice feature and is prevalent in all three games but can be glitch and you can end up doing something that’ll get you killed on accident. Perhaps the single worst part of this game is the driving and exploring in the M35 Mako which is the car you’ll find yourself in very frequently. It is the only thing that makes me dread another playthrough. The control scheme for it is very clunky and takes a LOT of practice to eventually get down. Other than that, the questing and interaction with NPC’s feels very natural and seamless. Everything that happens is there for a reason and nothing really feels out of place.
For a late 2007 game the graphics are pretty much on par and there isn’t too much to praise or criticize. Personally I don’t pay much attention to graphics and care a lot more about storyline and gameplay. Even though the textures and graphics aren’t that good the lore and storyline more than make up for the lack of amazing graphics.
The lore of this game is completely amazing and in-depth. There is so much to the lore in this game that even I, someone who has read three of the four books and read the codex multiple times, still doesn’t know everything there is to know. Everything that has happened in the game has some amount of information behind it. I could go on for hours about all the technology and alien races in the game but I intend to keep this review somewhat short. I honestly can’t explain everything there is, the only way to truly experience is to play it for yourself.
Rating: 9.5/10

I just got this for a couple of bucks, and after not playing it for several years, I got to say that this game has aged quite well in my opinion. And now,  let's talk about the heart of this game, and what makes it so special; the expanding, interesting, epic and completely immersive story filled with fully fleshed characters that you care about, amazing plot-twists, and an open ended narrative. This is what makes the ME series so special, along with it's bigger-than life space opera setting. Finally, I have to say that this game is a bargain. It offers at least 30 hours of gameplay, and if you explore every little corner and do every single side quests, those 30 hours could easily stretch to 50. Get this thing ASAP.

Bastion is a fun little gem of a game from a tiny team of passionate developers. It is an isometric action adventure RPG that tells the story of the Kid in the aftermath of a disaster called the Calamity.
There are three things that instantly stand out as you start a new game:
As mentioned above, Bastion is an RPG. The gameplay is pretty run and gun. You kill and roll your way from Point A to Point B, get what you need and fly back to your home base. You are introduced to several weapons throughout the game, which are upgradeable. You can acquire various passive buffs and you can buff up the enemies for extra XP. The game gets increasingly fun as you unlock more things. Levelling up can take a while though.
Bastion has a decent story with extremely well written dialogue. The story is short (3-4 hours) and tight and does not overstay its welcome. It feels like it ends exactly when it needs to. There's also New Game+ and Score Attack mode. Pretty self-explanatory.
Overall, Bastion comes off as a charming little game that oozes art, love and passion from each of its frames. Defeinitely pick it up either on sale or at full price as soon as you can.

If you played BG1 or BG2, you are familiar with this style of game.  The team at Obsidian however put their own spin on the genre and fixed a lot of the rule problems from the older D&D games.  This makes for a pleasurable and dynamic experience where you do not feel bottlenecked into picking certain classes or making complex min/max class combos just so you can rule the day.  Combine that with the fact you can customize your party with unique adventures and generated ones at taverns, and a very cool stronghold system with a 15 level dungeon below introducing challenges and breaking up the questing monotone, and you have a solid game experience worth every penny.  Personally my biggest problem is the sequal isn't here yet!  I can't wait to see what they do beyond level 12 and if they have plans to introduce prestige classes.  They have my money!

When considering Pillars of Eternity, you should think of games such as the Baldur's Gate series, the Icewind Dale series, or even Planescape: Torment, for this is the company this game keeps.  If you're a fan of old-school D&D type CRPG's, this one is for you, but be warned!  There is a lot of dialogue - also an old-school CRPG staple.  Approaching this game with the usual "choose whatever response you must to continue" whilst barely skimming the text could have detrimental affects to your gameplay experience, as choices affect how your story plays out!
Created using the Unity game engine, the game works smoothly.  While others may have experienced issues, I have not, especially since the release of the first patch, which corrected a few major bugs.
Let's talk numbers.  More specifically, the game has a pretty heavy framework of statistics, as most everything in the game is represented by a number.  Skills, combat (rolls, etc.)...most everything in a check of some sort, comparing the abilities of a character in your party against competing "rolls".  It is a pretty heft (and intricate) framework, and sometimes it can be a little confusing - especially if you do not understand the defensive rolls, which I myself had to take a good deal of time to wrap my head around.
Last, but not least, expect to be treated to a very interesting, original, and well-written story.  This game is for those who enjoy the journey just as much as reaching the end of it.  I would encourage you to sink yourself into the lore through the many notes, books, and pieces of dialogue in the world.  This game truly is a work of art.

This game quite simply sets new high standards in the world of computer RPGs.
If you were into old school cRPGs, you must absolutely play it (old gamer from the times of Ultima VII, Baldur's Gate and Planescape Torment here...). But even if you never played one of those games, you should definitely play Pillars of Eternity as well. Because it does much more than just offering an old formula: it innovates and rethinks an old formula to offer a new modern RPG experience.
Games like this tell you what an incredible experience you can have by investing into amazing writing quality over banal voiced lines, incredible stories over mainstream movie-like tropes, hand-painted landscapes over flashy 3D and FX, world building and immersion over cheesy entertainment. It's the difference between being amused by something and being fascinated and involved by something. There's nothing wrong in being amused, but you got to try the difference once in a while...

The mechanics of this simulator is pretty spot on, it's more realistic and much less "gamey" than others I have used.  As others have stated the graphics are pretty much Google Earth pics with a simulator played atop it, not really a negative in my book short of the pictures of planes on the runway that aren't really there, just part of the Google picture capture.
That said, there are a few bugs that make playing Frustrating as these bugs are mainly with the scoring.  Each successful action nets you only 10 points but every negative action costs  you 500.  I'll have the occassional plane that will never leave the terminal and every new plane that enters or exits a nearby terminal to that stuck plane costs my 500 points due to hazard warnings.  LAX is riddled with departure and arrival scoring bugs and they get a bit quirky because they're hit and miss when you get the hazard hit.  If I've got a plane on 7L lined up and waiting with a plane landing on 7R I get hit with a penalty.  If I've got a plane taking off on 6R and one landing on 7R I get hit with a hazard penalty.
If you completely ignore the scoring (which is the biggest negative to this sim) it is fun to play, especially managing the ground traffic.  I've never been in the positive numbers due to these scoring bugs, which is BIG negative experience to this sim.
Overall, I'm giving it a thumbs up simply because I do enjoy playing this app and hope the developers give the scoring another pass and fix these bugs.

If you knew that the world was going to end soon, how would you want to spend your remaining time? What would change for you, how would your priorities shift? Assuming you'd find an opportunity to escape, would you choose a future of perpetual narrow walls and cramped spaces over a short time of ultimate freedom followed by certain doom?
For the people living in the world of
, these questions are
.
delivers the English release of this 2009 title by
to Steam.
is a kinetic novel (a story without choices or gameplay) about the last few people on a
. Its most unique selling point compared to similar titles is its visual presentation: Instead of the waist-up character sprites positioned in front of static backgrounds that we are used to from most modern visual novels, it relies almost entirely on scene-by-scene
,
carefully designed to take character positions and camera perspectives into account. This gives the experience a very cinematic feel, quite literally reminiscent of movies, compared to other titles of its kind. Most scenes also features blinking eyes and lip syncing with the Japanese voices, which makes it impressively lively.
Needless to say, the asset quality is
, starting with the backgrounds ranging from the
to the
. The same attention to detail extends to the characters who, despite the multitude of poses and perspectives, always appear consistent, unique, and alive. From what I can tell as someone who does not speak Japanese, the voices really fit well, and coupled with the competent sound design and the soundtrack by Tenmon (if you happen to enjoy Makoto Shinkai's movies: yes,
Tenmon), which expands a small number of recurring motifs into a
, this is an aural experience that you are unlikely to forget.
The story revolves around Warrant officer
and his assignment to guard a remote research facility during the planet's final moments. A peculiar (but largely unspecified) astronomical phenomenon is going to wipe out all life on Earth, and humanity is putting the finishing touches on a centennial plan to migrate into space and search for a new home. One component of this plan are the felixes, genetically engineered superhumans whose intellect propels scientific progress far beyond its normal pace. However, there are dissenting voices claiming that humanity should face its ultimate fate head-on instead of trying to escape, so military protection is granted to essential actors within the plan – in particular to Sion, the supreme felix, mastermind behind the giant starships and humanity's savior.
The central themes of
include destiny and free will as well as the morality of living one's life for someone else. Ryou, as the self-described "military's attack dog," and Sion, as the people's only hope to keep on living, are both so devoted to their duties that they have fallen out of touch with
. Circumstances force them to confront their deeply buried sense of self and be thrust before the
: to keep on living in the narrow golden cages of their own design, or to choose the ultimate act of defiance and experience the freedom and joy that they had always denied themselves, living life to the fullest until the curtain falls.
The writing tends to focus on character interaction and personal growth over story complexity –
is all about the human condition, not about hard sci-fi. In fact, even the scientific details of the end of the world are almost completely glossed over. If you are looking for an apocalyptic sci-fi story with cool technology, this isn't it. Rather, the focus on the characters is so strong that it could be described as downright melodramatic in parts, insofar as that can be a good thing. It features countless
,
,

that easily smooth over the fact that some of the tension maybe could have been resolved in easier ways, or that there's a certain degree of plot convenience constructing the situations that are most interesting for the characters. It all ends up feeling very complete and satisfying.
All in all, I can recommend
without much in the way of caveats. If you dislike visual novels or anime-style art, odds are you have not read this far down. If you like visual novels but you're not sure if this one is worth your time, my answer is that it is. I also recommend avoiding playtime estimates. Reading speed varies from person to person anyway, but the later parts of this story work best if you can empathize with the sense of impending dread that the characters are feeling. For them, any day, any moment, could be the last one. It'll be more fun for you if you can get lost in that feeling as well, instead of calculating how many hours you might have left. Even if you have little to no experience with visual novels, this one is probably a better one to get started than most titles currently on Steam. With the above-mentioned reservations in mind,
easily gets a positive recommendation from me.

Since Starbound has finally been fully released, I figured now is a good time for a review.
First of all, I've had this game ever since it first came out in early access, so I’ve seen a lot of change in the game, but this is my review for the fully released game.
I cannot stress enough how good this game is in a short review, but I'll try my hardest.
Starbound is the best purchase I have could ever have made on Steam. Some people say it's just a Terraria rip-off in space, but it is so much more than Terraria could ever have been. It has so much depth to it and so much freedom. You start out as one of 7 different races, all of which have different styles of ship, background and dialogue. From the Normal Humans, who live and travel in typical human spaceships, own pet dogs, and give very optimistic, light-hearted analysis of things, to the Novakid, a race of 'interstellar gas-bag people' who appear as humanoid shaped clouds of gas that travel in spaceships styled like western trains, own weird gas puffs as pets, and speak like cowboys. As you can see, there is already so much more depth than what Terraria (which Starbound is often compared with) offers, with backstory and personality. And that isn't even close to the tip of the iceberg.
The story probably the main thing in Starbound that breaks away from being a Terraria knock-off. You start as a Student, about to graduate and become a Protector, which is a fairly self-explanatory job. The ceremony is interrupted by an attack from a bunch of big tentacles, forcing you to leave your planet, with only your ship and your newly obtained matter manipulator, a high tech tool that serves and a pickaxe and an axe, and eventually a liquid dispenser, wire cutter and painter. You escape safely, but with several damages to your ship, forcing you to beam down to the planet beneath you, which starts you on your quest to getting the resources to fix your ship. On this planet find a huge ancient gate, and when opened, transports you to a space outpost nearby in your solar system. This acts as your hub, with numerous quests, tech upgrades like double jumping, water breathing and even mechs, shopping and allows access to the main quest. I won't go into any more story detail because spoilers.
The atmosphere in Starbound is incredible, whether you are in the bustling industrial Outpost, to an eerie mining facility full of nightmarish, blood vomiting monsters, to a peaceful planet filled with villages, extensive, ambient caves and attractive scenery, the game tries it's best the fully immerse you into its diverse worlds. And I think it's safe to say that is does this really well. One of the greatest aspects of the atmosphere is the Music. The music is nothing like that of Terraria, which is a bunch of 'retro style' blinky noises which give you headaches and loop for hours on end. No, instead Starbound has 'proper' music, whether it’s the calm main theme, played on piano, or the ambient music that will play in a forest or a small village. There is an astonishing soundtrack that goes for an exact total of 6 hours, 39 minutes and 15 seconds, which I really recommend that you check out on YouTube before buying, just to get a taste of what you are buying.
The online community is also brilliant, with hundreds of different servers online. The game tries its best to let you interact with other players, with chat, pvp and instruments. There are loads of different instruments you can find and craft that automatically play songs from a list. You can download more songs from the internet, offering a huge library of music. You can actually make bands, by adding each other as band members, and the instruments all play to the same song, which can sound amazing and creates lots of fun. Last time I checked, the developers are very active, they would post dev. blogs and progress reports daily, and they always took in what people would say, and try to integrate all those things the best they can.
I think that’s all that can be said without going into too much detail. I feel like I haven’t said enough about this game, but there is just too much to say, so I implore you to check it out for yourself, take a risk and I hope that you enjoy it. I know that it is easily my best on steam, and that is saying something. And the most incredible part is, that all of what I have stated in the 5 paragraphs above, can be purchased for under $20 full price (I can't remember how much exactly, can't be bothered checking), That’s the price of 1kg of bacon, some cereal, a 12-pack of ice-cream cones and a 250ml bottle of thousand-island salad dressing (don’t even ask what I’m having for lunch)

SoD is the definitive zombie RPG experience. When I first started up the game, I instantly thought "Oh♥♥♥♥♥♥ did I just buy Dead Island again?". The answer was no, I didn't. The first few missions and maybe first hour are pretty directed in terms of gameplay and missions but after that, it's a free universe. Gather survivors, supplies, weapons, cars, and influence through a series of life-threatening missions. Wipe out entire hordes of zombies so they don't attack home. Build medical tents, workshops, sleeping quarters, sniper towers, and much more! Drive around the graphically appeasing world but be careful! It might be tempting to run through hordes of Zeds but your car will take alot of damage! Here are some of the highest points of SoD:
-Realism: melee weapons and cars all take damage after overuse. Nothing lasts forever!
-Challenge: Zombies are actually dangerous and it is always better to avoid them. Don't rush into a fight, bullets are few and so is your energy
-Immersive Environment: Witness the world fall apart around you. The military is not your best friend, niether is the established government in Marshal. Have the opprotunity to help total strangers or leave them for dead. It's the closest thing to a Walking Dead experience you'll get if you're looking for something like that.
-Defensive Battles: Home is never perfect or completely safe. Zed hordes can rush in any moment if you don't control the population of them yourself. When they come, they come. They climb over walls from all directions and it becomes an Alamo-esque atomosphere. Hold or die, it's simple.
-Death is a new begining: Since you can play as multiple characters, your death is not the end of the game. My first character, Marcus, I used to go out and look for survivors in the woods. I was surrounded by Zeds and torn apart. After one character's death, another one will give a quick eulogy and the whole camp's morale will go down.
-Home: Make it your own and get involved in that well known zombie apocalypse drama. Keep the morale of your camp up by scavenging and defending against zed hordes. If one character in particular is saddened or angry, do a mission with them to boost their morale and keep them going. Random events will generate (gun misfire, arguments, etc) that all effect the morale of the camp.
The Bad:
-Not fully optimized for PC: This is obviously a Xbox game, using a mouse can give you sometimes a more glitchy feeling. It does not fully hold back gameplay though, it can make it harder to get the full scope of your surroundings though.
-Invisible walls: In houses or other structures, it is common for invisible walls to pop out of nowhere and you will have to shake your mouse vigorously to be free.
All in all, the game is great besides for those few bugs. 8.9/10!

First of all, this game is nearly 8 years old (as of now). In newer machines it’ll require some tweaking to acquire the best results. Some things are unavoidable though, for instance, the max resolution is 720p, but other issues can be improved. In my experience the “motion blur” setting didn’t work out well: Shepard was always “shaking”. Other issue was the V-sync setting: no matter what I did, it simply wouldn’t work, the game was always at 62~63 fps and I would see screen-tearing literally all the time. Luckily there’s an easy solution for this: I simply activated triple-buffering in the GPU settings, overriding the game settings (then I activated V-sync in the game settings and restarted it: problem solved). Another issue was the Steam Overlay: in order for it to work with the game, I needed to open Steam as an administrator (Win 8.1).
Now that the technical issues are taken care of, let’s see the pros and cons:
•	Massive game: at least 30 hours of gameplay are guaranteed.
•	Over the top replayability value: you can play as Renegade, Paragon or any mixture of both. Your choices will affect not only the story of ME 1, but also the subsequent titles of the franchise.
•	The game is funny. Although Shepard appears to be serious, there’s a subtle humor to many of his lines/actions.
•	Outstanding voice-work: Seth Green (Joker), Keith David (Captain Anderson), and Mark Meer (Shepard) are incredible. Overall, the whole cast is consistent.
•	You can punch a NPC for no apparent reason.
•	Engaging story and interesting characters/classes/settings: Reapers, Protheans, Quarians, Krogans, Keepers, Turians, Volus, The Citadel, The Council, Mass Relays, etc… there’s a whole new sci-fi mythology to be found.
•	Great graphics for 2008: even though the graphics might seem outdated nowadays, they were really impressive back in 2008.
•	You’ll get to drive the best off-road vehicle ever: the Mako.
•	You can’t romance everyone.
•	You’ll get lost in Ilos, no matter what you do.
•	In the beginning you’ll have a hard time finding your significant ones inside the Normandy.
•	You’ll be annoyed by Shepard’s lack of endurance training (he can’t sprint for 200 meters without getting exhausted).
My favorite game of all time. No question.

State of George Takei --- er, Decay, is a Zombie Survival game. Yes. Another one. But this one is pretty fun, I promise!
In a market rife with extremely subpar games trying to ride off the success of DayZ. State of Decay does a very good job simulating the less flashy elements of survival; scavenging supplies, resolving conflicts that resonate among survivors ( Walking Dead soap opera, anyone? ) and introduces an interesting gameplay mechanic; your play time is not bound to a single character, allowing you to swap between characters as one gets tired, injured, etc. Included in State of Decay are RPG elements, allowing for leveling up a character, and a small degree of specialization.
The game is not perfect. The graphics are nothing to write home about, and the melee combat, while better than say, Infestation: Survivor Stories ( Formerly known as The War Z ) it still isn't an excellent Bruce Lee fighting scene, and the quests can and WILL pop up many times... the game is still damn fun. I enjoy it.
If you like zombie survival, then you should get this game. There are not very many games out there that do zombie survival well, but State of Decay is one of them.

In many ways Mass Effect could easily be an incredible Star Wars role-playing experience. After all, it has all the elements of that classic space opera, like memorable aliens, killer droids, and a special order dedicated to maintaining balance throughout the galaxy. Plus, there is the tiny little detail that BioWare has a history with this sort of thing. However, if it were a Star Wars game then Mass Effect probably wouldn't be anywhere as interesting or cool as it is. That's because discovery has an excitement all its own, and Mass Effect introduces us to a deeply immersive new galaxy fulThere are so many reasons why Mass Effect is so appealing. It's got a typical BioWare plot, which means that there's a mystery that's so well thought out and told that everything clicks into place during the big reveal. Yet it's also a game made by sci-fi fans for those who love sci-fi. There are so many elements borrowed and culled from decades of science fiction and movies, and there are countless moments that will remind you of Star Trek or Aliens or Firefly or some early John Carpenter movie (the electronic score is very Carpenter-esque, too). There's even an effective film grain post-processing effect that makes the game feel like a 70s or 80s sci-fi movie, before digital filmmaking and CGI made everything look and feel too clean.l of stories and mysteries.That's why I highly reccomend this game !!
