The Critter Chronicles is old school Point n Click adventure done right.  Simple story, excellent characters, and the most random and nonsensical ways of solving puzzles all while being humorous and referential.
There really isn't much to analyze about the game.  There’s no deep story or allegorical moral, just a straight adventure. But I've given too much credit to other games in this regards.  The Critter Chronicles is very clear on what your goal is in chapter and even in the subchapters.  Hold Space and tells you the puzzle you should be figuring out.  That's actually ground breaking when compared to other games that don't reveal what your goal is until after you do it.
The characters are great as well.  This story lends itself more towards a Star Wars parody with Nate being a reluctant Han while Critter is an amalgamation of Chewbacca, ET and several Muppets. Though, the love interest is definitely a Leia Organa clone, she plays opposite of Critter.  There aren't many characters but the ones included they got right.
Puzzle aren't too hard. Nate drops verbally hints as what to do, but even if you missed one they aren't so devious that you couldn't figure out with a bit of time. A few puzzle though left me frustrated. At one point I had run through all the possible combinations of interacting with objects that broke down a checked a gameboomers.  In bright Red Letters the guide pointed out I need to examine something I already had in my inventory because that would change it. That was annoying. I also accidentally skipped a puzzle not realizing the order I was supposed to do things. A few other puzzle were tough but not Goat level.
The real reason to love this game though is the referential humor. It pokes fun of 80s nostalgia while also being an homage. Star wars and Harry Potter references are clear, but a surprising one was day of the tentacle. Lots of little things were included that show a lot of love in the game.
My only real criticism is the lack of customization of controls. The mouse speed adjustment and middle click to reveal hotspots would have been a big plus.
Overall, it’s another excellent game in the series, a little short but if you like classic Point n Click adventures this one is for you.

This game has been on my wishlist for a loooong time. I finally bought it a few days ago, despite all the recent negative reviews about it on steam. So far, I'm not dissapointed that I bought it, but yes it does have negatives which should be mentioned.
Pros and what
really like about it:
+
: The creepy factor is really well executed. You'll
feel safe when exploring or gathering resources.
+
: Snowstorms are surprisingly "nothing-you-can-do-about-it" but sit and wait for it to pass. Also the night is definitely a hindrance to exploring, and brings a risk vs reward factor.
+
: I can't emphasize enough how this game will wash away any past RPG experience where you play as warrior and just run into the battle no matter what. Let me tell you my experience so far. A couple of times in the beginning I was running for my life from 4 wolves, and if I didn't have like 10 bandages which I thankfully prepared I would've died for sure. Even 1 wolf can do massive damage if you don't dodge properly. Today, I finally made it to the second island, only to get my first taste of death at the sword of a undead warrior skeleton. His blade effortlessly sliced through my tin armor in just 1 hit and I was dead.
+
: I like the interface, and how you can place anything even if you don't have materials for it. It's the first game I played where the buildings are premade, but surprisingly I don't mind. Before I bought this game I thought it would be a minus because I'm used to building my own structures (like in ROK)
+
: The health depends on cold, and stamina depends on hunger. I think it's tough, but enjoyable, especially when you are lost after being chased and then you realise you don't have any logs to make fire :)
Cons which I'm sure will be fixed or improved:
-
: At the moment there only seems to be 1 type of arrow and bow in this game, which is what you can make in the beginning.
-
: Animals walking through rocks or going underground is a bit of an issue on the second island.
-
: I lowered everything to low, turned off most things but anyway I get temporary freezes, low FPS.
Overall, I give this game 8/10. This game would be excellent, but performance issues right now is why I can't give it higher rating.

Since Starbound has finally been fully released, I figured now is a good time for a review.
First of all, I've had this game ever since it first came out in early access, so I’ve seen a lot of change in the game, but this is my review for the fully released game.
I cannot stress enough how good this game is in a short review, but I'll try my hardest.
Starbound is the best purchase I have could ever have made on Steam. Some people say it's just a Terraria rip-off in space, but it is so much more than Terraria could ever have been. It has so much depth to it and so much freedom. You start out as one of 7 different races, all of which have different styles of ship, background and dialogue. From the Normal Humans, who live and travel in typical human spaceships, own pet dogs, and give very optimistic, light-hearted analysis of things, to the Novakid, a race of 'interstellar gas-bag people' who appear as humanoid shaped clouds of gas that travel in spaceships styled like western trains, own weird gas puffs as pets, and speak like cowboys. As you can see, there is already so much more depth than what Terraria (which Starbound is often compared with) offers, with backstory and personality. And that isn't even close to the tip of the iceberg.
The story probably the main thing in Starbound that breaks away from being a Terraria knock-off. You start as a Student, about to graduate and become a Protector, which is a fairly self-explanatory job. The ceremony is interrupted by an attack from a bunch of big tentacles, forcing you to leave your planet, with only your ship and your newly obtained matter manipulator, a high tech tool that serves and a pickaxe and an axe, and eventually a liquid dispenser, wire cutter and painter. You escape safely, but with several damages to your ship, forcing you to beam down to the planet beneath you, which starts you on your quest to getting the resources to fix your ship. On this planet find a huge ancient gate, and when opened, transports you to a space outpost nearby in your solar system. This acts as your hub, with numerous quests, tech upgrades like double jumping, water breathing and even mechs, shopping and allows access to the main quest. I won't go into any more story detail because spoilers.
The atmosphere in Starbound is incredible, whether you are in the bustling industrial Outpost, to an eerie mining facility full of nightmarish, blood vomiting monsters, to a peaceful planet filled with villages, extensive, ambient caves and attractive scenery, the game tries it's best the fully immerse you into its diverse worlds. And I think it's safe to say that is does this really well. One of the greatest aspects of the atmosphere is the Music. The music is nothing like that of Terraria, which is a bunch of 'retro style' blinky noises which give you headaches and loop for hours on end. No, instead Starbound has 'proper' music, whether it’s the calm main theme, played on piano, or the ambient music that will play in a forest or a small village. There is an astonishing soundtrack that goes for an exact total of 6 hours, 39 minutes and 15 seconds, which I really recommend that you check out on YouTube before buying, just to get a taste of what you are buying.
The online community is also brilliant, with hundreds of different servers online. The game tries its best to let you interact with other players, with chat, pvp and instruments. There are loads of different instruments you can find and craft that automatically play songs from a list. You can download more songs from the internet, offering a huge library of music. You can actually make bands, by adding each other as band members, and the instruments all play to the same song, which can sound amazing and creates lots of fun. Last time I checked, the developers are very active, they would post dev. blogs and progress reports daily, and they always took in what people would say, and try to integrate all those things the best they can.
I think that’s all that can be said without going into too much detail. I feel like I haven’t said enough about this game, but there is just too much to say, so I implore you to check it out for yourself, take a risk and I hope that you enjoy it. I know that it is easily my best on steam, and that is saying something. And the most incredible part is, that all of what I have stated in the 5 paragraphs above, can be purchased for under $20 full price (I can't remember how much exactly, can't be bothered checking), That’s the price of 1kg of bacon, some cereal, a 12-pack of ice-cream cones and a 250ml bottle of thousand-island salad dressing (don’t even ask what I’m having for lunch)

I tried to play Baldur's Gate a few years ago but it seemed so old and I couldn't be bothered. Now this is the new and shiny one that plays like Baldur's Gate and it has a lot going for it.
The world is huge, the time I've spent so far feels like a fraction of it. I love how you can talk your way out of most stuff and solve some scripted events with your attributes or items.
It does get overwhelming from time to time because of the sheer size of the game but I can honestly say that I've had fun the whole time I was playing. I will definitely finish this game but it might just take me a few months to do so.
I have had a few problems with the game but the developers seem to be going at it to fix them and I haven't had any problems since yesterday's patch.
I will definitely recommend this game to everyone who has enjoyed Neverwinter Nights, Dragon Age, Fallout 1-2, Baldur's Gate type games. Just remember, it has a lot of micromanagement in combats. You will need to pause a lot if you want to play on a higher difficulty than normal and even on normal you'll need to pause more often than not because unlike Neverwinter and Dragon Age this game doesn't have auto-play on characters you don't control. They'll just attack another target if their current target is dead and that's it.
P.S. This one is a slow burner, don't try to finish it, just lose yourself in the game and let it take you wherever you might need to go. Also, don't try to clear out every single room because some monsters are way above your level and leveling up with those really hard ones will make the rest of the game too easy. It's a normal thing to get back and try to find some other thing to do before taking up on the bigger and more dangerous challenges.
Wish I'd waited a month before buying this game.

PROS
- Amazing, funny, nostalgic, sincere, absurd writing
- Amazing art
- Unique concept
- I would say it's fairly priced for the content you're getting (keep in mind other visual novels with considerably higher price tags and less content)
- Amazing (X3) music
CONS
- It's fairly short if you play it straightforwardly, which is not how the game wants to be played and can be frustrating if that's your preferred play style
- Many of the mechanics, such as the combat and the "hacking" puzzles, are just not fun/intuitive. In these areas the game doesn't make it clear enough what it wants you as a player to do, and even when you do figure these "puzzles" out it isn't satisfying, it's just frustrating. I understand they were going for classic 90s computer games but they could have updated the responses a bit more to feel good to play.
- On the other end, some puzzles are TOO straight forward, and feel like they're spoon feeding the player the answer. I find this more frustrating than the combat/hacking puzzles, because it just feels like there was no reason or thought for those obstacles when it was so obvious how to get around them. How many point-and-click adventure games have done the "find a key" puzzle by now? Once could pass for nostalgia, but in the first act, let alone the first scene they do the "find a key" bit upwards of 3 times. I wish a bit more of the attention given to the writing side of the game was given to the....game side of the game as well.
Despite all this, I still recommend HIVESWAP for people who love point-and-click adventure, regardless of whether you were a fan of Homestuck or not. The story is accessible for new audiences as well as paying a lot of subtle fanservice to people who read the comic, and doesn't have to carry a lot of the exposition baggage Homestuck is so famous for. Most of it's pitfalls are in the mechanics, but as it is it doesn't really need to be super engaging on that front, just a little more polish would make the experience more enjoyable. I was totally absorbed by the story and characters from start to finish and am very excited for act 2's release, which will hopefully be soon. X:)

It really is a 90's-style point & click adventure game.  For some, that will be fantastic.  Others may find it alien and peculiar.  There's one significant deviation from that formula though, in that the game features two minigames that are basically short sessions of Centipede.  The first is easy enough to be inoffensive to everyone, but the second is actually hard enough to be a genuine annoyance to P&C purists.
Assuming you actually LIKE P&C games, and are fond of all the reading and clicking things on other things just to see what the game will respond, there's a ton of material here. It took me 6 hours, and that's with only minimal "I know this won't accomplish anything, but I'm going to try using the X on the Y just for the lulz" shenanigans.
But if you DON'T enjoy reading all the text, the game is actually pretty short.  This first installment BARELY feels like it even manages to get the main story off the ground, which is a bit odd, because I don't think there are actually all that many more Acts planned.  Without knowing what the rest of the story will be, it's hard to say much of anything more about that.
All in all, a good time.  A bit slower-paced than just reading Homestuck was, even in the dialogue-heavy parts, but still a good time.  Recommend to anyone who likes both P&C games and Homestuck.  Ideally both, but there's probably enough here to tempt anyone who only likes one or the other also.

A quote from Eden*. Technically not a spoiler, but just in case I'll cover it:
This line is my favorite line from Eden*, and I really took it to heart. You never really know if the next goodbye will be the last.
Consider this your TL;DR version:
With a cute yet very sad love story, Eden* is out there with some of the best stories I've seen in a while. It's brought all together with brilliant characters, gripping story, beautiful art and astounding soundtrack.
The story to Eden* is fairly simple. The world is coming to an end and the human race needs to evacuate into space to avoid being wiped out by whatever the world is about to be destroyed by. Out of the characters we get to know throughout the story, two of them refuse to leave the planet. Instead they take up a life of solitude in the mountains and live the last few days they have left in peace. It's not something that looks very good on paper, but in my opinion it's handled extremely well. It's not only the story itself that makes Eden* an amazing visual novel though, it's also the characters. How they feel about one another, how they interact and so forth. With all the characters you meet, you grow attached to them. And with all the farewells you have to go through, it quickly becomes a very sad story.
The art... Not only is the art beautiful, it goes above and beyond of what a lot of other visual novels tend to do. The amount of detail and care that went into the art shows. A majority of the visual novel is not just one background with characters placed there like a lot of other visual novels are. Instead there are several backgrounds for a room from different angles. Also, the amount of pictures (not backgrounds where you can paste any character, but actual pictures with a character usually doing something already in them) is huge. The drawings give attention to even the little things that don't even really matter, making it a much more enjoyable experience in general. And to top all of it off, the opening is one of the best animated clips I have ever seen.
The soundtrack is one of the saddest yet most beautiful soundtracks I've ever heard. Pure and simple, it really knows how to set the mood for many situations. If there were an option to buy the soundtrack, I would probably do it.
Negatives are a tough one to mention, since there isn't a whole lot to mention. I guess you could say that I am a little disappointed with some scenes and how boring they were, but that's just me. Not a whole lot of things during the prologue were very interesting, and some scenes in general felt like filler. Thankfully, a majority of the content is interesting and what little boring content there was doesn't really affect the story telling in any way.
From a bunch of different visual novels that I've seen this stands out, because you can see how much effort was put into this to make it what it is now. If you're looking for a good, yet very sad story, this one is definitely something you should read.

Pardon my rambling thoughts ahead, afterwards I'll break down some basic pros and cons.
When I think about this game, I tend to gravitate towards comparing it to Narcissu.  Both are short kinetic novels, both deal with heavy topics like death.  But I think Eden* handles its topics a lot more interestingly than Narcissu.
A lot like Narcissu, death is a looming inevitability on the minds of the main characters.  For Narcissu, the constant talk of death and hopelessness turns the story into a drawn-out slog with an inevitable conclusion.  The characters don't really grow or noticably change over the course of the story.  Eden* handles the same concepts in a way that is a lot easier to swallow.  It isn't a spoiler to say that the main heroine dies in this story.  But how it handles that character death makes all the difference.  Eden* uses every chance it gets to develop its main hero and heroine into interesting characters with detailed motivations.  Where Narcissu was primarily about picking a better place to die than a hospital, Eden*s characters  use their struggles with their own mortality (either due to physical illness or the approaching end of the world) to learn to live life to its fullest with what time they have left.
Coming back and reading Narcissu again recently after having not read it for several years left me feeling depressed and almost...empty.  It was a soul-sucking experience.  But Eden*, despite being at times equally dark, sometimes even moreso because the characters were so much more three-dimensional, left me feeling uplifted and more positive about life.  I felt like it had really successfully communicated to me how important living my limited days on this earth to their fullest is.  So I think that's really a victory for this game's storytelling.
Now that that's out of the way, pros and cons.
+Great art.  This is subjective, of course, but if you don't mind the Key/Visual Arts-style GIANT ANIMU EYES, the spritework is great.  The occasional sweeping vista of fields or mountain lakes look great too.
+Great writing.  I only recall seeing a few minor typos, and it all read very smoothly over the 7 hour experience.
+/-  Music and general sound design was competent, but I don't recall anything hugely impressive.
- This isn't really surprising to anyone that has played a visual novel before, but there are no resolution settings.  You have windowed and fullscreen.  I just played in windowed.
Verdict: if you're looking for a book-like experience and don't mind moe-style eyes, pick this game up.  It's a beautiful story and you'll love all the characters by the end.

If you have played the previous game in the series, all I can say is that you won't be disappointed if you buy this one.
It has better graphics and arguably more humor than its predecessor, and more importantly, it will probably make Critter a much more adorable - or at least much less annoying - character for you.
As to those who haven't played the series yet, well... it's an old school point and click adventure game, and this game faithfully reproduces both the good and the bad characteristics of a typical game from that genre.
It means you will get tons of witty remarks, hilarious moments, and some clever puzzles while playing this game. But you will also find that the most of the gameplay involves walking back and forth between limited set of places, while moving your mouse cursor all over the screen with frustration, hoping to find some missed hotspot.
For a modern title, it pays notably little attention in mitigating such typical problems which pervade point & click adventure games.
So, if you feel like you are stuck, I'd like to suggest to try combining items in random manner or scrubbing the whole screen thorougly with your mouse, because there are number of not very logical puzzles, and very hard to find hotspots throughout the game.
But still, I have to conclude my review by assuring you that it's one of the better made classic adventure game you can get these days.
And the at very least, it also has PENGUINS and THE TENTACLE (yes, that purple one you remember from the old days). What can you expect more from an old school adventure game?

Got the game on pre-order waaaaay back in the day, played it a bit at the time.  When I eventually got tired of all the instability and frequent world-wipes and unfinished content (as there does tend to be in early-alpha builds, so no grudge there), I put it away so I could see with fresh eyes what it would look like when it was finally "ready".
First, some positives:
*The game does feel a lot more purposeful now with its over-arching story than it did way back in the early days. It also has a decent (if not exactly great) sense of humour.
*The tutorial mission is a nice intro to the controls (but badly needs to be optionally skippable).
*Lots of stuff to build with (if you can scrape together the pixels to buy it or the blueprints to craft it).  The possibilities for base-building are probably the game's strongest point.
*The graphics are still nice, while the soundtrack is full of overly-catchy "ear-worms" (although many are really not very appropriate for the overall atmosphere of the game itself: "You've just stumbled into a giant eerie cavern made of packed bones and tar-pits... let's play a cheerful little piano-ditty over that!").
*The addition of the outpost provides a nice mission-hub (although things are placed much too far apart and ultimately there's just not enough utility provided by it all).
*The addition of the various official "collections" is on the right track (but still feels a bit half-baked and incomplete).
*I still enjoy trying to gather together as many different crops as possible in a comprehensive megafarm (though the food system in general is about equal parts fun and frustration).
-=-=-
You may have noticed that even most of the positives have major qualifications attached to them.  Yet, all that said, I am seriously shocked at how user-unfriendly the game remains after, what is it, almost 5 solid years now (!) of supposed "beta-testing".  It's even more shocking given the (inevitable) example of Terraria standing right there beside it the entire time, showing plainly how to do stuff right for anyone who cared to look.  Here are just a few things that I can't believe didn't get fixed ages ago:
*Making storymission-progress with friends in multiplayer will make it impossible for you to complete the same story-missions in your single-player world without going into admin mode and cheating them completed!!  Blizzard handled single/multiplayer progression in Diablo 1 and 2 almost flawlessly nearly 20 years ago, yet this bug is apparently longstanding and doesn't seem likely to be fixed anytime soon.
*The controls are still clunky as hell, with too many important functions (hunting/farming/watering/healing/blockbuilding) being made dependent on too few equipment-slots.  The item-handedness is pointless and just makes the problem worse.  At least let us make something like a "farming build" with a hoe in one hand and watering-can in the other, since there is absolutely no reason a hoe needs to be "2-handed."  Or better yet, just make all those basic functions passively available if you simply have the appropriate item somewhere in your inventory.
*Movement-control is way too sloppy and loose for a game where a wrong move can easily send you falling off a mountain or down a pit to your death, resulting in the scattering of almost everything you happen to be carrying at the time.  And of course when you die you not only drop all your healing items but also all the materials you need to make more of them, so unless you have a big stockpile squirreled away at all times, have fun grinding up a bunch more of those every time you need to go retrieve your fallen loot, lest you finally make it back only to be immediately killed again by whatever got you last time. Wheeeee!
*Bad controls are made even worse by the amount of inventory management you need to do using an inventory-system that makes it almost impossible to do anything else while the window is open. Depending on your resolution, non-scaling item tooltips will happily pop up with the single bit of useful information sitting off-screen unless you either move the whole inventory window higher or shift the item you're interested into a higher row of the inv screen (I'm thinking here of the rottenness-status of food items, where it is all too easy not to notice just how far-gone something is until your nice meal suddenly turns into a puddle of green goo).
I could go on (and on and on). All of these things might sound like pretty minor quibbles, and individually it would probably be easy to get used to any one or two of them, but all taken together they paint a strange picture of a dev-team that either still doesn't actually know what "fun" is, or has a seriously warped definition of it.
Either way, Starbound remains a basically-promising game that, after nearly half a decade of work, still isn't nearly what it was promised to be, and basically just not much fun. Maybe I'll check it out again in 2021.

Alright, I have delayed this particular review long enough. Time to get cracking.
Starbound, I have probably played more of this is such a short space of time than any other game and again shows that even fairly small games and indie games can be just as good, if not better, than a massive, more well known games.
The short answer is this, Starbound may well be one of the best, if not the best game I've played in years. And that's saying alot.
Now, for the long answer.
For the record, I never played the pre alpha or the beta, so alot of the content people often talk about that appeared then I completely missed, so I cannot comment on that, though I assume there was a reason why.
However, what we get is still a very good game.
Starbound simply put, is Terraria in space. You are placed onto a 2D world with a 2D character of your own design, you then gather resources, craft new items and explore and fight your way across the world. However, the game goes further by giving you a ship, which upon being repaired, allows you to explore a vast universe. With numerous worlds to explore, there can be quite a bit to do.
I won't spoil too much, but Starbound is set somepoint in the future, where humans and other species haved joined together in the name of peace, forming the Terrane Protectorate. Your character is a Protector on their way to a graduation when... well... things go pear-shaped very fast.
If you want to know more, play the game! But I digress.
But of course, you will first have to create a character to play as. You can play as your good old fashioned Humans, the spiritual bird like race called the Avians, the intellegent apemen called the Apex, the cute but bloodthirsty sapient plant species known as the Florans, the peace loving, three eyed amphibious people of the Hyotl, the medieval, robotic Glitch and lastly, the 'stellar gasbag people' with a thing for the Wild West called the Novakids.
When you start playing proper, having teleporting down to a pleasent, lush garden planet, you can get to work collecting resources and crafting furniture, tools and weapons and armor. The crafting system is quick to learn and simple to learn, but is nice and complex in it's own way. You would use your crafting skills on their own to make the basic torches and such, plus your inventors table. The Inventor's table is especially important as it will allow you to make all the other crafting benches in the game.
As your explore the universe and gather more resources, you will be able to upgrade your crafting benches into more powerful versions, giving you access to new items to be made and new benches to use. Starting off from your typical wooden workbench and primative fernance, you can ultimately improve those into much more viable Industrial Workbenches and the Atomic Furneaces. You can also build more advanced benches such as the wiring station, for building more advanced systems, or the mighty Pixel Printer, where you can use your own Pixels, the games currency, to print out furniture at the drop of a hat.
Resources become quite important too, as you advance into the game, you are going to need to get your hands on more advanced resources in order to make better equipment, either making you travel to specific worlds to look for a specific creature type, or more dangerous worlds.
Worlds are typically divided into threat levels, those with higher threat levels will require you to equip more powerful equipment and in alot of cases, special items called EEPs which allow you to explore them. Each world level offers an ore that comes in high quantities. Starting with iron on the lowest level of worlds, you will have to go up the threat levels to obtain tungusten, titanium and durasteel to advance further.
This requires a little bit of extra detail. There are six tiers of equipment, Iron will allow you to make Tier 1 gear, tungusten Tier 2 gear and so forth upto Tier 4 with durasteel.
Six tiers of equipment may be small, but things get more interesting at Tiers 5 and 6. Three ores can be used to produce Tier 5 equipment, offering their own bonuses, Aegisalt, Violium and Ferozium. Tier 6 requires the Tier 5 equipment, the tier 5 ores and one final ore called Solarium to be made, offering the greatest bonuses.
But of course, you would need to get this stuff through the aid of pickaxes and drills. However, your primary tool is the trusty Matter Maniuplator. Not only can it be used for mining or placing items down, it can also colour objects, wire objects to buttons and consoles and be used to scan objects, some of which can later be made or printed. Your matter maniuplator can be upgraded to become more useful over time.
You also don't have to craft everything you need either. Out in the world you will find chests, challenge rooms and old ruins offering different items, some common, some hilarious and legendary, to aid you on your journeys. You will be able to teleport to an outpost when you can buy some supplies, continue a story and be also able to visit settlements in the game, filled with NPCs where you can trade or recruit crew members after helping out with certain problems. Such as helping make a present, or dealing with that bandit that is wanted for stealing chickens for example.
You can even build your own settlements on different planets and get gifts and pixels for building a nice colony and homes!
As your crew grows, you can expand your ships size, allowing for more crew members to join you on the ship, and for a few to follow you on the surface of planets. Also, a bigger ship means more to throw in! And don't be worried about leaving a nice colony or building of yours behind, you can set up a flag or even a teleporter, allowing you to teleport directly to it's location.
Combat is simple, but engaging and has some curious choices to built. You have two basic categories of weapons, one handed weapons and two handed weapons. One handed weapons tend to be weaker, but can be paired together to give you greater adaptability. Two handed weapons fill both slots, but tend to be more powerful and come with a special ability. Different tools can be used to aid your healing and your armor buffs up your weapons and allows you to use them more effectively.
And unlike most sandbox games, you can play through a story in your main game, which whilst perhaps simple, is actually satisfying to go through and challenging. With a nice story to boot.
So, gameplay wise, it is extremely fun, engaging and satisfying, and the precurdenally generated universe means that even though many worlds are similar, there will always be nice differences. And of course, building stuff is fun on a volacnic world, an ice world, a midnight world, a desert world, forest, savanah and all the like! Like I said, fun!
Now, the deeper technicalities. Being a 2D indie game with a very appealing art choice, this game will run smoothly on even low end computers no problem HOWEVER, once enough stuff starts happening on screen, which will inevitably happen, the game can lag out. So keep that in mind.
Multiplayer is also avaliable, and fun to go on. However, be careful as some servers might not be able to handle say, mods.
And speaking of mods, one of the best things about Starbound is the modding community, and the wider community aswell. It's very friendly when you look at the wider community, and the modders churn out plenty of mods to try out, including race extenders for playing more species, new items, new vehicles and all the like. A few mods I have been particularly enjoying are the Avali mod, introducing a very interesting new race of cute space raptors and items, and a mech mod for your robot mech needs.
So, to sum it up, engaging and addictive gameplay, plenty of easily used mods and a nice looking game which can run on older computers, what more can you want?
11/10. I am really looking forward to see what comes next!

I'm really disappointed in what's been done with this game. It had so much potential, and in beta was absolutely fantastic. I can say that in the time the game was pulled from beta to this most recent release, there have been no real positive changes that I can find (other than perhaps some very minor unit tweaks), and in fact all the changes are negative.
Biggest issues with the game:
- Population cap change: you can now only field a much smaller amount of units by end game, resulting in very stagnant and limited tactics/army compositions. Makes it much more boring than it used to be.
- Unskippable tutorial: the original tutorial wasn't the best, but it was MUCH better than this current one. It's incredibly long, not very clear, and even forces you to do certain things in the menu after it ends.
- UI redesign: Not sure what happened here, but the UI is more convoluted.
- Bugs: there are a ton of bugs, including a very annoying audio bug where the left and right channels are switched (i.e., if your units are attacking the enemy base, it'll sound like your base is being attacked).
Also, players will find the heavily reduced amount of in-game currency, meaning they won't be able to unlock the more advanced units they need for a long time. Instead, the devs have design decisions to make players feel like they need to spend real money to get currency for the unlocks they want.
It's obvious most of the effort was put into new unit skins, while somehow terrible change decisions were approved. I wouldn't mind the freemium aspect so much if the other changes to the game were reversed.
As it stands, I'm disappointed in what this game has become. It could have been amazing, but instead has been thrown away by terrible game design choices and mechanic changes.

Ok, so at the time of writing this I have 166 hrs on record. Updated After about 265 hours and top ranked 1vs1 player. (Which they removed 1vs1 Ranked because it showed the imbalances in their game and they didn't want to fix it).
First off, in beta, this was probably the most addicting fun, and strategic game that I have played in a long time. It is a Private map from SC2 turned into a full game. They had done such a great job in created multiple varieties of units and each of the 3 races had a "feel" to them. A play style if you will. This was the one game I just couldn't wait for release.
So why the bad review?
Well, basically this is no longer the game I played in beta. It looks the same, there are still similar units, but they mechanics were changed enough that it is a different game.
Is this new game good/fun?
Bottom line is no.
What changed?
For whatever reason may it be for balance, or server stability, or whatever they made it so mid game and end game units take up extra population.
Why is that bad?
Well, in beta, the "bad" players used to not build enough units. They used to spam maybe 2 types of units and try to build the biggest thing they possibly could. This usually meant they would get out this really cool unit and then get trashed by 3 basic units that had the same cost. This was mostly because the big units were supposed to be building late game after you had a core army and they would come in and trash your opponent at the end. Building this "core army" or a combination of units that worked well together and then building the awesome unit at the end never clicked for some players. But for those in the upper levels it was great.
Ok so lower population, so make fewer units?
Well now that the population is so low. (Actually building only 23 ish units end game instead of the full 60 [or more depending on race]) Means that end game has nothing to do with your early game. Once the third mine upgrade (turn 25) finishes you build only the biggest units. You have little if any starting units left and it comes down to a simplistic spam fight of big units. No strat required. When you only have 23 units to play with instead of 60 you over simplify the game and it is boring. There are cookie cutter teams that you just follow the formula with little adjustment. So it is now no longer a dynamic game, you are a robot doing the same thing every game and hoping that your teammate is doing the same.
Cookie Cutter? But there are so many units!?
In beta, about 40% of the units were obsolete. In release about 60% of the units are obsolete. They didn't buff/nerf/change most the units that nobody played. There were units that had a great concept but they just didn’t implement correctly. Now that you have even less options in terms of what to build there are even less reason to build multiple different units. You build your core 3 with some counter thrown in. Just because you have options doesn't mean they are good. There were a few units that I saw that were improved and I would love to have used them in the old beta but for the most part the game just got dumbed down.
How did play styles change?
Like I said before each of the races had a specialty. Terran was always at popcap and had good anti-air from the ground, but had weaker anti-air air units. Atlac had solid units with utility and could buff support the team while having either good ground or good air units. Yaoguai (Or however you spell it) had a slow early game, solid middle game that could clear waves, and then the strongest end game.  You used to want a balance so that you can use each race to your advantage. But they homogenized units (like WoW did with healers) to the point that except for some slight nuances the game play is the same between all three. The pop cap prevents you from fielding many different types of units to the point where they actually matter.
In conclusion, they made the game simpler and easier than it was. I am sure there are lots of gamers out there who like that. At least until you get bored. Unfortunately I will be playing far less of this game. Maybe if I didn't play the Beta I would like this game but since I know how good it used to be, playing a shadow of itself is rather disappointing.

I first purchased this product in October of 2016. It was fairly fun to use, I even used it in some livestreams. I refunded it not long after, however, not becausse I didn't enjoy the product--but rather because it kept reading my glasses as being my eyes and so my expressions would be distorted. It would make it look like Fluffo either had a severe case of lazy eye or some type of damage which prevented his eyes from staying open. While it certainly gave me many laughs, it bothered me that there was no way to effectively compensate for this without losing a degree of functionality. I need my glasses on to be able to see at all, being extremely nearsighted. It was my hope that they would come to accomodate for users who have to wear glasses all of the time, or otherwise have their trackability by the face-detection software be impaired.
Instead, when I reacquired the software on June 9th, I was disappointed to find that the face-detection still interpreted my glasses as being my eyes--even more so than when I first tried FaceRig. I had gotten a new pair of glasses since the last time and thought that maybe after a few months the software would have been improved or other methods of compensating for problems that wearing glasses cause with face-detection would have emerged.
FaceRig is a unique program, to be sure, and definitely one that you should try out for yourself. But be warned, if you have to wear glasses all of the time, the face-detectin owill in all likelihood see part or all of your glasses as being your eyes, and you'll be left with awkward, twitchy and otherwise unpleasant facial expressions.
All that aside, FaceRig is worth the cost. It's my hope that the program can be made more accessible to people who wear prescription glasses 24/7. A thoroughly amusing and at the same time frustrating experience, but one that I still enjoyed immensely.

One of the best zombie games to be released in my opinion. It's very different from most out there, bearing some MINOR resembelnce to DeadRising, in that it is 3rd person, open world (well deadrising is semi-open world, this is FULL open world) and finding and using weapons and food is a big part of the game. But, there are so many add ins it's amazing.
Pros;
Persistent survival. You have an entire base of survivors, you can pick where your base is, how to set up it, how to defend it, what people to keep in your group, you can swap between people, and when someone dies they are gone FOR GOOD. No reloading saves. It's got RPG aspects, so you can put most of your effort into leveling up one or two characters, but if all your good characters die in a freak accident, then your really screwed. The realism here is amazing. Also, if you don't CONSTANTLY find food, ammo, and mdecine, things can go down hill for your group fast. it's important to keep stocked up on supply. The persistents also applies to the game world, if you blow up a car, it's gone for good, if you loot a house, it's looted for good, if you drop some supplies in the middle of a field, a week later they are still there.
Well written. Despite the fact that the story has very little impact on the actual game play, the game is ASTOUNDINGLY well written for realism. every character in the game has a back story, special traits and weaknesses. In addition to this the way medicine, ammo, and guns are designed are very realistic, there are dozens of kinds of REAL ammo and REAL medicine, if you find a .22 bullet, you can ONLY use it in a .22 gun. If you find some asperin it will help with some light aches and pain, but it's no cure, morphine however is amazing and stopping the pain. There are 'trucker pills(nodoz)' That give you all your stamina back, but only for a while, you have a withdrawel and it drops back to lwoer then it was when you took them. This all adds up for a superb experiance when it comes to realism and connection to the game.
Nothing is impossible. Some zombie games like to make you feel like stuff is beyond impossible. If you've ever been rushed by two tanks in L4D2 you know what I mean. Even though some of the zombies in this game are a real ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to deal with (a BIG ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to be specific) nothing feels like it's impossible. Also, there is no 'magic protection zombies' where you will find 90 zombies guarding a box in the middle of a field or something. All the zombies are logically located, in big towns, there are lots of hoards, near army basis there are lots of SWAT/armored zombies, Near infestations there are useually screamers (which attract lots of other zombies, so it makes since zombies would gather around them)
NPC AI; most of the other NPCs in the game are respectably smart. From time to time, I have had followers abandone be for no reason and run home, and I'm not sure why, but other then that they never do anything stupid. They foxus on keeping themselves alive more then you, which makes since, they will run when weakened, avoid special zombies when not well eqiuped and go totally agro mode when they get the chance.
Cons;
A little wonky. The game is far from perfect, and combat is a little wonky. It's not impossible, and if you stick to melee it works 98% of the time, even if it glitches out visually sometimes. Guns howeve,r can be a pain in the butt. Zombies reandomly become "immune" to bullets during certian animations, which is VERY annoying, guns also become basically useless when a zombie closer to then about 5 feet/2 meters or so. This makes melee weapons MANDATORY. Also,  Zombie AI is very derpy. I've watched a zombie jump the same fence about 2 dozen times in a row, from one side to the other, for no reason at all, I've also seen them walk clean through doors, wall, windows, etc. The zombie spawning also derps out sometimes, I once had one jump oh top of me from ltiterally no where while I was surveying on top of a roof, but that is only once anything THAT bad has happend in about 30 hours of playing.
Graphics are pretty lame. I don't really care about this, but the game is choppy, weirdly lighted, badly animated, and poorly textured. I play on ultra specs, and tweaked with the settings a lot, and use some of my graphic cards game modifiers, and it looks a lot more acceptable, this however is not an option for people who did not have i5+ processers, or highly powerful graphic cards, as this game gets a very low frame rate, despite it's low quality. The only time I drop below about 45 FPS though is while driving really fast into an area I haven't driven into recently.
Night time. This game, REALLY needs some way of skipping night time. This makes me stop playing the game more then anythig. EVERYTHIGN is twice as hard as night, zombies are more abundent and hard to kill, it's hard to see anything, and the games wonky lighting is REALLY pushed. if flash lights were actually realisticly bright, it would be better, but it's like the batteries almost dead or something. When I shine a flashlight into a dark room, I can see the whole room in real life, but I doo good to see the zombie two feet in front of me with the flash lights on this game. maybe a future update could include a mechanic for batteries, flashlights, and upgradable flashlights? That would be fantastic.
I'd give this game a 8/10, it would be a solid 10/10 if they could clean up the animations, the wonkiness with the zombies, and the flashlight priblem (the lighting/textures on there own are not bad enough for me to drop a point)
All in all, it's one of the best games I have played in the past year. Undead Labs is setting itself up to be one of the greates, and most respected gaming companies in the zombie wheelhouse, which is saying a lot when up against games like L4D2, Deadrising 2, and the Walking Dead. (the good walking dead game!)
if you like zombies, RPGs, and survival-realism, this is a MUST OWN game, it is the single best zombie-RPG on the market at this time (blowing dead island clear out of the water, I'd only give it a 7/10) i really don't count deadrising as an RPG even though you can level up. lol

I give it a 8/10.
Short answer, I think this game has an incredibly fun mechanics and niches, although still needs TLC and polish.
It's a tug-of-war/rock-paper-scissors style game with lots of depth and tactics. It is NOT pay to win, 80% of the units are unlocked resonably fast with leveling, which in itself, is very nice as well (win a game, level up, lose a game get 1/2 to 3/4's of a level). I can fell the AI improvements since the EA release, which is much welcomed. They have since added skins, which are purely cosmetic. The 3 types of currencies, Gold, Green Gems, and Blue gems are all used fairly, gold for runes and units, greens for units and crates, blues for cosmetics and boosts. The game is pretty well balanced (Arhats have been nerfed but are still useful!) and no single game is won cause of a broken unit in perticular.
What I don't like/hate about the game :
-Weekly gold cap is pretty annoying, since I tend to put quite a bit of hours into this game.
-The voice overs are very low quality, and certain ones feel very out of place (ex : Fire Turtles, Blade Slaves, Outriders and Flamethrowers all have bad VOs)
-The AI, although improved since EA, is still off and wonky at times. Ex : Units standing still, walking into the middle of enemie waves, units pacing back and forth etc...
-Although not permanent, many units have been REMOVED since the EA, which is strangely backwards.
The movement slider feels...slow. I wish there was a sensitivity increasing slider. A clickable minimap would be great as well.
In all, a very fun FREE game, that doesn't require you to have to spend real money to fully enjoy it. A very fun game to play with friends, and I can't wait to see what this game evolves into, and what else Game Science can achieve in the future.

so i started out a fresh spawn like every other pleb.
i found a ton of gear, got pretty lucky, had a shotgun, two pistols with ammo, a sniper, hatchet, bunch of medical supplies. second largest backpack, combat gear. a sweeeet eyepatch.
i found a quad, looked all over for parts, finally found everything i needed except two tires..
another fresh spawn joined the game right behind where i was, he asked for a ride, graciously i gave him one.
we tooled around for a bit looking for two front tires, i found one and we were able to go much faster.
we arrived in a town called sultan, he said he found a .357 magnum, i already gave him a gun, just without ammo.. at this point we had been traveling together for about an hour, so i decided to trust him... i gave him some .357 ammo i had on me.
we continued to search through sultan, i found an ultra rare collectable item.. a "Garden Gnome". i was so excited, so happy. felt like the sad desolate world that makes up miscreated was finally started to pull itself back together, all was well.
we met back at the church where i parked the quad, i took the battery out so nobody could steal it, and he was waiting by it. i told him of my spectacular find, the ultra rare, ultra suave "Garden Gnome".
he asked to see it, so i showed him. then quickly picked it back up. he asked if it stands up, i said i dont know, so i dropped it once more, as soon as it dropped, he pulled out a gun, tensions rose, he aimed.. took 3 shots, and down i went, like a tree without a stump.. like a giraffe that lost its balance..
i was hurt, and dying. betrayed by my own apprentice, betrayed by a filthy disgraceful, despicable Gnome-stealer.
i laid there as he looted my bleeding body, took my gnome first, then my guns and ammo, stripped me of my glorious eyepatch, now blood-stained. he took my backpack and car battery, put it in the quad, looked back one last time in the grief and horror of his actions, then looked down at the gnome with one tear in his eye..
he wiped that tear, stuffed the gnome back in his new blood-stained backpack and pulled away on my old quad.

Unlike Terraria, Starbound has planets and spaceships, less stuff to explore overall, some cooler items, non-existant multiplayer, but tons of mod support.
The game is not very open-ended, forcing you to progress through the vague and repetitive storyline by going to a random planet that will always have what you're looking for, scan it, then go to the next planet. Building is difficult since the majority of resources aren't available until late-game, and random meteor showers or sandstorms will ruin your buildings anyway. You're better off hoarding everything in your ship.
The charm of the game is great, from the dialogue of the NPCs to having your crewmembers follow you around. But all of this gets old pretty quickly and your crew is pretty much worthless.
The only real value in this game is the huge selection of mods you can add to give some sort of replayability to your gameplay, but even then the game still doesn't hold up that well. However, the game is still worth playing solely because it feels like a watered-down version of Terraria in space, and you probably want something new to experience after spending countless hours in Terraria.

I bought this game for my children. It looked (still does) like a beautiful game with a story that kids could be happy with. But after noticing their lack of interest, I wanted to try it myself.
It's tedious. Annoying. Unforgiving. I can't believe they made an isometric game with ranged weapons so hard to aim. You need to spend a few attacks to get the right angle. AND it feels like aiming is not free-look. there are hops in your rotation angle so no matter how you try, sometimes you need to get a better location to hit a target. Playability gets hurt because of this. This FORCES you slowdown your pace. In the end, I was not caring much about enemies because why to bother with this tiring, kinda unrewarding task.
To top it all. You have a shield which allows you to deflect and counter attacks. Nice, right? A static enemy shoots an energy ball at you. You use your shield, towards it, right in front of it. And the darned energy ball hits the shield and goes sideways. Hmmm...kay, you think, let's deflect the attack to another enemy. Wrong. The next energy ball goes directly to the original attacker. WTH. What kind of math they used to code this? Random?
Oh, and the pauses in the controls. There are pauses after you attack, pauses even before some attacks (e.g., charging bow), pauses after you roll...this game does not make up its mind. Is this turn-based or what? Because I see the enemies constantly hitting you, like if this was more on the arcade side. And by "pause", please understand that annoyingly long period of time where you can't repeat the previous action. Just slowly move thinking of the next thing to do, and being punished in the meanwhile.
The scenary, beautiful. But the fact that you can fall down on the edges, yet fly over some holes, is beyond me. What are those holes in the platforms for? Showing us a cute transparency or parallax effect? The same rules should apply in the whole map.
Sigh.
There are some parts of this game absolutely well done. But in a nutshell, you can't combine a pretty eyes, a pretty nose, a pretty lips, etc., and inherently expect a pretty face.

Ok well. I had high hopes for this one. Put in just under 4 hours before getting frustrated. This product suffers from a serious case of "Unfinished" feel. So many issues with a game that has such enormous potential, but seems to have been rushed to release. I cleared my runway of arrivals and departs only for the camera to be stuck on the last depart until another aircraft checked in. In the mean time, I'm staring at empty sky watching a jet leave my view with absolutely no way to change the camera focus to something else at the airport or terminals. A free camera mode seems to be mandatory, but totally absent from the game. There also seems to be a total lack of a manual available here on steam, or even at the web site link.
While I can command the aircraft to change direction to avoid a mid air collision, there is no click menu option to change the altitude of an aircraft in flight, nor to assign one at take off. Flight strips also seem to be incomplete. While I'm use to the aircraft strips in Global ATC, this seems to make the Tower 3D version to be lacking useful information.
The game can have a lot of down time where you wait for something to happen. It would be nice to be able to change density of the traffic.
Sound effects of engines speed up and shut down are seriously cheesy. Even engine sounds in Airport Madness 3D are better. The computer voice acknowledgments of commands or check ins are also not polished. Traffic commands are not repeated or excepted in industry standard format, so just don't quite make it believable.
Sure seems like an early access game, not a polished simulation. For $29.99 with the future of pay to play DLC, and the additional cost for the PRO version, I can not recommend it. Maybe when/if it becomes polished or at least having the feeling of being complete.
EDIT - 6-15-2016 - Ok, I now have about 21 hours in this game. There are graphic bugs with planes parking in terminals, spinning 360 degrees over and over to finally stop in odd and unparked positions. Planes commanded to line up and wait, will spin 360 degrees in under 1 second as it turns onto the runway. If you fast forward time to get through a boring night, could find a bug where traffic just doesn't happen. I waited almost 12 "control hours" at one point waiting for new traffic to finally end up quitting the game.
I have a better grip on the "undocumented functions" of the game, still no manual available that I can find. The camera button will stop the annoying camera change focus. That's good. Again, I love this kind of game, but still see this one as not complete or rushed. Again, for $29 very over priced.
EDIT – 7-18-2016 – I now have more then 40 hours of game play in. The new patch finally released on the steam version has many of my gripes patched, but this should have been a while ago. Much more playable, but silly little bugs still exist. For example, occasionally when an aircraft turns on to the runway for takeoff, they make a 360 degree spin in under a second. Aircraft sound is still cheesy, I suspect that won't change. I'm not really sure what my expectations are of this game. After all, it is a game. But, if Dovetail follows their typical pattern, you will spend a ton of money on DLC, and see perpetual annoying bugs which will never be resolved.

Tower 3D is an Air Traffic Controller game aimed towards the casual end of the 'simulator' genre of games.  It's no ATC2 or Global ATC (and doesn't pretend to be), but it's not a lightweight time management game like Airport Madness either.  Tower 3D is aiming for a very neglected middle ground for ATC sims, so I had huge hopes for this one!
However, I'm disappointed at the missed potential here.  It didn't need to do anything different (all the basics for an excellent casual game are right there) but it should have done them all so much better!  Here's a list of the good and bad stuff so you can decide for yourself:
Hard to say.  If the developers voice intentions to improve it, then there IS a good game lying beneath all the faults.  Right now though, and without that commitment, £22 (current price) is just too high for the quality offered.  It's not an Early-Access title so (unless FeelThere declare otherwise) there has to be the assumption that no further improvements will happen.  As a result, I find it hard to recommend - yet wish I could because this exact game is needed badly on PC.  Hopefully, it will be improved and polished, and if that happens, I will adjust this review accordingly.
Airport Madness!  (stupidly fun, casual time-management game)
ATC3* (pitched at the same level as Tower 3D)
ATC2 (vintage, but still current and the most serious ATC to date)
Global ATC ('new kid on the block' but has a free playable demo you can try)

Please read this all text for an understanding of why I recommended this game despite its current deficiencies.  This is based on a very short stint (the tutorial, plus a few minutes outside of the tutorial).  So with that qualification:
While the premise is promising and there is definitely potential, the game has a very unfinished feel to it.  The very first tutorial aircraft I encountered pushed back from the the St. Thomas terminal like a proper airliner... wow, neat.... except for the fact that it was a Cessna.  OK then.  Then on the GA ramp that typically would have hosted the Cessna, a Dash 8 type turboprop taxiied right though the farm of its fellow turboprops to get to the taxiway.  The game took a slight hit to suspension of disbelief there.  And the Cessna thing seemed pretty darned obvious to me.
Rushed.  But could be fixed.
Pros: Promising mechanics, aircraft behave more or less as they should when commanded.
Cons: Rudimentary graphics and textures.  Aircraft movement is not terribly smooth.  View control is poor; zoom functionality is not terribly effective.
This has the potential to be a really good and engaging sim, but it's not there yet.
My advice - buy it to support the developer and encourage them to keep working on it.  Try it out.  You'll probably be disappointed.  But come back in 6 months and I expect (or hope) that it will be signficantly improved from its launch state.

The Total War series has at its heart managed to combine the best of turn-based and real-time strategy and has delivered fluent, thrilling - even cinematic - strategic battles on the one hand and scope for complex management and planning of cities on the other.
+ Total War Attila for me retains or reintroduces some of the best gameplay elements the series ever introduced (e.g. family and skill trees), while adding some well thought-out innovations (e.g. the horde mechanics).
+ Most factions are interesting, based on units selected from different general rosters and several to many (depends on the faction) unique units.
+ As befitting the time period the starting strengths of the factions range from one province to an empire, leading to very different gameplays.
- I concede, as many other Total War fans before me, that the AI is unfortunately one of the weaknesses in the series.
0 (neutral) It's hard not to be angry at SEGA for its DLC policy for several of the recent Total War titles. Attilla is no exception. Some DLC packs (Vikings, Longbeards) simply don't contain enough unique new content to justify their price. Others however (Desert Kingdoms, Celts) added some of my personal favourite factions into the game and are worth every cent. Also I would have been glad to pay some money for a DLC to add some additional siege warfare units.
Looking at Total War Attila in retrospective, also in the light of Total War: Warhammer, where the designers decided to greatly simplify the game mechanics, I realize it could also well be the culmination point of (well tuned and fun) complexity in Total War, which is why for me it warrants the "Test of Time" Nomination in the 2016 Steam Awards.

Chaser is a first-person torture simulator.
This game has a lot of weak spots, but the plot is not one of them. You play as John Chaser who is slow (and can't chase anyone unless he holds shift all the time). He lost memory and wants it back. Chaser travels the world to find it, visiting various locations. Random people help him in his quest (usually dying afterwards). Even though motivation of some characters is questionable, it is still hard to say that the story is bad.
What's bad then?
.
Weapons have bad sounds and weak animations, can't feel the gun at all. It's like you shoot using plastic toys.
Enemies are horrible in general. They have 2 modes:
First mode is fine, but second one sends shivers down my spine. Raged enemy can spot you even being hundreds of meters away. He can land shots while running backwards and capable of twisting his hands to shoot you without going out of hideout. Most of enemies are in raged mode and capable of 100-0 in like 2 seconds on
difficulty (quicksaves are almost mandatory). Sound detection is horrible. Enemies can hear you walking and there is no chance to sneak upon them. Why does this game has a knife if there is not a single chance to use it? Enemies also like to spawn right behind you, right in front of you and they do that frequently.
Game features HUGE levels with a lot of empty spaces and labyrinths. Prison level with red mist is one of the worst ones. Underwater level is vomit-inducing - what were devs thinking? Have they ever tried to play it more than once? Syberia level was a huge mess as well.
Missions have a nice variety: sniping level, train level, sneaky level, run without weapons level, defend the base in exoskeleton level and underwater level. Others are just plain corridors where you run around looking for objectives and shooting enemies.
Music is somewhat nice. Voiceover is so bad that it's amazing. Enemy battle screams are perfect (such as REEEEEEEEEEE and HOTSHOT). Protagonist sounds like he has Down's syndrome (which can be explained by the plot).
Camera work and character animations are terrible, but that's what makes them golden. Chaser's face moves like in gmod poops, other npcs are suffering from cerebral palsy as well.
This game is acceptable only in video form. Just watch it on youtube to save nerves and laugh during cutscenes.

Really old first-person shooter with futuristic background, heavily based on the movie "Total Recall". Somehow, up to the moment, Chaser is the best game its creators, Cauldron, made for all those years.
If you haven't played it before, when it was all fresh and comparable to the actual FPS on the market (2003, before such hits as Far Cry, HL2 and FEAR) - well, the game isn't aged well. If you're not down with old-school gaming mechanics, you'll most likely shouldn't try to play Chaser now. The game has many obvious and troublesome downsides, it is a real pain in the back for any casual nowadays gamer.
However, if you happen to know the drill of the old-school shooters (where, for example, you need to hit crouch button in the middle of jump to reach higher altitude) - I suggest you to buy and play the game. It is a real deal challenge, especially on the hard difficulty. If you manage to beat it now, without all those modern features like flashing directional arrows, checkpoints and all-mighty recovering chest-high wall - well, welcome to the club, man!
Let me tell you what was interesting in the game.
First, it's the space. Not the out-world nothingness we call cosmos, no, I'm talking about really big levels. Almost every level here is huge, by every FPS standard. Sure, it's still a shooter on the rail, the most of the times there is only one possible route from start to end. But, that means kilometers of walking. Or driving. Or diving (there is an underwater level). Yeah, the most part of those wastes will be filled with primitive copy/paste textures - same trees, same buildings with the same posters, same decals inside buildings... But that practice is still all over the industry! And even brighter in that parade of uniformity looks some noticable cool things on the background, such as actual rotating of the space station in the intro chapter, with different stars and views of the Earth in the portholes. Or the funny snowman somewhere in the middle of taiga.
All those big areas were made for the game to add some sense of realism. That kind of great achievement, when you to obtain some new thing have to actually do something, walk somewhere, elaborate, strive... and not just click two buttons on your phone to get all in your place - right away.
Sure, not too many people would like to change the comfort of modern games which telling you what you should do, for something odd-looking and not providing you with the safe and quick routes.
Second thing I liked in Chaser was the variety of missions. There is a sniping mission, where you need to protect a transport on its way through hostile military base. Exoskeleton mission, where you simply shoot your miniguns and rockets, defending the base. Stealth level, where you need to sneak around some goons to pick up some valuable conversation between some mobsters. Underwater level, where you swim... Swim, and then swim more, to get to some harbor "undetected". Well, on the way there are hundreds of aggressive droids which you need to shoot, and the route isn't too obvious even with markers, so maybe, that would not be the best entertainment in your life... But the whole game isn't! It's about to see of what you're made from. A challenge for your reaction time, coordination and patience. And your navigation skill.
Finally, the story. Yeah, it's trivial for the most part, and its major pieces you'll recognize much faster than the game plot shows them to you. But, it's a long story, really comparable with the Half-Life by its length and number of events and changes in the pace and alignments. It's much better than modern "don't ask questions, just shoot'em all!" standards.
Downsides are plenty, as I've warned you before.
The levels are so huge, that the most amount of the game time you'll be wandering, where to move next. In theory, it's quite simple - just follow the blood trail, more precisely, go where there are enemies waiting. But, in every level, there are some switches to click, holes to jump in or crumbled ladders you're still gotta climb. Well, train your wits about it... or just watch it all on the youtube, like all weaklings do.
The AI of your enemies... They aren't gonna find the cure from cancer, that's for sure. But their reaction time... Even if you catch someone off-guard and will try to shoot him in the nape, in a split second he'll be knowing where you are and shooting at you. If you ever played Counter Strike 1.6 (or earlier) with tough bots - that's them. Which is more - sometimes game spawns them on the cleared territory, behind your back. That's tough, unfair... but manageable, if you have your guts around.
Finally, the proposed layout of the game keys is outrageous. Just change it right before the game start. You'll need your nightvision, 'cause it's usually night time around. You'll need a quick button for "reflextion mode" aka bullettime/slomo feature. Yeah, it's not that cool as in Max Payne or at least in FEAR - but it's still useful, especially on the hard difficulty level.
Let's summarize again. The game is bad, by modern standards, it's not worth your time and money. It will hurt you badly.
On the other side, if you're a tough son of a gun, who have many old shooter games as kindergarten toys... try this thing. For example, it's much more variable, than Die Hard Nakatomi Plaza. More realistic, in many ways. And when it's not - it's a challenge for you to overcome. So come - if you're ready. In my library, I'll give it not too high mark of 6.8/10. But I'll honor the Chaser and its developers, Cauldron people, for at least one decent and sincere game.

First off, wow.  I was very impressed with this game (and I am not that easily impressed when it comes to things other than coffee or pizza).  Puzzle-based games seem very very difficult to execute successfully, in my opinion--I've seen many a well-thought-out puzzle game start strong and then fall victim to redundancy rather quickly (Talos Principle, anyone?).  This game was just long enough to be satisfying but without dragging on to the point of becoming tiresome.  The story was understated but still fascinating.  This one is a headache, but in a very good way.
What I appreciated most about The Swapper was the way it didn't just hand me everything I needed to be successful.  When a new mechanic was introduced, the game didn't go all tutorial, it forced me to learn by doing, by experimenting with this new device I've just discovered, much like one would be forced to do in real life.  As such, the game was very immersive.  On the whole, the puzzles were challenging, occasionally frustrating, but far from impossible.  They took a little juggling, a little concentration, but I only felt hopelessly stuck a few times, and mostly this was due to overcomplicating matters.  On a few occasions I actually laughed at how simple the solution to a seemingly complicated situation really was.  Controls felt a bit clumsy at first but quickly became intuitive.  Graphics make for a bit of eye strain, but fit the atmosphere.  Music is haunting and absolutely spot-on.
I really did love the story; even if the gameplay lacked it would have made the game enjoyable regardless.  Pretty critical points are touched upon, in particular the true nature of identity, but it presents its philosophies subtly and without being preachy, which is always a nice touch.  If you let it sink in, this one will stick with you for a bit after you finish playing it, but you'll be happy to have it there.

I have 100s of hours in DayZ, Arma II: Epoch, Arma III: Breaking point. I bought it a bit after update 36 which brought a lot of improvements to the game and update 37 added more vehicles and guns. Base building works pretty flawlessly. But it is limited to wood and tires for now. But they have some really complex wood structures you can build as you find more "guides" in the world that give you more crafting recipes. You can also build punji sticks, ballisades, and watchtowers.
With the latest update I get in the mid 50s with a gtx 960 and i7 4790k both overclocked. It runs very smooth the far majority of the time. But occasional stutters can happen for some players. The cryengine looks so much better than arma 3, the buildings and map in general look more to scale and detailed. There is a 36 play limit on servers right now at the moment, but they have been stress testing to try and increase it.
This dev team has some really unique ideas like "crafted guns" that look like they were made in someones garage, generators that need parts to power various things throughout the map. You have to take mags out of the gun to add ammo to them, But you can simply reload another mag by hitting a key. This is realistic.  Birds, rats, squirrels and frogs are in certain parts of the map which adds some atmosphere. There are tornados and rainbows, a long with a beautiful weather system.  It's well worth the price right now. I'm excited to see what they add next.

A short review with no story details.
eden* is a wonderful visual novel with brilliant art and a soundtrack that enhances the reading experience without being too overpowering. Simple details like having the characters blink add a nice touch to an already high quality work. This is by far my favorite visual novel currently (this review was created March 22, 2015) on Steam. The $20 price tag is quite steep, so I would wait for it to go on sale (mine was 50% off). If you're looking for a serious visual novel to start reading, I recommend this.
Notes:
- Length ~15 hours (assuming you listen to the voice acting)
- There IS voice acting
- There are NO choices/routes in eden* (Kinetic Novel)
- There is VERY LITTLE TO NO fan service
- This is the regular version of eden. The eden Plus+Mosaic version (not available on Steam) includes added blood to certain scenes and less censoring for certain scenes. It also includes an extra eroge side story that is not part of the main story. In my opinion I would have liked the added blood, but an eroge side story sounds incredibly out of place for this VN.
- I consider this a serious/emotional visual novel, unlike a VN such as Sakura Spirit. It tries to BE something and succeeds instead of appealing to absurd fan service.
- Originally released September 18, 2009

One could go on and write an extensive review for this majestic title in the video game industry, but when you finish the game in 42 hours, you really know the universe is speaking for itself.

-Massive galaxy to explore
-Immersive roleplaying game experience
-Complete skillful voice acting
-Intuitive character growth and skills
-Fun plot
-Original universe with original history and subplots to explore and learn
-Entertaining, memorable party members
-Two sequels that get even better
-Solid standalone game
-Comes with the DLC included
-The MAKO
-You have to actually endure elevator rides every time.  Bring companions.  Their elevator-only conversations make it less awful.  But it's still frustrating after about the fiftieth time.
-Good/evil choices with no middle ground
-Mass Effect 3 is not on Steam
This is one of the best roleplaying games in recent history, made even better by the fact that when you finish this one (which takes at least 40 hours), there are two more waiting for you on the other side.  Mass Effect 1 has the most problems technically speaking - particularly when it comes to using the MAKO to explore planetary surfaces.  This becomes tedious and aggravating very quickly.  And, like many roleplaying games, you can be good or evil, but not a mix without sacrificing some of the benefits that are only available to pure good or pure evil characters.
That said, the plot is great.  The game runs smoothly with few bugs or glitches, and the character cast is fantastic.
