There are few things to be said about Dark Souls that haven't already been said. Everyone has heard of the game, but only ever seem to hear that it's "difficult", despite the game having much more content and depth. I recommend
for help on your first playthrough. I just beat the game for the first time, so here are my thoughts.
There is no babying in Dark Souls. No pausing, no idle-healing, no experience to level up, no loading a previous save after you make a mistake. The game's mechanics punish you for haste and inattention, while it rewards precision, persistence, and mental fortitude. There are very few times that I died or came up short and felt like it wasn't my fault. A lot of games have gotten used to coddling a player, meaning that if you just put in raw time, you will always make progress (from experience, linear worlds, 1-to-1 resource allocation) since there are fewer choices. Sometimes you can sit down and play Dark Souls while making no tangible progress in the game, since you didn't play patiently enough. Yes, it won't always be an enjoyable experience, but, because it is not spoon-fed to you, the joy of overcoming a goal is unmatched.
Environments are absolutely top notch. I have always had a soft spot for overworlds that carefully intertwine each section, especially when revisiting an area changes later on in the game based on player made changes. Dark Souls is one of the best at this. Also, there is a lot of visibility in most places in the game. You've likely grown used to seeing backgrounds in games as inaccessible scenery, but Dark Souls shows you places in detail that you will explore later. As the game goes on, you will notice that you can see Blighttown from the ledge of the Firelink Shrine, or you notice the Demon Ruins from the Tomb of the Giants, or you notice any of
that are visible from other places in the game. All of this makes the world extremely immersive.
Choices matter. Without prior knowledge, a lot of the interactions with NPCs and merchants and your various yes/no decisions are highly impactful. You can miss out on access to a great item (or even several items) because of those choices. While it can be frustrating in retrospect, you can always make new decisions in New Game +. It also makes the game more exciting to know that you have an impact and be rewarded for exploring. Speaking of exploration, there is a lot of benefit to finding every nook and cranny.
Information is a bit limited. I relied a bit on
whenever I had a tough time, in particular when I didn't realize
. Lore and information is mostly given through item descriptions (so read them!) and soapstones (the orange things on the ground). You won't get much direction in the game otherwise, so just keep pushing forward. When you are lost because you can't attack someone or you are getting cursed/poisoned in 1 hit, read your item descriptions to see which tools you need to be using.
My biggest gripes are with some instances of artificial difficulty (instances in which the game screws you over for having no prior knowledge or requires rote memorization/luck to overcome something). This is something that has since been changed in the later games in the series, with the developers admitting that it didn't really add to the experience in a beneficial way. For now, you'll have to take it with a grain of salt. Also, the menu navigation/function is archaic for a 2011 game. Once again, just have to deal with it.
There is a 30 fps lock which can be remedied with
, and the game looks
better in 60fps (there are some games that I don't notice as much, but this one is an exception). I have had some problems with the platforming as a result of DSFix, though. It can get awkward in some particular spots, but is overall not very impactful. It can also randomly kick back into 30 fps if you alt-tab or bring up the steam overlay. In that case, just restart the game (autosave is great).
This is one of the few games that offers a truly unique experience, and I recommend that every gamer try it at least once.

This is the prequel to the original game and it tells the story of one of the 3 main characters from that game, with his sidekick getting a much expanded role in this installment.
And that is also one of the biggest drawbacks of the game, in the original game you had at certain points in the game the option to control 3 distinct and interesting characters. Here you can control 2, however one of them does not speak in a human language, so there are no helpful hints from him when you are inspecting items. This means that controlling him is annoying and a frustrating experience when you are limited to only that character for solving certain puzzles
It is interesting to see the genesis of a few characters, especially since in the original it was left as a big question unaswered. And the story itself is quite nice, however I will say that the puzzle design is noticably weaker this time around. And the game seems to be not up to the same quality as its predecessor, as there are quite a few issues with clipping, and a serious game crashing bug connected with a puzzle that can only be avoided by making sure the game is constantly busy during that puzzle.
The game does retain its charm though, and it makes for an OK entry in the franchise.

Action RPG at its best. Can not get better than that but the game is not for the average player who either does not have the time or the patience to invest a lot of time dying and dying and dying before rising up...
It is a fantasy RPG around an undead who starts fighting hordes of initially completely overpowered enemies. No surprise that in the beggining you will die A LOT (you can not say that the title did not warn you).
The RPG element is at maximum as it is one of the very few games that it captures so well the transition from being a helpless prey to a predator that turns the tables.
Strategy element is strong here as every enemy, from a simple undead to a huge boss, plays differently and requires adapting your play. Same for the environmental hazards.
And horror is here as well as even the weakest enemy can be a nightmare, not to mention that in most cases facing a few of them simultaneously is the fastest way to death.
PROS:
+ amazing dark and depressing atmosphere, imposing and impressive settings in almost all areas of the games
+ bigger-than-life bosses each one with distinct weakenesses and strengths, same for mini/mili/pico/nano bosses and for every possible enemy in the game
+ eerie soundtrack: not used very often but when it does it shines
+ excellent NPC voices
+ infinite combinations of weapons, spells, armors, upgrades, enchancements. Each piece has distinct cons and pros and unique play styles
+ unmatched sense of accomplishment when you manage to beat a boss or to pass to a new area, very-very few games manage to achieve this
CONS:
- the game is so difficult, especially in the beginning, that it will not be a surprise that most players uninstall it in the fist 10-15 minutes
- level of frustation when you die for the 100th time in exactly the same point; I wonder how many keyboards and gamepads paid this price...
- Very difficult keyboard controls, gamepad is almost obligatory
- Camera issues especially at confined spaces. In a super difficult game like Dark Souls this becomes very annoying
- Invisible obstacles/walls can lead to cheap environmental deaths, super annoying as well
- I could not make co-op to work. Seemed impossible to summon friendly phantoms even if the corresponding signs where there. Still, I was invaded a few times by player phantoms. It is a pity as I would definitely like to see the co-op aspect of the game (and it seems that it reduces the difficulty by a lot)
- very few instructions on the gameplay/inventory/progression options. For me it was impossible to progress in the game without spending a huge amount of time in Dark-Souls related wiki pages and watching videos.
- Graphics are not good (not to be confused with the visual design) and I could not install the third-party mods that improve the visuals.
All in all it is a very unique RPG game: at its best it is spectacular, a defining moment in game development that goes beyond the norms. In parallel it has its flaws and due to its super elevated difficulty many players will uninstall it without a second thought.
For me, it is simply a MASTERPIECE, one of the best games I have every played.

This was on pre-order discount on the localizers' site, so I thought "it looks better than Huniepop and it's all-ages" and picked it up. I wish I'd remembered that it was a Minori game -- I'm not a fan of the company for various reasons. I'm also not the target audience for this particular type of story, as the prospect of romance with Sion is not one I find appealing, so others may find value in this story that I didn't.
At a glance, the visuals of eden* are really impressive; they are technically adequate (I like the weathering effects on Elica's old radio, for example), but after a while you start to feel surfeited by the sheer volume of sweeping plains, elaborate vintage mansions, and dramatic winds constantly blowing the characters' hair around even when they're indoors. That's right, instead of static images, mouths move and eyes blink, which is (again) technically cool but also kind of weird. If you leave it on while making a sandwich or whatever, they'll just keep blinking, frozen in time. Spooky. The basic designs of the characters are generic, and everyone looks about half the age they're theoretically supposed to according to the text -- it's unintentionally hilarious when a vaguely teenage-looking dude announces "I'm not thirty yet" as if this is news. Of course all the girls have pretty much the same face (then again, that's true for 90% of visual novels, so it's hard to fault them for this). The opening theme is extremely nice, and I've no complaints about the background music or sound effects, which are serviceable enough. Sion's voice actress is the only one I found pleasant to listen to; I am grateful to Minori for including the option to turn off individual characters' voices, as this meant that I didn't have to listen to Lavinia.
The story here is that oh snap, the Nibiru people were right and the planet is going to be destroyed. The main character, who absolutely everyone falls over themselves to assure us is Totally Cool and Very Strong and The Perfect Soldier, is suddenly stationed at a remote research facility to act as a guard. It transpires that the reason they needed The Coolest And Strongest And Most Perfect Soldier is that The Smartest And Most Beautiful And Most Perfect Little Girl works at the facility. Apparently most of humanity is either dead from a massive war or in the process of leaving Earth on ships engineered by TSAMBAMPLG, so she is not just the smartest person ever (which she is, because she's the smartest of ALL the genetically engineered smart people), she is also the most important person ever. (Seriously, the other characters refer to her as "The Messiah" and literally dream of so much as catching a glance of her. Evidently the writer wanted to make sure absolutely no one missed just how wonderful and special these people are.) In practice, protecting TSAMBAMPLG entails sitting around chatting with several attractive ladies, followed by assassinating the evil spies who are trying to kill TSAMBAMPLG. The story routinely elides scenes that could conceivably be interesting (come on, a fade to black before the welcome party?) and telegraphs future plot elements with such gusto that readers are likely to sigh "finally!" when the main character finally figures out whatever was spelled out an hour or two ago. It's like trying to tell Dora that Boots is behind the box with this guy.
I was told by review after review that eden* had incredibly compelling characters, and so I was a bit put out, to be honest. I didn't find myself empathizing with Ryou at all, and honestly found him incredibly creepy, given the way he becomes obsessed with Sion after talking to her for maybe ten minutes. Sion herself is the "genius girl with no people skills or self-care abilities" archetype that can be found in a million other games, including compatriot Steam VN World End Economica; the standard hand-wave of a childlike character actually being super old is in play, because Minori knows very well how to make money hand over fist. Other characters include Elica, a mischievous and slightly ditzy maid (of course) who takes care of TSAMBAMPLG's everyday needs but seems to have a Dark Secret, and Lavinia or "Lavie", who is probably one of the most annoying characters I've encountered in some time. There's also the Major, who drinks and hits on civilian maids while on the clock and also has a Dark Secret. I'm used to stories in general at least having some sort of break point or divider when the POV changes, so I was jarred and confused when sometimes Ryou left the scene and the narration sort of hung around for a bit -- telling us what other characters are thinking or doing, often related to how awesome Ryou is -- before remembering that it had places to be and skedaddling back to Ryou without warning.
If you hunger for cheesy drama and animu chicks, especially those that are "totally like a hundred years old, so it's cool", this game has you covered. (The Clannad comparison made in other reviews seems apt.) There aren't really standing sprites and the overall presentation is supposed to evoke a movie, so it's not that different from watching a film that requires regular mouse clicks to advance. Still, as far as this type of game goes, I'd much sooner recommend Narcissu or Moonshine. eden* is just not for everyone.

I've played about 60 or so VNs in my time (some translated, some not) and I find Eden to be up there with some of the best. Probably one of the most striking things about this kinectic novel are the amazing visuals. The animation for the character's eyes and mouths immerses you far more than most VNs. Another great thing is putting the game on "auto" mode and displaying it on your HD TV really makes you feel as if you are watching an anime movie rather than simply reading a visual novel. I HIGHLY recommend playing the game this way for the best experience. The characters themselves I thought were quite interesting and deep, although I would have liked to learn more about them.
This game goes through a lot of emotions and you definitely go through these emotions while reading. I often empathized with the characters, felt sad when they were sad, or hopeful when something good happened.
Now for the stuff I didn't like too much: this VN is WAY too short. I was actually surprised at how quickly I read through it on auto mode (which is WAY slower than if I would read it myself). I read it in only 6 hours on the slowest mode! I find this to be far too short for a game like this that depends on character development. I actually wanted to learn about the early lives of the Felixes, more about Lavie, and have more interaction with Elica, who I felt needed more screentime (she was REALLY underdeveloped compared to the other characters I felt).

Undead Labs delivered a title onto XBox live like no other when it came to this particular niche of the zambonie genre. Even with a broken XBox that I had bought cheap, and a knockoff microsoft controller that had it's share of problems I was having a blast. I watched the world around me change as I began ransacking the county, ventiliating craniums along the way. My survivors honed their skills, as they were being equipped better and stockpiling more, still surprising me to this day with how many weapons there are. After maxing out the settings it looked like an entirely new game. Through its developement I was a bit salty about the title going to XBox Live, and still think UL would've been better off focusing on it as a PC title to start with but this more than makes up for it.

I am a big fan of the the original Book of Unwritten Tales and Critter Chronicles is certainly not a terrible game as adventure games go, but the thumb indicates whether I recommended it (not that it's an outright bad game!) and I unfortunately I just can't recommend Critter Chronicles - mainly due to the puzzle quality.
The original game keeps a nice balance between the puzzles being relatively intuitive, yet not quite so blatantly obvious that there's nothing to it.  Generally I could always figure out what needed to be done once I found the right items, without resorting to much trial and error.  Critter Chronicles, however, strays a bit too far into the territory of some of the more egregious 90s adventure game leaps of logic where the solution is stumbled upon only by exhausting all possible options.  More than likely at some point will need to resort to the process of trying to use every item on every other item and hotspot - which is made even more frustrating by having to rather slowly transfer items between two characters, one at a time.
Forgetting the puzzles, the game still retains much of the charm of BoUT.  It's still well acted (though Critter's "dialog" did start to grate on me as the game went on) and nice to look at, but the cast and overall scope of the game is much reduced compared to BoUT.  It comes out feeling a bit thin as a result.
To a certain extent it seems perhaps a bit unfair to hold it up to the standards of the excellent original BoUT, but that's naturally what one would compare it against, since Critter Chronicles is presumably meant for fans of BoUT.  The bottom line is unfortunately that all but the most fanatical of BoUT fans could safely skip Critter Chronicles without feeling like they missed out.  I don't regret playing the game, but knowing what I do now, I wouldn't regret having skipped it either.

You are undead, struggling to fight your way through the realms of Lordran on a quest whose final purpose is anything but clear. Where many games burden you with plot and background lore, Dark Souls lets the places you go tell their own kind of story, one lost in time and shrouded in mystery. The stone ruins at Firelink Shrine, the overrun town known as the UndeadBurg, the vast marble halls of Anor Londo. These all speak of a once prosperous realm rich with history, and rather than spelling it out in detail, Dark Souls lets you wonder about what has dragged this land into its current state of miserable disrepair. Item descriptions and brief conversations with non player characters occasionally illuminate the smallest aspects of Lordran's past, and over time, you may piece together a reasonably fleshed out picture of the crisis that has befallen the land. But you needn't concern yourself with these details if they don't interest you. The wondrous realms of Lordran are sure to seduce you whether you care to know their history or not.

It's been quite a lot of years now since this release so you probably know you are either going to buy this game or not. If you are, you like challenges. If you are not, you probably are not a fan of challenges.
Still, there are some things you should know about the game and the most important one, which you probably know by now is that this game IS A BAD PORT. Thankfully, there are fixes for it which makes things much, much better.
The second think you should, but probably know is that IT WILL MAKE THINGS MUCH BETTER IF YOU HAVE A CONTROLLER. I can totally play DS2 with keyboard and mouse. I actually prefer it that way. But DS1 doesn't have the same ease with configuring key bindings than DS2, probably because of the bad port. I never really bothered in going too deep in trying to customize keys for DS1 though.
Now, if you are willing to get this game, you have probably heard from friends that this game is AMAZING, IT IS AWESOME, THAT IS IS INCREDIBLY HARD, and I must be the one to tell you that IT REALLY IS NOT ALL THAT. The game is really good, but the bad port, some bugs that still exist and will probably never get fixed, the weird and clunky way to find players online (it may take a really long time for the game to notice you are online), some weird hitboxes (altough not as much as DS2) that will make you shout "THAT'S BULLSH-" and fps issues even on decent specs, specially a place named Blighttown may start to impress you.
The game isn't really hard. It even has messages on the floor to guide you through the commands! And I mean, the game is quite punishing and challenging, but it is really not that hard. This game most of the times offers a "hardcore" way to deal with things (mostly go melee against anything) and a "cheap" way to deal with things (basically with a Bow, but the game sometimes offers spots that you just can get nearly untouched and finish monsters and even bosses, for example the Capra Demon). Maybe such cheap ways exist just so that people don't complain too much about the difficuly and prorgess, though. Going full melee in the early game is quite tricky with lack of health, stamina and knowledge of enemy movesets. This game is one of those games in which the first playthrough is very interesting, frustrating, rewarding and everything altogether. If you are playing the game for the first time, I suggest you practice your reaction timing, and don't read any wiki or guide about it unless you are really having a tough time. This is the kind of game you will have suffered a lot to finish for the first time, but know that you learned so much you will probably want to start over just to have smoother, "better" progression and exeperience. And maybe try to PvP.
Also, regarding the game being too hard. You might want to use a Tower Shield and go Tanky, then you will see things getting much, much easier. Just don't expect to be unbeatable. You will still need to roll and dodge and parry efficiently, but the game will be much less punishing if you go through that path. If you want to play a light, glasscannon Dexterity build, then you will need to be much better at dodging and such if you don't want to die a lot.
PvP sometimes has hackers. PvP is really poorly balanced in DS1. The only thing that matters is level bracket. Meaning that in your early games you may find people who completely upgraded their pyromancy abilities (which can be upgraded parallel from levels) and one shot you. Or people who have progressed just a little on the story but already unlocked powerful Sorceries and have made dedicated builds that will one shot you with Soul Spear if you don't pay attention or roll properly. But because the PvP is also poor on the lag issue, you may see yourself rolling and get hit, even backstabbed (the famous lagstabs, which still happens even in DS2, that has a much, much better online system. But still not great when it comes to lagging, or maybe the hitboxes are still bad for the quick time event of backstab).
So now you know. If you buy this game, you probably won't regret it. But I suggest doing so when with a discount. The game is fun and all, but it is crearly not all that and you will know what I am talking about once you play it. But well, not everything is perfect, right?

-------------------------------------------------------------------------
-Cons-
*Graphical glitches can rarely occure forcing you to either restart the level or load a previous save.
(happened twice to me)

(Usually when loading the next level for me)

*Surfaces that aren't smoothed can cause you to become stuck to either floors or walls; forcing you to restart.
(be careful of jagged rocks or little trenches!)

(some levels have hidden passages or ducts you need ...it took me forever to find them)

- Very poor lighting
- Bad level design (it's a linear level but half the time I didn't know where to go)
- Your body snaps during certain sections making going through doors a fickle process
- Controls can be annoying to handle
-This level can be disorienting and make you feel sick if played for a long time
* Explosive weapons are bad.

- All grenade launchers are weaker than rifles
- Explosions do 5x more damage to you compared to the enemy.
- You throw grenades like 2 feet in front of you......? lol
-------------------------------------------------------------------------
-Story-
*Animation was bad but I thought it was funny
*Voice acting wasn't too great.
*Intersting plot twist, but I didn't really care about the writting.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------
-Miscellaneous-

*You can crouch-jump.
* Last level is full of soldier that spam rockets. They kill you in 1 hit....so be careful.
*You need to save often. There is no Auto-Save aside from mission starts.
*MULTIPLAYER IS DEAD. Not a big loss though.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------
-Conclusion-

Man oh man this game is awesome! think League of Legends with an RTS twist! No heroes here, there are 3 factions all with unique units and many abilities. Worried about hour long games? Worry not! There is a system that activates the "final battle" after a certain time if the HQ is not destroyed where the last units fight it out and the last man standing wins!
Pros:
"New" RTS style simulation mixxed with unit strategizing.
Casual for the RTS players who don't want to build bases or arrange units on a board, just plop them down and watch the fireworks!
Many types of units. There are many types of units for each faction. Each unit is well explained and has a good design, so far none of the units feel duplicated or the same.
Currency, there is no "pay to win" aspect, the developers give you free currency for winning a battle a day. With the currency they gave me I was able to unlock 4-5 different units as well as their upgrades. You also win free units by leveling up from battles. You can level up from both AI and player battles.
Graphics, the graphics in this game are very, very very good. The unit detail is amazing there is no clipping or glitching.
AI: Don't feel like playing against other players yet? worry not! The AI in this game can be very challenging! I took a team with 2 other people against 3 AIs and the AI beat us back at the end to where we had to hold the line at our base!
Cons:
Servers/Location
currently there are only servers in Asia, this could represent some connection problems for people. My game would stutter occasionally but I only lost connection once and there was no continuous lag or horrible game-crashing spikes. However the community there is nice, from what I have experienced nobody uses chat and they do not try to undermine or mess with you, they actually try to work with you. In my game I handled the artillery and minor unit control while they handled front line offense.
Grammar/language
this is barely anything to be upset about but it is the only other thing I could find wrong with the game. Some thing are not typed correctly and certain translations are not finished yet.

Okay. We should be fair with Starbound. I will bs nobody.
First off, I am a supporter from back when it was on Early Access.
The game has been dramatically changed since then.
I had to play through the whole game again, since my savegame was not compatible with V1 but who cares really?
So, what IS Starbound?
Well it started as an open world sandbox game. KEEP THAT IN MIND PLEASE.
So, since then a lot of stuff were added.
We got a great set of unlockable technology upgrades, so you can craft gradually stuff you are gonna need.
The game introduces you gradually to its universe with a set of missions, to do some essential things.
The whole tutorial is the lore of the game. Yup! A sandbox with lore as tutorial, how do you like that?
One step before going against the final boss, you know you are ready to explore whatever you want.
What a great idea! You also carry a codex, where you can collect a lot of wrriten stuff, like journals, stories etc etc, very rewarding for readers.
You can collect various stuff, like bugs, fish, fossils, and make collections out of them.
Randomly (?) generated quests occur all the time, with always interesting rewards and not useless stuff.
Challenges are available and a lot of stuff to do.
You can farm, you can have your own pets... what else can I say about this awesome game?
Oh! The world!
Well basically you start on a solar system. Then you go outside of it to another star. Stars are solar systems with planets inside them. Imagine that stars are generated gradually as you move through the universe map. And believe me, there are LOTS of stars, full of planets to explore.
Favorite changes (for early access users that wanna see what's new):
A] The pixel compressor has no penalty.
B] The fuel gathering became an interesting challenge instead of a freaking boring process.
C] Optimized not to lag.

I plan to give it more time to see how the developers improve upon the game, but it's definitely worth the price of the Alpha access.

A fantastic middle-earth adventure, with gameplay and mechanics as engaging as the lore-rich storyline.
Having long avoided this title for fear of what it might be like, I finally took the plunge in a steam sale and was utterly delighted by what I found.
The gameplay was intuitive, even for someone not used to or interested in action games, with the opportunity for fun and visually pleasing combinations of attacks.  Even the QTEs felt like they had their place rather than being an annoyance.  The Nemesis system adds a lot of choice and context to the playthrough, keeping the orc-slaying relevant long after it would have gone stale if it happened through plain open world encounters.  The world, though limited in size, is quite open and lends itself to exploration as you perform challenges and complete collections.
The story and characters should appeal to fans of the films, some being very familiar from the movies with others taken from Tolkien’s lore directly.  I found it to be a tremendous experience, with many nods to famous lines from the books/films liberally but tastefully sprinkled in.  Cut-scenes are deployed well but not excessively.
The visuals are fantastic, and performance is fine (mostly ~80-90fps, with occasional brief drops below 60) running on a 3770k + GTX 970 on a blend of very high and ultra settings.  It's an excellent game at regular pricing but when available on steam for less than £7 on sale, I’d say it’s an absoluete must-have for any LotR or RPG fan.

When I first heard of Dark Souls I was like, "Oh!  King's Field!"  I rented the first King's Field (second in Japan) a lot as a kid.  It confused the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of me.  It was slow, I didn't know where to go and I could only get so far as a six year old.  There were cryptic townspeople, savage plant monsters, out of the way spells that were not very useful and the slowest combat to ever grace the playstation.  But for some reason I enjoyed it.
Enter Dark Souls; as I missed Demon's Souls, Shadow Tower, Eternal Ring and the other King's Field games somehow.  From Software is a company that makes a game, and instead of moving on to a new idea, they just keep making that same game until it reaches perfection.  Dark Souls is the epitome of From Software dungeon crawlers.  It is their, in my eyes, magnum opus.
Don't be fooled by my playtime, as I also had it on the ps3 and played through it a bunch on there (only once all the way through, though).  Dark Souls is the kind of rpg you can experiment with over and over again.  It offers a ton of spells that are mostly situational, slow, methodical combat, weird enemies and cryptic npcs, except now, I'm old enough to appreciate it.
Dark Souls isn't about getting good or having a hardcore experience, although it can be; It's about a brutal, vicious world that respects your abilities and your time.  It is almost what being an adventurer in D&D would feel like if you were on the ground floor.  Forget the controller throwing, sissy nincompoops who can't handle a decent challenge.  If the game gets too hard, one can summon companions from their own game to help defeat the numerous bosses.
Now, to be fair, there are roadblocks in this game (a certain demon and a pair of archers come to mind), but once past them, going back through will almost be a breeze.
Dark Souls is a game that requires that you be alert at all times and to pay attention to your environment.  It is a refreshing game in an era of "press Q to blah blah blah."  I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys action rpgs, dungeon crawlers of all stripes and those looking for a legitimate, no nonsense experience.

Okay. We should be fair with Starbound. I will bs nobody.
First off, I am a supporter from back when it was on Early Access.
The game has been dramatically changed since then.
I had to play through the whole game again, since my savegame was not compatible with V1 but who cares really?
So, what IS Starbound?
Well it started as an open world sandbox game. KEEP THAT IN MIND PLEASE.
So, since then a lot of stuff were added.
We got a great set of unlockable technology upgrades, so you can craft gradually stuff you are gonna need.
The game introduces you gradually to its universe with a set of missions, to do some essential things.
The whole tutorial is the lore of the game. Yup! A sandbox with lore as tutorial, how do you like that?
One step before going against the final boss, you know you are ready to explore whatever you want.
What a great idea! You also carry a codex, where you can collect a lot of wrriten stuff, like journals, stories etc etc, very rewarding for readers.
You can collect various stuff, like bugs, fish, fossils, and make collections out of them.
Randomly (?) generated quests occur all the time, with always interesting rewards and not useless stuff.
Challenges are available and a lot of stuff to do.
You can farm, you can have your own pets... what else can I say about this awesome game?
Oh! The world!
Well basically you start on a solar system. Then you go outside of it to another star. Stars are solar systems with planets inside them. Imagine that stars are generated gradually as you move through the universe map. And believe me, there are LOTS of stars, full of planets to explore.
Favorite changes (for early access users that wanna see what's new):
A] The pixel compressor has no penalty.
B] The fuel gathering became an interesting challenge instead of a freaking boring process.
C] Optimized not to lag.

Miscreated is a promising survival fps with crafting & base building. At the time of making this review the game is very well optimized with impressive dynamic shadows and a large but somewhat barren landscape. Mutants & other players pose as the main threat although mutants are very rarely spotted, much like the zombies in DayZ. Exploration feels refreshing at first. You can enter every single building in the game world and loot melts in very well with the environment. I found it much easier to find them using my flashlight since all the small items on the floor and on shelves would cast shadows. It’s a small game mechanic that really gives it a lot of atmosphere.
It does feel like it becomes somewhat repetitive after a while though. It’s very time consuming to keep scouring every corner of a building in the hopes of finding some elusive ammunition and there doesn’t seem to be a lot of items in the game yet so there’s a lot of the same o’ same o’.
The sound is the games large downfall in my opinion. It’s awful.  The sound of gunshots does not have any dynamic. Even if you’re in an open field and fire a revolver there’s no echo. It sounds as if you’re firing it in a soundproof booth and it kind of just cuts off before the sound played through properly. Some effects sound very loud as if the source of the sound is very close to you although it could be a block away. The sound of footsteps sometimes repeat, making it sound as if there’s somebody else in the same building as you. Very annoying.
I do however understand that this is an early access title and that these are all issues that will probably be fixed eventually. It’s a good game for what it is & I am sure it will eventually be a very good survival game.
Worth the price right now? I would probably wait but keep a close eye on it. Buy it at a discount. If you love survival games but you’re tired of DayZ I’d give this one a go.

I personally really enjoyed the game, but I am probably capable of liking just about everything so I've decided to make a pros and cons list.
PROS:
+The art looked really nice. I liked the simple character designs against a more complex background, and all of the backgrounds were detailed and nice looking
+I really liked the dialogue and the text that popped up when you clicked on stuff. Almost everything you combined or made interact with other things had different text, which was really cool to me.
+I liked the characters and was interested to see what would happen next, which is pretty good because a lot of the times I don't care.
+A lot of people complained about the mini games, but I really liked them.
+The puzzles at the beginning were fun and nice to complete
CONS:
-The puzzles near the end were just clicking on random things and praying. The description said no dream logic but that was exactly what happened
-Very glitchy. This is probably the most major problem. If just this one problem were fixed, everything would be great. When I first played it, things weren't cropped right, and everything was just off centered. Sometimes I could see parts of other rooms I didn't even know about yet.
I actually got rid of steam and reinstalled it in order for it to be functional, Now it works great, but my computer is suffering. Why should a few videos and dialogue cause so much suffering?
-The strife scenes were very... strange? I feel like they would be better if there was some sort of health bar so you could feel that you were progressing in some way, and have you use some kind of fighting ability instead of relying on the random stuff you just pick up.
-There were a lot of homestuck references. While this is a homestuck game, so it makes sense that there'd be references, but there were some characters that were mentioned whose implications only someone who knew the character would understand. The storyline still makes sense, and its not completely void of entertainment if you haven't read it.
-The character animations were kind of off. They were kind of jittery sometimes, and other times they didn't quite match the action.
Also, some times the door opening animation doesn't quite match up with the door but at this point I'm just nitpicking.
-The game is pretty short. I personally was fine with it, I wish it was longer but it's like how I wish a book I was reading was longer. I don't feel cheated, I just feel excited for the next one. However some other people feel cheated and I can understand that.
-Really long production time. Why did it take so long, I finished in about 3 hours.
-"Everything has unique text when interacted with another thing" is a lie. Some things would say stuff, so saying that goes against the description.
-This is more of a misconception than anything else, but I thought there would be multiple endings and they did not exist. This makes the 3 hours worth that much less.
OVERALL:
Wait until the glitches are resolved and only then should you think about buying it. You do not want to go though the pain I went through. After the glitches are fixed, then continue to proceed cautiously. I love homestuck and I love a lot of the things in this game, but watch a playthrough if you just want to see the pretty pictures.

Let me start off by saying, if you liked Homestuck you'll like Hiveswap. Everything is here except this time around there's a lot less plot to deal with and only vague references and mentions. It helps to know the mechanics in Homestuck, but none of it is required. Now let me follow up and say that if you don't enjoy reading loads of text, using things with other things, you probably won't get a lot out of Hiveswap. There's cute characters, funny moments, and all sorts of little things going on if you just play the game through with the basic plot. If you start using everything with everything else you start understanding the characters as a whole. And that's Hiveswap's strength, getting you invested in the main characters through stupid completely optional interactions. And even if you don't do these interactions, the vast colorful cluttered environments come a close second, showing a ton of character in their own way.
But ultimately, Hiveswap is just a slightly more interactive version of Homestuck. Since accessibility to the craziness of the media is the concept, puzzles are very simple and interacting with objects will give you big hints that will tell you exactly what to do. It's a good thing that Hiveswap advertises this because adventure game veterans are going to feel a little underwhelmed. Again, however, this is a game where the completely optional acts of using things with things will fill in all those little spaces where the game may feel less than stellar. And nearly every thing you use other things with have unique dialogue! Hooray!
Big tip: if you intend to play the game this way, DIGEST IT. There is so much text, so much text, Homestuck is near legendary for its ability to completely smother pages with texts, Hiveswap is no different. If you really want to use everything with everything, then my friend, you have a 6 hour game ahead of you. So yes, take your time to enjoy it because you will get tired out if you don't. If you decide to just run through Hiveswap, it's considerably less time at about 2 to 3 hours, probably less if you know what you're doing or don't bother checking anything. But again, a lot of the fun is just those optional dialogues.
If you're interested in Homestuck but haven't read it or read very far into it, Hiveswap is... somewhat of a good jump in point. There's almost no spoilers to the main series, or at least any obvious ones. And from what I've seen, Act 1 doesn't reference the webcomic's plot at all. If you're a big Homestuck fan, then you're going to like Act 1 and it'll be over too soon. Just think of it as an update followed by a megapause. It's like Homestuck never ended. And if I'm going to be frank, given how much dialogue and text there is in Act 1, I'm pretty relieved that there'll be time to talk and speculate about every little thing. I feel like I have a headache after using a pidgeon on literally hundreds of items.

I find Savage Lands to be be strangely frustrating. I play single player and the difficulty is punishing. I'm glad that there is finally a health bar for enemies, but overall I think that I enjoyed the game more a year ago than I do now.
The new map is attractive and the graphics are good, but starting out is now even harder. I played for a few hours today and my little dude, Amy*, needs to eat about 5 pigs a day, just to not starve to death. Amy apparently has an amazing metabolism, perhaps it's the cold climate.
Chopping down a tree with low level tools now takes 4 times as long as before and pretty much destroys the axe after 1 tree. I'm not sure if it's been fixed yet, but the last time I tried building a house (which took ages what with the slow chopping and the rapidly disintegrating axes) I couldn't actually get inside it, because the doorway was too small. So now I am spending an excruciatingly long time building a stone house. Apparently, they are easier to enter. I sure hope so.
I frequently get a bug that makes it so that the crafting recipe for an item only appears if I
have the materials in my inventory, making crafting things a right pain in the posterior. Relogging does fix it temporarily, but it's really frustrating.
Getting cold reduces the health bar, but warming back up doesn't allow the lost health to regenerate. So I try to only eat when near a fire so that I can restore the lost health and frankly, it's just another annoyance. As soon as you walk away from your fire you are becoming injured by cold.
There are plenty of updates and the game is still in active development, unfortunately the development feels somewhat chaotic and it's very difficult to find up-to-date info on anything.
I would love to explore further and see more of the world and possibly it would be a whole lot more fun with a group of friends, but the way that I am feeling right now is that I cannot recommend it in its current state. Hopefully, one day things will feel more balanced and less buggy, but I suspect that the developers are focused more on creating the game that they want to play, rather than the game that I want to play, which is of course their prerogative, but I cannot recommend a game that I'm not really enjoying playing.
*My little dude is called Amy, in honour of the fact that I cannot play as a female character.

The Book of Unwritten Tales: The Critter Chronicles acts as a prequel to the first game in the series, The Book of Unwritten Tales. This game tells us about Critter and his(?) people and how he and Nate meet.

Although he'll show nice traits from time to time, especially when it's about something important, Nate acts like a self-centered, narcissistic buffoon when interacting with other people. Since the game has steam achievements some of which are bound to the difficulty setting the game basically requires two play-throughs. For that reason I would have liked to be able to skip the cutscenes between chapters.
Even more than the first game The Book of Unwritten Tales: The Critter Chronicles is easily recommendable. It's no Sam&Max or Monkey Island but still a good and solid game. I had fun with both books.

The prequel of Book of Unwritten Tales is shorter, a little more desolate, but has a tighter pace and most importantly, more Critter! It doesn’t exactly reach the same level of excellence as BoUT did, but it’s still a fun little adventure game.
Critter Chronicles was created to fix the greatest error in the first Book of Unwritten Tales: not enough Critter. It also serves as a prequel, telling the tale of how Critter and Nate met and eventually wound up as the two hapless travelling companions you found in the clutches of an ork bounty huntress.
As a game it functions more or less as an expansion pack: it’s about half as short, features only three main locations, and two controllable characters. Luckily the humour remained, albeit in much smaller doses.
The shortness is compensated by increased difficulty, including a larger dependence on character switching. The helpful hotspots remained, but even that is not enough to brute-force your way through everything.
The levels are less detailed– mostly because most of the game takes place on a desolate iceland– and there are very huge chunks where the designers just used high-resolution 2D images instead of elaborate 3D models. Since the engine is the same, the clipping issues remained too, but maybe they are a bit more frequent than they should be.
These mistakes don’t turn Critter Chronicles into a bad game, far from it, but they make it recommended mostly for those who are familiar with the original Book of Unwritten Tales.

Middle Earth: Shadows of mordor is absolutely an amazing game on almost every aspect (I said almost every, there are couple of things that does bug me, later more about that)
Personally I'm a huge fan of open world, stealth and brutal kills games, and this one offers everything.
Choose for yourself how you wanna handle a mission or just random encounters. wanna go from death from above or sneak in a bush and kill the enemy when they least expect it? Or just go screaming, head on into a fortress filled with orcs.
Even that there isn't much of variation in the missions and general gameplay. This game still offers a lot of varity in the way you choose to play: Sword head on into combat, Distance Bow and arrow or Stealth dagger. Every category has it's own perks that make is soo enjoyable.
The best part (and worst) imo are the captains and warchiefs, they have their own special abilities, fears, weaknesses, strenghts what gives you a way of varity on how to approach a captain or warchief. One becomes terrefied by fire but gets stronger when health drops below 50%. Others are invunerable for arrows and stealth but are weak against sword combat. makes you think on how to kill one.
then again, that 'worst' part is that sometimes the abilities combinations (mainly of warchiefs) are just ridiculous. I've had multiple times a warchief that was invunerable for sword combat, bow and arrow and stealth and can kill a caragor easely. that are some of those moments you have to think, how the f*** am I going to kill this guy. then again it makes you think and be creative, per say, take over 2 captains and command them to attack the warchief or find a graug and use him to kill the warchief.
Really enjoyable game, not only gameplay, but visual, 1st part you walk around in a dead and filled with fear land, second part, you walk around in a nice green and 'lovely' land. DLC's are nice as well, get to play and enjoy the story of the other characters you meet during your own campaign. classic hidden objects and collectibles. easy to understand ranking system and the skill tree, if you don't understand that, idk what you will understand. the side missions you randomly encounter during free roaming. One last thing that bothers me is that sometimes you have to kill a captain in a specific way or else he keeps coming back. I had to kill a captain 4 times before he was actually dead. something I don't really enjoy, but that is my opinion.

In my opinion, Bastion's gameplay is one of the least enjoyable things about it. Movement is slow, necessitating spamming the roll button repeatedly if you want to cover any ground in what I consider a reasonable timeframe, and the combat just didn't thrill me. The weapons are quite varied and have some nice upgrades, though. I much prefer my action RPG combat be more Diablo-styled, but that's neither here nor there. If you'll notice, I'm still recommending the game. Why?
Music, art style, and the buttery, sensual voice of the dude the creators of Bastion apparently have on permanent retainer for doing voicework on their games. Well, either that, or they keep him locked in a dungeon and let him out to voice act whenever they make a new game. Either way, I'm down with it. This one voice actor is the narrator for the game, and wow is his voice awesome. He says casual remarks about what's happened in the city, usually with an ecclectic bit of reminiscing, and it's just cool. You should know within a few minutes if you like it or not. If not, this may not be the game for you, but if you dig his voice, you're going to get so many healthy servings of it.
The game has a visual look that I really like. The characters look just okay in my opinion, but the backgrounds just delight my eyes. It's all aesthetically pleasing to me. And the music. WOW. I listen to this game's soundtrack at work. It's amazing. You can listen to the whole thing, posted free to YouTube by the developers themselves. It's superb, in my opinion. I love it, and it works so well with the visuals of the game, and there are some emotional scenes late game that the music absolutely elevates to a new high.
The story is also pretty good, though a few things are a little unclear, such as "Does the city normally float, or is that due to the Calamity?" and "What exactly happens in the Calamity itself?" (HOW it's triggered is explained, though) and other gnawing questions for me. That said, always listen to the narrator, because he drops some epic plot bombs on you while you're fighting and walking about. I do wish they would have timed some of these revelations so that it's not during an ambush attack that could kill me if I do something wrong, because then I get distracted and miss a little bit of what the narrator is saying, which is the story!
All in all, I enjoyed this game more than the first time I played it, a few years back. I didn't like the gameplay as much the second time around, but everything else was much better than I remembered. It's definitely a game I would recommend.

Action RPG at its best. Can not get better than that but the game is not for the average player who either does not have the time or the patience to invest a lot of time dying and dying and dying before rising up...
It is a fantasy RPG around an undead who starts fighting hordes of initially completely overpowered enemies. No surprise that in the beggining you will die A LOT (you can not say that the title did not warn you).
The RPG element is at maximum as it is one of the very few games that it captures so well the transition from being a helpless prey to a predator that turns the tables.
Strategy element is strong here as every enemy, from a simple undead to a huge boss, plays differently and requires adapting your play. Same for the environmental hazards.
And horror is here as well as even the weakest enemy can be a nightmare, not to mention that in most cases facing a few of them simultaneously is the fastest way to death.
PROS:
+ amazing dark and depressing atmosphere, imposing and impressive settings in almost all areas of the games
+ bigger-than-life bosses each one with distinct weakenesses and strengths, same for mini/mili/pico/nano bosses and for every possible enemy in the game
+ eerie soundtrack: not used very often but when it does it shines
+ excellent NPC voices
+ infinite combinations of weapons, spells, armors, upgrades, enchancements. Each piece has distinct cons and pros and unique play styles
+ unmatched sense of accomplishment when you manage to beat a boss or to pass to a new area, very-very few games manage to achieve this
CONS:
- the game is so difficult, especially in the beginning, that it will not be a surprise that most players uninstall it in the fist 10-15 minutes
- level of frustation when you die for the 100th time in exactly the same point; I wonder how many keyboards and gamepads paid this price...
- Very difficult keyboard controls, gamepad is almost obligatory
- Camera issues especially at confined spaces. In a super difficult game like Dark Souls this becomes very annoying
- Invisible obstacles/walls can lead to cheap environmental deaths, super annoying as well
- I could not make co-op to work. Seemed impossible to summon friendly phantoms even if the corresponding signs where there. Still, I was invaded a few times by player phantoms. It is a pity as I would definitely like to see the co-op aspect of the game (and it seems that it reduces the difficulty by a lot)
- very few instructions on the gameplay/inventory/progression options. For me it was impossible to progress in the game without spending a huge amount of time in Dark-Souls related wiki pages and watching videos.
- Graphics are not good (not to be confused with the visual design) and I could not install the third-party mods that improve the visuals.
All in all it is a very unique RPG game: at its best it is spectacular, a defining moment in game development that goes beyond the norms. In parallel it has its flaws and due to its super elevated difficulty many players will uninstall it without a second thought.
For me, it is simply a MASTERPIECE, one of the best games I have every played.

Before you read any further let me make one thing clear- this game is very, very good. Exceptional even, so many elements of it are masterfully designed to give a totally different and amazing gaming experience.
So, lets get the elephant in the room out of the way- Difficulty.
Yes this game is hard- especially the start. In fact you will probably doubt that you'll get to the end of it after the first hour or so, however, it is vitally important to stick with it. You will improve your skills massively in time, things that seemed nearly impossible will become almost trivially easy, this is part of the charm. You feel yourself grow in ability so much, relying only on your sharpened skills to take on truly overwhelming challenge and succeeding. The way difficulty works in this game is masterful. The gameplay is great, what feels clunky and unusable at first becomes very smooth and responsive in experienced hands, this game above any other I've played has one of the strongest connections of your wits to your performance, which is invigorating for tough fights.
The world in which it all takes place is despiringly bleak and desperate, the story is not told to you. Instead you are placed in a world and have to make your own conclusions about it's denizens and their motivations, the events that transpire and what it all means. This again is quite different to most games and triggers the curiousity in you much more than the standard formula, it has a feel almost like the old 'Myst' on PC (although it is not puzzle based).
Having the hindsight of multiple completions and nearly 300 hours play, I would rank this game as a modern classic. So much of it is a fundamentally different and richer experience than most games around these days. The more you play the more you realise the genius and originality of the design.
***As an aside- one word of warning. I would research online as to how to build your character and how to make strong weapons, it is not at all obvious and the game could be made much to difficult if you don't do it correctly.
***As a second and vitally important aside- Get an xbox controller for your PC if you are buying this. Mouse and keyboard was unplayable. They are fairly cheap and can be used for other games that work best with controller too. I already had one for use with a gamecube emulator.

Dark fantasy, action RPG that has some old school elements, such as its infamous high difficulty, and sports a great atmosphere.
It's true that the game is hard, but saying that it's its only real trait would be underselling its other great strengths.  The reason why it's hard isn't just due to brute force and cheap deaths, but like old school games, the enemies have very simple patterns and traps that you need to analyze first, then react accordingly with your easy-to-learn array to moves, either by blocking and timing counterattacks, or dodging like the wind, and you have to do all that for quite a while until you can get to the next campfire, the safe havens of the game.  It's a game that you can't just run through, there needs to be lots of care in your actions, and a certain degree of commitment.  If you are the type of gamer that play games as an hobby and not as a job, no matter how many times you die, I can guarantee you'll succeed.
The game puts at your disposition loads of options to customize your playstyle.  As I've said, the game has somewhat simplistic, but terrifyingly effective controls.
First, there isn't like a combo system, so you can only attack by doing light and heavy attacks, kicks that unbalance weaker enemies, dropping off from heights as you slash to deal massive damage, backstabbing, and parrying, an expert move that is very useful, but not necessary.  There are a lot of different weapon types, each with their own attack styles; there's the clubs that you mindlessly bash enemies' with, or the Halberd that allows you to stab from a distance and do arching attacks.
Furthermore, none of the weapons ever come as being inferior to one another of their own type, each of them has their own little strengths, such as providing a better boost if you have more Dexterity or Faith, and there are elemental damages, which can be a major factor in your success, as every enemies is weak to some type, so you have to take into account your equipment for every areas you take on.  The elemental damages may be often seen in RPGs, but it always keeps on providing a lot of strategy in return, Dark Souls being no exception.
You further customize your character depending on the stats you level up; if you level up Dexterity, you're better off using skillful weapons like whips and Shotels, or if you raised Faith, you'll be using "holy" weapons and Miracles using Talismans.
You avoid damage by blocking with your shield, or by rolling; said rolling, let alone the speed of your character, is heavily affected by your equipment load, so you have to sacrifice defense for more mobility.
Despite the somewhat simplistic nature, there's loads of ways you can play the game; you could block damage with big shields and tank with heavy armors, to then land perfectly timed, destructive counterattacks, or sacrifice all that for more mobility, taking the risk of receiving deadlier blows for having faster rolls, to then land backstabs or using magic at a safer distance.  Dark Souls perfectly displays your approach, you can either play it pretty casually, or use more complex strategies, there's isn't really a bad way to play it.
There's also a lot of replay value, in the way you can start fresh; in your next playthrough, you could maybe try for lighter swords, or take a shot at Dexterity weapons, or a mixture of magic and heavy axes.
The game's presentation is fantastic.  It gives off a very ominous vibe, due to its dark locales and grotesque hellspawns, the complete abscence of anything remotely cheerful, and the lack of music outside of boss battles and the Firelink Shrine, which are great orchestral themes.  This gloomy atmosphere gives it quite the strong identity.
So, despite its high difficulty, I would recommend this game to anyone who is ready to broaden their horizons, it's an old school experience that's rarely seen and executed so well nowadays.  Dark Souls has a lot of polish, and I do not regret any of the many hours I've spent on it, as it was such a great and unforgettable experience.
It may not have been long, but I was moved by the story and will never regret its purchase.

Stranded Deep is an Island Survival game, and is really well done. There are your normal Survival Crafting game ideas present: such as building basic tools, making a decent house, keeping your food/water levels up, trying to not get badly damaged or poisoned, etc.  The game does look fantastic on higher settings, and simpler computers should be able to run it (Probably not your mom's Commodore 64, however lol).  Since the game is island-based survival, the game does not require that much hard drive space (like you literally only need about 1 GB to actually install), and this should bring a sigh of relief because it seems that all present games require atleast a minimum of 20 or so GBs to play it.  Some may dislike the crafting now, but my personal opinion is that it is pretty simple to manage, once you get the idea that you need to be around an object you are trying to build, you pretty much have the hang of it.  Yes, the game does have some minor bugs, but really what would you expect from an Alpha build of the game.  All in all, the game is very fun to play even in such an early stage of development. Highly reccommended for those who like crafting, survival, and (as of right now) single player games.  Can't wait for future updates that will further expand the game....and multiplayer. :D

This game is very interesting, and, even in early development, has exceeded my expectations. As a game that has been played by quite a few popular Youtubers, it has certainly received a bit of well-deserved attention. It appears to be randomly generated, which certainly gives it a plus. (And even if it's not, the general lay out really puts you in a confused area every time, making the scenario more realistic as a lost survivor.) The graphics are very nice, and manage to be realistic even with rather simplistic and non-laggy designs, nor any form of motion blur and intense, system-crashing rendering, making it friendly for those with lesser computers (or multi-tabbers). The crafting system is very interesting, although it may be difficult to understand for beginners. However, it does make it easier to do things with a limit inventory, and has a more realistic feel to it then many other games that involve crafting. The developers of the game have also been very listening to their users and have been constantly fixing it and making updates, which shows very good usage of the Early Access feature. If you enjoy first-person survival games or enjoy a tropical ocean setting, this is a game you must have. For the price you pay, it is a very worthy experience.

While you can certainly tell that this game was rushed out or lacked funding or had some other issue in its implementation and polish stages, that does not stop it from being probably the best zombie game on the market. It really is about managing your survivor group and your base and staying alive, and due to the leveling system you grow to care about certain characters. It is a shame interacting with other NPCs is so basic and that there are not a very large amount of random events (they end up getting recycled fairly fast) because the way that events take place in the world mostly seamlessly is impressive. There are certainly some bugs with the AI, and it's not very smart to begin with. Despite these few drawbacks I have mentioned, the sheer massive amount of ambition in the features the game has to offer more than makes up for it's failings. If you are interested in sandbox games or survival games, this is probably your best bet.

When the region is gone crazy what will you do? Scavenge and fight for survival as the zombies prowl hungry for your flesh. Savage Lands is a work in progress, but it is worth your support.  You start play naked and alone on a hostile shore.  Your health declines due to the cold, and you need to eat to maintain stamina so you can run.  When you start out, the learning curve is steep and it takes a while before you get the hang of things, so you die, respawn and go and retreive your lost gear and try try again.  The game is unforgiving, and that is the charm of it.  If it were easy you would get bored of it very quickly.  To the Devs credit they are responsive and hands on and release changes ever week or two in my experience.  This is not Skyrim, it is its own beast, but frankly it has things that Skyrim would have benefitted from such as there being a point to eating and staying warm.  By the time this game is finished I think it will be pretty excellent.

So up until this point, I hadn't played a story driven game in years. Survival games and MMO's made up all of the games that I had played for a while and they were starting to get a bit stale. So I started looking for a game with an amazing story. I remembered back a couple years to my buddy walking around in his Mass Effect 3 gear a few years back when it first came out and how he talked about the series in such a high regard. So when I saw the steam series collection of the Mass Effect games (Mass Effect and Mass Effect 2) on sale for less than ten bucks, I immediately bought them. I wasn't disappointed.
The game starts rather abruptly but you're immediately thrown into an immersive universe with a massive library of lore which will continue to expand in the codex as your journey progresses. You play as Commander Shepard (or a character of your own creation), humanity's first Spectre. Humanity is a young species in the world of galactic politics and, as a spectre, you're a crucial step on the path to its acceptance by the rest of the council species. Your first mission: track down and stop the rogue spectre Saren. With a horde of Geth minions standing in your way, it's a race against time to gain the information needed to decipher a message implanted in your mind by a Prothean beacon
The combat is fluid and may be a bit too easy (not entirely sure until I replay the game on a higher difficulty). As long as you keep the enemy at a distance it's very easy to systematically pick apart any opposition with the help of two comrades whom you pick at the start of each mission. Each ally has their own skillset and special abilities which change the way you interact with the environment and fight your enemies. These allies range from a Krogan mercenary to an Asari scientist (who's a possible love interest if you've ever had a crush on Aayla Secura in Star Wars).
So the game has an epic story, a variety of interesting characters, fun, interesting squad abilities and gameplay; and fluid and satisfying combat. Where are the downfalls? Well the most annoying problem is the interruptions in dialogue that happen once in a while where the voices freeze while the game keeps going, cutting off the end of the character's statement. This can be remedied by turning on subtitles of course but it doesn't keep the occasional pause from touching a nerve. Another issue is that at certain points in the game, autosaves are few and far between meaning that if you do die, you risk getting set back 20 minutes or more in play time. At times the dialogue can also seem a tad robotic and the charm/intimidate dialogue choices seem to work a little too well with it convincing characters steadfast in one mindset to look the other way with very little to no additional effort.
If you like sci-fi and want a story of epic proportion to hold you over until the next Star Wars movies come out, look no further. At 40 hours, I've just completed my first playthrough without completing the DLC missions and a handful of the sidemissions so it's an extroadinary value for your money. I'm planning on playing it through again to finish up the content that I missed the first time around. If you can, wait for the series pack to go on sale again and pick it up for under ten bucks. You won't regret your purchase.

Graphics: I would say a 7 out of 10. Not Skyrim level or anything, but it has decent lighting effects, character and animal models aren't all that pretty, but not the worst you will see either.
Optimisation: 4 out of 10 in this area. Poorly optimised at this point and with a skylake i5, gtx 970 and 8gb of DDR4 RAM I max out in the 40s and 50s range of fps with stuttering, drops, etc.
Sound: 8 out of 10 as the sounds and atmospheric noise really fit the game. Animals, skeleton movement, wind, fire crackling, tree chopping, and mining all sound as you would expect them to and good.
Difficulty:
Couple of things affect Difficulty in this game and I will touch on them:
Attacks from enemies : You get attacked and you can bleed which can be healed by bandages which are not hard to find.
HUNGER: You can die from hunger really fast with the last update and you will either accept hunger related death as something you will just have to put up with or the alternative of spending most of your time hunting for food which isn't hard, but cheaply adds to the difficulty and is unrealistically difficult in my opinion.
being killed with one shot in R6 Vegas was fine because it's hard, but it's realistic, dying in a half a gametime day due to not eating 6 or 7 wolf meats is absurd and laughably unrealistic so I feel it's lazy and cheap hard in my opinion.
BODY TEMPERATURE: The elements can decrease your health bar which is normally red and replace it with a blue bar, which, when filled means your freezing and close to turning into a human popsicle if you don't seek shelter you've made or as usually the case in the beginning a fire. I actually thought this was pretty cool and loved the idea until you step into some water...When I did, then I realized, like my previous gripe, this game had resorted to another cheap way of inflating the difficulty level as it takes about 10-15 seconds to freeze the death with a full health bar if you're standing in the water.
COMMUNITY: 10 out 10. Aside from those who will defend this game like rabid fanboys if you criticize the game or point out it's shortcomings, the community is awesome and I've made friends with people on here that i hook up with in other games. Lose your stuff due to a bug (it will happen) and you can go to a server and chances are someone will help you get back on your feet.
SUMMARY
I struggle between recommending and not recommending the game because it's good and I enjoyed it, but I can't say it's a game for everyone. If you like hard games, then this is for you, but if you, like me, like games that are challenging in an honorable way ie no cheap and artificial ways of inflating the difficulty/making it an exercise in anger management then this might not be your cup of tea. You might also want to steer clear of this if you mind lag, bugs, fps drops, etc because unless you have a 980, equivalent, or better, i7, 16GB RAM or similar set up then you're going to more then likely experience these things as it is Early Access and optimization wise it shows.

The Swapper explores the iconic Theseus Paradox to it's fullest; how much can an object or, in this case, a person and their mind, change before they are no longer that same fundamental object or person.
What is identity and how do we defiine it, by the whole or by components, by the mind or by the body, by memory or by an active working consciousness, must we be animate or inanimate and who decides what exactly defines activity or passivity (maybe rocks are a higher, more intelligent being than humans but we lack the ability to communicate together). Is the core of a person contained in some ethereal soul or is it something more, perhaps it is something less.
Through the philosophical narrative within, The Swapper leads also to an existentialist exploration of the mind and body, yet I can't tell if the argument is pro 'existence precedes essence' or con 'essence precedes existence'. If we define ourselves by our ability to think and remember, a la Descartes, perhaps The Swapper is just a test to discover whether we are real. Whatever the answer, Sartre and indeed Aristotle would have enjoyed this.

Bastion. A lot has been said about this game, but let's cover the basics. Released in 2011; it was awarded with over a hundred awards; including "Best Debut Game." Does it deserve those awards?
Graphics
This game excels at three things, and this is one of them. The world is beautiful, even in it's collapsed state. Every frame flows well, and there are bright, vibrant colors that only watercolor games can bring. A few things are proportioned oddly, like the main character looks like someone that skipped leg day most of the time, aside from during cinematics; where everyone has a large head. That said, those little things add charm to the game, and are easily overlooked, and so I can't hold them against the game.
Controls
Perhaps the weakest part of the game. For an action RPG, it's pretty slow paced. The Kid moves slowly, and some of the weapons are also really slow. The controls also felt backwards throughout most of the first playthrough. I found myself using my ranged weapons a lot when I was intending to use my melee weapons, and this continued all the way to the final levels.
Disclaimer; this game is designed with controllers is mind, so it plays best with that, but it is slow enough paced that people without them that aren't used to the keyboard shouldn't have much issue. The keyboard controls are fine, though they also suffer from the same issues as the controller in regards to feeling off.
While your first weapon is slow, you acquire weapons of varying speed, and all are masterfully balanced, so you will find a loadout that you like, and will stick with that, saving for when you get new weapons, the game forces you to change to it, so that you can practice with it for a little while.
Overall, the game is simple, easy to pick up, but a little awkward on the controls.
Sound
In short: I have nothing but praise for this part of the game. It is good enough that it deserves recognition. Bastion's music is nothing short of outstanding. While there are only around half a dozen songs, they all convey the emotion of the scene well, and are not in the least distracting. They enhance the story well.

Story
Easily the best part of the game. Overall, it's short, only around six hours long on your first playthrough, and that's including the "Who Knows Where" sidequests. With that said, the brevity of the story is actually a strong point. No section feels long and drawn out, with each part of the story only as long as it needs to be.
I'm not going to go into detail about the story itself, but it is told through the use of a narrator, and while that normally is a problem, here, it works.
There are a few choices, which all matter, but they are more a moral choice, as they have no actual rewards or consequences for those choices. They are strictly about what you would do in those spots.
The story is easily the strongest point in an overall great game. While it doesn't stir any emotions, save for a few spots, it does a tremendous job of pulling you in and making you care about the characters and your pets.
Grade
Easy A. Bastion deserves those accolades. While not one of the best games of all time, it is a tremendous effort by a developer that hadn't created any games before this one. While there are a few shortcomings, mainly in the control side, it is one of the better games of 2011. Add in the New Game+ feature for added replay, and you have an overall excellent game.
