Action RPG at its best. Can not get better than that but the game is not for the average player who either does not have the time or the patience to invest a lot of time dying and dying and dying before rising up...
It is a fantasy RPG around an undead who starts fighting hordes of initially completely overpowered enemies. No surprise that in the beggining you will die A LOT (you can not say that the title did not warn you).
The RPG element is at maximum as it is one of the very few games that it captures so well the transition from being a helpless prey to a predator that turns the tables.
Strategy element is strong here as every enemy, from a simple undead to a huge boss, plays differently and requires adapting your play. Same for the environmental hazards.
And horror is here as well as even the weakest enemy can be a nightmare, not to mention that in most cases facing a few of them simultaneously is the fastest way to death.
PROS:
+ amazing dark and depressing atmosphere, imposing and impressive settings in almost all areas of the games
+ bigger-than-life bosses each one with distinct weakenesses and strengths, same for mini/mili/pico/nano bosses and for every possible enemy in the game
+ eerie soundtrack: not used very often but when it does it shines
+ excellent NPC voices
+ infinite combinations of weapons, spells, armors, upgrades, enchancements. Each piece has distinct cons and pros and unique play styles
+ unmatched sense of accomplishment when you manage to beat a boss or to pass to a new area, very-very few games manage to achieve this
CONS:
- the game is so difficult, especially in the beginning, that it will not be a surprise that most players uninstall it in the fist 10-15 minutes
- level of frustation when you die for the 100th time in exactly the same point; I wonder how many keyboards and gamepads paid this price...
- Very difficult keyboard controls, gamepad is almost obligatory
- Camera issues especially at confined spaces. In a super difficult game like Dark Souls this becomes very annoying
- Invisible obstacles/walls can lead to cheap environmental deaths, super annoying as well
- I could not make co-op to work. Seemed impossible to summon friendly phantoms even if the corresponding signs where there. Still, I was invaded a few times by player phantoms. It is a pity as I would definitely like to see the co-op aspect of the game (and it seems that it reduces the difficulty by a lot)
- very few instructions on the gameplay/inventory/progression options. For me it was impossible to progress in the game without spending a huge amount of time in Dark-Souls related wiki pages and watching videos.
- Graphics are not good (not to be confused with the visual design) and I could not install the third-party mods that improve the visuals.
All in all it is a very unique RPG game: at its best it is spectacular, a defining moment in game development that goes beyond the norms. In parallel it has its flaws and due to its super elevated difficulty many players will uninstall it without a second thought.
For me, it is simply a MASTERPIECE, one of the best games I have every played.

Before you read any further let me make one thing clear- this game is very, very good. Exceptional even, so many elements of it are masterfully designed to give a totally different and amazing gaming experience.
So, lets get the elephant in the room out of the way- Difficulty.
Yes this game is hard- especially the start. In fact you will probably doubt that you'll get to the end of it after the first hour or so, however, it is vitally important to stick with it. You will improve your skills massively in time, things that seemed nearly impossible will become almost trivially easy, this is part of the charm. You feel yourself grow in ability so much, relying only on your sharpened skills to take on truly overwhelming challenge and succeeding. The way difficulty works in this game is masterful. The gameplay is great, what feels clunky and unusable at first becomes very smooth and responsive in experienced hands, this game above any other I've played has one of the strongest connections of your wits to your performance, which is invigorating for tough fights.
The world in which it all takes place is despiringly bleak and desperate, the story is not told to you. Instead you are placed in a world and have to make your own conclusions about it's denizens and their motivations, the events that transpire and what it all means. This again is quite different to most games and triggers the curiousity in you much more than the standard formula, it has a feel almost like the old 'Myst' on PC (although it is not puzzle based).
Having the hindsight of multiple completions and nearly 300 hours play, I would rank this game as a modern classic. So much of it is a fundamentally different and richer experience than most games around these days. The more you play the more you realise the genius and originality of the design.
***As an aside- one word of warning. I would research online as to how to build your character and how to make strong weapons, it is not at all obvious and the game could be made much to difficult if you don't do it correctly.
***As a second and vitally important aside- Get an xbox controller for your PC if you are buying this. Mouse and keyboard was unplayable. They are fairly cheap and can be used for other games that work best with controller too. I already had one for use with a gamecube emulator.

Isaac has some problems in his family. His mother, watching a religious TV program, decided to kill her son in sacrifice to God. The kid managed to jump into the basement, a network of catacombs, densely populated by a huge amount of monsters. And the only weapon he has are his tears.
In The Binding of Isaac Rebirth you clean room by room, collect bonuses, find hidden places and shops, and then defeat the boss and jump into the next door in the floor. A new level begins and it gets harder and harder. You do so a few times before meeting his mother, then Satan himself or someone else.
The Binding of Isaac is challenging, really difficult. The farther you get, the easier it is to die and then you have to start from the very beginning. But there are many items which help you to become stronger. So many that I even used the Isaac Wiki to get the full understanding of every item and situation in the game (it really helps!). One item teaches Isaac to jump (finally!), other causes tears or enemies to explode and hurt everyone around. You can upgrade your max HP (Hearts), the devil will sometimes reward you with the power of the dark side (wings and other strong abilities for some of your hearts). The style of play often changes radically in the middle of the race. You just scribbled tears in different directions, hardly finishing even the smallest creep and then you suddenly get a power-up that changes your whole gameplay and you kill even the hardest boss without any problems. But the thing is, it can be the other way round, too! It is also always interesting to see how every item affects Isaac, because every item changes his appearance, so each time he looks different: he acquires tumors, horns or a bloody grin, pulls mom's bra on his head or... something else.
Failure is a part of the process. Play, die, start again, play, die, again. But every time we get something new (achievements open new items), so you do not want to stop completely.
Rebirth added a lot of new enemies, bosses, items and secrets if you compare it with the original game. And this is good! Edmund McMillen and his colleagues made an excellent job. A game full of the most horrible fears, bitter tears of childhood and exciting ideas.
You can also play it with you friend locally. But it’s not the local multiplayer you’d expect. Instead of a full second hero your partner takes control of a little Ghost accompanying Isaac. It can't go through doors or pick up items, it can only help to do more dmg. I would like more, although it is not clear how anything else would fit into the current mechanics.
So all in all this game is really fantastic! - 10/10!

This is my first time writing a review.  I bought this game Saturday night, and I already have 15 hours of gameplay.  Don't judge, we were trapped in the house all weekend due to the snowpocalypse.  :)
Yes, this is Early Access.  Yes, the game is very early in it's development cycle.  There are bugs, crafting is rather limited at the moment, and survival is incredibly easy.  The only real "threat" is the sharks, and even that is minimal.  Despite all that, it is still fun to play.
More importantly, this game has incredible potential.  The graphics are already good, the atmosphere is nice (bleak isolated), and that very rare plane flying overhead really kind of makes you feel hopelessly lost.
There are optimization issues at the moment, but they're not game breaking.  Some of the bugs do make things a bit more tedious than they should be (can't carry multiple items in the raft, items fall out of the raft easily, etc), and there's no concept of storage (just have your inventory and the ground).  Annoying, but solvable and not gamebreaking.
I would like to see some more variability in island size, the ability to engage in rudimentary farming, "mining", and possibly a move towards multiplayer support (kind of goes against the whole isolated nature of the game, but it could still be fun).
Overall, I'm happy I bought this game, will continue playing it often, and look forward to future updates.

This piece of software is not only badly designed, its fundamentally flawed from the get go.  This is just an outright bad idea to go with.
First off, the concept of face tracking itself.  This method of motion tracking using a visual camera is abysmal.  It takes far more resources than any other tracking method.  Its only benefit is that you can use a generic camera that any person will be likely to have, but more on that later.  It does not scale well at distances; in fact, it is very picky where you put your face at all.  Minute lighting differences or wearing glasses has a drastic affect on tracking quality.  Tracking with a single camera is also very limiting to this software’s uses.  Being “phuny” on a YouTube video or a Skype call is about all you can do with this.  Its so picky with tracking that you basically have to sit in a single spot, barely dispacing yourself from initial tracking or else risk losing all the tracked animations.  You can forget about looking in any direction that isn’t in the camera’s general direction.
Secondly, the hardware. If you use a $20-40 webcam you got at Walmart, you are gonna have a very bad time.  Of course you would want professional recording equipment if you wanted optimal results for something like this, but FaceRig performs so poorly its basically mandatory.  The developers even go so far as to say you NEED a 60FPS camera; something that is pretty important, but is NOT a standard for PC web cams.  Majority of web cams on the market cap at 30 FPS because they are not intended for this kind of use(expected use is video chats, which focus on limiting visual data for better streams).  This isn’t a big deal for YouTubers, who would have the necessary equipment AND the know how to configure a proper setting for it.  Your general prank Skype callers will quit of frustration.  Speaking of the YouTubers though!
Yall are gonna have to pay up for an extra, professional license if your channel is popular.  Honestly?  Spend your money else where.  Plenty of better, cheaper gimmicks that end up looking far more entertaining than this crap.
You know why all the screen shots have this excited, “:D” face to them?  Its because that is the easiest face for this software to pick up accurately.  In actual use, you will find awkward glitches in the tracking constantly.  Again, unless you are a YouTuber with good equipment, you’ll make a fool of yourself in a way you didn’t intend for; buying this garbage for $15.
Mentioning pricing reminds me: do you want to use all the anime grills people have made in the workshop?  Do you want to use workshop content at all?  Because ♥♥♥♥ you, that’s another $4 just to have the right to access them.  The entire workshop is filled to the brim with 2D Live content.  I could only find 3 regular FaceRig mods in my search.  I subscribed to 2 of them, 1 crashed the application.  In the off chance that you want to make your own 2D Live character, you are in for an even bigger world of hurt.  The application needed to make the characters is developed by an entirely different third party, whose based in Japan.  Majority of the quality tutorials are in Japanese. Its also quite a bit more expensive than this app itself; as opposed to regular 3D models which can be made in open source modeling applications such as Blender.
One thing that completely baffles my mind: a pre-recorded video of someone’s tracking performance can yield different results when fed into another PC opposed to the live performance.  Its so mind bogglingly ♥♥♥♥♥♥, I really can’t explain how you can mess up an app that bad.  Perhaps I should take it up with the forums, but I really don’t care at this point.  The tracking is inaccurate anyway.  You will be fighting with it constantly, trying to find the optimal sitting arrangement just so you don’t have to worry about it derping out every 3 seconds.
Lastly, to extend on the point of this awful design, visual motion tracking is both inefficient and, at this point, obsolete.  Emitter based tracking has taken over this department.  Its a bit more niche, considering that you need very specific, extra hardware along with the software, but it performs so much better with less overhead on the CPU.  It scales better, it detects better, and it can be run with a single standard design.  Even if you use visual tracking, using something similar to the PlayStation Moves colored ball design is far superior than trying to keep track of every possible configuration of skin tone, head/mouth/eye size, hair/glasses, etc.  It would be silly, but I would EASILY prefer wearing some skin tight mask and software specific camera than using this.  This app is worthless to me, and should be to just about anyone else.  By the time you spent money on professional recording equipment and the DLC packs you want, you could have easily purchased something a lot more entertaining and useful.
PS:  Why do you have achievements?  Why does any kind of software have achievements?  I don’t use software to feel like I have done something cool, I use them to help MAKE something cool.  That isn’t gonna happen with this.

This is your typical early acess open world survival game, if you've played one then you have played 'em all really.  It doesn't bring anything new to the table in terms of gameplay or content, not to mention the terrible performance. I know that alpha and beta games aren't really all that optimized, but I have been checking back occasionally on this game, and the performance has actually steadily gone down since I purchased it. It's not a hardware issue because the graphics are not that demanding, and i get the same frames on any settings. I can run a game like Deus Ex: Human Revolution at max settings with high frames and no drops, and anyone who has ever played that game knows how good it looks, and it is way more demanding than this. As of now, I wouldn't reccomend it, until some serious optimization has been done, it just runs like crap right now.
Update: I recently upgraded to a new computer. Here are some of the specs: Xeon 6 core hyperthreaded cpu @ 3.4 GHZ overclocked to 4 GHZ, 24 GB of DDR3, a 1050ti 4GB with a core clock of 1600 MHZ and an effective memory speed of 6500 MHZ. I still struggle to run this game over 40 FPS.

I understand that it is early access and there will be issues, however I cannot recommend a game that runs poorly (Not just for me, but a lot of people in the discussions as well) when in reality it should be running decent, especially when the requirements aren't even remotely high.
The game itself is enjoyable, but the amount of FPS is a killer. I will change my recommendation when they start doing some optimization fixes though, as it really isn't fun to play with frame drops quite constantly.

For the review, I will dodge the hype of being a Homestuck fan and look at it objectively. Even if you're someone who isn't familiar with the universe, you'll find a quirky storyline with very relatable characters (trust me, if you were a '90's kid', this is how you lived, besides the monsters of course. You will really appreciate all the little details you can find poking around even within the first few areas alone), humor, beautiful artwork, and an equally-great soundtrack. Those who have played Undertale may also notice some similarities in the overall "feel" -- which is no surprise, given that its developer has been involved in Homestuck to begin with (and this too, but more on the musical front).
It's not 100% perfect, though; I did have a bug with the first battle (don't use abilities on the basement monster when you first see it, or you'll glitch into a white screen), and I'm also not sure if there is any sort of auto-save option or quick-save keyboard shortcut (which would have been useful given said bug.cause I ended up having to replay a good portion due to that). Besides that, it has been great so far, and I hope that the remainder of this first chapter lives up to expectations.

A fun, openish-world zombie surivial light-rpg. At least that's what I'm calling it.
You transition form zone to zone, from the tutorial campground to a rural town to a larger city with the story. Basic combat elements are included, melee attacks with weapons that have degrading durability if overused and an assortment of firearms when there are just too many zombies to slice with a machette.
The most intriguing part of the game are the survivor camps you can build and strengthen. If you find survivors you can bring them back to your base, fortify the windows in case of attack and you build your repuatation with the other survivors so you can bring them along as a sidekick. There's a storage area where you can store your extra gear, and you're going to have it. Inventory space is very limited and dependent on the size of your backpack along with a weight limit on how much you can carry. Certain items, like bullets, snacks, and pain killers stack to small stacks to conserve space but you will constantly be returning to base to store your items. A downside to this is that you have to spend your reputation points with your group to withdraw items ythat you had just recently deposi9ted into the storage, a major drawback.
And when you're not playing, after you exit the tutorial, time continues on in the game and your camps can be attacked and your survivors killed mercilessly. It's is very annoying if you do not play it every day and I think it's a major drawback. You should be allowed to turn off ths feature but it is what it is.
I'd definitely say give this game a purchase if you can find it on sale. I wouldn't pay full price for it and I didn't. Alpha status suckas.

Summary: A great sci-fi RPG with fun dialogue and action.  It's a bit rough around the edges, but does not disappoint despite its age.
+It's an epic space adventure, in which you save the galaxy!
+Did the above sound awfully generic?  Well, I was surprised at the effort they put into creating a whole new universe with numerous alien races and technologies.  They even put this optional but very cool information in a codex whenever you interact with objects or people.
+A diverse cast of crew members with cool backstories, They even talk to each other when you ride the elevator (and thank gods for that)!
+Combat is generally fun.  Mostly with guns, as well as whatever technological or biotic (mass manipulating) skills you decide to learn.  You can also pause at any time to give orders to your party members.
+The "morality" tree isn't clear-cut good/evil, but renegade/paragon.  So your lawful actions don't cancel out your chaotic ones, or vice versa.  Instead each contributes to their own separate bar, which enables more dialogue options in the future should you invest the skill points.
+For the most part, you're free to do missions (both the main story and side missions) in any order you choose, flying around on your awesome spaceship
-The character movement can be clumsy.  I've gotten killed more than once when Shepard decides he can "take cover" behind a tiny piece of debris.
-Vehicular controls are extremely clumsy.  ♥♥♥♥ driving on hilly terrain, especially.
-Side missions can be pretty repetitive after a while, especially since ~70% of them involve driving around planets that are reskinned versions of each other to get to buildings whose layouts are also copies of each other.
-Inventory size limit is not a huge problem, but still a hassle.  Why did they bother?
-What the other reviewers said about elevators is true.  There's too many of them and take too freakin' long!

I must admit, I approached this game with skepticism. I absolutely loved The Book of Unwritten Tales, but the Critter parts? Not so funny. I never really enjoyed controlling this non speaking character, always having to guess what I might be saying, after a couple of minutes I always got bored or irritated. But this spin-off (and prequel), The Criiter Chronicles? Don't ask me why, but it totally works.
The story is simple but entertaining, in this game we finally understand WHAT is Critter. Part of an alien race crashed on the planet, we have to help him and his mates get a crucial part of their ship back from the... evil, for lack of a better term, Munkus. We will also meet again some of the characters from Unwritten Tales, like Ma'zaz, discover how Critter became friend with Nate and visit many locations of the previous game. Dialogues are funny and full of pop culture references, puzzles aren't extremely hard, but a couple of moments may be really challenging if you don't pay attention to your surroundings. Dark fantasy, action RPG that has some old school elements, such as its infamous high difficulty, and sports a great atmosphere.
It's true that the game is hard, but saying that it's its only real trait would be underselling its other great strengths.  The reason why it's hard isn't just due to brute force and cheap deaths, but like old school games, the enemies have very simple patterns and traps that you need to analyze first, then react accordingly with your easy-to-learn array to moves, either by blocking and timing counterattacks, or dodging like the wind, and you have to do all that for quite a while until you can get to the next campfire, the safe havens of the game.  It's a game that you can't just run through, there needs to be lots of care in your actions, and a certain degree of commitment.  If you are the type of gamer that play games as an hobby and not as a job, no matter how many times you die, I can guarantee you'll succeed.
The game puts at your disposition loads of options to customize your playstyle.  As I've said, the game has somewhat simplistic, but terrifyingly effective controls.
First, there isn't like a combo system, so you can only attack by doing light and heavy attacks, kicks that unbalance weaker enemies, dropping off from heights as you slash to deal massive damage, backstabbing, and parrying, an expert move that is very useful, but not necessary.  There are a lot of different weapon types, each with their own attack styles; there's the clubs that you mindlessly bash enemies' with, or the Halberd that allows you to stab from a distance and do arching attacks.
Furthermore, none of the weapons ever come as being inferior to one another of their own type, each of them has their own little strengths, such as providing a better boost if you have more Dexterity or Faith, and there are elemental damages, which can be a major factor in your success, as every enemies is weak to some type, so you have to take into account your equipment for every areas you take on.  The elemental damages may be often seen in RPGs, but it always keeps on providing a lot of strategy in return, Dark Souls being no exception.
You further customize your character depending on the stats you level up; if you level up Dexterity, you're better off using skillful weapons like whips and Shotels, or if you raised Faith, you'll be using "holy" weapons and Miracles using Talismans.
You avoid damage by blocking with your shield, or by rolling; said rolling, let alone the speed of your character, is heavily affected by your equipment load, so you have to sacrifice defense for more mobility.
Despite the somewhat simplistic nature, there's loads of ways you can play the game; you could block damage with big shields and tank with heavy armors, to then land perfectly timed, destructive counterattacks, or sacrifice all that for more mobility, taking the risk of receiving deadlier blows for having faster rolls, to then land backstabs or using magic at a safer distance.  Dark Souls perfectly displays your approach, you can either play it pretty casually, or use more complex strategies, there's isn't really a bad way to play it.
There's also a lot of replay value, in the way you can start fresh; in your next playthrough, you could maybe try for lighter swords, or take a shot at Dexterity weapons, or a mixture of magic and heavy axes.
The game's presentation is fantastic.  It gives off a very ominous vibe, due to its dark locales and grotesque hellspawns, the complete abscence of anything remotely cheerful, and the lack of music outside of boss battles and the Firelink Shrine, which are great orchestral themes.  This gloomy atmosphere gives it quite the strong identity.
So, despite its high difficulty, I would recommend this game to anyone who is ready to broaden their horizons, it's an old school experience that's rarely seen and executed so well nowadays.  Dark Souls has a lot of polish, and I do not regret any of the many hours I've spent on it, as it was such a great and unforgettable experience.

When I first heard of Dark Souls I was like, "Oh!  King's Field!"  I rented the first King's Field (second in Japan) a lot as a kid.  It confused the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of me.  It was slow, I didn't know where to go and I could only get so far as a six year old.  There were cryptic townspeople, savage plant monsters, out of the way spells that were not very useful and the slowest combat to ever grace the playstation.  But for some reason I enjoyed it.
Enter Dark Souls; as I missed Demon's Souls, Shadow Tower, Eternal Ring and the other King's Field games somehow.  From Software is a company that makes a game, and instead of moving on to a new idea, they just keep making that same game until it reaches perfection.  Dark Souls is the epitome of From Software dungeon crawlers.  It is their, in my eyes, magnum opus.
Don't be fooled by my playtime, as I also had it on the ps3 and played through it a bunch on there (only once all the way through, though).  Dark Souls is the kind of rpg you can experiment with over and over again.  It offers a ton of spells that are mostly situational, slow, methodical combat, weird enemies and cryptic npcs, except now, I'm old enough to appreciate it.
Dark Souls isn't about getting good or having a hardcore experience, although it can be; It's about a brutal, vicious world that respects your abilities and your time.  It is almost what being an adventurer in D&D would feel like if you were on the ground floor.  Forget the controller throwing, sissy nincompoops who can't handle a decent challenge.  If the game gets too hard, one can summon companions from their own game to help defeat the numerous bosses.
Now, to be fair, there are roadblocks in this game (a certain demon and a pair of archers come to mind), but once past them, going back through will almost be a breeze.
Dark Souls is a game that requires that you be alert at all times and to pay attention to your environment.  It is a refreshing game in an era of "press Q to blah blah blah."  I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys action rpgs, dungeon crawlers of all stripes and those looking for a legitimate, no nonsense experience.

After beating the game 2 times now, I have a better understanding on it´s strengths and weaknesses. A first Impression of mine when I first started was: Wow, this is like terraria in space!
Oh Boy,was I wrong.
This game simply cannot be compared to Terraria,even it´s artstyle is quiet similar. Terraria from my experience is more centered around exploring dungeons,fighting epic bosses and getting loot. Basically, a mix from dungeon crawlers. Action Platformers like Castlevania and other cellect em all games.
Starbound however is more focused on the idea of Exploration, Building colonies and... that´s pretty much it. Since the 1.0 Version,they have introduced Bosses and "Story" missions,but they are all pre made and not randomly generated like other planets.
That means you cannot influence the battle Arena like in terraria and have to fight the bosses and defeat the "Dungeons" as intended by the developers. A pretty big weakness if you ask me.
To even "unlock" These dungeons,or better called "stages", you Need to scan various objects from all the races (except Novakid), to Progress. It might encourage Exploration,as you Need to visit various planets and "starsystems" to find them,but due to the randomly generated nature of this game, some times you find These villages of the certain races you are looking for right away or after a hour of visiting planet to planet. It can get tedious really fast and put the game on a stopping Point.
One Thing to note is that all planets and Systems have a certain Level rank. It effects the Levels Monster and weapons you can find in chests. All fiery stars for example are the highest ranked System and contains the strongest enemies and also highest Level gear in the game, while gentle stars are the lowest leveled System and Serves as the starter System you will randomly spawn in.
Might be a safe way to Balance difficulty in the game,but it gets boring after a while, since the planets on These stars have a pattern in which they are randomly generated. You will quickly notice the limited generated Patterns and get quiet bored with it.
After you reached this Point in the game, I would suggest starting to build a colony on any Kind of planet. the more dangerous a planet is,the higher is your pay,that you receive from NPC´s that inhabit your colony. I would suggest starting of in a Level 1 planet, just to learn how the crafting works and after that move on to any other planet of your choice.
So far, with the 1.2. Version out and soon an update promised, this game is still worth it´s pricetag, despite it´s flaws I mentioned. I wasn't entirely sure about a VN priced at $20.00, but after about ten minutes in, I realized why. It should be noted that I'm fairly new to VN games in general, having only played six or seven personally. That being said, compared to those, this blows them out of the water.
First off, the story is not only moving and impactful, but long. You don't actuall come across the intro until about 30~ minutes in. That's just a estimate, but it honestly felt the opening came in where other VN closing credits would start rolling.
Secondly, the entire VN is voice acted. Voice acted tremendously well, for that matter. Even the main protagonist has not only a voice, but a face as well.
Not only that, but the art in this game is amazing. At first I thought I was delusional, but every character's eyes and mouths move. Every character and background scene really immerse you into the story the developer wanted to portray.
10/10, only regret regarding this game is the fact that I didn't buy it sooner.
Such an underrated game, a lot of depth, great graphics, devs who are working hard with the community to bring in solid gameplay and systems. I'd recommend picking it up

I've only started playing this game recently, years after it was released, and I was surprised by its quality. It's very well made, very solid and polished, with superb voice acting, sound effects, adequate combat and squad mechanics, and an intriguing story. It's true to the classic sci-fi traditions, probably influenced by StarTrek, but also by fiction that came before and established the genre. Highly recommended. Even if just to see what AAA should mean. I'm enjoying this more than most RPGs I played before. To tell the truth, I just switched to it after a few hours of Fallout 4 :)
Surprisingly, for a 7-year old game, the graphics look very pleasant, smooth, vibrant, clean and neat. Character animations are good, models are very realistic both visually and in movement. Often feels like watching a film. Also, very few things break the immersion, because the game is very polished. But it keeps you on a distance, as well... You know, on one hand, it doesn't try to suck you in, and on the other - it doesn't expose its guts on every corner with some glitch or logic loophole. The result is a very comfortable level of immersion and a smooth, intelligent gameplay experience.
Another thing that amazes me is the controls and UI. I suspect that this game was out on consoles, judging by dialogue selection interface, for instance. Yet it is perfectly adapted for mouse and keyboard, with sensible key mapping and no remapping restrictions that would prevent me playing like I prefer (Home-Del-End-PgDn instead of WASD). I'm quite used to the term "console port" and struggling with controls that were clumsily adapted from console controllers to keyboard and mouse. This game shows how controls should be handled in a PC title.
The story is also refreshingly free from clutches of cliches. It is not stuck in mimicking current political situation, or American history, but instead offers an original, mature fantasy with interesting characters and alien races. Also, you have to expect good and bad individuals in any alien race, and neither the game creates a racial archetype, nor it suggests you to do so. As a result, the story feels real and yet distant from our world - both in time, and in space.
Of course, I haven't finished the game yet, and it's just my first... well, second impressions. I might change my mind later, but I don't think the change will be drastic. It's a very well made, high quality title. It doesn't try to hook me or get under my skin, it offers a pleasant and enjoyable experience - which is always a respectable approach to winning the audience.

In England, the vision of a  “white christmas” as portrayed in films and TV programmes is a horrible lie. Even home produced TV content still pumps out fake snow during the Christmas specials despite us all knowing that it’ll only♥♥♥♥♥♥it down with rain.
So I was quite pleased that my assignment over the festive break was to review the snow heavy The Book Of Unwritten Tales: The Critter Chronicles. It’s a happy go lucky entry into the point and click adventure genre that’s full of warmth and good humour, if lacking in certain other departments.
A prequel to the first game, The Book Of Unwritten Tales, you start the game as Nate, on the run with a questionably acquired airship before you are attacked by a bounty hunter seeking to return the ship back to its owner, along with yourself for punishment.
After a lot of back and forth across the same few screen locations and some relatively easy puzzle solving to rid yourself of your pursuer. The plan immediately backfires and you end up crashing into the cold tundra of the Northlands. It’s here that you meet the star of the show, Critter, and the rest of his tribe. As with the previous game, you can switch between both characters in order to solve the puzzles that will help you both escape from the frozen wastes.
the book of unwritten tales the critter chronicles image
Solving puzzles in Critter Chronicles was relatively easy, and that’s coming from someone who usually struggles with such things. I assumed briefly that maybe I was no longer stupid but sadly that is not the case at all. The ease of the game is mainly down to one the fundamental issue I have with it. The heavy and repetitive use of backgrounds and locations. Even by two thirds of the game through I think I could count the number of backdrops on one hand. There is a significant amount of location re-use that does mean you’ll never get too lost trying to solve puzzles, there are only so many permutations you can attempt before you stumble across the right one. The net result is that the game that feels more like a smallish DLC episode rather than a title priced at £17.99, so I’m not convinced about the entry retail price here. It’s questionable.
So what does it get right? Firstly atmosphere, the game world is beautifully drawn and realised, even though the human characters don’t shine quite as much as the their creature counterparts. The game has a warm hearted comedic tone that gave me a few good chuckles throughout. Whilst the first chapter was rather dry and plodding in nature, the introduction of the Muppet inspired alien Critter and his species really liven up the second and third acts. Playing the game as Critter made for some very amusing moments, particularly as eats and pulls out of his stomach all of the items you acquire, and his imitation of certain objects when you click on them. The game also features an ultra adorable baby critter and an ingenious use for penguins that could solve the world’s energy demands if harnessed on a large enough scale.
the book of unwritten tales the critter chronicles image
The voice acting features some lively performances that could have easily been lifted from a Saturday morning cartoon. However it can sometimes sound as though the developers have rounded up a local amateur dramatics society, with some of the acting sounding very forced, particularly with the lead Nate. The score that accompanies the game is also quite enjoyable to listen to and fits in perfectly with the light hearted fantasy world that has been developed.
Overall The Critter Chronicles was an enjoyable slice of point and click adventure. It has a warm heart and some lovingly realised characters. Ultimately though, much like the frozen desolate wastelands, the game feels too isolated from the world itself. A sparse cast of characters and repetitive use of locations makes the game feel very narrow in focus.
Whilst the puzzles are quite simplistic, that could be considered a bonus for those of you that enjoy the telling of a story more than the taxing of the brain. I wouldn’t hesitate to snap up this game and its predecessor, The Book Of Unwritten Tales, if you see them going for a good price on Steam.

SHADOW OF ARKHAM'S CREED ...
I'm sure that I'm not the first person to point out how much this games plays like a mash-uo of the Arkham and Assassin's Creeds games, just set in Middle Earth.  That's not a knock on the game at all, though (at least in my book).  If you liked those series (and most people did), you're going to like this game.  Period.
That's not to say there is nothing original.  The nemesis system, for example, is quite fun, especially when defeated foes come back at exactly the worst possible time.  I was running a mission to defeat a pretty tough dude (for my level at the time).  There I am slowly wearing him down, trying to pick off his elite guard, dodging hurled spears ... and two other orc captains show up for revenge.  What was already tough fight suddenly because hilarious and insane.
The open world is also quite nice.  Sure, there are tons of side missions ... but never underestimate the sheer joy of just walking around the countryside at random, clearning out camps and strongholds on a whim.  There's something deeply satisfying about picking off archers from a distance, stealth killing your way around a small encampment, or just walking brashly into the middle of twenty-thirty orcs, and emerging victories several minutes later.  On a side note, this makes it a game that can still be very rewarding in 15-30 min segments, if that's all you can manage on a particular evening.
If you're still not sold, this game is on sale quite a bit.  I got the whole GOTY shabang for $10.  That makes it one of my biggest steals in years.
Finally, if you don't buy it, all the hobbits will die.

Let's get the obvious out of the way. Is this game challenging? Yes. Is this game hard for new players? Yes. Is this game impossible? Absolutely not. This game has a reputation for being a very hard game, sometimes being dubbed "The Hardest Game Ever." I will tell you right now that while the game is hard in the beginning, especially for new players, it can easily be learned. It is just another game in which the level designers introduce escalating challenges for the player to face. The game starts off showing you the basic controls (attacking, dodging, healing etc.) but those who pay attention can notice that the game is slowly introducing the player to how certain challenges must be approached (fighting one target, fighting multiple target, fighting ranged targets etc.). The golden rule is to watch your surroundings, and watch your enemies. You will be able to figure things out for yourself, because though the game may not tell you outright, it does show you the ropes before it throws you into the fire. Of course you may get stuck in some parts and there is no shame in looking at a guide. I did as well in the beginning. But before you do, look around the world and look for places you have not seen before. If the area is new, and the enemies are not too hard to fight, then you are going the right way.
This game is very satisfying. If you are new to Dark Souls then you will die, very often. But that is the whole point of the game so do not feel discouraged. This game will be hard in some parts, and you will come across an obstacle that seems impossible to defeat. But when you accomplish the task, and you will, you will feel amazing. You are also given a wide variety of weapons and armor to use. Each weapon has a specific move set that fulfills some task. When you find the armor and weapons that fit your play style, upgrade them and have fun. Weapons are another aspect of this game that are very satisfying. The weapons, ranging from practical to ridiculous, all have a weighted feeling to them. You don't just blindly swing a sword around like Skyrim, there is timing involved. When you get a hit in and you watch the enemies health go down, you will feel like a million dollars.
Along with the difficulty, the story also has a reputation. Much like the gameplay, the story is left up to the player for the most part. You are given an intro cinematic which lays down the history of the world. But once you are in the game proper the story is really only told through NPC dialogue and item descriptions. This makes the story a little bit of a mystery, you being the one who takes in information and clues to piece together the more in depth history of the world. Even when you have finished this game you can spend days watching videos of people explaining what happened in events before the game, and events that are happening in the game. Something as simple as armor next to a bonefire, or a suspicious item in someones treasure chest can open up entire stories.
The entire world is seamlessly connected. Except for a few areas that require special passage, the different areas are interconnected and it is possible to walk from each and every one without having a single loading screen. This helps  make the world seem more alive and grand, especially when, in some cases you are able to see one area from another. The visuals are also amazing. Whether it be from the top of a mountain peak or through a lush forest the atmosphere will certainly drag you in. However in some parts of the game, the framerate will go down drastically.
I don't believe Multiplayer was the main focus of this game, however it is present. Online play shows in the form of covenants, different groups that fulfill some role. Some covenants like the Warriors of Sunlight are available to help you out, while others like the Darkwraiths will join your game with the main goal of killing you. These days, the Darkwraiths are the only ones around, and connecting with people to COOP is nearly impossible. It has been patched but in my experience, online play is not very common.
DS Fix is a mod that I highly suggest players to get. One of the biggest problems with Dark Souls for some people is the fact that the game is locked at 30 FPS. This mod unlocks the framerate allowing one to reach 60 fps and solve some of the visual issues that people experience.
I highly suggest this game and I find it Overwhelmingly positive, however here are some things that one should keep in mind.
-Framerate is locked at 30, and in some places will go even lower making the game hard to play. Use DS Fix and this problem should be remedied
-Near the end of the game, some areas seem rushed in their design. One major boss in particular is notable for being rather lazy, and requires more luck than skill in order to fight. This is something the entire community will agree is the lowest point of the game
-Online play is not handled well. Though it is unique, you will have a better chance of being invaded by an enemy than you are being able to play with a friend. Though the strongest element of Dark Souls is it's single player so this should not be a problem
-This game can really only be played with a controller. If you do not have one I suggest waiting on buying this game until you can get one. There is a keyboard and mouse setting but it is very difficult to play with.
Dark Souls is truly a unique experience for any player. I've seen people put off by the difficulty at first and then eventually return to it hooked (This happened to me). If you are a fan of story and lore, this game is rich in it's atmosphere, world building, and unique presentation. Gameplay fluctuates from a fast panicked pace to slow anxious one. There are a variety of weapons that one can pick up and use to fit their play style. Overall this game is an experiment in determination. Every challenge can be completed and every enemy can be defeated. If you have learned the elements of the game, and have adapted to its rules, you will succeed. I highly recommend this game.

One of the best games I've played this year. Although there's a definite console feel to it, partly owing to the third-person perspective, State of Decay has a lot more depth to it than you might expect. In fact, I pretty much wasted my first run at it, by missing out on the higher-level features. Killing zombies is not the goal here, it's just a constant obstacle to building your colony of survivors.
The game has a pretty good tutorial intro for basic mechanics, but you will need to peruse an FAQ two if you hope to optimize your resource collection. For instance, when setting up an Outpost, you need to leave one bundle of supplies un-collected; that determines what resource the Outpost will generate. There's no indication of this in-game, and it's not something you're likely to figure out on your own.
Another minor concern is that once you start to fall behind the curve - too little resources, too many of your higher-level characters turned to zombie-chow - the game turns into a real hard slog. The obvious alternative would be to have it just end if your 'heroes' die, but that's a pretty stale cliche. In State of Decay, you're free to battle your way back up from the dregs. The lack of a user-save system leaves you with no other choices - just keep trying, or start over. Which is fair enough. It's great to see a game that doesn't compromise.
Combat is definitely simplified, console-style. It's not easy to be precise with melee weapons, and a bit too easy to get stuck behind a door or other obstacle. But the difficulty level is about right. You really need to think about your tactics, and avoid foolish risks.
I'm on my second play through Dead Island, and would still pick that as the best zombie shooter so far. But State of Decay gets some important things right that DI misses - most notably the base-building meta-game. It's great to have a positive objective for once, instead of the all-too-common "just survive" (as in DayZ, for instance). I'd put State of Decay high on my Must Play list for 2013.

This game feels like it was a bunch of lost potential. In fact, I had some fun with this one, and I figure with a little more polish it could have been remembered as a classic. However, there are two really big problems that prevent me from reccomending (or finishing) this... two problems that suck the life out of what could otherwise have been a decent shooter.
1) Bad Level Desgin:
In this game, YOU WILL BACKTRACK A LOT. For every path forward there are twenty dead ends... and most offer no reward whatsoever for exploration.
In a linear, story-driven game, this is an extreme indictment! Huge chunks of gameplay waste the players time and only bring boredom and frustration.
But there are also little problems to level desgin as well... things you would not normally think about until they go wrong. I will use an example from this game:
There is this level with a HUGE arena where a battle takes place. That is fine and well. But after the battle I ended up spending nearly 15 minutes searching for the way forward. There was this pile of rubble you are suppsed to climb up  and then a ladder above that. However, THE LADDER'S TEXTURE BLENDED INTO THE WALL TEXTURE. I ended up climbing that rubble no less than four times trying to get out of the arena and it was only on the fourth that I saw, just barely, that damned ladder.
Linear story-driven games, especially, cannot afford this kind of BS.
2) General Shooting Brokenness:
The second major problem involves a lot of minor issues with the shooting itself, but which add up to make a mediocure shooter downright frustrating. I will simply list them out:
-Enemies often point towards you and are ready to shoot at you before they have line of sight. Not only does this not make sense, but it also give them an unfair advatage.
-Enemies, thier weapons, AND THE PLAYER can clip through walls and doors, leading to many a BS damage (and the occational getting stuck).
-When one enemy knows of you... all do (think about the point at the top and see what problems that causes).
-Lack of varety. Enemies almost always consist of the same type (man with machine gun) with minor variations (now man has sniper).
-Samey corridor shooting. Rather than challenge the player with novel situations and varied, complementary ememies... 90% of gameplay is walking down a corridor and shooting the samey enemies.
-The game seems to depend on random health and armour pickups from enemies to sustain the player. Given how rapidly 100 health can go to 27 (which in most cases is as little as two shots from death) this turns certain portions of the game into peekaboo nightmares.
-Finally, there are rare enemies (man with genade launcher) which can one-hit-KO you. This is OK in shooters provided there is enough warning and enough chance to dodge. In Chaser... you get no such chance and have to simply eat a couple of deaths.
Fix the p i s s-poor level degisn and tweak the shooting? And you have something fun I would argue. But alas, Chaser has these problems, and I cannot reccomend it.

Well, I'll say one thing for Chaser: You definitely get a LOT of game for your money, especially considering that I got it on sale for a little over a dollar. This game is perhaps the longest FPS I've ever played. I finally completed it on medium difficulty after 36 hours of gameplay, (I know it says above that I put 47 hours into it, but I started a new game with 11 hours already clocked in). In addition to being long, this game is also extremely difficult. In fact, you will find yourself quick saving and quick loading A LOT; over and over again to get thorugh many areas and still maintain enough health and armor to advance further into the game. I don't think it's how the developers meant for the game to be played, but it's what needs to be done in order to complete it.
Chaser is a very well done  futuristic, sci-fi FPS with a bullet time mechanic that tells a very interesting story through well written cut scenes, has a good musical score, (particularly on the Siberian levels) and will take the player from a space station, to various points on the globe, and finally to Mars. Ammo and enemies are plentiful, and there is a terrific variety in both weapons and level enemies, from space soldiers, mobsters, ghetto trash and punks, to Japanese buisness men. All are out to kill you. There is one level fairly early in the game called "Kabir" that is in my opinion the worst mission in the game. You have to defend a truck from waves of enemies but they keep coming and coming relentlessly, and it is so difficult, that I actually quit the game and didn't pick it up to try again until several years later. Aside from that level, the game is pretty fun.
I recommend this game. As I understand it, it has quite a cult following, probably thanks to Inside Gaming's unfair treatment of it, (that youtube channel ripped apart some very brilliant games in my opinion - especially "Legendary"). But I will tell you that by far, the biggest flaw in this game is that there are WAY TOO MANY times in the game where you have absolutely no idea what to do. Ya, it's one of those games. Even after you've killed all the enemies in a level or a certain part of a level, you will almost always be wandering around forever trying to find that one tiny switch, or that one elusive ladder or hole in the corner that is too easy to miss, to advance into the next area. A few times there are level puzzels such as a board blocking a door that you have to shoot from a distance, so that you can open that door later in the level, but if you happen to not see that board, you will be wandering around forever trying to figure out what you're supposed to do. Every level of the game is basically like this and it gets old really quick. You will be scratching your head until you finally figure out what to do, or have to resort to a youtube playthrough. Also, I should note that the game has a very interesting twist at the very end with a completely unexpected ending. It's a challenging game that is best completed if, for nothing else, bragging rights. Anyway, I hope you enjoy it.
Considering the fact that this game was released years ago, one can say that it had nice graphics. However, the constant use of Bullet-Time effect can make the combat seem easier than it should be.

Tldr; I recommend this game to fans of old school shooters as long as you have plenty of patience and REMEMBER ADRENALINE MODE!
The Good:
-The story is decent for being 2003, even though I totally called their twist.
-The music is nice and the sound effects help bring a sense of life to the game.
-Old school shooter, a la Half-Life.
-The price. C'mon, its $5.
The Bad:
-This game is hard. Expect to die, a lot. Its rather unforgiving if you forget to use Adrenaline Mode (aka Bullet Time). The game NEVER mentions to use it despite it being probaby the single most important tool you have. On the flipside, once you've mastered going slo-mo to headshot everyone, the challenge seems to go away. There is just no middle ground. Seriously, try not to fight more than 1 guy at a time...
-The maps. So, the method of going through the levels is exremely linear, despite being very large places with interesting nooks and crannies. You end up going in circles just to circumvent one door. And this happens a LOT.
-The water levels. WHY!? Just... WHY!? We start on land and end on land, so why the stupid trek THROUGH a ship graveyard? Hello 3rd dimension, how are you?
-The A.I. targeting. Wow... These guys must ALL be professional snipers. You are targeted the second an enemy can make visual contact. Even across the furthest point of maps.
The Meh:
-The guns. There's a somewhat decent selection of these but they all feel underpowered. Grenades are especially bad; yours barely do damage, but the enemy's can kill you in one hit if done right.

Been really undecided on what to think of this game, since it has some good aspects and some not so good. In general, it's not a bad FPS game. If you like single player FPS games, you might like it, but it's a very average shooter in every sense, and a lot of the time it may also feel rather unpolished, so I can't really recommend it.
One thing that is commendable is that it has an actual story, something that FPS games normally lack, but the story is spaced out by overly long and repetitive linear levels, in many of which you only have a couple of weapons to use, and the same kind of enemy, so you keep ploughing through dozens of the same enemies in the same corridors. The progression through the levels also feels the same all the time. If you say come across 4 doors in the area, I bet you anything 3 will be locked and 1 is open for you to go through. And on a few occasions when every door is locked, means you just gotta find a good old vent.
The game also never really autosaves during the levels and there are no checkpoints. So if you've forgotten to save for a while and die for some silly reason, like falling off a ladder, then you'll lose a lot of progress. My very first death was in the first level, getting crushed by the sliding double doors. I've no idea who would build the doors to actually do that, rather than, you know, sliding back open again if someone is passing through.
The enemies always seem to be aware of your presence before you even know they're there. They'll spot you for miles and across the other end of a large map. Sure, it adds to the challenge, but it's also kinda cheap and annoying. If I am being shot at, I'd prefer to be able to see who is doing that without needing to squint my eyes.
I had to leave the game on a sniping section, which is equivalent to an escort mission, except you're sitting in a lighthouse and have to cover your allies in a truck that's trying to make it through a military base with enemies shooting at it from everywhere. Not sure if I'd be willing to continue anymore.

For those who have played the Infinity Engine games - Baldur's Gate, Icewind Dale, Planescape Torment, etc, then you will have an idea of the type of game this is. I would recommend this as a good spiritual successor to them with updated graphics, mechanics, and a new non-D&D fantasy game world to explore.
For those who haven't, Pillars of Eternity is a single-player Role Playing Game with real-time-with-pause tactical combat (as opposed to turn-based combat). This means that combat flows quickly if you leave it unchecked, but you can also either pause or slow down the game in order to quickly issue orders to your party in order to maximise their effectiveness.
You start the game with one character that you customise from 11 possible classes. From there you embark on a story in a swords-and-magic fantasy world where you can recruit others into your party of six from eight Obsidian-created characters (all classes except for Rogue, Barbarian, and Monk) with their own back stories, missions and conversational quips or you can alternatively create an equal number of 'hired adventurers' which are storyless NPCs that you create their class and progression similar to your own character.
As you go through the story you will find that the choices you made in building your character will give you a range of conversational choices that would be a bit different to if you created a different character with different stats and builds. There are also different factions in the two major cities of the games that you can help or hinder, and different types of conversational gameplay (benevolent, diplomatic, honest, cruel, etc) that can guide your interactions as well and offer different quest solutions and endings, which lends to replay value if you enjoy playing the game more than once.
Overall, the game is a very good addition to the genre without being perfect (some of the kickstarter backer content is distracting rather than engaging but it's optional and can be skipped over, pathfinding needs to be improved, modders will hopefully soon provide scripts for your NPCs to use in combat to reduce your micromanagement of combat in the future, and I won't mention the bugs as they're actively being patched as I write this review), reminding me of Baldur's Gate 1 rather than the improved and expanded sequel Baldur's Gate 2.

For those who aren't into Visual Novels:
I'm just gonna go ahead and say if you are a gamer in the sense that you wanna "play" with games this game is not for you. Visual Novel are about storytelling (or they should be) so most of the time you just advance the test.

Among Visual Novels this is one of the best I've ever read so if you feel you might be intrested in a good, heartwarming and bittersweetstory then you have my recommendation. This is one of the finest examples of what Visual Novels can be at their best.

This is not a nukige. If you just wanna buy it because "lol it has a lol" then shame on you!

As to which version to buy. I have the PLUS+ MOSAIC from the Mangagamer site and after reading trough the game I cannot in good conscience go to the adult content.  Belive me you wouldn't miss anything with the Steam version.

Pillars of Eternity can't decide the story it wants to tell and, in a game that purports to focus on storytelling, this is a fatal flaw. From the tutorial area, it is clear that the player character is The Chosen One. However, in the next area, there is a pesant bemoaning the fate of his friend, who was et by a bear. Clearly a quest for The Chosen One! No, actually, despite rolling characters specifically (and based on what the forums say are power builds) to be able to tackle one bear, The Chosen One is revealed to be The Inadequate One. Nevermind what appears to be a lack of actual choice in roleplaying if it did require a specific character build to kill one bear, making the first mob out of the tutorial area some kind of min/max powergamer test does not inspire faith in Obsidian's world-creation talents.
This illustrates the major flaw in the underlying systems of Pillars: Falling into the Uncanny Valley without explanation. It looks kind of like Dungeons & Dragons at character creation, as were the legendary Baldur's Gates of old (which it promises to resurrect), but is actually an almost completely new system where Might is required for healing and something called Resolve is needed for one of the three different kinds of defense your tank will need. Presenting a completely new system requires some explanation. Using a sort-of-familiar-but-not-quite system actually requires more explanation, Obsidian.
Sorry, Obsidian, C- for pretentious story-telling and RPG system over-reach. Come back when you can tell a story that doesn't ooze drama at every seam and devise a character generation system that doesn't require playing the game through several times before you know how to roll the character you want to play.

A well illustrated visual novel, with a moving, although somewhat empty story. Set in the future, the earth is facing its destruction due to causes left largely unexplained. The protagonist Ryou is sent to guard a secret facility. The facility was used to research a new genetically modified form of human with hyper intelligence. These modified 'felixes' were used to research and design the ships to be used to escape the destruction of the planet. The story is told half through flashback about the events surrounding Ryou, and the final days of the doomed planet.
Ultimately however the story comes off as somewhat unsatisfactory. Due partially to its nature as a kenetic visual novel. There are no choices, and no options for further reading. The game presents a lot of interesting material, but it is entirely set within either the research facility or the countryside. There is little to no opportunity to learn about the rest of the world. Ultimately this is a love story between the hero and heroine, and the rest takes a backseat with no chance to bring to light anything about the interesting background world. If you like a romance, this is a very good one. But it falls quite flat in other areas. Particularly as the story is actually at its core very simple and straightforward, it could take place in any setting with minor modifications. It therefore doesn't make the best use of the world nor characters it has come up with.
Pros:
- Overall well illustrated, pleasing on the eyes.
- Mostly realistic, likeable characters. No airheads or stupidity here.
- Decent length; my playtime is slightly inflated, it should take around 6-8 hours to complete.
Cons:
- Character illustrations ocassionally off model.
- Very limited animation, some lip-flap and blinking is the extent of animation.
- Kenetic story means no opportunity to explore areas of personal interest.

eden* is a Kinetic Visual Novel originally released in 2009 by minori (>inb4 minori is kinda paranoid back then that they sue someone and put region lock protection lel) that tells the story of a skilled soldier named Haruna Ryō and a felix girl named Sion.
The premise of the story is that in the far future, a huge mass energy called “Planet of Destruction” suddenly appeares in the sky as a red star. Lots of scientists starting to predict the end of the Earth, but at this point, 100 years before its predicted end, humankind started to feel another big threat - the Earth is dying: terrorist attacks and wars are ravaging badly that it decreased the human population rapidly. After some time passes, a United World Government was formed to prevent any further human destruction. When all the fighting stopped, the remaining humans came up with a plan to escape the Earth. At the same time, people were working on the “Felix Plan”: a plan to create a new technology to bring the remaining humans to a new planet. The story of Eden* begins 99 years later, when the Earth is on the brink of destruction.
Most of the stories were told via flashback and when you start the game for the first time, you could actually tell the ending since this is a kinetic VN. The flashback serves as to what is going on prior to the ending of the game and mostly consist of your SoL of Ryō & Sion.

The CG has that cold but warm hue to it that kinda adds melancholic feeling to the atmosphere, fitting the setting of what is going on around. I just wished that they did it on a higher resolution as most of the background CG is very calming, lushful and beautiful. The BGM is very well done, with based Tenmon also composing the BGM really gives that special feeling to it that somehow very calming yet at times is paced properly to what is going on around it.

This is a weird case for me, I want to like this game, and as such, would consider being on the fence. But not this one. While I do say, YES, it certainly has potential. As is? NO, I can not recommend Savage Lands to you or anybody else.
I played it sometime last year, and liked it for the most part. I just now came back to it, and quite a bit has SEEMED to change, and while, yes, it has, it has not been for the better. The game was already living up to its name before, this is a brutal game; you don't even need to make a mistake for it to punish you. But there-in lies the issue. The game, seems to have been made EVEN HARDER than the last time I played it.
I spawned, killed a skeleton with a stick, okay. Try to gather supplies before night, okay. The moment night falls, WOLVES. WOLVES WOLVES WOLVES. Your starting weapon does nothing. Your fists do nothing. You're forced to run, and if you're lucky, you'll get away. Alone, naked and cold, unless you somehow managed to scrap together clothing by day 1 (which won't be enough), or miraculously found enough (and managed to carry it with you) materials to build another fire, you'll freeze to death before morning. The water might as well be LAVA with how quickly it ends your life if you dare so much as wade up to your waist into it. Because yes, cold now consumes your life in the opposite direction. That is now health you no longer have access to. Even if you manage to warm up, that health will be missing! So if you so much as get a little chilly, you'll get one-shot before you have time to see that second skeleton, that wolf, or a giant boar.
Now, I'm not one who complains about difficulty in a game. But I am one to complain about PERFORMANCE of a game. They have gone out of their way in the last year I played this, to drive this to unfair and un-fun levels of 'hard', yet they have done NOTHING to improve the game's actual stability. Combat is still
, and even on the lowest settings, the random lag, slow-downs, or outright freezes, will most likely kill your fun before the nightly spawn-rates do.
TL;DR: If the game would perform better and had less clunky combat, it'd be cool.

This game asks "Hey, you know that press-x-to-attack-press-y-to-counter combat system that became so popular with Arkham Asylum? What if our sole goal was to make every single second of that game as fun as possible?"
Slow-motion bow headshots? ♥♥♥♥ yea! Incredibly brutal assassination animations that make you feel like an unstoppable killing machine? ♥♥♥♥ yea! Fun, fast RPG progresson? ♥♥♥♥ yea! The ability to take on a horde of 15 enemy soldiers and absolutely obliterate them single-handedly LOTR-style? ♥♥♥♥ yea! The chance of actually getting overwhelmed by enemy soldiers and dying brutally at the hands of an orc who will be promoted after your death into a position of power? ♥♥♥♥ yea!
While the combat has basically been optimized so that every single second is fun, it starts to wear thin about 20 hours in when you're alraedy an extreme bad♥♥♥♥♥ Fortunately, the game has a neat nemesis system that keeps things feeling fresh and dynamic for the first half, and the nemesis system actually has a neat twist halfway through that still keeps it relatively dynamic in the second half.
The story didn't move me much, and eventually gameplay wears a bit thin, but I'm INCREDIBLY hard to keep entertained when it comes to action games and this game is about as fun as it gets. Don't let my low Steam hours on record fool you, I've certainly logged 4000+ hours in DeS, DaS, DaS2, BB, and DaS3 across various platforms.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------
There is a certain stigma associated with Dark Souls, people seem to only use it as a metaphor for something that is extremely difficult or seemingly impossible to complete and that is just an unfair comparison.
Dark Souls is not easy, sure, but it will never kill you unfairly, it will never throw something that is impossible at you. What Dark Souls WILL do is give you an experience that is one-in-a-million in the modern age of gaming, it will not hold your hand and it will challenge you to something more than an interactive movie with QTEs or a game that gives you checkpoints every few seconds.
If you play one of these games for the first time you WILL die, you WILL spend hours trying to kill just one boss, you WILL miss checkpoints (bonfires) as they aren't just handed to you like checkpoints in other games, but if you persevere for a playthrough or two I think that you (like me) will find a saga of games that have near-limitless replayability, you'll finish the game with every weapon (there are somewhere around 100) and still want more, and unlike your standard game there will still be more for you to do.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------
If you've played a Souls game before then you know whether you like them or not, just buy it or don't.
If you haven't played a Souls game buy this one, it's the best you'll get without buying a PS3 or PS4 because Demon's Souls and Bloodborne ARE better, if you don't like the game then you probably won't like the other games.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------
If there's a game on Steam that is deserving of a positive review then in my opinion it's this one.

I write this after putting over fifty hours into the 1.0+ release as somebody who also played during the very early greenlight period. Starbound is an exploration sci-fi game with a charming 2d pixel sprite aesthetic and kind of frustrating play mechanics. Your character has upgrades that require items that are found in lootable items you encounter during exploration or are in loot bags given as quest rewards. Your ship is upgraded using loot found in a similarly. This all requires time but can be done independent of improving gear.
Acquiring higher tiers of gear and visiting different worlds is encouraged by the way resources are made available, but the way you get resources can be incredibly boring especially if you are not playing on casual difficulty, as you need to delve deep into each planet to explore for richer deposits of higher tier materials and you need to be above the underground point to teleport back to your ship. Getting back down can be simple with planting flags, but these also clutter your teleporter menu if you remove and replace destinations often.
Worlds look incredibly similar if you are mucking about the same underground biomes for hours and hours looting and mining similar areas whose only significant difference is how quickly the same enemies can kill you. The surface biomes and even large villages are usually expansive enough to be a chore to explore, and doing quests in villages and for random npcs can be annoying if you need to traverse a third the planet's surface for a simple loot bag.
The most enjoyable part of the game was the story Chucklefish added to flesh out the game, but the clunky interface, the annoyance of restocking+reequipping healing items after death, and the tedious inventory management for usable items, blocks, food, and other objects you can pick up is something that will hound your experience from hour 1 to hour 100.

As of writing this review I ahve mixed feelings about this game. For starters I love the games art style I find it very appealing. The gameplay is fun and addictive. Being able to travel around a universe and explore planets is very fun as well. However, I can not recommend this game to anyone in its current state. This game is horribly optimized. In areas with a lot of placed objects the frames will start to bog down and when there are a lot of npcs on the screen the game starts approaching slideshow levels of framerate. During combat large amounts of particle effects will cripple framerate to a crawl. Weather particle effects also effect framerate.The game even in single player has odd issues with what seems to be server lag. The player's character will be moving around freely while entities will freeze up and then shoot forward at incredible speeds like you are experiencing a lagging server.I do not have a top end gaming rig I have a high mid end rig which is well above the games recommended system requirements and there is no reason for a game like this to have such horrific framerate issues. If the devs ever Get the optimization sorted out to where this game can stay at a stable 30fps+ (preferably 60fps) I will change my review to recommended but in the meantime the framerate issues take the fun out of the game and make it very hard to enjoy playing.

In many ways, Bastion reminds me of BioShock: there's some good weapon and power customization, but the real star of the show is the world: a floating city torn apart before I even knew it existed, and one that I'm eager to explore.
That exploration makes up the bulk of the game: travelling through different areas and hacking-and-slashing baddies while gathering the necessary supplies to upgrade and enhance the titular Bastion. A sort of fantasy fallout shelter, the Bastion functions like a hub world between the levels.
Bastion has a great soundtrack, good story and overall good narration. The narrative side of Bastion is what makes it unique.

It is not the best when it comes to gameplay, but it is definitely playable and it has a great art style and soundtrack. It also has a unique take on in-game storytelling, and the arsenal you build up over a playthrough allows you to deal with combat however is most comfortable for you.
A note for ultrawide monitor users: It doesn’t run in full 21:9 (the BGs are all hand-painted and only extend so far), but it has an inverse letterboxed option. (i.e. You don’t have to add a launch command like you have to with Transistor.)

The closest to feeling like a zombie apocalypse that I've ever seen in an open world game.
The basic controls are adequate for whatyou want to do, the game switches well between stealth elements, melee and ranged combat, and social and resource management systems make it feel even less linear than the open world setting does.
Difficulty is generally forgiving, but the game autosaves and won't let you save more than one file, so the permadeath element is strictly enforced: in fact I have restarted the game once already due to a black fever outbreak and will do so again as my main protagonist just ran away from one swarm right into another and he's my best melee fighter.
The difficulty goes down when you've got NPC survivors with you, but the game is quite specific about alowing this (remember the resource management) and so you'll experience much of the game in the solo mode, which can get genuinely frightening at times. Often you'll be searching a building at night when a horde is making its way along an adjacent road, but you're not sure if the building you're in is empty. As well as trying to keep noise & light discipline whilst searching, you need to be on guard for something sneaking up on you or cutting off your escape routes.
The clipping is a bit of an issue, but everything else in the game comes together really well, and being on Steam and XBLA it's easily patched, so it should only get better.
Definitely worth a look, with more open world DLC on the way and a multiplayer being spoken about. Also, at only £15 (or less in sale)
