To be honest, there is too much I can say about this game but considering the amount of recommendation made by others I believe there really isn't a need to do so.
Below refers to the game as an entity rather than the dark arisen DLC per se.
One of the best ARPG of all time, still burns even by modern standard.
Brilliant class and character building system conferring free switching of playstyle. Classical medieval culture, detailed interaction among player and NPCs, beautifully structured natural world, and dynamic wildlife ecosystem offer definitely an immersive life as a fisherman-born hero.
While the setting has its charm, undoubtedly however, the best experience of this game comes from its battle mechanics: heavily action-based, fast-paced battlefield with all options the players have to give out certainly makes this game enjoyable; every class has its strength and playstyle - may it be climbing on the dragon and stab in its heart, sniping that orge you really hate in its eye, or even quadruble cast meteor storm and render all enemies reel in front of you. One must admit that the hit feel in this game easily outmatches most of its kind, making it outstanding in the forest of ARPG nowadays.
This game is simply a classic of Japanese-style ARPG by now. It may be surpassed by some due to its rather short main/side storyline and small map size, but the epic life of our arisens will never cease in shine.

It's 2004 and I had a factory built desktop from Dell ($500 then). It was in no way built for gaming, but I was determined to play on it anyway.
I browsed the net for games to play for free, and I found a multiplayer demo of Chaser. I downloaded it, waited several hours for it to load, and installed it.
For being the first ever fullscreen multiplayer FPS I have ever played, this game was incredible. It was like Call of Duty to me as with kids today. I played every. Single. Day. From what I remember the multiplayer being like, it was fast paced, VERY strategic, had amazing level design, and a wonderful array of weapons to choose from. Every time I see a FAMAS-designed rifle in any other game, I am instantly reminded of Chaser.
. I still often set my keybinds in other games according to Chaser's default keymapping.
Now, I know you're probably thinking, "Well this is a review from memories of a 9 year old kid. Of course it's going to be over-exaggerated." Well, it's true this is the first ever actual game I played on a PC. And it's true I had really no knowledge of what kind of game mechanics are good or desired. I never even touched the campaign because it was a multiplayer demo. But, if I could have compared the multiplayer in Chaser to anything today, it's very close to Counter Strike and Halo: CE. There's no extra crap. It's just you, some guns, some grenades, and an gritty and intelligent level design. It's simple, awesome, fast, and intense.
I love this game to death and I wish I could still play on multiplayer. If there are any graphic/multiplayer mods available for this game, PLEASE let me know.
Edit: I FOUND THE MULTIPLAYER PORTAL :D

You know what I love about this game...
It exists at the end of that small window in time between the original "forced 3d" shooter era of games like Doom and Duke Nukem, and before the modern era style of FPS took over.  It feels like a lost relic from a past era, and a hybrid of old and new concepts.
That being said...this game is ambitious and really dumb in a "so bad it's good kind of way".  You will quickly form a love/hate relationship with every aspect of this game.
The area to area shooting and combat mechanics are really quite good, but also really unforgiving. You can save anywhere, and you'll need to!
Cinematics and voice acting are really rough, but not dull or pretentious. It's a lot of tough talk and mafia stereotypes.
Now, the bugs and glitches...yes, there's a lot. They don't break the game or make it unplayable, but they do provide many good laughs.
So...enjoy this old school dumb shooter and buy it when it goes on sale.

Great ideas. Poor implementation. Buggy. Would like my money back.
It has a semi-persistent world feature, which is puzzling for a single player game. Let me elaborate: my play time in a single session is very limited. I returned to the game after not playing for a day, and I found that two of my fellow NPCs had died, my main character developed a fever and all of the home base supplies had dwindled to nada (all relayed to me by a nifty journal feature).
Fantastic. As a result of the above referenced events (that I had no opportunity to influence) the remaining NPC survivor morale dropped significantly. Due to their low morale, I could no longer directly control or request their assistance. I was then forced to venture out as a single character to find new survivors / supplies.
Every attempt ended in tragedy. The fever that my main character suffered from directly affected his stamina rating. With a low stamina, you can only attack zombies four or five times before becoming exhausted (aka defenseless). Each zombies at least four or five strikes to kill. The dwindled supplies meant that I had no potion like items to temporarily boost my stamina. Thus, it was virtually impossible to defend myself against more than two or three zombies at a time. Fine and dandy considering the game spawned a buttload of zombies during my downtime.
The impasse was further complicated by the fact that the game also features a "rogue-like" save system. It autosaves at the conclusion of each mission or boot up of the game. To the best of my knowledge, there is no other save function. Therefore, the several hours of playtime that I put into the game were rendered moot. I could not go back to an earlier save to try and stockpile extra supplies / find more survivors / not get a fever (not sure that's possible either). Due to the autosave upon boot up, I was stuck with a single, sickly controllable character with no supplies and a roomfull of NPCs that hated him. My only option was to completely start over (fat chance, after starting over once before. See bug below).
There are further game crushing bugs that occur (one neat bug stops you from aborting or completing a mission that was halfway complete, permanently halting progression of the story). Seeing as the developer is now releasing non-free DLC, it seems unlikely that they will fix said bugs.
Again, great idea on paper. Sadly, it never got off the paper.

State of Decay is the mutant offspring of The Walking Dead and Animal Crossing, in other words you need to make life or death choices that will affect the lives of a group of survivors, but you also need to do your chores and get along with your neighbors. While not all that smooth yet, the patches keep on coming and it becomes more of a PC game every day. Ultimately it can be a bit repetitive, but I find it comforting given just how wildly unpredictable certain aspects of the game are. Two playthroughs are very similar but also entirely different, since you never know who will become ill, or worse yet who will be torn in half by a large mutant zombie.
A good idea but the game is far too easy which rather defeats the point of a survival game.

An enjoyable romp through Earth and Alternia that left me wanting more (but in a good way).
PROS:
Excellent writing and humor
Immersive feeling of the 90's
Rewards inventory experimentation with clever dialog and/or achievements
Interesting but not frustrating puzzles
Very quality art and music
Enjoyable references and expands on the world of Homestuck, but doesn't require prior knowledge
NEUTRAL:
A few minigames exist, but they're nothing to write home about
If you don't like messing around with everything, you can beat the game, but you might not have as much fun
CONS:
Runs a little short, even with detail-hunting
Some audio and animation glitches, tho nothing game-breaking
Some puzzles can seem too simple, or are given away by the game
Would have appreciated a couple more battles in the second half of the game
Overall: As a Kickstarter backer of this project, I was worried that the gameplay might have suffered from its time in development hell. I am happy to find it an excellent, if not perfect, experience, and I look forward to more (hopefully before another 5 years pass).

Figuring out where to use what item does not make you feel clever, and is not rewarding, especially since the game often just tells you what to do. in the game, and I still haven't tried everything.

I personally feel I got my money's worth from Act 1 and will be sticking around for more, but I do hope future installments will have more interesting puzzles than this one.

I have to say, I am very pleased with the early development of this game. It is an indy game, with just a few people working on it. And they have been doing great in keeping in touch with the player community. When I first bought the game, my actual intention was to indeed take part early access development stages - not just to "play the game". And I'm still willing to do so. However, a few days after purchase, they took the game offline, but explained it was for good reason; they were updating from the now practically antiquated BlitzBasic3D engine (which I'm familiar with from another piece of software), to the Unreal engine. It took a while, but the whole time, the developers were keeping the player community notified on progress every few weeks. They're doing great, considering it's only a few people working on it. The game seems to be back up now. The tutorial still stalls in progression at the mining and industry section (but you can abort the tutorial if you want). And the chat composition field still doesn't allow backspace. But I'm certain this will be ironed out in due time. The game IS still early access and in development. But the devs are very involved. If you're willing to be part of the efforts to help improve this game beyond this stage, and you're looking for a fun multi-player online space pioneering game, then I highly recommend Sirius Online. Just remember, however, at this point of early development, to be ready for bugs and downtimes. And be sure to let the devs know about any bugs you find.

It's a great game. Not exactly playable on my Mac right now due to it being too laggy. And the menu for changing options is a little weird. Just control f helps. But I wish it was smooth. However, I did play before the updates and I'm just going to say this game has quite a lot going for it.

Keep in mind this is a rating for the current state of the game, and i'm sure it'll improve over the course of it's development.  With that in mind, if I do visit it at a later date I shall change things accordingly.
First off, as far I feel the UI is fine.  You can tell directly how the cold impacts your health and how hunger degrades your fatigue.  However, the bar's overlap the fifth slot a bit.  This could easily be rectified with repositionable HUD elements.  The game itself actually looks pretty nice, I'm playing on high graphics setting and am pleased with the overall care in sculpting the land.  It's easy to spot and recognize landmarks.  I should also note I'm pleased to see the mature toggle in the options, as this is a mature games, and it's nice to size the full figure from an artistic viewpoint instead of shy away from it like so many other Mature-rated games.
Now for the inverse of the visuals.  The game is forced to be fullscreen, and if you alt-tab to switch to another window and back, your mouse cursor is no longer locked inside the game, making it frustrating to be in the heat of battle and accidentally click off the game, shrinking it to the bar.  Using a torch in the off hand with a 2-handed weapon still has it equipped, but in an odd way.  Whenever you swing a two-handed hammer or axe with the torch still in the slot, the fire from it will often times sit right in front of the camera mid-swing, blinding you from seeing if a hit connects or not. This is frustrating when a torch has no other slots to be in due to the tight inventory constraints of the game.
Let's move onto Mechanics.  The crafting I found was alright, but heavily bogged down.  Not by functionailty, but literally   what there was to craft.  If they had tabs or folders for equipment, much of the valuable daytime wouldn't be spent scrolling through tin, iron, copper, bronze, gold, and silver items just to find the leather and wooden things you have can only really craft right off.  The day/night cycle as well, is interesting but double-edged.  on one hand, it makes daytime more valuable, and makes you want to spend what time you can gathering what you need.  On the other, night time takes -far- too long, to the point that it's disengaging.  In fact I'm writing this review over the in-game nights cause there isn't crap to do otherwise. It's understandable to make gathering wood for night fires important, but there comes a point where immersion can hurt the flow of gameplay.  It also makes building a leanto worthless, as there is no sleeping even to pass the night by.  Finally on the fact that there is no real pause.  This is especially a frustrating oversight on single player.  What am I supposed to do, take a♥♥♥♥♥♥in a bottle at my desk until I can build a house?  I'm sitting next to an open fire for most nights and a little knee-high leanto isn't gonna keep wolves away.  At least one good thing I can say about the game is the combat is actually alright, all the enemies have patterns that can be learned and bested the first try so long as you're careful and take the time to observe.
Finally, let's get to all the other little things that this game needs.  Firstly, I had to look up a  guide to find flint. Why? because at no point does the game state where to find one of the most essential resources to your survival.  You're just supposed to know there's designated nodes for it that only glow red where you're face to face with it. After you figure that out then sure there's plenty of nodes around for you to get up onto your feet, the game just wanted you to do trial and error for when hitting normal rocks hoping for flint doesn't work.  Another thing the irks me is the slow backstepping. I don't care how many games it's in, it doesn't fit when you're trying to strafe a wolf or skeleton and you try to backstep a little distance, so your character just leisurely saunters backward. The last thing is probably the lack of distinction between ore veins.  I found I couldn't tell any difference between tin, coal, flint, or other veins, so I'd have to smack any I find just to test which vein drops what.

So I just finished this game and what a journey it is!
It is an open world game set in the Lord of the Rings universe. You play Talion who is a ranger that gets imbued with the power of a spirit. This gives you extra powers such as the ability to drain enemies, read their minds to gather intel or even just mind control them.
As you progress through the game you will level up. Each time you level up you will get an ability point to spend on the current tier of abilities. To unlock more tiers and more abilities to pick you need to level up the power bar. This is done by completing power missions which mostly consist of killing orc captains and warchiefs.
The side missions give you Mirian which lets you unlock passive bonuses such as increased health, focus, more arrow slots etc. In addition you use it to unlock rune slots for your weapons. Runes are basically gems that you socket into your weapons to increase their effectiveness.
The side content isn't mandatory but I do recommend doing at least some of it as it's the only way to get Mirian and it will make things much easier for you in the long run. The combat of the game is excellent, very Batman-esque. You will be swinging your sword a lot and countering enemy attacks. There is a hit streak system and at 8 consecutive hits you can do a special ability such as an execution or an AoE stun.
You can do a lot of the game from stealth as I did. You can climb almost everything like Assassin's Creed and sneak up behind Orcs for a stealth kill. Your bow has limited arrows you can get from collecting them in the world or draining enemies. You have a focus bar that slows time when you use your bow but it is limited.
The game does a great job at making you feel powerful. There are cinematic shots of when you execute enemies and it feels so good to pop your late game cooldown and spam executes. Overall the game is very satisfying. The story is good, the combat is great and it's definitely a game for you if you are a fan of open world games or lord of the rings.

TL;DR:  If you plan on streaming/recording with this CPU eating program, just don't, unless you REALLY have the power-enthusiast build many gamers dream of.... but if you want a laugh, use it for Skype, or anything that doesn't really consume much of your CPU, go for it.
Before I say anything, I want to say that my PC isn't the greatest, but all components are brand new and I have well over the minimum requirements AS WELL as the recommended requirements. It is a decent gaming rig than can run almost any game on medium and high settings, even some Triple A typed games. Also, I am not negatively biased towards to program at all. I love Facerig. It runs amazingly without broadcasting/streaming and with a good webcam. Characters are well optimized with face tracking (some aren't) and I would recommend this to people who just want a laugh or those who have a powerful rig (if you want to stream, like me).
Looking at the program itself, I would presume that it wouldn't take up too much of my CPU, but even with the LOWEST resolution being a tiny box with barely visable text on the screen, it still consumes 30-40% of my CPU usage, even though my CPU has the performance equivalent of the reccomended. Add that with OBS, Then I'm using about 70-80% of my CPU, without even opening a game. It is just idle on desktop.
Note that I set the Facerig resolution to lowest and the FPS value to 30.
With it idle on OBS, the frames drop to 25. Also note that I'm not even using the broadcasting option. I decided to use window capture instead. The "broadcast" option is a horrible option if you want to opt out for green screen + chroma key without showing the UI. Using broadcast, I get an amazing 5 FPS average. It did not want to run at all. I did window capture and just cropped out the UI. Works just as fine as the broadcasting option.
I really think that with lots of people in mind wanting to use this for broadcasting and recording, not everyone has the powerful rig that can actually be used to create content with FaceRig to it's fullest potential. I am disappointed, but I am happy I still picked up the program. It just gives me a reminder that I should save up for the PC parts that I really want.
Maybe the recommended requirements should be set up higher, or maybe there should be ways and more options to make it so FaceRig doesn't eat up TOO much of your CPU, or just make it viable for those with a decent PC to run it more effectively.
I would rate it overall a 4/10.
But to categorize..
7/10 for the actual program itself, 1/10 for my needs.

Total war Attila is the 9th installment in the Total War franchise. Following the comercial and eventually critic success of Rome 2 Attila seem to be a very solid follow up to Rome 2, well after the trailers that is. Before I get into the pros and cons of Attila lets talk about the setting first. Attila is set in the late 300's till the mid late 400's ad, it follows the breakup and eventual end of the Roman empire at the hands of the fercious Nomadic warlord Attila. As with all total war games you can pick a faction to play as such as Huns, Romans, Vandals etc... and lead them through this time period. This time period though is one of the well apocolyptic times in history as barbarians storm western civilization, the earth cools leaving nothing to eat, people scramble over the leftovers of fallen kingdoms with bow and sword, and one more small thing only the scourge of god is now suddenly destroying all of settled civlization with millions of warriors leaving nothing in his wake but death and destruction. Sounds like the perfect recipe for a total war game right right? well just keep reading. Since we got that out of the way below I have a list of pro and cons and from there you can make your own decision.
CONS; Attila is far from a perfect game and below I will list my cons about the game.
Very lacking and similar unit rosters; Just look at the goths, vandal, and frankish rosters, yeah its bad.
More aggresive Huns; The huns in this game are well the center of the whole game and it makes me boil when the Hunnic AI sends maybe a stack or two to attack me and then kinda just sits there and just moves on. That was the biggest problem with my west rome campaign the huns were just disapointing.
Dumb Ai; In total war games it is not common to see ok AI but something happened in attila insted of better ai, The ai just gets ridiculous buffs. The ai still does dumd things like send the general first or suicide there units one at a time. When i ment total war needs better ai i didn't mean dumb ai With spartan stats.
Campaign map ai; all i will say for this is. Why would the franks raze all there neighbors and then take and keep territories in arabia?
Polotics and Diplomacy; In this game the politics is bare bones along with its diplomacy. When a Govenor has low loyalty all you do is press the secure loyalty button, and when you go into diplomacy with another nation no diplomats need to be send or anything, yop are always in constant contact with other people across the map it is like each leader has a smart phone with a few options: Declare war Make Peace Trade, and be my ♥♥♥♥♥.
Now that i have bashed this game half to death time to talk about good things in the game.
PROS:
Graphics; nothing else needs to be said
Horde Mechanic; The horde mechanic allows your faction to roam the map without a settlement you build large tent cities and dont have to worry about pesky city mangement. You can raze whole empires and keep the wealth all to your self.
Family Tree; For the first time since Medevil 2 family trees are back you can now it matters who rules your kingdom. You can marry into families and make alliances with them and if you play your cards right you just might inherit that land.
DLC well some of; DLC's in total war recently have been flakey, some are good and some just suck. In this game Empire of sands, Age of Charlemange, the last Roman, and the Celtic DLC bring much needed flavor to the main campaign, and in two of thoose cases whole new campaigns that in Charlemange case is better than the grand campaign.
Razing Cites; This campaign feature in my opinion is essential to the game especially for the nomads, and also the campaign graphics of a razed area is awesome.
Mods; This is the saving and high point of Attila. From unit mods to whole new campaigns you can find almost everything you need or want.
After that you can make your own decision on the game about the game, but i personally think this is still a solid game. Hope i can help I give Attila Total War a 3.9/ 5.0 or a 82/100 or even a B.

Before we start i just want to say; Chaser is by
means as bad as people make it out to be.
In fact, this is actually a GOOD game. Not SUPER good, not mediocore. No, it simply is GOOD.
With that out of the way, we can begin.
When i got this game, i went in, expecting a mediocore, if not ♥♥♥♥♥♥ experience. However, what i got was a lenghty, entertaining and mostly well executed game.
For a game that was released in 2003, it both looks and plays very well. What is very obvious to me, is that Cauldron set out to make a visually impressive and huge game, rather then a story driven game.
What i mean by this, is that the game's dialouge is completely off, and so are many sound effects, aswell as plot points.
But, the enviroments, the characters, serval other visual elements and the shear size of the game, are not only amazing for the time, but also make up for the cons.
Personally, i love the setting and design of the game, now it does use alot of grey and brown nuances like so many games do.
But the fact that the setting and level design is a combo of futuristic and present day architecture is making it all the more appealing. It also sets the tone for the game, humanity beat down by political and global crisis, rebels, savages and mafia scum all fighting for dominance, all helps to give the game a very distinct and depressing feeling.
One thing that most absolutely be commented individually, is the amazing 'breakable' glass. The glass will not break in one single point, it will break where ever you shoot it. Try it yourself, find a big juicy window and shoot out the corners and watch as it breaks as you want it to. Effects of this quality have not been matched by many games since, and Chaser defintly needs commenting for this. It is
Gameplay wise it's pretty solid, nothing too special or underwhelming here. It functions as any good FPS game should, you also have the ability to slow down time using "Adrenalin Mode" this especially becomes usefull at later stages, when you run into many enemies at once.
In latter parts of the game, everything becomes far more fast phased, and i had a short moment of throw back to the days of Doom.
The cutscenes are a real joy, as they have some truely funny dialouge, and often awkward yet funny situations. The main protagonist's look at the world is truely funny, and makes me believe he is not right upstairs... That making him even more awesome then he already is.
Alot of people probably want to know "Does the game have many bugs? Is it unplayable thanks to them?" the answer is; No.
The game does not have any bugs, that hasn't been disregarded completey in other "cheerished" titles. The only annoyance, and this is not a bug, is the fact that you do not recieve any kind of 'response' when you take enviromental damage, or fall from a ladder.
This can often cause you to die, while you thought you were beefed up on health. But it is a small thing, and incidents with it, are far and few between.
Overall, this is a good game, and defintly one i had alot of fun playing. The game is insanely long, and this is done very well, as it manages not to drop in quality the further you get. (Though some levels are abit repeatitive.)

Chaser is honestly one of the most innovative games of the past, present, and future generation. After playing over 100 hours of this game, it's obvious where the inspiration for Bungie's Halo: Combat Evolved came from. Sure, it came out two years after Halo, but that's because they only saw Jo Wood's amazing design. If the investors had given him his $17.26 before, Chaser could've revolutionized gameplay for PC and would've put the Xbox and PS2 out of business.
My favorite part of the game is how the enemies just run into the wall in such a beautiful way. Sure, some might call it a glitch, but I know that was there by design. When Jo Wood presented the concept for Chaser to his two cats and a parrot (RIP Jo Wood the Parrot), he wasn't just imagining another game, he was imagining the future!
By far the most interesting character is Thruster Man. (SPOILER ALERT) Thruster man is a deep and well thought out character that I know Jo Wood put hours into creation. His one goal is to appear for 30 seconds, shoot at you 3 times, then continue off into the sunset. You (John Chaser) must help him out by shooting him, otherwise he'll keep going, never to actually come back and do his one job, which is to kill you. The chemistry between him and John Chaser is one for the ages. I will be sure to tell my kids about Thruster Man when I grow up.
Overall, I recommend this game, and look wish Jo Wood luck with his new developer team, Homeless Studios.

The surreal art design, southern gothic soundtrack, and perhaps the greatest narrator in the history of games instantly create a perfect atmosphere for the world of Bastion. One of the most admirable parts about Bastion is the unobtrusive story-telling. The world, weapons, and enemies say so much on the story already that the game doesn't have to depend on cutscenes full of expositional dialogue. What little dialogue is in the game is short yet precise and manages to stay surprising, original, and funny throughout. You can really tell that the writers spent a long time to get the story to us as seemlessly as possible. When it comes to the gameplay, the main combat loop is engaging. The kid (the silent playable character) is given multiple new potions, upgrades, and weapons every level, which gives this short experience more variation than many triple A games are even able to achieve. While I love this constant progression in weaponary I do wish we could use each weapon a little longer before setting it aside for the newer, and almost always better, weapon. The only other negative I have for this game is that it seemed to be on a bell curve of difficulty, if that makes sense. I had a slight learning curve at first before the challenge ramped up in the middle. But by the time I got the fire breathing weapon and the mortar I only died once and didn't feel the same challenge as I did when I only had a machete and pistols. Overall, Bastion has a laser focus design that gives a beautiful story efficiently and constantly evolves both its combat and world throughout the game. 9/10.

For the gamers who are into RPGs, resource management, and base building of sorts, this game might be up your alley.
Whiel the visuals aren't SUPERMEGAFANTASTIC, they are good enough that they immerse you into the world fairly well, and as far as controlling characters are concerned, you don't control one specific character, it is best to switch to different characters to level up, and with the fatigue mechanic in this game, you kinda have to if you don't want to constantly run out of breath while swinging that crowbar.
As for base building, there are multiple site locations that provide different bonuses and drawbacks depending on which site you pick.  Some may have all the space to build every single facility, but be so far out of town that travel time doesn't really make things worth it.   To be honest though I've only found really one or two sites that really are worth the rtesources to relocate your survivors, the rest seem like a poor man's choice, but with enough resource management it's not impossible to afford.
The game that I have played seems to illustrate the scarcity of resources, which is great for being a primary driver of pushing you out of your starting town and into exploring different areas of the map.  Once your town's buildings are searched, the resources don't regenerate, so you'll have to make do with what you have and move on to the next town.  As a plot engine for the sparse storyline and as a gameplay mechanic, it works fairly well.
Now, if you're sick and tired of the zombie genres, there's only one thing I want to say to pique your interest in this game, and that is this; VEHICULAR MELEE COMBAT.  Being able to use your driver-side door as a melee weapon while driving in this game, is sheer genius, and very reminiscent of ZombieLand.  There's just something viscerally satisfying about opening your vehicle door at full speed and clocking a horde of zombies with your door.

Starbound is one of those games that instead of actually presenting the player with meaningful gameplay and progression, it gives the player a lifeless sandbox with no real incentive to do anything. Since I opted in Early Access, I've always thought this game has huge potential, but it just needs to take that extra step to make things interesting.
After 1.1 I feel that Starbound never took that extra step and kinda settled for less than it deserved in my opinion.
There is a lot to do, but in the end it's all the same busywork, whether it is collecting new items, fish or fossils, none of which to me is exactly very captivating. There are no epic adventures to be had, just the same-y planets and dungeons you've seen hundred times before.

Starbound has come a long, LONG way since release. Some of it good, some not so much. I'm not so much of a fan right now, but for someone who doesn't have fond memories of alpha and beta Starbound, you will probably like it a tonne.
Think Terraria, plus Space Engineers minus a decent combat system, you get Starbound. This game is mostly a exploration game, the enemies are meh at best. They have mediocre tracking skills and their attacks are more or less linear. But if you look from a exploration standpoint, it has a suprising amount of content. There are almost unlimited planets to check out, and now there are space stations, hostile/friendly ships, space anomalies, and mechs to explore them with.
What I think needs to be added or improved upon
-Mechs should have cosmetic slots. Like, I want a good mech that can get me more than 10 feet on a high level area, but I want a cool military style too. Cosmetic slots?
-Mechs should ALSO have more varied slots. The mech system, while pretty cool, is actually pretty basic. Start with low power and low defence, upgrade to medium of both, upgrade to high of both. If it had more of a rpg-esque approach with varying stats that would make customization more interesting.
-Enemy A.I. It is absolute trash. In fact, enemies in general are trash. They have never been interesting. They feel like they were added as minor inconveniences at most. Land enemies are slow, and usually just walk into you as a damaging method. Space enemies are kind of better, but I think space combat could be made more tactical? Like, when was the last time someone charged in head first during a space battle (ignore almost all space movies). Think Enders Game. In case of land enemies, play Terraria for a bit, get a feel for them.
-Weapons. Oh lordy me, they have fallen from a height. Now you can get a couple of random-generated weapons, which is nice enough, but you can only get these weapons-
1) Assault rifle
2) Pistol
3) Machine pistol
4) Shotgun
5) Sniper Rifle
6) Grenade launcher? Idk if that is still a thing
7) Rocket Launcher
There used to be things such as
1) Pulse Rifle
2) Floran Rifle
3) Avian Rifle
4) Plasma Pistol
5) Revolver
6) Flamethrowers
7) Shattergun (best weapon I actually loved them)
8) Plasma variants of most stock weaponry in current game
9) Grenades
There also used to be shields that applied buffs. With some cheating you could make invisibility watches. It was OP, but cool.
Those things above are what USED to be in the game, but now we just got some procedural generated guns and a couple swords, then the boring as heck unique weapons which fail to satisfy my customizable weaponry stash urges. Chucklefish, please add them back. I'll actually love you.
-Food system for all difficulties. Please.
-The space system
Alrighty, the space system now is fun, hands down. You can move your ship to anywhere, whether or not you can land at said place. There are space stations, mechs, space anomalies, other ships, etc. BUT, it can be improved with some concepts from beta/alpha and some new ones.
1) The tiered universe system. There used to be 5 different universe tiers, each a different difficulty, that you accessed slowly by defeating bosses and gaining a ship upgrade of some descript. This made finding a certain levelled planet quicker. Now thats gone, and you have to just hunt for one over the map screen. Also, please add back tentacle planets? Please?
2) Ya know how like, if a pirate ship draws up next to a navy ship, the pirates attack? Well ♥♥♥♥ it, fly right next to a hostile ship and they just let you go, no matter how much gold your ship walls are made out of. I think you should add an actual airlock to your ship like the hostile and friendly ships around, and make it so enemy ships can actually fly towards you and attempt a boarding. Maybe add ship combat too? That would be sweet. Yes, it would be hard to implement, but it would pay off.
3) Planets could do with a civilisation make-over. There used to be USCM bases, human lunar bases or whatever the ♥♥♥♥ they were, and god knows what. Now, theres a couple glitch things, maybe a hylotl settlement, possibly a novakid, and usually a floran town. Where is the equality?
4) In co-op, other people should be able to board your mech. Not pilot, just sit in the back. Makes it easier to escort people places.
- Option to hide your armour slots so you don't need to equip vanity items to hide that ugly helmet. I wana just see my face and my back. I don't want no ugly backpacks or glasses. I also want adequate protection at that time.
- Maybe, just maybe, fix the ♥♥♥♥ing quests. Honestly, they are boring as all hell. Make them INTERESTING.
- Make it so camping on planets is more important. Now its just, oh lets go here, oh theres night, oh lets leave. Maybe during the night you cant beam up? Make it more interesting as a survival mechanic.
I think Starbound now earns a like, 6/10 singleplayer, 8/10 multiplayer. Multiplayer is fun. Gotta give it that.

So I just finished this game and what a journey it is!
It is an open world game set in the Lord of the Rings universe. You play Talion who is a ranger that gets imbued with the power of a spirit. This gives you extra powers such as the ability to drain enemies, read their minds to gather intel or even just mind control them.
As you progress through the game you will level up. Each time you level up you will get an ability point to spend on the current tier of abilities. To unlock more tiers and more abilities to pick you need to level up the power bar. This is done by completing power missions which mostly consist of killing orc captains and warchiefs.
The side missions give you Mirian which lets you unlock passive bonuses such as increased health, focus, more arrow slots etc. In addition you use it to unlock rune slots for your weapons. Runes are basically gems that you socket into your weapons to increase their effectiveness.
The side content isn't mandatory but I do recommend doing at least some of it as it's the only way to get Mirian and it will make things much easier for you in the long run. The combat of the game is excellent, very Batman-esque. You will be swinging your sword a lot and countering enemy attacks. There is a hit streak system and at 8 consecutive hits you can do a special ability such as an execution or an AoE stun.
You can do a lot of the game from stealth as I did. You can climb almost everything like Assassin's Creed and sneak up behind Orcs for a stealth kill. Your bow has limited arrows you can get from collecting them in the world or draining enemies. You have a focus bar that slows time when you use your bow but it is limited.
The game does a great job at making you feel powerful. There are cinematic shots of when you execute enemies and it feels so good to pop your late game cooldown and spam executes. Overall the game is very satisfying. The story is good, the combat is great and it's definitely a game for you if you are a fan of open world games or lord of the rings.

It has been a long time since I've been truly hooked on a game. The story, delivered through an enchanting narrator, is given in small portions during gameplay that are easy for the player to swallow. It introduces new concepts slowly and gives the player immediate battle-ground application so they won't forget the controls they've learned. Each weapon is customizable/upgradable and there are so many to choose from that it this game is suitable to any play style. It introduces you to new worlds, characters, and concepts brilliantly; I dare say this is the first game since Portal to do this so masterfully.

Bastion is a beautiful action-packed indie game about a kid just trying to make it back home.
Before I get in depth, I want to say that this game is a solid 9/10. It deserves a spot right up there with the indie legends such as Cavestory.
The charm in this game is thanks to a high level of gameplay polish and innovative narration. I don't want to spoil it for you, but this is some of the best storytelling I've experienced in a video game for quite a long time. Really, THIS is how you make a game.
I will get the cons out of the way first. The balance in the game is somewhat questionable. Some weapons and bonuses (called spirits) are blatantly overpowered. Namely the brushers pike and leechade. (Leechade combined with Stabsinthe and lifewine is insane) Another thing that bothered me is how slow it is to get fragments, the game's currency. You will beat the game without even getting close to fully upgrading everything there is. Even with the use of idols (make the game more difficult in exchange for more fragments dropped ) the fragment gain is very slow for my taste. The best way to gain fragments are from vigils in the memorial but you can only do them once and they do not restart in NG+. My last gripe is that there is no reliable way to test your loadouts. There are repeatable levels called dreams, but it is not a super elegant way to test out damage and spirit interactions. I wish there was somewhat of a training dummy on the bastion. Oh.. and the game doesn't support my monitor resolution :( oh well.
With that out of the way, I can get on to what makes this game absolutely amazing. The art style is very unique and fun. You will enjoy looking at the diverse worlds and seeing the luscious colors. The graphics get an A+ here. The gameplay is very addicting. You will constantly be wanting to upgrade your favorite weapons to see just how strong they can become. Another thing that is great is the ability to choose your own favored weapon loadout. ALL weapons are viable in the lategame, but yes, some are better than others. All of the different weapons are fun and unique from eachother in some distinct way. Even within single weapons there are different upgrade paths that make the weapon feel even more diversified. You will love trying out all the different upgrade combinations on each weapon to see how they mesh with your playstyle.
The lore in this game is very well-written. It is almost entirely spoken storytelling and never shows you cutscenes of past events. This comes down to personal preference. Some may not like the way the game wants you to visualize the events in your imagination as if you are reading from a book. I actually adore it, BUT keep in mind that this makes the story a bit harder to follow along. You may not understand anything about the story until about halfway through where you get accustomed to how the game is designed. I think the fact that the replayability is so high makes this great because you can hear the story again. The distinct contrasts between the Caelondians and the Uras are a focus point of the storytelling. They draw a real connection between the different characters and their place in the post-calamity world. You'll meet a couple survivors and learn about their journeys.
There are a couple player-made choices that have an effect on the ending. You WILL actually want to replay the game over again to pick the other choices. You feel as if your decision has a really important outcome.
I highly recommend this game and I will definitely be picking up Transistor and Pyre. Deep down though I'm waiting for a Bastion 2...

Where most zombie videogames focus on a badass or a handful of badasses wandering around splattering undead brain matter all over the place, State of Decay instead chooses to focus on community simulation. I realize that sounds like the exact opposite of what gamers want from their zombie games, but let me assure you that community simulation makes zombie killing all the more satisfying.
In State of Decay, the main character is the valley the game is set in. Your success or failure has little to do with whether the character you are currently playing survives. And, believe me, characters WILL die, and once they're gone, there's no getting them back. I found myself more than once limping back to camp in a stupor, trying to come to terms with the fact that there was nothing I could have done to save my teammate from that horde of zombies. THAT'S the sort of game this is. As it should be in any zombie apocalypse, no one person is guaranteed survival and all that matters is whether your community can figure out a way to keep going despite the loss of one of its members. If your group's only auto mechanic gets eaten, you're soon going to find that gathering supplies and getting from place to place is a lot harder without a way to repair vehicles.
Every aspect of survival in State of Decay's valley is tracked and simulated, from the morale of your community, to the availability of supplies, to how much neighboring groups of survivors trust you. And every action the player takes affects the simulation-- if you want to grab that sweet shotgun out of the community's stash, you will have to prove that you've earned it first through contributing to the wellbeing of the community. This ends up being a very addictive game mechanic, as it isn't long before you find yourself overwhelmed with tasks the local community needs accomplished. For instance, if you focus too much on keeping morale up, you'll soon find that supplies are dwindling. And when you do go out on that supply run for desperately needed medicine, you'll often have to choose whether to ignore the frantic calls for help on the radio from the friendly group of survivors in the next town over.
Throughout all this decision-making and emergent drama, I hardly even noticed State of Decay's unpolished animation and clunky interface. They were there and I knew they could be better, but I was having so much fun that it didn't matter. What Undead Labs has got here is an incredibly addictive foundation to build upon and I can't wait to see what they come up with next. This is one developer that realizes when it comes to apocalyptic settings, the monsters are only a catalyst for revealing the true nature of man.

Dragon's Dogma or how some call it, "Japanese Skyrim", is a Capcom's attempt at a westernised RPG. And it's a good one, in my opinion.
The story, sadly, is the weakest part of the game. The start of the story is pretty standart: you play as an Arisen, a man or a woman who has been chosen by a Dragon to slay him and your goal is, well, to kill the Dragon. In the middle the story is almost non-existent and only at the end it becomes more interesting.
Most of the secondary quests are basically fetch quests and they can be pretty monotonous and boring though some of them may have consequenses in the future.
The best part of the game is its gameplay. I would call it a mix between Monster Hunter, Shadow of the Colossus and a wee bit of Dark Souls.The unique feature of the game is a pawn system. At early piont of a game you will be able to make a second character which will be your main pawn. After making your pawn you will be asked several question and your answers will determine your pawns behaviour. Beisdes your main pawn you also can have two additional pawns that you can hire from a rift. And this is where the online aspect of the game shows itself. You can either choose from random pawns made by the game itself in ofline mode or you can choose main pawns of other players as your companions in online mode. Your pawn is also may be hired. When your pawn will be sent away by the player that hired him, you will recieve a reward in rift crystals, one of the currencies of the game.
The more you fight the monsters with you pawn the more it learns and later will give you (or to the other player, that hired your pawn) advices about weaknesses of monsters and will use these weaknesses itself to fight more efficiently.
The roleplaying system is based around 9 vocations: 3 basic vocations (fighter, strider and mage), 3 advanced vocations (warrior, archmage and ranger) and 3 hybrid vocations (mystic knight, magic archer and assasin). Your Arisen may use all of the 9 vocations while your pawn may use only advanced and basic vocations. Your stats increase according to your vocation which is a bit uncomfortable in my opinion. Each vocation has several levels which get the more higher the more you use it. Each level of a vocation opens some skills, both active and passive ones. Each vocation can have 6 passive skills and 6 active skills used at once (warrior gets only 3 active skills at once which is strange because other advanced vocations get 6). You can change between vocations freely, there is no restrictions.
Now the part where The Shadow of Colossus and Monster Hunter aspects come in. There are different kinds of monsters in the game and some of them are pretty big. If the monster is big enough, then you can grab it and climb on it to get to its weak spots. For example, you can garb a cyclops and climb to his head and then attack his eye to deal increased damage. The giant monsters consist of different parts that can be hit individually and which can be crippled. If you attack legs of a cyclops long enough then it will eventually fall down and become vulnerable to attacks. Or you can burn the wings of a griffin and it won't be able to fly anymore. Also, damaging some parts may yield some materials. You can break off a tusk of a cyclops
and it will drop as a material which you can use to augment your equipment.
The size of the world is smaller compared to RPGs like Skyrim but is still big enough to have a fast travel system although weird one. In order to fast travel you need two items: ferrystones and port crystals. Ferrystones are used to initiate the fast travel and port crystal are the points to which you can travel. There are two permanent port crystal at two main towns and several mobile port crystal which you can carry and place where you you want.
The bossfights in Dragon's Dogma are pretty good although some of them may be very easy. The difficulty is a bit weird in Dragon's Dogma anyway. At the start you are very weak and simple bandits can kill you very fast if you are not careful. In the middle part of the game the difficulty feels much lower and then it suddenly raises up again at the end.
The music is mostly good although some of the tracks are ruined for me with a usage of electric guitar.
One of the music tracks for example:
Dragon's Dogma is a pretty solid game. It suffers from lack of a good story and pawn system could be done much better but the gameplay itself is very good. Also, the DLC that comes with it is very good too. It adds a whole new area to the game which is considered as the endgame area by many players and it's may be very hard for new players, several sets of new armor, 3 new weapons for each vocation and many more things.
I really recommend to try this game out if you are looking for some epic fights, especially when this game is on sale.

This was my first visual novel, and I'm really glad it was!  It was a great way to jump into the visual novel genre.  As a kinetic novel, you play through the game like reading a book, with no options for the player to make choices to influence the storyline.
But just because the playstyle was hands-off, it didn't lack in other departments.  The graphics are so beautiful - I am really drawn to games that are visually striking, where the art style is detailed and high quality.  This game is definitely gorgeous to look at, which is a major plus because I played the game for close to 20 hours.
Another thing I really liked is how the characters aren't static.  On any particular scene, the characters' eyes blink, giving the "page" a little extra visual oomph.  The scenes also change slightly every few sentences, making it seem like the characters are moving - a tilt of the head, a turn of the body, movement of the arms - they all add up to make the characters appear fluid when they are actually standing still for most of the game.
The storyline is a little more militaristic than I expected, but still enjoyable.  Warning!  This novel is a tearjerker!  There are several character deaths, which was very difficult for me to get through. I loved their personalities and backstories, and it was heartbreaking to watch them die.
Despite the sad parts, I would absolutely play this game again.  The artistry is magnificent, and the characters are intriguing and lovable.  Highly recommended!

For those whom haven't ever played a souls game before, then please read this. For those that have, and haven't played Dark Souls PTDE, then it's imperative you read this.
Firstly, for those that don't know, Dark Souls is the first in a trilogy of games that boasts ever growing popularity as they are released, and is the best introduction into Souls games you will receive - gritty, bitter, soul crushing disappointment... followed by frustration, determination, perseverance and eventually insatiable lust. Yes, this is not a nice game, but it has the potential to be the best.
Now, whilst you may have heard of the spiritual predecessor, Demon's Souls, and spiritual successor, Bloodborne; know that while they share similar mechanics, these game are not part of the Dark Souls trilogy, and shouldn't wholly determine whether you'll think you'll like this game - which they haven't otherwise you wouldn't be reading a review to make up your mind...
START HERE IF YOU ONLY CARE FOR THE WORTHWHILE STUFF ::
I'll start out by saying, this game isn't for the feint of heart. If you don't like difficulty, or you're not patient, or you think Skyrim can be hard... this isn't for you. I can tell you, I've played that crap with survival mods on legendary difficulty and all it does is bore me. Dark Souls brings difficulty and mixes it with ingenuity to create a whole new kind of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ tearing experience for the new player. But, it is a game that can be mastered, and within no time it shall be the player tearing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s... of newbs... using twink builds - because we're all sadists at heart.
Since we're on that topic, let's talk about combat. Dark Souls has one of the best, and most advanced combat systems of any RPG out there - easily combating that of Dragon's Dogma and other such games. FromSoftware has placed heavy focus on a mixture of tactical and reactive combat. One can win a fight using reflexes alone, but the game punishes you for not planning ahead. The player whom prepares properly, and learns their enemy, will find themselves breezing through most areas and bosses in no time.
Stamina management is a key feature in Dark Souls. Stamina, shown as a green bar on the top left corner of one's HUD, determines the players ability to dodge, attack, block, parry, sprint, jump and at times can even affect the speed and damage of one's attacks. It is infinite, in that it recharges over time, but poor management can lead to a temporary loss of stamina, leaving the player wide open, and 90% of the time will result in death, or something close to it. Always be wary of your stamina.
That aside, the combat system in Dark Souls is very complex. From 'sweet spot' attacks, which alter damage dealt depending on which part of your weapon strikes the enemy; to differing types of critical attacks, and the various damage types the game has on offer. One of the 'unseen' but easily recognised features of the game are enemies' weaknesses and resistances. While certain enemies will be weak to thrusting or slashing damage, they may be resistant to striking attacks... and vice versa. This same rule applies to the elemental types available in the game :
- Magic
- Fire
- Lightning
- Physical (which splits into Strike, Slash and Thrust)
And on top of that are status effects :
- Bleed
- Poison
- Toxin
This complex and diverse combat system allows almost infinite variety to every combat situation. Of course, certain things will work better against certain enemies, bosses, or even are better suited to the area (for example, using a smaller thrusting sword in a confined space yields better results than accidentally hitting the wall with your two-handed skyscraper)'
I don't want to pour out a wiki full of content on a mere review, so I won't go too into detail about everything that I have mentioned and chosen to omit.
Now, aside from basic combat, Dark Souls PTDE boasts some of the best boss fights in any game to date. This that have played other souls games can be prepared for on par and better boss fights than many of the best fights encountered in the Souls games, and Dark Souls 1 is home to the most renowned and notorious boss fight in the whole series (and one of the biggest souls memes) - so that should persuade you a bit.
For those that haven't played a souls game... well, prepare to die. It's in the title. Many of the bosses in this game will kill you. Many times over. It is the player's responsibility to learn the boss - their move set, their weaknesses and strengths, and to learn to be patient with it. Greed, impatience and thoughtlessness are the biggest enemies of the Dark Souls player. As I said, if you aren't patient, then it isn't for you.
Saying that, I do not wish. To imply, at all, that any boss in this game is boring and just a grind to do. Quite the opposite. Every boss, to me, in their own unique way is a fight to behold. Each will get your heart racing, as you battle epically against bosses a varying size and shape, from humanoids the size of you, to beasts the size of buildings, all accompanied by an astounding soundtrack - it will not disappoint... well, maybe one boss fight will, but we don't talk about that one.
Though it was the first thing I spoke about, Combat is not the most important thing about Dark Souls (well it might be to some), but to me, the defining aspect of this game is the design. Set in a dark, fantastical, medieval setting - Dark Souls sets the player in one of the most flawlessly designed worlds to be seen in an RPG. The interconnected world, which intertwines on itself, with twists and turns at every corner leading to new and exciting areas as often as the well needed relief of realising it was a shortcut back to your last bonfire (effective checkpoint), will leave most in awe of just how flawlessly created this masterpiece is.
The world itself is fully connected, with each area having a realistic and very visible geographical relation to one another. Most often, that place you see in the distance is somewhere you will travel later; and there's a peculiar sense of satisfaction in seeing the place you earlier surpassed off in the distance, and realising how far you've come since.
Disregarding that, the area design (each area is interconnected, but have their own names and environments) is absolutely top-notch. With various paths in each area, and an abundance of verticality almost everywhere you travel, the player will often find themselves stumbling upon surprises of both the good and bad variety... good usually comes after defeating the bad surprise though. Sorry. No reward without sacrifice. Alongside this, Dark Souls puts heavy focus on both the sense of relief and sense of accomplishment, and it's area design is something that does this very successful. Bonfires, a place where one may rest and replenish Estus, level up, and later use to fast travel (plus more), are scattered about the world - though scarcely. Areas focus on these bonfires, using shortcuts to provide the much needed relief to the player after their gruelling trek through an area. Some, however, are well hidden, so ensure you always fully explore every nook and cranny... but don't let your guard down. Dark Souls rewards exploration, but it also has its fair share of methods to stop you getting all its loot for free - watch your back, and shield up when rounding corners.
Now, with both combat and design vaguely covered, the next subject is narrative. Often the biggest complaint about Dark Souls is its lack of a compelling story, and lore. Well, to those that believe such lies, I slap you with a dirty dishcloth and tell you to roll up hill donning the Catarina Armour until you are dizzy enough to warrant thinking such things, at which point I will still say you are a fool. Dark Souls has an immensely complex, emotional and amazing storyline. I freaking ran out of space, so you'll just have to believe me. \[+]/

Seriously, just buy it. The original Dark Souls is as close to a perfect game as is possible to get. If you don't mind a little frustration, then the game is incredibly rewarding, and you won't regret the time or money you spent.

State of Decay is a very good, and exclusively cheap. The game has very unique features, but some downsides as well.
One good thing I liked is the ability to manage your home site, you can upgrade buildings or build new ones, things like a garage, a workshop, a sleeping house and much more, and it actually shows up in your area. Of course, it takes time to build or upgrade buildings and it requires you to have a decent amount of materials, which is a great realistic aspect of the game.
If you quit the game, time progresses even when you are not playing, this means your camp will consume the food you've collected while you were playing and you will need to restock, else people will die or get sick. You have 4 main resources in the game: Food, medicine, materials and ammo.
Food - as I said, it's the most basic and common thing to have. It isn't hard at all to scavenge for food, it's almost everywhere and you should have it before you quit the game if you want your camp to stay at good state, shape, etc.
Medicine - People can get sick, people will get sick. If you wound while using one character and another, and log off, it will surely consume some medicine to fix the injuries, you can even find medicine resource in pharmacies or vet-houses and bring them to your homesite.
Materials - These are used to build or upgrade buildings in your homesite, for example, in some stage in the game you will have a bigger population on your camp so you will need more beds for everyone to sleep. Then, you will need to build a sleeping house which can be upgraded to a bunkhouse and will provide beds for everyone, increasing their stamina and they will regenerate energy faster.
Ammo - Mostly used for the watch tower you will most likely have in your camp. The watcher will use his weapon to eliminate zombies off the perimeter and it will consume your ammo resources once in a while, if you want a safer perimeter, you want ammo.
One downside is the repetitive survivor quests, sometimes people in your camp will get angry or afraid. Your mission is to take them on a walk and eliminate some zombies while having a chatter. It's repetitive all the time, same lines and etc. I think it needs some new features.
Overall this is a great game, but you will need to spend a lot of time managing your resources especiall before you logoff, making sure your people can stay safe while you are not in game.  It's amazingly cheap (20$) and I would recommend anyone to try this game! Also check out the new upcoming DLC which brings new content to the game.

A really good, atmospheric brain teaser that was just the right amount of tricky for me. I bought it not really knowing it was a puzzle game (not my favourite genre) but I was hooked from the moment I launched it.
Things I Liked
- The puzzles. Obviously this is the bulk of the entire game. Never too hard, never too easy. Although saying that, there was ONE puzzle I had to look up. :-) But thankfully a lot of other people struggled with this one too so I didn't beat myself up too much!
- The atmosphere. Eerie, cold, dark and reminiscent of dead space without the jump scares/horror.
- The lack of back tracking and very linear progress. When I first realised that the game would be made up of one giant area to explore I worried that there would be much confusing backtracking. But no, although there is a little backtracking, it's very easy to navigate from one area to the next.
Thing I Didn't Like
- The graphics were a little bit blurry. Not a massive deal but noticable.
- The voice actors sounded identical. Especially the women. This made it hard to follow the plot.
- The story itself was not anything special. I was definitely playing for the puzzles alone.
- Not much replayability factor.
- The music was ok, but there was nowhere near enough of it. I much preferred the soft tinkling piano tracks I got in a few of the puzzle rooms to the ambient humming of most of the others.

It is an amazing game. Great visuals, relaxing music, and very cute art style.
The problem is balance, progression and gameplay.
The devs did a great job creating amazing aesthetics/presentation... but messed up with the gameplay, which is not very good. The problem with gameplay is that it often sends you searching for some item, except that in infinite random generated universe, you don't always know where the item is. Searching for needles in a haystack, again and again. Those searches pretty much destroy game pacing and "immersion" The intro mission is amazing, but when you're searching for one more thing in the infinite universe, it doesn't feel like that intro.
I have impression, that developer's attempt to focus on "survival" ultimately ruined the game, because it looks like a lot of effort was put into making stuff harder to obtain. Alright, so you wanna grow a certain plant. You can't buy the seeds, you have to find them. You want to make a sword.... you can't buy the ore, you have to find it. You need a rare material for a cool building? You have to find it. Prices for everything are high, cash is hard to obtain, and selling prices for items is incredibly low. Heck, at least in dwarf fortress you had creative ways of obtaining materials, were mostly fine with lower-tier materials (rarer metal didn't automaticlaly mean stronger weapon) and could buy stuff from passing caravans.  20 hours in you might discover that you CAN buy the ore, if you do a quest for a merchant, and said quest, will require you to hunt through half of the galaxy for some plant seeds and crafting stations. Meaning it is "To get A, find B, to find B, craft C, to craft C do X, and to do X, find Y and Z". Oh, and if you want to sell fifty thousand tons of rocks you mined? Well, their selling price is zero.
The experience is very uneven, searching for things in infinite randomly generated universe is very annoying, and many elements of gameplay feel strange. It is very tempting to just play on minimum difficulty and use cheats for any items you have trouble finding.
---------
In the end, it is a pity. Amazing visuals and presentation, ruined by flawed not well thought out gameplay component.

It's an interesting game to see how they've created an NPC rank system with the Uruks. However, it's mediocre combat system and storyline.
I spent about 3 hours or less to get the full experience of the gameplay. Masterminding the growth of certain Uruk leaders to only reap the rewards of their death later. Or planning out betrayals within the ranks with mindcontrol branding.
But as fun as this Uruk ranking system was, the novelty fades fast, and it's just grinding and trying to finish up the storyline, lore, etc. Took me roughly 17 hours to finish main storyline without rushing, and maybe double that for me to do a full completion run.
Combat skills and abilities doesn't really unfold well either. Abilities you unlock are only stronger and better versions of abilities you already have or applied to different enemies. So it's more of a vertical progression, rather than horizontal progression.
It's a bit hard to say if I recommend this or not...

Bastion is a beautiful action-packed indie game about a kid just trying to make it back home.
Before I get in depth, I want to say that this game is a solid 9/10. It deserves a spot right up there with the indie legends such as Cavestory.
The charm in this game is thanks to a high level of gameplay polish and innovative narration. I don't want to spoil it for you, but this is some of the best storytelling I've experienced in a video game for quite a long time. Really, THIS is how you make a game.
I will get the cons out of the way first. The balance in the game is somewhat questionable. Some weapons and bonuses (called spirits) are blatantly overpowered. Namely the brushers pike and leechade. (Leechade combined with Stabsinthe and lifewine is insane) Another thing that bothered me is how slow it is to get fragments, the game's currency. You will beat the game without even getting close to fully upgrading everything there is. Even with the use of idols (make the game more difficult in exchange for more fragments dropped ) the fragment gain is very slow for my taste. The best way to gain fragments are from vigils in the memorial but you can only do them once and they do not restart in NG+. My last gripe is that there is no reliable way to test your loadouts. There are repeatable levels called dreams, but it is not a super elegant way to test out damage and spirit interactions. I wish there was somewhat of a training dummy on the bastion. Oh.. and the game doesn't support my monitor resolution :( oh well.
With that out of the way, I can get on to what makes this game absolutely amazing. The art style is very unique and fun. You will enjoy looking at the diverse worlds and seeing the luscious colors. The graphics get an A+ here. The gameplay is very addicting. You will constantly be wanting to upgrade your favorite weapons to see just how strong they can become. Another thing that is great is the ability to choose your own favored weapon loadout. ALL weapons are viable in the lategame, but yes, some are better than others. All of the different weapons are fun and unique from eachother in some distinct way. Even within single weapons there are different upgrade paths that make the weapon feel even more diversified. You will love trying out all the different upgrade combinations on each weapon to see how they mesh with your playstyle.
The lore in this game is very well-written. It is almost entirely spoken storytelling and never shows you cutscenes of past events. This comes down to personal preference. Some may not like the way the game wants you to visualize the events in your imagination as if you are reading from a book. I actually adore it, BUT keep in mind that this makes the story a bit harder to follow along. You may not understand anything about the story until about halfway through where you get accustomed to how the game is designed. I think the fact that the replayability is so high makes this great because you can hear the story again. The distinct contrasts between the Caelondians and the Uras are a focus point of the storytelling. They draw a real connection between the different characters and their place in the post-calamity world. You'll meet a couple survivors and learn about their journeys.
There are a couple player-made choices that have an effect on the ending. You WILL actually want to replay the game over again to pick the other choices. You feel as if your decision has a really important outcome.
I highly recommend this game and I will definitely be picking up Transistor and Pyre. Deep down though I'm waiting for a Bastion 2...

Went in with very low expectations and I can say this game has delivered way more than I imagined. WELL worth the 20$ early access price. The dev team has come an extremely long way from early reviews and this game is a blasty blast. In comparison with DayZ, the bugs I've encontered have been few and far between. GREAT atmosphere and lighting. The weather effects may be the best I've experienced in any game. Fun enemies and PvP. Very respectable loot system. Cool base buiilding and crafting elements. Gun play is fun, and challenging. The enviroments are top notch, I really can't say enough about the wonderful atmosphere this game has. The citys are overgrown and have a lived-in feeling adding to the emersion, in my opinion this game is much more pleasing to look at than dayZ. In many ways this game feels so much further along in the development cycle than dayZ (which i compare it t often because its the only ther survival game I have massive time invested in). There are already cars and predators, which, at the time of this review are either not in dayZ, or are so buggy and complicated to get running they're not worth messing with.
The (minor) Cons
-Friends with lower end PC's have some trouble running the game, but its possible
- At this point the guns, in my opinion, do not sound very good. But from what I've read some are place holders to be fixed in the future. And the gun shots arent heard from more than 200m or so. (At least for me and I use TB's)
-Cars can be ninjas, that you cant hear until there right between your butt cheeks
-The server joining menu REALLY needs to be overhauled and more intuitive to make it easier to join friends
-Cant prone
-Items sometime get eaten by the earth if dropped in houses or bushes
- The UI needs a little work, but is respectable, and fairly easy to navigate
Bottom line, this game is a blast, and only getting better. Obviously this game is in early access, so the minor bugs I have foudn will be fixed. If youre looking for a survival game thats fun and beautiful, this is it.

So it's been quite a while since I've reviewed a game, but this game is getting too much hate. First up, ignore my hours in game, since I have nearly 50 hours on a different account. Secondly, this review will not include features from the July 30th patch, as I haven't played it yet.
So, Miscreated. Yet another open world zombie survival game. Another boring or broken early access game? Maybe. But this game is seriously underrated.
Miscreated runs on the CryEngine, which looks gorgeous, although it may require a beefy system to run on max settings. It got off to a really rocky start - glitchy, expensive, boring - but I eventually came across a GoldGloveTV video that featured him and a friend driving a pickup truck into a tornado. That convinced me to play this game. Even DayZ doesn't have tornadoes.
As of now, the game is gorgeous, with a huge map and base building. You can either settle down and grow crops, loot the cities and towns, or explore the many interesting locations in the map, including bunkers, crashed airliners, mineshafts, military checkpoints, and more. But what really adds on to the game is the ATMOSPHERE. Hayward City can easily be described as a "snowless version of the Division." There are burned out cars, collapsing buildings, trash piles, hanged survivors, weeds everywhere, etc. Other locations share these details, though not with the same intensity. It really feels like the world has gone to♥♥♥♥♥♥ And congrats to the developers for creating a city to rival a game Ubisoft spent three years making. Indie devs aren't always a bad thing.
Looting is a bit weird. While I love the realism of finding 12 9mm bullets in 2 hours of real time, it makes gunfights real intense when you run out of ammo entirely. Guns themselves aren't hard to find - just keep checking the burned cars, you'll get one eventually - but bullets are another story. And sometimes houses just don't spawn any loot. It's kinda random.
Cars and boats. I ♥♥♥♥ing hate them. You'll find everything you need to fix a car in about an hour - unless you're me, and spend 3 hours looking for oil, only to find 2 cans in the same garage - but they are easily damaged. Boats aren't worth your time as they get stuck on the shore way too easily. And if you just leave it in the water it'll just drift downstream or to shore. We need anchors/a launching system to push boats back in the water. It sucks right now.
Overall, the game is pretty far along, and much better than it originally was. It's essentially DayZ but with less items. That's not a huge complaint since DayZ is a cluster♥♥♥♥ when it comes to items. You can hunt, craft, loot, build bases, drive cars, kill players, grow crops, go exploring, or simply die in stupid ways. Hopefully there will be a story involving Algae Inc. or whatever the ♥♥♥♥ it's called. However, the game is fun and definitely worth it, despite the launch and small playerbase.
Miscreated: 7/10 (Great)
Tip: I don't know if this was a glitch or server shutdown or what, but my game would crash, and when relaunched, all of my stuff, including my spawn clothes, would be gone. Very frustrating, but it might just be that server, idk.
