For those whom haven't ever played a souls game before, then please read this. For those that have, and haven't played Dark Souls PTDE, then it's imperative you read this.
Firstly, for those that don't know, Dark Souls is the first in a trilogy of games that boasts ever growing popularity as they are released, and is the best introduction into Souls games you will receive - gritty, bitter, soul crushing disappointment... followed by frustration, determination, perseverance and eventually insatiable lust. Yes, this is not a nice game, but it has the potential to be the best.
Now, whilst you may have heard of the spiritual predecessor, Demon's Souls, and spiritual successor, Bloodborne; know that while they share similar mechanics, these game are not part of the Dark Souls trilogy, and shouldn't wholly determine whether you'll think you'll like this game - which they haven't otherwise you wouldn't be reading a review to make up your mind...
START HERE IF YOU ONLY CARE FOR THE WORTHWHILE STUFF ::
I'll start out by saying, this game isn't for the feint of heart. If you don't like difficulty, or you're not patient, or you think Skyrim can be hard... this isn't for you. I can tell you, I've played that crap with survival mods on legendary difficulty and all it does is bore me. Dark Souls brings difficulty and mixes it with ingenuity to create a whole new kind of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ tearing experience for the new player. But, it is a game that can be mastered, and within no time it shall be the player tearing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s... of newbs... using twink builds - because we're all sadists at heart.
Since we're on that topic, let's talk about combat. Dark Souls has one of the best, and most advanced combat systems of any RPG out there - easily combating that of Dragon's Dogma and other such games. FromSoftware has placed heavy focus on a mixture of tactical and reactive combat. One can win a fight using reflexes alone, but the game punishes you for not planning ahead. The player whom prepares properly, and learns their enemy, will find themselves breezing through most areas and bosses in no time.
Stamina management is a key feature in Dark Souls. Stamina, shown as a green bar on the top left corner of one's HUD, determines the players ability to dodge, attack, block, parry, sprint, jump and at times can even affect the speed and damage of one's attacks. It is infinite, in that it recharges over time, but poor management can lead to a temporary loss of stamina, leaving the player wide open, and 90% of the time will result in death, or something close to it. Always be wary of your stamina.
That aside, the combat system in Dark Souls is very complex. From 'sweet spot' attacks, which alter damage dealt depending on which part of your weapon strikes the enemy; to differing types of critical attacks, and the various damage types the game has on offer. One of the 'unseen' but easily recognised features of the game are enemies' weaknesses and resistances. While certain enemies will be weak to thrusting or slashing damage, they may be resistant to striking attacks... and vice versa. This same rule applies to the elemental types available in the game :
- Magic
- Fire
- Lightning
- Physical (which splits into Strike, Slash and Thrust)
And on top of that are status effects :
- Bleed
- Poison
- Toxin
This complex and diverse combat system allows almost infinite variety to every combat situation. Of course, certain things will work better against certain enemies, bosses, or even are better suited to the area (for example, using a smaller thrusting sword in a confined space yields better results than accidentally hitting the wall with your two-handed skyscraper)'
I don't want to pour out a wiki full of content on a mere review, so I won't go too into detail about everything that I have mentioned and chosen to omit.
Now, aside from basic combat, Dark Souls PTDE boasts some of the best boss fights in any game to date. This that have played other souls games can be prepared for on par and better boss fights than many of the best fights encountered in the Souls games, and Dark Souls 1 is home to the most renowned and notorious boss fight in the whole series (and one of the biggest souls memes) - so that should persuade you a bit.
For those that haven't played a souls game... well, prepare to die. It's in the title. Many of the bosses in this game will kill you. Many times over. It is the player's responsibility to learn the boss - their move set, their weaknesses and strengths, and to learn to be patient with it. Greed, impatience and thoughtlessness are the biggest enemies of the Dark Souls player. As I said, if you aren't patient, then it isn't for you.
Saying that, I do not wish. To imply, at all, that any boss in this game is boring and just a grind to do. Quite the opposite. Every boss, to me, in their own unique way is a fight to behold. Each will get your heart racing, as you battle epically against bosses a varying size and shape, from humanoids the size of you, to beasts the size of buildings, all accompanied by an astounding soundtrack - it will not disappoint... well, maybe one boss fight will, but we don't talk about that one.
Though it was the first thing I spoke about, Combat is not the most important thing about Dark Souls (well it might be to some), but to me, the defining aspect of this game is the design. Set in a dark, fantastical, medieval setting - Dark Souls sets the player in one of the most flawlessly designed worlds to be seen in an RPG. The interconnected world, which intertwines on itself, with twists and turns at every corner leading to new and exciting areas as often as the well needed relief of realising it was a shortcut back to your last bonfire (effective checkpoint), will leave most in awe of just how flawlessly created this masterpiece is.
The world itself is fully connected, with each area having a realistic and very visible geographical relation to one another. Most often, that place you see in the distance is somewhere you will travel later; and there's a peculiar sense of satisfaction in seeing the place you earlier surpassed off in the distance, and realising how far you've come since.
Disregarding that, the area design (each area is interconnected, but have their own names and environments) is absolutely top-notch. With various paths in each area, and an abundance of verticality almost everywhere you travel, the player will often find themselves stumbling upon surprises of both the good and bad variety... good usually comes after defeating the bad surprise though. Sorry. No reward without sacrifice. Alongside this, Dark Souls puts heavy focus on both the sense of relief and sense of accomplishment, and it's area design is something that does this very successful. Bonfires, a place where one may rest and replenish Estus, level up, and later use to fast travel (plus more), are scattered about the world - though scarcely. Areas focus on these bonfires, using shortcuts to provide the much needed relief to the player after their gruelling trek through an area. Some, however, are well hidden, so ensure you always fully explore every nook and cranny... but don't let your guard down. Dark Souls rewards exploration, but it also has its fair share of methods to stop you getting all its loot for free - watch your back, and shield up when rounding corners.
Now, with both combat and design vaguely covered, the next subject is narrative. Often the biggest complaint about Dark Souls is its lack of a compelling story, and lore. Well, to those that believe such lies, I slap you with a dirty dishcloth and tell you to roll up hill donning the Catarina Armour until you are dizzy enough to warrant thinking such things, at which point I will still say you are a fool. Dark Souls has an immensely complex, emotional and amazing storyline. I freaking ran out of space, so you'll just have to believe me. \[+]/

Seriously, just buy it. The original Dark Souls is as close to a perfect game as is possible to get. If you don't mind a little frustration, then the game is incredibly rewarding, and you won't regret the time or money you spent.

I'll start this review of by informing people that there is a slo-mo like ability mapped to the caps lock key by default. As far as I know (unless I skipped it somehow) the game doesn't actually inform you of this and I only found out by pure chance when I spazzed on my keyboard trying to get away from an explosion...so yeah there's that.
Anywho as far as the game itself goes although I'm giving it a recomendation it is a real mixed bag game design wise. This is probably a game you'll have a love/hate relationship with. Overall the gunplay is great. I really enjoyed the old school twitch based no iron sights shooting and good old fashioned health and armour drops. It's the level design that really starts to let this game down in the last few hours. The first level has you going through a space station with very linier corridors with very little room for deviation whereas the next few levels open up a little more. About halfway through the game the levels start becoming a little too open, with unessessary doors and corridors becoming accessible and some just plain huge open spaces with zero guidence or indication where to go next. This is bearable though and it's not until the last few hours that it just gets tedious. The game starts resorting to horrible half-life like platforming (crouch jump and all) and extremely obscure and hidden paths like barely visible vents and holes in the ground. The end mission is definitelly the lowest point of the game unfortunately. There's also a terrible stealth mission very early in the game but thankfully it's the only one and is over reletively quickly.
If you're looking for a game with a cohesive story I would look elsewhere as well. The plot is all over the place and the cutscenes and voice acting are laughable. It's a shame because the game takes you to some amazingly different locations like a space station, gang infested city slums, Russian bases crawling with soldiers and even eventually to Mars for the 'big' conclusion. The amazing variety of weapons is fantastic and they all handle differently making each of them very situational.
So in conclusion, if you're looking for an old fashioned shooter with some fun gunplay I would say pick this up. Even if you don't play it all the way through to the boring conclusion (honestly the story ain't worth it) it's still a lot of fun.

This has been needed for a long time, over 10 years.  Not only for the fans, but the industry as a whole, and those who simply don't know any better.  There are many people out there who don't even know what a good RPG is because they either never played them at the time or are too young to have played them.  All they know are the modern AAA titles that range from terrible to slightly better than mediocre.  To those of you who fall into that category, welcome to a real RPG.
It shouldn't be the case that this game is referred to as old school.  But at some point, many years ago, the industry decided that doing something different just for the sake of doing something different was somehow a good idea.  (Different just for the sake of making something different is terrible, it should only be made different if it's to better it.  You can't fix what is not broken.)  They then proceeded to fail at making good/great RPGs for over 10 years.  So this "old school" gameplay, to me, is just good game design that should never have ceased in the first place.  I have been saying for quite some time that all you need to do make a sequel or successor to good game is to take what made it good, maybe enhance it a little, utilize modern technology, and put in a new set of content/story.  This is what they did.
It stays true to the game experience of great RPGs such as Baldur's Gate and Icewind Dale even without the D&D rule set.  It is a very similar experience, and taking advantage of modern technology.  This was very well done.
The rule set is pretty good overall.
- The health and fatigue system is great, it's quite nice that going down in combat is not necessarily the end for that character.  Works well combined with limited camping supplies.
- Skills are not affected by stats at all.  This is a level of depth that I sorely miss.  For example, a high dex character is no better at stealth than a large, bumbling character.
- The armor system seems a bit flat.  It's an overly simple trade-off between attack/cast rate in combat and damage resistance.  I think there could be some more depth here.
I've encountered a couple bugs, but bugs can be fixed - not a huge deal.  There could definitely be more recruitable NPCs, the selection is quite small currently.  You can create your own, but those don't have the personality and side quests that the pre-made ones do.  Perhaps on some replays I will make use of that more.
It's a great game that I recommend for anyone who enjoys RPGs to pick up.  I give it a 9/10.  However, what this game accomplished - the resurrection of game experience that should never have died out in the first place, there is no rating system that could even handle such a high rating.  It is a bright ray of hope.  A hope that this is a sign of things to come.  This game proves that there is an audience for this type of experience (even though this should have been obvious the whole time).  Perhaps more developers will join in and we can have a new array of great RPGs.  That, I say without a doubt, is the greatest accomplishment here.  Well done, Obsidian.

which I dabbled most of my time into. I will mention more of that system later in this review, but first! The gameplay.
The game has cinematic combat and amazing character customization
But what I love most about DD:DA is that it doesn't do any hand holding when it comes to it's underlying mechanics.
There are a lot of instances where the things around you keeps hinting that you can do this and do that but never exactly tell you how...
I have never looked into forums with dead specific questions in my life. With that said, I truly enjoyed this experience.

The lore of Dragon's Dogma is interesting, I can definitely say that the ending is one of the most surprising things I've experienced in a game (Im not gonna spoil it don't worry)
but aside from that, the entirety of the plot is plain and generic.. Don't expect it to be Nier/FinalFantasy-esque when it comes to "emotional impact" or whatever cuz it's not that type of JRPG
Although, the side quests have these mini story arcs, which for me, is quite similar to side missions you see in Red Dead Redemption or other open world games. (I guess you get the point) I had lots of fun sinking my teeth into those.
So I mentioned the Pawn System earlier.
In the world of Dragon's Dogma, you have these side kicks we call "Pawns", these pawns are capable of learning from your actions and will practice what they've learned from you in combat.
You have your personal pawn who you can customize in a variety of ways, from appearance to equipment and even their traits, both in combat and personality.
The game has a system where you can upload your pawn online and other players will be able to hire them and your pawn will be able to learn from their travels with those other players.
"But what if I purchased this game a bit too late? Are people still playing?" Don't worry
I'm actually surprised how much people are still playing and how much are still discovering this game, there's a healthy community out there where you can share pawns and learn new things.

I think that itself is amazing. And THAT concludes my review and evaluation of Dragon's Dogma: Dark Arisen

If you love classic CRPGS like Baldur's Gate, Icewind Dale or Planetscape: Torment then you owe yourself to pick up this game. I've played almost 50 hours now and it's utterly brilliant. In a time where CRPGs have been reduced to AAA titles with QTEs, linear progression and being spoon feed every morsel of information Pillars comes as a blessing of both nostalgia and fresh air. The character creation is brilliant, the classes deep and interesting and the combat is strategic and tough, yet very rewarding. But it it's the lore and the graphics that really makes this game so brilliant. Your adventures in Dyrwood will immerse you into a world with a rich history, interesting races, frightful monsters, a pantheon of gods, and tons of interesting NPCs. The hand drawn graphics really brings this wonderful world to life in a way 3D graphics just can't.
For the younger players or those who never played the classics CRPGs of the late 90s, get ready for a bit of shock. Be ready to spend hours reading text, from old tomes, diaries to treaties on local history, books on culture, religion and factions. You'll also spend lot of the game time reading descriptions of characters and events. The game won't spoon feed you lore, it asks you to find out by yourself. It asks you to explore and understand, like all great RPGs should. This is a game that asks you to invest and apply yourself, but if you do it will reward you handsomely for it. The world feels more real and immersive because of it.
In short, this is wonderful game and all RPG fans need to pick it up, because we need more games like it.

Bastion offers a great story and fun, customizable, and challenging gameplay. You can tell that Supergiant (the developers) put a lot of effort into the visual and auditory aspects of this game.
- I really enjoy the art style. The colours are so vivid, yet not overpowering, and simple, yet very detailed.
- Narrator sounds like a wild west veteran. Total badass. Logan Cunningham (the voice actor) does an excellent job of keeping the story captivating.
- Intense music, very befitting for the story and progression of this game.
- Lots of melee and ranged weapons (and power up for the weapons) to choose from. You can easily customize your weapons to fit your preferred fighting style.
- Deflecting attacks with the shield is very satisfying.
- You can further customize the protagonist (the Kid) by equipping/unequipping Spirits; you get your standard buffs from these.
- I love how Supergiant decided to manage the difficulty setting. It is completely up to the player and can be changed any time the Kid is at the Bastion. There, you can visit a building called the Shrine where you can choose to invoke Gods (10 in total). Each God you invoke will grant you extra EXP and Currency from kills. However, they come with a side effect: enemies are more durable, move faster, deflect attacks, etc). So essentially, if you want a bigger challenge, you can invoke more gods, and in turn you will receive greater benefits.
- There are several optional challenge rooms for those willing to test themselves; fighting waves of enemies or mastering a weapon. Naturally you are rewarded for completing these challenges.
-
- Two endings and New game +.
- You will probably fall of the terrain often for two reasons. Firstly, it takes time to get used to the dodge roll. Secondly, it isn’t always clear where the edge of the terrain is.
I enjoyed playing Bastion. The story was sad but captivating. The combat felt smooth. Loved the customizable difficulty. Overall, a very solid game.

TL;DR: You need to play this game.
If you like games like Starcraft with a simpler, quick-paced experience where you don't have to worry too much about micro-managing resource collection and base building, you should give this game a try.
I say the game is near-real-time strategy because the style is like League of Legends in the sense that you spawn Minions to go out and do battle in the lane, but you don't have any hero that you control in real time. You can pick from a variety of units that you can bring into battle all with different strengths, weaknesses, and abilities. Units all cost a certain amount of credits to purchase and send into battle, and you only have a few credits to start with, so you can't just send in a bunch of bombers right at the start.
Credits are earned throughout the game, and there are two opportunites to upgrade the rate at which you earn credits. There is only one lane in this game which makes the combat focused into rounds of battles.  Eventually one side wins and before you know it, you're hooked.  There are details to this game that make it keep your interest such as management of runes which you can equip that give you boost to stats of units etc.  These runes are upgradeable, which makes you want to play to level your runes!  There is 1v1 and 3v3 PVE PVP and ARENA modes to be found, so a litle something for everybody.
You can purchase some XP and credits boosters to use during the rounds, as well as custom skins for your units, but the game isn't really pay to win.

Dark Souls, perhaps more than any other game on the market, is preceded by a reputation. From its ultra-imposing, ultra-intimidating bosses, to the alienating community mantra of "git gud", to the game's own subtitle of "Prepare To Die", the message seems clear: this game is hard, and you're going to die. A lot. The reality is, thankfully, quite a bit more complex than that. While Dark Souls seems destined to make an appearance on nearly every "most difficult games" list ever compiled, to place a disproportionate focus on some sort of perceived insatiable sadism is to sell the game far, far short of what it truly has on offer. Consider the whole picture, and it's little surprise that the Souls series has essentially spawned an entirely new subgenre unto its own.
At its core, Dark Souls is a game that demands to be respected. Every step you take, every swing of your sword, every swig of life-giving Estus is subject to an assessment of risk. New players quickly learn that while sharp reflexes don't hurt, it's caution, calculation, and preparation that make the difference between "VICTORY ACHIEVED" and the infamous "YOU DIED". Button-mashing and face-rolling will only see you sent back to the last bonfire, but with a bit of patience and a cool head you'll realize that towering demons and seven-headed serpents aren't quite so scary after all.
For as much respect as this game requires of the player, it returns it in kind. Save for a select portion or two of the game where it seems to momentarily forget that it's not actually part of the Uncharted series, fights are fair and frustration is shockingly minimal. While I won't go so far as to suggest that "no death is ever the game's fault", I will say that this game emanates a general ethos of measured punishment. Believe it or not, Dark Souls honestly
want you to succeed. It goes to great lengths to ensure that with enough observation, adaptation, and perseverance you will always have at your disposal every tool necessary to do so, even when your situation initially looks hopeless.
In addition to its punishing-yet-rewarding gameplay, there really is a lot to love about Dark Souls. For a game of few conversations and fewer cutscenes, its lore is surprisingly deep. While some exposition does exist as a more direct means of world-building, much of it must be pieced together through a combination of lore-bearing items and reasonable inferences made about the world around you. Much of the game follows a similar philosophy of content delivery, where there is always something new for particularly-astute players to discover. To this point, the game is perfectly content to allow even entire portions of the game world to be passed right by if a player doesn't happen to stumble upon them by chance (or by wiki).
Level design (for as much as "levels" exist at all in this game) is another area in which Dark Souls stands head-and-shoulders above the competition. Whereas many games seem to be satisfied with horizontal expanses of isolated chunks of content, Dark Souls has crafted an intricately-interconnected and startlingly-vertical world. During the course of my own playthrough, it was not uncommon for me to be suddenly taken aback at the realization that the passage I had just discovered had opened up an alternative route back to a previously-visited location, often in a surprising and pleasantly unexpected way.
Enemy design is varied and interesting. Few games have so effectively inspired within me such a mixture of wonder, awe, and intimidation as this game has with its enemies, especially with its area bosses. Combine this with the fact that each boss has its own dedicated (and often hauntingly-beautiful) audio track playing in the background as you take them on, and boss fights tend to be as mesmerizing as they are terrifying.
The way that Dark Souls implements its multiplayer is particularly interesting. Rather than a discrete mode of play, multiplayer is integrated directly into the core game. Players broadcast messages to the greater community by placing them into the environment, like graffiti on a wall. Through certain actions, with the aid of specific items, a player may even find themselves directly crossing paths with other players themselves (for better, or for worse), without even leaving their own play session. As far as I'm aware, all of this is (or at least was at one point) completely unique to Dark Souls.
Now, because I feel as though I've done nothing but gush about this game since my fingers hit the keyboard, I must note that there are, of course, flaws. As I mentioned, there are a few encounters in this game that feel rushed and cheap, and some that feel as though they would be more at home in a "high-octane" action-adventure game. A number of enemies are obvious near-carbon copies of one another with differing coats of paint. Some latter segments of the game suffer from level design that just doesn't stand up to what you've come to expect of it by those points. While the game's systems are generally refreshingly hands-off with regards to mechanical indoctrination, they can at times feel unnecessarily opaque, to the point where you'll be tempted to keep your web browser open to the Dark Souls wiki in the background while you play.
Finally, because no Dark Souls PC review would be complete without this mention, some light third-party modding is borderline-necessary here. The ubiquitous DSFix is such for a reason, as the game constitutes a pretty lackluster PC port. Frame rate improvements, a wider array of video resolutions, and a number of other graphical and performance-related options are likely to add immensely to one's enjoyment of this fantastic game.
What else can I say about this game? What else has already been said a thousand times over? If this game sounds at all intriguing to you, especially if you're somebody who has shied away due to its menacing persona, I'd urge you to try it anyway. With a bit of "can do" attitude, you may surprise yourself at your ability to push through a steep learning curve to uncover an experience that makes you feel rewarded in ways that most other games seem almost afraid to do. Play this game, and you may find that most other games just don't
do it for you anymore.
If you've found yourself on-the-fence about purchasing, give Dark Souls a fair shot - believe it or not, it'll do the same for you.
To anybody who enjoyed this review, consider checking out the following commentary video by Matthewmatosis. It's six-and-a-half hours long, but I found it quite informative and insightful, and it inspired my own review pretty heavily. If you're a big Dark Souls fan like myself, you might find it time well-spent.

I've been saving up for this game for a long time and honestly, even if there are some bugs and visual glitches, I still absolutely love it.
Cons first:
Once in a while the screen will shift to the side so much that another window of other scene appears (and the scene is also iteractable), tho I heard that this will be fixed in future updates. The default movements of characters while not walking are a bit choppy, but I guess that could be the style of the game.
And that's it, I didn't notice any other bugs, probably because I was too busy admiring the artwork.
First of all, ARTWORK. Man, the backgrounds, the animations, y e s. I would spend like 10 minutes just staring at the backgrounds, admiring the beautiful art. And then clicking furiously on everything with everything to get every single text box I can get. The humour of the game is also yes, very much like Homestuck, forced me to take out my translator app sometimes because it uses SO MUCH fancy words. Especially Jude. Jude's talking through walkie talkie kinda annoyed me.
Music. Oh god, the music. Every single piece I heard in this game is beautiful. Toby Fox and James Roach did an amazing job. My favourite was Xefros' theme Rustblood, a.k.a. WHERE THE ♥♥♥♥ ARE THE TREATS. Can't wait to arrange the song to piano.
Moving on. Strife scenes. They are a bit tricky, but I really enjoyed the generic Homestuck Strife texts after every attack. I loved that you needed to use stuff in your sylladex to win the fights. Rip bat monster, you will not be missed as you ate poor Frohiko.
The animations are really fluid and beautifully drawn. The "The Door is Open" animation is amazing. The facial expressions of the characters are very funny and perfectly drawn as well. Man, this game's visual are great and I will proceed to talk about it for the rest of my life.
Moving to Alternia, I was happy to find out some more stuff about this world that Hussie has crafted for us over the years. The violent nature of trolls never fails to amuse me. As Xefros kept talking about his moirail Dammek, who was probably sucked in to the cherub portal at the same time as Jude, I started to grow fond of this little sweet cinnamon roll Xefros and kinda feel bad for the boy, because his moirail was clearly using him? Let Jude kick Dammek's♥♥♥♥♥later for that please.
Where was I?
Discovered Alternian sports - Pusher ? I think? Later he referred to this sports as Arena Stickball so I dunno. Once again, morbid game: you win - cool, you lose - death. Like everything is in Alternia.
Also they have public transport which is great.
My favourite part about the Alternia part of gameplay was the ability to name Lususes. Lusi? I don't even know. I don't know why, but I got really excited when I got to pick a name for sloth Lusus.
Interactive walkie-talkie on Earth and trollian on Alternia was cool too. I wonder how will the real life dialogues go in the next Acts.
The personalities of the characters were also good. I feel like I know the characters as good as people I see everyday. Is that a good thing? Probably. Easier to write good fanfics :D
Man, I could go on and on about every single object in the game, but I'll spare you guys this time.

HIVESWAP is a well made point and click adventure game based on the Homestuck web comic. If you've read Homestuck, this is a great extension of the experience. You can totally play the game without having read Homestuck - it is not mandatory at all - and playing the game before reading Homestuck may actually be a good way to get into the series.
Currently, the game is very short, and has few actual puzzles. Thankfully, the price of the game is set at a point where that does not prevent me from recommending the game. Going into this game I was afraid it would be the same ol’ generic open world game that seem to be the trend these days (at least when this game came out back in 2014), but, to my surprise, Shadow of Mordor nails down the size of the world. It’s just the right size. Not too big and empty and not too small to make it a hub-game, like for say Deus Ex: Human Revolution. So traveling from one side of the map to the other doesn’t take long, but there is fast traveling nonetheless. Game also has a fair amount of collectibles to learn more about its lore.
The protagonist is your run-of-the-mill guy, nothing special about him, nothing makes him stand out. Story is nothing to write home about, another story about a guy getting revenge. No twists to keep you guessing, no real message behind it to make you think. But, that’s okay, because the meat and potato of this game is its gameplay.
While combat is technically speaking shamelessly ripped off from the Batman Arkham series, but with a slight twist from the usage of a Bow, which slows down time, Max Payne style, if you have the meter for it. If you played any Arkham game you know what you’re getting into. Press the button when you see it over the head of an enemy (or if he’s trying to swing at you if you turn it off), press 2 buttons to do various executions etc. Stealth is also extremely similar to how Arkham games handle stealth. Parkour is reminiscent of that from Assassin’s Creed. However, later on, you get to unlock an ability that will drastically change the way you go about things. Instead of killing the enemies, you then have the option to control them and make them obey you.
But the true enjoyment in the game comes from Nemesis System. Orcs or rather Uruks, all try to haunt you to climb up the ranks, but they will also fight amongst each other to take other’s positions and gain power. There are essentially 2 ranks in the game: Captains and Warchief, the latter being the highest rank in the game. The system is simply put: incredible. You could die to a random Uruk in the world, who then gets promoted to a Captain, you then could control him and make him start a war with a Warchief, aid him in the war and make him to the next Warchief and then finish him off. I was hanging on a ledge once, waiting for a Captain, who was also a bodyguard for a Warchief, and also weak to stealth takedowns, doing an execution, just as he executed he was just close enough for me to stealthily control him making him and his entire gang he commands mine.
The game seems to be very well optimized, loading times are short (though I did encounter once random situation where the game had to load for several seconds for some reason) and it has a fair amount of graphic options. Shadow of Mordor is a
game.

It's an interesting game to see how they've created an NPC rank system with the Uruks. However, it's mediocre combat system and storyline.
I spent about 3 hours or less to get the full experience of the gameplay. Masterminding the growth of certain Uruk leaders to only reap the rewards of their death later. Or planning out betrayals within the ranks with mindcontrol branding.
But as fun as this Uruk ranking system was, the novelty fades fast, and it's just grinding and trying to finish up the storyline, lore, etc. Took me roughly 17 hours to finish main storyline without rushing, and maybe double that for me to do a full completion run.
Combat skills and abilities doesn't really unfold well either. Abilities you unlock are only stronger and better versions of abilities you already have or applied to different enemies. So it's more of a vertical progression, rather than horizontal progression.
It's a bit hard to say if I recommend this or not...
If you're looking for a game to sink 100+ hours into with refreshing new content, then this isn't really that game.
But if you're looking for a quick game to just play on a weekend and be done with, then this is a good pick.

CoH: Eastern Front is a free expansion that adds a plethora of maps, balances, and 2 additional armies 1 per faction.
What I like:
-Armies: A soviet army is implemented in full force, serving the typial role you'd think of the army at the time. The Soviets feature a variety of cheap units to take over the field early but can hold their own late game with Strelky or guardsman infantry and the Tiger-rivaling IS-2 tank. All in all they are similar to the Amerians but have more complex nuance.
-The Ostheer are the new german army added to the axis faction. Unlike the "many-units-many-uses" doctrine of the Whermacht, the Ostheer have several versatile units but similar the former mentioned army, they require upgrades to advance into later game units.
Maps: Dozens of new maps, well designed, awesome.
What I don't like:
The soviets are too good, 1v1s against Ostheer result in usual consistent victory.  British have also been mysteriously removed from the game, I'm presuming because of balances, but why now after 3 or so years in the making? All in all the mod seems to be a lot of content but not a lot of polish, and acheivments don't work, fortunately the devs are constantly fixing stuff and invest a lot of time and passion which will hopefully be reflected in updates in the future.

Time to rewrite this old thing now since it's out of EA.  Let's start with an admittedly bad metaphor.
Imagine you see a food stand that makes sandwiches.  They have only one kind of sandwich, the 'Mystery Sub,' but it's promised to have the ingredients you like on it.  Specifically, pickles, butter, and white american cheese, with just a little bit of mayo.  It's also pretty cheap, so you order a sandwich.  You're told it'll be ready in five minutes.
Those five minutes go by, but still no sandwich.  So you go up and ask about it and the guy at the stand says he just started in the food service industry yesterday, and he misjudged how long it would take.  Since he's just starting out and he says it'll be the best sandwich ever, you decide to give him the benefit of the doubt and wait for a little while.
After half an hour of waiting, he finally gives you your sandwich.  You decide to open it to see what's in the 'best sandwich ever,' and you take a look at it.
Mayo.  Lots of mayo.  With one pickle, a big glob of butter, and half a piece of that awesome cheese you like all placed in different corners on the bread, covered in that white goop.  In other words, it's technically what you ordered, but it's not half as good as you expected it to be, and was given to you in much more time than you were told it was going to take originally.
Starbound is that sandwich.  It has everything they said it would have; exploration, building, even a few dark themes.  So technically everything they said it would be.  But there isn't nearly enough of that stuff, and mostly samey fetch quests and grinding.  The all-important story is shallow and derivative, with every quest pretty much being 'scan random crap, go though dungeon, kill boss.'  Rinse and repeat.
Over all, it's not a bad game.  It has plenty of stuff to keep you busy for a while, with tons of cosmetics and building items.  I would even say the building system is better and more fun than Terraria.  But there just isn't enough of everything else that would make it fun and unique; as the old saying goes, it's as wide as an ocean and as deep as a puddle.
There's plenty of bad stuff that happened in development; with the devs, with the missed release dates, and plenty of other problems.  I'm not going to go into it here; if you haven't heard of all the problems with the development and the devs themselves and are interested, you can look it up yourself.  God knows you'd get a better explanation from anyone other than me.
So I'll judge it on what it has in it now, not what happened in development in the past.  And for me, in it's current state it's a resounding 'meh.'  Good for one or two playthoughs, but you'll probably get bored of it before you even get to experience most of the main features.  I still haven't even tried the colony stuff, and I did very little farming after 1.0.  It's only fifteen bucks though, so if you think thirty or so hours is enough for that price, then go for it I guess.  Will you get as much play out of it as, say, Terraria though?  No, probably not.
I'm sure I've 'gotten my money's worth' out of it while it was in EA, but I still don't like the game much, so I'm giving it a negative review.  Maybe a 4 or 5 out of 10 for me.

As is, there are cool details in the game that make it neat, like the weather, deep foliage, etc. But when it comes to gameplay, it needs a lot of work. The combat system is clunky, guns have been super nerfed (a shotgun slug within 10 ft to the chest is only 25% dmg). You can craft some items but you have to find crafting guides, which give an objective but they are extremely rare on all the servers I've played. To date, I have only found 1 crafting guide. You have limited storage and unless you find the guide for a large storage, you can only make 1 ten slot storage box. Most of the time you're running around with good gear and will eventually get outgunned/outmanned unless you run in a group.
A pro is that the community seems to be fairly nice, but mainly as new spawns.
Base building is neat and a little different but is also clunky.
Overall, I don't recommend it because it's still clunky, there are hardly any mutants, and the game (for me) gets old fast.
It's about on par with the DayZ mod but once the newness wears off, youre still stuck with an alpha game that needs a lot of work still.
Kudos to the dev team for making good changes but I recommend buyers waiting a bit to make sure they continue the good changes and iron some of the kinks out. Otherwise, you'll be bored and irritated pretty quickly.

The three factions are unique in thier units, playstyles, and commander abilities. Ranked had bans on units and abilites both. If you feel like maybe there are some broken aspects of the game, they have that feature implemented which provides for some forced variety in ranked. I felt like the game was already very completed, that's why I was surprised when they brought it down.
If they still feel as though it needs work, than I am excited to see the finished product. I feel like it hit a nice sweet spot between casual and competitive. It's fun just making armies and watching them bash heads, with the minimal micro. But at the same time I feel like you do have to think quickly and adapt to your opponent at higher levels if you want to succeed.

Like many others, I suspect, PS3 game Demon's Souls smacked me upside the head around the turn of the decade after years of gaming complacency, and brought to mind many fondly remembered hours sat in front of 8 and 16 bit machines, learning by rote optimal routes through levels and the attack patterns of the brutal bosses at the end of them. Unlike those games, Demon's Souls had the technology to bring its artistic vision to vivid, decrepit, terrifying life and was always, absolutely, resolutely fair, despite its intimidating difficulty. I bounced off it, but the intrigue of its crumbling halls and the feeling of genuine elation at dispatching its eldritch horrors and reaching the next bonfire brought me back - and didn't let go 'til it was done.
Dark Souls is that game's spiritual successor - bigger, more refined mechanically, and more diverse in its environments, enemies, and ways in which to combat them. It's a long, slow crawl down into the pits of hell and back out again and despite some of the later areas feeling a little underdeveloped, you'll enjoy every minute of it through gnashed teeth and a steely, determined glare. The swordplay conveys a great sense of weight, with every weapon feeling a little different but equally deadly when mastered, and you'll want to do just that to see what lies down that next set of pitch-black stairs or within that ominous castle on the horizon.
Simply one of the best games I have ever played - the DLC keeps up the base game's quality too, if not exceeding it. A note, though - you'll want Durante's mods, and maybe a texture pack, to bring the PC port up to its potential.

Hussie and his crew have successfully turned this gigantic, beautiful spectacle of a webcomic into a game. Not surprising, really, as the webcomic was already in somewhat of a gaming format with its second-person perspective. But What Pumpkin Studios has really made their mark with their first installment of HIVESWAP. The animation and art is gorgeous, the story heartwarming and characters unique and lovable in their own way. The iconic, witty, and smart manner in which Andrew Hussie writes that is so prominently displayed in Homestuck has made its way here. Not to mention the deep meanings and themes either hidden between the lines or in plain sight; such as interactions and conflict between everyday people and big controlling corporations, modern-day technology used for the wrong purposes, mindsets of an alien planet compared to 1990s Earth, and rebellion and war.
What Pumpkin is going to make a lot of money with this series. There are likely to be many acts to come, and each act possibly being eight dollars? It is well deserved, though. I love this fandom, I love this franchise, and I can't wait for the installments to come. Well done, Hussie. You really put those 2.5 million bucks to work. Instead of wasting it on some ring for some fictitious scorpion chick.

This is a gem of a game that I highly recommend. I've had this in my library for a while but never properly played it until recently, and now I realise what a mistake that was. I'll start with the combat which is surprisingly good and satisfying, you gradually unlock a selection of melee and ranged weapons that are fun to use, and it's your choice whether you carry one of each or two of the same type, along with a shield and a special skill that consumes a tonic from your inventory with each use. Each weapon (including the shield) has a proving ground where you must complete a potentially difficult and fast paced challenge using the weapon to gain access to rewards, including materials to upgrade it or a first place prize of a special skill for that weapon. You can upgrade each weapon 5 times, with each upgrade tier allowing you to pick between one of two buffs to change the way the weapon performs, but these can be swapped around later. As you complete stages you can upgrade your home base and build up to six amenities, such as a distillery where you can customise your load out of permanent stat boosting "potions" (one can be carried per character level, up to 10), and a shrine where you can enable or disable idols that give you more xp and dropped currency at the cost of making enemies stronger or faster, making the game difficulty pretty dynamic. Top it all off with good level design, an interesting story and characters, and a well fitting soundtrack, and you have a very solid game.

The Swapper is a fascinating little puzzle game with just enough story to keep things interesting. The sci-fi horror setting fits it very well, and the ambiance contributes nicely: flickering lights keep things creepy and mysterious while you work your way forward, learning more with each dangerous step.
The story is told largely through discovering the background setup via text terminals, which I skimmed over in the beginning, but things spiraled out of control quickly and got intriguing enough that I went back and re-read all of them, which is something the game makes quite easy to do.
The key to making a
puzzle games is an appropriate level of escalating difficulty for the puzzles themselves. The Swapper did a great job of that, and most of the time if I was frustrated simply walking away and coming back with a fresh perspective some time later let me see the solution almost immediately. It's rare that a puzzle game gets that balance so right. Of course, there were innevitably a couple puzzles that I think required too much of a leap in logic. That's bound to happen with any game of sufficient length, so I'm not surprised, but I do think those few could've been better designed.
My only major complaint is about the achievements - it would've been nice for them to be tied to progression, but instead they're all hidden, and hidden exceptionally well. A very thorough explorer might find half during a play through, but I find it highly improbable that any one person would find all of them without a guide. They depend on invisible paths and fake walls without any clues to their location or even presence. They feel strangely obtuse and time consuming compared to the carefully thought out level and puzzle design present throughout the rest of the experience.
What limited voice acting exists is good. The soundtrack could have been the defining feature in a game like this, but instead it was sadly forgettable - a non-factor.
The Swapper isn't a totally amazing game, but it is quite good if you're looking for a story and puzzles that both make you think, even after you've quit the game.

If Facerig worked the way it was advertised... if...then I could see a lot of potential in it.
However, with the measly laptop I came to Steam with it wasn't going to happen. Was Facerig one of the reasons I decided to upgrade? Actually, it did factor in.
So, shiny new computer tower installed, widescreen monitor, webcam, microphone... everything was ready.
Facerig did not disappoint.
I was looking for something to create stories on for school, something the kids could take home or be sent to parents over social media, something a little more interesting than an audio recording and it hit that spot straight away.
So, I used it on and off until it came to organising a Halloween event for the school. With a little planning and a Skype setup, we arranged it so the students had a locked-room challenge, hosted by a Halloween monster (thanks to one of the DLC packs).
Sure, Skype support has been problematic lately, but that's Skype, not the software. Give yourself a half decent webcam, a decent lightsource and remember to keep your expressions animated and this will deliver the goods without fail. I've been following Starbound for a long time, and I absolutely love it. When Upbeat Giraffe came around, I wasn't really feeling the changes they made, what with the game becoming more linear and the removal of hunger (and a few other survival features). However, playing this version I feel like Chucklefish did everything right, and I'm also very glad to see that the hunger feature has been re-implemented. All in all, Starbound is still a top-notch game, and a must have for fans of pixel sandbox games.
PROS
-This gem is just about as gorgeous as pixel games can get, the artists have really out done themselves.
-Endless amount of galaxies to explore
-Build anything anywhere. Want to hollow out an astroid and build a science lab in it? Go for it. Wanna build a city on the moon? You got it! Want a nice little cabin on a lush forest planet? You can make it happen.
-Fun combat and interesting creatures.
-Lots of neat gadgets to use and weapons to suit your play-style.
-Just buy it.
Cons
-Some movement limitations are a bit annoying. The Dash tech isn't nearly as awesome as it used to be.
-I've noticed that the difficulty has gone down a bit compared to earlier versions. Perhaps it's just me, but it's something I thought I'd note.
-And finally, the biggest problem I have with this game will ALWAYS be how much of a pain it is to deal with having a decent light source when mining underground, because the ones given to you are awful in my opinion. Thankfully, there are mods to make it easier on yourself.
No game is perfect, but this one is pretty damn close! And with the current price, you can't go wrong. 9.5/10

Long read ahead.
I don't normally post game reviews, but felt compelled to make an exception. I was making an argument against PvE servers (more on this later), and received a permanent ban. Normally, I prefer to provide feedback on Steam games in person via forums, but that avenue has been closed to me, so I'll rely on this alternative.
First of all, how's the game itself?
It's not
bad, but if I were to sum it up with a title, it would be "H1Z1: Pre-Pre-Alpha Edition." It has a 36 player cap, runs on CryEngine, and is unable to support more than a few dozen entities in a ~25km² playable area. Speaking of the map, I
find it to be one of the game's high points. Unfortunately, this is where the "pros" list more or less ends.
I'll make this simple by going line-item with regard to what I believe to be the core concepts necessary to a survival game's integrity. You can decide for yourself whether these are done well or not, according to your own survival game experiences.
Nature is realistic enough (can actually hide in the bushes), but the (enterable) buildings are about as generic as they can be. It's pretty much a copy-paste job for a few "small home" types of buildings, a few shops, and a factory.
These perma-aggro on you if they spot you. They also die in about three swings from a melee weapon. You will encounter these less than a fifth of the time you encounter players on a full server; the engine simply can't support a decent amount of NPCs. There are also wolves, which interestingly enough try to distract you for others in the pack to strike from behind, but they tether and teleport back if you run about 300 meters.
By far one of the game's worst aspects, and something I brought up in the forums very often. Ammunition is
rare, which is
intended to mitigate player-killing. About 97% of what you find is food and clothing. In fact, food is trivialized to such an extent, that I'm not sure why it's in the game. Meanwhile, crafting materials are very rare, which brings me to...
Freeform base-building. Similar to other games, but you're not limited by structure part "latch" points. You can only build on a plot of land that you "claim" (one per server), and the structures are easy to break into, unless you use exploits to build in the air. The single most important aspect of base-building, storage, is trivialized because of
hoarding. You get to have one small box (8 slots) and one large box (never found the recipe) per server. That's it. As far as item crafting goes, the selection is
limited, and you'll rarely find what you want anyway. Example: there are 16 arrow/bolt recipes (making up 64% of all weapon recipes), but in the time I've played, I found arrows exactly
. Oh, and the inventory uses an outdated "slot" system.
The game runs...okay. That said, crashes are very common, and you will need to drop your settings to make the swings in frame rates tolerable. I had to drop shadows and AO on my stock GTX 980 just to not dip into the 30s all the time. Also, there are frequent lag-pauses, which is something that's
being addressed soon. There are some issues with getting stuck on geometry, and some "temporary" bugs, such as headshots not working.
The environment looks good, and the weather effects are nice, but outside of that, there's nothing that makes you really feel that you're "surviving," aside from the occasional encounters with other players, which, because of the low player cap, don't happen too often. And when they do, the players usually go their separate ways because no one is armed with a ranged weapon. The geared players, on the other hand, will almost always kill you, because the game lacks PvE content to such an extent that there's really nothing else they can do for fun. And because ammo is so rare, it's usually a very one-sided affair, as you can't reliably arm yourself with low-end ranged weapons until you've farmed for a while. You'll find guns, and you'll find ammo, but you'll rarely survive long enough to have matching sets. The few gunfights I've been in were against groups of 2-4 geared players when I at
had half a clip to fire. In their intention to combat mindless killing, the devs created a situation in which it's extremely difficult to deter better-geared players killing everything they see. In other games, it's easy to get some kind of pistol quickly, which, despite its inferiority, poses
danger to someone with a dope carbine.
Did I mention that nights are dark? They're
dark, to the point that you might as well be playing blind. If you have a glossy monitor and/or any kind of reflective glare, forget it. Fortunately for you, there's a fix: just turn up your driver gamma. But here's a quick anecdote with regard to that: when the devs were pressed as to why they don't balance the darkness a bit in the face of such a fix, they said that they didn't want to turn down the (let me paraphrase) "hardcore" darkness, because then they would essentially be "responsible for implementing a darkness-subverting exploit." That, and no one would be using the flashlight they put in the game. That's some logic right there.
Well, I feel that this has gone on long enough. I'd like to just touch up on what brought me here in the first place: the devs' treatment of the community. It appears to be, shall I say it, very "politically-correct." Disagreement is frowned upon, and rules are enforced arbitrarily. When I got in touch with a developer to inquire about my situation, he said he would look into it, and in a few minutes, blocked me without saying a word. It was pretty obvious that it was a matter of politics, and they just wanted to remove someone who publicly spoke about the game's issues (outlined here) instead of giving praise to meager iterations of progress. I know for a
that they didn't get rid of me to protect any of their "fans" from emotional harm. I was active for about three weeks, and during that time, I was pretty much the only one who logically addressed the game's issues, instead of either mindlessly praising or cursing it.
It was curious how they threw in "insulting developers" into the reason, considering I've done no such thing, and in fact wasn't even insulting the carebear advocates edging me on. Not a
cuss ever left my mouth. Of course they also ran the "remove all posts" toggle, so I can't prove it. Over twelve years and almost 11,000 posts, and this is the first game company to give me this sort of treatment. And I never expected
guys to do it, since I was advocating for
intent to create a survival game that's more hardcore than others on the market.
But in the end, if this game seems like a good investment (and I would've
still given it a thumbs-up if it was $6.99 or less, despite everything else), you have to ask yourself this: if you can't trust them to be honest with regard to how they treat their community members, can you trust them to deliver on the promises they're making with regard to their product? The game has been out for two years now, and I got it during the recent sale. It was in my wishlist during that entire time, and yet it doesn't feel much different from the videos I watched in 2014.

First off, this game is the very reason that cutscenes often catch flak today. In this game, they are literally five minutes long, often being slow and burning as much time as they can get away with. The first cutscene showed loads of action that the player is not allowed to participate in. The next one shows a space station breaking apart as slowly as possible, taking time to show off what is now laughably obsolete graphics. (Their attempts to show off their graphics are even more hilarious when strippers and cleavages appear.) In one cutscene, the character was warned against a danger that got him in the very same cutscene.
But enough about stupid cutscene/gameplay ratios, lets talk about the gameplay! Fairly early in the game, I met one of those stupid mandatory stealth sections where an enemy seeing one square inch of you results in an instant game over. The irritation there is enhanced by the game's complete lack of stealth mechanics. Not to mention that this section opened a plot hole; if the character is so valuable to his new owners, why are they so quick to murder him?
"What about the combat?" What about the combat! It's boring and irritating. It feels like you are playing counterstrike against an army of murderous bots, but with less strategy and worse gun mechanics. You die quickly, which would be fine if enemies didn't regularly spawn behind you. This game basically demands that you save scum through it.
All in all, Chaser promises a mediocre experience, but delivers far less than that.

So after playing through act one, I can confidently say that this game could become the next undertale, if it becomes mainstream, which I hope to god it doesnt because Im a damn hipster. However, this game is indeed downright AMAZING. It does a great job of incorporating references from the Homestuck webcomic, and the game itself is beautiful, graphicswise. Its humorous, story driven, and, to me, not being much of a point and click adventure type of person, was kinda challenging. The only downside to me is that you cannot physically lose any of the strife, or rather, battle, segments. However, I do believe this game was worth the wait. This is a must-own for any homestuck fan.

I'm a Homestuck fan, and have been waiting for this game to come out for quite some time, like most who have already played this. I was a little disappointed, but not shocked. I had a feeling that this game was going to be kind of a let-down from the trailers and screenshots.
It was fun for me to play, but mostly because I'm a fan and understood the references to the comic, which put a smile on my face. However, I wouldn't really recommend it to anyone who hasn't read Homestuck. To anyone else, it might seem very text-heavy, tedious, short and not that funny. I understand that the style of writing is in tribute to the comic, but maybe this didn't translate so well into a game. It made it boring. Also, I think having a hint button with no function is pointless, even if this was supposed to be a joke.
In summary, it was okay. But I would suggest waiting until the other acts come out to buy this.

I am going to make an adaptation of an reddit post I've made
Problems:
There are bugs. Which, leaving in account that this is an indie pc game is very normal. However, some stuff is really annoying, like cutscenes being skipped, and a resolution changing bug.
Most of the mid game cutscenes are just still images that change after one or two seconds. would not be too bad, bus most of the time there isn't a transitioning animation for the character before and after the cutscene, and some of the regular animations don't really interact withe the enviroment (I.E.: opening a door)
Joey opening doors animations annoys me. She should've interact with the door's handle. small nitpick but still
The puzzles are not challenging
It is Short. It can be divided in only two segments, and if you go running you can finish it in like an hour. Of course, that's normal for a point-and-click adventure game, since you usually have to interact with everything to extent it's time. but still, the game should have more playtime, speacially with the amount received with kickstarter money.
The good stuff:
The story. Nothing mind super blowing like the mid homestuck, but Honestly, it is probably because I know most of troll culture and have watched the trailers over and over again. It gives to me the same feeling I have with the initial acts of homestuck. If this indicates anything, Act 2 of hiveswap will be very good, like letters acts of the original work. It's a good introduction to both hiveswap and hauntswitch. It shows the protagonists of the games, the initial threats that they are fighting, the world(and house) they live in, and hints of other characters that will help or antagonize them. It has good potential, and I don't really like to criticize a story for it's beginning, the mid stuff is what matters. And a satisfying ending I guess.
Jokes: They are funny, and that's all I have to say on the matter
Music: I don't regret buying the album without knowing if the songs are good or bad.
Strife battles: They are all pretty nice, although there is a short amount of them
Characters: They are all lovely, and have all potential to grow, although if they do not in the following acts... they might look one-dimensional.
You can interact with everything with almost everything
You don't need to read homestuck to know what's happening. Everything  a new player won't know and need to know at the moment, the game will explain.
Neutral:
Animation:
They are good, however I wish there were more of them, especially in the middle of the game, the lack of transitioning between a character in the screen and a still image cutscene get's a bit annoying.
Dialogues: They are condesced in information and are funny sometimes. Although they can be a bit long.
Conclusion:
It's a good introduction, and if the following episodes expand on characters, lore and playtime it can be very good as a whole.
The price is a bit expensive for the size of the game, but might be worth it if the following acts are cheaper. like 4+ dollars cheaper
Now if you are a new player... even though I recommend this game you have to know that the game is around 3 hours, the following acts could get good or not. And you still will have to pay for them, are they going to be cheaper? What Pumpkin haven't given information on this yet. So, really think before buying.
I am going to rate this first act 7/10, 8/10 if the bugs are fixed. Going to update this in the next acts.

It bugged me that characters in a stressful situation were animated with smiles on their faces, I think a more neutral expression would appropriate at the very least.
I thought the play time was okay for episode 1. I think the price is okay for a single episode. Of course, I'm not young and broke anymore, so factor that in. I would normally wait for a sale on any game to be honest but I really wanted to support the community and buy this one at full price.
BUGS: I had one cut scene mysteriously not play, this is after it played once? I do not know why this happened, but it played the third time I tried it. Sometimes things appear off screen I think, but when you play in windowed mode, things look too pixellated (mainly the character). Sometimes the click areas felt needlessly tedious and off, especially descending the stairs in the Harley house. This game wouldn't run with my GTX 430 installed, I had to plug in my r9 290. Technically the lower card could've handled it, but it just wouldn't open. I saw people commenting in the community about this, so I thought I'd mention it because I think some compatibility issues might need sorting out.
Overall, it was a joy to play and I'm looking forward to the next act!

This is one of my favorite RPGs ever.
The pacing and variety in the combat, along with the scale of the action and world, make for a very interesting and fun game, especially compared to the more stiff combat seen in other fantasy RPGs like Skyrim.
For a simple example, you can scale and climb enemies in this game as well as use unique attack combos akin to hack and slash games. Thus, you can climb onto the wings of a dragon as it takes off into the air, creating an epic feeling battle.
The story is interesting enough to keep me invested, the combat and platforming are entertaining, and the amount of content in this game for the asking price is excellent.
I highly recommend this game to anybody looking for a great open world RPG.

Time to rewrite this old thing now since it's out of EA.  Let's start with an admittedly bad metaphor.
Imagine you see a food stand that makes sandwiches.  They have only one kind of sandwich, the 'Mystery Sub,' but it's promised to have the ingredients you like on it.  Specifically, pickles, butter, and white american cheese, with just a little bit of mayo.  It's also pretty cheap, so you order a sandwich.  You're told it'll be ready in five minutes.
Those five minutes go by, but still no sandwich.  So you go up and ask about it and the guy at the stand says he just started in the food service industry yesterday, and he misjudged how long it would take.  Since he's just starting out and he says it'll be the best sandwich ever, you decide to give him the benefit of the doubt and wait for a little while.
After half an hour of waiting, he finally gives you your sandwich.  You decide to open it to see what's in the 'best sandwich ever,' and you take a look at it.
Mayo.  Lots of mayo.  With one pickle, a big glob of butter, and half a piece of that awesome cheese you like all placed in different corners on the bread, covered in that white goop.  In other words, it's technically what you ordered, but it's not half as good as you expected it to be, and was given to you in much more time than you were told it was going to take originally.
Starbound is that sandwich.  It has everything they said it would have; exploration, building, even a few dark themes.  So technically everything they said it would be.  But there isn't nearly enough of that stuff, and mostly samey fetch quests and grinding.  The all-important story is shallow and derivative, with every quest pretty much being 'scan random crap, go though dungeon, kill boss.'  Rinse and repeat.
Over all, it's not a bad game.  It has plenty of stuff to keep you busy for a while, with tons of cosmetics and building items.  I would even say the building system is better and more fun than Terraria.  But there just isn't enough of everything else that would make it fun and unique; as the old saying goes, it's as wide as an ocean and as deep as a puddle.
There's plenty of bad stuff that happened in development; with the devs, with the missed release dates, and plenty of other problems.  I'm not going to go into it here; if you haven't heard of all the problems with the development and the devs themselves and are interested, you can look it up yourself.  God knows you'd get a better explanation from anyone other than me.
So I'll judge it on what it has in it now, not what happened in development in the past.  And for me, in it's current state it's a resounding 'meh.'  Good for one or two playthoughs, but you'll probably get bored of it before you even get to experience most of the main features.  I still haven't even tried the colony stuff, and I did very little farming after 1.0.  It's only fifteen bucks though, so if you think thirty or so hours is enough for that price, then go for it I guess.  Will you get as much play out of it as, say, Terraria though?  No, probably not.
I'm sure I've 'gotten my money's worth' out of it while it was in EA, but I still don't like the game much, so I'm giving it a negative review.  Maybe a 4 or 5 out of 10 for me.

If you're bored and need to be reminded why you have that crippling urge to kill yourself, Dark Souls hits the spot.

Much like Terraria, Starbound takes a new spin on a traditional grueling 2d routine of mining, refining, and crafting, with the option of either playing solo, or with friends. The game can be a bit slow paced at first, as the handheld matter manipulator takes a while to bust through tougher materials until you upgrade it, and even the weaker enemies can get the better of you before you’ve found the right rare resources to craft some half-decent gear.
If you are new, I highly recommend playing on Casual. The higher difficulties have you drop loot when you die which is very frustrating. Since this is one of those games where you can very easily die, especially if you're beneath the surface, dropping items just feels so anti-fun. I'm pretty sure I've seen jetpacks in this game, and I'd assume the feel of the game changes drastically once you can use a jetpack to save your♥♥♥♥♥if a monster hits you off a tiny ledge in a cavern. However, early on it's just pure frustrating.
Next, the missions/enemies you get, even early on certainly don't feel like they match the difficulty level I expected. Very first time going to a new planet as part of the tutorial, and a random NPC offers a mission. Pretty straight-forward "Kill a bandit" mission which I accepted. Little did I know that this bandit is damn near impossible to kill with my current gear. He fired rockets which did like 215 damage a hit, so he would always one hit kill me when I came close. I didn't even have a ranged weapon yet. I ended up having to abandon the very first side-quest I got because it just felt insanely unfair. I wish some scripted tutorial missions would give you set rewards of some upgraded armor and guarantee you have at least one ranged weapon. Maybe tone down some of the early enemies you see as well.
The combat system is decent, but I'm looking forward to more tweaks they could make. Just one example which is a bit frustrating are hammers. With a hammer, you need to hold the mouse button and you'll slowly raise the hammer over your head and you release to do damage. It feels a bit binary to me though. If I'm in a tight spot, why can't I just release the hammer when it's 50% full and do 50% damage? Instead it's either completely charged or you'll harmlessly lower your hammer. Lame. A nice change I read about, and I do appreciate is that when you damage an enemy you are briefly invulnerable to them. Supposedly this makes melee more viable, but I still feel like if you're up close to an enemy, you're going to have a bad time. That's why my preferences are with the chakram and spear. For true long range I have sort of a crappy pistol, but it does the job.
The inventory system is some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. I don't think there's really much else you can say about it. I hate that you can't directly use items from your inventory (such as food) but need to put it in your hand and then use it, and then put whatever actually useful item you had in that slot back. The game has some tabs it automatically puts things into, and so there's a lot of "Where the hell did that item just go?" feeling for a while. It highlights new items but the new item highlighting actually makes the icons very hard to see so you generally just need to hover over a bunch of them to get the tooltips. Having the option for a straight list with a scrollbar so I can see larger icons with item names would be great. Right now, the inventory just feels very compact when it could instead take up a larger amount of the screen for usability purposes.
Enemy designs so far seem pretty random. They have a nice variety of attacks and graphically have looked pretty different. It was cool going to a new planet and seeing all new enemies and NPC's. There is much room for improvment, but the game remains very diverse and expandable. There are a few things I would like to see added, without the need for mods/cheats. Items kept on death, more races, and a customizable difficulty. The client is buggy - continuously crashing, and you are unable to use mods on multiplayer unless both parties have mods. The game has potential, but currently there are a lot of problems that make the game un-fun or just tedious. As mentioned before, it suffers from lag in singleplayer, and crashed once for me. You have more options in decoration and base building, but the inventory management is so tedious. You need to go trough several menus to make basic items. For example to eat food, you need to open the inventory, move the food to the hot bar, and then use it, instead of just double clicking it or etc. Combat has potential, but it hampered by really stupid decisions. Some weapons have a fixed arc, so you can't hit enemies slightly under you. Fire arms use energy, so you can only shoot few times before you need to wait few seconds before shooting again. The game has randomly generated worlds, but they have some preset locations, so you can see the exact same mine, with the exact same npc's and rooms in two diffrent planets, which kills the immersion. Same thing goes to the "random quests". In the same village few npc's can give you the exact same quest. Overall I'm trying to give this game a fair chance, but I'm just not having fun. It has loads of potential, but it's hard to recommend it when you can play the more fun and polished terraria instead. On the other hand, I've been very impressed with the amount of content it seems to have. I did not enjoy this game. But for $15 I think this is definitely worth a purchase if you're a fan of survival games like Terraria.

There is this quiet before the storm. The sound of crunching snow beneath the feet of cold soldiers. A cough here, the clicks and clacks of MG42s being checked there. More artillery settles into place behind the pillboxes. Engineers slowly stretch springing barbed wire into place over the bodies of the last wave.
Through the quiet squeaks a sound. It is at first indistinct, and then suddenly unmistakable: the squeaking of tank treads, and on the right flank. Suddenly a Russian T-60 heaves into sight down the long main street of Stalingrad, and the first shot from its cannon booms out across the winter silence.
German guns explode in chorus, but their chorus is overpowered by the thunderous scream of countless Russian soldiers sprinting across the cold square. The engineers run, barbed wire half finished. The mortars pop, the artillery pounds, the machine guns rattle.
This is the third wave. If they break the line, the battle is surely lost.
In the distance, that battle is small to but one crew.
“King Tiger Reporting In.”
The Eastern Front Mod is one of those rare mods that just seems to be able to get everything right. So many mods have minor inconveniences one must overlook. Odd art here, a strange menu system there. Not so with the Eastern Front. They set forth to add two distinct, vanilla-quality factions to an already stellar game. In every single way, they succeed.
The Opposing Front expansion added new factions, new maps, and new game modes. The new game modes were a fine novelty, but quickly put aside to return to the meat of this RTS. If those new game modes were removed from Opposing Front, there would be almost no way to distinguish it, quality and content wise, from the Eastern Front mod.
Admittedly, I am more of an Allies player in all World War 2 games. The original Company of Heroes being no exception. As such, I am far more familiar with the Soviets than the Ostheer, the Axis’ added faction. I have fought against the Ostheer on many occasions, however, and can attest to the quality of their presentation and AI.
In short, the Eastern Front mod adds the Soviet and Ostheer factions to the game, along with a host of maps set in snowy Russia and neighboring areas. The mod is more or less feature-complete.
There is thankfully little to say beyond that simple review. Everything is as it should be in a mod like this. The factions look and sound exactly like they belong with the vanilla factions. The original factions are untouched, allowing the British and Soviets to fight side-by-side if you desire. The balance is spot on, with no one faction or tactic rising above the others to become dominant.  The new maps are of vanilla quality or better, with some unique terrain and layouts that encourage different strategies.
This is a mature mod which has been growing and improving for years, and the quality of every aspect is a testament to that. It is a mod that feels like an official expansion pack, allowing you to slide right back into the game unfazed.  The Soviets rely on masses of cheap units early, followed by guerilla tactics or powerful tanks later on.  The Ostheer, meanwhile, have access to unique units and defensive buildings that differentiate them significantly from the other two axis factions.
The AI of the original factions was given a boost to match that of the superior Soviet and Ostheer AIs.  Being a comp-stomper myself, this is a greatly welcome addition that makes the AI much more challenging and interesting.  I’ve noticed that all of the factions are more likely to build defensive structures now, which can make for exciting attack maneuvers.  They still won’t lay barbed wire or tank traps or anything like that, but at least pillboxes, trenches, and artillery is a big improvement over vanilla, where all 3 of those were virtually unseen.  They also don’t seem to spam single unit types, keeping a good mix into the late game.  In case all the new content wasn’t enough for you, the Eastern Front breathes new life into the old factions and maps as well with this new AI.
