It's great, quite frankly it's one of my favorite games of all time.
I've put more hours into the Binding of Isaac franchise than any other series. (My playtime isn't actually as stated, I've played a lot more offline and such)
There is a TON of variety in this game, you'll NEVER have the same run twice. There are hundreds upon hundreds of different items to pick up and experiment with.
Of course though, there are positives and negatives involved with such a huge amount of variety:
There are a lot of items that are just objectively bad and literally useless, which makes it a bummer at times to work hard for an item room/etc only to get "rewarded" with garbage.
There are also quite a few items that are ridiculously good. There are items in the game that make it an instant win if you aren't the worst player in the world.

Well, I don't really tend to write reviews for, like, anything. But this game here deserves this and much more.
I have to say that, being a Homestuck fan, I was really hyped waiting for it, but nevertheless, I will make this review as objective as possible.
It's an awesome first act for a point and click game. If you are a Homestuck fan like me, you're going to really enjoy playing this, looking into every detail and gasping at every reference or in-depth look at thing related to the webcomic.
Now, that doesn't mean that this game can't be enjoyed by people who doesn't know Homestuck, quite the opposite, indeed, the story is tailored in a way that no knowledge of the webcomic is needed to enjoy it. Sure, you'll miss part of the appeal of the game, but you won't have any "What? Am I supposed to know something?" moment while playing Hiveswap: Act 1.
Pros:
- A really nice and unique art style, with very fluid animations.
- A great soundtrack to enjoy every stage of the game.
- It's easy enough to assure you won't get frustrated by not knowing what to do to continue the story.
- The narration is very enjoyable, with humour everywhere, surely to make you feel like you are playing the likes of Monkey Island or Hollywood Monsters.
Cons:
- Maybe a little bit too easy, indeed. If you only enjoy point and clicks adventures that make you squeeze you brain out in order to solve an almost unsolvable puzzle, you're not going to enjoy this game, but hey! they point it out themselves, so...
- It is only the first act of a 4 acts series, so... Yeah, it really leaves you wanting more once you finish it, I'm not gonna lie. But well... It's only 8$, so it's a fair quantity of content for that price.
With all said, while I REALLY recommend this game to everyone who loves good humour and a great story, I must also say that, if you can, wait untill more acts are out, or have enough distractions at hand for when you finnish this one and find yourself craving for more Hiveswap.

If you love P&C games with good art and a ton of dialogue, then Hiveswap is for you.
The generous pricing model, to me, recouped the game's negatives which were: Sometimes frusterating navigation, a couple visual bugs, and even a single game-breaking bug.
Wish it didn't have those, but I was too busy having legitimate laughs to get hung up on it.
Soundtrack is on point as well.
Overall, I don't know how to recommend this to non-Homestuck fans. Even though the game is presented in a way that completely works for newcomers, a lot of the enjoyment I had was from being an already existing fan.
It's only $8 so, hey, it's worth a shot, right?

Being a big fan of Homestuck, I naturally backed this way back when it was first announced and had no name. All the trouble aside with Hussie being scammed out of his money in the production of this game, I have to say I was a little disappointed with just under 3 hours of content from the first act.
However, I do have to say, those were probably the best 3 hours I've had in a while. The dialogue is on point, the music is great and all the subtle hints to the Homestuck universe are fantastic. Overall, this is definitely for fans of the series, however it would probably be fun for anyone new to it as well. This is only one act, though, and there's 3 more to come from what I know, so we'll have to see what that holds, but so far I can say I'm absolutely into it.

You definitely don't need to have read homestuck in order to enjoy this game, but there are a lot of jokes and info that you will pick up on if you did end up reading the comic.  All in all, I recommend this to all those who read the comic, those who haven't but are willing to try it out, and those that just like point and click adventures.
One thing I will say though is that the first act is rather short if you just go ahead and try to progress, but seeing as how almost every combination of item has its own unique response, you can enjoy yourself experimenting to see what does what.
So yeah, I caved and bought

*Story so far and characters*
The story of act one is good but with a few flaws and tight strings.
"I felt like there could have been alot more character progression and more personel story for the protagonist of act 1"
*Gameplay*
The game progressively gets easier the longer you play since the game wont explain the basic's of the interfaces and possible scenarios where you can interact with surrounding objects using your items. Animations in cutscens are executed perfectly from Cuts and expressions of specific situations this includes [SPOILER) The mid battle sequence!

The game currently has a few bugs here and there but not something thats gamebreaking.

*Final word*
As a kickstarted game has this been a very well start.

-Gameplay is frustrating but very enjoyable after you "The player" learn the basic's!

Just to make a few things clear that most people have already make clear, but nonetheless: This game is in a VERY EARLY ALPHA. It is playable, and I enjoy doing the little quests and raiding some pirate ships (got balls m8?). It is difficult to write a concrete review complete with pros and cons as by the time somebody reads this, the features will have already been updated as the developer is CRAZY at work on this thing. That being said, I won't write many cons, as most the cons are either bug related and should go in the forums, or are planned to be fixed in the future.
So, some things I really liked are that the controls are relatively simple to pick up. They are really similar to the controls in StarMade, except MUCH easier and smoother. The weapon section in the market isn't implemented yet, but you still have 3 weapons to start with, excluding a mining laser. There is a short range rapid fire laser, a mid-range slower firing laser, and a long range and powerful sniping laser (I find it effective at taking out pirate ships from a distance).
Some things I didn't like (these do not include the bugs or things that I am aware of that are being worked on) is how every life you lose just seems disposable. Unless you bought a ship, dying just doesn't have that big of a consequence that I can feel. And speaking of the ships, whenever you die, the ship you are piloting (excluding the default ship) is removed permanently from your possession until you buy another one. This almost makes the entire idea of buying ships rather redundant in my opinion. If i grind for something, I'd like to keep it. I don't know, maybe there are some fans of systems like that found in Realm of the Mad God, where a death resets your character, but I am not one of them.
Other than that, I had, and plan to have, fun with this game in the future. Community is a little small but really die hard and passionate for the game, and the developer 10x that. Bastion is a small, stylish game that combines art, gameplay, and story in a unique manner to create what many consider to be a special experience. I think that in 2011, the idea of these cool, low-price indie titles still held some novelty, and a game like Bastion had a chance to stand out as something unique and cool. In 2017, the idea of a unique indie title providing gameplay, art, and story at a high level is not foreign to us. Many people now consider independent games to be capable of providing experiences that are as enjoyable as, or in some cases, more enjoyable than many AAA releases.
This is a game that has been in my backlog ever since it released in 2011. For whatever reason, I only ever got around to playing it recently. I very much enjoyed the game, and I would certainly recommend it to anyone. However, I think that I missed the time where I could find my experience to be particularly "special". I have played so many good games over the past few years, some of which have been smaller indie titles like Bastion. Bastion's unique style of storytelling, while certainly appreciated, does not carry the same weight as it might have before I had experienced games like Undertale, or other games that deliver intriguing narratives in atypical fashions.
I don't say any of this to knock Bastion; in fact, it is hard for me to think of any particular negative that I could write while reviewing the game. It is an all around good, enjoyable experience that should certainly be played by anyone who is interested in it. My recommendation is simply to set your expectations with the knowledge that this game might not surprise you like it did to so many of the people who may have recommended this game to you.
Bastion played a role in showing us what independent single player games can be, and by doing its part in driving the indie game scene forward, it has raised the expectations of the average gamer in such a way that Bastion is no longer a single standout game, but is instead one of many great games created by independent developers.

My expectations were pretty average when I initially bought the game, which kinda worked in my favour because they were immediately blown away by this spectacular game.
The first feature that caught my eye was the game's narrator; one of the best narrators I've ever heard/seen, right up there with the likes of Glados and Stanley Parable's narrator. Want a reactive but friendly narrator, with a bit of humor here and there? Want to feel like your journey is being narrated by a wise and calm sage? The Stranger's the right man for you. The only problem I had with him is that he only tells one story for each character in Who Knows Where (basically the game's arena) and repeats it every time you return there. It gets dull and repetitive pretty quickly if you try to farm in the arenas. Would've been nice if he had more things to say.
Then there's the breathtaking visuals and atmosphere. This game is unique in that the world literally builds itself piece by piece as you explore it; it really cements the fantasy-feel of the world. The artistic visuals look great as well. The game manages to strike a balance between colorful and welcoming visuals as well as dark and somber environments that together create a post-apocalyptic-yet-still-alive world. This game is a testament that you don't need realistic graphics to make a game beautiful.
Next is the gameplay and combat itself. For the most part, it's basically a third person hack-n-slash bullet hell. The controls are smooth and give you a lot of control over your character, so no problems here. The combat is pretty interesting; you get to choose two out of 10+ weapons to fight with (along with a shield for defense), and each of them are unique enough to have their own playstyle. You can also equip one skill to aid you in battle, most of which deal tons of damage, though others have certain functions as well (such as immobilizing enemies). Altogether, there's ~50 possible weapon combinations (not including skills), As for the enemies, there's a pretty decent variety of them, though I frankly wished that there's more. Most of the enemies are basically variants of a single enemy, so it would've been nice if there were more unique enemies.
Last but not least, the story. It's beautiful. The narrator did a wonderful job telling it. I won't say no more as I might spoil some stuff that you should definitely experience for yourself instead. Still, I'll be honest,
Overall, I give the game a 9.5/10. The gameplay and fantasy setting reminds me a lot of Spiral Knights, so if you liked that game, you'll most likely enjoy Bastion as well. Otherwhise, I still highly recommend this game for those who are looking for a casual and story-driven ARPG.

I am not sure whether to say that this game got the small things right or the big things right.  I am sure, though, that I want to say that the things it got right made it a real joy to play.  If you've somehow missed it despite the hype, bundles, and practically free sales prices, do yourself a favor and get it now.
Let me rattle off the things the game gets right.  I think I can sum them up by saying that Bastion feels (and "feel" is the critical word here -- it is a sensory but also in-your-bones-and-heart FEELING) like a superior evolution of a SNES game.  As someone who holds SNES games as the pinnacle of unaffected gaming pleasure, this is almost as high a compliment as I can give.  Many games that try to conjure SNES (or NES) qualities are excessively "retro," but many games that tried to evolve SNES games took them in really different directions (polygonal graphics, a first-person perspective, cel animation, and so forth).  While the graphics are higher resolution, the music more orchestrated, the narrative delivered by voice over rather than straight text, all of these things nevertheless FEEL the same, only better.  I guess I would compare it to going from a console port of an arcade game to the arcade game itself.  The latter is richer, but the same.
This overall great feeling is complemented by marvelous voice work by Logan Cunningham.  I'm biased because he was the lead in our Primordia, but I loved him in Bastion first.  The lines he delivers are clever and lend narrative without bogging the game down in expository cutscenes.  This, too, evokes Zelda and other SNES-era console games.  The story has a melancholy quality is reinforced by every audiovisual element.
That should be enough to buy the game.
Still, I have some reservations, and I can't be sure whether these are the "big" things or the "small" things.  Ultimately, I don't think the gameplay loop is very fun.  It's ... fine.  The controls are tight, the enemies are fairly varied, there is a true abundance of weapon types (each significantly different), and all sorts of gear and special abilities to obtain and power up.  There are secrets, and secrets within secrets.  But still.  Something about the gameplay was off.  I *think* the problem was that it was just too easy.  While there are elaborate finesse moves and devilishly hidden powerups, button mashing with basic weapons is typically enough to carry the day, even in many of the game's reward challenges.  Because there is not much of a difficult gradient, I never felt like I was particularly getting *better.*  Occasionally I would detour for one of those reward challenges and, for that purpose and that purpose alone, hone some trick.  But unlike, say, Mario or Metroid or Contra, where you inevitably end the game a much better player than you began, in this case it was only by dint of deliberate and gratuitous effort that I improved.  The game's many grind-oriented progressions and endless "you have X of Y" achievements and rewards contributed to this feeling of a baroque facade around a basically drab edifice.
And yet this problem, which may sound fatal, is absolved by the "feeling" discussed earlier.  The game is such a pleasure to experience that whatever shortcomings I perceived (misperceived?) in the gameplay loop are ultimately irrelevant.  They may mean that Bastion isn't a game that draws me back eternally, as say Super Mario World does, but it remains a game I recommend wholeheartedly.

much of this review is not just about Attila, but a broad overview of the Total War series as a whole, roughly since Rome Total War, and the lack of any real advancement in terms of AI.
The game basically fixes a lot of the problems introduced by Rome 2, while adding some others.  The absolute best new feature is the ability to just flat out destroy a settlement completely from the map.  Unfortunately, it can be near instantly rebuilt by any faction that seeks to do so, exact same name and spot.
As well, nomads can temporarily settle their armies into camps and build buildings to improve income and food and such, then pick up and move and settle elsewhere.
The settlement mechanics are still a frustrating, confusing mess for me most of the time.  Oftentimes I end up with sudden food shortages out of nowhere with no clear cause.  Other times, there's certain things which don't make much sense (like the Rivalry penalty) which only seem to escalate over time or don't seem to go away.  Some of them (like the Civil War penalty) doesn't go away at all, even if you've ended it.
the main issue of the game is the same with almost all the other Total War games, in that as technology advances and the demands of a grand strategy game becomes more complex, more gameplay features are needed to replicate not just armies that go and fight, but the proper elements to support and maintain an army, balance income, grow a nation-state, and interact with other nation-states in a way other than destroying everything.  Each Total War game handled this in different ways but in this and Rome 2 more so than ever, it's all essentially bunk because the AI is completely DOA.
Attila's AI is nowhere near as completely dead as Rome 2's is/was, but the issue is still there; the AI is such that diplomacy is completely dead.  Getting things like trade agreements that last longer than a few years is a monumental task worthy of a Steam achievement.  Things like creating tributaries, vassal states and so on are basically just filler options in the diplomacy menu because the AI will basically never accept half the options unless ground down to a single settlement and no armies.
The amount of coding necessary to create a complex, reactive AI is a massive task, but can be effectively done, as in Paradox games like Crusader Kings 2 and Europa Universalis.  Countless different statuses, constants, gameplay mechanics, and commands dictate how AI factions react and relate, leading to situations where diplomacy not only matters, but can be a powerful tool to either maintain a status quo among AI powers, or to simply prevent the AI from behaving brainlessly and having City-State X with 2 settlements and 500 soldiers from randomly declaring war on Neo Roman Empire Z with 840 settlements and 2,000,000 soldiers.
the Total War series has implemented several gameplay restrictions to help enforce this sort of thing, like in Rome Total War where the three separate Roman factions (Houses) are completely forbidden from declaring war on each other until the Civil War mechanic is unlocked.  Shogun 2 had the same with the Shogunate.
Nothing like that appears to be in play in this game or Rome 2.  Considering the immense amount of money poured in to Rome 2 and Attila compared to prior Total War games, they basically did no work on the game itself beyond aesthetics and the most barebones "arcade" style combat mechanics, with lots of different "special moves" unlocked based on the generals' stats or experience.
This would've been fantastic for an arcade game, but when half the achievements and gameplay is based on playing through an entire campaign of hundreds of turns, this becomes a monotonous slog which makes it impossible to play more than an hour or so at a time, to where I find myself going out of my way to auto-resolve most battles just because I'm completely and utterly sick of playing out every single battle only to have the brain-dead AI come back with a fresh army the next turn or two, because the game explicitly cheats by giving bonuses and money to the AI to compensate for the fact that it's completely incapable of doing much of anything otherwise.
When I play a game like Crusader Kings 2, I feel an actual sense of the faction I choose and its culture, politics, society, religion, and military.  I can literally see the differences in race in the different faces, skin tones, clothing, and coloring of the vassals and courtiers I see and interact with.  I can see a full-blooded French king with decidedly Arabic features, and scroll back on his family line far back enough to see when his French father married a Bedouin princess.  In EU4, wars are not a default state of being, but affairs with clear goals in mind that can be negotiated over, with the AI actually seeming overjoyed when it's down 50% in war score with no clear path to even a stalemate and you come and offer a White Peace out of nowhere.
There's essentially none of that in Total War Attila.  The difference in historical setting means there's less variety in terms of cultures and military units (less Greek/Macedonians, Phoenicians, Semites, Latins, etc) when more than half the factions are basically Celtic or Germanic.  That's not the fault of the game, that's just the historical setting.  But the game does so little with the sameyness compared to CK2 that many of the factions have the exact same units and there's no real sense of difference between them.
With DLC releases, both Attila and CK2 extend their timelines and overlap with the Charlemagne campaigns.  In CK2, the Charlemagne startpoint feels like a wholely new, different period from the rest of the game, while remaining fundamentally exactly the same map, colors, UI, and units.  Total War Attila's Charlemagne campaign looks and feels exactly the same as Total War Attila's grand campaign, just with decidedly more Christians and Muslims and significantly less Tengrii.

Dark Souls, perhaps more than any other game on the market, is preceded by a reputation. From its ultra-imposing, ultra-intimidating bosses, to the alienating community mantra of "git gud", to the game's own subtitle of "Prepare To Die", the message seems clear: this game is hard, and you're going to die. A lot. The reality is, thankfully, quite a bit more complex than that. While Dark Souls seems destined to make an appearance on nearly every "most difficult games" list ever compiled, to place a disproportionate focus on some sort of perceived insatiable sadism is to sell the game far, far short of what it truly has on offer. Consider the whole picture, and it's little surprise that the Souls series has essentially spawned an entirely new subgenre unto its own.
At its core, Dark Souls is a game that demands to be respected. Every step you take, every swing of your sword, every swig of life-giving Estus is subject to an assessment of risk. New players quickly learn that while sharp reflexes don't hurt, it's caution, calculation, and preparation that make the difference between "VICTORY ACHIEVED" and the infamous "YOU DIED". Button-mashing and face-rolling will only see you sent back to the last bonfire, but with a bit of patience and a cool head you'll realize that towering demons and seven-headed serpents aren't quite so scary after all.
For as much respect as this game requires of the player, it returns it in kind. Save for a select portion or two of the game where it seems to momentarily forget that it's not actually part of the Uncharted series, fights are fair and frustration is shockingly minimal. While I won't go so far as to suggest that "no death is ever the game's fault", I will say that this game emanates a general ethos of measured punishment. Believe it or not, Dark Souls honestly
want you to succeed. It goes to great lengths to ensure that with enough observation, adaptation, and perseverance you will always have at your disposal every tool necessary to do so, even when your situation initially looks hopeless.
In addition to its punishing-yet-rewarding gameplay, there really is a lot to love about Dark Souls. For a game of few conversations and fewer cutscenes, its lore is surprisingly deep. While some exposition does exist as a more direct means of world-building, much of it must be pieced together through a combination of lore-bearing items and reasonable inferences made about the world around you. Much of the game follows a similar philosophy of content delivery, where there is always something new for particularly-astute players to discover. To this point, the game is perfectly content to allow even entire portions of the game world to be passed right by if a player doesn't happen to stumble upon them by chance (or by wiki).
Level design (for as much as "levels" exist at all in this game) is another area in which Dark Souls stands head-and-shoulders above the competition. Whereas many games seem to be satisfied with horizontal expanses of isolated chunks of content, Dark Souls has crafted an intricately-interconnected and startlingly-vertical world. During the course of my own playthrough, it was not uncommon for me to be suddenly taken aback at the realization that the passage I had just discovered had opened up an alternative route back to a previously-visited location, often in a surprising and pleasantly unexpected way.
Enemy design is varied and interesting. Few games have so effectively inspired within me such a mixture of wonder, awe, and intimidation as this game has with its enemies, especially with its area bosses. Combine this with the fact that each boss has its own dedicated (and often hauntingly-beautiful) audio track playing in the background as you take them on, and boss fights tend to be as mesmerizing as they are terrifying.
The way that Dark Souls implements its multiplayer is particularly interesting. Rather than a discrete mode of play, multiplayer is integrated directly into the core game. Players broadcast messages to the greater community by placing them into the environment, like graffiti on a wall. Through certain actions, with the aid of specific items, a player may even find themselves directly crossing paths with other players themselves (for better, or for worse), without even leaving their own play session. As far as I'm aware, all of this is (or at least was at one point) completely unique to Dark Souls.
Now, because I feel as though I've done nothing but gush about this game since my fingers hit the keyboard, I must note that there are, of course, flaws. As I mentioned, there are a few encounters in this game that feel rushed and cheap, and some that feel as though they would be more at home in a "high-octane" action-adventure game. A number of enemies are obvious near-carbon copies of one another with differing coats of paint. Some latter segments of the game suffer from level design that just doesn't stand up to what you've come to expect of it by those points. While the game's systems are generally refreshingly hands-off with regards to mechanical indoctrination, they can at times feel unnecessarily opaque, to the point where you'll be tempted to keep your web browser open to the Dark Souls wiki in the background while you play.
Finally, because no Dark Souls PC review would be complete without this mention, some light third-party modding is borderline-necessary here. The ubiquitous DSFix is such for a reason, as the game constitutes a pretty lackluster PC port. Frame rate improvements, a wider array of video resolutions, and a number of other graphical and performance-related options are likely to add immensely to one's enjoyment of this fantastic game.
What else can I say about this game? What else has already been said a thousand times over? If this game sounds at all intriguing to you, especially if you're somebody who has shied away due to its menacing persona, I'd urge you to try it anyway. With a bit of "can do" attitude, you may surprise yourself at your ability to push through a steep learning curve to uncover an experience that makes you feel rewarded in ways that most other games seem almost afraid to do. Play this game, and you may find that most other games just don't
do it for you anymore.
If you've found yourself on-the-fence about purchasing, give Dark Souls a fair shot - believe it or not, it'll do the same for you.
To anybody who enjoyed this review, consider checking out the following commentary video by Matthewmatosis. It's six-and-a-half hours long, but I found it quite informative and insightful, and it inspired my own review pretty heavily. If you're a big Dark Souls fan like myself, you might find it time well-spent.

Truly a great spiritual successor to Baldur's Gate and Icewind Dale (and beloved Planescape Torment as well). Scenery is beautiful, character models fit in nicely (and have some nice animations), the ruleset takes something old and something new and makes for and interesting yet familiar experience. Writing in general seems sold enough, although some of the voice acting distracts because it's simply pretty bad. But the dialog allows for enough roleplaying opportunities, and it's nice that many stats of your character, not only primary stats and race but also history and religion, play a role in conversations. The combat can be challenging sometimes and requires some tactical positioning and use of abilities: sometimes my party died, but after reloading and doing things a bit different I came out victorious, which plainly proves that strategies matter!
One caveat however: the game is pretty buggy at the moment. (UPDATE - yay it's patched!) And these are not bugs like "character fell through scenery, reload is required", they are of the worse savegame damaging kind. And one point I could not reenter a certain map without crashing the game, which required some editting of the savegame file to fix. Also, my character has lost it's ability to equip a third weapon set for some reason... very annoying, but I guess these issues will be fixed in the following months, so I will still recommend this game. Just be wary, use save often and use multiple files, and you will be good.

Dark Souls easily gave me the most unique and indescribable gaming experience I have ever had. Yeah, you're going to die a million times but it will never be the game's fault, you will learn from every mistake you made. Dark Souls teaches you by its gameplay and not by its non-existant casual tutorials. Dying is not a frustrating thing in this journey, but the essence which makes this game so unique and outstanding. Sometimes you will get punished so hard even after you died, but you'll just want to keep playing. The gameplay is so simple at first glance, but in fact, it's deeper than the depression I felt in when I got cursed by those freaking frogs. I just can't tell how many secrets the game has, it's mind-blowing. And jeez, that level design... I have NEVER seen such genial, fluid and complex level design in any game, EVER, and at the same time it's so easy to memorize every inch of Lordran's amazing world. This universe is vital and thanks to its amazing community, Dark Souls is still a living, full of life experience.
After all, I thought I've seen everything in the gaming industry, then I did give a try to this masterpiece. Dark Souls is easily the best *game* I have played in my life and I only saw the tip of its nearly heightless iceberg.
10/10, would lose my soul(s) again.

Solid effort all the way around.  If you're a fan of the original Infinity Engine games or RPGs in general I recommend checking out PIllars of Eternity.  Enjoyed the experience all the way around.
It's a great game, I give it 92 out of 100.  Many of the issues I had playing through at launch have been addresses making this a well rounded experience, one of the best in it's genre.
Technically the game is very sound, never crashed on me, load times were a tad long at times but bearable.
(NOTE: Very light spoilers ahead)
Some random commentary on my experience:
- The use of voice overs in many conversations was very welcome, however the text itself was often written with descriptives ("soandso stares off into the distance, "blah blah").  So it was cumbersome to read along with the VO when the text was interspersed with these extra descriptives that were not in the VO script.  I wish the VO was a bit better integrated so that this wasn't an issue.  I'd end up listening to the VO then going back and re-reading the whole passage over again.
- I thought the NPC companions were decent, however I never did really feel an attachment to any of them.  Even once I started completing their quest lines I was left with a feeling of 'meh'.  Decisions I made with/for them didn't seem to have significant impacts on the characters themselves or the world.  Often I felt their writing (and some other areas of the game) was trying to be too sophisticated for it's own good and in the end left me feeling uncertain exactly what my party members believed or what was happening in the world.  I think it'd be better served if the storylines for your party members wrapped up towards the middle of the story instead of towards the end so that then the party members would have significant game time to live/act out the resolution of their quest lines within the story instead of ended up as minor sideshows compared to the larger story elements coming to a conclusion.
- My main character was a barbarian - barbarians seem to start off very weak.  I ended up having to micromangage the early battles until I reached level 5-6 where barbarians begin to shine.  Afterwhich micromanagement came down to boss level fights.
- Pathfinding in combat is wonky, sometimes my melee characters couldn't navigate around monsters w/o having to be handled manually.  This works both ways, difficult encounters can be made significantly easier by usage of +movement items and littering the field with summonable creatures making it harder for monsters to get at your squishy party members.
- The game does make a special autosave right before the 'point of no return' at the end of the game.  There is no continuing to play the game after it's beaten, you have to go back to this save if you wish to continue finishing up quests/content.
- This review, written shortly after launch, was originally ~twice this length, but the majority of sore points have been addressed!!  Bravo developers!

While I think I got my 1€ worth out of this game, Chaser can simply not be recommended. The shooting and the movement have the right feel to it. The music has the right ring to it. You even have a decent plot line with lots of skippable cutscenes. The maps are huge and range from cities and skyscrapers to space stations. Even the graphics are good enough for a game from it´s era. Sadly these things are not enough as Chaser has some *serious* flaws.
When a map starts, you don't have any enemies anywhere. Instead they get spawned each time you hit a preset location. At best this can mean enemies spawning to a room you just cleared a few seconds ago. Naturally these spawns make no sounds so you will simply have an enemy taking a free shot at you from behind. Very annoying.
The other major annoyance relates to the huge maps. Sometimes you have no clue where you are supposed to go or what on earth you are supposed to do. At least 1/4 of my gameplay time was simply running around checking which door can be opened in order to go forward. The best indicator of being on the right track is that enemies are still spawning around you. Otherwise you need to start guessing. To make this worse, it is possible to get stuck in some maps after which you are forced to restart the map. You can also get stuck in a lot of textures. Mostly this is just a minor annoyance cured by hitting your jump key a few times. Sometimes this means going for your last save. If you have no quick saves, this means restarting the map.
Chaser claims to have "Highly developed AI". In practice this means that AI always knows your exact position aiming at you in advance. Enemies don't always run straight to you though so I guess we need to give some credit for that. Instead they try to do some sort of flanking manouvers. The enemy also knows when you reload and will atempt to attack you during these moments. In other words you can sometimes draw enemies from cover by simply reloading your weapon. The AI always aims at your torso even when it is behind a cover. This made some fights quite hilarious. Another hilarious thing relates to scoped weapons. They make more damage with the same bullets when you have your scope on. Very logical.
To wrap it up, Chaser has some enjoyable moments but they are wrecked by aimless searching and enemies spawning from thin air. Add a few crashes with no autosaves and you will be feeling great for actually paying to play this game. Good thing it only cost me a few dota items. I'd give it a 6 ½ / 10.

As somebody who has had zero prior experience with anything Lord of the Rings related, I am very happy to say how pleasantly surprised I was with Middle-earth: Shadow of Mordor.
OVERALL RATING: 8/10
Gameplay:
The game controls wonderfully. The combat is like the Batman Arkham games, with some Assassin's Creed thrown in. Speaking of which, I see this game compared to Assassin's Creed very often, and I have to say; I only really see that in the stealth. You can sneak around and stealth kill an enemy, and it's oh so satisfying to take out an entire camp using only stealth kills and not being detected.
Story:
I honestly didn't really find the story very good, but it wasn't outright terrible. One word I can describe it as is forgettable. There's really nothing memorable here in the story department.
Graphics:
This game looks very very nice, no matter what settings you play it on. Even on low settings, the game manages to look fairly decent, and it looks even better once you bump things up to higher values. Shadow of Mordor with everything turned up to the maximum settings is truly a sight to behold.
Music:
Much like the story, the music is forgettable. Not a single track that I can distinctly remember, which is a shame really, because of how great everything else is.
Replayability:
This game is one that I can play over and over again and not get bored. The combat is so much fun to play and the stealth mechanics are well implemented. Jumping off of your tower when you spawn, brutally killing something nearby, and then immediately following up with an arrow to the head of a fleeing foe is a great experience to be had.
---Conclusion---
Middle-earth: Shadow of Mordor is something many other games nowadays fail to be: fun. Just fun. I love this game, and I think many others will too. If you're looking for a game to waste a ton of hours with, pick this game up. You will not be disappointed.

This will be a slightly unconventional review, in the sense that I won't be reviewing this game "in vacuum" (ie. independently of any outside factors), but instead I'll be reviewing it in relation and comparison to another game, The Talos Principle. It might seem silly and wrong to write such a review but there is a very strong reason to do so, for the two games have a lot in common, target the same audience and came out a mere one year apart from one another - I'd even go as far as to call them sister games. It could very easily be argued that both were trying to achieve sort of the same thing around the same time, therefore it'd be fair to compare them. That said, I'll try to assume zero knowledge of The Talos Principle on behalf of the reader, so that even if you haven't played TTP yet, you'll still be able to glean some useful information from this review.
Also, this is gonna be a long one, so if you need a TL;DR, I'll give it to you right here:
(as much as it makes me feel like an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to say "X is better" on an otherwise positive review of game Y)
So let's get started with the similarities first. The Swapper and TTP are both puzzle games, that much you've probably figured out already. They also both lie on the harder side of the spectrum, which I'm sure you'll be happy to hear (cause who wants to waste their time on weak puzzles, am I right?) But they're also both puzzle games with an underlying story - and it just so happens that The Swapper and The Talos Principle share one writer, Tom Jubert; he is the sole writer of The Swapper, on TTP he is joined by Jonas Kyratzes. The writer link is no mere triviality, for it explains the most prominent similarity between the two games; namely, an underlying narrative that touches on areas of cognitive science and philosophy of the mind. I admit that I'm a sucker for those subjects, and I'm happy to say that the writing on both games does them justice. Following the story isn't necessary for beating either game (at least it won't give you any hints on how to solve any puzzle), but you're strongly advised not to skip it, for it would be akin to throwing a ball of ice-cream in the garbage just to eat the cone that came with it. Other similarities include beautiful visuals and music, a set-in-the-future environment and a subtle feeling of being desperately alone.
So what are the differences between the two and why is The Swapper not as good as TTP? Well, for one thing, The Swapper is considerably shorter. I beat it in about 7 hours, and I'm nowhere near an expert puzzle-solver. There are some hidden terminals that you can find to unlock some achievements (which I've done as well), but other than that, there's not much replayability. Meanwhile, I've already clocked in 50 hours on TTP, I'm still not 100% done with it, and I know I'm gonna replay the whole game from scratch at some point, just to discover all sorts of easter eggs and hidden messages that I missed on the first playthrough.
Another grievance I have about The Swapper is that it's one of those puzzle games where figuring out what you have to do in order to solve a puzzle is not always enough. Sometimes you'll find yourself stuck on a level just because you have to fine-tune distances between clones, jumps, buttton presses etc until you get the desired result. It's just a cheap way to make a puzzle game harder than it really is IMHO. Maybe that's just me, but I enjoy playing puzzle games for the "figuring out what to do" factor, not for the "repeatedly trying to perform all the maneuvers right" one. YMMV.
But perhaps the Swapper's greatest weakness is that the story is not that well-woven into the game itself. I can't quite explain why without spoiling huge sections of the game, but suffice to say, it feels like the writer and the developers weren't working together as closely as they should while the game was being developed. It's a shame because the story is great, the game itself is pretty damn good, but the two don't form as much of a cohesive whole as I'd wish. That's not the case with TTP; you can tell that Croteam did a much better job communicating with the writers than Facepalm Games did.
So, in conclusion: Do I recommend this game despite its shortcomings? Absolutely. It may have its flaws but I still enjoyed it a great deal. That said, if you've already played The Talos Principle, you just might find this one just a tad bit underwhelming. To put it in terms of scores, I'd give TTP a 9.5 (though, honestly, sometimes it feels like a perfect 10) and The Swapper would get a 7.5, maybe 8.
PS and side note: I played The Swapper right after beating the main story in TTP, almost back to back, but I had no idea that I was getting into a game with that many similarities to the one I just finished (nor did I know about the common writer link, for that matter). Talk about a coincidence! Now I'm planning to play every other game these two writers have worked on.

The Swapper is a dark, atmospheric puzzler with a strong science fiction narrative that often delves into philosophical musings on life and identity. The game has many similarities to other games like Portal or QUBE (puzzle-solving gun, voiceovers, and a mysterious facility) as well as Braid (sidescrolling puzzler with a gimmick), but also takes many tonal cues from famous science fiction like Alien or Blade Runner. Putting these elements together, however, creates a unique story and atmosphere unlike anything else I've ever seen. This is certainly one of those games that'll stick with you long after you've finished playing it.

First, remember that this is Early Access.  It's not complete, it crashes, it has exploits, it has bugs, it has issues.  If you don't want to help make it better or want to spend you hard earned money on a finished product, don't buy this game.
Also know that this game has everything going against it.  A failed kickstarter, a single developer, and a game engine most people haven't heard of.  This is reason enough to simply avoid buying it.  I took a chance on it after hearing how involved the developer was - and every review that points this out is absolutely correct.  Dex is on ALL.  THE.  TIME.
If you want to see the developer ACTIVELY engaging players every day, getting feedback, revealing the short and long term plans, the ideas put into the game, then this is what you want.  Dex is super involved and the community is supportive of new players.  He has a Herculean work ethic, and that is why I'm glad to have bought the game - to support a developer who is passionate and consistent.
As for the game itself, there isn't a lot to do.  Blow up pirates, their hideouts, mine, PVP, complete missions, and explore around.  Only 2 tiers of spaceships are available at this time.  Combat feels soft, mining requires flying over chunks of asteroid to pick them up, and there's no customization to anything.  The list is long and changing all the time.
It's getting better, it's growing fast, and it's going to be a great product.  Get in now and help!

After 3 years of owning this game I finally buckled down and finished it, and man am i glad i did. I was initally hooked by the tight gameplay. This is a very story focused game so the majority of gameplay is very well designed dialogue trees punctuated by cover shooting. The dialogue trees a very intuitive: options that lead to exposition tend to be on the left and  and story advancing, and affecting choices tend to be on the right. The shooting mechanics are pretty simple, but passably enjoyable with the inclusion of biotic powers to add some stratagy to shake things up a bit.
As for the story of the game it is fantastic. The setting is a galactic community very reminicent of Star Wars with engaging intergalactic politics reminicent of the best of Star Trek & Babylon 5. In short an amazing sci-fi universe. What i like most in a story is the characters, and Mass Effect has some fantastic characters. My favorites being Liara, Garrus, Wrex, Joker, Captain Anderson, Tali'Zora, and of course Wrex. You may have noticed I just listed most of the potental party members and some of the side characters that is how likable and well written Mass Effect's characters are.
Long story short if you are at all a fan of RPGs (this is one of the best i felt fully immersed in the role I was playing), Sci-Fi (the game's universe is the perfect amalgamation of the best of popular Sci-Fi), or even simply great storytelling: Mass Effect comes highly reccommended from me.

It's an amazing game with flaws.
Right now if you're gonna play this game with mouse and keyboard, you're gonna experience quite poorly executed mouse controls, (Just as bad as Dark Souls' with the mousefix enabled.)
The mouse controls are better than what they were when the game first hit the Early Access program, but it's no way near as good as native PC games' mouse controls.
The mouse's sensitivity will go up and down along with your framerate, the sensitivity goes way up when the framerate's around 30-40 and will stabilize itself back when it's near the high 50s
The gameplay itself is quite satisfying once you get the hang of scavenging around and killing the zombies either stealthily or like a complete maniac.
You'll experience quite heavy framedrops quite often due to the fact that this game is a console port, and it's quite unoptimized with a lack of graphics settings (Only presets, Low - Ultra)
Although they have improved the performance a little bit, but it's no way near the 'well optimized' section.
You'll have a hard time aiming your guns at your foes with a mouse, so a controller is strongly recommended.
It's a fun game, but I'll be waiting for an update to fix the mouse issues that are still apparent in this game.
You'll be driving around in an open world doing missions for your fellow survivor npcs that you can also play as. (Most of 'em)
You scavenge the near houses you can find for supplies, and once you've emptied a house completely, there won't be any respawns like in DayZ, so you can't run around the same spot forever as there are actual missions taking place with a storyline for you to go through.
Playing as one survivor or another, they all have one life which means they won't be seeing you until you start a new game if they die during your current game, so you need to be careful as to how you approach a situation / horde of zombies.
It's a fun game but I haven't been able to complete it due to the issues I stated above, so that's all I have for now.
**The issues I've mentioned in this "review" have been resolved, more or less.**

My fiance bought me this game based on the hype from streamers. He also knew that I loved the Baldur's Gate games and Pillars of Eternity was being hailed as a spiritual successor. I bought in the hype myself, and was very excited to play it.
I'll overlook the glaring bugs that I encountered initially (having to do with Unity's network management [including Hamachi and wired ethernet adapters], which isn't even used for the game) because those don't have anything to do with the story, writing, shoddy combat system, or massive class imbalances.
I started with a rogue, which I quickly learned was a mistake. Any character can use rogue skills like stealth and lockpicking, and the backstab bonuses are negligible. The game's monsters ranged from easy one-shot skills to groups of Shadows that will ignore your warrior and pick off your party by swarming the weakest character first.
I don't have any problem with this type of mob, but when they occur within the first hour or so of the game without any learning curve, it's a bit imbalanced. I really wonder if people who aren't used to CPRGs even enjoy it.
The writing is cumbersome and extremely difficult to suffer through. There's just too much of it. Which wouldn't be a problem if it wasn't mediocre to start with. That's nothing new in games, but the writing borders on shakespearean levels of twisted, confusing wording without any of the art or cleverness. I find myself either re-reading passages to figure out exactly why they're over-describing some scene or I just read a few words and skim through.
This game is not unplayably difficult but the combat is extremely imbalanced and random. It just saps out the fun.
This is just not a good game. And it's frustrating that since this is a Kickstarter-backed game, there is nothing but insane hype and blind support. People who gave money to the development of this game will support it unconditionally. Even when I seek help for some difficult parts, forums are filled with "maybe you shouldn't suck so much" instead of acknowledgements that *MAYBE* Oblivion's custom combat mechanics are s***.
If you're thinking about buying this game, read the negative reviews first. Be prepared for what's wrong with it so there aren't any nasty surprises.

TL;DR If you liked Portal, pick this up.  Neat little experience while it lasts, but some puzzles will make you want to drive a stake through your monitor, which hurts the story's pacing a bit.
The game's strong point is its atmosphere.  There's a constant sense of contemplative melancholy, which fits  the game's mechanics quite well.  The narrative, while strong, isn't quite as clever as it thinks it is.  I get the sense that someone on the dev team noticed the macabre nature of the game's central mechanic, and they all sat around pondering the essence of conciousness for a while.
Definitely the most unique set of puzzle-platformer mechanics I've seen since Portal.  The puzzles themselves can be quite challenging.  They do a decent job of teaching the mechanics at the beginning, but in some of the later puzzles they ask you to think a little bit outside the box, but don't really give you a starting hint, which would have been nice.  I ended up having to look up 4 of the solutions, but, with one exception, I didn't feel particularly silly after seeing it done.  This is good puzzle design, but it can really kill the pacing if you get stuck for 20 mins, or have to alt-tab to find a solutions video that has jarringly happy music.
The game is mediocre. I'd recommend it if you like puzzle games but somehow it did not keep my attention.

The Swapper is a science-fiction puzzle platformer where you act as an astronaut exploring a crewless space vessel with some mysterious cargo. Using a cloning/soul-swapping handheld device, you traverse the ship and discover information about the crew's demise, primarily through mission logs and reports. Amidst mysterious environments and cryptic messages you puzzle together the ship's scientific and philosophical discoveries about consciousness.

An excellent platform puzzler, with the central mechanic of cloning and swapping pushed to its limit. The storyline is interesting enough to provide the impetus to advance from one puzzle to the next until it reaches a satisfying conclusion.
[Rating: 10/10]
Fun puzzles, interesting story, almost creepy atmosphere.  Fantastic game all around.

I'm a homestuck fan and was pretty hyped about this game. Not enough to contribute to the kickstarter campaign back in the days, but fairly excited.
So when it was put on steam greenlight, I supported it, and when it was released, I immediately bought it.
I started playing it - and then the first act was over. If I had to guess: probably after a bit over two hours.
That is an incredibly short amount of time.
During these two hours I had to play with massive black bars on my screen (because of some screen resolution bug? - apparently they plan to fix that with the next update).
During my time playing I certainly was entertained. Every item in the game can be combined with probably 95% of the other items available and will give you an reaction to it, which makes up much of the humor in this game. The characters are definitely interesting and homestuck-esque, as is the rest of the writing.
The backgrounds are also beautifully drawn, and the callbacks to the homestuck series hidden everywhere are very satisfying to find (even though a bit forced at times).
As a homestuck fan, who probably would've bought the game even if the overall reactions had been horrendous, I had fun.
Yet, I cannot with good conscience give a recommendation to it.
The short playtime, the extremely easy puzzles (with sometimes absurd solutions), the currently still bugged presentation, the soundtrack (definitely not as good as recent homestuck fan-albums), everything is basically bundled into an episode of an, for the foreseeable future, incomplete game, which on its own merits just doesn't stand out enough to justify a purchase.
In the end, I just don't know if you'll receive $8 worth of entertainment from this.
If I had paid 32$ for a hypothetical hiveswap season-pass (which, as far as I know, will be 4 acts in total, and if all acts cost the same: 4*8$ = 32$), and this was what I received for my money - I think I'd be pretty annoyed.
TL;DR: If you are a hardcore homestuck fan: buy it. If you think homestuck was pretty okay or you don't know anything about it: don't.

Yes.

The intentions of Mass Effect as the beginning of a series are apparent in damn near every aspect of the experience.  In a word: foundation.  It feels like it was designed to be built up upon, because what is here is aesthetically light, but structurally phenomenal.
What's immediately striking about Mass Effect given it's nature as an RPG is how well it plays as an action game.  Combat feels polished and dynamic, featuring an automatic cover system that works in tandem with largely artifical environments designed around boxes/wall/etc that leave no doubt as to what can and cannot be used for cover.   The shooting mechanics feel impactful and effective and the overall design accomodates both tactical and run-gun-hav'n-fun forms of play.  Battles can be as dynamic or degenerate strategy as you want them to be and not feel like either is more viable than the other.
But as an RPG, it's remarkable how many aspects of the game have been given this effectively tactile sense of physicality.  The ability to select responses through a conversation wheel with a mouse click creates a remarkably natural sense of rhythm to talking with NPCs that closely emulate real life.  There's no artificial time limit to responses either, this all happens as a natural consequence of the design of the system.  The physicality runs even to the more minor tasks such as hacking and navigation, extending the life of what would normally be sloggishly repetative tasks.  Again, as an RPG, it's rather startling just how good this game FEELS to play.
So what's not to love?  Well...yeah, we'll get to that, but first things first:
You are Commander Shepard, a human who's being eyed at by the Leaders of the Free Galaxy for the prestigious title of Spectre: an Intergalatic Man/Woman of Mystery with a License to Kill.  Things go♥♥♥♥♥♥up due a Spectre Whose Gone Rogue that leaves you with Information Vital to Saving the Galaxy and you are eventually tasked with Taking Him Down only to find that Behind His Power is A Much Greater Power that Threatens to Destroy the Galaxy!  If that all sounds cliche and routine well, that's cause it is.  Again, it feels like a foundation.  It's in the details - the subtleties and nuances they paint upon that very broad canvas - that makes the game's world so rewarding to experience.  The sheer amount of content they put into world building is astounding, but the restraint in not overloading the player with it if they don't want while still having it inform the situations the game creates is certainly worthy of note.
The thing to note upon a first run is how deceptively large the game is.  Playing the main quest takes you to only five planets before the endgame.  Some feature hub sections with a few sidequests, but taken as a whole, you could easily breeze through the entire game in only a few hours.  The bulk of the game's content is side quests that have you running willy nilly through dozens of systems in various clusters throughout the galaxy, usually touching upon some various world building content or minor character moments.  They can vary from a simple one-click scan of a planet for resources, to full on multi-planet hopping quests featuring both surface exploration, combat and tense negotiations...and there's SCORES of them!
So now...the price that's payed for all this polish and content: The game doesn't look very good.
Oh it's technically proficient.  Textures, faces and all are quite up to snuff.  But the design of the game is bare bones.  Any environment not devoted to the main quest is entirely pre-fab and not even randomly generated.  There's only some half dozen variations on them and since they do not change, it get's immediately repetative.  Even the main quest planets feel overly artificial and lifeless.  Mulitple quests end abruplty with nothing more than a pop-up window delivering silent flavor text and while the planet exploration goes a long way towards delivering on the scale the game, the actual landscapes were clearly randomly generated hieghtmaps ripped straight out of a late '90's 3d software program.  And yes, the way the game handles inventory is one of the worst I've seen anywhere ever.  Ya happy?
So that's Mass Effect.  A game where all the polish was put into the systems and design rather than the aesthetics, leading to a massive new world for players to explore that felt large, felt good to roleplay and simply play in...all so long as you ignored it'd been filled with blatantly copy/pasted environments.  Playing the game, the intent is very clear that this was to be the building blocks for a more fully realized world to build around their solid mechancis, design and world building.  Ah well...

One of the great RPGs of our time. Mass Effect excells in storytelling and characterization in ways that no other game has. This particular title is most memorable (for me personally) because of the way it introduces and develops the characters in such a fashion that the player truly cares about their fate and building relationships with each and every one.
Mass Effect also has solid shooter mechanics. I actually prefer the overheating weapons over the thermal clips from the later games. I also enjoy the combat storm and the way it is incorporated into the strengths and weaknesses of any particular character build. The abilites and leveling are also extremely well executed. I personally found it so rewarding and satisfying that I achieved level 60, but regardless the leveling system successfully helps to add reward during a playthrough.
Again, however, what makes Mass Effect such an amazing game is its characters and story progression. To avoid spoilers, I will just say that by the time I was nearing the end of the main story for the first time, I was deeply invested in each individual character's story and that is something that I cannot say about almost any other game experience.
Mass Effect exemplifies the great strengths of BioWare in its prime and will forever be a gold standard to which I will compare future titles to.

If I was giving advice to my past self, I'd want to wait until this game is finished- or at least a sale.

In terms of playability, the features that are present are nice. The mixture of construction, combat, and survival means that you're constantly switching tasks to stay on top of everything. On the other hand, individually, each aspect is very grindy and the balance is too straightforward.
The starting monsters are ridiculously easy, even with the most basic weapon, and yet until you get advanced weapons the very second tier are almost impossible. The hit boxes for the targets are sometimes awwkard, and the archery system is a joke. On the other hand, there's a decent selection of monsters and the drop rates are very well balanced, so once combat mechanics are refined this aspect should be above par.
Building is also above par, with a decent number of structures and an excellent placement system. HOWEVER, having to build an entire smithy just to have a forge feels like overkill and gathering the resources for a new base takes forever. In addition, for noncooperative multiplayer, defensive capabilities could be much improved.
Survival is very basic. Don't get cold, hungry, or injured and you'll be good to go. Some sort of meat vs. plant nutritional balance or a more in-depth breakdown of clothing's effect on the cold stat would tremendously improve this option.
The UI is... interesting. It's toeing the line between retro and just plain dated, but it isn't difficult to understand, though without information on weather or stamina its use is limited. In addition, colored boxes with the health conditions spelled out and visible percentages seem to be conflicting with the minimalist feel.
On the whole, I look forward to changing my recommendation when the game improves. Hopefully the pace will pick up and that day won't be years away.

Stranded Deep is a very interesting and promising indie game currently in early access, offering an unlimited world and awesome wildlife to interact with and discover. That said, there are a few annoying points. One of them is the bleeding debuff, this will be given to you if you get bitten by one of the two sharks in the game, a Tiger Shark or a Great White. It deals about .15% damage to health every second and whilst you will be able to survive for a very long time, you wont be able to get rid of it without finding two very rare items, only found at the bottom of the sea in shipwrecks, to craft a bandage to cancel the debuff. Whilst this is annoying, you can get around it by... not poking the shark with an axe. Yeah.
+ Graphics

When I was younger I remember having the demo-version of this game, which featured the Little-Tokyo and the following underground level and playing it over and over again. Maybe that's the reason I like this game so much.
Anyways - Chaser is a true old school first person shooter. Long levels in which you might even get lost in your first playthrough but even though it's a shooter you will have lots of different experiences in this game.
Some examples - you flee from a space station, fight your way through mafia goons, defend a truck from incoming enemies and even have a long underwater level in which you have to fend off sentry u-boats while navigating through boat wrecks.
There's also a very big range of your weapon arsenal that changes throughout the game.
And, even though its from 2004, the graphics are still pretty good (if you turn your resolution up enough).
Aside from shooting itself you have a Adrenaline-slow motion function that you can use against your enemies.
Another important aspect of the game is the story about the Protagonist John Chaser and his amnesia, which is carried on by cutscenes and dialogues throughout the game.
I give this game 9/10 because it was one of the first real shooters I owned and I'm never getting tired of the plain but awesome shooting mechanics in this game.

Let me get this out there right off the bat:  Shadows of Mordor is a AAA+ game with an amazing open-world with combat mechanics borrowed from the Batman series (and I'll take that combat system over just about anything).  Graphics are great, surround sound works flawlessly in both Dolby and DTS 7.1, they nailed the open world feeling where you're free to roam and can choose to do the main quests at your leisure, but you never feel rushed into getting them done.  With multiple ways to approach each situation, it almost reminds me of Dishonored in how you can choose to go balls-out or stealthy, the choice is yours.  So as far as the game goes, 9.5/10, it's a must-buy.
The problem is when I see that there's a new upgrade with some potentially new DLC.  It says "Buy ME: SoM - Upgrade to the GOTY Edition.  Awesome, I think to myself!  I can't pass up a good DLC bundle!  Then I read the 5.5 super light grey scale font in fine print that reads
.
That's odd, I think to myself.  I recall already owning BOTH the stand-alone Shadow of Mordor as well as the GOTY Edition Upgrade.  And you greedy *expletives* are trying to pull a fast one on your customers by not only making it confusing as to what exactly is included in the DLC package, but just for good measure, you might as well change the font size and color so that you need an electron microscope to find out if yuo're being screwed by what up until this point I had complete faith in.
So to reiterate.  I wholeheartedly recommend this game, it gets a 9/10 for me, but this new trend of making your customer spend an hour researching whether or not he's double-paying for some DLC he already owns so that you can potentially get a chance at making a quick extra buck is going to persuade me to find "alterior methods" of acquiring your game and leaving you with a negative review.  If you can make things right and make this customer proud to be an owner of Monolith Productions products, then I'll be glad to change my review and purchase your next game in the future.  All you're missing is some good PR and some solid transparency.
Other than that, keep up the fantastic work and please don't make me read the fine print when your next DLC comes out because I will most certainly be purchasing it!

My fiance bought me this game based on the hype from streamers. He also knew that I loved the Baldur's Gate games and Pillars of Eternity was being hailed as a spiritual successor. I bought in the hype myself, and was very excited to play it.
I'll overlook the glaring bugs that I encountered initially (having to do with Unity's network management [including Hamachi and wired ethernet adapters], which isn't even used for the game) because those don't have anything to do with the story, writing, shoddy combat system, or massive class imbalances.
I started with a rogue, which I quickly learned was a mistake. Any character can use rogue skills like stealth and lockpicking, and the backstab bonuses are negligible. The game's monsters ranged from easy one-shot skills to groups of Shadows that will ignore your warrior and pick off your party by swarming the weakest character first.
I don't have any problem with this type of mob, but when they occur within the first hour or so of the game without any learning curve, it's a bit imbalanced. I really wonder if people who aren't used to CPRGs even enjoy it.
The writing is cumbersome and extremely difficult to suffer through. There's just too much of it. Which wouldn't be a problem if it wasn't mediocre to start with. That's nothing new in games, but the writing borders on shakespearean levels of twisted, confusing wording without any of the art or cleverness. I find myself either re-reading passages to figure out exactly why they're over-describing some scene or I just read a few words and skim through.
This game is not unplayably difficult but the combat is extremely imbalanced and random. It just saps out the fun.
This is just not a good game. And it's frustrating that since this is a Kickstarter-backed game, there is nothing but insane hype and blind support. People who gave money to the development of this game will support it unconditionally. Even when I seek help for some difficult parts, forums are filled with "maybe you shouldn't suck so much" instead of acknowledgements that *MAYBE* Oblivion's custom combat mechanics are s***.
If you're thinking about buying this game, read the negative reviews first. Be prepared for what's wrong with it so there aren't any nasty surprises.

Of course, there was one issue with the game itself I had. Progression feels a little bit off. The only thing that i have a problem with the game which i dont know if the developers can do much about, besides more marketing is the fact that i can never find an avalible public server to play on. Bastion is a game where the art style, the narration, the sound, the music, and the story, are very satisfying.  The reason why I do not recommend it is because its gameplay, which is arguably its weakest aspect.
First, the core combat seems to be built on conflicting principles.  On one hand the player is supposed to rely a lot on muscle reflex, dodging and flanking enemies in between their attacks.  On the other hand, the terrain is rather punishing because it’s very easy to fall off the map while dodging around, getting hit by monster from different directions due to the inflexible switch-target mechanics of the shield blocking, and also where monsters’ attacks are largely not “telegraphed” but rather demands players to memorize the exact time between their attack animation finishes, and when the actual attack occurs.
Next, there is an excessive amount of weaponry compare to number of maps.  Due to weapons are discovered and players are expected to use them until completion of the map, the system where players upgrade and keeping a favorite set of equipment is weakened.  This issue is felt even more acutely at the final stage of the game, where just shortly before the player is given a “super cannon” that basically outranks every other ranged weapon in the game, but you aren’t so lucky to have any time enjoying it… as the latter half of the final stage locks the player into a new, and extremely unwieldy “environmental” weapon until the game ends.
These are just some of the highlight where I feel this game’s gameplay employs “difficulty by annoyance” kind of tactics, and is gating players from the good stuff, namely, the art style, the narration, the story (except the ending might be a bit let down).  This being said, the game doesn’t pass my own “should I play it or just watch gameplay video on YouTube” test.  So yeah, Bastion is a game that’s better “watched” than played yourself.

This game is an amazing example of that you don't need a title to offer a 60h long single gameplay for it to be good, enjoyable, and most of all - worth the money you paid. The relatively short time you'll spend on the whole campaign (around 7-10 hours, depending on how stubborn you are to nail the side challenges and how much you keep failing) is simply packed to brim with quality. The minimalistic design is at the same time beautifully crafted and well-detailed. The story is surprisingly complex and engaging with not very many words being said. In fact, the protagonist doesn't speak at all - his journey is instead narrated by one of the deuteragonists (who's hilarious by the way, if you enjoy some subtlety in your humour), another one of them only speaking at the very ending. The stages are fairly short, however each and every single one of them brings something new to the table, a different kind of challenge to face, which makes them memorable and fun. And finally, the soundtrack - gosh, the soundtrack! Playing Bastion without the sound is about as pointless as watching a musical with your ears plugged.
Overall, the game is not only very playable, but REplayable as well. The length actually becomes an advantage here, because it doesn't make the title overwhelmingly repetitive if you decide to play again. Sure, the plot is linear. The only side quests you can do are the challenges I mentioned earlier. There are only two plot-related decisions you can make -
and one of them has no consequences other than a different emotional, roleplaying experience for you while the other is just picking the ending you like better. But you know what? It's okay. The game is very honest about what it is (a sweet, quality indie experience) and what it isn't (an epic AAA RPG adventure). If you feel like slowing down a bit in your gaming exploits, but not so much as to play a grass growing simulator, Bastion is something I can very much recommend.

When people think Dark Souls, they think difficulty. What they might not realise is how that difficulty is used in encourage exploration and atmosphere.
Everything in Dark souls in linked to a story that only a video game can tell. It’s a story of triumph that means something, because you’ve seen how easy it is to fail... hundreds of times. The game design is perfectly linked to this story through the gameplay, the lore and the world design.
Most games use their world as backdrop for the action; a backdrop you often will barely notice. This is a game that will actually make you appreciate the world (and its ruined beauty) as you search for items and learn every nook and cranny as you attempt to overcome its obstacles.
While Dark Souls 3 may be an improvement on 90% of the Dark Souls formula, no game I have ever played can match the labyrinthine world design of Dark Souls 1. There’s a moment that I think every players has, after travelling for hours and what feels like miles where they find themselves in a familiar and safe place. I haven’t played a game that shown me how well together and believable a game world can be as well as that (admittedly I’ve yet to play Bloodbourne).
Through all the above, Dark Souls creates atmosphere by the bucket load and is truly a unique experience. Sure this port is pretty bad, and you’ll need DSfix if you even want to make it playable, but I suggest you do. My playthroughs here and my first one on PS3, have been the gaming experiences I’ve had since the PS1 era.
Unless you have a X-box controller, don't even bother buying it.

One of the great RPGs of our time. Mass Effect excells in storytelling and characterization in ways that no other game has. This particular title is most memorable (for me personally) because of the way it introduces and develops the characters in such a fashion that the player truly cares about their fate and building relationships with each and every one.
Mass Effect also has solid shooter mechanics. I actually prefer the overheating weapons over the thermal clips from the later games. I also enjoy the combat storm and the way it is incorporated into the strengths and weaknesses of any particular character build. The abilites and leveling are also extremely well executed. I personally found it so rewarding and satisfying that I achieved level 60, but regardless the leveling system successfully helps to add reward during a playthrough.
Again, however, what makes Mass Effect such an amazing game is its characters and story progression. To avoid spoilers, I will just say that by the time I was nearing the end of the main story for the first time, I was deeply invested in each individual character's story and that is something that I cannot say about almost any other game experience.
Mass Effect exemplifies the great strengths of BioWare in its prime and will forever be a gold standard to which I will compare future titles to.
The Mass Effect series is one of my favourite series of games, and I think I will always love the first one the most.

I am way over 40 hours into Pillars of Eternity, but not close to finishing it. So take this as what it is, a mid game impression. (I will update this once I am finished)
Pillars of Eternity is everything Dragon Age Origins was supposed to be and was not. A deep narrative combined with deep rpg mechanics. This is a game for people who care more about worlds and characters then about polygon count and extensive voice overs. That said, the graphics of Pillars are really nice, atmospheric, and for the most part varied. The voice acting is great and while not as extensive as in the high budget mass market products, it is more then enough and actually surprisingly extensive in its own right.
There is lots to read but you are never overwhelmed by vast amounts of expositional text that wont stop (well, almost never^^). The world and the story are very interesting and pretty unique. It does not fall into the trap of just putting all the fantasy cliches into it so as to appear deeper then it is. There are not dozens of quests at every corner of the world, but every single one feels meaningful in some way. There is no grinding. The inventory system in Pillars is pretty much the best in any RPG I have played. Combat seems simple and almost shallow at first until you start to realize the amount of options you have and how it all works and fits together. At that point combat will become very interesting and varied, and if you play on a harder difficulty and have to replay some of the harder fights they will remain enjoyable because of this.
There are actual reasons to replay the game, since the deep rpg mechanics allow for actual customization that will result in very different characters additional to the opportunities to choose differently in the many choices the games narrative offers you.
If you love RPGs, this is for you. If you thought DA:O was to shallow for your taste, Pillars is for you. It is by no means perfect and should have come out some 4-6 years ago, but as its is right now its by far and with pretty much no competition the best fantasy cRPG of the last decade.
