Blast from the past; if you're a fan of Baldur's Gate or any of its ilk, you owe it to yourself to get into this adventure.
Deviating from core D&D mechanics in ways that better suit a PC game, you'll find the UI and game mechanis cut right through a lot of the tedium and finicky issues with the old games. For example, if your main character a soft and squishy Rogue or Wizard, you will no longer be punished with an instant game over if they fall in combat. The endurance system allows you to play through a number of encounters without binge drinking potions or resting after each fight.
It is an very specific style of game to be sure; some might not like loosing battles on some crapy dice rolls. There are some things I also found lacking, like the ability to craft traps and a larger NPC companion pool considering the stronghold mechanics to keep benched companions busy.
Overall a great game so far, one I'm going to savor for a while yet.

This is a summary of my review video, which I encourage you to watch
if you are looking for a more in-depth review.
Pillars of Eternity is a nostalgia filled game in the same vein as Baldurs Gate, a top down RPG adventure. To start out, the options menu and control menu both have a lot of options to make the interface and game experience personalized, which is a great thing to see.  Graphically the game looks good, and has it's own atmosphere, which is nice. The game suffers from quite a few little bugs graphically, whether it be minor things like a dead enemies powers still triggering, or more annoying ones like debuffs that are supposed to last through a battle lasting even after I left the zone and rested in an inn. A detail list of more bug issues is in the video review.
The game also suffers from an excess of loading screens. From entering a house to going to another room in the house, and to another floor of the house, this coupled with the fact that the longer I played the game, the longer the loading screens were. This really breaks the immersion, and is disheartening the more you play.
The character creation is very well done, with lots of customizable options, and a great number of characters and styles to choose from, sadly no dual class system through. You also have the option to create and customize your entire party as you progress through the game, allowing you easily to play with six fully custom made characters.
The interface for the most part is sleek, with some customizable options, which is nice.  It offers an option of a stash, where you can put all of your gear. I really enjoy this option, because it makes the selling of items really simple. As a loot ♥♥♥♥♥, this is one of the best systems for gear and items that I have ever come across. The quest log is fairly well organized, and the game offers a Journal feature that literally provides a written account of your adventures, as though you were in a grand novel.
Visually, the level design is well done, but upon closer examination of the map, you see that the world is not that large, and the pathway to get through the world is fairly linear and limited in where you can travel to. Within towns and cities, the exploration is limited as well, as you can only explore homes and buildings that directly relate to the story line. This takes away from a sense of adventure never allowing you to wander yourself into loot or trouble.
The crafting system is simplistic, and while it's not a feature I enjoy, it is necessary if you play on a harder level.It also offers an enchantment feature, where you can craft and enchant items and better your weapons. You are limited in what you can chose, which some might find disappointing. It's more like a starter kit rather than an in depth crafting system.
The story doesn't really connect with the atmosphere and graphics of the world. The story is written more like a book than a game. Each encounter comes with story text, that is elaborate and over detailed.  Over and over again as you come across an event, person, or story driven device, you have to read about useless details such as the dew that glistened on the leaves in the early morning dawn. While this may be enjoyable at first, it becomes more of a tedious reading experience than a bonus to get through the game. Twelve pages to talk about one event. If you want more detail and in depth environment, the atmosphere should reflect this visually, not pages of reading. In spite of the extra details in the dialogues, the characters and villains in the game feel weak and extra. There is no weight behind your actions. If I slaughter an entire village, there is no consequences such as being ambushed by those seeking vengeance. It still feels like you are fighting against mundane mobs instead of affecting change in the world around you. The characters lack personality or depth. They are hypocritical in their beliefs; their actions do not support their words. Unlike Baldurs
Gate, where you had the option to go through dialogue with the option of leaving to battle something else and coming back if you got tired, here you have to read all the dialogue, complete the task that is required, then come back for more dialogue before you can continue in your adventure.
The combat comes down to experience more of which is by completing quests than by killing enemies. You only acquire experience by killing a certain number of a particular enemies, at which point you stop gaining experience at all after you kill X amount of them. The problems is that you come across many, oh so many of each opponents. It is annoying to have to continue to fight the same enemies, but not gain any experience, as humanoids of any kind never give any experience is just down right annoying as it wastes your time. The loot isn't all that amazing, and you stop gaining  experience, so what is the point of killing these beasts?  The amount of experience you gain is also scaled by the number of people you have in your party, which is poorly designed. If you want to distribute the experience gained but not have a in depth gain vs party member, it should be equally split between the members, they discourage playing with anything less than six party members as you get less Xp not more. You have an 'Awakened' soul, but your Awakened status adds little to no extra abilities to your character. You do not feel special in this game, sure having a fear style ability may be nice as a melee DPS but as a healer or ranged worthless. It does not customize to your class.

Each character has two health bars; health and endurance. This becomes more annoying than useful, as your character will naturally develop a higher level of health than endurance, but in battle it is your endurance that is drained 30x faster than your health. Once your endurance is depleted, your character is knocked out and useless, even if they still have a high level of health. There are magic spells, armor, weapons, buffs, and some natural race abilities that heal endurance levels through out combat. Yet they are still drastically lower than your health level, to the point where your health levels become unimportant. Having a tank character becomes essential, as the rest of your party can be easily one shot if an enemy gets to them. Beasts that are summoned with high defensive health numbers become almost pointless. As their low endurance numbers guarantees that they will be knocked out easily, for a creature with 400 health will be out due to their 70 endurance. Instead of balancing the damage taken versus the health you have, or adding tactical depth where people must have supplies to survive a dungeon, all you have to do is sleep and all your health points are restored. You have a camp kit and sleep whenever, and where ever needed, without the danger of ambush. There is no risk to your characters, or a need to prepare for a battle, as the threat of death is next to none, failure sure, death no. The combat becomes repetitive and disappointing. It limits your choices so far as gaining experience and getting low quality loot that I lose the desire to fight.

Each magical class had their own set of spells, (mages focus more on control and aoe damage, druid's debuffs the enemy and buffs the tank, priests are good for protecting the entire party, and ciphers focus on mental spells to confuse or control). Despite this, their class spells still felt too balanced with each other, with no impactual roles where having a particular class would give an advantage to a certain situation.

This game is an amazing example of that you don't need a title to offer a 60h long single gameplay for it to be good, enjoyable, and most of all - worth the money you paid. The relatively short time you'll spend on the whole campaign (around 7-10 hours, depending on how stubborn you are to nail the side challenges and how much you keep failing) is simply packed to brim with quality. The minimalistic design is at the same time beautifully crafted and well-detailed. The story is surprisingly complex and engaging with not very many words being said. In fact, the protagonist doesn't speak at all - his journey is instead narrated by one of the deuteragonists (who's hilarious by the way, if you enjoy some subtlety in your humour), another one of them only speaking at the very ending. The stages are fairly short, however each and every single one of them brings something new to the table, a different kind of challenge to face, which makes them memorable and fun. And finally, the soundtrack - gosh, the soundtrack! Playing Bastion without the sound is about as pointless as watching a musical with your ears plugged.
Overall, the game is not only very playable, but REplayable as well. The length actually becomes an advantage here, because it doesn't make the title overwhelmingly repetitive if you decide to play again. Sure, the plot is linear. The only side quests you can do are the challenges I mentioned earlier. There are only two plot-related decisions you can make -
and one of them has no consequences other than a different emotional, roleplaying experience for you while the other is just picking the ending you like better. But you know what? It's okay. The game is very honest about what it is (a sweet, quality indie experience) and what it isn't (an epic AAA RPG adventure). If you feel like slowing down a bit in your gaming exploits, but not so much as to play a grass growing simulator, Bastion is something I can very much recommend.

This game is a 2-D Isometrical, as I'd say, hack and slash, but honestly, it's much more than that. It's an impressive game, because it is so immersive. I've played quite a while back, so I do not remember any names, and niether the story seemed that deep (not too much of lore behind the world, imo), but I recommend it because of how amazing this game is holistically (overall). The storyline is cryptic, but it propells you towards new locations and looking to restore the world and save it from the Calamity, as well as understanding what happened. The graphics and the music only support those premises, drawing beautiful backgrounds and the inspiring sounds (oh, did I say, this game is also beautifully voiced?).
The hack-and-slash itself is very fluid, and even gives room for replaybility, as the player can choose from an arsenal of melee and ranged weapons and combine the two varieties to create his/her own battle style. The controls, as I remember, are very flud--and I've played with a keyboard!
The only real downside to this game, is that even though there is a vareity amongst the play-through options, once the story is over, it is very hard to replay the game, as you know pretty much everything, aside from an end choice that you get to make. Although the combat is still fun, going through the same locations and hearing and seeing the story repeat itself just seems a tad excessive. Nevertheless, there's always room for obtaining more achievements and trying out new play-styles.
Overall, once again, this game wonderfully brings together all of the elements I've talked above to create a piece of art. Hence why I recommened is so eagarly. But yet again, it's an experience that will be just that after its end--a great experience, which you might want to replay only in your memory.

Dark Souls is a game that does not really rely on a story, or set path to keep you going. It is a pilgramige, that forces you to struggle, adapt, and learn how to survive in its brutalizing, harsh enviroment.
The game blends multiplayer, with single player (you can turn off multiplayer interactions on the main menu). It plays alot like the legend of zelda mixed with a bunch of ARPG elements, such as allocating stat parameters (like vitality, strength, dexterity, ect...) and equiping different gear pieces and weapons that benifit you in different ways. Playing normally, you can find signs on the ground that do different things. orange signs have (un)helpful notes to guide you in the game, and white signs summon other players to your game to help you defeat bosses and stuff. Players can also invade your game to steal your humanity and souls.

There is TONS to explore in this game, Im even discovering new things every time I come back to it. Boss battles are tough, but once you beat them it is hands down one of the most satasfying things a video game can offer.

In a future where humanity has exhausted all of Earth’s natural resources, mankind has sent out seven interplanetary expeditions, dubbed the Sisyphus Project, to find something, anything to help them survive. But as they gradually lose contact with them, all hope relies on one space station. The Theseus has been orbiting the alien planet of Chori V for 192 years now and used the materials found there to build a new kind of technology that lets one swap bodies and consciousness with another. Ninety-three years have passed since its last transmission to Earth when a scavenger boards the functioning, yet desolate station to uncover the truth.
The Swapper (2013) is the first and only production by Finland based indie developer facepalm games. It is a side-scrolling puzzle platformer with action platformer (Metroidvania) elements that starts off on Chori V, but is mostly set inside a space station that has seemingly been abandoned almost a century ago. What makes this title stand out (apart from its premise), is that the playable character, together with its surroundings, was handmade out of clay and then filmed. Using something other than pixelart or meshes in a video game is quite the challenge, but definitely paid off as The Swapper looks and feels unique.
In an attempt to find anything worth scavenging, the player will explore the Theseus and not only unearth log entries from the crew, but also hear strange voices that seemingly come out of nowhere, as well as transmissions from somewhere inside the station. The controls are easily accessible and the title can be played with either a gamepad with an analog stick or a keyboard and mouse. To reach new heights or activate switches, players will need to use the swapper gun that lets them create up to four different clones of the scavenger. These mimic the original’s movements to a T. Not only will they jump when the scavenger does, but the distance between these versions always remains the same, unless, of course, one of them runs into a wall or dies. To create a replicant, players simply need to aim the gun in any direction and then shoot. They can then even transfer the scavenger’s consciousness into the copy, which comes in handy when a chasm is too wide to jump over or when the current body is about to be squished.
Unfortunately, the first couple of puzzles onboard the station are very uncharacteristic for the experience as a whole; they seemingly rely on high precision shots and quick reflexes that are common to shooters but not to puzzlers. Players then will likely get the impression that this game is not for them as The Swapper does not properly demonstrate that by aiming the gun and keeping the aim button pressed, time slows down considerably, so that quick reflexes are not at all needed. However, once that crucial element is understood, puzzle solving is much less stressful and becomes a matter of figuring out what goes where, which is what players came to this game for after all.
In that sense, the brain teasers that the The Swapper has are mostly marvellous in design and will keep fans of the genre hooked. They are tough, they are challenging, and they won’t let one go until solved as with every solution, one moves closer to the answer of what happened on the Theseus. With that said, there were three puzzles that I really couldn’t figure out and had to look up only for me to say, “How did I not think of that?”
Unfortunately, apart from giving players a false impression, the game does feature one truly unfitting design choice. Hidden inside the station are ten rooms, which contain messages from Earth and give additional information on the whereabouts of mankind. Finding these rooms also unlock The Swapper‘s achievements. Unfortunately, these hidden areas are so well stowed away that there are virtually no indications that they exist at all. The game doesn’t mention them, the achievement description doesn’t explain how they can be gotten, and all of their entrances are inside walls. Some of them – like with room V or room X – even disallow the usage of the gun to detect where the entrances might be found, while others – like room VI – require literal leaps of faith to get to them. What makes them painful to completionists, though, isn’t just that they are hard to reach, but that they won’t unlock.
Achievement hunters should be aware that the game won’t mark the achievements as unlocked on some computers, unless they do some tinkering beforehand.
Finally, even though The Swapper does have some setbacks in the secrets/achievement department and while it doesn’t properly teach that time slows down while aiming the gun, it nevertheless is a very enjoyable puzzle platformer. Fans of classical science fiction stories will love what they encounter in this roughly five hour long adventure that will have them ask for more.

State of Decay is a game truly like no other.  For those who talk of clones of DayZ or other zombie games, I urge you to try the game before making these statements.   This game plays as a third person action game, perhaps similar to others.  But where it really departs the other games in my opinion is the assembly of survivors that you have to put together, build shelter for and keep motivated through all the trials of the post-apocalyptic world.
In terms of gameplay, the pace is frenzied in general, with constant action, escalating quickly in some cases and quicker still if you don't take the appropriate action.  As mentioned, you need to assemble survivors and develop them, convincing other groups or individuals to join you and making sure you have enough skilled individuals so losing one doesn't drastically diminish your chances of survival.  They also tire out (making them far less effective) forcing you to rotate them often.  Building a shelter is critical and chosing the right location and structures to build (each has it's own function) is also critical to success.  The game is all about surviving and scavenging, ultimately to attempt to leave the area in hopes of finding shelter from the expanding zombie population.
For the price, State of Decay is a great deal for anyone craving another single player apocalypse survival experience.  Future expansion promises continued gameplay (the core game is not very long, perhaps 10 hours) and escalating difficulty.  I am thrilled this title made it's way to STEAM from the Xbox 360.

Dragon's Dogma stands out as one of the game's that I wish I'd played sooner. The medieval fantasy setting pits you against monsters from realms of fantasy and mythology: human enemies join griffins, chymera, dragons, harpies, ogres and goblins to name just a few.
The battle system is especially good, allowing the player to fight in nearly any style they'd wish, while also encouraging you to try a wide range of playstyles. You can set yourself up as a heavy-armoured warrior, mage, rouge/ ranger type, stealth specialist, or any combination thereof. The pawn system supports this, as you can choose new pawns that compliment your current playstyle at an town or city.
If I were to choose my issues with the game, I'd have to say that the 3rd person camera leaves something to be desired, especially in battle situations. In close or crowded situations, it can get hung up on the surroundings. The game also isn't the prettiest in terms of color scheme and texture quality, and it's locked at 60 fps, but the gameplay and the scale of the world (it's not 'open', but it is huge... which can make travelling for quests a pain) make up for the shortcomings.

Chaser is a horribly buggy semi-competent budget shooter. There are only two good things about it; the guns and the music. The story and voice acting are so bad it's painful, and good gunplay dosen't excuse many deaths that felt cheap. Additionally, I've become stuck in various objects that lay directly in my path, forcing me to reload from a past save. On multiple occasions I 've encountered horrible graphical glitches that made the game completely unplayable (see my screen shots for this game if your curious). Anything unrealted to shooting, such as a biref stealth section, is so poorly designed that I have to wonder why it's in the game at all.
The gunplay itself is a lot of fun. There are several guns, and all behave more or less effectively. There is usually only 1 or 2 good weapons that you'll find yourself using throughout a level however, so there really isn't much point in the decent array you have to choose from.
The terrible enemy AI is compensated for with a reduced ability for the player to take damage and a high level of accuracy on the part of the AI. Any single enemy can kill you if you arn't careful, and there are a lot of enemies, but the enemies themselves die so quickly that getting through a level without using the time-slowing feature is a completely viable option, provided you have good reflexes for whenever the enemies start popping out from behind corners. The time slowing feature itself is hugely dissappointing, as it recharges too slowly to be any fun.
I've seen estimates of length that go up to 50 hrs of playtime and higher. I'm over half-way through the game at 5 hrs. Excluding deaths, I doubt this experience is longer than 8 hrs.
Lots of people love this game, and while the shooting is good, the stealth section and an underwater section where I literally CAN'T SEE have me wondering why.

But Samuel Longwood keeps an ace up his sleeve for occasions like this…

Lots of potential but be warned....base building is very limited:
Base building is VERY limited, you cant build a roof till you find the recipes for the tall platforms, but the recipe drop rate is EXTREMELY low, ~50 hrs of play and have only found 2 of the recipe books, same for my friend.  At this rate it would take us ~500 hrs or more to have a chance to find them.  Base building is also limited by extremely low storage capacity, You only get 1 small storage chest (8 slots) per base.  If you can find a recipe you can also put down a large storage chest but again the odds of finding that are very low.  Collecting wood to build is a challege as it doesnt autostack as you collect it, which if you have any kind of gear makes it very hard, again you cant stow it away because of limited storage.  Once you find a hatchet or axe (fairly easy to find) you will be able to put down a foundation and a few walls and that is it, no ceiling or locking doors when you join.  A locking door requires metal obtained with a hammer (very low drop rates, my buddy and I have each found 1 in 50 hours of playing time. The security of your base....two guys with axes can break in with about 10 minutes of chopping.

Great campaign with a lot more depth than Rome 2.  Faction internal politics actually matter this time around!  There are plenty of factions to play that all feel different not just based on their starting position and units but by how their basic mechanics work.  It's definitely cool to preside over the crumbling Empire as Rome, but I think the most enjoyable way to play this TW installment is to play as one of the migrating factions.  As you lead your beleaguered hordes across the map, making enemies wherever you go, once you finally find a place that you can call home for a while really is rewarding and it invests you in the story of your tribe.  As someone who mainly plays RPGs, this was really neat for me.
CA seems to have put a lot of work into improving the campaign and battle AI for Attila as well, which is nice to see.  I actually had the Huns pull a hammer and anvil tactic on me in my last battle!  Never saw that in Rome 2.
Unfortunately, this game is not optimized for♥♥♥♥♥♥  I'm running a late gen i5 Intel CPU and AMD R9 390x GPU with High settings on this beast and I'm barely maintaining 45 FPS.  And it isn't like this game is any more graphically impressive than Rome 2, so I don't understand what could be causing the irregular performance other than bad optimization.
Apart from the performance issues, I've really enjoyed my time with this game.  It is rare for me to spend more than 60 hours on a game, but I'm addicted and can easily see myself playing Attila for over 100 hours.  This is definitely a buy for those that have computers that can handle it to a degree you're comfortable with.

Tutorial covers different classes of weapons, but doesn't indicate which are which. Then came some attempts at mining. At first, I found in strange that all the rocks that spawned off the asteroid looked the same, so I turned to get a different angle on them. Turns out, you can't even turn your ship in the same space as the rotational point is not the center of the ship. The rocks still looked the same-that's when it hit me, they're 2D sprites! Somehow, in the 12 years since Freelancer, Rene Marcel Dirks has found a way to reverse the trend of improving graphics. You'd be much better served playing Freelancer, you could probably find a more populated server. I tried to find a way to exit the game, but there's not even a menu!
Coupled with now being worked on by one person, development will be moving along slowly.
tl;dr: Avoid, try Elite: Dangerous, or X3:AP if you want a Freelancer experience. You'll even find the same number of players in X3!

Pillars of Eternity is a true RPG in the best sense.  It successfully resurrects the best aspects of its spiritual predecessors - Baldur's Gate, Icewind Dale, and Planescape - and at the same time manages to put a new, slightly different spin on the whole experience.  It feels both old and new, reminiscent yet adventurous, an homage and a brilliant original.  The execution is nearly flawless, and the journey is just as rewarding as the finale.  But be warned:  Pillars of Eternity isn't for your average, impatient gamer.  Be prepared to read walls of text, constantly pause and re-evaluate your battles, and throw your party against a seemingly unbreakable foe five-hundred times before finally working out a viable stratagem (a certain
comes to mind).
I finished my first playthrough at about 90 hours, give or take an hour or two.  I was being pretty thorough, taking every side quest I could find and completing all of them, and yet there is still more I could have done had I decided to.  And now, at this writing, I am at 93+ hours, starting my second playthrough.  And it isn't getting old.  Not even a little bit.
I tend to value a game based on how many play hours I can get out of it, measured against how much I spent on it.  I spent $45 on the Pillars of Eternity pre-order; already I've played double that number in hours (as mentioned above).  That, to me, is a success.  For purposes of comparison, take as an example FEAR3 - $60 at release for a campaign that lasted me about 17 hours on my first playthrough, if that.  And so Pillars of Eternity is a fantastic success in that department.
Certain bugs get mentioned on forums and in articles around the web.  I'll tell you up-front that I had absolutely no problems with any bugs beyond a character occasionally getting caught against a wall for a few seconds.  Nothing serious.
Overall, I give Pillars of Eternity a 9/10 - if only because nothing is ever truly perfect.  But Obsidian did a fine job here, taking an older, pre-established formula and re-implementing it in our modern gamer world to great success.
Highly recommended from this gamer.

So I started PE and I've been putting as many hours into it as I can to get through it, while also enjoying the game. I had no illusions that this game would be quite large, but the scale of it so far is quite impressive.
I've just finished the second chapter on Hard difficulty, my main character is an Aumaua Barbarian and I've opted to pick up NPCs as I go along. The experience has been great thus far, I got my face caved in early on, but after a few hard lessons I've picked up a few tricks to help me in the tougher encounters.
The game holds true to older games in the genre, however, it misses some of the finer details that really bring the world to life. Sound effects are the primary point I find lacking here. Don't get me wrong, the ambiance and music is beautiful, though it lacks smaller details like shouts and voices while moving through cities/towns. I've also found that the music can fall silent for long periods, breaking the mood at times. But since this is my biggest gripe about the game so far, I believe vehemently that it is a small and oft overlooked issue, which bodes well for the future of the game.
As for story and writing. I have been tested in my vocabulary on many occasions, and to my delight have enjoyed every minute of it. Obsidian have done a great job on the script and story so far and I'm eagerly awaiting more through the rest of my playthrough.

Would you read or watch a trilogy and then stop right before the end? Do you like cliffhangers that will never be resolved? Do you like to having the feeling you are in control while playing a game, only to be railroaded into doing something stupid later on? No? Then this game is not for you. Mass Effect and Mass Effect 2 are solid, if not excellent games. They have their flaws, but I can live with them. But it is a continuous storyline that runs across three games, not two. Mass Effect 3, the third installment, not available on Steam, but only on Origin, has a very controversial ending that ends the trilogy on a sour note. If you've somehow missed the controversy, just google Mass Effect 3 ending, read some of the many things that have already been said about it, and weep. Weep for the loss of something that could have been epic. Weep for the hurt feelings of countless gamers. Weep for the sorry fate of a couple of epic fictional characters, that felt like friends to so many of us.
If you think you will be able to live with the above and also love RPGs, then by all means, buy this game now, no hesitation, or just keep reading and then make up your mind.
Mass Effect is a great game. It is a game in which you are faced with a threat to the entire Galaxy and your character, Shepard, is the only one who can do something about it. The graphics may be a bit dated by now, the minigames may be more distracting than fun, the Mako may be near impossible to steer and eager to slide into the nearest ravine, the side missions may look like they were thrown together during a crunch time weekend, fueled by energy drinks and cheetos, and there may be some other minor problems, but, and this is a BIG but, the main storylines are excellent, the voice acting is close to perfection, the universe is vast and compelling. The greatest thing about this game is how engaging it is. You get a feeling for your character, always with the last name Shepard, but other than that, you can mold him or her any way you choose. You can choose a backstory, a look down to the gender, have intimate relations with humans and aliens alike, although there are no actual sex scenes, despite the uproar some people have tried to create. The average movie has way more skin than these games.
You get to know your squadmate pretty well, can even enter a relationship with at least one of them, and although your mileage may vary and may not like each and every one of them, you will probably find at least one or a few you will end up caring for. They can feel pretty real. They can't hit the broad side of a barn and are sometimes pretty useless in a fight, not hitting anything while one enemy is stomping your face and another is shooting you for good measure, but you take all that in stride because they feel and sound like actual people. The only written dialog is when you are presented with a choice. But that choice, once made, is then voiced marvelously, with depth and feeling, adding to the immersion. The choices make you feel in control, allow you to chart a course for your character, being a good person or a troublemaker or something in between, decide the fate of humanity or even the Galaxy, or on a smaller scale, who lives and who dies. Then it makes you feel sorry about that choice and perhaps restart from a savegame, or even create a new Shepard and do everything all over again, starting from scratch, rewriting history. Despite it all, it doesn't get boring. I played this game for over 120 hours, not just one playthrough, but many, with different variants of Shepards. Or with the same, trying to get better stats, righting wrongs, making left turns where earlier I had taken a right, just to see where it would lead. Or just play the game again on another difficulty level. Or using different powers or weapons. In and of itself, stand alone, ignoring, no, denying the great injustice that was Mass Effect 3, Mass Effect is a terrific game, and judged in that way, I would wholeheartedly recommend it.
In Mass Effect 2, more of the same, with better graphics. In Mass Effect 3, more of the same and then, right at the end.. They dropped the ball so hard, it made its way to the center of the Earth. I guess they ran out of ideas, out of time, out of money or out of writers or something. Maybe they just painted themselves into a corner, realised they couldn't live up to the hype they had created, couldn't realistically create several different endings without ending up shortchanging us anyway. Whatever the cause, it saddens me that I will never, ever get to see what happened to 'my' Shepards. That is the problem with Mass Effect as well. You are pulled into this universe, made to care about your Shepard and about your squadmates, come to regard them as friends. You do your best to keep them alive, try to work around their defects in targeting skills, despite their reputation, and love them for who they are. But you will never, ever get to see what became of them and are forced to make do with an ending that feels tacked on, even with the expansions. Even now I sometimes feel like I am grieving for these characters. Shame on you EA! Shame on you Bioware! I will never forgive you for this! Unless you belatedly release modding tools for ME3 allowing the communicty to finally fix this, or better yet, finally come up with a true ending, that lives up to all the pre-launch hype and really gives us different options and shows us what became of our Shepard and its squadmates. I would be desperate enough to pay for that too, just to heal this hole in my heart. *snif* If you're thinking: surely the ending to Mass Effect 3 can't be that bad? Then again, just google it. Then make your own decision. But don't say I didn't warn you. At least now you know what you are getting into.
If you do buy the game, it is useful to know that on Windows 7 the game won't run at all unless you run Steam as an administrator, that there is a guide to tweak the settings to prevent horrible audio stuttering, that you upon request you may be able to get the Mass Effect Bring Down The Sky DLC for free from EA and that you need to hang on to your final savegames for each character if you ever purchase Mass Effect 2. You can also buy all games together, but in that version the original game is completely unchanged, so other than it maybe being cheaper, there is no advantage. There are mods that allow you to play with better textures however.

Anyway, with all that mostly trivial stuff being said, end result is a game that I want to give a 8/10. This may change as I play it more, but I doubt it.

I don't think I've found myself saying how bad a game is so often as while I was playing Chaser. Chaser is a run and gun FPS that is overly ambitious, and falls hard in just about every possible gaming aspect. I want to say it feels like a cross between Serious Sam and Red Faction, but to put this title in the same sentence as those other two is blasphemous.
There are just so many bad things to rip on: The graphics are decent for a 2003 release although they could have probably toned down on the shiny, over-glossed textures. The shooter aspects are bearable and the story is kind of reasonable, albeit extremely disjointed and severely lacking any depth due to the main character's case of amnesia. Voice acting is respectable, although the character graphics make for a stiff delivery.
If one thing stood out it's that Chaser is god awful too long. It took me over 15 hours to finish, but I'd say there's only 7-8 hours of real content here. All the excess fat is just mindless killing of never ending spawning AI in a maze of bland and boring visuals.
The AI just sucks, period. They spawn above you, below you, behind you and you never really know where they are until you are taking damage. Toward the end of the game, the AI difficulty ramped up exponentially literally requiring me to quick save after each kill which reminds me, there's no auto save here so save early and save often. There has to be at least 1,000 grunts that are trying to kill you and there's not a whole lot of variety in the bad guys.

HIVESWAP: Act 1 brings the distinct flavour of 90s nostalgia into the Homestuck universe, beautifully displayed in rich detail. Be warned, however, that a bug that I (and many others apparently) faced caused this beauty to be tarnished slightly. When opening the game, the aspect ratio is messed up. You can choose a new display ratio, and it *looks* like it might've fixed itself - but it hasn't. If you experience this issue, relaunch the game, or else the backgrounds are going to appear incorrectly at times.
Back to the review. Hiveswap is a short adventure game with minimal difficulty and no "dead ends" from what I could see. The battle system is a neat spin on the way STRIFE works in Homestuck, and from what I could see it has no failure state. Think of battles in this as a series of puzzles that you have time to fail and get right. The puzzles don't involve any real violence, the main charatcer speaks for herself on this: "I don't use guns."
What you get instead of anything above "I whack the critter" is a very funny and entertaining battle system, with the iconic bizarre one-liners of STRIFE combat acting as gags or hints. The puzzles in combat do suffer, however, from a lack of clarity. There are times in combat where you'd think an option would work... and it doesn't. However this is an issue that all adventure games suffer, the dreaded "macgyver" solutions. But to say that Hiveswap goes to extremes in the way traditional adventure games do would be a stretch - rather, you can have multiple items that seemingly serve the same purpose, but only one works.
The environment is littered with interactable objects, and as any astute player would be wont to do, you'll spend most of your time clicking through the background looking for items. If you're the kind of person who couldn't care less about the story, and just look for items to solve puzzles, you'll probably only spend 20-40 minutes on this game. I'm a big fan of Homestuck, and spent a lot of time reading item descriptions and looking around this new part of its universe eagerly.
But that brings us to another point of contention for potential newcomers: the writing. I find the goofy and oftentimes slightly crude writing of Andrew Hussie to be amusing; it fits the theme of "a bunch of kids doing stuff" well, and can be very funny when it wants to be. However if you're the kind of person who's coming here looking for a tightly written and executed exploration of characters, then perhaps come into this game with an open mind. None of this is to say that Andrew's writing is bad, or lacklustre, or anything of the sort - heck, most adventure games also have corny writing. Rather I'd like to warn potential buyers that you're not walking into an oscar worthy piece of literary masterclass; rather, an emotional, epic, drama-abound script about kids being kids. It's great, but it's not for everyone.
Speaking of tone and atmosphere the music does the game much justice. I've seen comments about the music transitions being jarring but personally I never had issues with it. I did however spend a lot of time happily exploring with unobtrusive but pleasant melodies filling my ears. Homestuck has never been short of good music and Hiveswap is no exception. Don't let my description fool you however, when the game needs to get into full gear the soundtrack is happy to oblidge.
The story of Hiveswap so far has been very engaging. As an avid fan of Homestuck I found myself drawn, yet again, to the exploration of themes such as society and class, as well as the intriguing inclusion of green and red spirals... As someone who has no experience with the Homestuck universe, however, the game still has much to offer. It isn't quick to throw you into themes unbeknownst to anybody but the "niche audience." The game offers a steady introduction to the themes of the universe, with only a few things sticking out to me as lacking explanation; namely the STRIFE system itself.
The only remaining topic worth touching on is the animation. The idle animations for characters are very expressive and speak to their personalities; but they feel lacking. Rather than being fluid and pleasing to look at, they are stilted, as if they were merely a few frames thrown together. This becomes less apparent over time but it was still distracting at first. The game features many cutscenes, some of which are mostly fully animated and beautiful (the opening and ending cutscenes come to mind, the latter being wonderfully animated) - while the rest are stills being played with sound effects and music. I wish we had seen more of the former, but I understand the team were on a budget, and respect that they used their money wisely.
Overall I would recommend this game to anybody with £5 to spare, an open mind looking for a goofy, funny, and rather dramatic story, and a love of puzzles. If you are none of these then it might still be worth a try, but the refund option may turn out to be your best friend. If I had to rate Hiveswap as how I enjoyed it as a fan: 10/10. If I had to rate it as a consumer: 7/10. Hiveswap is let down by its length and minor technical issues. Even while taking my time and reading everything I could, I finished the game in about two hours and forty minutes. I thoroughly enjoyed that entire time, with no dips in my enjoyment whatsoever - but it was still a rather short time.
I will be back when Act 2 releases to continue the story, and hopefully, continue to enjoy myself immensely.

Great game. Combat is fun, challenging, and rewarding when you manage to play well. Lots of abilities that can make every fight different, and give you infinite choices on how to approach an encounter. You also aren't forced to choose if you want to specialize in stealth, combat, or ranged. You can do all of it, and are encouraged to do so!
Side quests aren't the most fun you'll have in the game, but they don't feel monotonous thanks to the optional challenges and varied objectives. At the very least the combat system is so good that you won't care if you spend hours doing the same thing over and over again. Seriously, I spent the better part of an hour in an Uruk Stronghold doing nothing but fighting everyone, and loved every minute of it.
At this time I haven't gotten very far into the story, but from what I can tell the basis is great. Being someone that is only vaguely familiar with LotR lore, I don't feel lost or confused (yet) due to references to other media. The protagonist is a badass, and you certainly feel like one while playing. The atmosphere and setting are very immersive, and suit the narrative extremely well.
The game also features frequent "mini-boss fights" in the form of Captains and Warchiefs and uses a system called "Sauron's Army". The system is kind of hard to explain, and would take a lot of time to type it all out, so I'll just say this: Boss encounters are fun and each one is different. You have to adapt and sometimes even find ways to get information about the bosses before you fight them, or pay the price for going into the fight knowing nothing about his strengths and weaknesses.
I could go on and on, but to conclude... You can't go wrong buying this game. I got it on sale, but I would've gladly paid a full $60.

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

Being just a tad too young to play the old swathe of Isometric Role-Playing games (e.g. Baldur's Gate, Fallout, Icewind Dale) when they first came out, my introduction to the genre came after a long relationship with their console counterparts. And - while I love KOTOR, Mass Effect, and friends - none of them have really caught what I really ended up loving about those old classics.
It's not the story (within reason almost any story can be told with any game), and it's not the characters (who again aren't really dependent upon the genre). It's not the visuals, or the disc-swapping.
No, it's the combat and the exploration.
It seems to me that most RPG's these days (with a couple of notable exceptions from Betheda) don't often just drop you down in a beautiful world and say "Eh, go do, you know... whatever." But that's one of the greatest things about the old school RPG's. Want to visit every wilderness area on your way to Nashkel in Baldur's Gate, sure go ahead. Want to completely ignore your vault's desperate need for a new water chip for a while and go talk to those cool looking Brotherhood of Steel guys, if you really want to. Incidentally guess how Pillars of Eternity works. It's just like that. Once you're out of the starting area, you can go pretty much anywhere. Don't really care about those creepy cultist guys and would rather go help liberate a keep from a crazed(?) despot? Whatever floats your boat man. Feel that diving into the seemingly never-ending chasm that is the Endless Paths is more important than figuring out this whole main-plot "Watcher" business, okay I guess. It's very, very liberating in a way that most games these days aren't.
Which brings us to my second point. The combat. There's just something for me that relishes in attempting a specific encounter multiple times, each time making it slightly farther in, methodically devising a strategy so that next time, I can take out one more guy before I fall. That's an experience most modern games don't give (some FROM Software games excluded to an extent), and even more having six characters each with a plethora of options (none of which seem always useless) allows for a seemingly infinite number of ways one could approach each encounter. That's a good thing. That's a very, very good thing.
If you haven't picked up by now, I haven't talked overmuch about the story of the game, and that was mostly on purpose, it's... good so far. Not amazing, not great, not phenomanal, but good. It serves the purpose of moving you from one area of the world to another where you get the really good content, the sidequests seem to be where the real heart of Pillars lies. I've stormed the aforementioned keep and taken down a drug den operating in the middle of the city. I've hunted down a notorious bandit and recovered the ancient scrolls of a God (only to dump them in a field... hey! The voices in my head told me to!). I've encountered a couple simple fetch quests, but every one had some clever story twist, or (failing that), an incredibly tough battle to flex my tactical muscles on.
tl;dr version: Pillars of Eternity is a great game, probably even Obsidian's best game. It goes back to the standard of a wide-open, engaging world, and supreme tactical combat that made all the old Black Isle games so great in the first place, and if you have any love in your heart for those old gems, you owe it to yourself to give this game a shot.

If you tedium is you thing, then this game is for you.  It delivers that good stuff in bucketloads.  You will spend countless hours sifting through menu screens and reading despcritions of items' stats trying to get all your party members equiped with just the right weapons, armor and spells to defeat the hoard of angry skeletons waiting just around the corner.  And when you finally do get your party just right, let the action . . . be stopped.  Because guess what you to do!  When combat commences you will really need to pause the action frequently so you can make sure each and ever party member is using just the right weapon or spell at just the right time in order to defeat the enemy horde guarding whatever McGuffin you are hunting.  What is badly needed is a tactics system like in Dragon Age Origins, where you can assign your party charaters many different rules of engagement while retaining the ability to step in at any time and take control of this or that charater as the situation warrants.  But in this game you have to reinvent your tactics every time.  It is just too much like work and too little like fun.
Visually battles are a mess. As your forces tangle with the enemy they become so tightly packed that visually understanding who is doing what to whom is difficult to see. Your best indicator of what is going on is a cluster of green and red dots above the characters to tell you what is going on.  And as often as not your view of the fight is obstructed by a wall thanks to the fixed isometric camera.
PoE's voice acting is competely mediocre (when it 's there at all.)  Seriously there are games a decade old that have better voice acting.  Obsidion should have invested more in voice acting or cut it completely.  As it stand the voice acting serves more to remind the player of what is missing rather than what the story is.
I really wanted to like this game, I really did.  I just couldn't bring myself to like a game that had me constantly concerned about the mechanics of the games rather than playing the game.  I couldn't develop any affinity for my own character, my companions or storyline. There just wasn't room to care about anything other than figuring out how to win the next battle.

Seldom do I write reviews. How many reviews start this way? It's indicative of those rare titles which, for some reason or another, touch and pull and twist at the heart-strings of the reviewer enough that they inevitably find themselves here, to hopefully reach out and convince some other person to support this new thing they have found and love. I only found out about Pillars when it made the splash page for steam. In my short experience with the game thus far, I am guessing there will be a lot of reviews that start like this one in the coming months.
This game is fantastic. Everything is there. But there's /more/ here, too. Whilst wandering out of a spider infested cavern, a small icon in the corner of the room popped up alerting me to click it for more information, revealing "there are bats the size of chickens caught amonst these webs." It's like Baldur's Gate with almost twenty years hindsight and feedback to improve the experience. Plus, I hear they're adding hats for bears and cats next patch.
If you've played the old CRPG's or not, you will delight in this game should you have a love of deep enriching story lines, tactical combat and time spent thinking imaginatively about fantasy worlds. Which leads to my other point, and I will try to be brief and wrap this up: Games like Skyrim and Dragon Age Inquisition are amazing in how detailed and beautiful the worlds are. They are well voice acted and well animated. But they are subtly limited by their reliance on these mediums, as well. Games like Baldur's Gate, Morrowind and this game circumvent that limitation though their storytelling aspects which, in a deliberate and wonderful way, demand the player to use their own imagination to frame parts of the plot. And in the end, this is a very, very good thing.

Obsidian Entertainment is the studio you go to when you want a good story and well-written characters, and they've delivered again with Pillars of Eternity.
This is an RPG in the old Infinity Engine style, specifically hearkening back to the classics: Baldur's Gate, Icewind Dale, and Planescape: Torment. This time the game isn't shackled to the old AD&E ruleset, instead coming equipped with a new set of mechanics designed to be used on a computer, taking full advantage of combat's real-time-with-pause system to allow a real difference between fast and slow actions.
There are eleven classes to choose from, each of which play very differently. There are eight NPCs in the game with their own quests and dialogue (and, as already established, they're all quite good), but you're not stuck with the adventuring buddies Obsidian selected for you if you don't want to be: you can hire adventurers at any inn, allowing you to decide their race, class, and stats just as you did your own. They won't have special dialogue, but it allows you to play with any party composition you'd like to.
The story is great, slowly revealing itself to you over the course of the game, ramping the stakes up as you learn more about what's going on. By the time you reach the end of the game and things start happening quickly, it feels as though the game has earned its payoff rather than coming across as rushed. Pillars of Eternity uses its conversations to convey the immensity of its endgame very well.
Conversations with party members – and with NPCs on the plot's critical path – are heavily voiced, though most conversations in the game are text-only. Make no mistake though: there are a lot of conversations in Pillars of Eternity, and they do a good job of expanding on the world even when they don't involve the main plot.
The combat in the game is fun and decently challenging. There can be a lot of micromanagement of your party members, but it allows for a big difference in outcome based on how well you position your characters and what spells you choose to have your spellcasters use. As mentioned, it uses the party-based real-time-with-pause system of the old Infinity Engine games combined with a system that doesn't force everything to happen in terms of very large-grain rounds. Characters equipped with melee weapons are "sticky", so if you try to move a character out of melee range the enemy will get a free attack against that character.
If you're a fan of RPGs, especially the ones from the Infinity Engine's heyday, then you will certainly enjoy Pillars of Eternity. Its writing, both its story and its characters, are great, and the combat is nicely done. Pillars of Eternity is an Obsidian Entertainment success story.

Anyway, with all that mostly trivial stuff being said, end result is a game that I want to give a 8/10. This may change as I play it more, but I doubt it.

The huns tend to get doom stacks of fully uprgraded soldiers until you kill atilla then they shrink into nothingness. This is no doubt meant to show a threat from the huns, and there really was weight to the final battle with Atilla. Overall Atilla total war is a fun experience, The DLC isnt neccesary, except maybe Charlamagne otherwise the DLC just adds more of what is already in the game. It is a fun game, and I think History and TW fans will enjoy.

If there was an openworld zombie game worth checking out this year, it's definitely State of Decay, because instead of trying to ride on the rise of DayZ-esque games, it tries to do its own thing and does it well.

This game demonstrates the overlooked importance of simplicity.
The game uses a lot of dirty methods to make you want to progress in the game. EVERYWHERE is an opportunity to level up or complete an achievement. This game would be a dangerous free to play game, it was apparently at one point was one. With the massive variety of weapon unlocks you need to grind for, there is ALWAYS something to look forward to that gets you practically addicted to the game.
It's a fun, relaxing, game with a great variety of color... something lacking in modern games, color. You have a vairety of modes, such as trying to shoot targets, trying to shoot through rings before hitting other players, a mode where everyone versus a single player with a massive amount of health, etc. It's great it has variety, but the modes basically don't deliver the same amount of fun as do the normal free for all or team battle modes.
It also has a variety of maps you can play on, a good number of them feeling unfair to some of the players balance wise, and they're so terribly simple I just don't understand why they don't just give players some form of map editor. Over time, these maps rebalnce themselves within battle, giving players otherwise potentially stuck in a hole some wiggle room. You cannot create tunnels in the game, which arguably is a good thing due to most weapons not being designed for them. So if you ever are in a hole and did not upgrade your tank to drive up steep hills, you're probably stuck until you make yourself a ramp which can, at anytime, be sabotaged by other players.
You can upgrade your tank in a variety of ways. It's not super diversed in exactly how you can upgrade it, some trees feel lacking in fact as if the developer ran out of ideas. Despite that, it does the job right and makes you really feel you're designing the tank based on your playstyle more than how the game wants you to play. You even have a "luck" tree which increases your odds  of getting good weapons, even if you have not unlocked these weapons yet.
Each weapon has its very own skill tree that can unlock an improved version for you to fire at some point. Even if you unlocked the best variant of a weapon, it doesn't mean you will get it and can very well still obtain an inferior version of the weapon. For most weapons, labeling the earlier variants of the weapon "inferior" can be inaccurate for it's more about trade offs on some. This is a game where you'd have to spend a long time to completely finish and you'll likely stop playing by the time that comes for a moment.
This game doesn't have a whole lot of gameplay, so you will likely play it a lot for a moment and then slowly take breaks and coming back until you stop all together. However, you will definitely most likely play it again at some point. Despite the simplicity and the grindy design of the game, it's a good game. For the price, it isn't too bad of an investment as long you have other friends on board.
There is some problems, however. Though few, some players use various exploits that is impossible to detect in game, such as rulers. Because of this, it's hard to know if players are good or cheating which causes a lot of drama. This game has, multiple times, attempted to fix this with various methods and all of them were more toxic than the cheaters in my honest opinion. One example was nudging, which only hurts the players playing honestly since what it did was adjust shots slightly, causing it so the good players no longer have the feel of the game and the cheaters to simply adjust their measurments method. Another example was like nudging, but randomized, meaning ALL players are going to have inconsistent shots, except the players already bad at the game will be even worse and the cheaters will still be dominate. There is a wind option, which is honestly a good mechanic despite it not being a good tool against cheaters since it makes the game fresh and more challenging.
Another problem is that the game implements tank customization, but you literally have like five options for each piece. This might be an exaggeration, it could be less. I feel that it could give more variety, some way. I believe it's difficult because of how simple the tanks are, the developer probably has no clue what else to really implement other than what is already available.
This problem exists in a lot of areas in the game. Maps and weapons have an overwhelmingly huge variety, but other areas do not most likely due to, as mentioned, lack of ideas. This doesn't hurt the game in anyway, but it's worth noting that the game does sometimes feel empty in some areas.
Pros-
Great weapon variety
Lots of progression opportunities to casually introduce other parts of the game
Solid gameplay
Cons-
Some bad maps for fair play
VERY grindy
cheating is very easy
lacking in content in some areas, such as tank customization.
Overall, I believe 7/10 is a deserved score. It's a great game and I think every gamer that likes laid back  gaming sessions should consider this. However, it's not by anymeans revolutionary but it never really was meant to be. It's just fun.

Great game. Combat is fun, challenging, and rewarding when you manage to play well. Lots of abilities that can make every fight different, and give you infinite choices on how to approach an encounter. You also aren't forced to choose if you want to specialize in stealth, combat, or ranged. You can do all of it, and are encouraged to do so!
Side quests aren't the most fun you'll have in the game, but they don't feel monotonous thanks to the optional challenges and varied objectives. At the very least the combat system is so good that you won't care if you spend hours doing the same thing over and over again. Seriously, I spent the better part of an hour in an Uruk Stronghold doing nothing but fighting everyone, and loved every minute of it.
At this time I haven't gotten very far into the story, but from what I can tell the basis is great. Being someone that is only vaguely familiar with LotR lore, I don't feel lost or confused (yet) due to references to other media. The protagonist is a badass, and you certainly feel like one while playing. The atmosphere and setting are very immersive, and suit the narrative extremely well.
The game also features frequent "mini-boss fights" in the form of Captains and Warchiefs and uses a system called "Sauron's Army". The system is kind of hard to explain, and would take a lot of time to type it all out, so I'll just say this: Boss encounters are fun and each one is different. You have to adapt and sometimes even find ways to get information about the bosses before you fight them, or pay the price for going into the fight knowing nothing about his strengths and weaknesses.
I could go on and on, but to conclude... You can't go wrong buying this game. I got it on sale, but I would've gladly paid a full $60.

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

A fun point and click adventure game that'll appeal to both fans of the genre with no prior experience with Homestuck, and to die-hard Homestuck fans. The story follows new characters living over a decade before the start of the comic, so doesn't require any prior knowledge; all relevant concepts are explained as you go. If you are a fan, you'll quickly notice links between the new cast and some existing characters though. *WONK*
It keeps close to the tone of the original comic, though backs a little away from the aggressive tone and removes the swearing for a more accessible overall feel (I didn't think Homestuck with clean language would work, but it actually does hold up well, way better than Namco High did), and has an absolutely ridiculous amount of unique dialogue for attempts to combine unexpected items.
The visuals are charming and the musical score is a great mixture of bombastic and whimsical.
Overall, I'd recommend this for people who want a fun, lighthearted adventure that's not excessively taxing on the old thinkpan.

Chaser is an old-school first-person shooter that was obviously heavily inspired by "Total Recall" (the original, not the remake). There was no "cover system". There's no leaning around walls. There's just shooting, and occasional jumping, and puzzles, and more enemies. You started with no memory of who you were or what are you doing on a space station. As you fought your way out of the station and continue on your own path of self-discovery (and destruction), you piece together your purposes,but it may not be the truth, as everybody seem to know you as something else... Graphics are lame as this is an old game, but the action makes up for it. Just be ready for the shocking ending. :)

Granted, there exists here and there glitches and faults, but holds a pioneering salvo of FPS, adventure, survival and tactic. The lengthy storyline may hold it back, however for keener gamers is certainly worth a gander. It is, if I'm honest and intertextual, a linear form of 'UT99', and as far as I'm concerned an alternative to 'Unreal: Gold' and 'Unreal II'. Worth a shot.

Chaser is about as generic as an FPS can get. It even has a useless pseudo bullettime mode.
You start off the game as John Chaser wakes up in some sort of cryogenic chamber on a space station with no idea who he is or why there is a small army destroying the space station in a rather over the top attempt to locate you.
You are immediately thrown in the action as the mindless hordes of enemies start attacking you from all sides as you make your way off the space station, through streets and sewers and even through a rather peculiar mini-submarine segment. It all feels very familiar though, it's all the same generic shooting you have seen before with nothing to set it apart.
The weapons all feel like plastic, the enemy AI is about as worthless as a blind guide dog and the maps are made entirely out of black and grey boxes.
The story is some of the most unbelievable manure you will ever encounter, not because it's surprising but because John Chaser appears to have no willpower whatsoever. Despite not know who he is, and everybody else seemingly knowing, he never bothers to ask. He also lacks the capacity to say no even when warned repeatedly not to go into the service of a particular sociopath.
All in all, this is one of those you can actually play twice without realizing it because it is all so generic and forgettable. Nothing stands out and nothing has been given that extra effort.

I was given a steam code by the developer in order for me to help promote awareness of the game, however in saying that any and all thoughts on Sirius Online are my own and I have tried to be as fair as possible
Sirius Online is a space-themed MMO by Vektor Studios run by Rene and Michael Dirks.
The game literally came onto Steam Early Access on 1st June 2015 and I am writing this after playing just over an hour, so call this a preview or first impressions if you wish!
I'll tell you now I'm a big sci-fi and space game nut, so excuse me if I sound a tad biased with this short writeup.
Sirius Online currently uses the Blitz3D game engine which is a free open source piece of software and honestly for what it is I feel that the guys at Vektor Studios have done a great job, pushing the engine to it's very limits and beyond its' capabilites.
In the current Alpha state you start with a small combat fighter and have to go round mining ores from asteroids to obtain more credits to buy a new ship, be it fighter, mining or transport "class" where there are several variations of ships in each of these.
I feel the gameplay in its' current form is impressive and will develop over time, extra weapons, hud options and even bigger ships are planned but so far Sirius has been very smooth and I have yet to drop below 50fps on my machine.
At present the game does feel a little bit grindy but it's a) In Alpha state and b) Early access, which means that it will have bugs, will have changes made and will be taking input from fellow gamers in order to improve upon it.
I have chatted to the developer and they are definately passionate about what they are doing, Sirius Online is a labour of love and they want to do right by it, I really hope they can pull it off because I can see a massive amount of potential in this game and I'm looking forward to covering it more as updates roll in.
I suppose the question you want to ask me would be "Is Sirius Online worth its' £6.99 pricetag?", my simple answer would be yes, however I'm not about one word answers, I not only think that you should buy into this game, but also help mould it because games like this need fellow gamers like you to come along, find errors/suggest content and really have the chance to build a game that you want to play, not what the developer wants to play.  Together as a community we are stronger so why nto become part of one?
I suggest...no I challenge you to buy this game and meet me in space, shoot me down in cold blood and then tell me you didn't enjoy it.
Reminds me of good old days when everyone was trading and fighting in cosmos. The world looks complex, maybe even too complex for me but those who like this kind of games will enjoy exploring it.
