I don't write reviews for games because I feel the need to keep my opinions to myself and let people exprience games for themselves and not be influenced by others to find themselves as a gamer. That beign said here it goes.
I remeber playing thousands of hours just playing Baldur's Gate: Tales of the Sword Coast and Baldur's Gate II: Shadows of Amn and it's expansion Throne of Baal. I remember Icewind Dale one and two. I remember playing Pool of Radiance: Ruins of Myth Drannor and other countless D&D and RPG titles like Niverwinter Nights. Very selddom does a game bring me back in a way to the feelings I had about those games. I love RPGs they, to me, embody what a game should be. It sucks you into your own world that is just yours, the decisions you make effect you, charatcers that have a special place in your heart, I'm talking about you, Minsc and Boo!
This is one of those rare games that I play and I feel the magic I felt about games when I was a kid. The trail and error, the building a character and finding what playstyle works for that class, the dungeon crawls that I play for hours and don't realize it is time to eat. Instead of my mother calling me down for dinner it's my wife, or my kids sitting next to me going "Dad we are hungry can you pause it after you kill this monster?" and when I pause it they groan with annoyance that it needs to stop. Now instead of playing solo like when I was a kid I have 3 of my own to share the magic with, and the memories I make I now share with them. I hear their laughs as the characters banter as you walk through the cities and caves and forests.
My oldest is now trying to battle her way onto my computer to play this game bcause it is like the games I loved when I was a kid. Simple yet complicated, easy yet hard, and it has all the makings of a classic. If you are a RPG fan or a fan of any of the Baldur's Gate games or Neverwinter Nights and you don't buy this game your are an idiot. This game will take you back to a time when games were amazing and not just good. I know I might catch some flak for that but how many games that have come out in the past 8 years have made you wanna go back and play them through 20 times? I can count the number on my hands. Yes there are fun games to play that are good for one maybe two play throughs but seldom suck me into my own world for hours and hours and hours of gameplay. I have about 50 hours on this game and I got it just a few days ago. I can't get enough and niether can my kids.
While it has it's drawbacks like any game and they are few and far between, such as the double clicking inventory bug, but they are so few I have yet to find one that is game breaking. you can't even say that for Skyrim or any other RPGs that have come out within the past 5 years. If you don't like RPGs then this game is not for you, if you never played Baldur's Gate and never will this game is not for you. But if you love them and want a game that takes you back then get this game.

Despite the ridiculous oversaturation of the whole Western World with zombies, this game does manage to create itself somewhat of a unique niche in such a crowded space. The game can essentially be divided into two primary components: a third person action game with light RPG elements and a sort of base management game.
The action aspect is the title’s primary focus and the player will spend most of their time engaged in fighting against, running from, or sneaking around zombies.  The combat, while not being outstanding, functions fairly well and is fun, although I suspect that if the game were much longer, it might become rather formulaic.  Most of the combat is melee based (as bullets are rare) but firearms do play a part and are useful against larger swarms of zombies.
The combat does suffer somewhat due to one particular problem that is almost inherent to third person action games in that it is sometimes difficult to get your character to face the direction that you want in the heat of the moment.  While this problem is nowhere near the level of old school Resident Evil games, it is occasionally a source of frustration.
The only truly bad aspect of the third person part of the game is the vehicles.  They just don’t drive well at all and are somewhat of a pain, especially considering how quickly they become damaged.
The RPG/base management side of State of Decay is what makes into something more than just another zombie action game.  You have to keep track of several different resources which are consumed steadily as you play, as well as deciding on different facilities that can be installed in your limited space.  Eventually your group can change bases and find themselves larger, expanded digs that offer more possibilities for development.  The game does present the player with some interesting choices here, because even the biggest bases cannot contain all possible facilities and most of the facilities are fairly useful.
You will not only manage bases, indeed you will spend more time dealing with the survivors themselves.  Some of these individuals are part of the story, but most of them will be found throughout the game.  On a conceptual level, the survivors are the most interesting part of the game, as you aren’t really playing as any one person but rather as the group as a whole.  If one character dies, you simply move onto another.  I’ve always wanted something like this in survival based games, as it allows for tragic disasters that don’t necessarily force you to reload because of a Game Over.
The game does seem to fall into the unfortunate hole that Grand Theft Auto IV did, in that you will spend much of your time babysitting your other characters, as they all seem to occasionally forget that they are in the middle of the apocalypse and wander off to do something utterly moronic.
State of Decay is more than a little buggy but there have already been patches which have fixed some of this.  Frame rate problems were pretty consistent, although it was never unplayable.
Many of the side quest arcs felt undeveloped, like a novel that ends 100 pages too early.  The game itself is short as well, but I enjoyed this aspect of it, as I don’t really have the time to dedicate to very many 40+ hour releases anymore, but I do wish that certain secondary arcs had a bit more meat to them.
Overall, State of Decay is one of those games that come very close to being truly great but is held back by a few problems.  It is inexpensive though, and is the ideal game to tackle when you have a free weekend, as it doesn’t take long to finish.  I am really looking forward to the expansions, as I think that they will polish the game’s faults and perhaps add more of a challenge.  Above all, while the game itself is good enough, it is the promise of future titles, made in light of the lessons learned from State of Decay that really excites me.   The developer has some great concepts that just need to be hammered out and hopefully the success of State of Decay will allow them to do just that.

State of Decay is a pretty solid and fun zombie game from Undead Labs. The game has a very smooth and nice feeling combat system for fighting the zombies, and sets up the apocalyptic world very nicely. Creating a home base with your survivor group, and managing it and the other survivors is easy enough to do, but at the same time very satisfying. Going on scavenging runs, saving survivors or hunting mutated zombies are things that you'll find yourself doing to help the group.
As far a realism goes, the game sits somewhere between Dead Rising and DayZ. The words "Realistic" and "Zombie" don't really go together, but as far as survival goes, your character becomes fatigued and injured over time, and will have to spend time at home to recover. Swapping between characters is essential to keep things running smoothly, and things such as ammo, food, medicine, fuel and materials can be gathered.
The game also allows the player to drive vehicles for faster movement, and has a large map to explore, along with many different home base points. There isn't a very forgiving atmosphere in the game, so if you die out there, the character is gone, just like real life. New survivors can be foud to replace them, but stats such as stamina, fighting and more will have to be built up to make them more effective.
Graphically the game looks good. As an Xbox port, it isn't extremely high end, but at the same time isn't very dated either. It runs nicely, but hasn't got any advanced settings, instead just "Low" "Medium" "High" etc. The lack of choosable features such as Anti Aliasing is noticable, and a lack of options such as texture quality, shadow quality and more are missed. I should also note that this game is far more enjoyable with a controller than a Keyboard and Mouse
Overall though, the game is very fun and has lots of content. If you like zombie games, I'm confident you'd like this one. 8/10

I gave this a thumbs down not because I think it's a bad game overall. But I do think that this is the one where they took a lot of the worst feedback from the Rome 2 debacle and implemented it poorly into this game. The result is a feature-filled, yet bloated campaign map that rarely gets you into RTS battles, which is a shame because they're possibly some of the best RTS battles in the series.
Cons:
-The campaign is a bloated mess. There are so many haphazardly-added features to the grand map that weren't balanced, like long periods of snow in North Africa as part of the climate change system,. Or a "Death" feature the Huns get where even if they have just a few dozen archers on your land, any of the units in your 20-stack army can't replenish losses. There are also these spergier elements like politics that just serve to add extra time onto the grand map or the fact that most buildings seem to cause public order penalties for no good reason.
-The AI gets lots of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ cheats and it exploits them. They'll use money bonuses to build all-elite armies that that they'll throw at you three stacks at a time. Or they get so many public order bonuses that you will never be able to use agents to make their populaces angry and rebel. Expect the start of every turn to be spam-clicking through a bunch of successful enemy agent successes while your spies can barely pull of the simplest tasks in the late game.
-The AI does everything it can to avoid getting into battles. I play these games because they tend to be really good RTS games that have a grand map thrown in to help get into big, fun battles. This game does anything it can to avoid battles. Enemies will exploit stances and space-counting to always be out of range of large armies and use movement cheats to speed past you to get to your tiniest setllements. They will NEVER attack you unless auto-resolve is squarely in their favor, so expect the AI to only ever use 2-4 stacks of armies at any time.
-The map itself is laid out really badly. Most of it is wide open ground and armies can just blitz across it for incredible distances per turn. You don't get the moments of S2 or R2 where you hold a chokepoint against armies. It's pretty dull.
-Horribly optimized. It's pitiful how badly this game performs. CW reasoned it by saying that  it's "not created with modern systems in mind" and that's just a really bad excuse for "we didn't have time to optimize this for 64-bit." Especially when the game will not recognize more than 3GB of GPU. It's especially odd since Nvidia puts my recommended at Ultra for everything, and it won't run above 30 fps for that.
- The voice acting is atrociously bad, and anything that leaves a character's mouth is the most unnatural-sounding combinations of words.
Pros:
-Some of the best RTS battles in the series. Fatigue and morale have been tweaked so that you they can play a major factor in winning or losing. I've won a few outnumbered battles by forcing the enemy to tire itself  while preserving my troops' stamina.
-Upgrading units into elite units on the map. Once unlocked, the click of a button will let you upgrade your lower-tier units into higher-tier ones.I really like this feature as it means less farting around with building types and putting armies into the right spot to get the right units. This is a feature I'd like to see in future TW games.
- Some nice minor features like the fact that archers will now fire in high arcs and most units have some kind of special skill like a sheild wall or other features. The former is useful for the defensive gameplay of things like the West Rome campaign while the latter is a nice balancing element.
-As badly optimized as it is, the game looks great. The dark mood is expressed well by the graphics, while still having a full, varied color palette.
-The music is a mixed bag, but a considerable improvement over Rome 2 or Warhammer. There are lots of really great tunes on this that sound great yet mix into the game well.

"The Swapper" is a game in which you need to think about how to combine options you have to gain access to areas, solving your way through the game and it's story.
It comes as a package of good ambience, music and story from start to finish.
During my playthrough I didn't notice any flaws, bugs or crashes. The game seemed very well done.
The newbie learning curve was commendable: Nothing was forced on the player but everything was explained when introduced as new mechanic.
There's an excellent level design, the game carries it's theme very well and makes good use of all mechanics. As far as I know the swapper in this game is something unique, so far. For an improved gameplay experience without stress and frustration the player may slow down the game when using the swapper device. Very well done.
Interface and menu design are pretty well done. Especially the map was very useful as it indicates where prograss has and hasn't been made, assisting the player in where to go and where already been.
Checkpoints exist frequently in the world. Also very well done.
Loading times for the game's sections are extremely short. Again very well done.
Later on teleporters may be unlocked to save the player travel time between the sections. Yet again very well done.
The only mediocre thing is the time period spent on a full playthrough: if you're solving your way through the rooms the game may be rather short.
Still the game doesn't feel rushed or unpolished at any point, it's just well done from start to finish.
Literally the only issue I had with this game was a minor one: No gravity rooms. In those you're supposed to use your swapper's swap-beam for drifting. I'm not 100% sure anymore but I think the game forgot to explain that single thing when it was a new game mechanic. Also the camera turns with the character when drifting through these no gravity areas which may cause health issues for some players (?).
The game is good to very good (depending on your personal preference) and in any case very well done.
However: This game is clearly not for people that lack patience or do little to not at all care about the story and ambience package.
Everyone else: Cleary worth buying and totally recommended.
PS: I'm impressed how well designed everything in this game is. I especially like the idea with the mouse cursor on messages: no longer overlapping the text.

This game demonstrates the overlooked importance of simplicity.
The game uses a lot of dirty methods to make you want to progress in the game. EVERYWHERE is an opportunity to level up or complete an achievement. This game would be a dangerous free to play game, it was apparently at one point was one. With the massive variety of weapon unlocks you need to grind for, there is ALWAYS something to look forward to that gets you practically addicted to the game.
It's a fun, relaxing, game with a great variety of color... something lacking in modern games, color. You have a vairety of modes, such as trying to shoot targets, trying to shoot through rings before hitting other players, a mode where everyone versus a single player with a massive amount of health, etc. It's great it has variety, but the modes basically don't deliver the same amount of fun as do the normal free for all or team battle modes.
It also has a variety of maps you can play on, a good number of them feeling unfair to some of the players balance wise, and they're so terribly simple I just don't understand why they don't just give players some form of map editor. Over time, these maps rebalnce themselves within battle, giving players otherwise potentially stuck in a hole some wiggle room. You cannot create tunnels in the game, which arguably is a good thing due to most weapons not being designed for them. So if you ever are in a hole and did not upgrade your tank to drive up steep hills, you're probably stuck until you make yourself a ramp which can, at anytime, be sabotaged by other players.
You can upgrade your tank in a variety of ways. It's not super diversed in exactly how you can upgrade it, some trees feel lacking in fact as if the developer ran out of ideas. Despite that, it does the job right and makes you really feel you're designing the tank based on your playstyle more than how the game wants you to play. You even have a "luck" tree which increases your odds  of getting good weapons, even if you have not unlocked these weapons yet.
Each weapon has its very own skill tree that can unlock an improved version for you to fire at some point. Even if you unlocked the best variant of a weapon, it doesn't mean you will get it and can very well still obtain an inferior version of the weapon. For most weapons, labeling the earlier variants of the weapon "inferior" can be inaccurate for it's more about trade offs on some. This is a game where you'd have to spend a long time to completely finish and you'll likely stop playing by the time that comes for a moment.
This game doesn't have a whole lot of gameplay, so you will likely play it a lot for a moment and then slowly take breaks and coming back until you stop all together. However, you will definitely most likely play it again at some point. Despite the simplicity and the grindy design of the game, it's a good game. For the price, it isn't too bad of an investment as long you have other friends on board.
There is some problems, however. Though few, some players use various exploits that is impossible to detect in game, such as rulers. Because of this, it's hard to know if players are good or cheating which causes a lot of drama. This game has, multiple times, attempted to fix this with various methods and all of them were more toxic than the cheaters in my honest opinion. One example was nudging, which only hurts the players playing honestly since what it did was adjust shots slightly, causing it so the good players no longer have the feel of the game and the cheaters to simply adjust their measurments method. Another example was like nudging, but randomized, meaning ALL players are going to have inconsistent shots, except the players already bad at the game will be even worse and the cheaters will still be dominate. There is a wind option, which is honestly a good mechanic despite it not being a good tool against cheaters since it makes the game fresh and more challenging.
Another problem is that the game implements tank customization, but you literally have like five options for each piece. This might be an exaggeration, it could be less. I feel that it could give more variety, some way. I believe it's difficult because of how simple the tanks are, the developer probably has no clue what else to really implement other than what is already available.
This problem exists in a lot of areas in the game. Maps and weapons have an overwhelmingly huge variety, but other areas do not most likely due to, as mentioned, lack of ideas. This doesn't hurt the game in anyway, but it's worth noting that the game does sometimes feel empty in some areas.
Pros-
Great weapon variety
Lots of progression opportunities to casually introduce other parts of the game
Solid gameplay
Cons-
Some bad maps for fair play
VERY grindy
cheating is very easy
lacking in content in some areas, such as tank customization.
Overall, I believe 7/10 is a deserved score. It's a great game and I think every gamer that likes laid back  gaming sessions should consider this. However, it's not by anymeans revolutionary but it never really was meant to be. It's just fun.

Over 250 hours on consoles in this game. TALK ABOUT REPLAYABILITY. Killing a boss with the same weapon over and over stays fun, then add in the game has so many different weapons, strats, armors, spells, equipment. It's an RPG where the the role you play is dude that slays monsters, the thing that makes it personal is how you do it, and in what order, and which you skip and so on.
If a person beats a game 1 time and then drops it I can understand because most games don't allow for largely different playthroughs. I don't often restart in single player games myself. In Dark Souls though it has a connection to Rogue Likes, where restarting isnt a chore or boring, its a core part of experiencing everything the game has to offer. Sure you could do everything on 1 character, some people do that, but the simplest way to taste the full variety of it is to "roll" new characters. I had atleast 10.
I would highly recommend at the least playing through the game with 3 largely different characters, dont try to be a jack of all trades. Find a theme you enjoy and make a character to fit it. There is a huge aspect of this game's community just relating to Fashion Souls or making a sick looking character. By having that cool character killing a boss you've killed times before stays fresh because the equipment you wear changes how you play.
The bosses in this game are the main attraction, mobs populate the world so it aint so empty. The bosses are designed to have wildly different types of aggression, attacks, defenses, and themes. Everybody loves to argue over who the best bosses are and who is their favorite. Some of my favorite are really easy, but they have an awesome theme song, or look, or cool lore. Some are also plain bad, the game basically ran out of funding near the end of development so there are a few notorious bosses in the game. I just like to think they add character, this game isnt an angel.
Something I never did do with this game is play it blind, I found out about it by watching streams on Twitch. So when I did buy it I had already seen every boss. Since this game however I have bought and played all the newer games blind and they are quite the experience. Although I do always look forward to getting into wikis to see what awesome armors and weapons I missed to be used for new characters.
This is most definitly an RPG series for the history books.

"There are a lot of zombie games, but this one looks old, but feels fresh"
Game overall is very good and deep, and has nicely executed gameplay mechanics that make you occupied for long time, just because you come back to it for more. You need to gather supplies in order to survive, but also you need to keep people in top shape by wiping out infestations, killing hordes, gathering supplies and eventually take them outside of base and kill some zombies together with them to make them feel more clever. Base too small? Find another one, and order everybody to move to it. You've been long time outside of base exploring the area? Your character will get tired and eventually run out of stamina (or the stamina bar will be impossible to fill fully). When you'll get hurt too many times, your health lowers and you need to switch to other characters. Lost your character? It's gone. You cannot have it back. This is the main thing I love in this game. When you loose one of characters, it hurts, this character is gone. This is when I realised that dialogs and overall - story - of characters is very good and nicely written. At some point I felt so emotionally connected with Markus (main character you start as first time) that when I died while playing as him, I've started game again from the beggining, because I didn't want to loose him. Did I mention that game is open world? Yes it is, you can do whatever you want untill whole map will eventually run out of resources. That is another unique thing about this game. Nothing respawns. Crashed your car and it exploded? You loose it. Gathered supplies from nearby house? They're gone. They never respawn. This adds so much realism to the game, and fear that you need to take risks in order to survive. You can also get some new freeloaders to your base. Of course it will be possible to switch to them, after you fullfill tasks they give you (going to their base and dropping supplies), or just after bringing them to your base. Generally speaking, there is a lot to do, and this review will not cover all of this stuff, you just need to find out more by yourself.
Technically speaking, this game is pretty outdated. Graphics are somewhat old looking, but they're not ugly. Just textures could use better resolution, and animations could use some more fixing. Well, we cannot expect much as Undead Labs ported this game from Xbox 360, where it was successfull as it is now on PC. It runs on CryEngine 3. First I thought it was Unity 3D, but after some readings I've discovered it uses Crytek's engine. I thought that it pretty much wasted it's potential. As mentioned above animations are sometimes jerky, and doesn't fit the situation. Some textures are ugly, low res, but overall, it's not ugly to the point to make you puke. Performance is pretty poor on Ultra Spec. It does run noticably better at High Spec (Graphic options are named like this) with 60FPS, but does have some drops to 40 in towns. My PC is not top notch, I have i3-3.2 GHz, 4GB RAM, Radeon HD7850 2GB, but still it could use some more 'love' to make it run smoothly. Game has very limited graphic options (one slider) but it does job well improving the performance.
Controls. Game lacks some stuff that could come in handy for some group of players. I dislike forced Mouse Acceleration. Thank god Undead Labs added rebindable keyboard bindings, so it's easier to configure and play.
Game does not have multiplayer and will never have. Developers stated a lot of times that this game won't have any possible coop or multiplayer. It's all reserved for upcoming Class4 (this game is Class3) and honestly? In single player it plays so well that I didn't even noticed lack of multiplayer.
Overall, game is worth the money, so is upcoming 'Breakdown' DLC which will only add some more of gameplay. Game has enough content to make you occupied for looooong time. It's best zombie game to date, it looks old, but feels fresh despite it's obvious flaws. Undead Labs - Congratulations.

This is the game I have been looking for since the Zombie Hype following "DayZ".
It combines a Survival Game with fun fights (nothing beats fighting zombies with wrestling moves), several home bases, which can be upgraded and customized for your way of playing and rudimentary role-playing elements.
And it is all completely Single Player. For some this might be a reason not to buy, but for this player it was the argument that sold the game. The game has a permadeath system and adapted it perfectly for a SP game. The player does not start with "his own" character. You rather start the story join a group of survivor, all playable for the character.
All the characters in the game get exhausted and get debuffs through this. The player than has to return to the home base and choose another survivor to continue. This system is extremely fun as you can develop several different characters and ways of playing the game within one playthrough.
Another mechanic which makes this game great is the resource management. The survivors don't spend all day with slaying zombies and driving around town. Most of the time cabinets, crates and all kinds of storage stuff is searched and looted. The player has to do this as the home base needs four resources. Food, to keep everyone well fed; Ammo, with a lot ammo in stock the home base has a decent supply of ammo for every firearm; Materials, to build and upgrade the home base and outposts, and medicine, this act the same way as ammo does a lot of supply equals lots of drugs at the home base.
The most fun part of the game is the fighting. The player can either fight with blunt, sharp or heavy melee weapons or several firearms. The range of melee weapons goes from table legs to sledgehammers to cavalry sabres. Melee combat is mostly used in the game as guns are loud and the zombies react to sounds.
This review just touches the surface of the game but I really hope that it helped you in any way.

Attila TW is probably the most frustrating to play out of the entire TW series
Why?
The entire premise of city management is balancing population "public order" (happiness) and resource production
City buildings give maybe 1-5 happy while it costs 30= food each season
Building food producing buildings causes social unrest for some reason, offsetting the happiness gained from your city building. To cover this you need to build "communal grounds" which give +public order but costs enormous food consumption. Building industry also causes enourmous unrest. Trying to balance this will plunge your cities into social unrest very quickly.
Food is shared amongst your entire empire, but individual regions suffer unrest if they aren't producing enough food for themselves, making it very difficult to see where the food is being produced and who needs it the most. You have to station a full army stack in a region to give enough public order to come out even. Sending this army out to do army stuff will often cause negative order and will cause a rebellion if not stationed back in the city soon.
One stack vs one stack battles are normal and mostly problem free. The problems arise when four or five armies (stacks) do battle. Auto resolve lets the game resolve the battle without playing them. Unless you have a huge numbers superiority it is almost always better to play them yourself. When you have more than one army, the game only lets you control one army at a time, with units trickling in from the borders (often far enough away that they will have no effect on the main combat). If you need certain units that could turn the tide for you, like cavalry, archers or seige engines you are unable to choose your army makeup before or during setup.
The main antogonists of the game, they will rampage through the map razing any cities in their way. So what can you do against them? Almost nothing really, when you have one stack in your borders and they do the plundering thing, your food production can be crippled, causing famine and decimating your armies very fast. When the Huns have no other target except you, expect 4 or 5 death stacks ready to seige you. If you like getting BTFO at turn 150 then you might enjoy the game. Battle AI for the huns is really cheesy as well. If you are in terrain advantage like a steep hill, the huns will refuse to attack you and will sit in thier deployment zone and not move. If you move against them they will use mobility and encircle you and surely win. Waiting out a 60 minute battle on x3 acceleration is not fun. On th ecampaign map if you find a lone stack of huns and can beat them, they will retreat farther than you can follow them, even if they are completely surrounded by stacks, they will still be able to run away.

Attila is a highly frustrating game that highlights many flaws with TW series as a whole.
Now that many of the bugs have been worked out, Total War Attila is a very fun game. Don't give it bad reviews because of DLC because no one is forcing you to buy them.

After 400 hours I think I can give a review.
IMO its not the best Total War, but it is a strong contender for 3rd or 4th place. Basically all the problems of Rome II are fixed, the campaign, with all the events, climate change and marauding hordes, feel dynamic and are quite challenging. As always the game starts getting good only had difficulties hard or higher, but that is to be expected.
The rosters are generally thematic, but varied, even though the rosters of some Germanic factions fall a little flat in diversity and distinctiveness. Instead, play style, starting positions and specializations (like the Naval Supremacy of the Vandals) influence and partially dictate your play style. The Eastern, Nomadic and Roman factions do not suffer from any sort of limited rosters and feel distinct from each other, as well as prior factions of earlier Total War games.
The Migrating factions really are an amazing addition, even if they are not as fun to play for some people, they are a great AI addition at worst.
The Huns specifically are menacing, but they behave very differently from the Mongols of TWM2. Instead of basically being a natural disaster, they start more like a band of bandits and and ruffians and as they accumulate wealth and have 6 to 10 elite fullstacks around the map they become a real threat to even the most developed empires.
Desolation is also a pretty great mechanic, however it should be adjusted with a resettling/ colonization mod, since otherwise whole swaths of the map remain basically empty until the end of the game, which is interesting for some time, but ultimately it adds very little.
The unit-balancing is fine, but cavalry seems a little to strong, missiles are very deadly, which is fine and adds a lot of momentum to the battles. Naval battles are actually very fun now and the Naval factions of the game are extremely fun to play. Instead of overloading every ship with an insane amount of commands they are now split into range, ramming and boarding, so that even the AI knows what to do.

Love the depth, you truly feel immersed as the ruler of a kingdom, the commander of an army, and within the politics and infrastructure of your nation. This game even has a certain degree of customization, you can name your armies, pick their battle standard, choose the traditions such as increased attack, higher income from raiding, decreased to no attrition from winter conditions and much much more. You can also rename cities, and villages. Every decision you make has good or bad consequences. Choosing to name another man within the family tree your heir and disinheriting your current heir causes a drop in loyalty. To much disloyalty can lead to a civil war and a separatist off shoot faction of your own faction. Sacking a settlement vs occupying can get you riches but lead to provincial instability. Moving your army from a city or town to invade another faction or fight a battle can lead to victory and the capture of new lands, yet leaving your lands unprotected open the way for other armies to invade wreaking havoc amongst your lands. This game is all about strategy, well thought out choices, and finding the balance between military, economic, religious, political, and many other things concerned with the success of your kingdom, empire, nation, etc. I recommend this game to any one that enjoys history, watching armies fight bloody battles sometimes down to the last man, and feeling like the ruler of your own faction. I have logged countless hours in this game, conquered 75% of the map as the Saxons, and played several other campaigns as the Visigoths, Picts, Alemans and Langobards, (my favorite factions tend to be Germanic tribes due to their fierce warriors), but all of the factions have their perks. This game can be somewhat unforgiving to new players but if you play on easy and listen to all of the advice and play the prologue you can learn quickly. It took some mistakes and failed kingdoms to teach me a few lessons but this is without a doubt my favorite game and I've owned it for atleast a year or two.

I've quite a history when it comes to playing infinity engine games and D&D oriented games in general and I can not in good faith recommend this game for the price it's being offered. I've played Baldur's Gate 1 and 2, including the expansion throne of Bhaal. Yes I've played Icewind Dale 1 and 2 and even Neverwinter nights 1 and 2.
Pillars of Eternity just doesn't measure up, in large part due to the laziness of the developers and an overall lack of innovation. This is the first time I've played through a Bioware/Obsidian rooted game and skipped through the text conversations out of the shear dreariness/tediousness of the story in PoE. If the idea of micromanaging every action of your party members sounds appetizing, then you might very well enjoy this game, that is if the bugged AI and invisible walls don't ruin your experience, as quite regularly you will find that your party members will twitch or stand around aimlessly while you attempt to slog through the game's ever boring world. I paid $38 for this and regret doing so, for those infinity engine fans wishing to purchase this game, I would suggest waiting for a price drop and paying no more than $8. Don't believe the hype, this is not the lovingly made Baldur's gate successor you had hoped for.

The game has amazing visuals, good music, and endearing writing that you'll feel right at home with if you're familiar with Andrew Hussie's other works. Because of all those reasons, I can look past the minor bugs, the horrendously limited video settings, or even the fact that it's supposedly only 3 hours long. But one fatal flaw that I cannot forgive is that it's the most poorly optimized game I've ever played, no joke.
Seriously, as good as the visuals are, a game of this magnitude could have been pulled off in the early to mid 2000's and run butter smooth on low end machines of that era no problem. Instead, the game overheats my admittedly dated laptop in a matter of minutes, and chugs during cutscenes. By comparison, I can play both seasons of TellTale's The Walking dead for hours and only occasionally have to close it to let my laptop cool down. There's no excuse as to why I can run those games, but not this.
I'm not forgetting that this is a freaking 2D point and click adventure. HD or not, what could possibly be eating up so many resources? The most taxing thing it would need to do is render a few layers of animated bitmaps. The other things like music, cutscenes, and UI are all things that have been around and haven't been innovated on since 2000. I suspect it's due to a combination of flimsy programming, and a bunch of junk tacked on by the Unity engine that the game doesn't even need. The game honestly would have been better off being built from the ground up.
You might not be able to empathize with me if you have even a decent computer by today's standards, but if you're like me and you're too broke to afford a new computer to replace your toaster that you've managed to keep running for half a decade, then I can't recommend this game. The minimum requirements page is misleading, and even then, it still shouldn't take that much processing power to run a 2D point & click adventure.

Varied and in some cases quite challenging Grand Campaign start conditions, objectives, and playstyles save Attila from being just a glorified Rome 2 expansion pack.  The addition of horde mechanics, nasty disease systems, the razing of cities, and various other intricate and reactive systems make the Grand Campaign experience notably deeper and more chaotic.
The combat experience is much like my preferred mod loadout for Rome 2: fast and lethal, rewarding creative engagement positioning and well-timed unleashing of hell.  The AI here is solid as it's ever been, covering its units well and generally reacting to threats, but it was never the spotlight of the Total War series, nor particularly creative; and that doesn't change here.  The campaign AI, on the other hand, seems as devilish as it's been since the magnum opus that was Shogun 2.
Many of the game's other downsides like limited vanilla faction selections tend to tie in to the game's DLC model, by now familiar to Total War fans.  I can't recommend this one at full price even adoring Total War, and increasingly loving Attila, just because of the piecemealing of content that is usually roughly twice as expensive as it should have been, and of inconsistent quality and quantity.
From the brutal demands of prioritizing your many needs and your limited resources as the Western Roman Empire to the brutal reality of razing settlements as the Huns only to realize you can no longer feed your army, Attila delivers exactly the experiences it promises, and might have alternately been titled Total War: Dark Age.  With Workshop support and the admirable Total War mod community, this one is especially fun to conquer.

ShellShock Live is a game that initially started as a flash game on Kongregate, however the developers evolved it into much more by having it be a paid game with a new coat of paint and a lot more features and improvements over the flash game. However the one thing I do miss is the ability to play pong in-game when you're dead. It's sort've like Worms where it's either a free-for-all, where one player lines up his shot and fires, and then the next. Or one entire team lines up their shot and fires, then the next team. There's special shots, such as 'earthquake' and 'backroller' (which rolls backwards if you shoot behind an enemy, hitting them anyways) or the 'tunneler' which is self-explanatory. There is, in-fact, at least a few hundred different kinds of shots that you can unlock as you level up and finish more matches. As you level up you can also customize your tank and upgrade its abilities which are not by any means gamebreaking, as the matches are recommended by your level.
All in all, for seven dollars, it's a pretty solid game especially if you're poor and bored.

Puzzle difficulty ramps up at a nice pace, and you get all your abilities in the first five minutes of play, so it's not like a game where you bang your head against a wall only to learn there's some other gizmo you need first.  I did have to read a walkthrough for the solution to one puzzle, but only because I didn't realize a certain something could be done slightly differently than I'd been doing it for all previous puzzles.  The story is excellent, and wonderfully delivered.  The only tip I have for new players is turn on subtitles, as the occasional dialogue can be lost due to ambient sound and music.
Big thumbs up from me.  It didn't have quite the emotional impact of Limbo or Inside but it was close.

Some players might argue that since you only control what amount of what type of creatures you summon, makes the game too simple, and does not give the player enough strategizing options, but i have to disagree, the fact that your options are limited makes strategy even more important in my opinion.
Hear me out on that one, if played in ranked, one player of each team bans a commander skill, and another bans a troop. What you think your ennemy might play factors a lot into that choice, let's say you faced an oponent before, and you know he prefers terrans, banning terran skills and troops might force him out of his comfort zone.
then once in-game, MANY choices are in front of you, do you produce mass low tier troops? do you produce minimal amount needed to hold back the ennemies to save for early tier 2 or 3?? then you need to make decisions to counter the ennemy tactics, for example, they have no anti-air early on, instead of your usual tactics you then produce flying troops to force them to adapt, etc.
Also after playing a while and gathering a lot of currencies you start unlocking advanced troops, then again adding another level of strategy to the game, as some troops are "weaker" but have amazing active abilites you then must decide when to use.
All in all, GREAT game!! can't wait for the actual release!

Okay so I finally finished Act 1 and I believe it's about time I talk about it properly ;
Hiveswap is a pretty good game. Sure, it's short. But when you rule this out, the game is really good imo. The characters are very likable and dynamic - even the ones who're not introduced properly yet, the artstyle of the game is really pleasant and reminds me of the comic without being too sketchy, the musics... are good, since james roach and toby fox did the job, and the writting is honestly well done even though Hussie wasn't the one in charge.
If you're searching for a game including reflexion and deep puzzles, or action and reflexes, I can't recommand Hiveswap to you. Hiveswap is a game about exploring, going with the flow, experimenting with various items or simply following a story without worrying about how good you're doing. If you're the kind of person who'd attempt to spray spices on a pigeon, feed a poster or that kind of dumb♥♥♥♥♥♥ then yes, consider Hiveswap because the game expects you to test it.
Also, I saw some non-homestuck persons wondering if the game was accessible for them : yes, it is! It happens 15 years before HS begins, so most of the characters weren't even born, and overall the game explains pretty much everything important. It just involves some references you won't catch, but nothing really problematic.
Anyway I'm hella hyped to see the rest. WP announced the other acts will take less time to come than this one, hopefully in 2018 we'll get something!

The writing and story are on point, and frequently had me genuinely laughing, not that amused snort that is often equated to "lol". Yeah, it's not the longest game ever, and there are a few finnicky niggles here and there (The resolution starts out at the minimum, and you need to restart the game for the resolution change to take effect, the cutscenes are a little glitchy), but its certainly worth all of five quid for 3 hours first playthrough and double that to mess around and hunt for things, when its just _that funny and engaging_. This is Act 1 of 4 (supposedly), and there's talk of a counterpart game series telling the other side of the swap later called Hauntswitch. That said, it doesn't end on a massive cliffhanger, merely a open pause, and I doubt the next parts will take as long as Act 1 took to materialise (They've been working on them simultaneously, the engine is written, etc). Maybe you' also be disappointed too if you'd built up grand expectations in the meantime, but for what it is? I'd say it's a new classic of point-and-click.
Now if you'll excuse me, I'm gonna go grab some lunch and dive back in to go hunting for things.

Normally I wouldn't write full in-depth review for an early access game. It would be kind of unfair to do so considering the full experience of the game has yet to come. However there are things I would like to talk about and address to both new players and the developers.
The best way to describe Savage Lands, it's like a combination between The Forest and Elder Scrolls.
Keeping in mind that this game is early access, it does have its problems. Unlike the typical early access game where you usually experience connection issues, lag, glitches, etc. this game is actually pretty well built without these issues. Loads times are actually pretty phenomenal and there are little issue involving bugs/ glitches, at least from what I have experienced. A couple de-syncs every so often, however that is most likely becuase we had three players connected to a private hosted server via the same local connection. The main issue with the game is the lack in overall content however that is to be expected.
In the feature list under the game description, there are two 'features' I would like to address.
Robust Item Crafting and Intuitive Build System.
Before I delve into the issues with these features, I would like to state that I am fully aware and understand that Signal Studios has not released all the content yet, hence 'early access', however at this time, the descriptions of these features are not accurate. Mind you, these are listed as "Early Release Features", which means that they were intentionally listed as features being currently in the game. I disagree.
Robust Item Crafting
Crafting works and it's not bad, however in the description for this feature it states "Limitless Options". There is a lot of potential with the crafting, so I have no doubt that the developers are going to be progressing the possibilities making this description more accurate, currently however, it's just to far from limitless for this description to be accurate. There are only a handful of craftable weapons/ tools and armor, and a good portion of them require harder to get and rarer materials.
Intuitive Building System
If you have ever played The Forest, the building system is exactly the same. Its simple, but there isn't really much you can build other than a few structures. I would really like to see more structures added as well as customization, decoration, and more function added for the structures as well. As of right now, other than getting a couple of achievements  it's really not worth the time and effort to build anything. Find a pre-existing city on the map and make base, it will have everything you need already minus strong boxes.
As for the rest of the listed current features, the descriptions are fairly accurate. The world is anything but forgiving and you never know when an enemy is going to charge at you out of nowhere unless you are in an open area and even then, if you aren't paying attention to your surroundings, you will find trouble pretty quick, or rather trouble will find you. The AI system is spot on and the combat is indeed brutal and can get pretty intense. Perhaps a little too intense. One minute you are chasing a deer, then suddenly you are fighting a Dire Wolf that popped out from the bushes. Next minute you are fighting a whole pack of them. But hey, what fun would the game be if the combat were too easy? The game certainly teaches you to stay aware of your surroundings. The game is more fun in multiplayer, albeit if you want more of a challenge, play solo.
Overall, the game is very fun and addicting. I would even go as far to say it is the best early access game I have played to date, even with its limited content. With that said, there is still plenty to do while the developers are working hard to bring us more content. I actually would not mind collaborating with the developers and sharing ideas for future content, as this game has some great potential to be one of the best open world survival games to date and I would love to see this game succeed. So if any developers are reading this, feel free to add and/or message me. I would gladly share some ideas and options. Nonetheless, keep up the great work.

A lot of people will tell you "play it, it's hard". I'll tell you "play it, it's hard, AND good".
The game is really good.
This game is basically the Chuck Norris of JRPG. It's so new and refreshing in the genre that most people don't even think it's a JRPG.
-Universe-
Finally a game wich understand the importance of realism. Instead of being all monster Hunter like, it shows you normal soldiers, with normal armors and normal sized weapons, and when you get used to it, they show you dragons and giant knights. So when you see them for the first time, you're like "god, those random guys were tough, so how the hell do I beat THIS guy ?!"
You play the oh so classic random guy who doesn't know anything about the world you're in, and you get the lore through dialogues and item descriptions.
Also, this game doesn't care about cutscene. You have some cutscenes, yeah, but only for non-interactive moments. In most game, when someone betray you, you have a big♥♥♥♥♥cutscene with the music and the dialogues basically telling you "be careful, he's a bad guy". In this game, you just get attacked in real time. In other games, when someone sacrifice for you, they will simply put a cutscene and ask if you want to save him or not. In this game, you can fight by his side or leave in real time, you even have the choice to kill the ennemies before he encounters them. Hell, some actions are so logical you don't even think you could do them in games. Like, killing an ennemy supposed to kill you're buddy before he get's there, and it actually works. And he actually has dialogues for the rest of the game.
The universe is really intriguing, not because it's particulary original, (after all, it's all knights and dragons...), but because you discover it yourself, you make your own theories, and everything collapse because you find another item that contradict the rest.
Personaly, I was so enticed by the world of Dark Souls that I kept coming back to it even though the game bashed my skull against the floor.
Also, the levels are really complexe, there are a lot of paths, and the game rewards observance, via secret passages (a lot of them), or even shortcuts (wich are incredibly useful, because you can't teleport until like three quarters of the game).
-Gameplay-
Your guy evolve with stats. Weapons have treshold, wich means that, unlike in Skyrim, where leveling up let you do the exact same thing but with bigger numbers, in Dark Souls, a mage characters will stumble with a greatsword, being unable to carry it even with two hands, only being able to wave it around, nearly falling down, while a strong character can wield two of those with ease.
On the opposite side, a strong character might not even be able to cast a basic spell, while a mage can spam the strongest spell in the game. This way, you actually have a meaningful progress. You work toward having enough dexterity to wield this katana, or enough strenght to carry this armor, or enough faith to summon this miracle.
You can have a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of builds this way, and the armors are really bad, wich is actually a good thing, because it means you can wear what you want, for stats are only useful on weapons and shields.
The game is hard, but it's not artificial difficulty, good players who knows how Dark Souls Work can complete the game very quickly, sometimes without even dying. It's all about timing (for rolls and parry) and knowledge of patterns.
I did not play a lot of PVP, but it has been one of the core aspect of the franchise since the beginning, spawning entire memes (looking at you, giantdad). Compared to Dark Souls III, poise is a thing, so the meta is a bit more varied, allowing you to try funny builds (even saw a fast roll smough with a katana...)
-TL DR-
It's good, not because it is difficult, but because it's simply good...
It's so good that it makes you come back even though it kills you and make you rage.
In the end, when you "git gud", you'll find other games disappointing, you have been warned.

I've quite a history when it comes to playing infinity engine games and D&D oriented games in general and I can not in good faith recommend this game for the price it's being offered. I've played Baldur's Gate 1 and 2, including the expansion throne of Bhaal. Yes I've played Icewind Dale 1 and 2 and even Neverwinter nights 1 and 2.
Pillars of Eternity just doesn't measure up, in large part due to the laziness of the developers and an overall lack of innovation. This is the first time I've played through a Bioware/Obsidian rooted game and skipped through the text conversations out of the shear dreariness/tediousness of the story in PoE. The combat is dull and a step backwards from the scripted companion AI in the infinity engine games. If the idea of micromanaging every action of your party members sounds appetizing, then you might very well enjoy this game, that is if the bugged AI and invisible walls don't ruin your experience, as quite regularly you will find that your party members will twitch or stand around aimlessly while you attempt to slog through the game's ever boring world. I should also mention the fact that your party stops getting xp from battles after getting enough kills of certain mobs and completing that mob's beastiary, making battles an annoyance and borefest later in the game).
I paid $38 for this and regret doing so, for those infinity engine fans wishing to purchase this game, I would suggest waiting for a price drop and paying no more than $8. Don't believe the hype, this is not the lovingly made Baldur's gate successor you had hoped for.

Well, this is clearly an Obsidian game.  As.. bugs.. more  bugs than a cheap motel.   More on that in a minute though.
This is what an RPG should be in my opinion.  You can make your own custom characters, or not.  You can pick up people you meet in the world and take them along doing their story driven quests, or not.  You can build your little castle up, or not.  There is a lot of stuff in this game that if you do not wish to do you can skip.  You are never boxed into helping a companion with their side missions, but you will want to.  They are just that well written.  Each has their own personality, each has their own opinions about the things you do and see.
Combat is also fun, but a challenge.  Early on I kept losing a fight in the endless dungeon.  A room full of Lizard people and a drake kept demolishing my party.  Finally I got it in my head that I was going to park my 2 heavy soldiers in a door way and use them to force the on coming enemies into a narrow path so I could control the situation better.  Sent my ranger out, shot a little lizard person for his attention and ran half way across the level to my waiting party all kinds of bad things in tow.  I owned that fight.  The fight that had beaten me several times before.  It was extremely rewarding to not only beat that battle but beat it in such away that none of my people took a lot of damage either.   Tactics matter.
So the game is fun.  The game is compelling.  The game is also broken.   I cast a spell with my wizard Aloth (sadly he's the one that you meet not one I made) and now he can't do anything.  He can't swap weapons, he can't cast anymore spells.  Anything you hand him dissapears he is broken.   Other companions forget their spells when you take them out of your party for a while.  My chanter forgot most of his chants when I parked him at home for a while.  These are very frustrating things.  If you notice them quick enough you can just reload an earlier save and be alright with it.  If you don't and you save several times before picking up on the fact that your chanter in fact no longer chants it is not a really great feeling.  Also, I made a ranger, who comes with a companion pet.  If the pet dies and my character does not but I choose to reload because I did almost die or everyone else got killed my pet vanishes.  You can't leave the level, you have to gather your party before venturing forth.. but you can't because mr wolf is now in the ether.   It doesn't matter which save I load at that point he's gone in all of them until I completely quit the game and go back in.  Less of a problem than my wizard, but annoying.
So.. bottom line is I'm pretty sure Aloth is just broken.  My chanter has forgotten the chants that seriously helped my party... and I think I am going to start over again and avoid the things that caused both of those problems.. and that should say everything.  It's busted but I'm still going to work through it.  It's a great game if you can overlook it's flaws.

One of the best FPS ever.
That's the short review, but here's the rest.
This is definitely the best game from Cauldron, a small developer that was able to make their own, amazing, engine (kinda like few other small ones, like Croteam). It's weird because many of the other games developed by them ranges from "meh" to "uninstall right away", and most are just average.
That's why this one comes by surprise when you play it: it looks awesome, it's huge, has the old-school feeling that, even in those years, was getting lost, and has that something that makes you keep playing until you reach its end.
It's not perfect by any means, and it shows its age in many aspects, but once you get used to its bugs and the quick-save key, you'll be fully immersed in this fun, and very hard, classic FPS experience.
The main problem about this game is the enemies, that are able to see you and "snipe" you with any weapon they are carrying from any place they are hiding in. You always have to be on the lookout for them, and always have a cover spot to quickly use in case of an encounter (which, in most cases, is a multiple encounter). That isn't making the game impossible, but you gotta have a very good aim, even at normal difficulty, to take them down before they do the same to you (headshots highly recommended). You also need to save often, and I really mean it.
The good thing is that this game uses healthpacks and armor bonuses, so you can just not collect them until needed, like we all old gamers used to do back then.
It's easy to ragequit this game, because some enemies are simply unforgiving, or because you died and forgot to save close to there, but you'll come back to it until you finally complete it if you like old-school shooters. The graphics still are enjoyable to this day, in my opinion, because of the nice quality of the textures and models, the amount of the special effects (including the spectacular glass breaking) and the sci-fi setup. Good music and proper sound effects, though the voice acting is the usual B-movie kind.
Last but not least, there's some variety in the levels. Not only in their looks, that are very different from level to level, which keeps the experience fresh, but also because of some different from the usual objectives, like sniping enemies from a tower, or diving underwater. This game has basically them all, just like in AAA titles.
I have no idea if multiplayer still works or is populated. When I played this game ages ago it was basically dead already, but it felt fun when I actually could find someone online, with some different modes than just DM/TDM.
I think that if you're a FPS lover, this must be in your library. I already had it from back then but I purchased it again on Steam while on sale just because it's worth keeping it around, forever.

The CloakNT engine remains one of my favorites, as I love its scalability, looks, feel, and editing tools. Cauldron pulled off some interesting effects in the engine like dynamically lit particle effects, tesselated water surface that reacts to gunfire impacts, hybrid static/dynamic lighting and shadowing, realistic glass/wood breakables engine, environmental effects (environment impacts scope ring [fog, ice, dirt, etc], emissives from bullet impacts (shoot pipes or pressured glass windows), etc. A lot of these things are absent entirely from modern games/engines. It is a sad testament to the negative impact of console gaming.
The engine also is capable of rendering very large areas with long viewsheds with minimal performance cost. They did some really awesome things behind the scenes in the CloakNT engine, which is made even more impressive by the fact that the engine was created in-house from the ground up.
Combat is pure oldschool and twitchy; good stuff.
Music is superb, visual style is great (if inconsistent), and levels sprawl! They're huge, if sometimes a bit lacking in interactivity.
I love the variety of environments you find in this game, as well as the various play mechanics you'll use along the way.
Story is a cliche made of tropes and other cliches, but it works to good effect.
Main voice actor sounds like John Wayne. What isn't to like?
Multiplayer is fun and quick, a nice mix of Q3A and CS IF you can find a low-ping server. Lag compensation is ♥♥♥♥♥♥ at best and anything above about 100ms you'll start to have lots of wtf moments.
There are a few cheaters unfortunately, but a good game can be had most of the time.
Do yourself a favor and get it for the massive singleplayer alone (20+hours)

In my opinion this game is the best of the Series, because it's the least streamlined one with the most choices and freedom of play and with the least amount of completely linear nerfhearding tunnelmaps. The combat in ME3 is better, but the cost is too high.
Pro:
+ Lots of different guns and armor with a ton of different mods. Lots of useless ones too.
+ Lots of dialogue and very few cutscenes.
+ Pretty funny dialogue choices at times, especially the Renegade options can be pretty funny and abusive.
+ Big square planet maps & the Mako. The only game in the ME series with a tactical choice.
+ Experience points for Kills. Time to go hunting for Thresher Maws & Geth!
+ Unlimited ammo, but with overheating and recoil. Nice diversity of guns and mechanics.
+ Import of previous 'veteran' characters.. Practically no level limit..
+ Lots of skills.
Cons:
- The dialogue choices doesn't quite reflect what's being said. Quite often far from it. It's a gamble. How's that RPG?
- Quite often different dialogue options leads to the same result or none at all. Just for show.
- Once you are overloaded you can't sort through your entire inventory to scrap the least useful ones in favor of the last additions, which often happens to be a lot better than anything else you've got.. (Bleh, Of course).
- No three-some!! Just like any other BioWare game it enforce ancient and unnatural monogamous relationships.

Also, Jennifer Hale's voice acting as Femme-Shep is exquisitely charged with passion and verve!  Strong female protagonist, if you choose for Shepherd to be female.   I, frankly, found the male voice actor to be neutral in his emotions too often.  I don't believe he threw himself into the role as much.
Jennifer Hale sounds like she's the hero who held off a Batarian raid of a human colony single-handedly and against all odds.
Anyway, I digress.  If you have the money to burn, and want a good story, this is one of the best in sci-fi. (Mass Effect 3's ending being the only highly-contested part of that statement.)

In my opinion, Mass Effect is like what Knights of the Old Republic could have been if Bioware had more freedom. Which they did. It's obvious from the story, and from the gameplay, that Bioware wanted to make a truly interesting and captivating experience. I've always considered myself more of a fan of traditional fantasy RPGs, but Mass Effect's characters and world are more than enough to earn this game a spot in my favourite RPGs of all time. I have very few complaints about this game, the only major one being Kaidan.
He sounds exactly like Carth, for God's sake. And I don't know a single person who likes Carth.

If you’re a fan of either sci-fi mystery or puzzle games, I can’t recommend this enough. Fantastically atmospheric, with a compelling philosophical theme that reveals itself at just the right pace, and nicely ties the central gameplay mechanic to the story. The score is stunning and perfectly complements the dream-like feel of the game.
The compact puzzles that make up the substance of the gameplay combine just a few simple concepts to produce a surprising amount of variety, and I felt the difficulty was pitched just about right. There are refreshingly few technical demands, but plenty to test your spatial reasoning and imagination.
I played this on a Core i3 laptop with onboard HD4000 graphics and it was mostly fine, with a little bit of chugginess towards the end, but not enough to interfere with gameplay.

On a lot of technical levels, this game is good. It's well executed, at any rate. But is that enough?
When I play a puzzle game, I want something that *really* makes me think - about the puzzles, about myself, about the world, something. Technical excellence simply isn't enough. Without the depth of gameplay that many other games can provide - through combat, creating things, destroying things, economics, strategy, character building - and without a world with exploration or characters to get lost in, I can't really find anything to this game that makes me stop and go "wow".
The clay animations are excellent, the voice acting is good, the plot's alright, and the puzzles are tricky, but nothing about this game made my jaw drop, although right up until the end I was hoping it might do so. In the end, it just kinda felt like yet another puzzle platformer with a single gimmick. And even though it was a competent specimen, that's not enough to recommend it by. Not for me.

First let me start off by clarifying that yes, my time on record is minimal (not sure why, seeing as i've played way more than 4 hours). But, I don't need 2000+ hours to accurately describe this game.
Let me cover some pros/cons for you.
+Beautiful graphics and atmospshere (night time storms got me shaking in my boots): At first i never realized that this game ran off of cryengine. But, it does and the weather and atmoshpere in this game are AMAZING because of it, especially at night. That being said, this game is probably a bit resource heavy for older computers.
+Comprehensive crafting and loot system: You can craft a lot of stuff, from structures to storage and various other things; and place it uniquely in the world. Granted some things require plots to build by, this is a minor nuisance.
+Enemies are not all zombies: Thank the heavens, the enemies are not all the same generic zombies like a certain survival game (ehem...dayz). At its current state, it has wolves as well as various types of mutants.
+UI is nice: It is clean and easy to use. Characters react decently to the enviroment and the ability to eat food quickly without having to pick it up first is a godsend.
+Combat is engaging: All weapons are a bit different in their use and range, and they fixed the reloading issue so guns are more viable now.
-
: This is my number one gripe with these survival/openworld zombie games
Yes, you die and you lose everything on your body (rather it stays on your corpse until you run back and get it if someone hasnt stolen it) and spawn somewhere completely random.
Further explanation: I get it, it is supposed to be hardcore. But here is the thing, the point between when you become well-established (meaning: you dont have to spend 4 hours looking for a hatchet to build shelter, or a backpack to carry more then a can of peaches and a flashlight, etc) in the game and when your a lonely fresh spawn is quite a while. Meaning, you can reach what is essentially "getting-by" and then end up just getting killed and starting all over. Which sucks. Especially, if you have a base and supplies and your just figuring out where everything is. Add on top of that, you dont start with a map or compass even. You just end up in a bush somewhere.
My solution? Add a bedroll or bed or something like the game Unturned has that you can craft and then claim and respawn at when you die, giving you the 60sec respawn timer to spawn at your bed or a 10sec timer to spawn in a random spot if you so wish. This will give players a sense of hope in that if they die, they don't have to spend 12+ hours re-finding everything they just slaved hours beforehand finding. They won't have to search for their own base. Make the bedroll destroyable and make it so you can only utilize one. If this idea is too extreme (which, from what i've seen it works
, even on a super small map like Unturned's) make it so players
start with a map and compass so they can find the base they spent hours, if not days working on; instead of wandering around in some bushes lost AF. Please Devs, do this.
-Finding the necessary items: Don't get me wrong, the loot system in Miscreated blows DayZ's out of the water in my opinion. See con number 1. Finding the proper tools as a fresh spawn takes time and dedication. Just tonight, it took me a few hours to find a hatchet. Finally get one and get established and players will end up dying and spending another 3 hours looking for a hatchet. repeat.
-Global chat: Would like a global chat to communicate with all in the server. Option to hide it would be swell as well.
-Nameplates: I don't know if i missed this, but i think you have to be right next to someone to see their name. If it even pops up. I don't know. All i know is every person i've looked at i've had to ask for their name.
This game is great, it just needs polishing. The state it is in now is 100x better than it was a few months ago. Fix the respawn issue and i think the game would be
. Hopefully, the devs over at Miscreated see this or try the implementation of bedrolls like i suggested. Maybe stats like in unturned would be cool too. Anyhow, that is all. i give it a 8/10.  -2 for respawn problem :)

The game is making its way there and i still may try to play it, but essentially its not worth buying yet. Follow it because it may go somewhere eventually but as of right now its a beautiful looking box thats only 1/8 full.

As an avid fan of the Total War series, I had pre-ordered Rome 2. After that debacle, I swore off the Total War series and Attila just passed me by. I finally picked this up on sale after reading about it while playing Rome 2's Emperor Edition.
For me, this is the best Total War made to date. The era has never really interested me historically, so it's basically the gameplay that keeps dragging me back again and again, especially when contrasted against Warhammer. This is Total War. You can't just build full stack armies and run around adding more square footage to your empire, you have to actually manage it. Every effect has a counter effect. Balancing pros and cons actually makes you feel like you're governing an empire and that the people in it are actually there, the faceless seething mass of mankind that call themselves your subjects (or don't - steamroll the rebel scum!).
The politics, family trees, diplomacy and loyalty mechanics are beautifully executed, giving you things to do when you're not crushing skulls and burning houses. The addition of army integrity, horde factions, reinforcement direction indicators, razing or abandoning settlements, seige escalation, walled minor settlements, changing climate, disease and sanitation, fertility (!), sea sickness (!) and war weariness (I wish it were in the base game!) makes you really savour each move you make. The immersion is real. The varying play styles and huge differences in campaign objectives between the base factions make the game an insanely different from any Total War before. For example: one faction is looking for a new home, one is trying to hold on to its past glories, one is trying to unify its people and one just wants to see the world burn. This makes sure that the game is different every time you choose a new faction.
There are cons though. You definitely need an overhaul mod to make the game satisfying (like Fall of the Eagles), the AI (though drastically improved over Rome 2) is still not the sharpest tool in the shed (reinforcing armies abandon their artillery to my cavalry Every.Single.Time.), the food surplus doesn't transfer to other provinces (or.maybe my people are just greedy ♥♥♥♥s) and the fact that they removed (!) the weight icons from the unit banners (circle for light, square for medium, diamond for heavy, shaded for cavalry). These issues aren't game breaking though and mods can fix everything (still waiting for one for the last thing though).
If you want a really detailed, extremely satisfying, highly immersive, ridiculously difficult, satisfyingly (yes I know I already usd that, shut up) realistic, terrifyingly dynamic and a hair tearing paranoia inducing Total War (should I End Turn? Did I resolve all political issues? Is there an impending rebellion? Is any army in snow or in the desert? Is there a Roman army on my doorstep? Do I have to change a governor? Is my sanitation okay? Will any building get completed that will cause food shortages or maintenance penalties? What's the next season and what will be the penalties? Are my agents shamming? Are my enemies' agents shamming? Oh god I hope I don't get the plague!), then this is for you (its more fun than I made it sound). If they made a Total War: Empire 2 with these gameplay mechanics, I'd blow everybody at CA every day for a year.

This means, in the end, you're still sitting there and clicking a box a hundred times to craft each individual item.
Almost every UI is like this. There are no key shortcuts, so everytime a menu opens (such as opening a chest) there is a tedious time rearranging windows and clicking buttons that could easily have been mapped to a shortcut.
Crafting generally just feels slow and bad. There are items that you will want to craft multiple times, but they are hidden in nested menus, which makes them really annoying to get to. Since the game centers on finding items for crafting, upgrading, and building, this is a big turn off for me.
Also there are a lot of bugs and it's poorly optimized. Sometimes performance drops for no reason, and things will fail to load. My character died once, but when I respawned in the ship, the ship didn't load in, so I sat in the empty screen while a falling animation played until I died again for no reason.
I didn't play long enough to get to any interesting space-related things, but from what I've seen the early crafting trees and progression are nearly identical to Terraria, which in turn is somewhat similar to Minecraft. For something that is supposed to be Starbound and exploring the universe, it's disheartening that I'm wasting my time sorting through the same rock-and-wood-based recipes yet again on a slightly different-colored planet.
Buy it later when they fix the bugs and the gameplay. It's a promising concept and game, but it's just not fun for me and feels terrible to play.

I've been a fan of Homestuck for a few years now. I got into it maybe two or three years before the comic ended and I followed it pretty religiously to the end. So naturally going in, I was expecting Hiveswap to have the requirement of understnading the comic and all its complexity.
I am happy to report that is not the case. While reading the comic will make you catch certain references and draw conclusions, Hussie is 100% correct when he says there is NO requirement to read the comic to understand this game. So if you've never read Homestuck or are thinking about reading it, this game is still really good.
The achievements are ridiculous and that is part of the charm. The writing is over the top and that's sort of Hussie's brand of humor. If you like quirky writing Hiveswap is the game for you, even if you're not a fan of Homestuck. That being said though if you're not a fan of quirky writing, you probably won't enjoy this game.
The soundtrack is excellent, there is nothing more to say about that. Get the soundtrack edition, you won't regret it.
The game also is very easy to pick up and play even if you've never played point-and-click adventure games before. It avoids the pitfalls of the genre such as accidentally putting the game in an unwinnable state (there's always a way to progress in Hiveswap).
I would highly recommend it and for $8 it'll be a great way to spend 2-4 hours. Will definitely play again.

Overall, this game was wonderful to play and delved me deeper into the Homestuck world. The characters have a nice introduction and everything, and things are really just set up well for the first and upcoming acts. There just needs to be more meat to this all. . .
