PROS:
- Open-ended sandbox gameplay with a focus on exploration
- Large amount of building and customization options
- Great sprite art and graphics
- Wonderful soundtrack
- Better execution than No Man's Sky
CONS:
- Major bugs have not yet been fixed, such as the crew duplication issue
- Performance problems when loading busy areas and the pixel printer
- Multiplayer has a good chance of breaking your save files
- Combat is much too simplistic outside of missions
- Could use additional content and progression
Despite the numerous technical issues, I can't help but recommend "Starbound" for those looking for a fresh new sandbox game to try out. While it has a number of flaws, I feel that it does reflect that rare spirit of exploration and discovery where many other games fall flat. Just be sure to look up how to backup your save files in case of that inevitable game-breaking bug, crash and/or file corruption...

This game is fun; it has a large variety of factions (some admittedly with considerable overlap but less so than usual), the battle gameplay is much improved and the AI is far more difficult to trick and indeed defeat than ever before. However, the usual DLC issues aside, there are a few things that really irritate me. Towers have much too high an attack, siege weapons are ludicrously accurate and the building cap is the real reason I wrote this review. Please please can CA scrap this! It makes absolutely no sense - cities expand in the real world to meet the needs of their populations. I understand this is supposed to force players to make 'tough' choices but this is ridiculous because the state of your food, sanitation, economy, happiness (integrity), and military already do this.  It's time to go back to the days of Medieval 2, where you were limited by money and time not space. Food and sanitation are nice additions and add complexity but the building cap means that these buildings take up precious slots that are needed for military and cultural buildings. In addition, since when has building a large farm instantly made the whole population utterly furious? Again, Total War has always placed emphasis on balancing the happiness of provinces, but the building cap means that players can't combat unhappiness by building entertainment buildings because they have no building slots left. All this does is discourage investment in high level buildings to keep happiness balanced. Luckily, some of these issues can be modded out but only insufficiently and the most important ones not at all. Please remove the building cap for future games; it makes the game far less enjoyable and has apparently facilitated the removal of sanitation and food in Warhammer, two things I'd far rather have than an arbitrary number of building slots.

Mass Effect is a sci fi RPG set in the future. You travel between galexies trying to save the univers from a massive threat.
The choices you make matter. People will live or die because of them, some choices you wont even see the results from until you are playing the second or third game. You truely shape your own story and it's fantastic in every way.
The game play mechanics are a bit dated, as are the graphics but the mod listed above should help with the later. While the game play mechanics are dated, they aren't lacking in fun. They aren't tedius, they just aren't stream lined. ME2 has a change in this, and 3 alters game play even further. In this installment you have a inventory and can buy different weapons, armor, ammo types, and get some resonable depth with the leveling system. The next installments simplify this and you lose a lot of that old style mechanic. (I like the armor system and weapon system a lot in the first game but the ways to improve in the second game are good  as well, just different.) You work as a squad, and command each member. That beind said they do have AI and work on their own as well. You can choose to let them use their powers by themselves or, to have complete control of what they use and when they use it by issuing commands.
You get to explore planets, there might be random people trying to fight out for their lives, giant creatures waiting to kill you, or little monkeys stealing tech you really want to get your hands on. There is so much I would like to say, but won't at risk of spoiling the adventure for you. Get out there, suit up, and have some fun.
If you are going to play any of these games, I highly suggest starting with this one and playing all the way through. If you don't, there are things you will miss. Big things, and little things that make the series shine so bright.

Mass Effect is the flawed yet massively enjoyable beginning to what has become one of the most epic storylines in gaming history. The Mass Effect trilogy is the analogue to Star Wars in the gaming industry, and it all started here. The first Mass Effect is my personal favorite out of the three for several reasons. While the game is quite action heavy, it has a much higher emphasis on decision-making and role-playing than its two heavily streamlined sequels. Mass Effect is from my point of view, the one game in the series that can stand on its own as an isolated storyline. The same can generally be said about the second game, but the second is made much better by playing the previous entry in the series. Mass Effect can be fairly overwhelming when it comes to the amount of lore packed in to the game, but for the most part all of it is intelligently written and quite interesting. The game performed fairly well on highest settings and i didn't run into to many graphical hiccups, but that's not to say this game is polished. I encountered quite a few minor bugs during my playthrough, but none of which were game-breaking. Mass Effect is a fantastic game in its own right and i highly reccommend playing through it at least once. I would reccommend the series as a whole if it didn't have such a ♥♥♥♥ing atrocious ending.

I am very impressed by The Swapper. It is a wonderful puzzle game.
The key mechanics are duplicate player agents between which the player can swap which agent they actively control. Several other games on Steam use a similar mechanic (where the player controls multiple agents simultaneously who all move in the same way) I've played some of these ("I and Me" comes to mind) but The Swapper builds on this mechanic and uses it in some new and creative ways.
The atmosphere is excellently done. The screenshots on the store page don't fully do it justice. You have a sense of the isolation of space and the deterioration of the space station you are exploring. The atmosphere also enhances the underlying themes of the game and the questions it raises about life, the mind and identity. You don't have to engage with any philosohpy to enjoy The Swapper. But I think it is remarkable that the developers have created both an excellent puzzle game and an experience that can cause the player to reflect on their own thoughts.
Highly recommended for anyone who enjoys puzzles, logic challenges, or atmospheric space games, The Swapper is a solid 8/10, even by 2017 standards.

Imagine a PC game flavored with chunky bits of old school 2D. The Swapper's not quite a platformer, it's a puzzle game packaged with a brooding mystery sci-fi story set in space.
The essence of the game is getting to smaller puzzle rooms generously dispersed throughout the desolate space station.
The puzzles have a rising difficulty curve, but you may not find yourself stumped until the later ones appear. That said, more systems are added as you advance, deepening the puzzle complexity by with more buttons that you have to stand on simultaneously, with new conditions that interfere with your cloning abilities.
The heavy sci-fi atmosphere is heavy with prolonged isolation and sounds of shuttle doors closing, vents breathing and space-inspired sounds. It's not monotonous, however the setting sometimes takes you to lusher greener spaces punctuated with wonder-inspiring piano segments. A good pair of headphones is a must.

Obviously Miscreated is in Alpha, obviously it is a lot like Dayz or H1Z1 or 7 Days to Die. However from personal experience with Dayz Standalone, and 7 Days to Die, this game is leagues ahead of its counterparts in my opinion. Miscreated is a beautifully crafted game and you can tell a lot of dedication has gone into making it's world. From graffiti giving you a sense of the world before the mutants came to be, or the rats that now crawl in the alleyways through every city scavaging for food, you can surmise the events that came to be.
Miscreated's controls are fluent. It doesn't feel as clunky as Dayz Standalone for example.
Loot is generally easily to come by, but you'll still have a harder time finding the more rare things such as crossbows or that desperately needed sniper scope. There have been times that I've nearly died but I finally found that Tomato Juice I was searching for to hold me over until my friends were able to reach me and help me out.
Speaking of which, Miscreated has a very creepy atmosphere when playing alone, you feel like a survivor in the wilderness just trying to survive, there are many fantastic RP servers to choose from that I have never encountered someone who KOS'd. Everyone I've come across is playing this game for the fun of it, they mostly enjoy that player interaction and will at least give you a chance.
This game absolutely shines with friends though. I have already met about 8 new people and group up with them on a daily basis to go exploring through the towns, cities, and even magnificent caves with waterfalls inside of them (Bring a flashlight cause they get DARK.)
I highly recommend this game if you enjoy games like DayZ or H1Z1.

This is as close to the feel of free form zombie survival as as anyone has gotten so far. It's not perfect, but the ambiance gives you that sense of, "This could be me if this were to actually happen." A lot of classic ideas like supply conservation, stealth and fostering your own stamina are present. A few really great ideas didn't quite work out mechanically. You can barricade windows in most homes, but it doesn't really help any. If you've got a horde on you they are either going to climb in someplace you hadn't boarded yet, or are simply going to tear through your fortifications eventually. Given that those barricades don't stay up once you leave the area there really is no reason to do it. At best you're creating a bottle-neck, but you're usually better off just running for it or saving time by fighting it out to begin with. Still, the choice of shooting a zombie in your way or trying to sneak around it while you have a horde lurching up behind you gives a great sense of urgency and weight to your decisions on the fly. A MUST HAVE for zombie enthusiasts!

State of Decay fills a void in the "zombie genre" of gaming that has desperately been in need of filling since the first zombie game has created.  It hands you a (mostly) open world filled with survivors and zombies, and leaves you to make the big decisions, scavenge, and help others depending on where you want to go with the game.
The game itself is a mission based apocalypse simulation with a smattering of RPG elements.  You're periodically handed missions - of varying types, everything from scavenging for supplies, to rescuing survivors, to establishing or upgrading home bases and outposts.  Along the way you meet several new communities of survivors, both good and "not so good", who you can assist and then even invite into your own enclave for protection.
You're not limited to playing any one character.  As characters tire or become injured, you can switch off to another character in order to further complete missions or to simply "level up" their skills.  Speaking of skills, this game cleverly includes several RPG elements;  you can increase your cardio, fighting, shooting, and other skills for general character improvements, and as these skills level up, you're allowed to choose specializations for each character in order to make them more effective at the tasks.
SoD also takes things a step beyond other zombie games by adding group morale/moods.  The occasional pep-talk must be given to keep other survivors in good spirits, and your enclave as a whole has a "morale" that must be kept up by wiping out nearby infestations, providing adequate supplies, and progressing the game.
By far the most interesting and exciting feature of the game is that the game continues on even after you've stopped playing.  If you exit the game and leave your enclave with few supplies or someone in bad spirits, you're likely to log in to find survivors missing or killed, morale has dropped a great deal, and even your entire enclave wiped out.  However, if you leave your group in good spirits with plenty of supplies, outposts, and a high morale, you're likely to log in to increased supply reserves, your group in good spirits, and several new mission opportunities.
After all, this is a game of survival, and only the most fit will do so.
All in all, desite a few minor (IMHO) flaws, this is the zombie game I've been waiting for - if you're looking for a game that puts you in the shoes of a zombie apocolypse survivor, this is definitely the game for you.
Pros-
Fairly open world zombie apocalypse simulation.
Missions are for the most part interesting and applicable.
Character skills and specializations add variety to playable characters.
Scavenging adds to the realism of the game.
The group morale is a clever idea that keeps the game moving along.
Combat is generally fun, with a decent variety of weapons and supplies.
Persistent world - your group continues on, even after you've stopped playing.
Mod community - the mod community for this game is growing every day.
Cons-
There are still a few bugs to be worked out.
The occasional crash (I've had 3 in 7 hours of playtime)
Graphics could use some polish and better textures.
Enemy clipping through walls, fences, etc.
Combat animations are a bit long and stamina depletes a bit too quickly.
State of Decay is a solid 8/10 and easily worth the price of admission.

Dragon's Dogma is a wonderful game hampered by coporate cuts and deadlines.  This is not a game that you can simply pick up and play - it requires an investment of time in order to enjoy.  I'd expect most people to quite honestly dislike the first 5 to 10 hours of play for this game.  Because of some poor decisions when it comes to gameplay, I'd most unabashedly advice looking through a wiki or walkthrough of some sort in order to power yourself through the beginning of the game.
However, when you can finally reach the meat of the game, it turns into a fantastic action game where only a few mistakes could mean your defeat.  For the most part, this game is about killing giant monsters, and it does that fantastically well.  I recommend this game, but only if you are willing to invest a great deal of time into a perhaps boring and grindy beginning.

Pillars of Eternity excels at its storytelling and its ability to bring together most of the elements that made Infinity Engine games so great. It's certainly a game that evokes nostalgia, reminding us of what a true PC RPG used to be like.
Baldur's Gate fans, you will quickly catch up to the fact that the writing on this game is generic at best. Not bad, but uninspired and tired. AD&D was such a long time ago and it was a convoluted mess. Even so, I feel Obsidian did not do any better with the combat and mechanics they came up with.
There are 11 character classes but it doesn't feel like they are unique. Spell-casters have their own place, of course. Melee, not so much. If only for a few class-specific traits and abilities, they remain largely the same. Rogue, for example, has no roguish elements. Anyone can pick a lock if they have a high enough stat. Same with trap detection and disarming. So my rogue ended up as a heavy armored melee fighter, since there's no restriction in equipment, either, or bonuses for equipping characters with proper gear.
Spellcasting is weak and, after a few levels ahead with stronger enemies, it became relatively ineffective. Debuffs became more beneficial than actual offensive spells. Healing is... you're better off hoarding healing potions.
Not everything about the game is bad. The game world is a joy to explore. Seeking quests and resolving disputes is as satisfying as it ever was. Lost caravans, murder plots, missing blacksmith supplies cargo, overthrow an insane lord. It's all there, and it's fun to go from town to town seeking to restore peace or become a villain. It's all up to you.
Despite its shortcomings, I enjoy the game for what it is, not a true Baldur's Gate successor, but a fair attempt. It's my understanding that this is but the first of a series of games in development. Hopefully they'll fix what needs to be fixed and deliver what is expected.
For now, I will avoid pre-ordering and wait for the buzz to pass before I jump into another Obsidian adventure.

After having just finished the game a few minutes ago (as a dull human male warrior), I can definitely say that Pillars of Eternity captures what people loved about the Baldur's Gate, Neverwinter Nights and Icewind Dale series along with Planescape: Torment while improving little bits to that timeless formula.
What I enjoyed was the amount of freedom in shaping your character along with their backstories and type of individual with fun and (while heavy) intuitive gameplay. The storytelling freedom in this game is astounding and for any roleplayers, this is a great game to do such roleplay. Interaction with the characters can shape and mould their views which relect in the endings. The endings themselves are satisfying to say the least and I wouldn't mind starting a second playthrough to try out new choices and classes to see more of this game.
Not too many bugs when I was playing though there was sound cuts from moving the camera away from the characters in towns (though these are minor) and the jerky movements from fast mode. These are minor ones though and the only gripe I have is the lack of pre-buffing before bossfights (though cooking food sort-of replaces that)
Overall, my game of the year (unless something else proves me wrong) and would play again.

Recieved this as a birthday gift, one of the best gifts I've ever recieved.
I'll start by saying, however, that this is the single worst PC port I've ever seen. Very nearly unplayable without modification; 30 fps lock and if you happen to lack the power to stay at 30 (which isn't unlikely, given the poor optimization), locked at 15 and the mouse cursor never fades from the screen (even when using a controller), etc (most problems can be fixed with mods, thankfully).
Moving on from that tangent, this game is well made on the whole. The world and enemy design, boss concepts, difficulty curves/spikes, and the co-op and PvP systems. Every area has a story, a meaning and a purpose; all connect at some point (mostly by unlocking shortcuts or hidden paths). Unlike most games npc don't throw information at you, you won't find an exposition guy telling you every detail of the story or reminding you that you still need to slay the boss of the 3rd area. NPCs are few, making the land feel desolate and lonely, and have goals of their own (that they may or may not share with you) and aren't mere quest-givers or henchmen. Most will have something of a quest-line, though it isn't immediately obvious (no map and quest log here, folks) that may have several paths, depending on your actions.
If you want a true challenge, then you have come to the right game, you'll need to treat every fight with care (yes, even mere skeletons) or you'll die, on what most games would consider a meaningless encounter and/or free exp or loot. As you move on, new mechanics are introduced, not by a tutorial pop-up or a convenient moment for a companion to mention that sewer rats may carry diseases or that certain creatures may fear fire: The status effect/enemy/damage type is thrown at you, and you must learn for yourself (or die) and eventually come to understand the means in which you can handle it. This game is undeniably diffucult, only through patience and persistence will you succeed. Only the foolish will continue to blindly rush through an area, and eventually they will break.
Overall, I highly reccomend this game to anyone has yet to play any of the Souls/Borne franchise or anyone who has played any of the other games in the series and found some amount of enjoyment in it.

I often see this game describes as "hard but fair". I see two problems in that statement.
First, "hard". It's not hard, at least not in a sensible way. Instead, it punishes you for the tiniest mistakes (and even for non-mistakes sometimes) and forces you to repeat yourself over and over again. By forcing you to walk long distances repeatedly and kill enemies you've already killed every time you failed, the game wears out your patience, thus making it feel harder, and inflates the playing time, thus making it seem bigger than it is.
Second, "fair'. Enemies can attack through walls, whereas your own character is constantly looking for the nearest wall to smack his sword against every time you swing.
This, allied to the extremely pompous and joyless feel of this game, the unnecessarily complex and obscure mechanics, the sluggish pacing and one of the worst soundtracks I've ever heard, make this one of the most oppressively boring experience I've ever had in gaming. The only difficulty in this game is in wanting to play it, and that's not what I expected from this purchase.

Written as of update 2/0.0.02
This game is very fun. With frequent updates and a currently small community you can ask the developers to add in things and have a say in the development. Many people complained that it got boring but I found a way to stay entertained. I used to go to an island, make a bed, sleep 1 night, and then move on. Now I go and build a small-large shelter with a door (added 3 days ago as of today 2/16/2015), use all resources, leach every wreck, then stay for a few more days and move on. I like to stay for atleast 5 days.
Shipwreaks are common and contain suspense every time you explore them even though most items are trash. There are usually 2 or 3 useful items like airtanks or axes.  While frequent, they are balanced. Plane wrecks were just recently added 3 days ago and contain mostly garbage resources.
Killing sharks is moderately challenging but they tend to flee to easily even after the recent AI change.
Deep in the ocean there are World War 2 ocean mines. I don't think they explode. In the deepest trenches of the ocean you can find UFOs but you need a flare to see them. They are on a small hill in deep trenches. They currently serve no purpose. This game will be improved over time but there is currently no way to be rescued. I can't wait to see how hypothemermia and hyperthermia (opposite of hypothermia) will play into the game. I just build shelters to store food and now that beds can be dragged around, I store beds in my huts. My first home was a 2x2 scaffolding (I don't remember what the floor is called) with walls, 1 set of steps, 2 doors, a bed, and full roofing. I built it today. My first house was pretty good.
You don't have to worry much because the only predators at the moment are 3 breeds of shark (new one added 3 days ago) but the Tiger Shark is weak and not very aggressive. The Great White is the one to worry about. That new breed of shark doesn't seem to even attack. I high doubt you will die from a shark. They are more scary to the player than they are deadly. If this game had respawns, they might be deadly but since this game is perma-death, the sharks cannot be too powerful.
Just in case of emergency I back-up my save every time I do anything important such as going to a new island or exploring a wreck.
I would love a co-op mode. This game is 3 weeks old and people have modded it. Somebody figured out how to go into multi-player. I know this game is perma-death and meant to be scary but having a friend to help would be fun. Also, it would remove scare-factor. I would enjoy having a friend to explore wrecks and the scary dark UFO depth waters.
In Summation:
This game is enjoyable at the moment but you might want to wait a while for more updates so you have more to do in this game so you know if you want to spend $15.00 USD on this game. I enjoyed it but if you have an irrational fear of water or have a water and/or shark phobia, you may not enjoy this game because a decent bit of it is exploring wrecks and paddling between islands. If you do not want to take the time to make large shelters and gather resources and would rather just loot wrecks that you find on each island and then move on, you will become bored quickly. This game may never have an option to be rescued so if you plan on waiting until rescue, you may be shocked if you never will be.  On the other side: There are jets that fly an estimated 20,000ft above you that could potentially be used for rescue.
No matter the amount of updates, this game is love it or leave it: some gamers will enjoy this game and have a blast and will play this all the time, the latter will find this game pointless and avoid it. I enjoy this game but sometimes I feel like there could be something more that the game is just lacking. Co-op is a huge thing when I say "something" but there is more than just that. I can not pin point exactly what but I just have that feeling that there is more to add to the game. This game has a lot of potential. It could be like Minecraft. It starts small and grows huge.

The game is an intelligent semi-linear puzzle-platformer that has you managing clones to grab orbs. But that's not really the main selling point.
The game's masterful depiction of the mind-body debate really calls into question its central mechanic—swapping between people. Clones or not, the potential unseen consequences of the main tool the protagonist has to progress brings an existential thread into the equation. It isn't beaten over your head like in SOMA, but if you bother to follow up a bit on the nice references to Dennett and Chalmers you get yourself into a right philosophical knot.
Add that to the heartbreaking story, household visuals, and pensive/atmospheric soundtrack, and you've got yourself quite the afternoon. Two afternoons, if you'd like to read up on the achievements—which offer some great narrative closure—and experience the story again after you understand what's going on.

The concept of Singularity is very interesting - being able to leap through time and change the past so that you can alter the present and prevent catastrophic events in the future. The setting of the game is similarly captivating; you and a team of U.S Marines are dispatched to an abandoned ex-Soviet island called 'Kotorga 12' to investigate a recent anomalous EM surge.
What makes this game so horrible is that it's not fun to play because the enemies are easy to kill, there's a lack of enemy variety, the majority of the weapons (the Seeker notwithstanding) are boring and the levelling system effectively boils down to being able to kill bullet-sponge enemies faster. Combined with no memorable characters and a horror atmosphere almost completely negated by bad AI as well as the aforementioned criticisms, Singularity does not do justice to the premise at all.
It's a shame. These kinds of games are always irritating because there's great conceptualisation, yet in bringing it to a game format they've managed to bury it in shallow and repetitive gameplay.
Whilst I heavily do not recommend this game, I still firmly believe that a game like this could be great if it addresses said gameplay issues and involves more memorable and likeable characters.
Took quite a few ideas from multiple games, and somehow made it work. Graphics are a bit dated, but if you're looking for a quality single player FPS, you can't go wrong here.

This game follows the style and feel of Baldurs Gate and Icewind Dale in almost all aspects, it's a very long game with a rich story and massive amount of content.
Battles can be somewhat unforgiving if you dont save scum a lot (just as given with the other 2 games).

What we have here is a graphic novel with interactive areas and a bolted on RPG system, leveling seems to take place once every blue moon and I have found characters with a 7 in lore could not use scrolls that needed 2 in lore, so the RPG side is simply not working.
It relies heavily on text based story telling to create game play, combat, exploration, all seem secondry to this one part of the games design. Unfortunately the story just is not that interesting, I have put books down that have been more interesting than this.
If you check the steam stats and achievements for the game, you will notice a trend, most of the advanced features of the game are not getting used, most folk use the create an adventurer feature, only 25% have actually finished act 1. This should tell you a lot.
It actually reminds me of a computerised version of the old paper and pen RPGs where the dungeon keeper tells you what you are looking at. Trouble is, this is computer game where we can see what we are looking at and half the time it does not match the text.
I have seen this compared to Baldurs gate a lot, honestly, it is not Baldurs gate, its not even in the same league as Baldurs gate but the game does have its charms if you sit back and treat it like an interactive book with pretty average if long winded story line.
If I was to give it a score it would be 7 out of 10. Worth owning but not for £35. I would say pick this up when the price hits £22 which is closer to its truth worth.
I would ask obsidian one question though, where did the $4 Million dollars from kickstarter go because this game is not worth $4.
Worth buying but wait for the sales.

My favorite campaign map to date, with fun/enriching story campaigns (Charlemagne and Last Roman) with the same ***DLC scheme since Rome 2. You have the decline and fall of the Roman Empire at your finger tips, with many legendary leaders scheming to make their people the supreme. You have many groups running west, fleeing the rising Hun menace, and old barbarian tribes finally seeking conquest as opposed to survival. And, in the wake of such wanton conquest and the tragic demise of the great empire, The Scourge of God has been born: Attila, King of the Huns, has come to turn this world into ash. If you know the history, the map and factions are so awesome. If you don't know the history, the map is great with a plethora of factions to see and be where you can put many hours into the game.
Hordes are a revolutionary addition to Total War, with some not so savory parts to it, yet still very fun. The new sacking mechanics are a good step up from prior games, as is the new raze function. You can spend many years just roaming and looting and have a lot of fun.
Battles remain more or elss the same, with the same development that occurs in each game, but with an increased focus on skirmish cavalry. Naval battles are still the same, with land and sea battles/sieges still a thing. Navies are hefty on upkeep, and kinda not worth it considering few factions use boats or have to embark and travel via the sea.
The refined family system is great, with some new emphasis on characters and familial/tribe actions. I like it.
This game, it's good. The best single player Total War that ever was or will be (sorry Warhammer, not really interested). Multiplayer still remains in the hands of Shogun 2, sorry Attila.
***Yes the DLC factions are ridiculous, don't buy them. The base factions are good, plus, with each faction dlc they release one free faction for all players.  The game itself is great, don't downvote because you don't like DLC purchases. Plus Charlemagne and Last Roman are great.

Hiveswap is finally out!  And it's...  Good?   Yep!  Hiveswap is pretty much a love-letter to 90s, adventure games, and homestuck.  What's homestuck?  That's not important!  While Hiveswap is based off of homestuck, I was actually surprised to see that they kept their word about homestuck knowledge being unecessary.  There's a ton of references thrown in, but they shouldn't look too out of place if you haven't read any.
But what about the gameplay?  The puzzles are decently challenging, but usually after finding the solution I think "oh, that actually makes sense."  It's not the type of game where you'll have to try everything with everything to figure out some insane logic puzzle that makes no sense, and in fact the game usually hints pretty hard at what you need to do for most of the puzzles.   Speaking of trying everything with everything, you don't HAVE to, but you'll probably WANT to, since there's a unique line of dialogue for almost every single combination of items.  That being said, there are a few interactions that don't have any lines.  It didn't happen very often, but it would have been nice if there was a generic "that's not how that's used" just to fill in these gaps.
(edit: there's apparently been an update that's supposed to fix some interactions not having lines, so that's pretty cool.  Also I forgot to mention, there's a hint button in the game, but it was completely unhelpful.  Maybe future acts will feature harder puzzles that require hints, but for now you should be able to deduce most problems by just reading the hints the text provides.)
The soundtrack is... weird.  It wasn't bad, but the whole thing has a fairly unique sound to it that's kind of hard to describe.  It's not the type of soundtrack I would purchase, but there were definitely some songs I did enjoy.  Also, the battle music kind of cut in really suddenly and poorly.  The transition was pretty bad.  Other than that though I didn't notice any issues with transitions between songs.
(Edit:  I've relistened to a few of the songs and they definitely grow on you.  I still don't think the album is really worth purchasing at full price, but you may consider getting the game + soundtrack bundle.)
I absolutely loved the art style.  It completely captured the feeling of homestuck and the 90s.  The houses are filled with all sorts of random trash and posters, and the majority of it is interactable.  The animation is also really good.  It's not super fluid at times, but even the lower quality cutscenes look very nice.
The writing is also surprisingly good.  They do a good job of introducing the alien concepts without just having a massive info dump, and the jokes were pretty on point as well.  There were a few grammar and spelling mistakes, but nothing too major.  I will say though the main character, Joey Claire, is a bit boring.  She does have a variety of interests, but other than that she acts pretty typically for a main character.  Luckily, the other characters have been a lot more interesting.
The game, however, is pretty short.  It took me about 4 hours to get through it in one sitting.  How much time it takes the average person will probably vary a lot though, since you can waste a lot of time just interacting with random things.  Normally I would say hold off on purchasing a game this short, but for  8 dollars it really isn't too much of an investment.
Overal, I really enjoyed my time playing hiveswap.  If you're a fan of adventure games, you should check it out.  I definitely look forward to ACT 2, even if we will probably have to wait another 5 years for that to come out.

Dragon's Dogma is a wonderful game hampered by coporate cuts and deadlines.  This is not a game that you can simply pick up and play - it requires an investment of time in order to enjoy.  I'd expect most people to quite honestly dislike the first 5 to 10 hours of play for this game.  Because of some poor decisions when it comes to gameplay, I'd most unabashedly advice looking through a wiki or walkthrough of some sort in order to power yourself through the beginning of the game.
However, when you can finally reach the meat of the game, it turns into a fantastic action game where only a few mistakes could mean your defeat.  For the most part, this game is about killing giant monsters, and it does that fantastically well.  I recommend this game, but only if you are willing to invest a great deal of time into a perhaps boring and grindy beginning.

State of Decay.
If you like survival games with zombies and base building, then this is the game for you. Starting off in the state park you find yourself Marcus Campbell with your friend ED. Quickly learning that zombies have come. This game is at a medium pace with being able to get through the entire game in around 13-14 hours if you go straight through. (3-4 ingame days)
There are multiple activies starting with gathering supplies such as food, medicine, building materials, ammo. Please note that the looting system is unique as if you find crates of resources it will give you an option to open it, and give you an option to put it in your rucksack. If you break it down it counts towards takable gear, if you put it in your rucksack you can put it towards  your camps resources.
The game also has multiple zombie types. You have your standard single zombie, you have your zombie hoard, you have your screamer, you have your ferrel, you have your stinker, you have your giant, and you have your armored zombie. In my opinion the two zombie types you do NOT want to engage on your individual self are the giants, stinkers, and ferrels.
The game is between a set storyline and a grind openworld. You will have your missions that progress the game. However you will also have your "clear the infestation" missions, you will have your "hunt the ferrel" missions. You will also have your "go get x supplies"
These resources are used towards but not include building up your little home. From building items like medical faciliites, a library, a guard tower and bunks for people to sleep on. Now with upgrading, do not be concerned if you use your resources at one base when you are thinking of moving to a different location. There are plenty of resources. They are finate. BUT there are enough.
A few problems I have found with the game, for example DO NOT use Marcus Campbell for anything. Once in your first home, (Which is a church, go figure) Switch immedicately. Trust me, if he dies you will be sorry. Apparently a few missions require for him to live. Such as a mission to find a new home.
Another little glitch I found that you can run over streetsigns. However 3 minutes later they appear standing again.
What I would like to see is better use of the facilities. For example at the warehouse (if you take that as your home) It seems that the warehouse isnt used to the best if its abiliy. There is alot of empty space that could be utilizied.
I also see that you have a radio, refrigeration, and other electronics. BUT WHERE IS THE GENERATOR? I mean it would be nice if you could add generators so you could add lights that turn on during the night.
The outposts are nice because they can be used as a buffer between your house and zombie hoards (due to having mine defences) however what I would like to see more hands on when it comes to them. Like there are more options with them like .. should it be a manned outpost, should it be an unmanned outpost.
Another thing I have noticed is that when you call for salvage assistance, they dont use vehicles, even though you can have like 3 or 4 vehicles. speaking of vehicles, if your person dies, your gear, and vehicle used to get there, stays there. However does NOT despawn. (Dont quote me on it)
Another thing I wish to point out is that this game is NOT easy. (Then again I couldnt find a way to change the difficulty) Trust me it takes a little while to actually get accustomed to how the game is played. So do not feel discouraged if you find you have to restart your game 2 or 3 times before you are like. "Alright, lets do this the right way"
Overall this game is entertaining, I would recommend it. I would also recommend looking into mods if there are any out there. (Preferably a mod where you can change the outfits, or equip armor, or larger backpacks, more efficitient camp layouts.

I picked it up on sale, and I'm sad to say it still wasn't worth the money.  It looks like the game might be playable with mods and a controller, but the base game with mouse and keyboard just isn't for any but the most determined.  I thought I could get past a clumsy interface, but I was wrong.  It had the basic terrible-port issues--within the first minute of playing I'd consulted guides twice for basic "how do I even" type stuff, because the game only gives you the console commands, and escape for some reason doesn't open the menu.  I could have gotten past that (I'm persistent) but the actual combat is unplayable.  The camera is the real terror--it doesn't stay at a useful angle long enough for you to get your bearings, and since the combat is timing-based it just doesn't work.  Frankly, even outside of combat, the camera is still a liability--I had trouble with friggin' doorways and hallways!  If the (immobile, nonhostile) backdrop is almost as bad as the enemy, you know you're playing a poorly designed (or ported) game.
Still might try to pick up one of the later games, if the porting is better.  It's a shame, because the gameplay does look fun, if it had worked properly.
----------
Let me just add, as well--I only got to see the opening cutscene as far as story goes, but I have to say--it sounded like a fifth grader trying to be "edgy" and "mysterious" wrote it.  Not impressed.  Giggled the whole way through.  Can't speak to the rest of the story, but that did not make a good impression.

While it is a rewarding experience, I think that many of the puzzles are extremely complicated and require juggling of several gimmicks at once. Mass Effect is a role-playing shooter in a beautifully realized sci-fi world. It was the second-to-last game made by the – legendary – game studio Bioware, before the inevitable quality decline set in, that occurs when a studio is incorporated into the EA roster.
Even though Mass Effect was originally an Xbox 360 exclusive, Bioware did not let the limited hardware hinder the game's potential. The game was a visual masterpiece, and the tight movement and combat naturally inherited from the Unreal Engine played wonderfully into the game's core shooting mechanics. The intense firefights with lasers, explosions, and kinetic powers, kept you at the edge of your seat – but it was the expansive universe, and heavy story elements, that kept you from leaving it.
If I were to make a parallel between another much beloved piece of media, I'd say that Mass Effect followed the Matrix formula to a T. Much akin to the Matrix trilogy, the first part of the Mass Effect trilogy is an independent piece that stands on its own, it builds up a mysterious and interesting world, and let's you take it in however much you like – but just like the Matrix trilogy, the second and third parts thoroughly disappoint.
Why The Matrix trilogy went the way it did is a mystery only the Wachowskis can answer for, but as for Mass Effect, we can clearly point our fingers at EA and say: “They did it!”. Mass Effect, along with Dragon Age: Origins, were Bioware's final games that showed the brilliance of the studio. The games that followed are little more than fan-service on top of bad writing. Let's not even start with The Old Republic.
As for Mass Effect, it's one of the most fleshed out worlds ever created. The game hooks you from the start, and won't let go – even when the credits roll. You're gonna wanna go back, and it's recommended, as the game has twists and turns that will only reveal themselves on second or third playthroughs.
I recommend this game to anyone and everyone.

I enjoyed this game playing from start to finish, something that you could expect to take the better part of a day to do.  The story follows a Spec Ops soldier Renko on a mission to the island of katorga-12 off the coast of Russia.  There, he encounters a time anomaly that sends him back into a burning building, where he saves a man's life.  This man goes on to conquer the world under Soviet rule.  Thanks, Renko.  The rest of the story is exploring the island with the Time Manipulation Device (TMD) to try to fix things, all while gunning down the mutated denizens of the island and the flow of soldiers from the new dictator's regime sent to stop you.
In terms of gameplay, the game is Half-life mixed with Bioshock.  The TMD is both your gravity gun and your plasmids, being useful in puzzle solving and combat, and usable alongside your firearm.  You can explore the levels to find more E-99 (read: ADAM) and use those to upgrade your weapons and character.  Gunplay is right out of Bioshock, with varied enemy types that require different approaches, and very satisfying.  Using the TMD to remove or create cover, or to create a bubble of slowed time is genuinely fun.  Certain levels just scream Half-life though, to such an extent that I was wondering at one point if an ichthyosau-like monster was going to dwell in the water.
The game is quite easy on normal, and the puzzles are solvable with the expected tools.  Level creation is a bit shoddy in parts, relying on invisible walls often as not to prevent unitended exploration.  Though the character upgrades are a bit more interesting, all weapons have the same three upgrades with two levels each, so they lose a little personality compared to bioshock.  The major complaint would be the controls in the upgrade screen requiring the use of arrow keys and forbidding the mouse.
Solid game for $15.00 on a steam sale.  If you liked Bioshock and Half-life, this will feel like a good purchase.

An fps from 2010 that gets criminally overlooked nowadays. It's hard to decribe Singularity perfectly, but all the unique abilties and weapons come together to form a campy romp through familair territory with a few surprises along the way.
Here's the positives:
The most interesting part of this game is easily the TMD (Time Manuipulation Device), which adds extra layers to gunfights and makes combat a real treat instead of the usual shooter affair of "shoot the guys until they're all dead". Without going into too much detail, the TMD allows you to do everything from aging your enemies to dust to creating a bubble where time is slowed to a crawl. It adds a lot of dynamic features to fighting and I honestly wish there was more game just so I could keep playing with the fantastic uses of the TMD.
While the starter weapons are fairly standard pistol, rifle, shotgun etc., the weapons that come later on are nothing short of inspired. One of the most interesting comes in the form of a sniper rifle that allows you to steer the bullets into your enemies, and it never gets old! Although there are only a little over 10 weapons over the course of the game, they all become a lot of fun in combination with the TMD as well as feeling nice to use on their own.
There is also an upgrade system called "hero perks" to give your character more health, extra ammo for weapons, more power in TMD abilties and so on, but it's a minor feature that doesn't have a lot of unique stuff going on, it serves primarily to scale your power to meet the growing difficulty curve of the game. There's also the abiltiy to upgrade your weapons to reload faster, do more damage and other standard power upgrades, but again, there's nothing too unique about it.
Now on to the negatives:
The game seems to move really fast through some of its areas. There were genuinely interesting ideas or gimmicks that I wanted to see utilized longer, especially when it comes to the monsters, as there are a lot of specialized monsters that only appear in one area of the game and then disappear for the rest of the game. Speaking of length, I finished the singeplayer campaign in 7 hours, which is a little light for games of its kind.
My other major complaint is that the upgrades offered for weapons and the hero perks felt boring. Not bad necessarily, I still made sure to be on the lookout for hidden perks I could discover in the world beause I genuinely wanted to find them all. However, the overall premise could have been expanded into something more interesting. The real bulk of my problem comes from the fact that the upgrades really didn't feel that impactful. They did improve the weapons, yes, but because it's not possible to upgrade every weapon in every way, I found myself prioritizing specific wepaons I liked best and by the end of the game only using those weapons because they were simply better than the others since they had upgrades.
Overall though, this game is still worth checking out for combining some really unique features together to make a fun shooter in a pretty cool location. If I had to give it a score, I'd give it a 7/10. Get it on sale though, the price is way to high for what you're getting.

I really enjoy this game, it's well made and definitely worth $15 even in it's current state. Here's a breakdown of gameplay, graphics, environment, crafting, bugs, and ultimately - why I would recommend this game.
-Pretty fun to explore shipwrecks and find stuff
-Made a motorized raft (which totally kicks♥♥♥♥♥
-Conquered multiple islands for my own greedy needs
-Built a fortress with a lookout tower and used binoculars to spot sharks
-Still haven't found my good friend Wolly
-Murdered crabs and ate them in front of their friends
-Drank then ate numerous coconuts
-Palm trees are now extinct
Gameplay is great, crafting system is really unique and I like it, it seems realistic, like you're actually putting stuff together instead of some wizardry where walls and foundations just appear. Although at this point there's not much to do, this game has really good potential (I'll elaborate more on this at the end).
This game is very nice looking, and has a really nice feel of realism to it. The only thing I'd want more with the graphics is better antialiasing, a fix for the weird lines you can see in the distance separating the areas of water, and further render distance.
The environment is very nice, there are plenty of sea animals and dangers. Sharks, whales, crabs, many types of fish, and more to come in the future. The islands are all pretty standard and have numerous palm trees, rocks, and a few yucca plants for lashings (rope). My favorite part about the environment is the water and shipwrecks. The water is awesome and it really feels real when you're swimming around exploring. The shipwrecks are interesting to explore and often have very useful loot like buckets (which you fill with seawater then boil to make it drinkable), parts to make an engine for your raft, and other useful items like flashlights and bandages.
I love the crafting system in this game. I've never seen anything like it before. Instead of having to combine recipes through a crafting menu, you actually put the stuff together on the ground, hold left click, and select the item you want to make. To make tools you hold anything, but to build foundations, walls, and other building materials, you need to be holding a hammer. The crafting is very well done, no complaints about it.
This is the least buggy early access game I've ever played. At initial release, there were a few bugs such as disappearing raft, flying sharks, and low sound quality rain, but those were all fixed very quickly. As of now, the only bugs/glitches I know of are the double/triple paddle and flying with palm trees. Very solid game with few bugs.
The developers of this game are great, because the game actually gets updates, and said updates
add content and fix bugs (looking at you, DayZ). This game has so much potential and with the development roadmap going the way it is, I'd love to see multiplayer co-op and much more content in this game in the future. Keep up the good work, devs!

I waited until the early access phase had ended and until the game was in full release. I have to say; this is by far the most polished and refined zombie survival sandbox experience I've ever had. The only limitations I belive it had was its budget; things such as amazing graphics -not that they're bad -I'm just used to high end AAA titles which boast amazing visuals. Knowing that the budget wasn't massive; Undead labs have reached for something quite ambitious. Have they pulled it off? I belive they have. This game is immersive and has enough variety between missions and sidemissions for it not to feel like a 'grinding' or 'mechanical' use of your time but an meaningful and deeply engaging experience.
The great thing about it is you get the hoard fighting feel of L4D2 without the sense that you're just passing through but actually warding off hoards to defend yourself or your home. And when people die -espcially characters you put a good deal of time into; well it's meaningful; not in a tear to the eye way the Walking Dead boasts but in a way which means something to you because you played through the experience of the game, trained that character, equpped them, knew their skills and hobbies, had seen them interact with others and that's why it sucks when they die -not just because the narrative told you it was sad but because of the time you invested in that character. Thankfully the permadeath system does not halt your gaming experience but reverts you to alternate characters within your home base. Every decision you make and even to an extent, the WAY you carry out that decision (eg: reckless driving, putting things off too long or even friendly fire) can really make a difference to how the characters in the game react to you and the situation. Ammo is fairly rare and weapons arn't that common themselves, so you have to really mean it when you choose to draw your weapon instead of using melee combat -which makes the guns feel so much more desirable and your persona far more secure when you use them. Thankfully they're not too rare so if you miss a shot or decide to shoot a zombie that you'll fell bad.
It isn't a complete sandbox like DayZ, there are missions and randomly generated side missions which keep coming so while you're free to prioritize hunting ammo or supplies you'll never have a sense of aimlessness.
There is an element of stratergy invovled with SOD when it comes to upgrading and deligating resources for differrent things; do you want to prioritize defences around the perimiter of your homebase? Or is putting resources into a family dining arrangement to avoid discord within the walls of your base more important to you? There are many other decisions you can make with the investment of your resources which will directly impact on the readiness of your characters, weapons and vehicles when they are called upon.
It's a pretty slow start and will initially require some more patience than the opening segments of most games but by the time you're 2 hours in you won't want to stop playing. It's managed to even pull me away from the latest release in my favourite game frachise ever within a month of it's release -the game I built this high end machine to play. And yet I find myself perfectly content lobbing off zombie's heads, or jumping in a car and running over zombies hordes at a time.
SOD is an immersive, meaningful and addictive gaming experience which gives back so much more than what you pay for it by the gaming industry's standards today. Having said that I'm the kind of gamer who will persevere with what others consider to be punishing and sometimes repetitive games which demand persistence and patience such as Metro 2033, Far Cry 2 and the original Assasin's Creed. All things considered (including the liklely budget for the developers) I can not fault State of Decay. Personally; I'd give it a 10/10.

First of all I have to say I'm a huge fan of computer role playing games, some of my favorite ones being Planescape Torment, Baldur's Gate series, Icewind dale series, Arcanum and Fallout 1 and 2 which I've re-played a number of time over the years. I'm also a pen and paper player of D&D. I have been waiting for years and years for a true successor to Baldur's Gate to come, and sadly, I've fell to the hype and foolishly believed this is finally it.
In few short points I will try to describe why I'm disappointed with this game.
- It was widely advertised as a spiritual successor to Baldur's gate series so I was naturally expecting an epic storyline similar to a "child of Lord of Murder" and addictive combat mechanics similar to AD&D ruleset. Both are missing from this game.
Obsidian tried to invent their own ruleset which just doesn't work as well and in the end makes every class too similar to each other. I rolled a rogue and was surprised to see my only rogue skill was mechanics, which every other character in the game could also level up, so why have the rogue class at all? There's no hide is shadows skill, only hide in shadows combat ability which can be used only 2 times per rest (which are very limited in this game), so in the end I outfitted him in plate and went full melee ignoring my rogue skills completely. Even though there's perception attribute, you have to use stealth mode to actually find hidden caches and since there's a lot of hidden items in the areas you visit, you'll be stealthy (and thus slow) almost all the time. No wonder this game brags with 100 hours of gameplay.
Every class or race can use every item in the game, the only penalty being the reaction time (speed) of the character influencing casting or weapon attack time. Everyone can also use scrolls, all potions, etc.
Spellcasting is also very bad and limited in this game, as almost every spell is combat only, meaning there are no pre-battle buffs, and taking into account that many useful spells are area of effect, and that there is friendly fire - nothing bad with that per se, but since your spellcaster has to get real close to cast them, it's virtually impossible to use them effectively.  There's no traditional spellbook but a grimoire which can hold infinite amount of spells but only 4 per level can be selected for use at a time, and then again you have a limited per rest usage of them. And since they are combat only, expect generic boring spells, different by damage type only (fire, ice, poison, etc.). Transcribing the spell from another caster's grimoire costs money, depending of the level of the spell. Why? I guess the grimoire you carry has a slot that says "insert coin here" or something. There are no actual materials used in the process, so... A lot of these immersion breaking and irritating little things in the game.
There's also a infinite shared item stash which is carried by you all the time, there's no encumbrance, so strength makes no impact on how much you can wear or carry, you get the picture.
- The story.
It started interesting but very quickly went to "visit this guy, oh he's dead, visit that guy, oh's he's dead also - let's visit another guy and hope he gives us some answers". I'm 25 hours in the game and don't know crap about what's going on except I'm some kind of Watcher that can see the person's soul. There's a skill you get early on which let's you reach into someone's soul and read about that person's past life. There's a ton of those people around and it's not interactive in any way or integrated into a story, just walls and walls of texts. I started fearing visiting new locations because of it, just how much pointless stories I will have to read in this tavern? In the end I beat my OCD and just skipped those.
The game just bombards you with lore, names and history from the get go, even on the character creation screen. It's very hard to process all that information, the names are not memorable, and I'm not even familiar yet with the layout of the world, so dumping all that information all of the sudden can be overwhelming. Races, provinces, wars, deities, cities, islands... OK, OK... let me care about something at least a bit before you hit me with info over the head. I had like 50 books on me in the first 5 hours of the game.
- Crafting and loot
There's crafting in the game and it's available to every character, you do it from your inventory screen. Some items can be enhanced, some can not. You can put some properties on your gear and increase it's damage potential or defense. It' very generic and uninspired and I guess it's there only to serve as a money sink. In 25 hours playing or normal (which people say it's hard compared to similar games), I haven't used one consumable or a scroll. I don't see a situation where I'm spending thousands of coins to make a single scroll.
Loot is also very generic, there are some named items in the game, but nothing special, nothing that lets you feel really powerful. In the end you can make your own stuff by crafting, I had everyone dual wield flaming weapons, which I made myself. If there's no good and interesting loot, there's NO REASON to explore. take into consideration there's also no XP from killing stuff, and you lose interest in exploration completely.
Skyrim and Dragon Age Origins made the same mistake. RPG's are all about risk and reward. You risk your party to overcome an obstacle to get riches, items, artifacts, experience and with it new skills that again make you feel more powerful. The game should ideally throw increasingly difficult obstacles onto you, and in return giving you nicer things, it's a very simple process, really. Makes you feel satisfied. Do I feel satisfied with PoE when after a fight I find just same old vendor trash I found 20 hours before? No, I don't.
I did not feel compelled to explore in PoE, at all. You literally explore the whole map, and find nothing except for a few crafting herbs.
- Quests
Nothing special or original, at all. Fetch quests. A guy in the woods I've never seen before asks me to overthrow a local noble. I accept and go to the keep of that lord, only to be attacked on sight. Why? Is that standard practice to attack everyone who comes to the door? I guess the interactivity lies in the 3 different entrances into the keep (main gate, sewer, over the wall). OK, so I kill them all, the crazy lord included and the first guy reappears and just takes the throne and keep over. That's it. No more conversation with the guy. NPC 1 changed by NPC 2. I actually still enjoyed that part of the game, the art of the keep was very nice but was surprised how shallow the writing was. Is that really the best what you could do with that story?
Perhaps it get's better later on, but in 25h I've yet to see a memorable NPC or an enemy who has something interesting to say. Think of first level of BG2, I'm sure you remember the genie you encounter. That genie has a lot more personality than any NPC I've seen in this game so far.
Final thoughts:
The Pillars of Eternity is not a terrible game, it's OK, I guess. In fact, I liked it considerably more that the Wasteland 2. What PoE is missing is addictive gameplay, and better writing. I wish they bought the D&D license and went with Forgotten Realms setting and ruleset. This way it feels more like Drakensang: The Dark Eye than Baldur's Gate. A missed opportunity.

I'm not sure I will finish it at all, in fact it reminded me how Arcanum was great and I got a craving for that game, over this one.

Well. Its here. After 5 years of hype, HIVESWAP: Act 1 has finally been released.
The gameplay resembles a classic point and click adventure style of game, with beautifully drawn backgrounds, HEAPS of dialogue and world building, and wonderful music. In addition, there is SO much lore for those who have read homestuck. I would say the game fills in many aspects of daily troll culture and life that we knew little to nothing about before the game.
Its cute, funny, enjoyable, and I highly recommend to anyone who enjoys puzzle/point and click, even if they have not read through homestuck.
However. Was it worth the 5 years of hype, a long and drawn out release, and 8$ for one of four acts? No.
The movement is point and click, and while usually not too intrusive, can be extremely annoying for just getting your character out of the way of what you need to click on. Should have been a WASD movement system. Its a core mechanic that feels very unpolished relative to the rest of the game. In addition, upon startup there are a few EXTREMELY glaring bugs, the foremost of which is if you change your resolution and dont restart the game, it WILL make the UI look super weird and terrible. Which is how I played the entirety of the game.
Which is not hard to do, as the game is not long. For something that had 5 years to be developed and raised over 2.1 MILLION dollars on kickstarter it is entirely underwhelming, especially with the 8 dollar price tag. Even though I took my time in exploring every interaction, I finished the game in exactly 2 hours. Not only that, but the game ends just when the story picks up, RIGHT as things get serious. Blueballs for sure. I mean, they didnt HAVE to leave it on a cliffhanger, and considering that this is act 1 of 4, seems like they could have condensed 2 acts into this one game and chosen a more resolved point in time. And what seems more ridiculous is that even though they left it on a cliffhanger, they couldnt bother to give us a date for the next installment.
To conclude, I loved it, 5 hats out of 5, 8 out of 8, 10 decapitated Dirks out of 10.
Ps. F**K YOU Hussie where the hell is our epilogue you cant just END the comic when GAMZEE IS STILL IN THE FRIDGE I mean come ON.

I think the word "relaxing" best fits this game, ironic I know since it's about war.
Coming from DesertStrike (Starcraft 2 arcade map), its game mechanics in the BETA came pretty intuitively. Have a bunch of dps and put tanks in front to soak damage, stick in some stealth units to fk with your opponents, and most importantly counter your opponents' army composition with your own. Simple enough.
NO LAG, and best part is I can play this game in bed on my laptop mostly with just the keyboard, with the rare one or two clicks from the trackpad for upgrading units and using commander powers. Like, imagine coming home after gym at night and you just want to play something with low-as-fk APM and fun. This is your game.
For the RUNES, I personally didn't care too much about them. It's pretty much League-of-Legend-like and too much hassle for such little difference (like.. you need to level them to pretty high levels to actually feel any impact in matches, which needs many many hours invested into grinding, ain't nobody got time for that, well... maybe kids. iuno.) I can sort of see this mechanic as a potential pay-to-win source. uhoh.
The UNITS though, very cool designs mostly, especially the variations of the standard units. Actually, the standards all seem to look worse than the variations, probably because they want you to invest to unlock them. ATLAC race looks really cool. YAOGUAI is kinda weird, since they're pretty much just furries, trying to fight against the other races which got rockets and plasma weapons or wteva lol like srs? There's some little things, like TERRAN race using arrows, spears, and horses, but also guns, motorcycles, and mechs?! Some weird age-difference in terms of technology right there. Doesn't look quite right when you see them together.
COMMANDER POWERS - Could really use some detailed descriptions of these things when you hover your mouse over. Like, if it's summon a unit or something, have it show the HP/DEF/DMG/RANGE/DURATION/etc. If it's an AoE thing, show the maximum number of units it can affect, just GIVE US MORE INFORMATION cause right now it's just going on feel for me at least.
CANNOT play against FRIENDS - I really wish I could invite my friends to a custom game and square off against them, but that didn't exist in the BETA. Hopefully it'll be in the full game release.
NO TEAMCHAT - Everything you type is talk-to-all. So how da heck do you plan strategies without letting the enemy team know?! There's only so much the emote lines can say. Most the time people just don't talk period. I've had to spam chat to get any response.
SOUL ESSENCE MINE UPGRADE - For new players, I think just having the cost and down-time-duration as a hover-text over the icon is good enough, cause right now, if you don't already know how much it costs to upgrade at the 2 periods, you won't know until you click it and get denied.
UNIT PATHING - For the majority of the time, it's pretty alright, but occasionally, especially early game around the lootboxes at the middle, they do some weird merry-go-round stuff, which mostly gets the melee units killed since they're just kinda spazzing out and not hitting anything. Also, units will just chase surviving enemy observers into the cannons and get melted instead of shooting at the crates, kinda weird.
Overall IMO, a very fun game requiring little effort to play. Runs super smooth for the amount of units it's showing even at high graphics. Designs are cool, matches are quick to queue for AND play, GOOD STUFF YE. Get it.

Although it has been several years since I played this franchise, I still remember playing it as if it was yesterday. However, let's begin with the one that started it all: Mass Effect.
Like any RPGs done well, Mass Effect has the story and the gameplay mesh marvelously together. Wihle you can't customize your own armor and accessories, the items in your inventory still serve a purpose and it's easy to equip either your main character or the supporting cast with the right set of armor.  The FPS part is challenging enough for the player and has multiple difficulty settings to accomodate players from newbie status to those used to FPS and want a challenge. All in all, I can spend hours just playing the game and not notice the time has gone by until I've finished it.
However, what stands ME above almost all of the existing RPGs out there, is its outstanding narrative. With unique NPCs, talented voice acting, and indelible cutscenes such as a planet blowing up (trying not to give out spoilers here), I would definitely recommend this game to all who would declare themselves a hardcore gamer, RPG fan or not.

This game is a contemporary masterpiece and although flawed (it's obvious that the game was rushed and there was a lot of cut content), no other game delivers on the fantasy of gathering a party of merry adventurers and embarking on an epic journey as well as Dragon Dogma does.
The combat system is the best in its class, with its responsive and intuitive controls (keyboard and controller are both equally viable options) this game is just a joy to play. It features one of the best character creation systems in any RPG and a versatile class system in which you can freely switch between classes while mixing and matching your abilities.
However, this game is known to be very divisive among RPG fans, it does have a number of negative aspects, like the overworld being quite barren and undercooked, an irregular pacing or some obfuscated user interface and gameplay elements. Still, the positives outweigh the negatives and this game is without a doubt and excellent and unique experience that oozes with style.

Not great. I hear the director has done some other good short films though. I'd check them out. This one is just lacking a bit as far as acting goes and some of the effects.

If a practiced scifi author had written this as a short, it could be a fantastic story.
If one of the experienced producers with a budget had hired the talent, it could have been a good screenplay.
If the director and actors would have had a bit more experience (and perhaps time), it could have been a little more polished as a finished product, rather than looking like a hobbyist production.
Keep in mind, it's a decade old now, so the effects are pretty good for an indie film from 2008... but still, if you don't like FILMS then this probably won't be of interest.
This is neither a good nor a bad short; it's just a marginal production with marginal production value and inexperienced actors and (imo) director, but has the bumpkin-charming feel of a bedtime/campfire story.  These are aspects more related to limited time and a simple plot, and by the end I was glad they chose to keep it simple because once you get what's happening, the substantive story has already been told, and it's only about seeing it played out.  There are some minor stereotype references
but no overtly political or social commentary on that level.
While I don't think I wasted my money at a sale price of $.50, I also wouldn't recommend the film to anyone without a disclaimer to the effect of, "It's not bad, but you WON'T be impressed."  This is one of those products that makes me wish for a neutral rating option; as anything other than an indie production, or if it was longer than 22 mins of your life, I would say to avoid this product.  That said, it's inoffensive (nothing graphic, no harsh language), would carry about a PG rating, and could be shared with young kids as a thought provoking resource.
The only thing I didn't understand as a focus was with the fruit:

Future Farmer. It's like a messed up sci-fi horror with more twists than you thought possible in 20 mins. This short movie doesn't get enough credit I think. Sure the acting is B grade and some of the characters feel not fleshed out enough (I'm looking at you Clarissa).
This movie builds a believable world of dystopia. The struggling farmer is confronted by corporations trying to steal what he's achieved in this futuristic world, with all the androids and gadgets you'd expect from your typical sci-fi. This film was created with a small team on a small budget, and they achieved a polished 20 mins of entertainment.
So skip your next Google Play app and spend $2 to support the small independent entertainment industry.

Notice: The Contagion developers seem to be so busy with their retail game that ZPS' updating has slowed to a crawl, if it's even being updated anymore. I would really, really like for a developer or two to give evidence that I'm wrong, as I still love ZPS and would prefer that it does not befall the same fate as it's GoldSrc brother, Zombie Panic.
Ladies and gentlemen, Zombie Panic Source. This was a great mod back in its prime. I would go so far as to say it was one of the best, if not THE best, multiplayer SMods of its time. An update on February 11, 2011 (if i recall correctly) made the game even more difficult by "fixing" knockback, though this made things even harder for Survivors when attempting to win. It has not been "re-broken" since, adding to the steep difficulty curve for humans.
one of the best SMods of it's time. Not anymore.
It's core idea is this: two teams, humans and zombies, are 100% player-controlled, battling for either the sake of humanity or for the world to be a bit more overrun with undead. Unlike Contagion, there is no AI here. None. Every single moving entity is controlled by a living, human being. It also is unlike Left 4 Dead in the sense that humans are not able to take tons and tons of damage; with normal health and no armor, four scratches (3 from the Carrier) and you're dead. Meanwhile, Zombies literally eat bullets for breakfast, and it's gonna take a lot to their face for them to fall.
This game encourages teamwork, but it is not mandatory, meaning you could totally be a jerk and leave your fellow survivors to die and still win. That being said, there's the chance that they will come back with a vengeance, making your job of surviving much harder than before. Every bullet and survivor counts.
Unfortunately, in a game like this, balance is always an issue, and right now there is a lack thereof. When knockback was fixed on zombies, instead of bullets pushing them back, zombies are "slowed down" instead, and sometimes this mechanic doesn't even work properly. There's lots of indie games out there have good but unfinished games that completely drop work on it as soon as they make enough profit.
Then there's games that may release poorly but the developers continue to polish the features and pour their attention into improving things.
Miscreated falls into the second category.  The initial release, from what I heard, was pretty bad.  But it's gotten steady updates with very open and hard working developers to craft it into a very promising survival game.  This is the kind of indie game that we should be supporting.  Maybe then other developers will take notice and realize that spending your time on a game and talking to the community can make a game that was once a complete bust into a very popular title.
As far as the gameplay itself think DayZ but with better controls, inventory, and graphics.  There are a few areas still lacking but the developers are hard at work and I have little doubt that this game will only get better.

This game is a contemporary masterpiece and although flawed (it's obvious that the game was rushed and there was a lot of cut content), no other game delivers on the fantasy of gathering a party of merry adventurers and embarking on an epic journey as well as Dragon Dogma does.
The combat system is the best in its class, with its responsive and intuitive controls (keyboard and controller are both equally viable options) this game is just a joy to play. It features one of the best character creation systems in any RPG and a versatile class system in which you can freely switch between classes while mixing and matching your abilities.
However, this game is known to be very divisive among RPG fans, it does have a number of negative aspects, like the overworld being quite barren and undercooked, an irregular pacing or some obfuscated user interface and gameplay elements. Still, the positives outweigh the negatives and this game is without a doubt and excellent and unique experience that oozes with style and charm.
