Before I say this game is great, which it is, let's address the fact that it is early access and I will change this review in the near future. Stranded Deep is awesome. Beautiful graphics, unique crafting, immaculate exploring potential, and overall great dynamics. However, like all other "survival" games, the developers have failed to properly order the aspects of survival properly: shelter, water, and food. I'm sure everybody's heard the term 3 hours without shelter, 3 days without water and 3 weeks without food. Stranded Deep is yet another failed attempt so far ( as of Alpha 0.02 ) as a survival game to graps these 3 simple things. The island concept is unique and fresh, but it just falls alongside the others of constantly eating ( with little variety ), hardly ever needing to drink ( with also little variety of how to obtain water ), and finding or creating shelter doesn't pose any risk if you feel like being nomadic. In addition, sharks are given a bad name, being dropped in as the only true "enemy" of the player, sharks are made the feared pinacle of the game. Though fun and heart-pumping, the elements are what you should truly fear. Sharks should be portrayed as their curious, harmless selves and the aspects of survival, including the effects of the environment on the player, should be emphasized. I can't stand swimming around worrying more about the next time a great white will take a chunk out of my leg than I am the next serving of fresh water I'll have. It's utterly unrealistic, and in order for this game to be at it's best, survival and realism should be pushed to their fullest, most immersive state.
In short to the developers, great work on such a beautiful game, but get your survival aspects on track and IN ORDER OF IMPORTANCE. Keep your sharks curious, majestic, and human-avoiding as they really are. I can speak on behalf of most people that watching a shark gently swimming beneath the water, not attacking you, is just as humbling (and enjoyable) as having one charge right at your throat. Don't remove their aggression, but make them more of an attack-only-if-attacked AI, or make it a *VERY RARE* occurance that they will attack. Lastly, make your islands more diverse in terms of size, wildlife, natural structures and distance from each other. It wouldn't hurt to add very large islands with unique characteristics that players can inhabit for long, if not permanent, periods of time. The possibilties are truly endless, and this game is the prize gem of open canvases.

Go play Baldur's Gate 2.
More detailed review here, if you are interested...
The game will give you your money's worth, timewise - if you do the side quests, you will easily hit 60 hours on hard difficulty.
Act I and Act II are well made, but unfortunately they set up the stage for Act III, which is a major letdown.
Combat system is either unfinished or not thought through - it is acceptable for trash mob fighting, but for big fight or boss fights, it is lacking and transforms challenge into needless frustration. What am I ♥♥♥♥♥ing about?
- there is no reliable aggro system; mobs just tend to rush the first party member they see
- engagement system seems an interesting idea, unfortunately many mobs have traits to ignore it and rest just does not give a♥♥♥♥♥♥ so it is detrimental only to your party members; this results in constant choke point fighting, where at least you can control the movement of enemies
- because the aggro system is based on proximity and not on individual aggro (except when you have a wizard, who is likely to be mass teleported on or rushed by a zerg of reckless madmen), you might have hard time meleeing anything, as mobs tend to turn away from the tank and hit your cipher for no reason - yeah, nevermind that guy in heavy armor swinging a mace at you, the most prudent thing to do is to turn around and completely ignore him
- lack of defensive choices for "squishies" makes this even more annoying; a horde of mobs absolutely ignoring four other party members in their way and headlessly rushing a wizard in the back seems rather comical; poor dude has a few deflection oriented spells (pitiful) that are probably get interrupted anyway, no matter how high resolve he has
- many scrolls/abilities/potions not working; for high difficulty or difficult fights in general, the game encourages you to use every weapon in your arsenal, which is a valid principle; unfortunately for you, those weapons are broken; many triggered abilities do not work at all, for example Second Chance or Unbroken for the main tank
- you can't prepare for fight, since potions, scrolls and majority of spells can be used only in combat; you can somewhat mitigate this by scouting ahead and positioning your party before encounter starts, but that option is not available when you fight the tough fights, ie where you need it most
- the two hardest fights in the game are pretty much just RNG, depending on if your tank get oneshot/grazed/missed by the big attacks
- you quickly find out that despite the variety of spells and abilities, you will be mostly using just those with Raw damage in harder fight, as Raw damage is the only kind that completely ignores any resistances and defences.
Story itself is well written and mostly interesting, until you get to Act III, where everything seems rushed and chaotic, plus the endgame big story revelation is one HUGE CONTRADICTION of Mass Effect 3 ending proportions. COME ON, OBSIDIAN, YOU ARE BETTER THAN THAT!
The NPC characters are rather unremarkable. They do have funny interactions when in group with each other, but apart from that, there is nothing. Their personal quests do not give much information about them, you really do not get more invested in their past or anything. I was hoping for characters of Baldur's Gate 2 caliber, both in group NPC and bad guys. I was disappointed.
There is also no romance between characters. None. You would expect a group of people that travels together for months, daily facing the prospect of death, to develop some tight bonds. Not here, though.
----------------------------------------------------------------
Look, Pillars of Eternity are not a bad game; they are certainly way better game and RPG than so-called "game of the year" Dragon Age: Inquisition. However, in a direct comparison with Baldur's Gate and BG2, it is very lacking. It is encouraging that Obsidian took the task of making a honest, old school RPG, and, by Stendarr, they tried hard. Maybe the next title will get all the bugs and imperfections sorted out.
6/10 - would have been 5/10, but I believe Obsidian deserves some credit here and encouragement for the future releases.

You and group of survivors, search and scavenge your way through a fairly large map dealing with mobs of zombies.   Smacking, hitting, shooting, all work well and is richly satisfying. The story is… Okay…  You rescue survivors, and work on trying to figure out why the dead are eating people. At first blush, Attila was a little disappointing because its superficially so similar to Rome 2, same army animations etc. However, once you play more than a few turns, this disappears and it is truly a totally different and much, much better game.
There are some questionable design decisions, for example virtually every faction gets similar units (but there is still a wide diversity) eg saxons get pikemen, lancers, and cavalry that are good at attacking other cavalry despite having none of these historically.  However there's so much unit choice and such a wide diversity of units (especially when you start recruiting client state/horde units) that they're all fun to play as + I find the combat far more complex. Different factions have different stats, for example Barbarians have high attack but generally lower defence and armour, while with Roman units its the other way around.  Roman units get chewed up by barbarians, so you need to play quite tactically with them now and make full use of terrain and your Levis Armaturae and cavalry. Especially appreciated is the (finally!) addition of a 'missile block chance' for all units.  This is so good it would be impossible to go back to a time without it, and I have NO idea why it wasn't in Rome 2 (what were they thinking???).
But now to the gameplay. People have complained that all the factions are 'the same' but in truth I really don't see this. Excluding DLC, there are four main playstyles,  'Roman', 'Germanic Barbarian' (eg Suebi, Visigoths), 'Eastern' (Sassanid, Garamantians), and 'Nomadic' (Huns, white huns) etc but each plays very differently, and further playstyle differences are added even between factions depending on their religion (which actually makes a real difference in terms of buildings and effects now), whether they're a horde or not, and differing units. I've completed games on hard as ERE, WRE, Saxons, Sassanids, Garamantians, and White Huns. Horde tribes are a real challenge, since your city travels with you, and I haven't mastered this yet.   I found legendary difficulty too awkward because of the pause-delay that gets added to all of your actions from the auto-save, so I play only on hard or very hard.
I'm currently playing the absolute best campaign of my 10 years playing total war  (i've played all TWs except the first shogun) as Western Roman Empire on Very Hard.  An early decision to hold one province too many (Belgica) rather than falling back to Narbonensis as I usually do, as well as a subsequent (still early) decision to switch to Graeco Roman paganism stretched my empire to the absolute breaking point. I spent until 417AD  'treading water' fighting battle after battle, marching my legions all over hells half acre to put down rebellions, fight off rampaging hordes, et cetera. Along the way I lost my alliance with the ERE and had no other trade allies or client states, so it was tough. It also played out very diffierently to an identical campaign on hard. I didn't get my usual economic buildings built early because I had to spend on troops, so I was behind from the get-go.
After I wearied my foes enough I was able to sign a stack of peace agreements but I was busy for many more years putting down rebellions and spending spare cash (that now wasn't being spent on soldiers) building buildings. Now in 422 AD, I've stabilised my religion, have taxes stably on high (its a net benefit to public order once all the immigrants are gone) and I control all of italia, north africa, hispania, most of france and most of britain with the Varinians as my client state in Scotland. The thing is, even with 12 legions my empire is still stretched to the max as I have hordes through the interior, the franks have 4 provinces and a few stacks near colonia agrippina, i have five or six hun hordes, rugians and another horde faction hanging all around illyria and in my interior, and I have the garamantians (who have 8 regions) on my border in Africa.  I have two legions in Britain keeping that pacified, two in gaul, one in hispania, two in Africa, three in north italy/illyria, and my expeditionary legion is sailing towards Aksum under Flavius Stilicho (he just died, now its his son) to keep the ERE happy.
I can't move any of those legions for fear of attack, and now the Gaetulians in Cydamus have launched an attack with three full stacks on my two under-manned (saving $$ on garrison expenses) African legions - there's some tough fights coming up. I'm surprised the garamantians haven't pitched in yet, since they're at war with ERE but mercifully neutral (yellow face) happiness with me.  On the same turn, my former clients, the Saxons, seceded and declared war.  Unfortunately they helped me wipe the Visigoths out of Greece and Constantinople, and they captured much of the ERE's former territories, so they're quite a threat. Ordinarily I'd get Macedonia (Roman, graeco-roman pagan, religiously tolerant, admires empires, reliable, defensive) to help me sort them out since they're pliable and also control four regions in illyria, but since they're at war with the ERE (which holds virtually all of the middle east except Egypt, having for once wiped out the Sassanids) I can't do that either and I'm likely to be at war with macedon soon also.
Words don't do it justice but its an incredibly engaging campaign.  One word of advice if its achievable on harder difficulties (for all campaigns really, not just WRE) is to crank your taxes up to high. Initially it will hurt public order so you should try not to be at war,  but you can save yourself up to -18 (or is it 20?)  (-9 as WRE) in immigration penalties.  Normal taxes give -4 to public order, high taxes give -10.  So you spend 6 public order to gain 9 public order as well as a huge increase in income. It's a great idea but I think its a bit too beneficial to the player once you can pull it off.
Whew, that degenerated mostly into my WRE experience but honestly, I don't know if this is the 'best' total war ever as I've had a lot of fun with all of them,  but it is really a phenomenal game, is much better than Rome 2, and i feel sets a new high water mark for the series.  I downloaded the last roman campaign but only played 3 hours so far (seems fun, loving the later time period and new units) and i have the empires of sand DLC but i haven't finished a campaign with it yet.  I tried a couple of starts and the new units definitely make Himyar and Aksum more threatening and the Tanukhids seem like a lot of fun, but I always got stomped early as the Tanukhs. (instead play as ERE and recruit their awesome cavalryt!) . Do recommend.
**EDIT** I have subsequently edited this review after discovering some problems.  There are several bugs in the game that are unresolved and are unlikely to be resolved by CA. They're a little devious but can have a very profound effect on gameplay. The first is that a number of traits and retinues appear to have no effect - especially those that give +exp to units. Pankration gloves etc are entirely useless.  Also there is an easily reproducible bug where faction members that remarry the wife of another dead faction member will disappear, yet still be available for employment as a general.  you can never give them offices etc so eventually they accumulate a huge amount of influence and revolt leading to a separatist conflict. There are other problems in charlemagne such as not being able to recruit archers after researching a certain cavalry tech....these bugs have been around for a long time and aren't going to be fixed. This knocks a lot of the gloss off my review - but I tried going back to Rome 2 today and Attila still beats it by an order of magnitude. Also, the encyclopeia isa piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥that doesn't load half the time and takes an age to navigate when it does. Its obscure, difficult to use and doesnt make life easier. Some stats like rate of fire should be on the main unit card not encyclopedia.

ShellShock Live is a really fun game, in which you brutally destroy your opponents' tanks with many different weapons, and by many weapons, I mean
weapons. Have you ever imagined a grenade that just broke into a bunch of smaller grenades? How about launching a rainbow? How about a cat? There's all that and more.
When you start, you're able to get right into the action in multiplayer, or play through singleplayer missions, starting from a simple and quick tutorial. The singleplayer missions are mostly fun from what I have played, albeit infuriating sometimes. For example, one of the missions further in pits you against an opponent that teleports almost every turn. Another one I am currently stuck on pits you against 2 enemies, each with slightly less starting HP, but they have more powerful weapons than you, being able to drain over half of your health in one use of one of their weapons, meanwhile you can barely take down ~20% of their health with 1 GOOD shot of one of your weapons. As you progress some of the missions begin to feel slightly unbalanced. However, they do yield XP when completed, which can be used to level up. More on that in a sec.
The multiplayer mode has a wide variety of settings you can play in, having a quick join feature, which sometimes likes to apparently join me into games that are already in progress, and allowing players to create their own rooms or tournaments with their own rules or join other rooms or tournaments. In Multiplayer mode, there are several modes, my favorites being Juggernaut(which seems to not be played much, as in big rooms, the Juggernaut is OP) and the classic Deathmatch. Juggernaut is essentially a 1 vs the rest of the players in the room, and has more starting health than everyone else, which is dependant on the HP setting and the amount of players, not sure exactly how though. The Juggernaut wins if they defeat everyone else, but everyone else wins if the Juggernaut is destroyed. Deathmatch is the most popular mode, and is usually played in teams, but can also be played in FFA. Regardless, the objective is to use the various weapons you are given to reduce your enemies' HP to 0. The last team/player remaining is the victor.
As you play, you will gain 2 things over time, XP and Gears. XP is collected by completing singleplayer missions, dealing damage in games, skill shots in games, winning games, being alive at the end of games, and being the MVP(Dealing the most damage in a game). After getting enough XP, you'll level up and gain an Upgrade Token, along with a weapon and/or map. Upgrade Tokens can be used to upgrade your tank in 4 categories: Tracks, Chassis, Gun, and Luck. Upgrading Tracks will let you climb steeper surfaces, and get some extra fuel per turn for movement. Upgrading Chassis will increase the amount of armor you start with, and get a chance of restoring some armor and/or health at the start of each turn. Upgrading Gun will increase your chances of a Critical Hit, which is normally 1.5x the normal damage, but that can also be increased. Lastly, upgrading Luck yields more weapons in crates, and can let you get more armor and health per crate or even be able to use a grappling hook to automatically grab nearby crates without having to move to them. I really like the rate at which you can level up, as it keeps things interesting, not to mention the weapons have their own XP as well, which can let them be upgraded.
Gears can also be found as you play in a few different ways. Your most common way of picking up gears is when they occasionally blast out of a tank that's been hit. Mousing over these gears will pick them up, adding a gear to your balance. There is also a power-up crate ingame that can occasionally spawn, that when you shoot it, it will drop several gears, letting you mouse over them all. Another way is the Daily Win Bonus. All you have to do is win a single game per day, and you'll be able to spin a wheel that can yield no gears to a whopping 100 gears. The last, but risky method is the Wager Gears option in multiplayer rooms. This option can make players wager up to 3 gears per game, in which the winner(s) have the gears split amongst them. This can be a goo way of grinding gears if you play big FFA games and you're good at the game. Gears can be spent on a few weapons, maps, and other cool cosmetics including tank parts or victory music. Again, I really like the rate at which you can get these gears, and unlike the Flash version of this game, Gears can't bought with money, and are actually obtainable in game.
Overall, this game is really fun, and it's worth it. You don't even need to wait for a sale like I did,
It also runs well on lower end computers, so there's another plus.

The bugs that people are citing as reasons to avoid the game simply are not that bad. Don't double click inventory. If you encounter one of the other bugs, sorry, but the game itself is imminently playable as is. The combat is hard but fun (once you get past the first town's temple which has inexplicably engagement breaking enemies). The art is beautiful. The character creation is extensive and meaningful. The story is rich. The world is rich. The quests are varied. The companions are varied (though they can't compete with nostalgia). The dungeons are deep.
It's not perfect but it's one of the best RPGs in years. It's not trying to be an MMO like some modern RPGs. It can be obtained legally without DRM! That in and of itself is amazing.
While the Dragon Age series has gotten more and more faceroll with thin plots and a built in dating sim, Pillars has focused on making intense, tactical combat and a rich game world, and they did it very well.
Does the might stat make sense? No. Are there a couple bugs? Yeah. Is it fun as heck? Yes. It's an experience I would recommend to anyone, as it doesn't jerk you off while picking your pocket as is the modern trend. It delivers a real game, with real depth, and many hours of play. It's exactly what games should be.

After having almost 200 hours played, Starbound has been a real joy with me and my friends. You can go explore planets, build things, just aimlessly wander, etc... I've mostly enjoyed the building part myself. Lots of weapons to find, interesting towns to visit, and the best part is being able to play it with your friends.
The graphics are beautiful, the sound is lovely and appropriate, mechanics make sense (for the most part), and crafting is actually enjoyable. It's pretty open that you can play it however you want and it doesn't restrict you from progressing on your own pace, or even force you to play along with the missions. Upgrades unlock pretty independently from the missions, which is a good thing. The missions are also pretty challenging, although short.
The game is also moddable, so you can expand and enhance your gameplay experience. Just keep in mind that mods don't quite play well playing multiplayer.

Disclaimer: this is my first review, and the reason I'm writing this is that the line between "good" and "bad" game is not so visible to a person who is not familiar with Starbound, and therefore I feel obligated to end my juorney with Starbound like this.
Starbound got into Early Access in 4th of December 2013. Before that, the lead developer Tiy had formally announced Starbound in February 2012, and a kickstater-esque pre-order opening was launched on April 2013. Starbound was released on 22 of July, 2016, when it had been on development for over five years.
Starbound sets you up in a planet with no other resources except your ingenuity and a Matter Manipulator, a clever tool used to harvest wood and ore for your use. As you get familiar with the crafting, you notice that the interface is a bit clunky and finding what you'd like to make gets harder as the game progresses and you are given more crafting recipes. The planet you're on contains many secrets, such as dungeons and chests for you to explore. The procedural generation gives a noticeable difference to all planets, and even though certain biomes on different planets look the same, there is a difference in my opinion. After you have explored the planet you're on, you can teleport back to your ship and find a new planet in your current system, or use space fuel to travel into other systems. As you progress, your stuff gradually gets upgraded from medieval style to sci-fi.
Starbound has many different resources obtained trough different ways, like farming and mining. Although all the planets are beatiful and have something to explore, the player wants to progress in the game; getting better armor and survival gear is necessary. However, once you notice that making some armor requires cotton, your nice and perilous adventure in the planet's core isn't as nice as it was. It's good that Starbound doesn't hold hands on telling you where to find certain items, but that brings me to one of my strong points on my critique: exploring isn't fun if that exploration doesn't guarantee you to progress, and on the other hand progression is meaningless if nothing changes. Unfortunately Starbound achieves both of these bad points, even though it seems that it tries so hard not to.
There is no guarantee that a dungeon has something rare for you, or if it does, it's stuff like one or two pieces of matter manipulator modules. Which you need a lot more if you hope to upgrade your manipulator. On the other hand, when you find your items you need to progress, you're thrown into more dangerous planets but the premise is still the same: find out what stuff you need to upgrade your crafting stations, dig deep, don't die. Return, notice there's a resource you need but don't know what that is, get frustrated. Also, building shelter / a fancy house to yourself serves no use, as you need to switch planets to progress; meaning you need to bookmark that planet to return to your nice dwelling.
Starbound tries so hard to not be repetetive it's almost funny. I understand that these procedural concepts are really hard, but that is not an excuse if you have five years to polish your game.
The story of Starbound is like a children's fairytale to indie developers. There's the good things, the bad things, and the moral of the story. The good things in my opinion are the promising setting, full mod support and enough customization to feel that you are truly unique.
The bad things: Let's just say that I don't want myself to get cencored by Mollygos or Tiy. There is evidence of that, there is evidence of Tiy shilling the game in reddit with alternate users, there is evidence of people getting banned in the official forums for asking how their product is progressing. I strongly suggest every reader to dig bit deeper into this, it's actually pretty funny how this thing was managed. Like the combat system was revised at least three times. Also, the design failures that had been reflected to Steam include a period where Starbound had not had a patch in one year. When Starbound was in Early Access. The excuses to this include stuff like moving into an office in London and what have you. Some games stay in Early Access for a year and they get released. Starbound was in early access for almost three years.
The moral of the story is that you should respect your playerbase, keep your promises especially if you receive money for a product that doesn't exist yet, and that doing freelancer work without any guarantees is a coin flip. I do not personally feel this way, but Tiy has been described from various sources as being "egomaniac". Take it as you will.
If you like repetetiveness, go ahead. If you like illusion of progression, go ahead. However, Starbound is still to me an unfinished product with broken promises of features, and most likely will be forever. My own personal opinion is that you should not buy this game, or any future titles from Chucklefish without those titles being of exceptional quality, and nominated for Game of the Year in mainstream reviews.

Having now finished the game and majority of its quests, I can clearly say it is a good game - a solid piece of craftsmanship. Is it good enough to stand its ground when compared to BG/IWD/P:T? Just about.
Graphics:
I had no isues with anything, the game looks neat and doesn't displease the eye. Nobody plays those kind of games for the graphics anyway. Having said that, the absolute lack of any cut scenes and the fact we are 10+ years since last Infinity Engine game makes it look dated. Obsidian could have included at least one animation at the very end of it. What we are getting are stills.
Sound:
All tracks sound like they have been taken from somewhere else. It isn's a complaint per se as I actually liked them but they lacked consistency and epicness of for example BG2 soundtrack. Voices were fine and overall sound (ambience and "other stuff") was good too. My only complaint is the music during the combat - it sounds like cheap BG2 rip-off and loops in such way it makes me cringe every time it starts.
Now, the sound has tendency to stutter when map is moved somewhere very fast (it sounds like engine is trying to play old map's location sounds and the new ones, while at the same time gets all the samples from objects on the way... :/). It is obviously a bug and it may (or may not) be fixed later.
Gameplay:
I personally hated it. It isn't bad mechanic per se because it works and is playable, but the chioces made by devs created very "damage spongy" opponents which I personally hate as it dictates the way game HAS to be played.
Example? Basic level ~8th Ogre has nearly 300hp while my level 11, full-on constitution tank has ~220hp. It happens due to the fact the attack rolls are made based on d100 roll (less than 15 - miss, less than 50 - graze, over 50 - hit, over 100 - crit) modified by attackers accuracy and defenders deflection. That creates system, where all characters will nearly aways hit (as accuracy and deflecton are usually a wash and mostly ballance out) but for varying damage (due to grazes, hits and crits) and Damage Reduction armor provides further reducement to the damage suffered. The effect is: monsters are balanced vs party but borderline broken vs solo characters because solo lacks adequate DPS.
Yes, this is a party orientated game, I get it. But because of that system my OP tank Fighter will rarely be hit by anything (Deflection 130+) getting grazed all the time while my Wizard/Priest are getting two-shotted if anything gets to them. Because everything always hits vs ballanced characters and damage control is based upon Damage Reduction (which 2nd line characters often have none). Overall - it isn't a bad mechanic but it feels counter intuitive and isn't very opaque, reqiring plenty of research to get it. It also may not be to the taste of everybody. It certainly wasn't for me. Bring back AD&D2ed!!! :)
Additionally, poor pathfinding was a PITA. Micro management while moving is something I'd rather not do. It got better after 1st patch (or maybe I have got used to it? ;)) so there is hope for the future.
Story (spoiler free):
FIrst of all - NPC's characters in the game are weak. Nowhere near Planescape's or Baldur's Gate's. I know it is a high bar but I don't even feel they could hold a candle to Dragon Age Origins' characters. I personally found them all just boring and uninteresting. Doing 2nd playtrough now with entirely custom made group.
Main story is ok. Not spectacular, no explosive twists and turns. It is rather common fantasy themed thing. Solid enough to keep player interested.
I personally didn't like the fact I never felt like there was a solid adversary. Yes, there is "this dude" and "this organisation" but they lack characteristics that would make me want to stop him. PoE effectively tells the story of PC's journey when on a quest of self discovery. It desn't really work for me.
As a side note, all references to Kickstarter ruined the game immersion for me. In game there are characters with gold plated nametags - those were designed by Kickstarter backers. One could feel those were rather randomly dropped into the game and the gold tags only made it more obvious. Completelly skippable stories that don't really add anything (and introdiction od crapload of immersion breaking Godlikes with bad names in the game for no reason... :/). It is still better than reading "monuments to backers" where your character can read some internet handles and bad, backer-made writing. I hope there will be a button that turns all that crap off.
Summary and explanation (TL;DR):
Pillars of Eternity is a solid game in a genre that I thought dying. And while it caters to a nostalgic fan base, it is solid RPG for anybody willing to spend time with it's bugs and unintuitive fighting system. Will it bring new players into RPG genre? Probably not. Will it please old fans of the genre? It should. While BG3 it isn't, I don't regret 45h+ spent on my 1st playtrough and will go for a 2nd one. But only after I finish Planescape Torment for the n-th time...
My grade: It's a good game, get it if you ever played any Infinity Engine game and liked it. If it's the first time - Baldur's Gate will be better for you to start with.
Original (negative) comment:
First of all - the game is a solid piece of work, but man, it's the buggiest game I've ever played. After the game repetedly crashed to desktop during Raedric's Hold exploration (making it impossible to be finished), I managed to calm down, grind my teeth and swear silently in solitude.
Now, after 20h+, the game doesn't load any of my saves and even trying to start new game crashes it. It actually gets better - it took me couple tries to even launch it as it kept crashing when trying to load main menu!
Great game. Love the create-an-adventurer, because my only complaint is there aren't enough NPC's and they're sort of lame.

I've done my best to avoid spoilers in this, I don't think there are any, as the only name I've dropped from in the game is mentioned at the start (and I mean in the very start).
The game's UI is clean, sensible in design, and there are divisions between the "musts" and the "wants" and the "boy that'd be nice".  For "questing" this is a three part division, with the "Quests" being what you MUST do to complete the game, and two lesser categories below.  (This only gets confusing when you need to appease some group and it isn't a quest; in context it makes sense, but you need to stay on the ball.)
The length of the game is also nothing short of fantastic.  You can choose to spend forever playing this game (my first run took 30 hours on Path of the Damned, Expert, Iron Mode and I didn't attempt to complete every quest or search for much in the third act), or you can blast through it with a sensible class designed to speed run in 4-6 hours (for the purposes of, say, resting less than 10 times as an achievement, or killing less than 175 monsters, while simultaneously going for Solo and Triple Crown Solo achievements).  Being able to adapt to the length this much is clearly beneficial.
The items, the companions, the general conversational style of the game is both shocking and awesome.  The range of linguistic styles employed is, upon closer examination, significantly more limited than you'd have thought (which, truthfully, is to be expected given the size of the team), but the way in which they present themselves masks how small the team is, and gives a richer, deeper, gameplay, including tying certain linguistic norms to certain groups (i.e. dwarves speak differently to humans, not so much in phonetics/phonology (sound) , in as much as the lexical choices (syntax and thus semantics)).
Perhaps the most intersting part of the game from an interpersonal/social perspective is your choice to go about your business as a nice person (forgiving, etc.), or to adopt what might be
described as a sociopathic rampage (with no feeling, just doing your thing).  I'm not suggesting a Hotline Miami style bloodbath (though you can attack just about anyone you want), nor am I suggesting you can complete the game without killing anyone or anything; I'm simply suggesting that there's always a plan A and a plan B (kill or talk them down).  You can even keep the murder to a minimum (and, in fact, must, if you want one of the achievements -- at least in that run).  The downside to going with "Plan B" (murder murder murder) is that sometimes you'll find your characters (your hero or the companions) dislike what you're doing.  It will impact their abilities to fight (or heal) unless you take a specific attribute.  So if you're the sort of short tempered "must kill" type when things go sideways, the ability to do this without severe penalty is great; if you're the type of person who realises how damn powerful that extra non-class attribute is, then you'll realise the penalty is pretty severe (depending on how you choose to play it is or isn't).  I guess the point is that it's well balanced in this sense, and they obviously put in some good work here.
The
Bugs (without spoilers):
If you're someone who habitually double clicks things without needs to, you've no doubt hit the clothing bug.  I'm not, so I didn't, so I'm not sure if I should file this under the "why are you doing this?" pile or the "gamebreaking bug" pile.  Help is on the way with a patch due to land sometime soon.  Either way, I hope you learned your lesson.
on changing tiles is another bug.  There's a tentative fix involving modifying your save slightly (removing files from an archived file) which sorts it out, but requires you to re-run an area.  My second complete run through the game didn't trigger this so perhaps there's something weird going on.  Either way, I believe this is also being addressed.
There are some graphical bugs which can happen if you alt-tab a whole lot while playing.  Again, could be system related, could just be that alt-tabbing during a game is an awful idea, and it could be chance.  Restarting the application (i.e. not the run, the game's binary file) fixes these.
The game is one which requires a lot of talking to NPCs, to your companions, and sitting through (unskippable) cutscenes.  While this initially irritated me (namely after a bug made me repeat things), the cutscenes are important to the story, and eventually you'll find yourself surrendering to the particle effect-driven pretty narrative.
If you like cRPGs, if you like Baldur's Gate, Neverwinter Nights, Icewind Dale (etc., etc.), you should consider this game.  It's the first in quite some time I've enjoyed in this way.  If you're coming from something like Diablo then you probably won't enjoy it as much, as the game is truer to the tabletop style of gameplay, and relies far less on the "all must die" emphasis Diablo has is its franchise.  For those on the fence I'd say this game is good, and on the lower difficulties is no doubt forgiving.  For those looking for a hardcore, ultra-brutal, unforgiving experience, there's also the Path of the Damned difficulty, which, when coupled with Expert mode and Iron Mode, means you'll be playing the game almost like a rogue-like (there's a single save, it'll let you take the last one, even if you die).
it's very pretty, somewhat excessively for a cRPG, which in turn adds a level of depth supporting the rich lore.

Perhaps the best way is to suggest you are not the "great man" of history, but rather someone thrust into the role by circumstances (and chance), right at the beginning (at the end of the "tutorial" style phase, so you see the change).
The content, it is there.

I nominated this for THE “JUST 5 MORE MINUTES” AWARD.
Just 5 more minutes. Just 5 more hours. Just 5 more days.... Yeah I wish. Finals are coming, I had to rush the main campaign so that it wouldn't distract my any further. Hopefully.
In this game, you play as Talion, a Ranger of Gondor. He was forced to witness his wife and son slain by The Black Hand of Sauron and was killed himself. Yet he was resurrected by Celebrimbor the Ringmaker, an elf who crafted the three rings of the elves, and together they use this chance to seek revenge.
And to kill uruks.
And be killed by uruks.
Resurrect again.
Turn uruks against another.
And kill them all.
Endlessly.
The story is not that great. It's a rather straightforward revenge tale. But as a LOTR fan, I think it's a nice addition to the lore.
Aside from the open world which is good but not exceptional, this game has a rather unique stuff known as the Nemesis system. The uruks are uniquely generated for your playthrough, each with his unique personality, strengths to be wary of, and weaknesses to exploit.
Each uruk have the same goal: to be in power, to be in charge. They want to be a warchief. In order to do that, they have to do missions, known as power struggles. They include dueling with another uruk, recruiting followers, etc. We can interfere with their missions, not just to make them fail but also to ensure their victory when needed.
An uruk, even the random guard one, can get increase in power and even get promoted if he kills you. When you encounter him again, he will remark about how noob you are. Vice versa, if you kill an uruk, there's a chance that they'll be resurrected in lower ranks, and when you encounter him he will blurt about revenge. Of course, it's a pleasure to kill him again.
10/10 will kill Ûkrom the Handsome again.

Middle-Earth: Shadow of Mordor is by far one of the best games I have ever played. Its like combining the moving controls from any Assassin's game and the battle mechanics of the Batman games. Now, sure it brings together the controls from two other great games, but what really makes this game shine is the nemesis system. What this is, if you don't already know, is a system that sets up ranks for the enemy. There will be 30 or so random and unique enemies all with their own names. What I loved, playing throuh this, is that I found an Orc named Zog Brawler. He killed me instantly. When I came back to fight him again, he made a little remark about how he killed me once and would do it again. Except this time I killed him. Usually in games, when you kill an enemy, the enemy stays dead, but with the nemesis system, unless you decapitate your enemy, there is a possibility of it's return. I ended up fighting Zog Brawler 10-20 times before he finally stayed dead. At first it was frustrating because I wasn't used to gameplay like that, but after a while I started to make a history with this orc as my arch nemesis if you will. No longer was Zog an ordinary orc, but he was the Joker to my Batman, and when he was finally gone for good, I kind of started to miss battling him and hearing his witty comments on how he would kill me. Without the nemesis system, this game wouldn't be what it is, and quite frankly I am surprised you are still reading this. Stop reading this and buy the game already, you'll thank me after you stop playing your first binge play of a couple of days.
